The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele



The point
Structure is something a machine can hold and act on. Which things belong together,
which change preserves a relation, which earlier act a later move depends on: those
can be part of its state and its rules. That is the commitment behind the Thiele Machine.
I want to take those relations apart, put them to work, and ask what survives when
the machine changes or when we look at it through a smaller window.

The way into that question is two computers with the same answer. The answer
leaves something out. We can give that difference a place in the machine, let the step
maintain it, and ask what an observer can recover and what a change costs. A record of
a checked claim will be the first case I work through. It gives the argument something
definite to stand on: states you can point at, moves you can follow, and rules you can
try to break.

Start with one small picture. I’m going to take it apart, and keep asking what each
piece means, as far down as I can get before I hit something that holds or something I
can’t get under. I’ll tell you which. Then I’ll put it back together at the end and you
can check whether it still stands.

One warning about how this went, because it explains the shape of everything after
it. Most of the time I had the hunch first and found the names later. Over and over,
somebody had been here before me. Sometimes that made my day. Sometimes it
pissed me off. You’ll see both.

Two computers that end up the same
Put two computers on a table. Hand each of them the same list of a thousand numbers.

The first one sorts it. It compares, swaps, walks the list again and again until nothing
is out of order. Then it does one more thing: it walks the whole list front to back and
checks that every number is no bigger than the one after it. That check could have
failed. It passes. Then it tidies up after itself, wipes its scratch work, and leaves the
sorted list in memory. (That check compares neighbours, so what it settles is that the
output is in order. That the output holds your thousand numbers and no others is a
second claim, and it would take a second check comparing the output with the input.
When I say sorted below, I mean in order.)

The second one never looks at your list. Somebody typed the sorted version into it
earlier, same thousand numbers, same order, and it puts them in memory.

Now wait until both are done and look inside. Same bits in memory. Same bits on
the screen. Set it up right, which you can, and it’s the same everything, down to the
last bit. The first compared the entries and checked their order. The second loaded the
same answer without doing either. The list is in order in both; the difference is what
each run did with it. Wheel them out on a cart, swap them, wheel them back, and ask
me which is which. I can’t tell you. You can’t tell me. And the part that bugs me most:


                                           8
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


built the ordinary way, neither machine can tell you either.

Sure, while they ran they were different. One did thousands of comparisons, the other
did a copy. But the runs are over and the runs are gone, and nobody was being sloppy.
Ordinary computers are built to forget how their bits got there, on purpose. Later in
this chapter there’s the sentence where a physicist said so in 1961, and why he said it
costs heat.

Who cares? Anybody who’s been handed a sheet that says “all tests passed.” Anybody
who’s looked at an inspection sticker on a windshield: the sticker looks the same
whether somebody checked the brakes or somebody sold the sticker. An audit, a
proof, a ledger, an AI that sounds very sure of itself: every one of them is a pile of
bits that could have come out of either computer, and the question that matters is the
one the bits can’t answer. Did something establish this, or did it just print it? I’ll come
back to every one of those at the end of this chapter and say which of them this book
actually helps with. Fair warning: fewer than you’d hope.

I’m going to call the first run’s relation to that answer established: it checked the order
of this list. The second run has the answer without that relation. The list’s order is
there either way. What can a machine keep of the difference between the runs? The
rest of this chapter takes that question apart.

Look harder
The obvious answer is: just look harder. Don’t look at the end, look at everything.
So make the computers as lookable as computers get. Scale them up to the size of a
warehouse, every wire a lamp that’s lit or dark, every switch something you can walk
up to and touch. Nothing hidden in a chip too small to see. Put both of them side by
side and walk the floor.

While they run, sure, you’d see the difference. One has a whole wing lighting up,
comparing and swapping, and the other just copies. But they finish. The comparing
wing goes dark. Now walk the floor and look at every single lamp. The sorted list is
spelled out in lit and dark lamps in both, the same pattern, and everything else is dark
in both, because both cleaned up.

There is no lamp anywhere that says “a check ran here and passed.” Not hidden. Not
encrypted. Just not there. You can see everything there is, and the thing I’m after isn’t
one of the things there is. Looking harder doesn’t help, because the problem isn’t that
you can’t see enough. It’s that nothing was kept.

That’s the shape I want you to carry through the rest: the problem was never visibility.
It’s keeping.

So keep the trace
Then the fix is obvious, isn’t it? Don’t let the run go. Keep the trace: every comparison,
every swap, the check and its answer, written down as it happens. Wheel the com-

                                            9
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


puters out on the cart and back, read the traces, and you’ll know which one sorted.
Problem solved?

It’s the right instinct, and it gets most of the way to this book. But take it apart, because
“just keep the trace” has three things wrong with it, and each one is a piece of what
comes later.

First, a trace is bits, and bits can be typed in. Whoever typed the sorted list into the
second machine can type a trace in too: “compared, swapped, checked, passed,” a
few thousand lines of it, every one of them plausible. A trace written by a program is
something the program produced, and the machine running the program doesn’t care
whether it’s true. So keeping the trace doesn’t answer the question. It moves it. Did
something establish this trace, or did it just print it?

Second, the way out of that is to take the pen away from the program. Don’t let
the program write its own trace. Have something underneath it write the trace, one
step at a time, as the steps actually happen, so nothing a program does can add a
line that didn’t happen or erase one that did. Airplanes do a version of this. Flight
recorders go back to a prototype David Warren built in Melbourne in the 1950s. He
was an Australian scientist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories, working on jet
fuel, and after a string of unexplained airliner crashes he wanted a box that would
hold the instrument readings and the voices in the cockpit for whoever came looking
afterwards; I know his story from museum and encyclopedia accounts, and I haven’t
read his own report. The recorders that came out of that idea are fed by the aircraft’s
own instruments. Nobody’s account of events goes into them. And they’re built to
survive the crash, so the investigators don’t have to depend on anyone’s memory
of what happened. That’s the right shape, and it isn’t mine. Later in this chapter it
gets its name from computer security, a reference monitor, and I’ll say outright that a
machine built that way would be doing what this book describes. What the book adds
is narrower than a rulebook for everything underneath. It’s about the records that go
up and never come back down: what that something has to keep for good, and what
keeping it costs.

Third, you can’t keep all of it. A full trace grows with every step and never stops
growing, and a machine with finite memory runs out. Even the flight recorder doesn’t
keep everything. The cockpit voice recorder is a loop. I went looking for how long
the loop is, and it has kept growing: for decades it held the last thirty minutes, an
American rule in 2008 raised that to at least two hours, and big airliners built since
2021 carry twenty-five hours. Whatever the length, everything older gets recorded
over. Every real machine that keeps a trace keeps a window of it, or a fingerprint of it,
and forgets the content.

The fingerprint is the sharpest reply, so take it seriously. Fold every new line of
the trace into a fixed-size scramble of everything before it, and you’ve got a hash
chain. The timestamps of Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, two cryptographers at


                                             10
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Bellcore whose story comes later in this chapter, work that way; so do the audit
logs the cryptographers Bruce Schneier and John Kelsey designed in 1999; and so do
the measurement registers in the security chip a lot of computers carry, the TPM. A
running program can only extend those registers, folding a new measurement in. It
can’t write a value of its own into them, and the ones that matter here start over only
at the next reboot. That really does keep something about the whole trace in a few
dozen bytes. But look at what it keeps. It keeps a binding. The content isn’t in it: to
read the history you still need the trace stored somewhere, and the fingerprint only
tells you whether a copy somebody hands you is the one that went in. The binding
holds only because nobody knows how to find two traces with the same fingerprint,
which is a bet on how hard a search is. No law of nature backs it. That part isn’t only
my opinion. The computer scientists Moni Naor and Guy Rothblum proved a sharp
version of it in 2005, and they even call the thing a fingerprint: keep a small private
fingerprint of a big file somebody else stores, check the file by reading only a little
of it, and against an opponent with unlimited computing the size of the fingerprint
times the amount you read has to be on the order of the whole file. Do even slightly
better than that against an opponent with limited computing, and you’ve shown that
one-way functions exist, which is the hardness bet in its barest form. Their setting is a
stored file. A growing trace is a different setting, but it’s the same bet, with its terms
written down. And squeezing traces that keep growing into a fixed number of bits has
to land many traces on one fingerprint. That’s a merge, hidden behind how hard it is
to find which traces share a seat. It’s the same merge as the people and chairs further
down, where four people have to sit in three chairs. Fingerprints are great. They’re
not a way out of forgetting. They’re a very clever way of forgetting.

So the real question was never “save everything.” It’s this: what’s the smallest thing
worth keeping for good, and what does keeping it cost? The answer this book ends up
with is the commitment, in the database’s sense, a question closed, and the trace drops
away. (The cryptographer’s sealed envelope also goes by the name commitment. It’s a
different thing, and both come up later.) Not every comparison the sort made. Just the
one fact that a check of this very claim passed and the question got closed. And here’s
the part that matters most: on a finite machine, keeping even that one fact for good
forces the machine to forget something somewhere else. That’s the chairs, further
down. And keeping things for good fills up, which Part II turns into a count.

So the premise was never that computers can’t keep records. They keep records all
day. It’s that nothing in the rules of an ordinary computer makes the record paid for,
permanent, or earned, and those three come in at different places, so here’s where.
Paid for is the model’s one rule: in the Thiele Machine, the step that raises the record
has to cost something. Permanent is a premise, the one the chairs need, and one of the
conditions Part III puts on a record. Earned, meaning a check of this very claim passed
first, isn’t in the model’s core at all. It’s what the step of the small machine in Part IV
enforces, proved for that machine and every program on it run from a clean start. One



                                            11
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


more word rides along with permanent, and it’ll come up when I line my record up
against other people’s: dated. A record that goes up and stays up went up at some
particular step. The first raising occurs at a definite step in the execution history. The
latch itself does not store that step number. So dated, in this book, means dated in
the execution history, and carrying a timestamp is a different property that the record
doesn’t have. A machine that charges one mark for every step it takes meets the first
rule, and the charging does nothing toward the others, and I’ll keep pointing that out.

Computed, stored, established
Three words that get used like they’re one.

Computed is about the steps. The first machine computed the sorted list. The second
didn’t.

Stored is about the bits. Both machines stored it.

Established is neither, and that’s the whole problem. It isn’t the steps, because they’re
gone. It isn’t the bits, because they’re identical. It’s something like this: the first
machine has a right to lean on “this list is sorted,” because it ran a test that could
have failed, the test passed, the test was about this very list, and then the question got
closed. The second machine has the same sentence and no right to it. That’s a true fact
about the two of them, and it’s written down nowhere, in either one. (Whose right,
strictly? A machine doesn’t lean on anything, any more than a filing cabinet does. It’s
the right of whoever reads the first machine to lean on what it says, and the machine
is where the grounds for that right would have to be kept. “The machine has a right”
is shorter, so I’ll keep saying it, and now you know what it’s short for.)

Four words I’ll hold still from here on. A check is the test, the thing that could say no.
A commit is the closing, the question shut for good, about that edition of that thing.
The record is whatever stays behind to say so. And established is all three, about one
thing. That’s the working sense. The book cashes it at three depths: a paid closing in
the bare model; an object with a checked relation and a paid event, in Part III; and the
whole chain on the small machine, in Part IV. Each place says which one it means.

Which raises a fair question. What if the second machine, handed the typed-in list,
runs the check on it? Then it has established that the list is sorted. Full stop. It
didn’t do the sorting and it doesn’t need to. The line I’m drawing is between checked
and unchecked. Whether the list was computed or copied doesn’t enter into it, and
“without doing either” up there was about the copier that never looked. So whatever
this book ends up counting, it isn’t how hard anybody worked.

People say “a right to lean on it” about a lot of things that turn out to be vibes, so I
had to find out whether this one was anything. So I went looking. Here’s what I ran
into.




                                           12
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


The clerk who forgets everything
The picture of a computer I started with is a person with a pencil, a strip of paper and
a short list of rules. So I went back to the source, Alan Turing’s 1936 paper, to see how
far he actually takes it.

He takes it a long way. Back then a “computer” was a job, a human doing sums by
hand, and Turing modelled that person. He’s careful with the person’s mind: whatever
the clerk knows, beyond a handful of states, has to go down on the paper. Then he
goes all the way. He imagines the clerk getting up, walking off, forgetting everything,
and coming back later. To pick up where he left off, the clerk leaves himself “a note
of instructions,” and Turing says that note is the clerk’s state of mind, as far as the
computation is concerned. Marks on paper and a note. That’s the whole state.

My two computers are sitting right inside that. Suppose the clerk didn’t write the note.
Somebody slipped it under the door, in the right form, with the right instructions. He
comes back, reads it, carries on, and every mark he makes from then on is exactly
what he’d have made if he’d written it himself. Turing’s model can’t tell the clerk who
did the work from the clerk who was handed a note saying he did. It was never asked
to. Turing wanted something you could check without crawling into anybody’s head,
and a note on a desk is about as checkable as it gets. That’s why the paper still works
ninety years later. It’s also why there’s no place in it for the thing I’m after.

So the founding picture of computing is a man who leaves his desk, forgets everything
he was doing, and trusts a sticky note. I relate to him deeply.

And now the question nobody needs answered to follow the argument, which is
exactly the kind I can’t leave alone: who were those clerks? Real people. In the late
1800s the Harvard Observatory hired rooms full of women to do the arithmetic of
the sky, cataloguing stars by hand for a fraction of a man’s wage, and some of them
made discoveries of their own, Henrietta Leavitt’s way of telling how far away a star
is among them. (I took the wages and the discoveries from Dava Sobel’s history of
those women, and from the historians at the American Institute of Physics, who put
the men’s hourly pay at nearly five times the women’s.) Rooms like that ran artillery
tables in both world wars; that part I took from David Alan Grier’s history of human
computers. So when Turing modelled “the computer,” he was modelling somebody’s
actual afternoon. Does that change the argument? Not a bit. But it changes the picture,
for me anyway: the sticky note was always a person trusting another person’s work,
and the question of whether the work behind it was really done is older than any
machine.

Information doesn’t have it either
My next guess was information: one machine got some, the other didn’t. That one
died fast. Claude Shannon, who turned information into a number in 1948, says on
his first page that the meaning of a message is “irrelevant to the engineering problem.”


                                           13
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


His number measures how many messages you could have sent. What the one you
sent did is outside it, which is exactly right for building telephone lines and exactly
no help to me. Same message out of the same set, same number, for both computers.
He’d give them the same number if one of them got hit by lightning and came out
right by luck.

Fine, forget the set and look at the one message. In the 1960s three people, sepa-
rately, worked out how to measure the information in one string: Ray Solomonoff,
an American who was after a theory of guessing what comes next from what came
before; Andrei Kolmogorov, the great Soviet mathematician; and Gregory Chaitin,
an Argentine-American mathematician who later worked at IBM. Their measure is
the length of the shortest program that prints the string. Same two computers, same
string, same number. And then there’s the thing in that theory I keep going back to
and standing on, to see if it creaks. Running a program can’t add this kind of informa-
tion. What comes out can’t hold more than what went in plus the program, give or
take a little. Leonid Levin, who studied under Kolmogorov in Moscow and later left
the Soviet Union to teach at Boston University, proved a general version of this, and
he has a one-liner for it that’s too good not to repeat: you can torture an uninformed
witness all you want, you won’t get information about the crime.

Which means, as far as information goes, sorting your list told you nothing. The sorted
list holds nothing that “your list, plus the word sort” didn’t already hold.

Logic says the same thing in a different coat. The standard logic of knowing, the one
the Finnish philosopher Jaakko Hintikka worked out in 1962, has a property people
call logical omniscience: if you know some facts, you automatically know everything
that follows from them. So by that logic, once you knew every number on your list,
you already knew whether it was sorted. Hintikka flagged the problem himself, in the
same book, and people have been trying to fix it since. The fixes read like a pile until I
asked each one the same thing: when it lets you write known next to “sorted,” what
does it make you write in the margin? Hintikka’s margin is empty. Each fix writes one
thing there.

The fix that comes closest to me is from 1995, by Sergei Artemov, a logician at the City
University of New York as of 2026 who studied under that same Kolmogorov (the 1995
report came out of Cornell). He wanted a logic that could name the proof itself. What
I think he’s saying: you only get to know a thing if you’ve built an actual justification
for it, and the justification rides along with the claim. That’s a reason traveling with
the claim, which is almost a record. Only almost, because it’s a way of writing things
down and reasoning about them, and nothing in his margin says the reason was ever
run, or when. People have taught it to count, too: Ho Ngoc Duc, a logician at Leipzig,
in 1997, made knowing take reasoning steps, and Artemov and Roman Kuznets, a
logician then at Bern, in 2014, asked how big a justification can get before knowing
by it stops being feasible. I took those for rivals at first. As I read them now, Duc


                                           14
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


counts the steps the knower takes and Artemov and Kuznets weigh what you’d hand
somebody to check it, one distance from two ends. It has a computational side, too:
Francisco Bavera and Eduardo Bonelli, two Argentine computer scientists who work
on what programming languages mean, in 2018 turned justification logic into a lambda
calculus whose terms carry, and can inspect, the history of the computation that made
them, and Samuel Bucheli, Meghdad Ghari and Thomas Studer, three logicians, Studer
the head of the logic group at Bern, put justifications on a time line in 2017, where they
persist and change.

Line that up against the margin this book wants: earned, paid for, permanent, dated.
Artemov’s reason is nearly earned, the steps and the sizes are prices, the time line is a
date. Their time line keeps its dates. Mine is dated only in the execution history: the
raise happened at a definite step, and the latch doesn’t keep the step number. What
none of it has is the closing of a question as a step with a price. Their prices are on
reasoning, and the Bern justifications change, the one thing a closed question doesn’t
do. Push on mine, though, and it gives twice. Artemov’s margin holds the reason
itself, and mine only says a check passed. And their prices grow with how hard the
thing was to know. This book charges the step that raises the record, and how long
the checking took never enters it, so for a measure of effort, read theirs.

So the two most careful accounts I could find, one about bits and one about knowing,
say the same thing: the sort added nothing.

And yet you know something after the sort that you didn’t before. You can read the
smallest number off the first slot. You can stop worrying. Something happened. That’s
the clue, and it’s the first solid thing I’ve got: whatever established is, it isn’t new bits.
It’s the same bits, settled.

The guy who got closest
Somebody had that clue before me, and on that clue he’s the closest neighbour I’ve
found, so he gets the most room and the hardest push.

Charles Bennett, a physicist at IBM, wrote a paper in 1988 that starts where I just ended
up: information isn’t the same as value. His example is an almanac of where the moon
and planets will be every day for a hundred years. It has no more information than
the equations it was calculated from, but it saves you doing the calculating. So the
value is the work. He called the amount of work a thing carries its depth.

Was this my idea, already done, by a guy at IBM? The only way to find out was to find
where it parts from mine, because if I couldn’t find that place I’d just be renaming his
idea. And it’s one word: plausibly. Depth is the amount of work a thing was plausibly
made with. Bennett says straight out that you can’t know how a message actually
came to be; for all you know it came from flipping coins. Depth is read off the finished
thing, the way a fossil’s age is read off the fossil.



                                             15
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Bring the two computers back. The sorted list in the first one has some depth. The
identical list in the second has exactly the same depth, because depth looks at the
list and nothing else. A photocopy of a deep thing is just as deep. Depth tells you
what work a plausible way of making the thing would take. It’s not a record that this
machine did it, and it’s not a receipt for what doing it cost.

So Bennett’s standing right next to the line, on the other side of it, and as far as I can
tell he got his own question right. He asked how much work a thing embodies. I’m
asking who has the right to lean on it and what they paid to get there. His answer
lives in the object. Mine, if I’ve got one, has to live in the machine.

Statues that walk off
If it isn’t in the information, maybe it’s in the knowing, so I went and read the philoso-
phers. And there it was again: people had been arguing about the difference between
having the right answer and knowing it for a couple thousand years.

Plato’s version is a joke about statues. There was a story that the sculptor Daedalus
made statues so lifelike they’d walk off if you didn’t tie them down. Plato says true
opinions are like that: they wander off, and they’re not worth much until you tie them
down with the reason why. Once they’re tied down, they’re knowledge, and they stay
put. Knowledge tied to a reason, and knowledge that stays. Of everybody I’d have
bet on to hand me that shape, Plato wasn’t on the list.

Then in 1963 a philosopher named Edmund Gettier broke the tidy version in three
pages. Smith and Jones are up for the same job. Smith has good reason to think
Jones will get it, and he’s counted the coins in Jones’s pocket: ten. So Smith figures,
with good reason, that the man who’ll get the job has ten coins in his pocket. Then
Smith gets the job, and, unknown to him, Smith also has ten coins in his pocket. True,
believed, backed by a reason. Not knowledge. He was right by luck, because his
reason was about the wrong pocket.

That’s the push that matters for a machine. Checking one pocket and committing to
a claim about another is right by luck. So whatever a machine commits to, the check
underneath has to be about this very claim, and I’d better say exactly what that means,
because it carries a lot of weight later.

A check is about this very claim when four things hold. It tests the same property the
commit names. A cousin of that property won’t do. It tests that property on the same
thing the commit names, and the thing next to it won’t do either. Nothing has written
to that thing between the check and the commit, so it’s still the same edition the check
looked at. And the check is honest: it says yes when the property is true and no when
it isn’t, on every value it could ever be handed, this one and all the others. Break the
first three and you’re Smith with his ten coins. Break the fourth and the check is just
a rubber stamp. Later in the book I build a machine whose step won’t let a commit
through unless the first three hold, and whose checks come with a proof of the fourth.


                                           16
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Two notes on those four, because they matter later. The fourth asks for more than
it needs. To rule out luck, a check only has to never say yes when the property is
false; saying yes every time it’s true is a bonus. And the third is a very old bug in
computing wearing Gettier’s coat. Security people call it time-of-check-to-time-of-use:
check a file, use it, and something swaps the file in between (Matt Bishop and Michael
Dilger, two computer security researchers at the University of California, Davis, wrote
up how to hunt for it in 1996). Databases guard against the same thing by making
sure, just before a commit, that nothing they read has been written since; H. T. Kung
and John Robinson, two computer scientists at Carnegie-Mellon, called that optimistic
concurrency control in 1981. A philosopher’s pocket and a sysadmin’s race condition,
same bug. One limit, said now: a machine can only promise “nothing has written to
that thing” about its own memory; for brake pads or a voter roll the third condition
becomes a premise about whoever measured (Section 14).

And here’s where I went further than this chapter needs, because the obvious next
question is: does anything fix Gettier? People tried for years. The first patch is “no
false steps in the reasoning”: Smith’s mistake was believing Jones would get the job,
so rule that out. Then a philosopher named Alvin Goldman came back with barns,
and he credits the barns to Carl Ginet, another philosopher working on what it takes
to know something. You’re driving through a county that, unknown to you, is full
of fake barns, just painted fronts propped up to look like the real thing. You look
at the one real barn in the county and think “that’s a barn.” True. Believed. Good
reason, your own eyes, and no false step anywhere. And still you were lucky: if you’d
glanced at the next one over you’d have believed the same thing and been wrong.
Every patch gets a new barn, and as far as I can tell the arguing hasn’t stopped. Which
tells me something I’ll keep: whether a check was good isn’t only about this one case.
It’s about what the check would have done on the cases next door. Hold on to that,
because it’s the next section.

What “could have failed” means
I keep saying the first machine’s test could have failed. Take that apart, because it’s the
piece everything else hangs off.

The machine is deterministic. Given your list, the check was always going to pass.
So in what sense could it have failed? By “could have failed” I mean this: hand the
checking stage an out-of-order candidate output and it says no. I do not mean hand
the whole sorter an unsorted input; putting that input in order is its job. The relevant
counterfactual is a defective candidate reaching the checker. An ordinary unsorted
input reaching the sorter isn’t it. Chance has nothing to do with it. The copier that
never checks has no corresponding rejection.

Here’s the shape. A check is a question asked of every possible input, and it splits
them into two piles: the ones it says yes to and the ones it says no to. “Could have
failed” just means the no pile isn’t empty. A check that says yes to everything has


                                            17
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


an empty no pile, and it distinguishes no inputs, however long it runs and however
official it looks. It can still be sound, when its property holds of everything, and then
it’s sound and tells you nothing you didn’t have. A philosopher, Robert Nozick, made
a version of this a condition for knowing, in 1981: you know a thing only if, had it
been false, you wouldn’t believe it.

Push on it once more, because this is where it really gives. “Could have failed” is
a fact about the procedure, about what the check would have done on other lists. It
isn’t a fact about the end state at all. Look at the first machine’s memory when it’s
done: a sorted list. Nothing in those bits says “and whatever made me would have
caught a mistake.” That’s the warehouse again, every lamp visible and none of them
saying it. The one thing that makes the first machine’s answer worth more is exactly
the kind of thing those bits can’t hold: the copier ends with the same bits, and neither
machine kept anything else. An end state can hold more than the answer, and the
only way a machine can own this is to write something down at the moment the check
passes, and to have that something mean what it says. More than anything else in this
chapter, that’s why I ended up needing a record. A better answer wouldn’t have done
it. Even then the record only carries half of it. It can say a check ran on an edition and
passed. That the check would have said no on a bad list is a fact about the checker,
and that half rides on a proof about the checker, which somebody outside the machine
has to read and accept. Where that kind of chain of reasons stops is the swamp of the
philosopher Karl Popper, a little further down.

One more thing that tripped me up and then didn’t. Rig a check to pass only on your
one list. Is that cheating? No. It’s a perfectly honest check of a different claim, “this is
that exact list,” and it has a big no pile: every other list. It establishes exactly that and
nothing more. What a check establishes is whatever it’s honest about.

Put that next to the empty no pile and the two fit together: a check establishes what
it’s honest about. An empty no-pile means the check distinguishes no inputs. It can
still be sound for a property that holds on every input; soundness and nontriviality
are different requirements. One thing I’ll say plainly now, so it doesn’t ambush you
in Part IV: the small machine I build there doesn’t police this. Its step makes sure a
commit was checked first, about the same thing, by a checker proved honest. It doesn’t
stop you asking a question that can’t come out no, like “is this number at least zero.”
Ask one and the whole chain runs, three marks paid, and nothing is established but
the chain. The certificate I show off there asks one that can fail.

Settled, whether it’s true or not
Then I ran into Charles Sanders Peirce, an American scientist and philosopher, in an
1877 essay called “The Fixation of Belief.” He was asking what inquiry is for, and
his answer named the thing I’d been running together without noticing. The point
of inquiry, he says, is to get out of doubt and settle on a belief. And when someone
objects that surely what people want is a true belief, he answers like a guy who’s


                                             18
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


watched a lot of arguments end: “as soon as a firm belief is reached we are entirely
satisfied, whether the belief be true or false.”

That’s funny, and then it isn’t, because he’s right. Settling and being right are two
different events. A question can be closed on a wrong answer, and once it’s closed it
acts closed. Peirce cares a lot about which ways of settling hold up (science wins, for
him, because it has to answer to something outside any one person), but the settling
itself, the question snapping shut, is there every time, and it never comes with a
guarantee.

Karl Popper came at it from the other side. He was a philosopher from Vienna asking
what separates science from everything else, and in his 1934 book, the one that came
into English as The Logic of Scientific Discovery, he says every test has to stop somewhere,
at some statement somebody decides to accept, and nothing in the evidence forces you
to stop there instead of one step further. You stop when you’re satisfied. His picture is
a jury: the verdict is a decision about what happened, and the jury deciding it doesn’t
make it true. Science, for him, is a building on piles driven into a swamp, and the piles
stop where somebody’s satisfied they’ll hold. They never reach firm ground.

A real jury has a problem Popper doesn’t mention, because a real jury is twelve people.
Lewis Kornhauser and Lawrence Sager, two law professors writing in the Yale Law
Journal, noticed in 1986 that a court that votes by majority on each premise of a case
and also on the verdict can end up contradicting itself: every judge is consistent, and
the court isn’t. Christian List and Philip Pettit, two philosophers writing in Economics
and Philosophy, turned that in 2002 into a theorem. No way of combining people’s yes-
or-no judgments on connected questions meets a short list of conditions that each look
harmless on their own and always hands back a consistent, complete group judgment.
A group’s settling is a rule’s settling, and which rule you pick decides which of the
honest settlings sticks. Try the problem with three ballots and a rule that a payment is
due only if a contract was signed and a deadline was missed. One voter says yes to
both, one says signed but not missed, and one says missed but not signed. Each voter
applies the rule consistently. Count separately: a majority says signed, a majority says
missed, and a majority says no payment. You can point to the disagreement on the
paper without blaming any one voter’s logic. I haven’t tried to put a group on the
machine, and that’s where I’d expect the first wall to be.

Popper’s swamp sent me further down, because it’s the oldest problem in the book and
it doesn’t have a bottom. Ask why you believe something and you get a reason. Ask
why you believe the reason and you get another one. Sextus Empiricus, a skeptic and
doctor who lived probably in the second or third century and whose whole method
was holding off judgment, wrote down the ancient version, credited to someone called
Agrippa, and in 1968 the German philosopher Hans Albert, who with Popper led the
school called critical rationalism, gave it a name with a joke in it: the Münchhausen
trilemma, after the baron who claimed he pulled himself out of a swamp by his own


                                            19
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


hair. Every chain of reasons does one of three things. It goes on forever. It loops
back on itself. Or it stops somewhere, because somebody decided it stops. People
have argued for a very long time about which of the three to live with. So “when do
I actually know, and when am I done checking?” doesn’t get a clean answer from
anybody. What you can do is be honest about where you stopped and why. That’s a
lot of what the rest of this book is: every place it stops is written down, with its name
on it, so you can decide whether you’d have stopped there too.

Lay Peirce and Popper on top of each other and here’s what shows through. The check
is one act. The stopping is another. The check can run as long as you like and it never
makes you stop; at some point something decides, and the deciding is its own event.
That’s the second machine’s whole trick: it skipped the check and kept the answer.

And a logician said the part I didn’t expect a logician to say. Per Martin-Löf, a Swedish
logician, says a proof is an act, and once it’s done it’s done. His words, from lectures
he gave in Siena in 1983: “a proof is, not an object, but an act . . . Only secondarily,
and irrevocably, does it become the act that has been performed.” That took me a few
reads, and the tenses unlocked it: first the act being done, then, for good, the act that
has been done. You could say that’s true of everything that ever happened. Fine. But
it’s the two computers again: the first machine’s check happened, irrevocably, and the
machine right now carries no trace of it. The past can’t be undone. The record of it can
be lost, unless something keeps one. That gap is where this book lives.

Then the intuitionists got there first, which by now I should’ve expected. The Dutch
mathematician L. E. J. Brouwer, who held that a mathematical truth is something a
mind makes evident, argued from 1948 on about an idealised mathematician working
in stages, the creating subject. The people after him only came clear to me once I sorted
them by three words: the act, the object, and the trace the act leaves behind, which
Martin-Löf’s sentence has no room for. The logician Georg Kreisel (1967), Austrian-
born and then at Stanford, wrote it down as a formula: the subject has evidence for A
at stage n. That’s a trace, something you can come back and ask about after the act is
over. Anne Troelstra (1969), a Dutch logician who studied under Brouwer’s student
Arend Heyting and became one of the leading authorities on intuitionism, added that
the subject never forgets what it has made evident, so the trace never fades. That’s
how Mark van Atten (2018), a philosopher in Paris who has spent years on Brouwer,
credits it; the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on intuitionism lists the never-forgets
axiom among Kreisel’s own, and I haven’t settled which is right. Van Atten, going
through the whole history, reads the formula as “by stage n the Creating Subject has
made A evident.” Look at the tense. Has made is Martin-Löf’s “the act that has been
performed,” reached from the other end. And look at what that carries. It’s tied to a
stage; at any stage you can ask whether it’s happened yet; it never goes away; and it’s
never wrong. Van Atten even says the subject can’t just accept a proof handed to it
from outside: it has to go through the steps and rebuild the evidence itself. That’s the
copier who runs the check. And then there’s Göran Sundholm, a philosopher of logic


                                           20
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


at Leiden. He has long kept a proof as an act apart from a proof as an object (1998),
and, as I understand his work, apart from its trace as well. In a 2014 paper he worked
through how Brouwer’s theory of the creating subject sits beside the thesis that every
effective procedure is a program, which is the side this book’s machines live on. I
know that second paper only by what it sets out to do, so I lean on it lightly.

Set their trace beside my record and the columns nearly all fill: their stage is my dated,
their never forgetting my permanent, their never wrong my earned. Their stage is
written into the trace, though, and my dated is only a step in the run that the latch
doesn’t keep. The empty one is the price, and I think I see why. For a mind with
unlimited memory, never forgetting costs nothing. On a finite machine, writing a
record that stays up forces the instruction to merge some states. Charging for that
merge is a further premise. Those are the chairs and the price rule, still to come. So
it’s the closest thing to my established that I’ve found. The formula is around sixty
years old, and the idea under it, Brouwer’s creating subject, is older than that. Push
on my side from theirs, though, and it gives twice. Van Atten’s subject won’t take
a proof from outside, and my machine takes exactly one: its checker is trusted on a
proof about the checker that somebody did outside every run. And their evidence is
never wrong because, for Brouwer, made evident is what true means. Mine is right
only as far as that checker is honest. Where they differ, the difference is honest: their
subject is an idealised mind with unlimited time and memory, and mine is a machine
with a finite table that establishes only the claims its program checks.

Not a switch
So far I’ve been talking about established as if it were a light switch: on or off, the first
computer on and the second one off. That bothered me the whole time I was writing it,
and for a while I couldn’t say why. It felt too small, the way a word can be technically
right and still not cover what you’re pointing at. I don’t trust that feeling on its own,
because I’ve had it plenty of times about things that turned out to be nothing. So I
went looking for something outside my own head that would either give the feeling
something to stand on or show me I was imagining it.

I didn’t know what I was looking for, at first, beyond a rough shape: two things that
look exactly the same and differ in how far something about them has been settled.
So I started collecting anything that seemed to have that shape, and most of what I
collected fell apart as soon as I looked at it closely. How each one fell apart taught me
more than the thing itself did, so I’ll go through them in the order it happened. Every
story below is the version I could piece together from the records I could reach, and
where I couldn’t reach a record I’ll say so. Check me.

The first batch was all hidden things. A pea under one of three cups. A tree, whose
age you can’t see from the outside. A forged painting that looks right until somebody
tests the paint. A glass of gas, where the thermometer shows one temperature and
underneath there are uncountably many arrangements of molecules that would all


                                             21
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


show the same reading. Plato’s prisoners in the cave, who see shadows on a wall. The
things casting them stay behind their backs (Section 7 tells their story). Every one of
these looked promising for about a minute. Then I noticed they all fail the same way:
look harder and the hidden thing shows up. Lift the cup. Cut the trunk and count
the rings. Run the paint test. Look at the molecules, at least in principle. Turn around
in the cave. In each case the hidden part is a fact about the object that better eyes
could find. That isn’t what the two computers have. You can see every lamp in the
warehouse and not find the check.

That failure gave me the first real tool I had, and it’s a crude one. Give an observer
perfect vision of the visible thing, as much detail as they want, and ask whether they
could read the difference off it. If they could, it’s something hidden, and that’s not
what I’m after. If they couldn’t, it might be. I want to be honest about how much
weight that test can hold. It’s a judgment, and I’m the one making it, with whatever
blind spots I have. Somebody careful can look straight at the evidence and still read
it wrong, because of what they expected to see. So I treat the test as a way of sorting
my own examples. It isn’t a verdict, and if you find a case where it sorts wrongly, that
tells me something about the test and about me.

The second batch got past that test and failed a different way. A clock face reads three
o’clock and doesn’t show how many days have gone by; no amount of staring at the
face tells you. And a computer can keep a complete history of what it did. That one
has a story behind it. In 1961 Rolf Landauer, a physicist at IBM, argued that a computer
has to give off heat whenever it throws information away, and that real computers
throw information away all the time. Twelve years later a younger colleague of his,
Charles Bennett, asked whether they had to. His answer, in a 1973 paper, was no. A
machine can write down every step it takes, copy out its answer, and then run itself
backward, retracing its steps and wiping the history as it goes, until it holds only the
input and the answer and has never thrown anything away. It takes a forward run, a
copy of the answer and a backward run, with scratch space for the history. Bennett
thanks Landauer at the end for raising the question in the first place, which I like: the
man whose principle says forgetting costs is the one who asked whether you could
get out of it. The history it keeps along the way is real extra information, sitting out
where anyone could read it, so it isn’t a hidden fact of the first batch’s kind. And
keeping it and unwinding it throws nothing away, so by Landauer’s own reckoning
it carries no heat floor; the construction accounts for steps and scratch space, without
establishing zero heat for a physical implementation. It can also be run back down.
Neither of those two, the keeping that carries no floor and the running back down, fits
what happened to the first computer, which did something that can’t be undone and
paid for it in work. If the standing I’m after could be added for free and taken back
for free, it would just be bookkeeping. So that batch taught me what else I needed:
something that only moves one way, and costs something to move.

The third batch came closer and still didn’t quite fit. In 1782 James Six, a Canterbury


                                           22
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


man from a family of silk weavers who had taken up watching the weather, described
a thermometer for the Royal Society. He wanted the coldest moment of every night,
and he’d found that with an ordinary thermometer you had to be looking at it when it
happened, because, in his words, “if it be not immediately noticed, it can never after
be known.” His fix was two little steel markers in the tube that the column pushes up
and that stay where they’re left. That’s a record that only moves one way. Then he
spoils it, for my purposes, in the same paper: every evening he wrote the numbers
down and slid the markers back with a magnet, “without a touch.” A record anybody
can reset with a magnet is not the thing I’m after, and Six would have been the first to
say he wasn’t the first to build one; his paper lists the thermometers that came before
his.

Since 1996, starting with oral polio vaccine, vials of vaccine bought through UNICEF
have carried a small sticker, a square inside a circle. The square darkens as the vial
takes on heat, and the darkening doesn’t undo when the vial cools. When the square
matches the circle, the vaccine shouldn’t be used. One way, and it can’t be reset. But
it’s chemistry. The reaction in the square is chosen to run about as fast as the vaccine
itself spoils, so the sticker is really reading the vaccine’s own condition by a proxy.
Nobody ran a check; the heat did.

Closer still: the International Vocabulary of Metrology, the reference book that mea-
surement laboratories work from, says a result is traceable only if it “can be related to
a reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing
to the measurement uncertainty.” That’s a lot like what I want, a standing earned
by checks, step by step. The same document adds that traceability “does not ensure
. . . that there is an absence of mistakes,” which is the true-versus-established split
written into an international standard. And the top of the chain wasn’t fixed either.
When the official copies of the kilogram were compared with the prototype in 1889,
1946 and around 1991, they had drifted apart by tens of micrograms over the century,
and nobody can say which one moved, because the prototype was the kilogram. In
2019 the kilogram was redefined by fixing a constant of nature, Planck’s constant,
instead. A chain like that can also lapse: if the calibrations stop, new results stop being
traceable. The standing has to be kept up, which my record doesn’t.

The rules of chess have the shape too. The current Laws of Chess of FIDE, the inter-
national chess federation, say in Article 9.2.3 that two positions are the same only if
“the same player has the move, pieces of the same kind and colour occupy the same
squares and the possible moves of all the pieces of both players are the same,” and they
spell out that a king that could still castle and one that can’t are in different positions,
even on an identical board. That passes the perfect-vision test. And the official text
says why it passes: the castling right changes which moves are legal. So the hidden
part steers the game: it decides what can happen next. In the machine I’m building,
the record never steers. It never touches the ordinary computing at all. Each of these
got something right and missed something else.


                                            23
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


The one that fit best, and I want to say clearly that it only fit best among the ones
I found, was the standing of a mathematical statement. Here’s how it went for one
statement, as far as I could follow it.

In 1611 Johannes Kepler, the emperor’s mathematician in Prague, owed his friend
and patron Johann Matthäus Wackher von Wackenfels a New Year’s present and, he
said, had nothing to give. Wackher, Kepler wrote, loved nothing, for the games you
can play with the word, so Kepler wrote him a little pamphlet about the nearest thing
to nothing he could find, a snowflake, which had landed on his coat as he crossed a
bridge. Why six corners? Kepler couldn’t say in the end. But along the way he stacked
equal balls in his head and asserted that one way of stacking them, the way grocers
stack oranges, packs them so tightly that, in the 1966 English translation, “in no other
arrangement could more pellets be stuffed into the same container.” He didn’t prove
it. He said it.

Then the sentence sat. In 1831 Carl Friedrich Gauss, reviewing somebody else’s book
on a piece of number theory, proved what amounts to the special case of stackings laid
out on a regular grid. In 1900 David Hilbert put the general question of packing equal
spheres on his famous list of problems for the new century, without mentioning Kepler.
In 1953 the Hungarian geometer László Fejes Tóth showed how the whole thing might
be cut down to a problem with finitely many numbers in it, and a decade later he
guessed that computers might one day finish it. Thomas Hales, a mathematician then
at the University of Michigan, started on it in earnest in 1994, and in August 1998
he and his student Samuel Ferguson announced a proof that leaned on a great deal
of computer work. The Annals of Mathematics gave the paper to a panel of twelve
referees, led by Gábor Fejes Tóth, László’s son. They ran seminars on it for years. A
journalist, George Szpiro, later reported that by July 2002 they were 99 percent certain
it was right; I couldn’t find those words in anything the referees wrote themselves.
What Szpiro printed in Nature in 2003 was the editor’s letter as Hales reported it: the
referees had “not been able to certify the correctness of the proof, and will not be able
to certify it in the future, because they have run out of energy . . . ” The Annals printed
the human part in 2005, and the whole proof appeared in 2006. Hales started the
Flyspeck project in 2003 to have the entire proof checked by proof assistants. It was
finished on 10 August 2014.

Lay those dates out on the table and look at what moved. The sentence never changed.
Hilbert’s version of the question didn’t even name the man who first said it. Whether
it’s true never changed, as far as anyone can tell. What changed was how far it had
been established, and it changed in stages, each one paid for by somebody’s work: a
guess, a special case, a place on a list, a plan, an announcement, a panel’s reported
ninety-nine percent and their exhaustion, a printing, a machine check. A perfect reader
of the sentence can’t see which stage it’s at. And it only ever moved one way.

Then I tried to break that one too, because by this point I’d watched a lot of good-


                                            24
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


looking examples fall over, and there’s an obvious place to push. Standing can fall. In
1852 a student named Francis Guthrie, colouring a map of the counties of England,
noticed that four colours always seemed to be enough to keep neighbouring counties
different. The question passed to his old teacher Augustus De Morgan, who wrote
to the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton that a student had asked him
for “a reason for a fact which I did not know was a fact,” and that he didn’t know it
yet either. In 1879 Alfred Kempe, a barrister who did mathematics on the side and
sang counter-tenor, published a proof, and his description of finding it is wonderful:
“After a somewhat arduous search, I have succeeded, suddenly, as might be expected,
in hitting upon the weak point . . . ” The journal’s associate editor, William Story,
added a note saying Kempe had “substantially proved” the theorem, and tightened
the counting part of the argument. Eleven years later Percy Heawood, a lecturer at
Durham who by one account brought his dog to his lectures, showed that one step of
what he called “the now apparently recognised proof” doesn’t work. Kempe swaps
colours along two chains at once, and swapping the first can spoil the second.

So standing can fall, and I went back and forth on what that does to my picture. Where
I’ve landed for now: the check that got Kempe’s proof accepted, Story’s note, went
through the counting and never examined the double swap. A check that never looked
at a step can’t have said no to that step. In the sense of the previous few pages, the part
that fell was never earned in the first place. I’m aware that’s a convenient reading for
me, and I’m wary of convenient readings, especially my own. Take it as where I ended
up. It isn’t a settled answer. It is, though, the reason the machine later in this book
only lets its record go up after a passing, sound check and a matching commitment.
It supports nontrivial claims whose checks can fail. It does not require every certified
claim to be nontrivial.

And then the part I didn’t expect. The four-colour statement was true all along. Ken-
neth Appel and Wolfgang Haken, two mathematicians at the University of Illinois,
proved it in 1976 with a computer, and the proof was met with suspicion for years; a
cleaner version came in the 1990s; and in 2005 Georges Gonthier, a computer scientist
at Microsoft Research in Cambridge, finished a proof of the whole thing checked by a
small proof-checking program. So here’s a statement that stayed true the entire time
while its standing went up in 1879, came down in 1890, went up again in 1976 against
a lot of doubt, and went up further in 2005. The fall wasn’t a fall of the truth. It was a
fall of how far the truth had been established, and it was the right fall to have, because
what had been established was less than anyone thought.

Laying all of that out together is what changed my picture. If there are stages, then at
each one there’s a line, and the line has two sides: not this far yet, and at least this far.
Each line amounts to its own yes-or-no question. But choose the question carefully.
“Do we still trust this proof?” can turn back to no, as Kempe’s did. “Did we carry out
this particular check?” asks about a completed act. Cross out the acceptance and the
act still happened. To keep its answer available, the machine must retain a record and


                                             25
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


have no move that resets it. A check’s ability to fail does not supply that permanence
by itself. Maybe the switch wasn’t wrong. Maybe it was just incomplete, the first
of many lines, and the real shape is a direction with lines drawn across it. I’ve gone
around many times on whether the lines create the direction or the direction comes
first and the lines are just places where you cut it, and on whether yes and no are
even different from each other until something draws the line between them. I don’t
have an answer to that. The one part I could actually settle is that a single switch isn’t
enough once there are three or more stages, and that is proved (Section 11). Everything
else in this paragraph is me thinking out loud.

Flatland, where this hunch started (Section 1), turned out to belong in the first batch.
It’s a novel Edwin Abbott published in 1884, narrated by a square who lives in a flat,
two-dimensional world (Section 7 says more about him and it). When a sphere passes
through the flat world, the narrator sees a line whose ends fade wrong and whose
length keeps changing, and only when he feels it does he find a circle, a perfect one.
Then the sphere tells him it will rise, and he watches it dwindle to a point and vanish,
and come back larger and larger. The hidden direction leaks into his view, faintly,
and a sharp enough flat observer could in principle work out where the sphere is. In
this machine, as far as I can make out, you could move a state all the way along the
established direction without changing a single bit of the ordinary machine. That may
be exactly why the ordinary machine can’t see it. It may also be why, if the direction is
worth having, someone has to build it in on purpose and keep it on purpose. Whether
keeping it costs anything is what the rest of this chapter tries to find out.

None of these people were writing about what I’m writing about, and none of them
is the reason any of this is true or false. Reading them didn’t make anything truer.
It raised how far I’d established a few things for myself, and I could still be wrong
about every one, the way the people who read Kempe in 1880 were. I went through
them because I needed something to test the feeling against, and most of what I tested
failed. The failures told me what the thing isn’t: not hidden, not free, not reversible,
not steering. What’s left after all that is mostly a list of what it isn’t, and I’m still not
certain I’ve described what it is.

Computing already had a word for it
Here’s the slightly embarrassing part. Computing already has a word for this and
uses it every day. Anyone who’s used a database has seen it: COMMIT.

A database does a pile of tentative work, and then there’s one moment, the commit,
written to a log, after which the change counts. Jim Gray, who more or less built the
theory behind that, opens his 1981 paper on it by saying the idea comes from contract
law, and his example is a wedding. People negotiate, somebody asks, two people say
“I do,” and from then on it’s binding. If it was a mistake, you don’t erase it. You do
another transaction to fix it, the way a bad contract gets a second contract. Nobody
reaches for a time machine.


                                             26
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


The wedding was a philosopher’s example first. The Oxford philosopher J. L. Austin,
lecturing in 1955, said “I do” makes a marriage. It doesn’t describe one, and sayings
like that aren’t true or false. They can misfire (the wrong person says it, a step gets
skipped). They can’t be false. That’s a commit exactly. Writing the commit record
doesn’t report that a question got closed. Writing it is the closing. And a commit can’t
be false. It can misfire: committed without the check, committed about the wrong
pocket. Gettier and Peirce again, from a third direction. Then somebody else reads the
record, and for them it stops being a performance and turns into a report: “this was
checked and closed.” A report can be false. On the small machine in Part IV it can’t be,
about the machine’s own history: if its flag is up from a clean start, some claim was
checked and closed, and that claim held of that edition when it was checked. That’s
the one place in the book where a commit and the truth get tied together, and it took a
proof to do it.

Robin Milner, building a proof checker in the 1970s, ran out of memory, so he decided
to keep only the finished theorems and throw the proofs away, like a teacher rubbing
out the blackboard to make room. The obvious worry is forgery: if the proofs are
gone, what stops someone just writing a theorem down? His answer was beautiful.
Theorems got their own type in the programming language, and the only way to
make one was through the rules of logic. You couldn’t forge one because the language
wouldn’t let you build it any other way. He named that language ML, for Meta
Language. I wanted to call my machine the meta machine. I’m choosing to treat that
as a coincidence. Calling it a sign would be more my style, so this is more restraint
than I usually manage.

Bitcoin is the loud modern version. Its records can’t be changed without redoing all
the work that came after them, and a computer that drops off the network and comes
back trusts the longest chain as the story of what happened while it was gone. That’s
Turing’s clerk again, coming back to a note. The difference is that the clerk’s note costs
nothing to forge and Bitcoin’s costs a mountain of work. It’s the clearest case I know
of somebody making a settled fact expensive to fake, and they got there by paying for
a search. The settling itself carries no price.

That’s a different job from the one this book’s price does, the mark it charges for raising
a record. I’ll name that price the toll when I state it, a few pages on, and I’d rather say
this now, before you read the toll as a deterrent. One mark deters nobody. Bitcoin’s
work is tied to something scarce, electricity and hardware; a mark in this book is tied
to nothing. Eric Budish, an economist at the University of Chicago, built a model in
2025 of what that tie has to cost. As I read him, for Bitcoin’s kind of trust to hold, the
honest work has to stay expensive at every moment compared with what an attacker
could win, and the bill grows in step with the value being protected. A flat mark can’t
do that job, and it isn’t trying to. What makes a raised record mean something, on the
machine where it means anything, is an order rule: check, then commit, then certify.
That rule would work just as well at a price of zero. The price is there because, on the


                                            27
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


premises of the chairs a little further on, a finite machine that prices its merges can’t
avoid it. Scaring anybody off has nothing to do with it. The machines I actually build
don’t meet those premises, so on them the price is a choice made to match (Section 16
says why).

And Bitcoin wasn’t first. Pull on its footnotes: three of the eight references in the paper
that started it point to Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, who in 1991 worked out how
to stamp a document with a time nobody could fake later, by chaining each stamp to
the ones before it. A company built on their idea, Surety, printed a short fingerprint
of its chain in the classified ads of the New York Times once a week from 1995, and it
was still doing it in 2018. I found that in a piece the journalist Daniel Oberhaus wrote
that year, which says the ad runs under “Notices & Lost and Found.” Think about that
for a second. To make a record nobody could quietly rewrite, they put it somewhere
a million people would keep a copy of without even meaning to. A physicist named
Wojciech Zurek has spent decades arguing that the world does the same thing with a
measurement, copying the result into so many places that nobody can take it back. I’ll
get to him properly near the end of Part III.

There are more fences like these: logs that can’t quietly change, certificates you can
check. Later in the book I take five of them apart. I lean on all of them. They work. I
want that said plainly, because the next thing isn’t “they’re broken.”

The next thing is where they sit. The database’s commit is bits in a log, kept by
a database program, on a machine whose own step will overwrite those bits the
moment some instruction says to. Milner’s guarantee is a type checker; it holds inside
programs written in his language and nowhere else. Bitcoin is a protocol on ordinary
computers that will do whatever they’re told. Every one of them is a program or a rule,
on top of a machine that can’t tell my two computers apart. The machine underneath
keeps nothing and charges nothing for what got settled.

The obvious comeback: so put the rule one level lower, in the operating system, or
what security people call a reference monitor, the small always-on piece everything
has to pass through. Yes. Exactly that. A monitor that wouldn’t let any program raise
its record without paying would be doing the thing I’m talking about. In this book’s
words it would be implementing the model, and I’d count that as agreement. What I
care about isn’t who builds the fence. It’s what the fence has to obey, wherever it’s
built, and whether that’s forced or just a good idea.

That comeback has a history, and it’s older than me by a lot. In 1972 James P. Ander-
son’s planning study for the US Air Force described a reference monitor: a piece every
access has to pass through, that can’t be tampered with, and small enough to check. In
2000 Fred Schneider, a computer scientist at Cornell, argued that a monitor that only
watches a run as it goes can enforce only rules whose breaking shows up at some finite
point, the kind computer scientists call safety rules. “No certificate without an earlier
passing check and a commit” is one of those. And in 2015 Arthur Azevedo de Amorim,


                                            28
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


a computer scientist then at the University of Pennsylvania, and six coauthors built
monitors that check a rule at every single instruction, and proved them correct. So
putting a rule under every program, so nothing can get around it, is their move. I
didn’t invent it. What I’m putting under that move is narrower: a record that has to be
paid for, on the small machine one that has to be earned, and a reason, from counting,
why a finite machine that prices its merges can’t make the price of a record that never
comes down zero.

What settling looks like
The chapter on what structure is (Section 2) ends with a pile of things sorted into
buckets. Settling a question is that, plus one more thing.

Picture every state the machine could be in as a field of dots. A yes-or-no question
about the state splits the field into two rooms: yes and no. That’s a sorting, the smallest
one there is. And remember the no pile: if one of the rooms is empty, there’s no sorting
at all, just a field. Now the extra thing that makes it a settlement: once the machine is
in the yes room, no step it can take leads back out. The door opens one way. A settled
question is a sorting plus a door that only swings in.

At its best, what goes through the door is a relation: these numbers are in this order,
these two things belong together. There’s a chimpanzee named Sultan, later in the
book, who fitted two short sticks into one long one and reached the food. Nothing
new got added to the cage. Two sticks became one tool. That’s what I’d want the door
to be for.

But the door doesn’t care, and this is the honest edge of the whole picture. Hook the
door to a check that says yes to everything and the machine walks through even when
the claim is false. If the claim happens to hold of everything, that same check is sound
but distinguishes nothing. Settled whether true or false, like Peirce said. A door that
only swings one way tells you a question was closed. It doesn’t tell you it was closed
right. Price and correctness are two different books, and I keep both, separately.

One more edge, the one Gray’s wedding already hinted at. What stays shut for good
is that the question got closed, about that edition of that thing. Whether the claim is
still true is another matter. Change the list after the commit and the record still says,
truthfully, that the old edition was checked and closed. And if the claim turns out
bad, the fix is another act on top, a second record that says “withdrawn.” The first one
never quietly comes back down. So “entitled to lean on it right now” is three things at
once: closed, not withdrawn since, and the thing unchanged.

Why it has to cost
This is the part I’m proudest of, because once you’ve picked a record that stays, the
choosing stops and the counting takes over. And the counting is chairs.

Take any machine with a finite number of states. Its step is a function: give it a state


                                            29
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


and a move, it gives you back one state. Pick a yes-or-no reading of the state and make
it permanent: no step ever turns a yes back into a no. Now suppose some step takes a
state that reads no and lands it on one that reads yes. Then that step has to land two
different states on one. It merges.

Do it with chairs. Draw a box on the floor, three chairs inside, one chair outside by the
door. Four people, one per chair: the four states the machine could be in. The three
inside already read yes. One step moves everybody at once, each to the chair the rule
sends them to. Nobody inside may leave, because yes is permanent. The person by
the door has to come in, because this is the step that flips them to yes. Now finish the
move, one person per chair. You can’t. Four people, three inside chairs: somebody
shares. Maybe the newcomer ends up on a lap, maybe two insiders squeeze onto
one chair; either way, two starting places share a destination. The people stand for
alternative starting states; a running machine occupies only one. Draw the move’s
arrows, then have somebody choose one starting place without telling you which and
report only the destination chair. At a shared destination, that report cannot tell you
which of its starting places they chose. Watching the person walk would give you extra
information; the destination alone does not. That’s the pigeonhole principle, which is
old and not mine, and the checked version, with exactly those three conditions (finite,
permanent, one flip), is in the chapter “Why the toll isn’t arbitrary.” No physics in it
anywhere. Counting.

(How old is it? I went looking. A French Jesuit, Jean Leurechon, used it in 1622 to
argue that two people somewhere must have exactly the same number of hairs on their
heads, which is the kind of thing you can be completely sure of and never check. The
first name for it I can find came two centuries later, from the German mathematician
Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet, who used it in print in 1842 without naming it and in
later work called it the drawer principle, the Schubfachprinzip; the pigeons came later
still. Benoît Rittaud and Albrecht Heeffer, who wrote a short paper in 2014 on what
came before Dirichlet, looked for a source for the year 1834 that turns up next to his
name and found none, and neither have I. Is 1622 the bottom? I can’t tell you. History
is like that: it’s where you start digging.)

Turn it around and it gets better. A reversible computer, one where every step can be
run backwards, never merges anything, because a step you can undo never puts two
people on one chair. Bennett, the same Bennett, showed in 1973 that any computation
can be done reversibly if you give it room to keep its history while it works. But
give a reversible computer a finite memory and, however much it computes, it can
never raise a flag that stays up. It can always back up to before the flag. Settling
needs exactly the kind of step a reversible computer refuses to take. (In a reversible
description of the machine and its surroundings together, the distinction lost from the
machine remains somewhere in the surroundings. Turning that transfer into a lower
bound on heat needs the thermal assumptions below. The chairs establish the merge;
they do not measure a heat bill. Section 4 comes back to that.)


                                           30
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


Now the physics, as an assumption with its name on it. Rolf Landauer, at IBM, 1961,
said that a step that can’t be run backwards, that merges, “requires a minimal heat
generation.” That’s the rule people call Landauer’s principle. On a finite machine,
settling something for good takes a merge, and under the adopted Landauer premise
a preparation giving positive probability to both members of a colliding pair has a
positive mean heat bound. The instruction’s collision is one fact; which starts actually
occur, and the physical device’s heat, are further facts.

And here’s his next sentence, the one I promised at the start. That heat, he wrote,
“serves the purpose of standardizing signals and making them independent of their
exact logical history.” That’s my two computers, in 1961. Ordinary machines spend
their merges, and their heat, on forgetting how the bits got there, on purpose, so a 1 is a 1
no matter what path made it. That’s why the sorter and the copier end up identical,
and why the comparing wing goes dark. And the very same kind of step, a merge, is
what it takes to close a door for good.

So here’s the deepest thing I can say about settling. Not every forgetting settles
anything: wiping a scratch pad closes no question. But on a finite machine, every
settling forgets. The step that closes a question for good lands two states on one,
somewhere, maybe not where you happen to be standing, and afterward nothing can
tell which one it was. A verdict keeps the decision and lets go of the arguing. An
ordinary computer pays for the forgetting and keeps nothing to show for it. What I
want to know is what a machine looks like that pays for the same forgetting and keeps
the receipt.

Every assumption in that is a way out, and you should know where they are. Give the
machine unlimited memory and it never has to merge; it can write its history down
forever, and the chapter “Why the toll isn’t arbitrary” builds exactly that machine. Let
the flag come back down and the chairs lose their grip. And the heat isn’t owed by
every run. Landauer’s principle, in the general form Part II adopts, bounds mean heat
by the uncertainty actually removed from the prepared inputs. For a deterministic
run from a known start, it supplies no positive heat floor; that doesn’t show the
device gives off none (Theorem 4.13). Preparing both members of a colliding pair can
give a positive floor. The ledger toll still charges its mark on a known run, because
merge pricing prices the instruction regardless of which input was prepared. That is a
premise of the ledger, not another conclusion about heat. And Landauer’s principle is
physics. No proof in this book reaches it. In 2012 a group in Lyon erased one bit held
in a tiny bead, kept in place by a laser, and found the average heat it gave off coming
down toward Landauer’s floor as the erasing was slowed. The principle has serious
critics too, the philosopher John Norton among them. So the counting is proved and
the price is an assumption, and I never let those two swap places.




                                             31
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


Somebody got there first, goddamn it
Bennett also says looking can be free. His famous move with Maxwell’s demon (the
whole story’s later in the book) is that you can write down which side of a box a
molecule is on without paying anything, as long as you write on a blank page. What
