costs is wiping the page to make room for the next one.

I’d been sitting on this idea that committing is what costs, and learning doesn’t, and
I thought: this one’s mine, I finally had an original thought. Then I found Carlo
Rovelli’s 2024 paper, “The Thermodynamic Cost of Choosing.” Nope. Somebody got
there first, goddamn it. A real physicist, with a real paper, saying that making a choice
that sticks costs at least the same heat Landauer charges for erasing a bit. He even
quotes a German saying, Wahl ist Leiden, to choose is to suffer, and at that point what
are you going to do but laugh.

And then, taking him apart properly, it got good, because he seems to contradict
Bennett. Bennett says measuring can be free; Rovelli says any measurement costs.
So which is it? Look at what Rovelli calls a choice. A coin in the air hasn’t chosen
anything; it has to hit the ground and stop. And then the sentence I’d put on my
wall: “stabilization must be irreversible, otherwise it is not stabilization.” Bennett’s
free measurement is one that could still be undone; that’s why it’s free. Rovelli’s choice
is one that’s been made to stay; that’s why it costs. The way I read them, they’re
standing on opposite sides of the same door: learning on Bennett’s side, committing
on Rovelli’s. (Bennett’s demon still pays in the end, when it wipes the page.) Neither
of them puts it that way, so push on it. But if it holds, it’s the best sign I’ve got that the
line I keep drawing between knowing and settling isn’t something I made up.

Push on it, then, with his paper open, and it gives in four places: his choice is unpre-
dictable, it’s a branching where mine is a merge, it’s stable only for a while, and he
stands against Bennett’s free measurement, where I’d have put him beside it (Section 5
goes through all four). So the two-sides-of-one-door picture is my reading. He doesn’t
draw it, and the piece of it that’s really his is the one sentence about stabilizing. That
sentence I’ll still put on my wall.

So he’s my closest neighbour, and here’s the difference, exactly. His is physics: a
price in heat, at a temperature, for a choice that sticks. Mine is a rule in a model of
computation: a charge in the machine’s own count, on the step that flips a permanent
reading on, with no temperature anywhere in it. Same instinct, different place. I’ll
take it. It’s annoying to be second. It’s worse to be alone and wrong. And he’s the
closest only on choosing. On copying there’s an older neighbour, in the physics of
molecules, and Section 5 gets to it.

What the Thiele Machine is
So here’s what I built, and which parts I was pushed into and which parts I chose,
because you should know which is which.


                                             32
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


The Thiele Machine is a model of computation, the way Turing’s machine is: math you
can reason about. You can’t buy it in a box. It isn’t a device, a CPU or an instruction set;
those are things you build to carry it, and Part IV builds one, as small as I could make
it. Unlike a Turing machine, it computes nothing new. It adds what a computation
establishes, and what establishing it cost. The event it accounts for happens on any
computer, whether anybody keeps track of it or not, and the record exists only if
something keeps it. It has a few parts. A state. A step that moves the state. A record:
a yes-or-no reading of the state that says whether something’s been established. A
charge on each kind of move, added up on a counter that only climbs. One rule, which
I call the toll: the step that flips the record from no to yes has to cost at least one mark
on that counter. And a window, what an outside observer gets to see, which is there
because the two computers already showed you the problem: the usual window, the
bits, can’t see the record. The toll’s first name, the one I gave it before I understood it,
is No Free Insight.

One what, and why one? One mark, in the model’s own count. One because it’s
the least a whole-number count can charge and still not be free, and the toll only
says not free. The model doesn’t say a mark is worth a joule or a dollar; whether it’s
worth anything physical is Landauer’s assumption, named, and nowhere else. And
one is just the floor: Part II shows that if you charge one mark per halving, a step
that squeezes a lot together pays at least the logarithm of the squeeze, roughly how
many times it halves the number of states it can tell apart. Don’t read that backwards,
though. One mark isn’t one halving. A single state flipping into a big room of states
that already read yes, with every state in play equally likely, squeezes things together
very little, much less than a halving, and the whole-number count rounds that up to
one. Read in the worst case over what the machine might be holding, the same flip
can remove a full bit; Section 4 has both readings.

What “new model of computation” means here. The Thiele Machine makes chosen struc-
tural distinctions explicit in the state, the step and its cost. In the case on the table,
that includes which object a check concerned, which edition it saw, and which later
act may rely on it. A record keeps something of those relations; a window determines
how much an observer can recover. Change what is kept or what the window shows,
and you change which questions the resulting state can answer. The computing base
supplies the operations. The record adds no computable function.

Which leaves a fair question hanging: if it computes nothing new, does it even get to
call itself a model of computation? I think so, and not only on my say-so. Computer
science has long kept models that compute exactly what Turing’s does and differ
only in what they count, how long a step takes, what reaching into memory costs,
because the counting is the reason to have them. The random-access machine of the
computer scientists Stephen Cook and Robert Reckhow (1973) charges each instruction
one unit, or a cost that grows with the logarithm of the numbers it handles. The cell-
probe model (1981) of Andrew Yao, a computer scientist who later won the Turing


                                            33
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Award, counts only the memory cells a program reads. The input-output model of the
computer scientists Alok Aggarwal and Jeffrey Vitter (1988) counts only the blocks
moved between a small fast memory and a large slow one. The bulk-synchronous
parallel model of Leslie Valiant, a computer scientist at Harvard (1990), charges for
rounds of communication between processors. Closest in kind are the two axioms the
computer scientist Manuel Blum gave in 1967 for any measure of computational cost:
they name no machine, and say what every cost has to satisfy, the way the toll is a rule
every price list on the model has to obey. That’s the family the Thiele Machine belongs
to, with an axis of its own: what a run established, and what that cost. Part III lays the
toll over a register machine of the first kind, and over a Turing machine and a lambda
calculus, and none of them computes one function more afterward (Section 10). What
each of them gains is a record and a bill.

What was I pushed into? That on a finite machine, a record that never comes down
can only be raised by a merge: counting, proved. That merges cost: physics, assumed.
What did I choose? To put the count inside the step, as part of what a step is. Nothing
forces that, and a log off to the side was always the other place it could go. It’s my
claim about where the account belongs, and the rest of the book is the case for it.

About the name. I named it after myself, on purpose. Half of that is a joke and half
of it is a stake in the ground. Turing got a machine, so here’s mine. The longer story,
meta machines and all, is in “How I got here” (Section 1).

The names work the way Turing’s do, and I’m going to be a little annoying about
them. The Thiele Machine, capital letters, is the model and nothing else. A Thiele
machine, lower case, is any particular system proved to fit the model, the way one
rule table is a Turing machine; a two-box toy on a sheet of paper counts. A Thiele
machine is Thiele-complete when the machine under the record can compute anything
a Turing machine can (under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine), for
free and without ever touching the record; a record that goes up stays up; and, from a
clean start, the record goes up only after a check of some claim passes, by a checker
proved to mean what the claim says, in a language of claims and meanings fixed
before any checker is named, then a commitment to that same claim with nothing it’s
about changed in between, then a certificate, with exactly one mark charged for each
of those three acts; and at least one claim on the machine has a check, commit and
certificate that raise the record on some inputs and leave it down on others. And a
universal Thiele machine is one fixed program that runs other machines as guests, with
each guest’s record earned again by the host’s own steps and each guest’s toll paid on
the host’s own ledger. Nothing is left to the guest’s good manners.

The first bar, being a Thiele machine at all, is low, and I’d rather you hear it from me. A
machine that charges one mark for every step it takes, whatever the step does, obeys
the toll for any record you like; a clock is enough to make something a Thiele machine.
If Thiele-complete only meant a Thiele machine that can compute anything, a clock


                                            34
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


bolted to a computer would pass that too, and so would a machine whose record
never goes up. That’s why Thiele-complete asks for more, and both of those fail it,
by theorem: a clock charges for computing, and Thiele-complete says computing is
free; and a machine whose record never goes up fails the clause asking for at least one
claim whose check, commit and certificate raise the record on some inputs and leave
it down on others (Section 16). The small machine of Part IV meets it, and so does the
same machine over any properties with an exact test for telling two of them apart and
a checker proved to mean what it says, as long as one of them is true of some number
and false of another, sorted lists included. And every machine that meets it has the
same blind spot built in, also by theorem: the part a Turing machine would call the
whole machine, the line it’s on and the numbers it holds, can’t tell you its record or its
ledger. That’s about an observer who sees only where a run ended. One who also has
the program and the start can work both out.

the counter written out, so you can watch it happen. You don’t have to take my word.

to commit, and to certify (raise the record), and nothing for ordinary work like moving
numbers around.

At the end, the bits on both machines are still the same sorted list. Everything else
differs. The sorter’s record is up and its counter reads 3. The copier’s record is down,
and it’s paid 2 for two refusals, because on that machine a refused attempt still costs
what it costs. (Read those as two separate attempts. Written as one stored program,
the copier would stop at its first refusal and pay 1.) Nothing the copier can do raises
its record without first running a passing check of the claim it then commits to. And
no outside window that only shows the list can tell you which is which; the difference
is all in the part the window doesn’t show. Walk that warehouse now and there’s
finally a lamp that’s lit in one and dark in the other.

Now how literally to take that table. It’s a picture of the chain, and the chain is what’s
proved. The small machine’s own checks are three questions about one counter: is it
zero, is it even, is it at least some number. What its proofs need from the questions
is a checker proved to say yes exactly when the answer is yes, and an exact test for
telling two questions apart. That’s enough for “sorted”: a version of the machine that
takes any questions with checkers like that proves the same chain once for all of them,
and with a list packed into one counter it certifies a sorted list for three marks and
refuses an unsorted one forever (Section 16). Without a proved checker for “sorted,”
the chain would be honest about a counter and only by convention about your list,
which is Gettier’s pocket again, one level down.

And a lamp for whom? The record is bits too. It’s a lamp on the machine, for anybody
walking that warehouse. Hand somebody a printout of it across a desk and you’re
back at the sticker on the windshield: they have to trust whoever hands it over, or
have some way to check the box that says it ran. That crossing is a different problem
with its own tools, signatures, attestation and proofs a stranger can check, and this
book doesn’t solve it. Section 7 says what those tools rest on, and the small machine’s
record, like any record kept in a machine’s state, carries nobody’s signature. What the
step changes is the question, from “did it run?” to “do I trust the box that says it ran?”
That’s a smaller question. It isn’t no question.

Now the honest half. Take away the small machine’s rules and keep only the bare toll,
and the copier has an easier move: pay one mark, flip the record to yes, done. The
toll is satisfied. The receipt is real. It’s a receipt for nothing. The bare toll prices the
closing of the door. The check behind it goes unpriced.

                                            36
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


What putting it in the step buys
So here’s the hardest objection, and I’d rather make it myself. You defined a flag
and a charge, then proved the charge gets paid when the flag goes up. That’s your
definitions agreeing with each other.

On the bare model, that’s fair, and the copier’s receipt for nothing is the proof. What
makes the record mean established is the small machine’s step, which won’t let a
commit through unless a check of that very claim passed, meeting the first three of
the four conditions from Gettier’s pocket, with the fourth, an honest checker, proved
about the checker separately. And what it proves isn’t about one program. It’s this:
on every list of instructions anybody can write, starting clean, if the record is up, then
somewhere earlier a check of some claim, about some edition, passed; then a commit
of that same claim; then the certificate; with nothing touching the thing between the
check and the commit.

From a clean start, a raised flag guarantees that some claim went through a passing
check, a matching commitment about the same edition, and a successful certification.
The flag retains that historical fact. The channel names the latest earned commitment,
which need not be the commitment on which the flag first rose. The final state does not,
in general, identify the claim certified at that first rise or the step at which it occurred.
And the flag doesn’t say the claim still holds, at the certification or at the end, since
the counter can change after the commitment.

That “every” is the whole answer to what the step buys. A log kept by a program gives
you a fact about that program: if the program’s right, the log’s right. The database’s
guarantee holds for work that goes through the database. A rule in the step gives you a
fact about every program the machine can run, the buggy ones and the hostile ones too,
because there’s no way to run anything on it that isn’t a string of its steps. That’s what
moving the rule down a level changes. Not what can be computed. Which programs
the guarantee covers: this one becomes every one. Here the relation between a check
and its object has a job in the machine: the step reads it and refuses a commitment
when it no longer fits. That is one concrete way to make structure part of what the
machine does.

Two limits on that “every,” said now so you don’t have to find them later. First, it’s
every program. It isn’t every everything. The guarantee covers any list of instructions,
run from a clean start, one step at a time, on a step that does what its definition says.
Hostile programs, yes. A hostile start (a table of facts nobody checked, a reset), hostile
hardware (a soldering iron on the flag’s bit, a second writer the step can’t see) or
a hostile reader, no; Section 24 lists the whole fence. That’s the same shape as the
database’s guarantee, true if the layer underneath is faithful, with a much bigger class
of programs inside it.

Second, the flag and the counter on their own are what people who verify programs
call ghost state: erase them and every program computes exactly what it did before

                                             37
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


(Section 6 has where that idea comes from). What isn’t ghost on the small machine is
the table of checked facts, which the step reads and refuses on, at run time, for every
program. And the move of putting a rule under every program isn’t mine either. It’s
the reference monitor’s, and its history is a few sections back.

What it isn’t
It isn’t more computing power. Anything a Thiele machine computes, the machine
under its record computes without it. The book proves that over any machine at
all, a base-driven record is a switch the machine’s own events flip once and nothing
flips back; it watches the computing and adds nothing to it. That’s a sentence about
the record. The checker belongs to the machine under it, and the definition of Thiele-
complete doesn’t ask the checker to be a program. Hand it a checker that knows which
programs halt, and whether a CHECK of “this program halts” traps tells you whether
it does, so that machine decides halting (Section 16 has the details). With a checker
that is a program, as every checker in this book is, nothing in the machine goes past
what a program can do. The record makes nothing faster either: erase the flag and the
counter, and every run takes the same steps to the same places. CHECK is another
matter. It’s a test at unit cost, and one CHECK of “A ≥ m” settles whether A ≥ m in
one step, where the two counters alone would count A down. It isn’t quantum. It says
nothing about which problems are hard.

And an ordinary computer can keep a record like this. Give a Turing machine a spot
for the record and a track for the counter, write its rules so it never sets the spot without
bumping the counter, prove that, and it is a Thiele machine. It’s no counterexample
(Section 16.16). What an ordinary programmable computer, as built, doesn’t do is
make its own step enforce a record for the programs it runs. When it runs another
program, that program’s record is just data in memory the program can write, and
a buggy program can flip it for free, because the host’s step has no opinion about it.
Could it be built otherwise? Sure. A universal machine with one fixed table, the kind
Turing built, could have that table written so it mirrors each guest’s record and charges
for the raise, and it would qualify. Nothing about ordinary computers stops that. They
just aren’t built that way. That gap, between the machine doing the stepping and the
program it runs, is where the databases and the proof checkers and Bitcoin built their
fences, and it’s the gap the universal Thiele machine later in the book closes, first for
the programs of the small machine it’s built on, and then for every Thiele machine
whose workings a program can compute.

There’s a cheap version of a universal machine, so here’s which one this is. A host with
a move that means “run one guest step” runs any guest because I wrote it that way,
and the book has one of those, as the simple picture. The universal Thiele machine
doesn’t get that move. It’s one fixed program, written in the small machine’s own
six kinds of instruction on a host with more counters, and it fetches, decodes and
carries out each guest instruction itself, the way Turing’s universal machine does. The
theorems are about that program: it halts exactly when its guest halts, with the guest’s

                                             38
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


answer in its counters; its flag goes up at some step of its run exactly when the guest’s
goes up at some step of the guest’s, by its own check, its own commit and its own
certificate; its ledger equals the guest’s at every point where the two runs match; and
the machine it runs on is Thiele-complete (Section 16.13). Its guests are the small
machine’s programs, from every clean start, and those programs compute everything.
Add one move that pays a mark and does nothing else, and the same kind of program
runs every Thiele machine whose next move, step, prices and reading are computed
by programs: it halts when the guest’s run stops, its flag goes up at some point exactly
when the guest’s reading is yes at some state of its run, on a chain whose check is the
guest’s own reading, and its ledger is the guest’s prices plus at most two marks at the
raise when the guest’s reading starts at no (when it starts at yes, the host has to raise
its flag at once and pays three on a ledger of nothing), a surcharge no program on that
host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest’s whole ledger at the raise is
below three (Section 16.14). A Thiele machine whose reading no program decides isn’t
covered, and I say exactly where the edges are.

What’s proved, what’s argued, and what I just believe
Every claim in this book has a status and I’ll tell you which, every time. Here’s the
whole list at once, so you know what I’m on the hook for.

Proved, for any system with the named parts: anything that obeys the toll pays at least
one mark to get from not-established to established (short enough that you’ll prove
it yourself on paper in Part II). With finitely many yes-states and a record that never
comes down, every move that raises it merges states, which is the chairs; consequently
every schedule that prices merges charges that move, and every run from no to yes
has positive total cost. The price is an assumption with a name. Finding out can be
free: you can learn something from a step that merged nothing and cost nothing, so
the toll lands on committing. A window that shows a certifying step and a quiet one
alike, before and after, can’t price certification exactly, however clever it is. And over
any machine, a base-driven record is a one-way switch on an event, with two choices
left free: the price list and which event.

On the smallest machine I could build, six instruction kinds on two counters: the
chain in the table above (check, commit, certify, same claim, same edition), for every
program anybody can write, that one included, with claims about any property that
comes with a checker proved to mean it and an exact test for telling properties apart,
“sorted” included (Section 16). From a clean start, a raised record always went through
a passing check, then a commit, then a certificate, of exactly the same claim about
exactly the same edition; nothing gets into its list of checked facts without a check
writing it. Every run from a clean start that ends with the flag raised has incurred at
least three marks of instruction cost, and this bound is attained: check “this counter is
zero,” commit to it, certify, and when the counter is zero that pays exactly three; when
it isn’t, the check traps with the flag down and nothing after that ever raises it. The
machine doesn’t stop you asking a question that can’t come out no, and I say so where

                                           39
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


it matters. It’s Thiele-complete in the strong sense from a few pages back, and that
sense has teeth: every clock-style machine, one that charges for computing, fails it,
and every machine that meets it hides its record and its ledger from its own window,
both by theorem. Its computing is that of the two-counter machines of Marvin Minsky,
one of the founders of artificial intelligence at MIT, which Minsky proved can compute
anything a Turing machine can, under his 2n encoding, done outside the machine. The
two universal programs described under “What it isn’t” run on top of it, and what
they’re proved to do is said there.

Argued only: that an account of computation should carry what was established, and
what it cost, in how it steps. The proofs show that it hangs together, what it follows
from, and what it costs (six instruction kinds and three marks, on the small machine);
whether it ought to be adopted is argued, and it’s a claim about what matters, which
those mathematical results do not decide.

Guessed at, with the ways to kill it written down: that the event worth recording is
certification, because its records are the ones that get copied and relied on all over the
place by parties who didn’t produce them (the pointer thesis, Part III).

Not proved, and I’ll say so every time it’s tempting: any physical price for one mark,
anything about a physical device running any of this, or anything about which prob-
lems are hard.

Which of the proved part is new? Not one big thing, and I’d be suspicious of me
if I said otherwise. By my own sorting at the back (Appendix C) it’s four smaller
ones, each with its neighbours standing right there. The toll derived from finiteness,
permanence and a price on merging: the pigeonhole principle, Landauer and Bennett
on merging, and the finite heart of the German mathematician Ernst Zermelo’s 1896
recurrence argument, about whether a closed box of gas has to come back around to
where it started, are all next to it. A window that shows a certifying step and a quiet
one alike, before and after, can’t price certification exactly: an old fact about functions,
the 1956 thought experiments of Edward Moore, at Bell Labs, on what you can learn
about a machine you may only watch from outside, and the engineer Rudolf Kalman’s
observability, the same question asked of control systems. What I put in is a price. A
base-driven permanent record, over any machine, is a latch on one event: the 1918 flip-
flop and write-once memory are its neighbours. And the small machine, a definition
of Thiele-complete that a clock can’t meet, and a universal Thiele machine written as
one fixed program: a record that’s priced, and earned, under the reference monitor’s
every-program move (Anderson in 1972, Schneider in 2000, monitors from Azevedo
de Amorim and coauthors in 2015), carried to every program of the small machine
and, with one paid move added, to every computably presented Thiele machine. That
fourth one is built and checked; the idea under it isn’t new. The first is a ledger form
of a core that’s classical and already priced in physics; the second and third are small
exact statements I didn’t find stated before, where I looked. The two-player game


                                            40
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


check later in the book is careful engineering on known mathematics. It doesn’t make
a fifth.

At the bottom: what I suspect and can’t prove
This is underneath the proofs, so read it with the lights on. None of it is a theorem,
and I’m not going to dress it up as one. It’s why I care, and I’m telling you going in,
so you don’t catch me sneaking it in later.

Physics has a word for the moment a question closes: measurement. And the people
who thought hardest about it keep describing it in this chapter’s shape. They ran
together for me until I put them on one picture. Flip a coin in a crowded room. Before
it lands, it could go either way. After, it’s settled, somebody chalks it on a board, and
the result gets copied out into the world, the light and the air, so many times that it
can’t be taken back and everybody who looks agrees. Five pieces: the question, the
landing, the chalk mark, the copies, the agreeing. Each person leans on a different one.
Wojciech Zurek has spent decades on how the copying works. Rovelli’s coin has to hit
the ground, so his piece is the landing.

Niels Bohr, the Danish physicist whose institute in Copenhagen was where quantum
mechanics got argued into shape, leans on the mark. In a 1954 talk he said seeing
anything at that scale depends on an apparatus that works irreversibly, like permanent
marks on a photographic plate: a door that swings one way. I found that line quoted
in a recent paper and haven’t seen the page in Bohr’s book myself. John Wheeler, the
Princeton physicist who named the black hole, went further in a 1989 talk in Tokyo
and leaned on the question: every physical thing gets its existence from yes-or-no
questions answered and registered, boiled down to “it from bit.” As I read him, the
coin has no face until something asks and something writes the answer down. How
literally he meant that, I can’t tell. And Peirce, way before any of them, leans on
the agreeing: the kind of settling worth trusting is the kind that has to answer to
everybody. Laid out like that, they pair up. Bohr and Rovelli lean on a step that only
goes one way, in the plate and in the coin. Zurek and Peirce lean on many onlookers
who agree, one with light and one with people.

Lay that next to everything above and the parts line up: a check that could have come
out either way, a result that’s now settled, a price paid in forgetting, a record that stays.
I suspect that isn’t a coincidence. I suspect the event this book prices on a machine is
the same kind of event physics calls a measurement, showing up in a different place.
The forgetting is my step. Bohr only says irreversible, and getting from a record that
stays to a merge is the chairs, on a finite machine. Push on it and it gives at Zurek. In
Zurek’s picture the world settles a result by copying it, and copying merges nothing
(Section 15 pushes on that). As I read it, that’s Bennett’s free measurement, writing on
a blank page. So physics’ own word lands on both sides of Bennett and Rovelli’s door:
the chalk on the paying side, the copies on the free side. The landing I’d put with
the chalk, and when Section 5 pushes on Rovelli’s paper it slides toward the free side,


                                             41
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


the side of finding out. So two pieces already stick out, and I’ll leave them sticking
out. Which picture a settling on a machine matches is part of the suspicion, and the
suspicion doesn’t settle it. That’s as far as I’ll take it here: a suspicion.

Now let me point the biggest gun I can find at it, and that’s John Bell, the Northern
Irish physicist at CERN whose 1964 theorem comes back in Part IV. In 1990 Bell wrote
a short, furious essay against the word “measurement,” with a list of words he said
have no place in a physics that wants to be precise. On the list: system, apparatus,
environment, irreversible, information, and measurement, which he called the worst
of all. I used half of them in the last few paragraphs without even trying. Bell would
have taken my suspicion apart in an afternoon, and he’d have been right to, because
every piece of it leans on words physics hasn’t pinned down. Nothing in this book
proves any of it. The proofs are about models and machines, and whenever physics
shows up in them it shows up as an assumption with a name on it. The suspicion is
why I went looking. It isn’t what I found.

Where this goes
So here’s the picture, put back together. Two machines can hold the same bits and
differ in what they’ve established, and you can’t see it even walking the floor between
them, because it was never kept. It isn’t a difference in the algorithmic information of
the final list: the list is the same. A retained record of the runs would be additional
information, and these two machines kept none. It isn’t depth; depth belongs to the
bits, and a copy has just as much. It’s an event: a check that could have said no, about
the claim, then a question closed for good, with no promise the answer’s true. The
could-have-said-no part lives in the procedure. Two end states with the same bits and
nothing else kept can’t tell it apart, so only a record written into the state can carry it.
On a finite machine, a record that never comes down can only be raised by a merge, a
kind of forgetting, the same kind ordinary computers pay heat for so their bits forget
where they came from. A preparation that actually loses uncertainty through that
merge has a mean heat bound under the physical premise. The merge by itself does
not give every run that bill. The Thiele Machine puts the record and the charge in
the step itself, and what that buys isn’t more computing. It’s a guarantee about every
program. A log a program can freely write does not by itself supply that guarantee.

Every time I thought I’d found something new on the way down, somebody had a
name for part of it already, and that last sentence is no exception: a rule under every
program is the reference monitor’s move, from 1972. Fine. What I think is put together
here is smaller and more than one thing: the four small things I listed under what’s
proved, each with its neighbours named. There’s no one big one.

And the stuff from the start, the audit, the proof, the ledger, the test sheet, the sticker,
the confident AI? Here’s the straight answer on which of those this helps. The sticker
is a question of whether a piece of paper is genuine, and nothing here touches it. The
“all tests passed” sheet fits only if the test is a checker proved to mean what it says, in


                                            42
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


the machine’s own language; a set of tests that can miss a bug certifies “this procedure
said yes,” which is true and smaller. An audit and a ledger get the test sheet’s answer:
kept by a program on an ordinary computer, they’re bits the program wrote, and they
fit only where the step underneath keeps the record and refuses to raise it without
the check. A proof is one example: checking its steps is a procedure that can reject
them. Whether its statement says what you meant is still yours to read. The AI that
talks as if it’s sure of itself isn’t addressed at all. What the book gives you is a record
on the machine itself, with a proof of what a raised one means. Getting that record
to somebody across the room who has to believe it is a separate job, and Section 24,
under “Outward consequences,” says how little of the outside world I’ve reached. If
you came for a tool, that’s a short list. If you came for the question, this is where it
starts.

The rest of the book is me trying to break all of it. First where I came from, then the
word I couldn’t define when I started, structure. Then the smallest thing that could
carry the bill, on a sheet of paper, with one rule I’ll hand you without a reason, and
then the chapter where I find out whether I had to pick it. If it breaks there, the book
ends there. I’d rather know.

The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele



Before the book: the short version
The book in one paragraph. The Thiele Machine is an account of computation that holds
structure in the state and makes its treatment explicit in the step. Start with things
and their relations, then ask which moves preserve them, which lose distinctions, and
which distinctions an observer can see. The worked core is a state, a step rule, a cost
for each move and a yes-or-no reading, with a toll on turning that reading on. A
ledger adds the costs; a window shows some of the state. This small case lets us derive
definite consequences: a permanent reading over finitely many yes-states can only
rise through a merge; a price on merges then forces the toll. A window may hide that
change and its price. Over any base, a driven permanent record is a latch; records
with more stages give a direction of such readings. These are results about the pieces
they name. Part IV gives them a concrete form in a machine with six instruction kinds,
where checks and commitments are tied to the same edition of an object. The later
constructions change the base, join machines and run one inside another, asking what
structure and accounting survive. That is the route from the picture to the machinery.
The five steps below follow it, with the premises and the limits of each claim.

I didn’t invent a machine. I found one. That’s how I see this work, and I’ll be straight
about the difference between that conviction and a theorem before I do anything else.

That sentence walks straight into one of the oldest fights in mathematics, so here’s
a short trip into it first. G. H. Hardy, a Cambridge number theorist who wrote A
Mathematician’s Apology in 1940 to defend doing mathematics for its own sake, came
down on the found side about as hard as anyone ever has: mathematical reality, he
wrote, lies outside the people who study it, and the theorems they like to call their
creations are really just notes on what they saw there. The German mathematician
Leopold Kronecker supposedly split the difference: God made the whole numbers,
and everything else is the work of people. Supposedly, because push on that line and it
gets thin fast. It comes down through Heinrich Weber, another German mathematician,
in a memorial piece written after Kronecker died, pointing back to a lecture from 1886,
and that’s the only source I could find anybody citing. A great line with one witness.
(The first chapter of Part II stops early on to ask how many witnesses a claim ought
to need. The answer is more than one.) So does any of this settle whether I found
the Thiele Machine or made it up? No. A proof doesn’t settle it either: showing what
follows from the premises doesn’t decide whether you found the theorem or made
it. That’s why it’s labelled a conviction. What it changes is how I hold the thing: like
something that was already there, which means I can be wrong about its shape and the
shape won’t care. And to be exact about what “found” covers: the parts the counting
forces on you, the latch shape and the merge. The event to record, the price list, and
putting the count inside the step are choices, mine, and “The point” said so where it
sorted what I was pushed into from what I chose.

What this book is. An argument about what an account of computation should pre-



                                          44
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


serve. An answer, a run and a view of a run keep different things. The sorter and the
copier make that difference visible; the model lets us ask exactly which distinctions
a description retains and what follows when it drops them. My proposal is to carry
those structural relations and their accounting in the step itself. Here is the argument
in five steps, each with where it stands.

Holding a sorting costs something; standing behind one might. That’s Part I: one word,
structure, pushed on with you through as many of the people who wrestled it before
me as I could reach. It finds three different acts that people run together. Building and
storing a sorting you can read back costs work and space. Forgetting where things
came from costs heat, if Landauer is right. And standing behind a sorting, vouching
for it, is a third act, and nobody I read had put a price on it. The nearest was Rovelli’s
price on a choice that sticks, and his is a choice nobody could predict, which Section 5
shows is a different act. Whether that act has a price is the first accounting question
the book takes up.

Writing a permanent record. If the step that turns uncertified into certified has to pay,
every run from uncertified to certified has paid. Proved, for any system that follows
that rule, whatever its states and steps. And the rule isn’t arbitrary: on any system
with finitely many states, a certificate nothing takes back can only be switched on by
a step that merges two states. That part is pure counting, proved. If every merging
instruction is charged at least one mark, the rule follows. That is an abstract price
on the instruction; a physical heat bound also needs the input distribution and the
device premises. That part is proved with the charge as a named premise, its critics
named, and every premise refusable with a counterexample built. Learning isn’t what
costs: a measurement that forgets nothing can be priced at zero by an honest price list,
and an observer still learns from it. Proved. What can’t be free, on those premises, is
committing to what you learned in a record the machine can’t take back.

Two more things belong to that step. First, which steps a price on merging has to
charge, when move names can be told apart: exactly the ones that merge. On a finite
machine, every step that writes a record nothing takes back is one of them, and a step
that switches a certificate on escapes the price only when the same step switches one
off somewhere else. The tidier guess, that the priced steps are exactly the permanent
records, is false, and three states show it. No theorem picks out a wider class of events
every account must price. With one mark per halving, the step that writes a permanent
record costs at least the base-two logarithm of how much it squeezes together (how
many times it halves the number of states it can tell apart), and, from an even spread
over the states in play, the same bound holds in bits of Shannon entropy, the standard
measure of information. Proved, with the price as a premise. Second, where the
machine I built stands, and that’s a fact Part IV settles. The small machine of Part
IV isn’t a finite machine of that kind: its counters have no top, so it isn’t finite, and
some of its free steps merge states too. So the chairs don’t reach it. The merge premise
asked of the record layer alone does: a move that sends two different states with the


                                           45
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


same line and counters to one state costs at least one. The small machine’s own prices
meet that premise, and every price list that meets it charges the flag-raising step, with
no finiteness premise (Theorem 4.15). What the chairs do reach is a finite piece: an
eight-state machine, four slots and a flag, on which every premise is a theorem and
the toll follows outright (Section 4). And the small machine runs that piece: seen
through a window that shows only the line number, read modulo four, and the flag,
a program of the small machine, after a two-mark setup, does what the eight-state
machine does, one move at a time, and from then on pays exactly what the eight-state
machine charges (Section 4, with the construction in Section 16.17).

A window can hide what was paid. Two runs can look identical through the usual window
and differ in what they established and paid, and nothing reading only the window
gets the difference back. The machine I built has such a pair for the window a Turing
machine would point at, the line and the counters, and every machine that meets the
definition of Thiele-complete has one through its own window: two runs from one
clean start that end looking the same, one certified and one not. Proved, both. And
when two single steps look the same through a window, before and after, and only
one of them certifies, no price read off that window charges the certifying step exactly.
Proved, for any window with such a pair of steps.

Leaning on a fact takes a paid history. A computation is entitled to lean on a structural fact
when it holds the object, a checked relation, and a paid event on its record. Defined,
for the model, with a counting fact beside it. Number eight cards and hide which one
you chose: three yes-or-no answers suffice to identify any choice, while for two cards
one suffices. The difference is two questions. That change in the size of the pile does
not itself put two marks on a ledger; a premise must connect the questions to paid
steps. The cost floor that ties those questions to steps a run actually paid for holds
for any system with a counter, once somebody supplies three things: the list of rivals
before, the list of survivors after, and a tree of yes-or-no questions with enough leaves
to cover the narrowing. Then if a run paid at least as many charged steps as that tree
is deep, those payments cover the index bits, the questions it takes to point at one
entry of the first list less the ones it takes for the second (Section 8). No run is shown
to have to pay them. The run doesn’t hand back the tree, and nothing in it says why a
candidate was dropped; the lists count repeats, and the index bits aren’t the number
of questions anybody asked. On every Thiele-complete machine, the small machine
included, the paid steps are the record moves, each exactly one mark, and a run from
a clean start that ends with the record up, having narrowed a list that way, carries
an earned chain and pays at least the index bits in record moves (Section 16.17); and
when the questions are counted as the run’s own checks, the floor needs no tree to be
supplied, with a limit stated where it’s proved. Entitlement is a license to lean on a
claim. It doesn’t prove the claim is true.

So the axis belongs in the step. An account of computation should carry what was
established and what it cost as part of how it steps. Bolting it on after isn’t enough.


                                             46
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Proposed. The proofs around it show it hangs together and what it costs; whether it
should be adopted is argued, and no test settles it. What’s proved around it: over any
base machine, a base-driven record is a latch on an event, with two free choices, the
price list and the event; no decider whose flip a substrate can itself represent decides
which programs admit a shortcut, given a recursion theorem (the fact that a program
can act as though it held its own code). “Admits a shortcut” there is a label for any
property of programs that two programs doing the same thing always share, and
that some programs have and some don’t; Section 13 says why the label is all the
argument gets to see. A substrate is the model’s bare shape, a kind of state and a rule
for stepping, and here the extra pieces it’s asked for are programs written as states and
that recursion theorem. The wall comes by the same self-referring trick, the diagonal,
that put a hole in the foundations for arithmetic built by the German logician Gottlob
Frege (Part I tells that story). Which event deserves the record is a thesis, with its
refutations listed.

Certification is one point I could pin down. It gave me a law I could state, a machine
I could build and run, and proofs I could put in front of someone who didn’t share
my intuition. It’s one witness in a larger argument about structure and observation. It
isn’t the argument.

How the book is laid out. Part I is the picture: how I got here, and what structure
is. Part II is the axiom: the smallest thing that could carry a bill, why its one rule
isn’t arbitrary, and why learning is free where committing isn’t. Part III is the logic:
the counter, the windows, entitlement, insight, the latch, the whole direction, the
exact shadow, the diagonal (the lambda calculus L gets its recursion theorem there by
proof), five real systems, and a thesis. Parts I to III develop the abstract arguments and
their examples. They also point ahead to instances and limits on the machine built in
Part IV. Part IV builds one machine, the smallest honest machine I could make: two
counters, six instruction kinds, a table of checked facts, a ledger and a flag. On it a flag
raised from a clean start provably went through a passing check, a commitment and a
certification of the same claim, in that order, and it computes everything Minsky’s two-
counter machines can, so whether it halts is undecidable. There Thiele-complete gets
its definition, the one a clock fails, and the universal Thiele machine gets built as one
fixed program that runs every program of the small machine and earns its own flag,
and then, with one paid move added, every computably presented Thiele machine.
The machine that universal program runs on gets Kleene’s recursion theorem by proof
too, with Rice’s theorem beside it; on the two-counter machine itself Rice’s theorem
holds on every input, Kleene’s holds with inputs written as powers of two, for the
function the program computes though not for the facts it records, and with plain
inputs Kleene’s is false, which is proved too. Then a check worth earning, the two-
player game and its integer test: a flag raised from a clean start can stand on a passing
check of eight counts, and the check passes exactly when every question pair was
sampled and a fixed moment matrix is positive semidefinite, which forces Tsirelson’s



                                            47
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


bound, the ceiling quantum mechanics puts on the score of a two-player game, for the
tally it’s handed. It’s there to show the toll charges the same however deep the check
is. It isn’t a physics tool: it doesn’t sort data into quantum and not, and a tally above
two doesn’t by itself rule out a local model with chance in it. Then what the counter
has to do with physics. Part V is where to challenge it and what would break it. The
vocabulary I had to learn is at the back.

If you want the argument without the whole tour, read “The point” and this short
version, then Section 2, Section 3, Section 4, Section 7, Section 10, Section 11 and
Section 12. Then follow the construction in Section 16 through Sections 17 and 18, and
the conclusion in Section 25. If physics is your thing, add Section 5 and Section 21. If
you mean to check me, add Section 22 and Section 23. The appendices are reference:
everything in them is there to be looked up when a claim points at it. Nothing gets
cut for that. It’s a map. Nobody’s on a diet.

I think there’s something foundational here. The results in this book have statements,
premises, and arguments. The larger claim is a conjecture. No theorem proves it. I
built the machine so that the work could be done in public, with something firmer than
my confidence to argue over. If you’re the skeptical sort, and I hope you are, the two
places to aim are the appendix that sorts what’s mine from what isn’t (Appendix C)
and the chapter of ways to break it (Section 22).

Let me be straight with you
What this project is. An account of the relations a computation carries, the moves that act
on them, and the views through which they can be read. The smallest accounting case
uses a yes-or-no reading and a toll; structural entitlement adds an object, a checked
relation and a history that earned it. The generic flag-raising step pays to set a flag
and checks nothing. In the earned version, a checker establishes a stated property of
a particular object, and the step keeps that check tied to the edition it concerned. The
model, the results under its premises and the instructions of a particular build each
have their own scope.

The permanent-record result. For the yes-or-no case, the universal certification result
is this: when the yes-state set is finite and the reading is permanent, every move
that raises the reading merges states. Consequently, every cost schedule satisfying
merge pricing charges that move at least one mark, and every run from no to yes costs
at least one. This is a theorem over all systems satisfying those premises. It isn’t a
property peculiar to the implementation in Part IV. The counting under it is classical,
the finite cousin of Zermelo’s recurrence argument and folklore among automata
theorists; what’s mine is reading it as a price on a ledger, and Appendix C gives the
neighbours. Three layers stay separate through the book. The first is the structural fact
that a permanent raise merges states, which needs no prices at all. The second is the
pricing premise, merge pricing, which turns that fact into a ledger bound. The third
is the small machine of Part IV, which has its own stated prices and enforces earned

                                            48
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


certification. Its unbounded counters do not meet the finite-state premise; its toll is
established directly from its instruction rules.

The proved core, in three steps. Anything that follows the toll pays something to get
from uncertified to certified. A window that shows two states as the same, when
they disagree on the counter or on some other question, can’t answer that question
on every state. Those two are about any system with the named pieces, and so is the
third, argued in three lines in Part III: a checker that only sees a window where two
states collide can’t be both sound and complete about the claim that separates them
(Section 7). All three are statements about named laws and named windows, and
the third is checked too, over abstract transcripts and then for every Thiele-complete
machine (Section 7). An ordinary machine can keep a richer encoding, or enforce the
same invariant through its own transition table. What I’m proposing is about why the
extra distinctions matter. It isn’t a theorem that every Turing-equivalent system lacks
them. And if you want the list of what I think is new, it’s the short one at the end of
“What’s proved, what’s argued, and what I just believe” in “The point,” four small
things, and nothing bigger.

The layers, once. The core definition (Definition 3.1) is a certification system: states,
moves, a step, a cost for each move, a yes-or-no reading, and the toll. Everything else
is added on top, and each theorem names what it adds. First come extra structures and
requirements: a ledger that sums the costs, a window, permanence of the reading, a
price on merges. Then an earned implementation, the small machine of Part IV, with a
checker proved sound and a provenance theorem. Then an interface, Thiele-complete,
that any machine can be read through. Then a universal interpreter for a stated class
of guests. The bare definition doesn’t ask the step to be computable, so when I say the
record adds no computing power, I mean relative to a fixed base.

Substrate versus scaffolding. Two layers run through the book, and confusing them
makes the theorems quietly stop meaning what they say. The substrate is the shape: a
kind of state and a rule for stepping. Different theorems ask that shape for different
extra pieces, and the pieces aren’t the same. The universal floor (the “pays something”
result above) asks for a certification reading and the toll on it. The counter’s unique-
ness (only one count fits a chosen start and price list) asks for a starting value and a
schedule of increments; Part III gives the argument, a short induction that works for
any system with those two pieces, and on the small machine of Part IV the ledger is
the sum of the charges by theorem (Section 16). The diagonal asks for a way to write
programs as states and a recursion theorem for the transformations the substrate can
express, and needs no toll at all. “Substrate-level” doesn’t mean one fixed plug that
every theorem shares. A theorem only gets to use the parts it asks for. Ask it what
it needs and it’ll tell you, and whatever else is lying around the workshop isn’t the
theorem’s. So each result is stated over exactly the extension it uses. The substrate
with the extension a theorem names is what I mean by the model, and the name Thiele
Machine belongs to the model. The scaffolding is everything that holds the shape up


                                           49
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


so you can touch it, and when I say my machine, the small machine, the machine I build or
the build, this is what I mean: the machine of Part IV, with its two counters and their
versions, its table of checked facts, its channel, trap, ledger and flag, its six instruction
kinds and their prices, the host with a register for every whole number, and the uni-
versal programs that run on that host. The build fills in several extensions at once and
borrows, for any one theorem, only the extension that theorem names. Let that line
blur and a theorem stated over one extension starts reading as if it carried premises
it never uses. “Substrate” never means the build, and it never means the side of a
simulation doing the stepping; for that I say “the machine doing the stepping,” as
against “the program it runs.”

So here’s how the book keeps the two apart. Parts I to III are about any system with
the pieces each result names, and their pictures are toys you can hold (two boxes on a
sheet of paper, chairs in a room, a row of dots). My machine isn’t one of them; it first
appears in Part IV. Every Part III claim that has a machine instance gets that instance
in Part IV, with its own theorem, and Part III says so in one sentence at most. When
the origin story, a few pages on, says the shape “was the substrate the entire time,” it
means this layer, the model’s shape. It doesn’t mean any piece of the build. Same story
with two more of its words. When it says “the machine” about the thing it named the
Thiele Machine, or calls that thing a meta machine, it means the model; “my machine”
is the build, and the build doesn’t show up until Part IV. And when it lists what the
model asks for (a state, a step, a record, a ledger, a window), read the ledger and the
window as two of the extra pieces: a result asks for them only if it uses them.

Part IV has one piece of scaffolding, and I’d rather you know up front how small it is.
Section 16 builds the smallest honest machine I could: two counters, six instructions,
a table of checked facts, a ledger and a flag. Earned commitments are proved there
(a flag raised from a clean start was checked, then committed, then certified, on the
same edition, with nothing touching that thing between the check and the commit),
and so is universality, through Minsky’s two-counter machines and a halting result
due to Minsky, using the construction of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors.
Then one fixed program, on a host made of the same kinds of instruction with more
counters, runs every program of it, and with one paid move added, every computably
presented Thiele machine. None of that is the model. It shows the model fits in six
instruction kinds.

The names again, this time with every part pinned down, because I’ll hold to them
for the rest of the book. The Thiele Machine, with capitals, is the model and nothing
else. A Thiele machine, lower case, is any particular system proved to be an instance
of the model’s core definition, a certification system with its five parts and its toll
(Definition 3.1), the way one rule table is a Turing machine. The toys on paper in
Part II count, the same way trivial Turing machines do. The small machine counts
too, with its toll proved, and Part IV names the theorem. A Thiele machine is weakly
Thiele-complete when its base is Turing-universal, and that bar is nearly empty: a


                                             50
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


machine that charges one for every step is a Thiele machine for any record, so a clock
bolted to a computer clears it, and so does a machine whose record never rises. So
Thiele-complete asks for four things (Definition 16.7). A universal base whose moves
are free and can’t touch the record, and a record that stays up once it’s up. A record
that, from a clean start, rises only after a passing check of a claim, then a commitment
to that same claim with nothing it’s about changed in between, then a certificate, with
the checker proved to mean what it says: the claims and what they mean come from
a language fixed first, and the proof is that the checker’s yes makes the claim true in
that language’s sense. An exact toll: one mark for each of those three acts and nothing
for anything else. And a claim whose check, commit and certificate raise the record on
some loaded starts and leave it down on others. Every clock-style machine fails the
definition, because it charges for computing, whatever its record, and every machine
that meets the definition hides its record and its ledger from its own window, both
by theorem. None of the four clauses is there for decoration: for each one there’s
a machine that meets the other three and fails it, a Thiele machine with a universal
base that no interface makes Thiele-complete (Theorem 16.23). The small machine
meets it, and so does the same machine over any properties with an exact test for
telling two of them apart and a proved checker, as long as one of them can come out
both ways, sorted lists included. A universal Thiele machine is one fixed program that
runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with the guest’s record earned again
and its toll paid by the host’s own steps. Part IV builds one, U: a fixed program in
the small machine’s own six kinds of instruction, on a host with more counters, with
no step of any guest built in. Its guests are the small machine’s programs, so every
computation runs on it under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine, and
it matches each guest’s halting, answer, flag and ledger exactly, raising its own flag
by its own check, commit and certificate. Then UP , the same program with one more
handler for a paid move that does nothing else, takes as its guests every computably
presented Thiele machine, one whose next move (picked by a driver), step, prices
and reading are computed by programs, with the reading decided on every state. It
matches the guest’s halting, raises its own flag on its own earned chain exactly when
the guest’s reading has said yes, and keeps the guest’s prices to within a surcharge
of at most two when the guest’s reading starts at no, which no program on that host,
run from a clean start, can avoid in general. And a computer that runs the small
machine, your laptop say, isn’t a Thiele machine. It implements one, inside bounds,
the way a laptop implements a Turing machine. Push on that comparison, because it’s
loose, and the looseness is the point. Does a laptop implement a Turing machine? Not
exactly. Turing’s tape never runs out, and a laptop’s memory does; strictly, a laptop is
a very large machine with finitely many states, and it behaves like a Turing machine
only on computations that fit. Nobody minds, because the bound is known and most
computations people care about fit inside it. That’s the same deal any device running
the small machine gets: its counters stop somewhere, and the theorems speak only
for runs that fit. The bounds aren’t fine print. They’re the whole difference between
implementing a model and being one.

                                          51
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


How much can a difference in width matter? There’s a famous answer, and it’s worth
the detour. On 4 June 1996 the first Ariane 5 rocket lifted off and broke apart about
forty seconds after its engines lit. The inquiry board, chaired by the mathematician
Jacques-Louis Lions, traced it to one conversion in the inertial reference software:
a sixty-four-bit floating-point number, an alignment value called BH that’s tied to
horizontal speed, squeezed into a sixteen-bit signed integer. On Ariane 4, where the
software came from, that value could never get big enough to overflow, because of
how that rocket flew in its first forty seconds. Ariane 5 flew differently. The value got
too big, the backup unit failed on it, the main unit failed the same way about seventy
milliseconds later, and the function doing the converting didn’t even serve a purpose
on Ariane 5; it was kept for commonality with the old rocket. The board’s report says
the assumption that made the conversion safe had been agreed on and never exposed
to outside review. A width premise that holds on one machine is a fact about how that
machine gets used. The code doesn’t carry it, and yet it travels with the code without
anybody noticing. The only defence I know is the dull one: write the premise into
every statement that needs it, where the next person will trip over it.

What this project is not. Not a solution to P versus NP, and not a complexity-class
separation of any other kind. Not a theory of everything. Not a claim that computation
is physics, or that physics is computation. Not a physics result: the game result (the
integer check and Tsirelson’s bound from the short version) is pure mathematics, and
Landauer’s principle enters only as a premise with its name on it. Nothing here derives
it. Not a quantum computer. Its theorems about quantum strategies are mathematics
about vectors and matrices, with no claim about a physical device. Not a verified chip
or a verified device of any kind; a mathematical model and an abstract machine, with
proofs of their properties. Not a claim to priority on the ideas it builds from. What
it does add, with the closest earlier work beside each item and the difference spelled
out, is sorted in Appendix C: chiefly the price as a named rule on a ledger and the toll
derived from it (on a counting core that is classical), the pricing form of the window
fact, the latch form of a record that never comes down, and a checked machine and
universal interpreters that carry the toll, whose every-program idea is the reference
monitor’s. Not closed on every question: the ones I couldn’t settle are listed at the
end.

What I do and don’t know about prior work. I came to this with no formal training in the
fields it turned out to need, and I’ve read what I could reach, with every tool I had.
The prior-work map below is orientation. It doesn’t pretend to be scholarship. For
each piece of this book it says who did the thing it leans on, and what, if anything, this
development adds. I’d welcome correction on any row.

There’s a law about rows like these, and it’s a joke that keeps turning out true. In
1980 the statistician Stephen Stigler proposed that no scientific discovery is named
after the person who first found it, and then credited the idea to the sociologist Robert
K. Merton, who had been writing about fights over scientific priority since 1957. So


                                           52
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


Stigler’s law is an example of itself, which is either the best joke in the history of
science or a very tidy accident. Is it a law? No. It’s a pattern. Nobody proved it. But
this book has already tripped over it once, in the opening chapter: the pigeonhole
principle wears Dirichlet’s name, and Leurechon had it two centuries earlier. And I
put my own name on a machine. By Stigler’s law, that makes it somebody else’s. The
table below is my best attempt at finding out whose.

What I compare each time is what a result is about. Landauer’s bound is about heat, a
physical cost under a thermodynamic model. No Free Lunch (an optimisation result,
in the list below the table) is about averages over a whole spread of problems. The toll
is a floor on one kind of step, the step that turns a certification reading on. Rise-only
pricing adds a second rule on top: charge nothing on a step that doesn’t turn it on.
So the comparisons are about the shape of each result. They aren’t claims about who
got somewhere first, and they don’t show that certification is the only event worth
pricing.

Three kinds of exact. The word exact does three jobs in this book, and each job keeps one
name. Rise-only pricing charges at least one mark on every step that raises the reading
and nothing on any other step; its tightest bill, one mark per raise and nothing else,
is the exact schedule. Instruction-exact pricing charges every instruction a fixed listed
price. On the small machine of Part IV that’s one mark each for CHECK, COMMIT
and CERTIFY and nothing for the rest, and the definition of Thiele-complete calls it the
exact toll. CHECK and COMMIT raise no flag, so the small machine is instruction-exact
without being rise-only, and no rule is broken by that. Simulation-exact accounting is a
host whose ledger equals its guest’s ledger at every point where the two runs match,
as the universal program U’s does. A machine can meet any one of the three and fail
the others.

The right-hand column uses words the book only builds later (the latch, the fibre, the
universal program, the integer check, the matrix test), so read it as a list of places to
go. You aren’t meant to follow it yet.

Everything in the right column is stated with its premises in the body of the book,
and everything in the middle column is cited where it’s used. The table is the short
form. The long form is Appendix C, which takes each row, says what was already
known with sources, and sorts what’s added into new result, new proof, mechaniza-
tion, implementation, synthesis, or conjecture or thesis. Most of the right column is
mechanization, implementation, and synthesis.

A few more labels I went and looked up are neighbours. Some of them also sit in
the table above, and one, the reference monitor, is the move the small machine’s step
makes. I list them so you can see why I don’t think the toll is one of them under a new
name. Each is a claim inviting correction.

   • Linear logic (Girard 1987) treats an assumption as a resource that gets used up.
     It constrains what a program, or a proof, may consume. The toll constrains the

                                               56
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


      model’s step function instead. Same instinct, different layer.
   • Foundational proof-carrying code (Appel 2001) checks safety proofs against the
     smallest trusted base it can: a logic plus the machine’s semantics. Here no proof
     rides along with the program. The step rule writes the receipts as the run goes.
   • Session types (Honda 1993) constrain how programs talk to each other so the
     conversation can’t go off script. The toll is about what one computation has paid
     to establish. Different problem.
   • No Free Lunch (Wolpert and Macready 1997): averaged over every problem,
     whatever an optimiser gains on some problems it gives back on others. That’s
     an average over a whole problem space, and the edge is paid for elsewhere. The
     toll charges one step in one run, with no refund anywhere.
   • Kolmogorov complexity (Kolmogorov 1965): the description complexity of a
     string is the length of the shortest program that prints it, relative to a fixed
     description language. That’s a property of a finished string, with no steps and
     no moment of paying. The toll is a law about a step.
   • Cook and Levin (Cook 1971; Levin 1973): checking can be cheap while finding
     looks expensive, and whether finding is really harder is the open P-versus-NP
     question, a gap in how difficulty grows with size. The toll puts a fixed floor
     under the one step that commits, however easy or hard the finding was.
   • The thermodynamic cost of choosing (Rovelli 2024): settling a binary choice
     at temperature T gives off at least kT ln 2. That’s the closest thing to the toll
     itself I’ve found, because it charges a commitment. An object or an average
     isn’t what it prices. But it’s physics, indexed to a temperature, and its choice is
     unpredictable, a branching, and stable only for a while, where the toll prices a
     deterministic no-to-yes transition. Finiteness and permanence are the additional
     conditions that force its instruction to merge states. The toll charges the commit-
     ment in a model of computation, with no temperature in it. Closest neighbour.
     A different chair.
   • Persistent copies (Ouldridge and ten Wolde 2017; Ouldridge, Govern and ten
     Wolde 2017): making a copy that stays correlated with its original after the
     two come apart has a thermodynamic bill. The nearest physics I’ve found to
     “learning free, committing priced.” It’s heat for a correlation, in chemistry; the
     toll is a count in a model of computation.
   • Thermodynamics of finite automata (Ouldridge and Wolpert 2023): if the small-
     est automaton for a language has a letter that sends two states to one, recognising
     that language on a device that repeats one local step produces entropy, and if
     the smallest automaton only reshuffles, recognition can be free. That’s the chairs
     with a physical price on them, and one of their worked examples is the latch’s
     language turned inside out. It’s the closest neighbour of all to the road the toll is
     derived on; Section 4 says exactly what’s left over for me.


                                           57
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


   • CerCo, the Certified Complexity project of Amadio and coauthors, builds a
     verified C compiler that carries the object code’s execution cost back up to an-
     notations on the source. There the cost decorates the program and survives
     compilation. Here it lives in the model’s step rule.
   • Reference monitors and execution monitors (Anderson 1972; Schneider 2000;
     Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors 2015). A small piece every action passes
     through, enforcing a rule on every program. Schneider argued that a monitor
     watching a run can enforce only rules whose breaking shows up at a finite point,
     and “no certificate without an earlier passing check and commit” is one of those;
     the micro-policies check a tag rule at every instruction, proved correct. That’s
     the move the small machine’s step makes, so this one is the house itself. What’s
     added is the edition-bound check-then-commit with a paid, permanent record
     on top, and the derivation of why the payment can’t be zero. Kevin Hamlen,
     Greg Morrisett and Fred Schneider (2006) went on to sort which rules monitors,
     program rewriters and static checkers can each enforce, and they differ, which
     is one reason this book doesn’t claim that every enforcement mechanism is a
     Thiele machine underneath.
   • Trusted components in replicated services (Chun and coauthors 2007; Levin and
     coauthors 2009; Veronese and coauthors 2013; Decouchant and coauthors 2022;
     Clement, Junqueira, Kate and Rodrigues 2012): a small record inside each replica
     that a replica taken over still can’t make say two things, with a proof of exactly
     what that buys. The record is theirs. The toll isn’t in their picture.
   • Ghost state (Owicki and Gries 1976; Filliâtre, Gondelman and Paskevich 2014):
     variables added for a proof that can be erased without changing what the pro-
     gram computes. The flag and the counter are ghost in that sense. The small
     machine’s table of checked facts isn’t, because the step reads it and refuses on it,
     for every program.
   • Verifiable computation and proof-carrying data (Parno, Howell, Gentry and
     Raykova 2013; Chiesa and Tromer 2010): a short proof, checkable by a stranger,
     that a computation’s output is right. That establishes the claim for the stranger,
     and anyone with the inputs can make one, the copier included. The record here
     is about one machine’s own history. A proof like that is one way to carry the
     local record out of the box.
   • Commitments and entitlements (Brandom 1994): talk as score-keeping, tracking
     who is committed to what and who is entitled to it. Brandom’s entitlements can
     be defeated and can be passed on by testimony. Here entitlement is priced, step
     by step, and a copy carries it only as far as the copy is genuine. Same words,
     different machinery.
   • Correspondence assertions (Woo and Lam 1993; Gordon and Jeffrey 2003). In
     protocol verification, “this end event must be preceded by a begin event for
     the same thing” is a correspondence assertion, and a type system can prove


                                           58
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


      a protocol keeps it against any opponent. “No certificate without an earlier
      commit, and no commit without an earlier check of the same claim” has that
      shape. Theirs is proved about programs by typing. Mine is enforced by the step,
      which is the LCF comparison again, at the level of single instructions.
   • Monotonic parallel composition (Åman Pohjola and Parrow 2016) and persis-
     tence in the pi-calculus (Palamidessi, Saraswat, Valencia and Victor 2006). Åman
     Pohjola and Parrow separate models where a neighbouring process can never
     stop a step from models that can solve consensus, and test-and-set, an instruc-
     tion that writes a cell and reports what was there, is on the consensus side.
     Palamidessi and coauthors compare messages that are used up with messages
     that stay, and the end of their study is a reduction from Minsky machines. The
     small machine, put into Åman Pohjola and Parrow’s setting with threads pooled
     on one shared state, has a consensus process in their sense, so it lands on their
     non-monotonic side; that, and their theorem, are checked. The comparison with
     Palamidessi and coauthors’ persistence stays a comparison.
   • Constructor theory (Deutsch and Marletto 2015; Marletto 2016; Marletto, Vedral
     and coauthors 2022; Violaris and Marletto 2022): physics as which tasks a device
     that runs in a cycle can do, with irreversible meaning possible while the inverse
     isn’t. It’s the nearest physics I know to “committing costs” stated for a cycling
     device. It’s quantum and approximate, and the chairs are classical, finite and
     exact (Section 4).
   • Accountability and fault detection (Haeberlen and Kuznetsov 2009; Küsters,
     Truderung and Vogt 2010; Treitz and Künnemann 2026): when an outside party
     can tell who misbehaved. Their windows are this book’s windows, and the trust
     they leave over, an honest log or a trusted step, is left over here too (Section 7).
   • Transferability (Easwaran 2009): a deductive proof lets you learn from someone
     you don’t trust because you can check every step, and a probabilistic proof
     doesn’t. That’s the argument for carrying the object and re-running the check
     (Section 7).

And then the silly question that list raises, which I’m going to chase anyway: why
is an optimisation theorem named after lunch? Wolpert and Macready borrowed an
old saying, “there ain’t no such thing as a free lunch,” and the saying is older than
almost everyone who gets credit for it. American saloons in the 1800s put out a free
lunch for anyone who bought a drink, and the drink paid for the lunch. A Washington
newspaper was already saying in 1909 that somebody has to pay for a free lunch; a
