Labelled, though, isn’t the same as unplaced, and a hedge isn’t a position, so here’s
mine. Earman and Norton’s objection is a dilemma. Either an information-theoretic
exorcism of the demon assumes the second law, which they call the sound horn, and
then it adds nothing the second law didn’t already give; or it rests on a new principle
tying information to entropy, the profound horn, and nobody has given that principle
independent grounds. A named premise is the sound horn, on purpose. That’s where
Bennett ended up in 2003, and Norton’s “Too Good to Be True” (written in 2025,
published in 2026) says the careful literature almost always accepts that horn, and


                                           107
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


argues that whatever succeeds there is ordinary thermodynamics relabelled. I’ll take
that. Ordinary thermodynamics, relabelled onto a ledger, is all this section asks of
the physics. And on the counting I’m on Norton’s side outright. His 2018 paper
“Maxwell’s Demon Does Not Compute” exorcises the demon with Liouville’s theorem
and nothing else, no information and no computation: dynamics that keeps every
patch of states the same size can’t crowd a big set of states into a small one. The
counting core of this section, that a step losing nothing can’t carry a no-state into a
set that stays up, is that point in finite, discrete form. And if you want the best case
for the premise itself, the one I found is James Ladyman, Stuart Presnell, Anthony
Short and Berry Groisman (2007): from one of the standard statements of the second
law, the one named for Kelvin, they derive that a logically irreversible operation can’t
be carried out thermodynamically reversibly by any of their L-machines. That’s a
physical argument under their stated model of a machine. It deserves to be argued
with on those terms; it does not by itself establish the book’s whole-number ledger
charge.

One question a physicist asks before any of that, and it’s a good one: the laws under-
neath never merge anything. Classical mechanics carries each exact state forward to
exactly one next state and could carry it back again, and Liouville’s theorem adds that
a patch of states keeps its size as it moves; quantum mechanics is unitary, which is
one-to-one too. So when this section says a step merged two states, where did the
difference go? Out of the machine. The merge is in the machine’s own description,
the states its reading is about. The machine together with everything around it still
runs one-to-one, and the distinction the machine forgot survives. It gets pushed out
into the surroundings. Another memory could keep it as a readable record; when
uncertainty is removed into a thermal reservoir under Landauer’s conditions, heat is
the relevant transfer. The surroundings play the part of door one’s endless strip. That
door is always open for the universe as a whole and shut for the machine, because
the machine isn’t the universe and its memory fills. The heat claim needs more than
moving a distinction outside the machine: another memory could retain it. Under
the physical conditions used here, when resetting removes actual uncertainty into a
thermal reservoir, Landauer bounds the mean heat handed over. None of that heat has
to be heat wasted. Takahiro Sagawa’s 2014 analysis says that erasure can, in principle,
approach a process that produces no entropy overall: the reservoir’s entropy goes up
by what the machine’s goes down. A positive mean heat transfer can therefore be
unavoidable without being wasteful. A known input has no uncertainty to remove,
and this entropy-loss premise alone sets no positive heat floor for it.

4.6 How much: the price grows with the squeeze
The toll says “at least one mark.” That’s a floor for raising one flag. The room argument
says more if you let it. Say there are m people already inside and k more come in
through the door in one move. (That’s a different k from the one in Landauer’s kT;
when the two meet, below, Boltzmann’s constant gets a little B hung under it, k B , so


                                          108
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


you can tell it from a head count.) All m plus k of them end up in m chairs. That’s a
squeeze, by a factor of (m + k) over m, and if you accept a slightly stronger version
of the forgetting price, that each mark pays for at most one halving of the number
of distinguishable states, then the move costs at least the number of halvings in that
squeeze, which is the base-two logarithm of (m + k)/m.

Back to door three’s stamp, but give the reading four possible values this time: A, B,
C and YES. Write them on four cards. Choose one secretly, then cover its face with
an identical opaque YES label. Read only the new face: all four possibilities now give
YES. Before the move, identifying the original face took two yes-or-no questions (one
of the first two? then which one?); afterward there is only one possible face to report.
Two bits gone from that reading. Two halvings. Peeling the label off would recover
the old face, so this tabletop version models the loss from the reading; it does not
demonstrate physical erasure. So that move costs at least two marks, and two marks
is enough: a cost of exactly two satisfies the halving rule. The general statement is m
+ k at most 2 to the cost times m, and there is also a logarithm form that rounds both
logarithms up and is weaker for it (three states and one newcomer round to the same
two bits on both sides, and the rounded form says nothing). The halving premise, like
the one before it, is a definition used as an assumption. The units are halvings. To
turn a halving into joules of heat you multiply by k B T ln 2, and that multiplication is
physics; the counting stops before it.

That little k B deserves a short trip of its own, because it sits exactly where counting
turns into physics, and its name is a small history lesson. Ludwig Boltzmann’s grave
in Vienna has S = k log W carved on it (that k is the same k B , before anyone hung a B
under it): entropy is a constant times the logarithm of the number of ways the parts
could be arranged. The idea is his. The constant, and the equation written that way,
came from Max Planck, in his work on radiation around 1900. In his Nobel lecture in
1920 Planck said the constant “is frequently termed Boltzmann’s constant, although
to the best of my knowledge Boltzmann himself never introduced it,” and guessed
that Boltzmann never believed anyone could measure it accurately. I’d assumed
Planck named it after Boltzmann. His own words point the other way: it was other
people calling it that. Who first did, I couldn’t pin down; one recent paper points to
Paul Ehrenfest in 1906, the year Boltzmann died, and I haven’t checked that myself.
Ehrenfest was an Austrian physicist who had done his doctorate under Boltzmann in
Vienna. So the most famous constant in this corner of physics wears the name of a
man who didn’t write it down. Does that change the bill? No. But look at the job the
constant does in that equation. Take it away and what’s left is the logarithm of a count,
which is a number of halvings, which is what the squeeze bound hands you. The
constant is the exchange rate, and whether the world honours that rate for a merge is
the premise. No theorem here settles it.

Exactly, with one new piece of notation: for a list D of states, write | D | for how many
it has, and imgi ( D ) for the number of different states the move i sends them to.


                                          109
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Premise 4.4 (Halving price). Each mark pays for at most one halving: for every move
i and every list D of states with no repeats, | D | ≤ 2cost(i) · imgi ( D ). (It implies merge
pricing, since a merge sends two different states to one and so needs cost(i ) ≥ 1.)


There’s a plainer way to read that premise, and it’s worth having because it says what
the premise is about. Look at one landing spot of move i and count how many states
land there; call the biggest such count the move’s worst pile-up. The premise holds
exactly when every pile-up has at most 2cost(i) states in it, which is to say the cost is
at least the base-two logarithm of the worst pile-up. One direction: take D to be one
whole pile, which lands on a single spot, and the premise says the pile has at most
2cost(i) members. The other: any list D splits by where its members land, each part fits
inside one pile, so | D | is at most the number of landing spots times the worst pile-up,
which is the premise. So the halving price asks a move to pay for the worst it could
ever do, whichever state it’s actually handed. That’s worst case on purpose, and it
has a home in physics. In the branch of thermodynamics that prices a single run that
has to succeed every time, with no averaging over many runs, Philippe Faist, Frédéric
Dupuis, Jonathan Oppenheim and Renato Renner derived in 2015, in that framework,
what they give as the least work any logical process needs, and when every input
might occur and no error is allowed, their bound comes to k B T ln 2 times exactly that
logarithm. Take an AND gate as the example: three inputs land on 0, so it needs at
least log2 3, about 1.6, halvings’ worth of work (two marks, in whole numbers). The
premise asks for that bound of a device that has to work whatever it’s handed, and it
counts it in marks. Joules don’t come into it.


Theorem 4.6 (The squeeze bound). On a finite machine with a permanent reading and a
cost satisfying the halving price, let m be the number of states that read yes, and let a move i
turn k different no-states to yes. Three numbers, then: m counts every yes-state of the machine,
reachable or not; k counts a list of distinct no-states that the move turns to yes, and the move
may turn others too; and cost(i ) is the price the cost assigns to the move. Then

                                                                               m+k
         m + k ≤ 2cost(i) · m,       and, when m ≥ 1,        cost(i ) ≥ log2       .
                                                                                m
The counting inequality holds as stated. When m ≥ 1, it is equivalent to the displayed
logarithmic lower bound.

Proof. Put the m yes-states and the k newcomers in one list; it has m + k different
members. By permanence every yes-state lands on a yes-state, and by hypothesis
every newcomer does too, so all m + k land among the m yes-states: imgi ≤ m. The
halving price gives m + k ≤ 2cost(i) · imgi ≤ 2cost(i) · m.

The four card readings are the case m = 1, k = 3, where the bound is reached. With
k = 1 the bound says cost(i ) ≥ 1, which is the toll again. The counting argument also



                                              110
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


shows that at least k states collapse, without any price premise.

The bound is reached for every m ≥ 1 and every cost c. Whenever m + k ≤ 2c m, a
finite machine with a permanent reading and the halving price has m yes-states and
a move of cost exactly c that turns a listed k distinct no-states to yes. The move turns
every other no-state of that machine to yes as well, (2c − 1)m of them in all. No cost
meeting the halving price on that machine charges the move less than c. So the least
whole-number cost that meets the bound is exactly ⌈log2 mm+k ⌉.

Four more facts about the halving price, and the last one is a limit. First, the plainer
reading above is a theorem on a finite machine: the halving price holds exactly when
no move has a landing spot with more than 2cost(i) states landing on it. Second, for
the eight-state machine described later in this section that’s a theorem about its own
price list: no move has a larger pile-up than 2cost , so the halving price holds, and the
toll follows from it; and the price list is the least that meets the halving price, since
any price list that does charges every move at least what this one charges. Third, the
squeeze bound is met with equality there: its stamp turns on the four states whose flag
is down, beside the four whose flag is already up, and 4 + 4 = 21 · 4. Fourth, and this
is the limit, the small machine of Part IV as a whole does not meet the halving price,
whatever procedure you use to decide whether two of its states are equal, because one
of its free moves, the one that takes one off a number the machine holds, lands two
different states of the whole machine on the same state (the pair is in Theorem 16.42).
That the halving premise fails there is a theorem. What does hold there is the same
premise asked of the record layer alone, and it gives the toll on that machine too
(Theorem 4.15, below).

4.7 The same bill, written in bits, and when it’s zero
There’s one more way to say all this, and I include it because it’s the way physicists
say it and because it hands you the one case where the bill is exactly zero, which I find
more instructive than any case where it isn’t.

Claude Shannon, in 1948, gave a number to “how much you don’t know”: if something
could be in any of n states and you have no idea which, your uncertainty is log base
two of n bits, and that’s the most it can be for n states. If you push your uncertainty
through a step that forgets nothing, it stays the same; through a step that merges
two states you might have been in, it drops. Now run the room. Before the move,
you might be in any of the m + k states in play. After it, you’re in one of m. So
your uncertainty afterward is at most log2 of m, whatever you believed before. If you
started with no idea at all, every one of the m + k states equally likely, your uncertainty
was exactly log2 of (m + k), and the move removed at least log2 of (m + k)/m bits: the
same number as the halving count, now in Shannon’s units. Landauer’s principle, in
the form physicists write it, then says a step that removes that many bits from the state
gives off at least k B T ln 2 of heat per bit. Put the two together and the flip gives off
heat, and the exact statements below say how much and under which side conditions,


                                           111
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


one of which (the temperature has to be taken as zero or above) is easy to skip and
shouldn’t be.

Why does Shannon’s number share a name with the physicists’ entropy at all? There’s
a story about it. Shannon wanted to call it uncertainty, and the mathematician John von
Neumann told him to call it entropy instead, for two reasons: the same formula already
lived in statistical mechanics under that name, and nobody really knows what entropy
is, so in an argument he’d always have the upper hand. It’s a great story. It comes
from Myron Tribus, who spent years tying information theory to thermodynamics,
who said Shannon told it to him in 1961, and who printed it, with Edward McIrvine, in
Scientific American in 1971. Then in 1982 an interviewer, Robert Price, asked Shannon
about it, and Shannon said he didn’t think von Neumann had told him any such thing.
So it’s a legend with one witness, and the person the witness quoted doesn’t remember
saying it. What doesn’t hang on the story: the two formulas really do have the same
shape, and it still takes Landauer’s premise, a named assumption, to turn a count of
bits into heat.

Exactly, with the notation built first. A spread (probabilists say distribution) is a way
of giving each state a chance p( x ) ≥ 0, with the chances adding to 1. Its Shannon
entropy, in bits, is
                          H ( p) = − ∑ p( x ) log2 p( x ),
                                         x: p( x )>0

where the big sigma means “add up, over every state x with a chance above zero,”
and each term is a state’s chance times the bits it would take to single that state out.
That comes to log2 n when n states share the chance evenly and less when the chance
is lopsided. Pushing a spread through a move i gives the spread of where you land:
q(y) = ∑ x: step(x,i)=y p( x ). The bits the move removes are H ( p) − H (q).

Try four equally likely cards, A, B, C and D. Send A and B to a box marked X, C to
Y and D to Z. Beforehand each card has chance 1/4, so the four terms in the sum are
each 1/2: two bits. Afterward the box chances are 1/2, 1/4, 1/4, and the three terms
are each 1/2: one and a half bits. Half a bit was lost on average. You can see where:
half the time the box is X and leaves one binary question unanswered—A or B? The
other half of the time Y or Z tells you the starting card exactly. An actual draw never
loses half a card; the half belongs to the average uncertainty over repeated draws.

Start with the half of the claim that costs nothing, Bennett’s half. A move that forgets
nothing sends each state somewhere different, so the chances just get carried to new
addresses, one for one. Nothing piles up and nothing spreads out. The uncertainty is
the same number before and after.


Theorem 4.7 (A move that forgets nothing removes no bits). Let the states be finite,
listed once each, and let f send states to states with f ( a) = f (b) only when a = b. Then for
every assignment of chances p, the pushed spread q has H (q) = H ( p).


                                              112
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


Proof. An injective map on a finite list of distinct states is a reshuffle of that list: every
state is hit exactly once. So q( f ( x )) = p( x ) for every x, and the sum defining H (q) is
the sum defining H ( p) with its terms in a different order.

That’s why a price on removed bits can leave every reversible move free, which is the
shape the toll needs: the bill lands only where something was forgotten.


Theorem 4.8 (Entropy after a permanent flip). On a finite machine with a permanent
reading, let m be the number of states that read yes, and let a move i turn k ≥ 1 different
no-states yes. For any spread p whose chance lies on those m + k states, the spread after the
move has H (q) ≤ log2 m. For the even spread on the m + k states, the move removes at least
log2 mm+k bits.

Proof. After the move, all the chance sits on the m yes-states (permanence for the old
ones, the hypothesis for the new). There is at least one yes-state: the image of a state
that flips. Thus m ≥ 1. Write q1 , . . . , qr for the positive output probabilities, where
r ≤ m and their sum is 1.

For y > 0, ln y ≤ y − 1: the derivative of y − 1 − ln y is 1 − 1/y, so its minimum is 0 at
y = 1. Apply this with y = 1/(mq j ), multiply by q j , and add:

                             r               r
                 − ln m − ∑ q j ln q j ≤ ∑ (1/m − q j ) = r/m − 1 ≤ 0.
                            j =1            j =1


Dividing by ln 2 > 0 gives H (q) ≤ log2 m. The even input spread has m + k probabili-
ties each 1/(m + k ), hence H ( p) = log2 (m + k ). Subtracting the output bound gives
the claimed loss log2 ((m + k)/m).


Premise 4.5 (Landauer’s principle, as a premise). For the chosen physical memory
and its input distribution, assume that a step lowering its logical-state entropy by ∆H
bits transfers mean heat Q ≥ k B T ln 2 · ∆H to a bath at temperature T, where k B is
Boltzmann’s constant. Here Q is an average over that preparation, not a bound on
each individual trial. Applying this premise requires a physical model in which the
logical entropy loss has this thermodynamic meaning; a bare state-transition table
does not supply one.


Corollary 4.9 (Heat floor of a permanent flip). Under Premise 4.5, with k B T ≥ 0, the
flip of Theorem 4.8 from the even spread gives off at least k B T ln mm+k ; with k B T > 0 that is
strictly positive.

Proof. Theorem 4.8 gives an entropy loss of at least log2 ((m + k )/m) bits. Multiply
by the nonnegative factor k B T ln 2 and use Premise 4.5. The identity ln 2 log2 x = ln x




                                                 113
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


gives the displayed floor. Here m > 0 and k > 0, so (m + k )/m > 1 and its logarithm
is positive; if k B T > 0, the heat floor is strictly positive too.

How big is that? Take the case where the squeeze is two, one state flipping in beside
one that was already yes, so m = k = 1 and the floor is k B T ln 2. At room temperature,
about 300 kelvin, that’s roughly three zeptojoules: three thousandths of a billionth of
a billionth of a joule. And that’s the biggest bill a one-state flip gets from this corollary.
With k = 1 the floor is k B T ln mm+1 , and it shrinks as more states already read yes: with
a thousand of them it’s about a thousandth of k B T, some seven hundred times less
than the case of two. So, for an even spread over the states in play, one mark is not
one halving. It’s one halving exactly when the squeeze is two; for any thinner squeeze
and an even spread, the physics asks for less than a halving, and the toll still charges a
whole mark, because marks come in whole numbers (that’s the rounding the entropy
road to the toll leans on, a little further down). Read in the worst case over what the
machine might be holding, the way the halving price reads a move, it’s at least a full
bit every time. A permanent flip merges two states (Theorem 4.1); put half the chance
on each, and the move removes a full bit, whatever m is. So the gap between the mark
and the bits is a fact about the even spread. In the worst case the flip removes at least
the full bit the mark pays for. Whatever the size, it’s a bill only if you grant the premise;
nothing on this page measured anything. And even granted, it’s a bill nobody will
ever see on a meter: real logic gates spend many thousands of times more than this
on every switch, even the frugal ones. One 2023 tally of the numbers puts switching a
single CMOS gate at a hundred attojoules at the low end, over thirty thousand times
this. The point of the number isn’t that certifying is expensive. It’s that, on the premise,
it isn’t zero.

A related logarithm appears in a different physical question. Yûto Murashita, Ken
Funo and Masahito Ueda (2014) study processes whose reverse histories can include
ones with no forward counterpart. They call this absolute irreversibility. If those reverse
histories have total probability λ, their bound on mean entropy production contains
− ln(1 − λ). In their free-expansion example, gas initially confined to a fraction l of a
box gives ln(1/l ).

Setting l = m/(m + k ) gives the same logarithm as the squeeze bound. That numerical
match does not identify two physical processes. Our arrows specify neither a thermo-
dynamic reverse experiment nor its path probabilities, so they do not determine λ. We
cannot infer absolute irreversibility, its absence, or a heat equality from the state count
alone. Gonzalo Manzano, Gülce Kardeş, Édgar Roldán and David Wolpert (2024)
study such trajectory-level questions for computations with one-way transitions and
random stopping times. Their physical premises are additional to the counting done
here.

The even spread is the easy case, and you might worry the heat depends on picking it.
It doesn’t. Any spread that gives a real chance to every yes-state and to the state that


                                             114
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


flips will do.


Corollary 4.10 (Positive heat for any full spread). On a finite machine with a permanent
reading, let move i turn a no-state s yes. Take any spread p that gives positive chance to s and
to every yes-state. Under Premise 4.5 with k B T > 0, the heat the move gives off is strictly
positive.

Proof. After the move, s and the yes-states all land among the yes-states, and there is
one more of them than there are yes-states, so two distinct states with positive chance
land on the same state. That merge removes a positive number of bits (Theorem 4.14
below), and a positive temperature times a positive number of bits is positive heat.

There’s a third road to the toll here too, and it’s the same shape as the merge road,
with bits in place of marks for forgetting.


Definition 4.6 (Entropy-priced). On a finite machine, a cost is entropy-priced when, for
every move i and every spread p, the cost of i is at least the bits the move removes:
cost(i ) ≥ H ( p) − H (q), where q is p pushed through i.


Theorem 4.11 (The toll from entropy pricing). On a finite machine with a permanent
reading and an entropy-priced cost, every move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at
least one. So the machine with that cost is a certification system (Definition 3.1), and every
run from a no-state to a yes-state costs at least one.

Proof. Let move i turn s yes, and let m be the number of yes-states; m ≥ 1, since
step(s, i ) is one. Take the even spread on the m yes-states and s. By Theorem 4.8
with k = 1, the move removes at least log2 mm+1 > 0 bits, so the cost of i is a whole
number above a positive number, which makes it at least one. The run-level floor is
the universal floor (Observation 3.1) applied to that system.

There are three roads to the toll, with two different strengths. Entropy pricing and
the halving price are equivalent: the most bits a deterministic move can remove is the
base-two logarithm of its largest pile of starts sharing a destination. Merge pricing asks
only for at least one mark whenever any pair collides. It is the two-state restriction of
the stronger conditions.

Try eight equally likely cards all sent to one box. The loss is three bits. A charge of one
meets merge pricing but fails entropy pricing and the halving price, which require at
least three. All three conditions give the permanent-record toll; only the stronger two
give the full squeeze bound.


Theorem 4.12 (Entropy pricing, halving, and pairwise merge pricing). Take a finite



                                              115
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


machine whose states can be decided equal or different, and a move i. (1) If no state has more
than K ≥ 1 states landing on it under i, every spread loses at most log2 K bits through i;
and if some state has exactly K states landing on it, the even spread on those K loses exactly
log2 K bits. (2) A cost is entropy-priced (Definition 4.6) exactly when it satisfies the halving
price (Premise 4.4). (3) A cost satisfies merge pricing (Premise 4.2) exactly when it satisfies
the halving price for every list of at most two different states, and exactly when it satisfies
entropy pricing for every spread whose chance sits on at most two states. The first of those two
equivalences uses no finiteness, only the test for equal states.

Proof. (1) Split the bits removed into one term per state, as Theorem 4.14 below does,
and bound each term with ln y ≤ y − 1 at y = q(step( x, i ))/(K p( x )). Adding up, the
total is at most log2 K plus a multiple of K1 ∑ x q(step( x, i )) − 1, and that sum counts
each state’s chance once for every state landing beside it, at most K times, so the extra
part is at most zero. For the even spread on a pile of K, the chance starts on K states,
log2 K bits, and ends on one, which is zero bits. (2) If the cost is entropy-priced, take
the even spread on any pile: by (1) the cost is at least log2 of its size, and a whole
number c at least log2 n has n ≤ 2c . That every pile is at most 2c is the halving price
(the plainer reading above). The other way, (1) with K = 2c says no spread loses
more than c bits. (3) Two different states that land together have one image, so the
halving price for that pair reads 2 ≤ 2cost(i) , which is cost(i ) ≥ 1; a pair that doesn’t
land together, or a single state, asks nothing. A spread on two states loses at most one
bit, and none unless they land together; the even spread on two that do loses exactly
one.

Thus merge pricing is weaker than full entropy pricing, though both force the one-
mark toll under the permanence and finiteness premises. The mathematical prices
are rules on instructions. A physical interpretation additionally needs Landauer’s
premise for the actual distribution and an explicit conversion from bits or marks to
thermal quantities.

Now the zero. Toss a fair coin under a cup without looking at how it lands. Rule: set it
heads up. You might have had tails; now you have heads; one bit of what you didn’t
know is gone, and that’s the bit the principle charges for. Now lift the cup, see heads,
put the cup back, and apply the rule again. Nothing you didn’t know changed. No bit
was lost. And the principle, applied to a state you already knew, demands nothing:
the premise holds exactly when the heat is zero or more, which is to say it sets no
positive floor. The entropy-loss bound depends on the preparation and on what the
move does to it. Here “known” means a preparation concentrated on one logical state,
or a conditional ensemble whose side information is explicitly included in the account.
Merely telling a spectator which way the coin landed does not change an unchanged
device’s heat. This is the generalized form of Landauer’s principle, worked out by
Owen Maroney in 2009, in a paper he wrote at the Perimeter Institute in Canada (he
has been a philosopher of physics at Oxford since 2011), and by Sagawa in 2014, and


                                              116
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Landauer himself had the seed of it in 1961: for a row of bits all already ONE, he
wrote, there’s no need to carry out any operation, so no entropy changes and no heat
is given off, and resetting a row all ZERO to ONE involves no entropy change either,
because neither row carries any information.


Theorem 4.13 (A known state gets no heat floor from the premise). On a finite machine,
if the spread puts all its chance on one state s, then any move removes zero bits, and Premise 4.5
for that move holds exactly when Q ≥ 0.

Proof. A spread on one state has entropy 0, and so does its image, which is again on
one state. So ∆H = 0 and the premise reads Q ≥ 0.

Be careful with that one, because it’s easy to overread. “The premise sets no heat floor
for a known state” does not mean a stamping machine run on a known-blank sheet
gives off no heat. A device can dissipate on a known input too: heat can go into the
room even when no uncertainty is removed from the data. Its dissipation depends on
its physical implementation and control protocol. What the theorem says is only that
the premise sets no floor there. The floor comes from what you didn’t know. That’s a
sentence about the bill. The device is a separate matter. And notice that the toll still
charges the known-state stamp one mark, because the toll is a rule about the move,
and the move doesn’t know what the observer knows. That’s the worst-case gap from
door three showing up again, and it’s the price of having a rule a machine can follow
without asking who’s watching.

The physics of all this has a standard review, the physicists Juan Parrondo, Jordan
Horowitz and Takahiro Sagawa’s “Thermodynamics of information” (2015), which
sets Landauer’s bound, its generalized form and the costs of measurement and feed-
back side by side. And the gap between a device and the spread it runs on has a
physicist’s number on it. Artemy Kolchinsky and David Wolpert (2017) showed that a
fixed process built to dissipate as little as possible for one spread over its states pays
extra when it runs on another, and the extra is how much closer the process brings the
two spreads, measured in relative entropy; the extra was later named mismatch cost.
That’s the worst-case gap again, priced for an actual spread, where the toll prices the
move.

There’s a second piece of fine print on that theorem, and it’s about who works the con-
trols. The entropy-loss bound supplies no positive floor for a known input. Whether
a device can approach that floor also depends on its controls: lower this barrier, tilt
that well, raise the barrier again. Those operations have a timing and a physical
implementation. The entropy calculation alone does not price either.

Paul Riechers, Alexander Boyd, Gregory Wimsatt and James Crutchfield (2020) anal-
yse metastable memories under time-symmetric control: the prescribed control is the
same played forwards or backwards, with the relevant time-reversal conventions. A


                                               117
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


symmetric clock pulse can meet that restriction; an arbitrary clocked pulse need not.
For memory states unchanged by time reversal, their low-error result distinguishes
inputs m for which applying the desired logical map C twice fails to return to m. They
call those transitions nonreciprocal. With equal local-equilibrium free energies, the
leading minimum-work term as the error allowance ε tends to zero is proportional to
                                                           
                            k B T ln(1/ε) Pr C (C (m)) ̸= m .

The probability is over the initial memory states. This is a low-error scaling with
physical premises, not an exact finite-error heat charge on every execution.

A permanent flip from no to yes is nonreciprocal at that no-state: a second application
cannot return it to no. A known input at that state can therefore face the extra work cost
in their restricted control setting, even though its initial logical entropy is zero. Their
class also includes a three-state cycle, which merges nothing. The distinction is about
the permitted controls as well as the logical map. It neither changes Theorem 4.13’s
entropy calculation nor identifies the book’s abstract merge price with a universal
physical bill.

A deterministic run from a known start has a known state at every step. For such a
run, the adopted entropy-loss premise reduces to Q ≥ 0: it supplies no positive heat
lower bound. That does not establish that a particular device attains zero heat. The
chairs guarantee a collision among the already-yes states together with the entering
no-state. They do not guarantee that the entering state takes part in the collision
(take four states s, a, b, c, with only s reading no, and a move s 7→ a, a 7→ b, b 7→ b,
c 7→ c). For an input distribution supported only on no-states, this counting argument
alone therefore forces no positive entropy loss. Whether other states in that support
merge depends on the move. The operation-level ledger toll still follows under merge
pricing.

So here’s what this section actually earns. A finite machine’s permanent flag-raising
instruction has two allowed starting states that land on one state. Prepare those two
with equal chances: that instruction removes one bit, and under the adopted physical
premise its mean heat is at least k B T ln 2. That is a worst-case preparation, not a
positive charge on every execution. A known start gives no positive entropy-loss
floor; whether a device can attain zero heat also depends on its dynamics and controls.
The ledger charges the merging instruction regardless of the preparation because
merge pricing explicitly requires that. The counting proves a collision, the preparation
determines the uncertainty removed, and the physical premises connect that removal
to heat.

Here’s the general case, and it’s the one that shows you where the bits go. Split the
bill state by state. Each state x you might be in carries its chance p( x ) along to where
it lands, step( x, i ), and finds whatever other chance landed there too. If nobody else
landed there, its term is zero. If others did, its term is the difference between how


                                           118
The Thiele Machine                                                                            Devon Thiele


crowded its landing spot is and how much of the crowd it brought.


Theorem 4.14 (The bits removed, one term per state). On a finite machine, for any move
i and any chances p( x ) ≥ 0, with q the pushed spread,

                                     ∑
                                                                                         
              H ( p) − H (q) =                  p( x ) log2 q(step( x, i )) − log2 p( x ) .
                                  x: p( x )>0


Every term is zero or more, so a move never adds bits. If two different states x ̸= x ′ , both with
positive chance, land on the same state, the sum is strictly positive.

Proof. Group the sum for H (q) by where things land: the chance q(y) at a landing spot
is the sum of the p( x ) that land there, so H (q) = − ∑ x: p(x)>0 p( x ) log2 q(step( x, i )).
Subtract from H ( p) term by term. Each term is non-negative because the landing spot
holds at least what x brought, q(step( x, i )) ≥ p( x ), and the logarithm keeps order. If
x and x ′ share a landing spot, that spot holds at least p( x ) + p( x ′ ) > p( x ), so the term
for x is strictly positive.

4.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not
Let me total it: what have you earned the right to conclude, and what is still a door?

You’ve earned this: on any machine with finitely many states, a move that raises a
flag either forgets something or takes a flag down somewhere else. Pure counting, no
physics, no premise beyond finiteness, and the half of it where nothing comes down
is the four chairs. You’ve earned this: on a finite machine, if a flag, once up, stays up,
then raising it has a collision somewhere. If it raises k distinct no-states, the yes-states
together with those newcomers have at least k fewer distinct outputs than inputs. This
does not say that each newcomer shares its destination. Counting again. And you’ve
earned this: if forgetting is charged for, the toll follows, and if forgetting is charged per
halving, the size of the toll follows too; each of those derivations hands back a system
with the five parts and the toll, so Section 3’s floor applies to it as it stands. That’s the
rule from Section 3, now derived, with every premise named, for any finite machine
with a flag that stays up. In that section I only declared it.

Here’s what you haven’t earned. I’m listing it so you don’t assume it. You haven’t
earned that forgetting costs anything in the world; that’s Landauer, it’s measured for
beads and argued over for the general case, and in this book it’s an assumption with
a name. And even granting it, Landauer’s entropy-loss bound demands no positive
heat from a run whose state is known (the lifted cup), so what the physics forces is
a floor on a device that has to work whatever it’s holding. Any one run can come in
under it. You haven’t earned that any machine you’d actually want to build is of this
kind, either, and there are two easy ways to miss. A machine that keeps its running
total inside its own state, as a number with no ceiling, has infinitely many states, so
the finite premise fails for it as a whole. And you can’t patch that by giving the total a


                                                    119
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


ceiling. A total that only climbs, held in finite memory, eventually either stops at its
top, and then two different histories leave the same top value, which is a merge, or
rolls back over to zero, and then it doesn’t only climb. So any running total a finite
machine keeps for itself has a horizon: it’s honest up to its width and no further. And
a machine whose price list charges the step that raises the flag, but lets some other
step merge two states for nothing, raises the flag honestly and still doesn’t charge
for forgetting in general, so the merge-pricing premise fails for it. Either one puts a
machine outside these theorems as stated, though a finite piece of it can still sit inside.
The machine I build later (Section 16) misses in both ways. It keeps counters with
no ceiling, so it’s infinite outright, and some of its ordinary steps, counting a counter
down among them, can land two different states on one for free. So the chairs, as
stated, don’t reach it: they force the toll only on finite machines that price every merge,
and it isn’t one. It doesn’t need the chairs, though, and that comes after the eight-state
piece below.

A finite piece can still sit inside, and here’s the smallest one I could build where every
premise is a theorem. None of them is left as a hypothesis. Four slots times a flag, eight
states. Three moves: stamp (set the flag, go to the next slot, cost one), jump to slot a
(cost two), next slot (cost zero). It’s finite and permanent; the next-slot move forgets
nothing; the stamp and the jump merge; merges are priced, and priced per halving.
So this section’s two conclusions hold on it outright. The counting lemma underneath,
that a duplicate-free list with at most K preimages per image has at most K times as
many members as images, is proved generically. Merge pricing alone would take
any price of at least one for the jump. The jump’s price of two is what the halving
price asks, since the jump squeezes four states into one. One more fact about it, also
checked: each move’s price is exactly the number of halvings in its largest squeeze.
For a move that costs c, no state is landed on by more than 2c states, and some state is
landed on by exactly that many (stamp squeezes at most two states into one, jump to
a slot squeezes four, and next-slot squeezes nothing).

The machine Part IV builds runs this eight-state machine. Seen through a window that
shows only a line number, read modulo four as the slot, and a flag, a short program of
that machine, once a two-instruction setup has run, does what the eight-state machine
does, one move at a time, and pays exactly what the eight-state machine charges
(Section 16.17 has the construction and the exact statements). The machine as a whole
is still not merge-priced: some of its free steps merge states, so the finite piece is a
piece. The toll on the whole machine comes another way.

Finiteness did one job in the chairs. It forced the step that raises a permanent flag to
merge two states. On the machine of Part IV nothing has to force that, because the
merge is in plain view. Its CERTIFY takes a state with the flag down and the same
state with the flag up to one place, since a flag that’s already up just stays up. Its
COMMIT overwrites the channel, so two states that differ only in what the channel
names land on one state. Both are checked. So any price list that charges every merge


                                           120
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


of that machine’s own step charges the flag-raising step, and finiteness never comes
into it.

That leaves the other miss, the free merges. Clause (c) of Thiele-complete, in Part
IV, asks for base moves at zero, and a base move merges (DEC, counting a counter
down, lands two states on one), so full merge pricing and clause (c) can’t both hold
on that machine. They don’t have to. Split a state into its base part, which is what
a two-counter machine would show (the line number and the two counters), and its
record part, which is everything else: the versions, the table of facts, the channel, the
trap latch, the ledger and the flag. Then price only the merges the record layer makes.


Premise 4.7 (Record-layer merge pricing). A move that sends two different states with
the same base part to one state costs at least one.


The merges among base parts are the ordinary computer’s business, the ones any
two-counter machine makes, and whatever heat they cost is the ordinary computer’s
heat. Merge pricing implies this premise, so it asks less, and on the record distinctions
it is still an assumed operation-level price; identifying it with heat needs a physical
model.


Theorem 4.15 (The toll on the machine I built). For the small machine of Section 16, with
no finiteness premise: (1) CERTIFY merges, and so does COMMIT of every claim, and each
joins two different states with the same line and counters. (2) Every cost that satisfies merge
pricing for that machine’s step charges CERTIFY and every COMMIT at least one, and obeys
the toll, so the machine with that cost is a certification system. (3) No INC, DEC or HALT
sends two different states with the same line and counters to one state. So the machine’s own
prices, base moves at zero and each record move at one, satisfy Premise 4.7, and merge pricing
fails for them. (4) Every cost that satisfies Premise 4.7 obeys the toll, so the machine with that
cost is a certification system.

Proof. (1) Take a state whose channel holds a commitment, once with the flag down
and once with it up. CERTIFY raises the first, leaves the second up, moves both on a
line and charges both one, so they land together. For COMMIT, take a table holding
the claim about the current version, once with an empty channel and once with the
channel already naming that claim; COMMIT writes the same name in both. (2) Only
CERTIFY raises the flag, and it merges. (3) A base move keeps the table, the channel
and the trap latch, adds nothing to the ledger and leaves the flag alone, and when it
writes a counter it moves that counter’s version up by one; so two states that agree
on line and counters and land together agree on everything. A trapped state keeps
everything but its ledger, and a live one stays live, so a trapped state and a live one
never land together. Merge pricing fails because of the free DEC of Theorem 16.42,
whose two states differ in a counter. (4) Only CERTIFY raises the flag, and by (1) its



                                               121
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


merge is a record-layer merge.

So this section reaches the machine I built. On that machine the toll follows from
record-layer merge pricing, and the machine’s own price list, clause (c) included,
satisfies that premise. This is a result about its ledger, not a heat bound. There’s
a second way out, which I note and didn’t take. Morita’s reversible two-counter
machine, from the history earlier in this chapter, runs every step backwards and is still
universal: with its input encoded, it computes anything a Turing machine can. Put
the record layer on a base like that and every base move is one-to-one, and full merge
pricing permits those base moves to cost zero. Choosing that schedule would meet
clause (c); the lower-bound premise alone does not require zero charges. I haven’t
built that machine or checked it.

And you haven’t earned anything about what the flag means. Four chairs don’t know
what they’re certifying. The bill is for raising a flag that stays up. Whether raising
that flag ever amounts to standing behind a structural fact, the “vouching” I keep
promising and keep not delivering, is a question for the machine of Part IV, and here
it has moved exactly this far: on a finite machine that charges for every merge, if that
flag stays up, it was paid for.

One last thing, because it should nag at you. The toll is forced by the premises, but the
premises were chosen, and “permanent” in particular was chosen by me. Why should
a certificate stay up? Why not let it come down, pay nothing, and be honest about it?
That’s a fair question, and merge or revoke is the start of an answer (the three-card
machine only showed that the converse of Corollary 4.5 fails): on a finite machine
that charges for every merge, a flag that goes up for free is a flag the same move takes
back somewhere, and a record that can be silently taken back is the thing the bulla
and the hash chain and the write-once disk were all built against. “Permanent” here is
exactly that: the flag can’t be lowered. The toy in Section 3 didn’t have it; the lineage
in Section 3 was built around it; I chose it. Whether that was the right job to pick out
of the five is something you can argue with me about, and I’d want you to.

And “permanent” is an idealization, which I should say before a physicist does. No
physical record lasts forever. A bit held behind an energy barrier leaks over it at some
rate, however slow, and a closed finite system comes back around, which is Zermelo’s
point from the chairs. The theorems in this section need permanence on every state,
including states the machine never visits, forever. Weaken that to “the flag stays up on
the states that actually turn up, for as long as anyone cares,” and merge-or-revoke tells
you what goes wrong: the move could take the flag down somewhere nobody ever
looks, and then it isn’t forced to merge at all. A version of the toll stated in chances
and time spans would be a different theorem, and I don’t have it.

One piece of it I can hand you. Take one move and repeat it from one start, forever. On
a finite machine the states that run passes through are finitely many, so it falls into a



                                          122
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


loop. If the move forgot nothing on those states, it would be a reshuffle of them, and a
reshuffle brings every one of them back around, the start included, where the flag was
down. So if the flag goes up along that run and stays up from some point on, the move
merges two states the run itself visits. The shared chair is one the machine actually sits
in. And it doesn’t touch the known-state point above: a merge among states the run
visits still receives no positive lower bound from the entropy-loss premise when its
state is known. The argument holds for any map iterated from a start whose flag is
down, with the flag up at every step from some point on; no permanence premise is
used.

Runs that mix different moves split two ways, and the answer is short enough to give
here. If the moves are picked from outside, in any order at all, the answer is no. Take
two states, one reading no and one reading yes. Move a swaps them; move b does
nothing. Run a once and then b forever: the flag goes up at the first step and stays
up for good, and neither move merges anything anywhere. The swap would take
the flag down from the yes-state if it ever ran there; on this run it never does, and
that’s exactly the weakened permanence this paragraph is about. But if the machine
is closed, picking its next move from its own state, the run is the orbit of one map, the
step with whatever move the state picks, and the single-move argument applies to
that map as it stands. Now say the moves come in a pattern that eventually repeats,
one word w of moves over and over. Suppose the flag is down at some step after the
repeating starts, and goes up and stays up after that. Count the repetitions from a
step where the flag was down (start w at that letter if you have to) and run the same
argument on the composite of w’s moves, at the states where such a repetition begins.
It merges two of those states, both visited; follow the two through the letters of w,
and the first letter where their paths meet merges two states the run visits at that
letter’s place in the pattern. So: moves picked from outside, no; a closed machine or a
repeating program, yes.

There is also a limited statement about how long a noisy record lasts, using a different
quantity: total entropy production during relaxation. Take a device with no outside
hand: a random process hopping among finitely many states at rates that never change,
with a reverse for every hop and local detailed balance, able to get from any state to
any other. Require at least one up-state and one down-state. Left to run, it settles
into a long-run spread π. Measure each up or down stretch from its entrance, with
entrances sampled in the stationary process, and call the mean lengths Tup and Tdown .
Start the device in a known no-state s. The total entropy it produces over relaxation is
at least ln(1 + Tup /Tdown ), in units of k B .

The argument is three lines once the pieces have names. With fixed rates, total entropy
production is at least the drop in relative entropy to π; that follows from Massimiliano
Esposito and Christian Van den Broeck’s split of entropy production (2010). A known
start s has relative entropy − ln π (s), at least − ln π (no), and the relative entropy runs
down to zero as the device settles. The stationary chances of up and down have the


                                            123
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


ratio of their mean stretch lengths, because crossings up and down balance. Hence
− ln π (no) = ln(1 + Tup /Tdown ).

For a large up-to-down ratio, doubling that ratio raises this lower bound by about
k B ln 2. Making both stretches longer by the same factor leaves it unchanged. Across
a family of devices whose ratio tends to infinity, the bound diverges; no single finite
irreducible device in this class keeps its flag up forever. This is a relaxation bound, not
a heat charge on each flip. It uses neither a thermodynamic reverse-path construction
nor time-symmetric control, so it does not identify the quantities in those other results.
It also does not close the known-input escape from the deterministic entropy-loss
bound: this noisy evolution and its total entropy production are a different question.
Hold that argument to what it says. The entropy is added up from the moment the
device sits in the known no-state s until it has settled, over one whole relaxation.
The starting spread is all on s, and π is the device’s long-run spread. The inequality
rests on fixed rates, finitely many states, every state reachable from every other, a
reverse for every hop, and local detailed balance to relate the entropy balance to heat
exchanged with the reservoirs. Total entropy production includes the change in the
device’s entropy too; it is not heat alone. It’s one bound on one relaxation, and it
doesn’t charge each certification again. It also isn’t the permanence of the finite-state
theorems on a noisy device: on this device the flag comes back down, and Tup and
Tdown are average stretches. The discrete-time core is checked, for a finite chain whose
steady spread π is positive and satisfies detailed balance: the entropy produced in one
step is exactly the drop in relative entropy to π, and never negative; from a known
start s the entropy produced in the first T steps is − ln π (s) minus the relative entropy
left at step T, so it never exceeds − ln π (s) and reaches it in the limit exactly when
that remainder goes to zero; − ln π (s) ≥ − ln π (no) for a start among the no-states;
the flow from the no-states to the yes-states equals the flow back; and with each mean
stretch taken as its mass over that flow, − ln π (no) = ln(1 + Tup /Tdown ).

Try the stretches with a bag of ten counters: nine marked YES and one NO. Draw,
record the answer, replace the counter and mix again. Each draw gives YES with
chance 9/10, whatever the last answer was. A YES stretch ends on the next draw with
chance 1/10, so its mean length is ten draws: the mean L obeys L = 1 + (9/10) L. A
NO stretch similarly averages 10/9 draws. Their ratio is nine, just like the ratio of YES
to NO counters. In a long record, count all the YES entries and divide by the number
of YES stretches; that is the measured mean stretch length. Divide both counts by the
total number of draws and you have mass divided by flow.

For this rule the long-run flow from NO to YES is (1/10)(9/10) = 9/100 per draw,
and the reverse flow is the same. A start known to be NO has relative entropy
− ln(1/10) = ln 10 against the long-run spread; after one draw the spread is already
1/10, 9/10, so none of that relative entropy remains. This bag shows the probability ac-
counting. The entropy-production interpretation still needs the stated physical model;
shaking counters in a bag does not measure that heat.


                                           124
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Two things need establishing for a general device: that it actually settles, and that
“mean stretch length” means what it sounds like. Here is what each says, and why it
holds.

Settling first. A chain doesn’t have to settle. It can get stuck in a corner, or cycle
round forever. What rules that out here is a condition named for Wolfgang Doeblin, a
German-born French mathematician, son of the novelist Alfred Döblin, who took his
doctorate at the Sorbonne in 1938 for work on chains like this one and died in June
1940, at twenty-five. In words: from wherever the device is, its next step lands on each
state with at least some fixed fraction δ of that state’s long-run chance. No state is ever
out of reach in one step, and none is favoured so heavily that the others starve. Under
that condition each step shrinks the distance between where the device is and where
it’s going by the factor 1 − δ, so the distance dies off geometrically and the spread
converges to π at every state. Here’s the payoff for the bound. The entropy produced
from the known start stays under − ln π (s), and it also gets there: after T steps it falls
short by at most (4/m)(1 − δ)2T , where m is the smallest long-run chance of any state.
So − ln π (s) is the exact total entropy production of the whole relaxation, in units of
k B , and the bound − ln π (s) is reached.

For rates satisfying detailed balance with π, the same equality holds when the device
hops at random moments, with no clock ticking. At every instant the relative entropy
to π falls at exactly the rate entropy is being produced, and that rate is never negative;
add the rate up between two times and you get exactly the drop in relative entropy
between them. For settling, Doeblin’s condition becomes a condition on rates: the
rate of hopping from any state x to any state y is at least c times π (y), for some fixed
c > 0. Then entropy is always being produced at least c times as fast as the relative
entropy still left, and that forces the relative entropy down at least as fast as e−ct . One
wrinkle needed its own proof. A known start puts all its weight on one state and none
anywhere else, and the logarithms in the relative entropy go bad at zero. The check
shows the relative entropy is still continuous at the starting instant, because u ln u
goes to zero as u does. So adding up the production from the start out to infinity gives
exactly − ln π (s).

I should say what Doeblin’s condition costs. It asks for every hop to be possible
directly, in one step or at a positive rate. A device whose states reach each other only
through other states can still settle, and the standard theory of these chains says the
conclusion holds for it too, but the proofs here don’t cover that case. For a chain that
ticks, the condition holding for some fixed number of steps would be enough for the
same argument; I’ve checked it for one step.

Then the stretches. The bound used the fact that the long-run chances of up and down
stand in the ratio of the mean stretch lengths, and I took the mean length of a stretch
with the flag up to be the long-run weight of the up-states divided by the flow into
them. That’s a theorem. Here’s the argument. Start each stretch the way the flow starts


                                            125
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


them, count the steps until the chain leaves the up-states, and the average is exactly
π (up) over the flow, again under Doeblin’s condition. The proof is a telescoping sum:
the long-run weight that has stayed up for k steps splits into the stretches that started
just now and the weight that stays up one step more.

With the stretches measured in seconds, when the device hops at random moments, it’s
checked too, and the route is different. Ask, for each up-state, how long on average the
device takes to leave the up-states from there. Call that its leaving time. The leaving
times obey one plain rule: from any up-state, the rate out of it times its leaving time,
minus the rates into the other up-states times their leaving times, comes to exactly one.
Rates measured per second times times measured in seconds give a dimensionless one.
Average the leaving times over the way the flow starts stretches, multiply by the flow,
and the rule plus the balance of the steady spread (as much weight flows into each
state as out of it) rearrange the sum into exactly π (up). That the rule has a solution
at all needs proving, since nothing promises it in advance, and Doeblin’s condition
supplies it: run a clock that ticks faster than any rate in the chain, and the leaving
times are the limit of a count that only grows and never passes one over c π (down).
Last, the seconds themselves. Take the chance that a stretch started by the flow is still
running at time t, with the chain stopped the moment it leaves the up-states. That
chance starts at one and falls at least as fast as e−c π (down) t . The time spent up, which is
that chance added up over time, comes out to the averaged leaving time minus what’s
still running, and as time runs on it closes in on π (up) over the flow. Mass over flow,
in seconds. The bound’s two premises are both checked now, in steps and in seconds.

The next section is about a different door entirely. Forgetting has had its section; the
question now is whether finding out costs, because the demon’s whole trick was that it
knew which way the molecule was going, and I owe you a straight answer on whether
knowing is free.

5 Learning is free, committing is not
I ended the last section owing you an answer about knowing. The bill so far sits on
forgetting: under merge pricing, a finite machine’s permanent flag-raising instruction
was paid for because it merges two states somewhere. But there’s a thing that looks
like the opposite of forgetting and feels like it ought to cost at least as much, probably
more. Finding out. Every time a machine rules out a possibility, it knows more than it
did. If forgetting a bit costs, does learning one cost too? I had a strong feeling about
this, and you probably have it too, so here it is first: learning is the expensive part.
Most physicists had that feeling as well, for a long time. It’s why the demon took a
hundred and fifteen years to exorcise. Or didn’t. “Exorcise” is the word the people
who think it worked like to use. John Earman and John Norton, the doubters from the
last section, called their two-part paper on it “Exorcist XIV: The Wrath of Maxwell’s
Demon,” and I read that Roman numeral as a joke about how many times the demon
has been declared gone. So hold the word loosely. This section is me finding out


                                             126
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


where the feeling goes wrong. I’m going to tell you the version where the exorcism
worked, because it’s the version that says where the bill goes, and the door from the
last section stays open behind it.

5.1 A small being at a small door
You met Maxwell’s demon in Section 3, in one paragraph. It gets a whole section here,
because the step it seemed to pay for and the step it actually pays for are what this
section is about.

In December 1867 James Clerk Maxwell, who had published his equations for electric-
ity and magnetism two years before, in 1865, and to my mind had as good a claim as
anyone to being the most important physicist alive, wrote a letter to his friend Peter
Tait describing a problem he couldn’t get rid of. Take a box of gas at one temperature,
with a wall down the middle and a tiny door in the wall. Now imagine, he said, a
“very observant and neat-fingered being” sitting at the door, who can see individual
molecules coming. When a fast one approaches from the left, it opens the door and
lets it through. When a slow one approaches from the right, same. Otherwise it keeps
the door shut. It never pushes anything; it only opens and closes a frictionless door
at the right moments. After a while the right side is hot and the left side is cold, and
you’ve got a temperature difference you could run an engine off, made out of noth-
ing but looking. That’s supposed to be impossible. It’s the thing the second law of
thermodynamics says can’t happen, and the second law is the law physicists are least
willing to give up; Arthur Eddington, the English astronomer, wrote in a 1928 book of
popular lectures that a theory found to contradict it has nothing for it but to collapse
in deepest humiliation, and nobody has had to test that yet.

Maxwell put it in his textbook in 1871, and it got named Maxwell’s demon, though
not by Maxwell. William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, called it a demon in Nature in
1874, and Maxwell, in an undated note to Tait headed “Concerning Demons,” tried
to take the name back: “Call him no more a demon but a valve . . . ” Nobody listened,
which is probably for the best, because “Maxwell’s valve” would not have lasted a
century. But keep his correction, because it’s exactly right and it’s the whole problem:
the being does no work. It opens and shuts a door. So physicists spent the next century
trying to find where the being was cheating. I want you to feel the pull of the obvious
answer, because I felt it and so did most of them: the being has to see the molecules.
Seeing costs. Case closed. In 1929 Leo Szilard built a one-molecule version of the box
and did the arithmetic, and said the second law survives if finding out which side the
molecule is on costs at least as much entropy as the being gains. In 1951 the French
physicist Léon Brillouin made it concrete: to see a molecule you have to bounce light
off it, and the way the philosopher of physics Jeffrey Bub sums up the result, finding
out that way costs at least k ln 2 of entropy for every bit, which is kT ln 2 of heat,
Landauer’s number before Landauer, and there was your toll on looking. For thirty
years that was the answer. Information costs because getting it costs.



                                          127
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


That’s a price on one way of looking, and it doesn’t show that every possible way of
making a record has to pay it. A device can burn energy without that being a law.

Szilard is worth one more minute, for a reason that has nothing to do with the demon.
Four years after the one-molecule engine, in September 1933, by his own later telling,
he was waiting at a traffic light on Southampton Row in London, having just read a
newspaper report in which Ernest Rutherford, the physicist who had announced the
atomic nucleus in 1911, called the hope of getting power out of atoms moonshine, and
as the light changed it occurred to him that an element which gave off two neutrons
when it swallowed one could keep a reaction going by itself. That’s the nuclear
chain reaction, thought up crossing a street. It’s his memory of himself, and Richard
Rhodes’s history of the bomb opens with it, in a first chapter called “Moonshine,”
which is where most people meet it, so hold it as the man’s own story. A timestamp
it isn’t. Does it change anything about the demon? No. What it adds is a picture of
the man: the same mind looked at one molecule in 1929 and one neutron in 1933, and
both times the question was what a single small step forces downstream.

5.2 Bennett moves the bill
In 1982 Charles Bennett, who’d already shown in 1973 that computation can be done
without forgetting, took the demon apart one step at a time. The being looks at a
molecule and writes down which side it’s on. Is writing that down a merge? Picture
the being’s notepad, which starts blank. After looking, the notepad says “left” or
“right.” Two possible worlds before (molecule left, pad blank; molecule right, pad
blank). Two possible worlds after (left, “left”; right, “right”). Nothing merged. Two
in, two out, and you can read the before off the after. Copying what you see onto a
blank page forgets nothing, and a step that forgets nothing is a step Landauer doesn’t
charge for. Brillouin had priced one particular way of looking (bouncing light) and
took it as the price of getting information at all. Bennett gave a way of looking that,
on his account, doesn’t pay it.

So where is the bill? The being has one notepad and a lot of molecules. After the first
molecule the page is full. To do the next one it has to wipe the page. And wiping takes
two possible worlds (pad says “left”; pad says “right”) to one (pad blank). That’s the
merge. That’s the step with no way back. The demon pays every cycle, and what it
pays for is making room to see again, and the amount it pays is at least what it gained,
and the second law sleeps soundly. That’s the rule from his 2003 notes I quoted in
Section 3: erasing and merging cost, and copying onto a blank place to write doesn’t.

Section 3 separated making a record from resetting it. Now you can see exactly which
step pays, and why the other one was tempting, because looking feels like the active
part. It’s the thing the being does. Wiping feels like housekeeping. The housekeeping
is where the money goes. If there’s a sentence in this section I’d want you to carry out
of it, that’s the one, and the idea in it is Bennett’s.




                                          128
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


5.3 Two different things called “narrowing”
Here is what I had to get straight in my own head before any of this made sense, and
I’ll give it to you as a picture because that’s how I eventually got it.

Draw the machine’s possible states as a row of dots. Now draw a second row above it:
the dots that you, standing outside, still think it might be in. Those are two different
rows. The first is a fact about the machine. The second is a fact about you, about
what you’ve seen and what you’ve ruled out. Both rows can shrink. They shrink for
different reasons, and only one of them costs.

The machine’s row shrinks when two of its states land on the same state. That’s a
merge. That’s what the price charges. Under the halving rule from Section 4, a run
can’t shrink the machine’s own row by more halvings than it paid for. That’s the
theorem just below, and it’s the Section 4 squeeze bound run forward along a whole
program. That section took it one step at a time. No new idea; the same chairs.

Exactly. Write ⌈log2 n⌉ for the index-bit count of n: the smallest whole number k with
2k ≥ n, the fewest yes-or-no questions that can guarantee identification among n
things when arbitrary binary splits are allowed. It is 0 at n = 1, and I set it to 0 at
n = 0 too, a convention for empty lists, since the logarithm of zero isn’t a number.
Wherever I write an ordinary logarithm without the rounding, its argument is positive.
For a run t and a list D of starting states, let imgt ( D ) be the set of states the run can
end in, starting from somewhere in D, and write |imgt ( D )| for how many there are
(in Section 4 the symbol for one move already meant the count; here I need the set and
its size both). Let cost(t) be the run’s total cost.


Theorem 5.1 (The machine’s own narrowing is priced). If the cost satisfies the halving
price (Premise 4.4), then for every run t and every list D of starting states with no repeats,

                        ⌈log2 | D |⌉ ≤ cost(t) + ⌈log2 |imgt ( D )|⌉.

Proof. By induction on the run. A single move of cost c shrinks a list with no repeats
by at most a factor 2c (that’s the halving price), which costs at most c in rounded
logarithms; the states reachable after the rest of the run from the shrunk set are exactly
those reachable after the whole run from the original. Add the costs.

The run itself is the witness; nothing else is handed in. That will matter in Section 8,
and I’ll say why at the end of this section.

Your row shrinks when you see something that some of your candidates couldn’t have
shown you. You cross those candidates off. Nothing happened to the machine. It
didn’t merge anything; it didn’t know you were watching; it would have done the
same thing with nobody in the room. The physicist Edwin Jaynes had a name for
mixing these up, and I think it’s one of the most useful names in all of science: the


                                             129
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


mind projection fallacy, treating what you know about a thing as if it were a property
of the thing. Your list of candidates is in your head. The machine’s row is in the
machine. The halving price is about the machine’s row, and crossing a candidate off
yours doesn’t move it.

And here I have to be fair to Jaynes, because he’d argue with where I just took his
phrase. In a 1965 paper on Gibbs’s and Boltzmann’s entropies he wrote that entropy is
“an anthropomorphic concept” (a phrase he credited to the physicist Eugene Wigner),
and by that he meant a property of the particular experiments you or I choose to do
on a physical system. On his account the system alone doesn’t carry it. So for Jaynes
the second law is about what’s known too, and the line I’d have liked to draw, that
the second law has opinions about the machine and none about you, is exactly the
line he’d refuse. Who’s right is one of the oldest fights in statistical physics, Jaynes’s
reading against Boltzmann’s, and I can’t settle it. I don’t have to. The spreads in
Section 4’s entropy theorems are spreads over the states the device might be in when
the step runs, and every theorem there holds whether you read those chances as
ignorance or as physics; “the floor comes from what you didn’t know” is the same
sentence in either reading, with “you” being whoever built the spread. What I need
from the fallacy is only this: the two rows are different rows, and only one of them is
the machine’s.

5.4 The demon on a sheet of paper
Build it, because the whole claim is four dots and two arrows and you should see it
merge or not merge with your own eyes.

The machine has a hidden bit (think of it as the molecule’s side) and a display (the
notepad). Four states: write them as pairs, hidden then display. 00, 01, 10, 11. Two
moves.

MEASURE copies the hidden bit onto the display, by adding it in the way that a light
switch adds: if the hidden bit is 1, flip the display; if it’s 0, leave it. Draw the arrows.
00 goes to 00. 01 goes to 01. 10 goes to 11. 11 goes to 10. Look at the arrowheads:
every state has exactly one arrow landing on it. Nothing merged. MEASURE forgets
nothing.

WIPE sets the display to 0 whatever it held. 00 goes to 00; 01 goes to 00 as well. 10
goes to 10; 11 goes to 10 as well. Two arrows land on 00 and two on 10. That’s a
merge, twice over. Under any price that charges per halving, WIPE costs at least one.
MEASURE is allowed to cost zero.

Now be the observer. You can see the display and not the hidden bit. What you’re
shown, the display here, is what I’ll call a window: the part of the state an outside
observer gets to see. Section 7 is about windows in general; here the window is
just the display. The display starts blank, so your list of candidates is {00, 10}: two
possibilities, one bit you don’t know. The machine runs MEASURE. You look at the


                                            130
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


display. If it shows 1, the only candidate that could have produced it is 10. If it shows
0, only 00. Your list went from two to one. You learned the hidden bit. The machine’s
price for that move: zero. Its own row of possible states went from {00, 10} to {00, 11},
still two; nothing it could have been got merged with anything else. You narrowed.
It didn’t. That’s the measuring half of Bennett’s argument on four dots, and WIPE’s
charge is the wiping half. So the demon just broke something: one bit gained, nothing
charged. Here’s the thing it broke, written out so you can see exactly where the crack
runs: for every list of starting candidates, every run, and every actual start in the
list, the index bits the observer gains (log2 of the candidates before minus log2 of the
candidates after, both rounded up) are at most what the run was charged. Four dots,
and that sentence is false.


Definition 5.1 (What an observer knows). Fix a window w from states to what can be
seen. Given a list Ω of candidate starting states, a run t, and the actual start s0 ∈ Ω,
the observer’s knowledge K (Ω, t, s0 ) is the list of candidates s ∈ Ω whose run shows
the same thing through the window at every step as the actual run does.


If that definition looks familiar, it should. It’s the standard way logicians of knowledge
set it up: what you know is whatever holds of every case you can’t tell apart from
the actual one, given everything you’ve seen (Fagin, Halpern, Moses and Vardi’s
Reasoning About Knowledge, 1995, builds a whole subject on it, runs and observations
included). And it’s the logically omniscient kind from the opening chapter, the kind
where knowing some facts means knowing everything that follows from them, for
free. I’m using it on purpose, flaw and all. This section is about learning, and learning
in that sense is exactly the thing that’s allowed to be free. Settling is the separate act
with a price, and nothing in this definition settles anything.


Theorem 5.2 (An observer can learn for free). There is a four-state machine (the demon),
a window (the display), a cost satisfying the halving price, a run of cost 0, and candidates with
|Ω| = 2, for which |K (Ω, t, s0 )| = 1. So the claim “for every Ω with no repeats, every t, and
every s0 in Ω: ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ − ⌈log2 |K (Ω, t, s0 )|⌉ ≤ cost(t)” is false for that machine and that
cost. In the same machine, every cost satisfying the halving price charges WIPE at least one.

Proof. The machine and run are the four dots above: MEASURE is a bijection, so cost 0
satisfies the halving price; the observer’s two candidates show different displays after
MEASURE; WIPE sends two pairs of states to one each, so the halving price needs its
cost ≥ 1.

The demon is the picture. The smallest case is smaller. The claim as written already
fails on a machine with two states and every move free, because the observer’s very
first look tells the two apart, and it never fails on a machine with one state. That’s why
the interesting version is learning after the first look, which is where the three states


                                              131
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


of Theorem 5.3 come in. And WIPE’s price needs less than the halving rule: merge
pricing alone charges it at least one.

I have to be exact about one thing. The halving rule is a floor. It says merges cost
at least this much; it does not say anything costs zero. So what the theorem exhibits
is one price schedule that meets the halving rule and charges MEASURE nothing. A
different schedule could meet the rule and still charge MEASURE; nothing in counting
forbids overcharging. The claim is “learning is not forced to cost.” It isn’t “learning is
free on every machine,” and on a given machine a schedule may still charge it. That’s
