weaker than the section title. The title is the short form you’d say before checking the
fine print, so the title stays and this paragraph stays next to it.

The physicists had this freedom on the books long before me. Paul Fahn (1996), doing
the entropy accounting of Szilard’s one-molecule engine step by step, argued for a
symmetry between the measuring step and the erasing step: on his account, which of
the two you hand the bill to is partly a choice of bookkeeping, and the total is what’s
fixed. Sagawa and Ueda (2009) derived a bound on that total, with the split depending
on the memory. So, on their accounts, “a schedule could charge MEASURE instead”
is a known freedom in how the books are kept. I didn’t find a loophole. And the other
reading is very much alive. Ruth Kastner (2025) argues that Brillouin was essentially
right after all: once the physics of a real measurement is put back in, it’s measurement
that pays and foils the demon, erasure drops out of the bill, and Bennett’s free copy
fails as physics. The theorem above is about price lists, so it stands either way. What
hangs on her is whether a real demon can look for nothing, which is the same door
the next paragraph’s doubter pushes on.

And the doubter from the last section cuts this side too, so I owe it to you, since I
leaned on him there. In 2013 John Norton argued for a no-go result: at the scale of
molecules, thermal jiggling keeps any process that’s supposed to be thermodynami-
cally reversible from ever actually finishing, and finishing it takes more entropy than
Landauer’s amount. If he’s right, Bennett’s free measurement isn’t free in practice
either, because it’s one of those processes. The theorem above survives that, because
it’s about price lists: a schedule that meets the halving rule isn’t forced to charge the
copy, whatever a real device spends. What wouldn’t survive is the physics I’ve been
hanging on it, that a real demon can look for nothing. If Norton is right, the line
between learning and committing keeps its counting and loses its physics. I can’t
referee that one either.

5.5 Who holds the pen changes the bill
Now the part that I think is the most beautiful fact in here. You find it by playing with
the four dots. Thinking about them won’t get you there. Run MEASURE twice. The
first copies the hidden bit onto the display. The second adds the hidden bit in again,
and adding a bit twice with a light-switch add gets you back where you were: the
display is blank again. Check the arrows: 10 to 11 to 10. The display went full and


                                           132
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


then blank, and nothing merged, and the price was zero both times. So a display that
was blank before the first MEASURE can be put back to blank for free, by a second
MEASURE. Just not by WIPE.

What’s the difference? MEASURE consults the hidden bit when it clears the display. It
knows what’s written there, because it has access to the thing it was copied from, and
so it can undo the copy. Nothing gets erased. WIPE doesn’t look. It sets the display
to 0 regardless, and “regardless” is exactly the many-to-one. Bennett has the general
form of this in the 2003 notes: he lists the “erasure of one of two copies of data known
to be identical” among the logically reversible operations, because you’re removing a
duplicate, and no information is destroyed. And it goes further than Bennett in work
that came after him: the quantum physicist Lídia del Rio and colleagues argued in
2011 that the cost of erasing a system depends on how much the eraser already knows
about it, down to zero and in the quantum case past zero. The bill for clearing a record
is sent to whoever clears it, and it’s smaller the more they know. Try it with a red or
blue card under a cup and a note that is blank or marked. Start with the note blank.
Lift the cup: for red, toggle the note (blank to marked, marked to blank); for blue, leave
it alone. The note now reports the colour. Repeat that same rule while the card is still
available, and the note returns to blank. Check all four card-and-note combinations:
the rule undoes itself, so no two land together. Erase the note regardless of the card
instead, and for either card both note values land on blank. That rule merges on the
full set of combinations. On the correlated pair you actually prepared, the card still
keeps the information. The difference is which information the rule can use and which
states it must handle; these paper operations do not measure a heat difference.

5.6 The smallest machine that teaches for free, and the one that can’t
Two more small facts, and then the point. The demon measures what you learn by
comparing the start to the end, but an observer’s very first look already rules things
out before any step runs, so the fairer question is: after that first look, can a step teach
you more, for free? Yes, and the demon still does it. And the smallest machine that
can is three states in a ring: U goes to V, V goes to W, W goes to U, and the window
shows “true” only at W. Start with candidates {U, V}; both show false. Take one step.
From U you now see false; from V you now see true. One step told them apart, and
a ring forgets nothing, so a zero price meets the halving rule and is the price chosen
here.

Two states can’t do it, ever, with any arrows, and this is the one that needs no price
premise at all. If a machine has only two states and you can’t tell them apart at the
first look, then the window shows the same thing on both, and those two are all the
states there are, so the window shows the same thing everywhere, forever, and you
never learn anything. Try to draw a counterexample. You’ll draw the same two dots a
few times and give up, and the giving up is the proof. Three is the smallest number
of states on which two states that look alike at the first look can come apart at a later
look, and that’s what teaching is.

                                            133
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


Theorem 5.3 (Three states are the minimum for free teaching). Call a machine a free
teacher when it has a cost satisfying the halving price, a list of candidates with no repeats
containing the actual start, and a run of cost 0 after which the observer knows strictly more
than after the first look, |K (Ω, t, s0 )| < |K (Ω, [ ], s0 )|. There is a free teacher with exactly
three states, and there is none with two or fewer.

Proof. Three: the ring U → V → W → U with the window true only at W, candidates
{U, V }, one step, cost 0 (a ring is a bijection, so cost 0 satisfies the halving price). Two
or fewer: two candidates that agree at the first look are, on a two-state machine, all
the states there are, so the window takes one value everywhere and no later look can
separate them. This half never uses the price at all.

5.7 What the toll prices, said at last
Now I can say, more precisely than I could two sections ago, what the mark in Section 3
is a mark for. Not for learning. What you know can be narrowed at no cost, with
nothing merged, on some machines under some honest price lists, and the demon is
one. Not for looking, not for copying, not for finding out. The mark is for the one
thing in Section 4 that couldn’t be done without merging, on a machine with finitely
many states: raising a flag that stays up. Learning is the demon writing on a blank
pad, which merges nothing. What the demon pays for is the wipe, a step with a shared
chair. The mark in Section 3 is paid for the same reason, because raising a flag that
stays up also has a shared chair, but it’s a different step: the demon machine has no
flag, and its price list prices merges; commitments never appear in it. Same chair.
Different room.

This is also where I settle up with Rovelli, my closest neighbour from the opening
chapter, because I put him and Bennett on opposite sides of one door, and I owe you
how much of that is mine. All of the reconciliation is mine. Rovelli’s paper doesn’t
make it, and in four places his own framing points somewhere else. He reserves
“choice” for an outcome that is stable and not predictable, and he rules out a thermostat
because it runs on a predictable mechanism; the commit in this book is a step a rule
fixes in advance, so by his own definition his result doesn’t cover it. His choice
is a branching, one possibility splitting into two, and he calls choosing in a sense
the inverse of erasing, because branching is the inverse of merging; the toll comes
from a merge, the opposite shape. His stability is for a while: he says stabilization
means something only on times that aren’t too long next to the time it takes things to
thermalize, and past that nothing stays chosen; my permanence is forever (and the
last section owned up that forever is an idealization). And he doesn’t stand beside
Bennett at all: he holds that any measurement is dissipative, credits the point to the
philosopher of science Hans Reichenbach, and doesn’t cite Bennett. So what Rovelli
and I share is a sentence, that a choice that sticks costs something like Landauer’s
bill. There’s no shared mechanism. Push on it and his coin hitting the ground, a fact
gained from something nobody could predict, sits closer to what this section calls


                                                134
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


learning than to committing. I still think it’s the same instinct. That’s my reading, and
he doesn’t make it; you now have everything you need to disagree with it.

And on one point Rovelli isn’t the nearest physics. The nearest I’ve found is in bi-
ology. Thomas Ouldridge and Pieter Rein ten Wolde (2017) derived what they call
the fundamental costs of making a persistent copy of a polymer, one whose sequence
stays correlated with its template after the two have physically come apart, and of
destroying one. On their account a copy like that is a state out of equilibrium, and
making it has a thermodynamic bill they measure efficiency against. A companion
paper the same year, with Christopher Govern, does the same kind of accounting for
the molecules a cell uses to read out the state of its receptors, which is a measurement
in all but name. The way I read them, the copy that has to stay is the one with the
bill, and that’s the closest thing in physics I’ve found to the line this section draws
between finding out and committing. The differences, so it doesn’t get borrowed for
more than it is: theirs is heat, in chemistry, for a correlation between two molecules,
and their title has the destruction of copies in it too, so their copies don’t last forever;
mine is a count in a model of computation, for a reading that never turns off, with no
temperature anywhere. Same instinct again, from a different direction.

The chemistry has the sharp form of it, too, and it came two years later. Jenny Poul-
ton, Pieter Rein ten Wolde and Thomas Ouldridge (2019) studied minimal models of
polymer copying, and in those models, when the copy grows at equilibrium, with the
weakest chemical driving, a persistent copy’s accuracy and the efficiency of making it
both vanish; only driving the growth out of equilibrium, paying, buys a copy that still
carries information about its template after the two let go. That’s finding out against
committing, in chemistry, with the bill attached, and I’d rather say plainly that biology
had the distinction before I did. What stays different is the kind of thing the record is:
theirs is a correlation in a chemical ensemble, mine is a reading enforced by a step in a
model of computation.

Two more neighbours have “learning” and “commit” in their titles, so the slogan
shouldn’t be read against them by accident. Sebastian Goldt and Udo Seifert (2017)
did the stochastic thermodynamics of a neural network learning a rule, and argued
from it that learning has a thermodynamic cost: on their account, the entropy the
network produces bounds how much it can learn. That doesn’t contradict this section,
and here’s why. Their learner isn’t copying onto a blank page. Its weights are a driven
thermal system, jostled by noise and dragged toward what the data push them to,
and what they price is that physical process. This section’s free learning is narrower:
one way of finding out, a copy onto a blank, is allowed to cost nothing. Nothing here
says every way of learning is cheap, and theirs isn’t. From statistics, Aurélien Garivier,
Tor Lattimore and Emilie Kaufmann (2016) gave a proof that in a two-armed bandit
with Gaussian rewards, a strategy that explores first and then commits for good ends
up, as the horizon grows, with at least twice the regret of the best strategy that keeps
deciding as it goes. That’s the closest published sentence I’ve found to “committing


                                            135
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


isn’t free” with a number on it. Their price is reward lost, which is a different unit
from a mark on a ledger, so it’s a cousin. A twin would have to count marks.

So here’s exactly what “No Free Insight,” the name I gave the toll before I understood
it, covers, because I don’t want the name doing work it hasn’t earned. Insight in the
sense of finding out can be free. The insight the toll prices is the kind you’ve committed
to, written into a record the machine can’t silently revise. Whether that narrower thing
deserves the name is a fair thing to argue about; I kept the name because it’s the
question I started with, and because the narrowing is the finding. I don’t count it as a
retreat.

It also tells you how to read a bound that’s coming. Section 8 counts what it takes to
narrow a list of candidates down to a shorter one: at least as many yes-or-no questions
as it takes to point at the survivors among their rivals, a counting fact that holds for
anything with a list in it. Turning that count into a bill, saying a run actually paid that
many marks, is a different claim, and when the book makes it, for any certification
system in Section 8, the payment goes in as a hypothesis: a decision tree (a branching
chart of yes-or-no questions, which Section 8 builds) no deeper than the number of
paid steps the run took is handed in, along with the lists themselves and the fact that
the tree’s leaves cover the narrowing. This section is the reason it has to go in that
way. The narrowing alone doesn’t force anyone to pay; the demon just showed you
a narrowing that cost nothing. So wherever narrowing gets a price in this book, the
payment is a premise, and I’ll keep calling it one.

And one more boundary. This whole section is about a machine that’s finite and
deterministic and a watcher who crosses candidates off a list. There’s no quantum
anything in it. This narrowing has nothing to do with “observation collapses the
state”: the narrowing here is bookkeeping in the watcher’s list, the machine never
notices, and the result would be the same if the watcher were a filing cabinet. In 2010
a group in Tokyo (Toyabe, Sagawa, Ueda, Muneyuki and Sano) did run a real demon,
a tiny particle walked up a staircase of potential by feedback on what a camera saw,
and the energy it gained was paid for by the information the camera took, with no
violation of anything. The demon is real, it works, and it pays. Where it pays is the
part that took a century.

What I still owe: everything so far says “at least one mark” and I’ve been keeping
the marks on the side of the page, a running total you tally as you go. What happens
when the machine keeps that total itself, inside its own state, where a step could in
principle reach in and change it? That’s the counter, and it’s the next thing I have to
build.

The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


Part III

The logic

6 The counter
Everything so far has kept the marks on the side of the page. You played the toy, you
made a tally as you went, and the tally lived in your hand. The machine never saw it.
That’s fine for a toy. For anything that’s going to run on its own, with nobody tallying,
the total has to live somewhere the machine can reach, which means the machine can,
in principle, reach it. So this section is about what a counter has to be before you’re
allowed to call it a receipt. I mean the counter of any machine whose state carries
a running total that every step bumps by whatever a price list says that step costs.
Section 3’s five parts don’t need one (there the total was a sum you did on the side),
so this is one piece added to the five, and the facts below are about anything that has
it. I’ll give you the answer first, because it’s short, and then spend the section on why
each word is there: a receipt is a total that lives in the state, that only climbs, that
equals the sum of what was charged, and that nothing else could have been.

6.1 A stick, split down the middle
The oldest receipt I could find that you can still hold is a piece of wood. From about
1100, under Henry the First, until 1826, the English treasury recorded what it was
owed on tally sticks: a strip of hazel, notched across with cuts of set widths (the
treasury’s own handbook from around 1180, the Dialogue of the Exchequer, gives them:
a thumb’s width for a hundred pounds, a swollen barleycorn for a pound, a bare cut
for a penny), then split lengthwise so that each half carried the same notches. The
payer kept one half, called the stock, which is one story for where the word stockholder
comes from. The treasury kept the other. When the time came to settle, you laid the
two halves together, and only the two original halves fit, because wood splits along a
grain nobody can copy. Add a notch to your half and the other half shows a gap where
the partner should be. Try to remove a notch and you find that wood can’t be uncut.
When they finally stopped using them, the clerks burned centuries of old tallies in the
furnaces under the House of Lords, overheated the flue, and burned down the Palace
of Westminster, which I mention because it’s the best fact I picked up for this book
and because it tells you how many of them there were.

Do it: draw a border round a strip of card, notch it once for every coin you hand a
friend, then split it lengthwise through the notches and keep half each. Keep the same
strip: no trimming its edge away or substituting another. Add a notch to one half and
put them back together. The mismatch is visible. You cannot fill a cut back in with the
card you cut away; an attempted patch is an alteration to inspect. The total you made
is the notches, one per coin (conservation), and under that rule the count only climbs.
Both halves began with the same count. If they disagree now, something changed; the


                                          137
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


mismatch alone does not tell you which holder changed it. The demonstration gives a
comparison you can make, not an unforgeable object or a verdict on who cheated.

Economists read the same stick another way, and they’re not wrong either. Alfred
Mitchell-Innes (1913) made the exchequer tally his star witness that money is credit:
the crown paid the people it owed by “raising a tally” on some branch of its revenue,
a wooden acknowledgment of debt. A receipt to me, money to him, and it’s the same
piece of wood. Narayana Kocherlakota (1998) later proved a version of his point: in a
wide class of economies where nobody can be held to a promise, anything money lets
people do, a memory of everyone’s past dealings lets them do too. His title says it in
three words: money is memory.

6.2 Why it has to climb
Start with the second property, because it’s the one that does the most work and the
one people fight hardest. Why can’t the counter ever go down?

Because of what the toll is for. The floor it buys, back in Section 3, says a run from NO
to YES costs at least one. That sentence is a floor: it says the run paid at least this much.
If the counter could come back down, a run could pay the toll, get its flag, and then
take the payment back, and the floor would be a floor on nothing; “this run cost at
least one” would be true of a run that ended having cost nothing. So a counter that can
fall is an accountant you can lean on to revise the books, and a floor stated in terms of
it isn’t a floor. The counter only climbing is not a flourish. It’s what makes “at least”
mean something. This ledger records cumulative charges, each a whole number of
marks and none negative, so it never decreases. A refundable balance, one that pays
money back, would be a different accounting object with a different invariant, and the
floor here says nothing about it. (In Section 3’s abstract theorem the total is a sum of
whole numbers and climbing comes for free; this paragraph is about why a total stored
in the state, where a step could in principle write it, has to be designed so that no step
ever lowers it.)

The same rule turns up in two places that have nothing to do with each other, pointing
in opposite directions, and that’s a big part of why I trust it. In 1978 Leslie Lamport
asked how a set of computers that pass each other messages, with no shared clock,
could ever agree on what happened before what. His answer is a counter per machine
with two rules: add one before you do anything, and when a message arrives carrying
the sender’s count, jump your own counter above it (never below your own). Those
counters, he showed, respect cause and effect: if this caused that, this has the smaller
number. And they do it “with no actual timing mechanism,” his words; they’re clocks
only in name. Try it with three people passing notes and you’ll see it work in two
minutes, and then let one of them reset their counter to zero after reading a note, and
watch a reply come out numbered before the note it replies to. A counter that goes
down can’t be leaned on for order.

Where did Lamport get it? In the notes he keeps on his own papers, he says the

                                            138
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


timestamps came from an earlier note by Paul Johnson and Bob Thomas on keeping
copies of a database in step, whose algorithm wasn’t quite right: it let things happen
in an order that broke cause and effect. What let him see the fix, he says, was special
relativity, which teaches that the one order of events everybody agrees on is the order
of what could have caused what. And he passes on a line from Jim Gray, the same
Gray as the commit at the start of the book: Gray had heard two opinions of the
paper, that it was trivial and that it was brilliant. Lamport’s answer is that he can’t
argue with the first and isn’t inclined to argue with the second. His account stops at
relativity, so the chase does too. The picture it leaves is a good one: a number that’s
allowed to climb and never to fall is enough to write “this came after that” with no
clock anywhere.

Now the other direction. In 1949 Alan Turing, and in 1967 Robert Floyd, each asked
how you prove a program stops. The answer, both times: find a quantity that goes
down on every step and can’t go down forever (a whole number that can’t go below
zero, say). If every step lowers it and it can’t fall forever, the steps can’t go on forever.
Up-only gives you order. Down-only gives you stopping. They’re different rules (one
needs the jump-above-the-message step, the other needs a floor it can’t fall below).
They have the same shape, seen from the two ends: a one-way quantity is something
you can build on, and a two-way quantity is a number that happens to be written
down somewhere.

And the real-world case where a counter was allowed to go down, and got gamed
exactly there: Ethereum, one of the largest blockchains, charges “gas” for every step
of a program, and for years it refunded gas when a program freed up storage. Someone
noticed you could fill storage when gas was cheap, hold it, and cash the refunds when
gas was dear, and a token was built to do exactly that, and the real work in a block
could reach nearly twice the block’s stated limit. In 2021 a change called EIP-3529
cut the refunds sharply (none for self-destruct, a smaller one for clearing storage, and
a cap of one fifth of the gas used). The written reasons are the gas token and those
overfull blocks. I read both as the same lesson: a counter that goes down was being
leaned on at the place where it went down. Ethereum’s gas comes back in Section 14
as one of five small models of systems people actually run, and it’s the only one of the
five that prices a write at all, and it’s instructive that the part they had to fix was the
part that could fall.

6.3 Conservation: the total is the charges and nothing else
The first property is the plainest one. The counter after a step is the counter before
plus what that step was charged. Add up a whole run and the middle values cancel
out, the way a sum of differences collapses to last minus first, and the total is the sum
of the per-step charges. Why state it?

Because it’s the property that fails quietly. Say a machine charges one for raising a
flag, and also, somewhere in its error handling, forgets to add the charge when the


                                            139
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


step fails halfway through. Or charges two in one code path and one in another for
the same move. Or has one step that writes the counter directly. Then the counter is
mostly the sum of the charges, and “mostly” is the whole gap between a receipt and
a note that says “trust me, about this much.” Conservation is the sentence that there
is no “mostly”: every step, every outcome, every error, adds exactly its charge, and
a step that fails is charged the same as one that succeeds, because the charge is on
the attempt. For a machine built the way I’m describing, that sentence is the rule the
counter is updated by, so it can’t fail by definition. What can fail is the claim that a
real machine is built that way, and checking that means going through every move it
has, the failure branches included, one at a time, which is dull and is the whole job.
The run-long form, counter at the end equals counter at the start plus the sum of the
charges, then follows from the one-step rule by the cancelling sum; it’s below. It’s the
kind of theorem that looks boring and is the one you’d most want if you were going
to rely on the number. One thing it doesn’t say: that every mark bought something.
The ledger is exact about what was spent. What the spending was worth is another
question, and whether a mark bought a real narrowing is Section 8’s question, and it
needs a witness on top of the ledger entry.

6.4 Only one honest count
Here’s the property that surprised me by being provable at all. Suppose you fixed
the schedule: this move costs one, that move costs zero, and so on, for every move.
And suppose someone else keeps their own books: their own function from states to
totals, which starts at zero and, on every step, goes up by exactly what the schedule
says. Could their books disagree with the machine’s counter, somewhere, on some
state you can actually get to?

No. And the proof is the tally stick. Both totals start at zero. On every step both
go up by the same amount. So on every state you can reach by steps from the start,
they’re equal. That’s it; it’s an induction, the one-step-at-a-time argument from Sec-
tion 3’s floor. The mathematician’s word for this is initiality: the counter is the one
bookkeeping that all the others, if they’re honest about the schedule, turn out to be.
Given the schedule, the count is forced. Two things about that sentence I had to be
careful with, and they’re worth saying before the symbols. It doesn’t assume the other
books climb: climbing follows from the schedule, since the schedule never charges a
negative amount, so “only one honest count” and “it only climbs” aren’t two separate
demands on the other bookkeeper. And it holds on reachable states only. A state you
can’t get to from the start is one where it says nothing about whether the other books
agree, which is the right thing for a receipt to say.

Here are the properties exactly. First the piece being added to Section 3’s five, a counter
and a price list, and then the two facts about it. The counter gets the Greek letter µ
(mu), which is the letter the machine in Part IV uses for it (Theorem 16.5).




                                           140
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Definition 6.1 (A counter kept by a price list). A counter machine has a set of states,
a set of moves, a step function apply that takes a state and a move, a start state sinit ,
a schedule c giving each move a cost in N, and a counter µ from states to N, such
that µ(sinit ) = 0 and µ(apply(s, i )) = µ(s) + c(i ) for every state s and move i, with no
exceptions. A run of a list t of moves from s applies them in order, and c(t) is the sum
of their costs. A state is reachable when it is the start or is apply(s, i ) for a reachable s
and some i.


Theorem 6.1 (Conservation). In a counter machine, for every state s and every list t, µ at
the end of the run of t from s equals µ(s) + c(t). In particular µ never decreases along a run.

Proof. Induction on t. For the empty list both sides are µ(s). For a list i followed by
t′ , the one-step rule gives µ(apply(s, i )) = µ(s) + c(i ), and the induction hypothesis
from apply(s, i ) adds c(t′ ). Since every c(i ) ≥ 0, the counter never falls.


Theorem 6.2 (Only one honest count). In a counter machine, let B (for “books”) be any
function from states to N with B(sinit ) = 0 and B(apply(s, i )) = B(s) + c(i ) for all s and i.
Then B(s) = µ(s) for every reachable state s.

Proof. By induction on why s is reachable. At the start both are 0. If s = apply(s′ , i )
with B(s′ ) = µ(s′ ), then B(s) = B(s′ ) + c(i ) = µ(s′ ) + c(i ) = µ(s), the last step by the
counter’s rule.

Those two proofs are the whole of it, and they’re about any counter machine. They’re
on the page, where you can check every line. The machine I build later is one of these,
and on it the run form is a theorem: the ledger after any list of instructions is the start
plus the sum of their costs (Theorem 16.5). The uniqueness half holds even with the
books’ rule asked only of reachable states.

I want to flag what initiality does not do, because the fact is smaller than the word. It
doesn’t pick the prices. The schedule is an input: somebody decided that raising the
flag costs one and adding two numbers costs zero, and nothing here says that decision
was right (Section 4 is where I argued the floor isn’t arbitrary; the rest of a schedule
has to be defended by whoever writes it). It doesn’t turn marks into anything physical.
And it isn’t the category theorist’s “initial object,” though the word is borrowed for a
related reason.

There is a universal property nearby, and I’ll say exactly how far it reaches so the
borrowed word doesn’t reach further. Take any other machine that understands the
same moves (call it the target), and pick a state of it to start from. Walking a list of
moves through it, one at a time, is the one and only way to send lists to its states that
starts where you said and keeps in step as the list grows by one. Programmers call
that walk down a list, one item at a time, a fold, and I’ll borrow the word. That’s an


                                              141
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


induction on the list from its end, the same shape as the proof just above, and it never
looks at the other machine’s reading or its prices, which tells you how much the toll is
doing here: nothing. It’s a fact about lists of moves; states haven’t come into it yet.

Coming down from lists to the states of the machine running them is where it gets
interesting, and where the borrowed word stops. Two different lists can leave a
machine in the same state. If they leave the target in two different states, there’s no
single place to send that state. That’s the whole obstruction, and it’s exact: the map
from states exists on the reachable ones precisely when equal states always come from
lists that agree on the other side. Call that the descent condition, because it’s what
lets the fold come down from lists to states. A toll doesn’t force it. Take the one-bit
machine whose set costs one and whose reset is free. It obeys the toll, yet a single
set and a reset followed by a set leave its bit in the same state. A target that keeps
its whole history as its state tells those two runs apart, so nothing comes down. So
the fold is unique on lists, and that’s what the word “initial” earns. It doesn’t make
anybody’s states initial among everything that obeys the toll, and I won’t say it does.
The fold and the descent condition are proved over any machine: the fold is the one
such map, descent holds exactly when each reachable state goes to one target state,
and a map the fold factors through gives descent; the history-keeping machine is the
example that shows where descent fails.

And the borrowed word has a home. I didn’t build it, so I’ll point at it. That lists
of moves are the starting object, and that a machine’s behaviour factors through its
reachable states exactly when a condition like descent holds, is the theory of minimal
realization. Joseph Goguen put it as a universal property in 1973, in a paper whose
title says it outright, “Realization is universal,” and Thomas Colcombet and Daniela
Petrişan redid automata minimization in the same functorial terms in 2020. Their
machines can have any output at all, which is the honest point: the fold and the
descent condition never use the record, so the toll is doing nothing here, just as I said.

The nearest classical parallel to “only one honest count” is in thermodynamics. The
mathematical physicists Elliott Lieb and Jakob Yngvason showed in 1999 that once
you fix which states of a system can be reached from which by adiabatic processes,
and that relation meets a short list of axioms, there is an entropy, a function that goes
up exactly along the relation, and it is unique once its zero and its unit are chosen.
Their uniqueness, like this one, comes after the fixing: the order is the input there, the
price list is the input here, and in both the count is forced by it.

6.5 The toll is an old trick with a new name
Now a thing I first took as a let-down. It would be nice to have a new kind of cost
argument. This isn’t one. The toll is a case of a technique that algorithm people have
used since 1985 and that a mathematician studying the stability of motion had, in a
different costume, in 1892. I’m telling you it’s old so you don’t think I invented it.

The trick is called the potential method, and here’s the whole of it. Give every state

                                           142
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


a number, call it the potential, that measures how much “owing” is stored up in that
state. Then look at each step and ask: does the cost of the step, plus the change in
potential it causes, ever come out negative? If it never does, you’ve got a bound: any
run costs at least the amount the potential dropped from start to finish, because the drop
had to be paid for by the steps along the way. The computer scientist Robert Tarjan set
it out in 1985, crediting the potential view to Daniel Sleator. Tarjan’s use goes the other
way (potential as prepaid credit, to bound a run from above): he used it to analyse
data structures that are occasionally expensive and usually cheap; and the decreasing-
function idea underneath it is the one the Russian mathematician Aleksandr Lyapunov
used in 1892 to prove that a system settles down. Do the coin version, which runs
Tarjan’s way, as a ceiling: a stack of coins, PUSH adds one and costs one, POP-ALL
removes them all and costs as many as it removed, potential equals the number of
coins. PUSH costs one plus one potential; POP-ALL of k coins costs k and drops the
potential by k, net zero. So any sequence from an empty stack costs at most twice the
number of pushes, however many expensive pops are in it. That’s the method. Three
lines.

Push on that 1892 for a second, because a date like that hides a lot. Lyapunov wrote the
idea up as his doctoral thesis, in Russian. A French translation came out in 1907, made
by a French naval engineer, Édouard Davaux, and corrected by Lyapunov himself. The
English one came out in 1992, a hundred years after the original, and it was translated
from the French: a translation of a translation. So for most of the twentieth century
a reader with only English met the idea secondhand or not at all. Did the algorithm
people of 1985 get it from him? I can’t tell you, and nothing here needs them to have.
Whether anybody walked from one to the other on purpose is a question I’d like
answered. What I do have is a picture: the same idea, a number that only goes one
way along a run, turned up in a thesis about whether a moving system settles down
and in a paper about data structures, close to a century apart.

Now point it at the flag. Potential: one if the flag is down, zero if it’s up. A step
from down to up drops the potential by one, so for the step’s cost plus potential
change to be non-negative, the step has to cost at least one. That’s the toll, exactly,
and the two are the same statement: the toll holds for a machine if and only if every
step has non-negative amortized cost under the flag potential (“amortized cost” is
just that sum, the step’s cost plus the change in potential). Then the universal floor
from Section 3, “any run from NO to YES paid at least one,” is just the potential
method’s standard conclusion, the drop in potential from one to zero, and every
system with the five parts that obeys the toll is an instance, which is exactly what a
certification system is. Two more facts fall out of the same picture. Under the toll, a
run raises the flag at most as many times as its total cost; each raise uses up a unit
and a unit isn’t used twice. And if you demand the upper-bound version too, that the
potential before a step covers its cost plus the potential after, then the two together
hold exactly when raising the flag costs exactly one, everything else costs zero, and



                                           143
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


the flag never comes down; that’s the sharpest version of the schedule, and notice that
Section 3’s toy doesn’t meet it: the toy’s VOUCH move, played from YES, makes a
mark although it raises nothing, which the floor allows and the exact version forbids.
(These two facts hold even if the price depends on the state as well as the move’s
name, which is wider than Section 3’s per-name cost; a per-name cost is a special case.)
Two older tools sit beside these, named for completeness: running a list of moves in a
“writer” that accumulates a number returns the final state and the run’s cost, and a per-
move schedule is a “grade” fixed before the run; neither embeds those frameworks’
full type systems. The writer is the move the programming-language researchers
Norman Danner and Daniel Licata make in their cost semantics, a translation that
carries a cost alongside a program’s result (Danner, Licata and Ramyaa, ICFP 2015;
Danner and Licata, Journal of Functional Programming, 2022). The grade is Shin-ya
Katsumata’s: a computation carries its resource as a grade, and the grades compose
as the computations do (“Parametric effect monads and semantics of effect systems,”
POPL 2014). Dominic Orchard, Vilem Liepelt and Harley Eades put grades into the
types of a working language (“Quantitative program reasoning with graded modal
types,” ICFP 2019). And the potential method went into types before any of those: the
computer scientists Martin Hofmann and Steffen Jost (POPL 2003) gave a type system
that attaches potential to data and predicts, before a first-order functional program
runs, how much heap it can use, which is where type-based amortized analysis begins;
the multivariate work of Jan Hoffmann, Klaus Aehlig and Hofmann (2011) carried it
further. Read against them, the counter is a grade carried in the state by the step rule.
No type carries it. And what does that difference even mean? A cost that lives in a
type gets checked before the program runs, by whoever checks the types; a cost that
lives in the state gets written during the run, by the step itself. Same number, different
moment of truth.

So is mine an embedding of their frameworks, or something weaker? Half of it is
exactly theirs, and the other half is left out on purpose. The counter is their writer:
a step that moves the rest of the state without looking at the counter, hands back its
cost, and has the cost added on is a computation in the writer over whole numbers
with addition, and running a list of moves in that writer gives back the final state
and the total cost, nothing more and nothing less. Every system in this book whose
step never reads its own counter has that shape. What doesn’t come along is the part
of their frameworks that works before anything runs: the type systems that carry
grades, Danner and Licata’s bounding relation and the recurrences they extract for
a program’s cost. That isn’t a hole waiting for a patch. It’s the moment-of-truth
difference I just named. Putting the count in the step is choosing the other moment,
so the grade here is written by the step at run time and never checked ahead of it.

How close do the two moments come? Close enough to say exactly, in a limited form.
Take a small structured language over a machine with this kind of counter: sequencing,
branches whose two arms carry the same grade, and paid acts each graded with their



                                           144
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


charge, and grade every program the way Katsumata’s discipline does, adding grades
along the program. On loop-free programs the two agree on the nose: on every run
that doesn’t trap, the counter rises by exactly the grade. The argument is conservation
set beside the grade rule; the counter’s rise is the sum of the charges along the run, and
the grade rule adds the same charges in the same order. Loops break the agreement,
and in one direction only. A loop that runs a paid check once for every unit in some
register, where the check always passes and is charged one, costs that register’s value
on entry, and no fixed whole number is an exact grade for it; a grade that’s a function
of the inputs, the kind cost-aware type theories like calf (Niu, Sterling, Grodin and
Harper, 2022) allow, gets exactness back. So the counter carries their semantics exactly,
agrees with fixed grades wherever a fixed grade can be exact, and where a run’s cost
depends on its data it holds the exact number that a fixed grade can only bound. What
has no counterpart in the step is the checking ahead of time: a type checker turning a
program away before it runs.

There’s one more neighbour, closer than any of those, and I’ll name it before somebody
names it at me. A number the step keeps up to date and nothing else ever reads is
what program-proof people call an auxiliary variable, or ghost state. Susan Owicki
and David Gries added auxiliary variables to parallel programs in 1976, because
some true facts about such a program can’t be proved without one, under the rule
that an auxiliary variable never steers the program. Jean-Christophe Filliâtre, Léon
Gondelman and Andrei Paskevich, in 2014, worked out when ghost code can be erased
without changing what the program computes. By that test this section’s counter is
ghost whenever no step consults it, and Section 10’s base-driven records are built
exactly that way: the base moves the same whatever the ledger and the record say. So
what does putting it in the step buy, if the number is ghost anyway? Two things, as far
as I can see. The number is there while the machine runs, where a window can show
it (Section 7), and not only inside a proof somebody wrote afterwards. And the rule
that keeps it is one rule for every run of every program. An annotation covers only the
one program somebody happened to prove. Whether a record stays ghost depends
on what else the step does with it; the machine in Part IV has a part that isn’t ghost,
its table of checked facts, because the step reads it and refuses on it, as the opening
section said. One last relative, from the graph side: Section 3’s floor is a cheapest-path
bound in a system with weights on its moves. Every path from the no-states to the
yes-states crosses the line between them, and every edge across that line weighs at
least one. Weighted automata go back to Marcel-Paul Schützenberger in 1961, and
priced timed automata, which add clocks, were set out in 2001. The floor is about the
smallest case of what they compute.

Exactly, for any certification system with states S, moves I, step, per-name cost, and
reading:


Definition 6.2 (Potential, amortized cost). A potential is a function Φ : S → N. A step


                                           145
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


has non-negative amortized cost under Φ when cost(i ) + Φ(step(s, i )) ≥ Φ(s). The flag
potential is Φcert (s) = 1 if cert(s) = no and 0 if it reads yes.


Theorem 6.3 (The toll is the potential method). (1) The toll holds exactly when every step
has non-negative amortized cost under Φcert . (2) For any Φ with non-negative amortized cost
and any run t from s, cost(t) + Φ(run(t, s)) ≥ Φ(s). (3) Hence, under the toll, a run from a
no-state to a yes-state costs at least 1 − 0 = 1.

Proof. (1) Check the four combinations of the reading before and after: only no-to-yes
has Φcert dropping, by one, so the inequality there is exactly cost(i ) ≥ 1; in the other
three it holds for any cost. (2) Induction on the run, adding the per-step inequalities
so that the middle potentials cancel. (3) Apply (2) with Φcert , which is 1 at the start
and 0 at the end.

So what’s new, if the method isn’t? Only where it’s pointed. The potential method
is a way of proving things about costs. What this book adds is a claim about which
potential, the flag, and about what happens to that claim when you can only see a
window of the state. The method is Tarjan’s and Sleator’s. The reading is mine, and
I’m about to find out what it can and can’t survive.

The flag potential has relatives in physics-flavoured mathematics too, which I found
after the fact. Resource theories study what you can turn into what when some oper-
ations are free: Bob Coecke, Tobias Fritz and Robert Spekkens gave the general defi-
nition in 2016, Fritz worked out its algebra in 2017, and Tomáš Gonda and Spekkens
catalogued the numbers that never go up under free operations, which they call mono-
tones, in 2023. Read with “certified” as the resource and one mark as the currency, the
flag potential is the kind of cost monotone they build, measured in that currency, and
the floor is its simplest case. Does that make the toll a resource theory? Only as this
simple resource-accounting example: the floor is one mark for a no-to-yes run. An
exact one-mark conversion additionally needs a run attaining it. It’s a neighbour to
know about. I don’t count it as a result.

6.6 What the counter is, said once
A receipt is a total that lives in the state, only climbs, equals the sum of the charges on
every path including the failures, and is the only such total for its schedule. Each of
those had a home before this book: the stick for a total that lives in the state, Lamport’s
clocks for climbing, Turing’s and Floyd’s ranking functions for the same one-way rule
run downward, the telescoping sum for conservation, the induction for the single
honest count. None of them is physics. None of them says what the charges should
be. What they say is that once you’ve chosen the charges, the counter is the arithmetic.
It’s no second opinion. And the toll on top of it is the potential method with the flag
as potential, which is to say a trick from 1985 wearing the question from Section 2.

Here’s one thing the counter can’t do just by existing: if you can only see part of the

                                            146
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


state, can you tell what the counter is? Can you even tell, from outside, which step
paid? The stick works because you can lay the two halves together. What if you’re only
ever shown one half, through a window, and the window doesn’t show the notches?

One piece of that has a short answer, and I’ll give it now so the next section can
start from it. A window, for now, is just the part of the state an outside observer is
shown (Section 5’s display was one, and Section 7 is about windows in general). Call a
window counter-complete when some rule, applied to what the window shows, returns
the counter on every state; flag-complete likewise for the flag. Say a window forgets the
counter when changing the counter and nothing else never changes what the window
shows, and likewise for the flag.

The short answer: a window that forgets the counter is never counter-complete, what-
ever else it shows, and a window that forgets the flag is never flag-complete. Take any
state and make two copies of it, one with the counter set to 1 and one with it set to
2, everything else held still. The window shows the same thing for both, so any rule
gives the same answer for both, and one of the two answers is wrong. The flag is the
same argument with yes and no. On the stick: a window that shows you the wood’s
colour and its length, and hides the notches, can’t tell you what’s owed, and staring
harder at the colour won’t help. (The argument needs a state space where the counter
can be changed on its own, the rest held still; that’s what “forgets” quietly assumes.
The machine I build later is such a space, and it has a checked pair of its own: two
runs with the same window, one paid and one not (Theorem 16.14).)

Be careful what that doesn’t say. It says neither part can be dropped. It doesn’t say
a window showing both is the smallest window that works, because nothing here
orders windows, so there’s nothing for it to be smallest in. And it’s about reading the
counter back. Which step paid is the harder question, and it’s the next section’s.

7 Windows and shadows
I left you with the stick split in half and asked what happens if you can only ever see
one half through a window that doesn’t show the notches, and with a harder question
under that one: can you tell, from outside, which step paid? This section is about
windows. It’s a section where the mathematics is so small that I’m going to state it in
full and then spend most of the pages on what it’s not, because the smallness is the
trap: the fact is a one-liner and it’s tempting to climb over it with cleverness, and you
can’t, and seeing why you can’t is the content.

7.1 A cave, and the people who got good at it
This one is Plato’s, and the part I need is near the end. In the seventh book of the
Republic, Plato has Socrates, the main speaker of the dialogue, describe prisoners
chained in a cave since childhood, facing a wall, with a fire behind them and people
carrying objects along a walkway between the fire and their backs. All the prisoners
have ever seen is the shadows on the wall. To them, Socrates says, the truth would be


                                          147
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


nothing but those shadows. Further on, Socrates reads the story out himself: the cave
is the world of sight, and the climb out of it is the soul’s climb toward what’s really
there. So a real world hidden from anyone who only looks is in the story on purpose,
and Plato put it there. It still isn’t the part I need.

What I need comes a little before that reading, when one prisoner, freed and taken
up into the daylight, thinks back to the cave. The prisoners, Socrates says, hand
out honours to whoever is quickest at spotting the shadows as they pass and best at
guessing which comes next. Read that again. The prisoners get good at it. They build a
whole science of shadows, with experts and prizes, and it works, on shadows. What
they can’t do is say anything about a carried object that leaves no mark on the wall.
Not because they’re stupid. Because the information isn’t on the wall. Skill inside a
window doesn’t reach past the window, no matter how much skill. That’s the fact.
Plato dressed it as a lesson about education, and it is one, but strip the dressing and
it’s a sentence about functions, and it’s going to be the whole section.

7.2 The shadow of a cube
Do this one tonight with a lamp and a flat wall. Keep the lamp well back, hold a cube
face-on with its face parallel to the wall, and mark the outline of its shadow. Replace
it with square card and adjust the card’s size or distance until the outlines match as
closely as you can judge. Show your partner only that outline. It does not tell them
whether the object has thickness. For the exact mathematical version, take parallel
light rays and let the window report only the silhouette: an aligned cube and a square
face of the same size then give exactly the same square. Ask them, and they’ll tell
you, truthfully, that they can’t know, and if they’re honest they’ll also tell you that no
amount of staring at that square will change it.

Now turn each a quarter turn about its vertical centre line. The card’s shadow becomes
a narrow edge; the cube still casts a broad face. With ideal parallel rays and zero-
thickness card, those are exactly a line and a square. Now the wall-watcher knows.
What changed? Not their cleverness. The window. A second look from a different
angle is a bigger window than one look, and what bought it was the turn. Edwin
Abbott wrote a novel about a window like this in 1884, Flatland. A Flatlander never
sees a shape. Abbott’s narrator says it in his first section: nothing was visible to them,
or could be, except straight lines. Put a coin flat on a table and lower your eye to
the table’s edge, and the coin turns into a line; that’s the whole view. What gives a
Flatlander anything more is fog. A line that’s near is bright and a line that runs off
into the fog goes dim, so a trained eye can read a triangle or a pentagon off how fast
the brightness fades toward the ends. The training takes time and money, and in the
story only people with money get it. That’s a window that got bigger, and it was paid
for in time.

Then a sphere comes through the narrator’s plane. What his eye gets is a line whose
ends fade too fast for any flat figure he knows, changing size in a way no flat figure


                                           148
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


could. He only settles that it’s a circle by feeling it, and the circle grows from a point to
its widest and shrinks back to nothing as the sphere rises through. From one slice he
can’t put a sphere together. From the slices one after another, seen and felt and argued
over, he starts to. The escape from a window is never “think harder.” It’s always “a
different window,” and a different window that answers the question always has to
show apart two states the old one showed alike; that’s Theorem 7.1 below, applied to
the new window. In every story here, getting that window cost something: a turn, a
second look, training, time. What a change of window costs in general is a separate
question, and no theorem in this section prices it.

Who was Edwin Abbott? Not a mathematician by trade. He was headmaster of the
City of London School for twenty-four years, a clergyman, and the author of more
than forty books, a Shakespeare grammar among them. He put Flatland out under
the name “A Square.” His full name was Edwin Abbott Abbott, two A’s, and the pen
name may be a joke on that, A squared; nice if true, but take it as a lead. Here’s the
part I like best, from a sketch of his life on the geometer Thomas Banchoff’s pages:
Flatland, by far the most read thing he wrote, isn’t mentioned at all in his obituary in
the London Times or in his entry in the Dictionary of National Biography. The official
record of the man was a window too: it showed the headmaster and the grammarian
and left out the one book people still read. That changes nothing in the argument. It’s
the argument, acted out by an obituary. (Flatland already turned up in Section 1, where
the hunch behind this book started, and in the opening section, The point, which first
told the sphere’s visit.)

7.3 The whole fact, in one paragraph
Here’s the mathematics, and I promise it’s all of it. You have a set of states, the real
things. You have a window, which is a function that takes a state and gives you what
you can see of it: the shadow, the slice, the half-stick without notches. And you have a
question about the state, which is also a function: it takes a state and gives an answer.
The thing you want is a decoder: a rule that takes what you can see and gives the right
answer to the question, every time. When does one exist?

Think about two states that cast the same shadow. The decoder sees the same shadow
for both, so it gives the same answer for both. So if the question has different answers
on those two states, the decoder is wrong on at least one of them, and there’s nothing it
can do about it, because it never saw the difference. That’s the whole fact. If a decoder
exists, then the question must already give the same answer on every pair of states
that look the same through the window. Mathematicians call the set of states that cast
one particular shadow the fibre over that shadow (think of the shadow as a point on
the wall and the fibre as the bundle of all the things that could have cast it), and the
sentence is: a decoder exists only if the question is constant on every fibre. That’s the
theorem just below, and the “only if” is the direction that bites. The other direction,
“if the question is constant on fibres then a decoder exists,” is true too, but it needs you
to be handed, for every possible shadow, one actual state that casts it, so you can look

                                            149
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


up the answer there, and the handing is not free either, since someone has to supply
a representative for every shadow. (You can always fill a gap with a default answer.
The default doesn’t recover what was really there.)

Exactly. Let S be any set of states, V any set of views, w : S → V a window, and
q : S → A a question with answers in any set A. A decoder is a function d : V → A with
d(w(s)) = q(s) for every state s. The question is constant on fibres when w(s) = w(s′ )
implies q(s) = q(s′ ).


Theorem 7.1 (Decoders need constant fibres). If a decoder exists, the question is constant
on fibres. Conversely, if the question is constant on fibres and you are handed, for every view
v, a state r (v) with w(r (v)) = v, then d(v) = q(r (v)) is a decoder.

Proof. If w(s) = w(s′ ) then q(s) = d(w(s)) = d(w(s′ )) = q(s′ ). Conversely, d(w(s)) =
q(r (w(s))), and r (w(s)) has the same view as s, so by constancy its answer is q(s).

The result holds for arbitrary sets of states and observations.

Try the smallest case, by hand, because it’ll keep coming back. A state is a pair: a
position, 0 or 1, and a hidden flag, up or down. The window shows the position only.
Two moves from (0, down): one sets the position to 1 and raises the flag; the other sets
the position to 1 and leaves the flag alone. Both land on position 1. Now write down
every possible decoder from “what I see” to “is the flag up”: there are exactly four
functions from two positions to two answers. Check each against both results. None
of the four gets both right, because both results show position 1 and one has the flag
up and one doesn’t. That exhaustive check is the theorem on this example; the general
statement is the one-line argument above, and that’s the one that carries the weight.
There’s no fifth function hiding somewhere.

7.4 People who found this on their own
The fact is so plain that it got discovered separately in every field that has to deal with
seeing part of something, and I want to lay them beside each other, because that’s the
kind of evidence I trust: people who’d never met kept walking into the same wall.

In 1956 Edward Moore, working on the small switching machines that became com-
puter hardware, asked when an experimenter who can only feed a machine inputs
and watch its outputs can tell two of its internal states apart. His answer gave a
precise meaning to “indistinguishable from outside,” and a theorem with a sting in
it: even when every pair of states can be told apart by some experiment, there are
machines where no single experiment tells you which state you started in. What you
can always do is run an experiment after which you know which state you’re in now.
In 1960 Rudolf Kalman, whose filter went on to aerospace and industry, asked the
same question for continuous systems, called it observability, and gave a test (a matrix
rank, which you can compute) for whether watching the output over time pins down


                                             150
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


the internal state. His unobservable states are exactly a fibre: states whose difference
never reaches the output, and never will, however long you watch. That second half
took me longest to take in. More samples help only when the states eventually show
different outputs. States in the same fibre of the whole observation history remain indis-
tinguishable. Try it on a car: if your only instrument is the speedometer, two cars a
mile apart at the same speed read the same forever, and nothing on that dial will ever
tell you which mile marker either one started at. Read the mile markers instead and,
over time, you recover both position and speed. Same car, different window.

Where did Kalman’s filter go first, before aerospace and industry at large? Toward
the Moon. In the autumn of 1960 Kalman called an acquaintance, Stanley Schmidt, at
NASA’s Ames Research Center, and came to visit, not knowing what Schmidt’s group
was working on. The group, a branch with eight people doing the analysis, was stuck
on how a spacecraft going around the Moon and back could work out where it was
from what its crew could measure through an optical sight: a few angles to the Earth
and the Moon. That’s a window problem with a capsule in it. The state is position and
velocity, the view is a handful of angles, and the job is to keep a running best guess
at the state from a sequence of views. Kalman presented his new filtering paper to
them, and with real work (their problem wasn’t linear and his theory was) it fit, and it
went into the feasibility studies for navigating Apollo. Leonard McGee, of Schmidt’s
group at Ames, and Schmidt, telling the story in 1985, call it a fortunate sequence of
events and say the solution might have gone undiscovered but for that meeting. What
it changes: it shows the limit from the useful side. The filter didn’t make the angles
show more. It made a sequence of views, over time, pin down the state, and it can
only do that when the state is observable from those views, which is Kalman’s own
condition. That’s the mile markers. A cleverer speedometer would never have got
there.

In 1977 Patrick and Radhia Cousot built a whole discipline of program analysis, called
abstract interpretation, on throwing information away on purpose. You run the pro-
gram over coarse descriptions of its values, and the exact values never enter. And you
accept that the answer you get has to be true of every real value the coarse description
could stand for. For example, an input known only to lie between −1 and 1 has a
square between 0 and 1; the interval does not tell you its exact square. That is a sound
bound over the hidden possibilities. Exact recovery would require the stronger con-
dition of fibre constancy. And in 1970 Edgar Codd, inventing the relational database,
made programs independent of how the data is stored, and the relational systems
that followed gave users views, deliberately partial windows onto the stored data. A
decade after Codd, in 1981, two database researchers, François Bancilhon and Nicolas
Spyratos, gave the view-update problem an exact semantics. The problem is this: if a
user changes what they see through a view, which of the many underlying states that
cast that view should the database move to? Several are legitimate. The fibre, from
the writing side.



                                           151
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


Two more fields have the fact as a founding definition. In the theory of knowledge,
what an agent knows is modelled by a partition of the possible states into cells, the
states it can’t tell apart, and it knows a fact at a state exactly when the fact holds at
every state in that state’s cell. The economist and game theorist Robert Aumann used
that model in 1976 to prove that two people who start from the same prior, and whose
estimates of an event’s chance are common knowledge, can’t agree to disagree; the
computer scientists Ronald Fagin, Joseph Halpern, Yoram Moses and Moshe Vardi
built a whole logic of knowledge on the same partitions in Reasoning About Knowledge
(1995). Theorem 7.1 is that model with the cells written as fibres: a window knows
the answer to a question exactly when the question is constant on its cell. And in
computer security, the computer scientists Joseph Goguen and José Meseguer defined
noninterference in 1982: one group of users doesn’t interfere with another when nothing
the first group does changes what the second can see. A window that can’t see the
counter is the counter not interfering with the window’s view, and the clerk below is
what that costs.

And Parnas, from Section 2, hid things on purpose: a module is characterised by the
design decision it hides from its callers. Hiding is a window. The caller can’t later read
back what was hidden, including the things it later wishes it could check, and that’s
the price side of the coin whose benefit side Parnas was selling. None of these people
were doing philosophy. They were trying to build filters, databases, compilers, and
modules, and the wall is the same wall in each.

One more, from information theory. Oliver Kosut, at Arizona State, and Jörg Kliewer,
at the New Jersey Institute of Technology, two information theorists, asked in 2018
when a receiver on a channel with a possible attacker, and no shared key, can always
either get the message right or notice the attacker. The answer is all or nothing: the
rate is zero, or it’s everything the channel would carry with no attacker at all, and
which one depends on a condition they call overwritability, that the attacker can make
what the receiver sees look exactly like an honest transmission of some other message.
That’s a printer, a way to put the same thing in the window without the event behind
it. The fibre fact is their condition in its plainest form, with the probabilities taken out.

And one from machine learning, where the two computers turn up with a lawyer
attached. Four machine-learning security researchers at the University of Toronto and
the Vector Institute, Anvith Thudi, Hengrui Jia, Ilia Shumailov and Nicolas Papernot,
asked in 2022 how a company could prove a trained model had forgotten someone’s
data, and found that the same model can come out of different training sets, so the
finished model can’t show whether a point was used or removed. The only claim they
found you can audit is about the procedure that was run. Same wall: the finished state
is a window, and what happened is in the run.

Philosophers who study testimony, which is the trade of being told things, have the
same wall from the other side. Read one after another they blurred into a list of


                                            152
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


opinions for me, and the list didn’t tell me anything until I built a picture that showed
where each one sits. So here’s the picture first.

Somebody passes you a note across a room. It says the answer to question seven is
42. What crossed the room? Ink. Whatever made the writer believe 42 stayed on their
side: the working-out, how careful they were, whether they knew or guessed. Pull
that apart and there are five things in play: the claim on the paper, the writer’s head,
whatever process got the writer there, the trip across the room, and your head at the
other end. Every position I found puts its weight on one of those five. Once I saw that,
they stopped being a list and became a map, and the map has connections the list hid.

The two ends of it are Locke and Burge, and they’re the same dial turned opposite
ways. The philosopher John Locke, in the first book of his Essay in 1690, says believing
something because someone with authority said it isn’t knowing it. If the reason
didn’t cross the room, you don’t have it. Tyler Burge, a philosopher of mind and
knowledge at UCLA, argued in 1993 that you’re entitled to accept what you’re told, if
it’s presented as true and it makes sense to you, unless you have a reason not to. Locke
says only ink crossed, so you’ve got nothing. Burge says the ink comes with a default,
and the default holds until something knocks it over. I get the pull of Burge. Nobody
could get through a day checking every note. But a default anybody can trigger by
writing something sensible is a free record, the thing this book keeps refusing, so on
that dial the book sits at Locke’s end. And sitting there has a price: staying there
means carrying the check across the room every time.

Jennifer Lackey, a philosopher at Northwestern who has spent much of her work
on testimony, cuts the wire between the writer’s head and what arrives. Her case,
from 2008, is a teacher who doesn’t believe the theory she’s required to teach, and
her students come away knowing it anyway. I went back and forth on whether those
students really know it, and I haven’t settled it. But look at where the case cuts. If
it’s right, what arrives at your end never had to be believed at the other end, and the
writer’s head drops out of the map. Sanford Goldberg, also at Northwestern, moves
the weight one more place over, onto the process. In 2010 he argued that whether
your word justifies me can depend on how reliable the processes behind your word
were, which sit outside my head. That one took me a few reads. What I think he’s
saying is that part of my reason for believing you lives in you, in machinery I can’t
see, and he’s fine with that. I’m not, quite, and why I’m not is why this book exists:
machinery I can’t see is machinery I can’t check. Christoph Jäger and Nicholas Shackel,
philosophers at Innsbruck and Cardiff, built a model of degrees of belief in 2025 in
which the writer knowing is neither necessary nor sufficient for the reader to know.
That lands where Lackey’s teacher landed, from a completely different direction, a
story on one side and a calculation on the other. Agreement like that I trust more than
either piece alone, as long as I remember a model only shows what can happen inside
its own rules.



                                          153
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


Then two sets of people who drew arrows. Wesley Holliday, a logician then at Stanford,
put testimony into a logic of belief change in 2009, with an authority graph recording
whose word each agent takes and rules for what hearing a speaker does to a belief.
I’ve only read a summary of Holliday’s paper, so I’m taking that on somebody’s word,
which is a funny thing to admit in this paragraph. Security people had drawn the same
kind of arrow two decades earlier. In the logic of authentication of Michael Burrows,
Martin Abadi and Roger Needham (1990), two computer scientists at Digital’s research
lab in Palo Alto and one at Cambridge, if I believe an authority has jurisdiction over a
statement and I believe the authority holds it, I believe it. Set that beside Burge and
it’s his default with one change: the authority is named before the note arrives. That
one change is the whole difference. Burge’s default trusts whoever is writing. Theirs
trusts only a writer you picked in advance.

Kenny Easwaran is the one who goes after what crosses the room itself. He’s a philoso-
pher who works on probability and on how mathematicians know things, and in 2009
he took up a question I’d never have thought to ask. The philosopher Don Fallis had
pressed it in a series of papers: why will mathematicians accept a proof that’s long
and complicated, or partly carried out by a computer, and turn down a probabilistic
one that can be far more certain? That looked backwards to me at first. More certain
should win. Easwaran’s answer is a property he calls transferability. A deductive proof
puts the reason on the paper. Every step crosses the room, so you can learn from
the writer without trusting the writer. A probabilistic proof leaves the reason behind
and sends only the writer’s word about what the dice did. Once I saw it that way it
stopped looking backwards, and it’s the cleanest statement I found of what this book
does: make the reason cross the room, carry the thing, and run the check on your own
side. That reading is mine. His subject is proofs passed between mathematicians, so if
it’s wrong, it’s wrong on me.

Now push on my own spot on the map, because it gives. The book carries the check
across the room, but the check runs on a checker, and I trust the checker because it was
proved honest once, outside every run. That’s a jurisdiction rule. It’s Burrows, Abadi
and Needham’s arrow with the checker as the named authority, so I’m not sitting at
Locke’s end as cleanly as I’d like. What I can say is that my authority was picked in
advance, that it’s a single named thing while Burge trusts every writer, and that its
honesty rests on a proof you can examine yourself. That’s a smaller trust than Burge’s,
and a different kind from Goldberg’s, because the machinery is out where you can
look at it. It isn’t zero, so I’m pointing at it here myself.

Only Burrows, Abadi and Needham write about machines passing messages, and
even they write about the computers as if the computers held beliefs. The rest are
about what survives the trip from one head to another. Either way it’s the copier’s
problem, with philosophers’ names on it and, in one case, computer scientists’.

Distributed-systems people hit the wall too, and one pair of them measured how far


                                          154
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


it goes. Their papers were a pile of acronyms to me until I put them all in one room.
People at desks work from one rulebook and pass slips to each other. Nobody sees
into anybody’s head; all anyone gets is the slips handed to them. Somebody may be
cheating. What can the honest ones do about it with nothing but slips?

Andreas Haeberlen, then at the Max Planck Institute for Software Systems in Saar-
brücken, and Petr Kuznetsov, then in Berlin, asked in 2009 which faults an outside
observer can detect at all. As I read their answer, it sorts cheating by where it sits. A
cheat can break the rulebook without changing any slip. A cheat can write a slip an
honest player could have written too, for all anyone holding it can tell. A cheat can
fail to send a slip that’s due, an omission fault, or send one the rulebook would never
produce, a commission fault. The first two, they argue, no algorithm can detect. The
last two can be caught, and they put a floor under how many messages the catching
costs, which I liked for obvious reasons. My first guess was that the classes ranked
how bad a fault is. They don’t. They rank how far the fault gets toward a slip, and the
first two are a fibre: an honest room and a crooked one that hand out the same slips.
That’s the fibre fact with an auditor attached.

Their group’s PeerReview system (Haeberlen, Kouznetsov, the same Kuznetsov
spelled another way, and Peter Druschel, the institute’s founding director, 2007) is
the ladder up to that wall: every node keeps a secure record of the messages it sent
and received, and a checker replays the record against a reference implementation,
a copy of the rulebook it can run, which exposes the faults a correct node got to see.
That’s close to the whole-state escape from the three escapes below, built: ship the log,
and the checker re-runs it. Close, because a log of slips stands in for a whole state only
if the rulebook can rebuild what a desk did from them, and only if the checker’s copy
of the rulebook is the right one.

The next three ask what you can say once you’re at the wall. Ralf Küsters, Tomasz
Truderung and Andreas Vogt, three security researchers at Trier, asked what a ver-
dict should hold. They gave in 2010 a general definition of accountability, a verdict
naming who misbehaved, and argued, with a proof inside their own definitions, that
verifiability, the property that an outsider can check a result, is a restricted form of it.
The way I read the restriction: verifiability says something went wrong, and account-
ability points at a desk. Radha Jagadeesan, Alan Jeffrey, Corin Pitcher and James Riely,
programming-language people at DePaul in Chicago and, for Jeffrey, Bell Labs, asked
when the verdict comes. They built in 2009 an operational model of systems that
enforce a policy after the fact by audit, and studied the trade between the power of
the auditor, the cost of the audit and what’s asked of the agents. Robert Künnemann,
Ilkan Esiyok and Michael Backes, at the CISPA security center in Saarbrücken, in 2019
made the idea a mechanized check, with Certificate Transparency (CT), the public
logging of the certificates web browsers trust, among their examples. As I understand
it, they did it by turning accountability into a property of the trace, the whole run.
That’s Thudi and his coauthors’ wall again: what happened is in the run.


                                            155
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


In September 2026 Timo Treitz, a student at Saarland University, and Künnemann gave
CT the full treatment (Section 14 has my fragment of it) and found, in their model,
that plain CT gives accountability only if the log is assumed honest, an assumption
the SCT auditing extension (SCT is the signed certificate timestamp a log hands out)
can drop and the gossiping extension can’t. In my room, CT hands PeerReview’s log
