of slips to a third party to keep. An honest log is the commitment bit from the three
escapes below, with a name on the contract: somebody’s promise that the bit is set
when, and only when, the claim holds, trusted at the step.

Turn the room on me and it gives twice. A flag raised for free that never reaches the
window is Haeberlen and Kuznetsov’s first class, and no auditor outside catches it;
that’s the clerk’s trouble, next. My way out is PeerReview’s, and it trusts a copy of the
rulebook too: the checker, proved honest once, outside every run. And every verdict
in this book is accept or reject on one claim. It never points at a desk. In Küsters,
Truderung and Vogt’s terms that’s the restricted form, and the rest of accountability
isn’t here.

7.5 The clerk with two photographs
Now point it at the counter, because that’s why this section is here. Suppose you want
to bill for raising the flag, exactly: at least one mark for every step that raises it, and
nothing for a step that doesn’t. And suppose the person doing the billing is a clerk
who sees only a window on the state, a photograph before the step and a photograph
after. The clerk’s bill is a function of the two photographs. Can the clerk bill exactly?

Not if the window has the wrong kind of blind spot. Here’s why, and it’s the cube
again. Suppose there are two steps that give the clerk the same before-photo and the
same after-photo, and one of them raised the flag and the other didn’t. (The two-move
toy above is exactly such a pair; so are “a stamp goes onto a document inside a closed
drawer” and “someone opens and closes the drawer.”) The clerk has one bill for that
pair of photographs. If the bill is at least one, it overcharges the step that didn’t raise
the flag. If it’s zero, it undercharges the step that did. Any bill that never misses a raise
bills something that wasn’t a raise, and no bill from those photographs is exact. The
fix is the plain one: put the flag in the photograph. If the window shows the reading,
then “one when the reading goes from down to up, zero otherwise” is exact, and such
a window has no pair like the one above. That’s enough. It isn’t the only way: a
window can hide the flag and still have no colliding pair, in which case a bill from the
photographs can be exact; what the argument proves in the other direction is only that
a colliding pair rules exact pricing out. And “exact” here means rise-only pricing: at
least one on every step that raises the flag, nothing on any step that doesn’t. That’s all
the clerk’s problem needs, and the bill “one for a raise, zero otherwise” meets it. So
it’s exact about which steps get charged. It isn’t exact about how much, and it doesn’t
pick out one bill: “two for a raise, zero otherwise” meets it too. Pinning the bill down
takes one more demand, a ceiling: over any run, the total never exceeds the number
of raises. With the floor and that ceiling there’s exactly one bill left, one per raise and

                                            156
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


zero otherwise; that’s an if and only if for any system whose bill is decided step by
step: apply the ceiling to a one-step run. These are stated for any states and any steps.
The window version, the cube theorem with a price in place of a decoder, comes next.

Same clerk, now in symbols, so you can check every word I just used. Take the five
parts of Section 3 with a window w : S → V, and say a step (s, i ) raises the flag
when cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes. A price is any function of a state and
a move. It meets the floor when every raise costs at least one, and never overcharges
when every non-raise costs zero; together, it is exact (about which steps are charged;
the amount is pinned only by the whole-run ceiling above). A window price is one
computed from the two photographs only: price(s, i ) = b(w(s), w(step(s, i ))) for some
bill b : V × V → N. A collision is two steps (s1 , i1 ) and (s2 , i2 ) with w(s1 ) = w(s2 ) and
w(step(s1 , i1 )) = w(step(s2 , i2 )), the first a raise and the second not.


Observation 7.2 (No exact window price across a collision). If the window has a collision,
every window price that meets the floor charges at least one on some step that is not a raise; so
no window price is exact. If instead the reading is a function of the view, cert(s) = r (w(s))
for some r, then the window price “one when r goes from no to yes, zero otherwise” is exact,
and the window has no collision.

Proof. Across a collision both steps get the same bill b(v, v′ ). The floor makes it at least
one because the first step is a raise; the second step, not a raise, pays it. If the reading
is r of the view, the window price reads the raise directly, and two steps with the same
photographs either both raise or both don’t, so there’s no collision.

So the exact price of raising the flag lives in the step itself, or in a window with no
colliding pair, and a window that shows the flag is the plainest such window. A
window that contains a pair like that one can’t carry it. Whether a particular machine
has such a pair, for a particular window, has to be checked machine by machine and
window by window; the theorem only tells you what a pair does once you’ve found
one.

There’s a tidy way to say what the best window prices are, and it isn’t mine. Start with
the charge one for a raise and zero otherwise. Give each attainable pair of before-and-
after photographs the highest charge of any step that casts that pair, and you have the
cheapest window price that never undercharges; give it the lowest, and you have the
dearest one that never overcharges. Those two are the “there is” and “for all” of logic
taken along the window, which F. William Lawvere, an American mathematician best
known for his work in category theory, the mathematics of maps between structures,
showed in 1969 (“Adjointness in foundations”) are the two adjoints of pulling a state-
ment back along a map. Four researchers at the University of Calgary, Robin Cockett,
Isabelle Geng, Carlo Maria Scandolo and Priyaa Srinivasan (2023), used the same
move, as Kan extensions, to extend resource measures along a map. In those terms



                                              157
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


the theorem says that an exact window price exists exactly when the two coincide on
every pair of photographs, and a collision pulls them apart. That restatement is mine,
and nothing checks it.

Control engineers have been hunting pairs like that for a long time, under other
names. Discrete-event systems is the field of machines that jump from state to state
on events, some of which an outside observer sees and some of which it doesn’t. In
1995 five engineers, Meera Sampath, Raja Sengupta, Stéphane Lafortune and Demos-
thenis Teneketzis of the University of Michigan and Kasim Sinnamohideen of Johnson
Controls, asked when such an observer can always work out, from what it sees, that
a hidden fault event has happened, within a bounded number of further steps. They
called that diagnosability and gave a test for it on finite machines. Anooshiravan Sa-
boori, then a doctoral student at the University of Illinois, and Christoforos Hadjicostis,
the engineer who supervised his doctorate there, asked in 2007 the question the other
way round, for secrets: a system is opaque when an observer can never be sure it’s in a
secret state, because some run outside the secret always looks the same. Read the raise
as the hidden event and the window as what the observer sees. Then a collision is the
raise failing to be diagnosable with no delay allowed, and a window that can’t tell the
flag is the flag’s state being opaque to it (Theorem 16.15, later, is that, for the small
machine). That’s my reading; they don’t put it that way. Their versions are richer than
mine: they allow delays, look at whole runs, and come with algorithms. What this
section adds is only the price: what a bill computed through the window does across
one such pair.

Why can’t the clerk just watch the step itself? A clerk who does, who sees the whole
state before and the move, bills exactly with no trouble at all: “one for a raise” is a
function of exactly those two things, and it’s the step price above. So the collision bites
an observer who doesn’t see the step, or who’s handed an account of the step and can’t
trust the account. That second kind is the opening chapter’s trace problem come back.
If the names of the moves arrive in a log the program wrote, the program can write
whatever names it likes, and a clerk reading that log is reading one more window, one
the program painted. Seeing the move means being underneath the program, where
the step is.

7.6 The three escapes, and what each one costs
Suppose you’re the person outside, and you want to be convinced that a run paid. The
window you’ve got doesn’t show the counter. Here’s how bad that is, in the smallest
setting I can build. Take a counter machine from Section 6, give its states a position
and a flag as well, and give it a window that shows the position and nothing else.
Now take two runs from the same start, with the position at 0, the flag down and
the counter at 0. Run A makes one move that raises the flag, costs one, and lands at
position 1; its counter reads 1. Run B makes one move that does nothing but step to
position 1, at cost zero; its counter reads 0. Call the pair of photographs, position 0
then position 1, the transcript. Both runs leave exactly that transcript. A verifier is a

                                           158
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


rule that takes a transcript and says accept or reject. It is sound when every transcript
it accepts comes only from states where the claim holds, and complete when every
transcript from a state where the claim holds is accepted. The claim is “the counter is
1.”

No verifier on these transcripts is both, and the proof is three lines. Suppose one were
both. Run A ends with the counter at 1 and leaves the transcript, so completeness says
the verifier accepts it. Now soundness, on that same accepted transcript: every state
that leaves it satisfies the claim, and run B’s end state leaves it. So run B’s counter is 1.
It is 0. That’s the cube again, with a verdict in place of an answer: a verifier sees only
what the window kept, and two states that the window can’t tell apart get one verdict
between them.

Now dress the transcript up. Take any richer kind of transcript, with a way to squash
one down to its bare photographs, and say a verifier on the rich ones only looks at the
bare part when two rich transcripts that squash to the same photographs always get
the same verdict. If some rich transcript left by run A and some rich transcript left by
run B squash to the same photographs, then no verifier that only looks at the bare part
is sound and complete either: it gives those two the same verdict, completeness makes
that verdict accept, and soundness then lies about run B. Notice what that needs. The
pair has to survive into the richer kind of transcript; a design whose extra part tells
A from B doesn’t meet the premise, and the argument says nothing about it. So it
doesn’t classify every transcript design. What it says is that a verifier that only reads
what the bare window keeps fails on that pair.

Economists got to the same wall by another road. Jerry Green and Jean-Jacques Laffont
(1986) asked what a mechanism can do when people can claim about themselves only
what their situation lets them back up, and Jesse Bull and Joel Watson (2007) built that
into mechanism design as hard evidence. In their terms, an audit can tell apart only the
cases the evidence on offer tells apart. That’s the cube with a ledger in it.

What can you do? Here are three things that work, and nothing says they’re the only
ones; as far as I can tell, cryptography uses all three. Each rests on something you
have to trust, and I’ll say what, because “a price” in the counter’s sense is not what
any of them costs.

You can be shown the whole state. Then there’s nothing to decode; you read the counter
off the state. The price is trust: you have to believe the state you were shown is the
state there was.

You can be shown a commitment: the ordinary window plus one extra bit that is set
when, and only when, the claim holds (here, that the counter reads exactly one).
Reading that bit gives a verifier that is sound and complete for that claim, if the
bit is binding (set only when the claim holds) and honest (set whenever it holds).
The trust is in those two “ifs,” which are a contract about who can set the bit. The


                                            159
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


contract can be met, and a bit anyone can set breaks it, which is the one-line version of
why an unsigned log is just another window. Nothing in that picture has a hardness
assumption in it; whether a real commitment scheme meets the contract is a question
for cryptography, and this book doesn’t take it up. (A clash of words I should own:
“commitment” here is the cryptographers’ word, something bound to a claim, which in
their schemes also hides the claim until it’s opened, and this bit doesn’t bother hiding
anything. The opening chapter’s commit is a different act, the closing of a question.
Same word, two jobs. The sealed envelope has an exact theory of its own. Three
information theorists, Andreas Winter, then at Bristol, and Anderson Nascimento
and Hideki Imai, then at Tokyo, found in 2003 the best rate at which a noisy channel
can carry commitments, and the cryptographers Claude Crépeau, Rafael Dowsley
and Nascimento (2020) worked out how that rate drops as the committer gets some
control over the noise, which is the opening chapter’s “take the pen away from the
program” with a formula on it.) In 1999 the cryptographers Bruce Schneier and John
Kelsey worked out how to make a log that an intruder who takes over the machine
can’t quietly rewrite, and the honest scope in their paper is the honest scope here: it
protects what was written before the break-in, through keys, and nothing after. Two
cryptographers at the University of California, San Diego, Mihir Bellare and Bennet
Yee, had named that property forward integrity in a 1997 report and proved their
scheme has it. Point it at an AI agent that keeps its own log of what it did, and the
line moves to the very start: an agent that writes the wrong thing from its first step is
on the far side of the break-in for the whole log. A 2026 preprint on tamper-evident
audit trails for such agents, built from hashes anchored on a public blockchain, is even
called Agent Flight Recorder (by Laurent Bindschaedler, of the Max Planck Institute
for Software Systems, and Quentin Botha and Christoph Siebenbrunner, of the Vienna
University of Economics and Business), which is the opening chapter’s word, and the
opening chapter’s fingerprint paragraph is the part of this book that applies to it.

Or you can ask. Interaction: the outside party gets to put a question and gets an
answer that pins the thing down. The price is the honesty of the answerer; a liar’s
answer is another shadow. Moore’s experimenter chose inputs; the zero-knowledge
proofs of the cryptographers Shafi Goldwasser, Silvio Micali and Charles Rackoff in
1985 are the refined form, where a verifier is convinced by a conversation designed
to cut exactly the line between true and false and nothing else, with a mathematical
guarantee against a cheating prover. I mention zero-knowledge to say what I’m not
claiming: the asking in this section is one round, with one fixed question (“tell me
your counter”), and nothing in it models a cheating prover; the honesty is assumed,
and nothing enforces it. That’s a toy of the real thing, and I’m not going to let the
real thing’s reputation stand behind the toy. (Joseph Halpern, Yoram Moses and Mark
Tuttle, computer scientists who work on reasoning about knowledge in distributed
systems, gave zero knowledge a knowledge-based analysis in 1988, which is where
I’d start for the logic of it.)



                                          160
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


The real thing even has a cave in it, which after Plato I can’t resist. In a paper for
the 1989 CRYPTO conference called “How to Explain Zero-Knowledge Protocols to
Your Children,” two cryptographers, Jean-Jacques Quisquater of Philips Research and
Louis Guillou of the French telecommunications lab CCETT, with their families and
Tom Berson of Anagram Laboratories on the byline, told it as Ali Baba’s cave: a ring-
shaped tunnel with a magic door at the back that opens only for a secret word. Peggy
goes in down one side while Victor waits outside; then Victor walks to the fork and
shouts which side she should come out of. If she knows the word, she always can.
If she doesn’t, she gets away with it only when Victor happens to call the side she
went in. Play it at the table with a coin for Victor’s shout: one round, a cheat gets
through half the time; twenty rounds, about one time in a million. And here’s the
part that belongs in this section. In the story, Victor ends up convinced, but a video of
the whole thing convinces nobody else, because a staged run, where the two agreed
beforehand which sides he’d shout, makes exactly the same recording. The recording
is a window, and the real run and the fake one cast the same shadow. That’s the cube
in the cryptographers’ favourite bedtime story, and it’s why the real thing has to ask
live, many times, against a prover who might be lying: everything my one round
leaves out.

Each escape is a window with something added: the whole state, a bound bit, an
honest answer. None of them is “a smarter verifier on the old window.” Cleverness
lives on the wrong side of the projection. What’s true of any machine is the cube.

Here are the three constructions exactly, for the pair above, with the relations written
down. The relation matters: it says which state a transcript is allowed to describe. If
it quietly assumes a truthful answer, then a verifier sound for it is sound only against
honest answerers, and it says nothing about a liar. Write A and B for the states runs A
and B end at, µ for the counter, and τ for their shared transcript.


Definition 7.1 (Three richer transcripts and their explanations). Keep the states A, B
and their shared bare transcript τ, with µ( A) = 1 and µ( B) = 0. Write E0 (s, t) for
t = τ ∧ (s = A ∨ s = B). The claim is µ(s) = 1.

A full-state transcript is a finite list t of states. Define ES (s, t) to mean that t is nonempty
and its last entry is s. The verifier rejects the empty list; otherwise it accepts exactly
when the last entry’s counter is 1.

A commitment transcript is a pair (t, b) of a bare transcript and a Boolean. For any
chosen explanation relation EC , the commitment contract is the pair of implications, for
all s, t, b:
                       EC (s, (t, b)) ∧ b = true =⇒ µ(s) = 1,

                           EC (s, (t, b)) ∧ µ(s) = 1 =⇒ b = true.

These are binding and honesty, respectively. The verifier accepts exactly when b is


                                              161
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


true. One relation meeting the contract is EH (s, (t, b)) ⇐⇒ E0 (s, t) ∧ (b = true ⇐⇒
µ ( s ) = 1).

A response transcript is a pair (t, r ) of a bare transcript and a natural number. Define
E I (s, (t, r )) ⇐⇒ µ(s) = r. The verifier accepts exactly when r = 1. This relation
imposes no condition on the bare component t; the response alone carries its entire
truth condition.

Each construction assigns verification the constant abstract cost 1.


Theorem 7.3 (Three conditional escapes). The full-state verifier is sound and complete
relative to ES . For every EC satisfying the commitment contract, the commitment verifier is
sound and complete relative to EC . The response verifier is sound and complete relative to
E I . Each has cost 1 under the stipulated cost assignment. The honest relation EH satisfies the
commitment contract; the unchecked relation EU (s, (t, b)) ⇐⇒ E0 (s, t) does not.

Proof. For the full-state verifier, an explaining state is precisely the last entry. Reading
that entry’s counter therefore accepts exactly when the explaining state’s counter is 1.
An empty transcript is rejected and has no explaining state.

For the commitment verifier, acceptance says b is true. Binding then gives the claim
for every explaining state, which is soundness. Conversely, honesty says that any
explaining state satisfying the claim has a true bit, which the verifier accepts. The
equivalence in EH gives both implications directly. Under EU , however, B explains
(τ, true) even though µ( B) = 0. That violates binding.

For the response verifier, explanation gives µ(s) = r. Acceptance adds r = 1, so
µ(s) = 1. Conversely, µ(s) = 1 and explanation give r = 1, hence acceptance. The
three cost claims follow from the assigned constant.

The argument holds for any pair like A and B, over arbitrary sets of states, claims,
transcripts and explanation relations; it uses only their claim values and their shared
transcript. A verifier sound and complete for the claim under an explanation relation
cannot look only at the bare part once two transcripts with that same bare part are
explained, one by a state with the claim and one by a state without it. The three
escapes use full states, a commitment satisfying the contract, or truthful responses.
The cost 1 in the definition above is not used in any of these arguments; it is a chosen
price.

On a real machine the collision is a theorem, and it doesn’t depend on the toy. Give a
run from a loaded start (Part IV’s word for a start at line 1 with the two counters set
to a and b, written (1, a, b)) the bare transcript made of a, b and the base window the
run ends with, and say a state explains a bare transcript when some run from that start
ends at it showing that window.



                                              162
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


Theorem 7.4 (No bare verifier on a Thiele-complete machine). Let a machine be Thiele-
complete through an interface (Definition 16.7). (1) No function from bare transcripts to
Booleans is both sound and complete, under that explanation relation, for the claim “the record
is up.” (2) There is a clean loaded state such that no function from bare transcripts to Booleans
is both sound and complete for the claim “the ledger is at least 3 above what it was at that start.”
(3) For the small machine of Part IV, whose moves CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY and
whose counter move DEC are defined there: a run CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY from the
loaded start (1, 0, 0), which ends with the ledger at 3, and three DECs of a zero counter from
the same start, which end with the ledger at 0, end with the same window, and no function on
bare transcripts is sound and complete for “the ledger reads 3.”

Proof. Observation 16.26(2) gives a loaded state and two runs from it that end with
the same window, one with the record up and one with it down, and, from one clean
loaded state, two runs with the same window, one whose ledger rose by at least 3 and
one made of free base moves that leaves the ledger where it started (that observation’s
proof builds it). Both end states explain the same bare transcript. A verifier complete
for the claim accepts that transcript, since a state where the claim holds explains it; a
verifier sound for the claim then makes the claim true of every state that explains it,
including the one where it’s false. That’s (1), and (2) is the same with the ledger: the
paid run’s end state satisfies the claim, and the free run’s doesn’t. For (3) the two runs
are written out in the statement: three moves land on line 4 in both runs with both
counters at 0, and the same two-state argument applies.

Put with the three escapes, the whole picture holds for every Thiele-complete machine
and for the small machine: the bare-transcript verifier doesn’t exist; the collision
survives into any richer transcript that keeps it, so no verifier that only reads its bare
part works either; a verifier on full states exists; one on the bare transcript with a
committed bit exists, sound and complete when the bit is honest, and the unchecked
bit breaks the contract; and one on a truthful response exists. The collision is a premise
of the richer-transcript half, and the contract is assumed; no fourth way is claimed to
be impossible, and no hardness is proved.

In the three escapes the collision is gone, and no trick did it: the extra information
pulls A and B apart. The full-state transcript shows the counter outright. The honest
commitment for A carries a true bit and the one for B a false bit. The honest responses
are 1 and 0. In none of the three is the verifier asked to tell identical inputs apart,
which was the impossible job.

Now the limit, and I’d rather say it before you find it. A list of states has no authen-
tication built into it, so nothing in it stops a liar from handing over whatever the
verifier wants to see. The commitment contract is assumed, and the unchecked bit
above is what happens when the assumption is dropped. The response relation only
allows a truthful counter value, so asking a question here does not buy resistance to a
cheating prover. And the cost 1 is an abstract price I wrote down. It doesn’t measure

                                               163
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


what it takes to authenticate a state, check a cryptographic proof or send a response.
What these three show is which extra distinctions a verifier can use. They are not an
adversary model, a security parameter or a hardness reduction.

So what would it take to make that commitment bit binding for real, against somebody
who wants to cheat? Cryptographers had to face that one in the open, and the place
I’d point is a short paper the computer scientist Manuel Blum, whose Turing Award
was for complexity theory and its use in cryptography, presented at the CRYPTO
meeting in 1981, “Coin Flipping by Telephone.” His setup: Alice and Bob have just
divorced, they live in different cities, and they want to flip a coin over the phone for
who gets the car, with nobody they both trust to do the flipping. If Alice flips and
announces, Bob has to take her word. If Bob calls it first, Alice can lie about how it
landed. Blum’s way out is for one side to commit first: send something that fixes the
choice without showing it, and open it only after the other side has called. And what
keeps that commitment binding isn’t anybody’s promise. It’s a bet that a certain kind
of big number is hard to factor. Push on that and you’re standing on the honest edge of
this subsection. In Blum’s protocol, binding is earned, on the condition that factoring
is hard. Here it’s written into the contract and assumed outright, and the unchecked
bit above shows what’s left without it. That’s why I won’t say these escapes beat a
cheater. Blum’s paper is the kind of thing it would take, and nothing like it is in this
chapter.

Now point the three escapes back at the record we have been constructing, because
that’s where they bite hardest. A record kept in a machine’s state is bits too. Hand
someone outside a copy of those bits with a note saying “the flag is up,” and they’re
reading a window: the run that really raised the flag and a box built to print that it did
cast the same shadow. So putting the record in the step answers “was this earned?” for
whoever can see the state and trusts the step that wrote it. For anybody else it moves
the question, from “did it run?” to “do I trust the box that says it ran?” Crossing that
line takes one of the escapes: the whole state, from a box you already trust; a bound
bit, which in practice means a signature over the record or a quote from measured
hardware (and Section 14 shows a quote vouches only for what was measured); or
asking, against a box that might lie, which is the cryptographers’ business. One more
relative deserves its name here, verifiable computation: the box hands back its answer
with a short proof that the answer is right, which a checker can verify without redoing
the work (Pinocchio, built in 2013 by the computer scientists Bryan Parno, Jon Howell,
Craig Gentry and Mariana Raykova), and proof-carrying data passes proofs like that
along a whole chain of parties who don’t trust each other (the computer scientists
Alessandro Chiesa and Eran Tromer, 2010). That’s the strongest export there is, and
notice what it exports: the claim. The history stays behind. The proof shows the
answer is right for that input. It doesn’t show which machine did the work, or when,
and any box with the input can make one. Nothing in this book supplies any of
these escapes. The model’s record is local to the machine that keeps it, and the small



                                           164
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


machine of Part IV keeps its record in its state with no signature on it at all.

7.7 What this isn’t
Three things this isn’t, and I’d rather take them off the table now.

It isn’t mysticism. Nothing here says the window is false or the state is unknowable.
The wall is a function, the objects are its inputs, and the only claim is that the function
isn’t one-to-one on the thing you asked about. A richer window recovers it. Plato’s
prisoners could have turned around.

Rice’s theorem is the neighbour this looks most like. It isn’t Rice’s theorem, though it
rhymes with it. The logician Henry Rice, in a paper of 1953, proved that no program
can decide any interesting property of what another program does from its code, and
a cousin of the fact here is that a run which hasn’t halted yet looks, so far, exactly like
one that never will. But Rice is about what’s computable. The cube is about what’s
there. The cube theorem holds for a toy with two states and nothing to compute;
the obstruction is missing information, and cleverness doesn’t come into it. I’d be
overclaiming if I let the famous theorem lend its weight to the small one.

And it isn’t “with enough data you can recover anything.” Kalman’s unobservable
states stay unobservable for all time. The question is never how much of the window
you’ve got. It’s which window.

The counter lives in the state, and whether anyone outside can read it depends entirely
on what they’re shown, and a window with a pair like that in it can’t price the flag
exactly, with any rule, ever. Which raises the question I’ve been pushing in front of
me since the buckets. Fine, the flag went up and was paid for and I can see it in the
right window. What does that entitle me to? A paid flag is a paid flag. What’s the
claim behind it, and when am I allowed to lean on it?

8 Structural entitlement
I keep writing the word “vouch” and then taking it back. Let me stop doing that and
say what it would take. A reading went from NO to YES, the toll charged the move
that did it (Section 3), maybe the reading stays up (Section 4 says what it costs to make
it stay), and the right window shows it (Section 7). Now: what is a later step allowed
to do because of that? That’s a different question from “is the thing true,” and the gap
between those two is the subject of this section, and I’d argue it’s the subject of most
of the arguments people have about evidence, so give me the long way round.

8.1 The coin that moved
Here’s an experiment you can run on a friend, and I’d ask you to actually run it,
because the feeling of it is the point. Put a coin under one of three cups while they
watch. Say, cup one. Send them out of the room. Move the coin to cup three. Then,
and this is the trick, put a second coin under cup one. Bring them back and ask: “Is
there a coin under cup one?”

                                           165
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


They say yes. They’re right; there is. And they have a reason: they watched you put
it there. True, and believed, and justified by what they saw. And it’s not knowledge,
and you can feel that it isn’t, because their reason points at a coin that left. The coin
that makes them right is not the coin they’re thinking of.

That’s the trap from the opening chapter, done with cups: Edmund Gettier’s three-
page paper from 1963, “Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?”, which broke a definition
of knowledge in about the time it takes to read it. The definition was that you know
something when it’s true, you believe it, and you’ve got good reasons. Gettier took
it from two philosophers of the 1950s, Roderick Chisholm and A. J. Ayer, and the
only place he mentions Plato is a footnote saying Plato “seems to be considering”
something like it in the Theaetetus. I’d assumed people had leaned on that definition
since Plato. As far as I can find, they hadn’t. The Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry
on the analysis of knowledge calls the idea that it was ever widely held “a bit of a
convenient fiction,” and Julien Dutant, a philosopher at King’s College London, wrote
a 2015 paper called “The Legend of the Justified True Belief Analysis” arguing that the
older tradition asked for something stronger: a mark on the belief that can’t be wrong.
I’ve read only summaries of Dutant’s paper, so take that last part as his, secondhand.
Gettier’s two cases, and the cups, show a belief that passes all three tests and still isn’t
knowledge, because the reasons and the fact aren’t connected; they just happen to
agree. Bertrand Russell had a related case in 1948: somebody looks at a stopped clock
at the one moment it happens to be right, and they’re right about the time, and they
know nothing.

Is 1963 the bottom? Not even close, and 1948 isn’t either. The Stanford Encyclopedia’s
entry on the analysis of knowledge, which is where I’d send you to check me, gives a
case from the eighth-century Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara: you’re looking for
water on a hot day, you see water ahead, it’s a mirage, and when you get there you
happen to find water under a rock. And one from Peter of Mantua, a logician of the
late fourteenth century who died in 1400 and whose Logica survives in manuscript:
Plato is running right next to you, you take him for Socrates, so you believe Socrates is
running, and Socrates is in fact running, in Rome, where you can’t see him. Older still?
Maybe. This is where the trail goes cold, which isn’t the same as where it ends. What
it changes is how much I trust the shape. People in different centuries, languages and
traditions kept building the same trap by hand: a reason that points at one thing, and
a truth that happens to be sitting on another.

What’s missing is a wire from the reason to the fact. Ask your friend what they’d need,
to be entitled to “there’s a coin under cup one,” and they’ll tell you: lift the cup. Not
“remember putting it there.” Lift it, now, and look. That lifting is an event, it happens
on the record, and after it the reason and the fact are the same object.




                                            166
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


8.2 Plato nearly had it
Who was Theaetetus, though? The dialogue is named for a real person, and I wanted
to know who. He was a mathematician. In the dialogue he’s a teenager, and he tells
Socrates that his teacher Theodorus had been showing them, one case at a time, that
the side of a square of area three, or five, and so on up to seventeen, can’t be named
by any fraction: the Pythagoreans’ diagonal from Section 2, done again case by case.
The young man’s idea was to stop going one case at a time and find one word for all
of them. Euclid’s tenth book, on lengths that share no common measure, is thought
to be largely his work, and he’s credited with being the first to study the eight-faced
and twenty-faced solids, the two Plato assigned to air and water in the Timaeus. The
dialogue opens with him being carried home to Athens from the army at Corinth,
badly wounded and sick with the dysentery going round the camp, barely alive; the
usual date is 369 BC. And the conversation itself has come down as a record. Euclid
of Megara (not the geometer) says he took notes as soon as he got home, filled them
out later, and had Socrates correct them whenever he came to Athens, and he has
the result read aloud. So the dialogue about what turns a true belief into knowledge
survives as a checked record of what was said. That changes nothing in the argument.
I just like that the book about knowledge is named for the man who took the diagonal
and made it general.

I want to be fair to the Theaetetus here, because it’s easy to be quick with the ancients
and they deserve better. Socrates, in that dialogue, doesn’t just say “true belief plus
reasons.” He tries three different senses of what the “account” behind a true belief
could be: a statement you can say aloud; a list of the thing’s parts; and, third, the
mark that sets this thing apart from everything else it could be confused with. He tries
each, and each fails, and the dialogue ends with nobody knowing what knowledge
is, which is one of the more honest endings in philosophy. But the third sense is the
one I’d underline. An account as the thing that distinguishes: the test that gives the real
case a value no rival gives. He couldn’t make it work because he had no way to say
what the account had to be attached to. Two and a half thousand years later, here’s
this book’s guess: the thing it has to be attached to is a state, and the account is an
object sitting in it. I’m not claiming that settles Plato. I’m claiming he was pointing at
the right thing, and that’s my reading of the dialogue, which you can check against it
in an afternoon.

Push on that once more, because Socrates gives his own reason for dropping the third
account, and it isn’t the one I just gave. If the account means knowing the mark that
sets the thing apart, then knowledge has been defined as true belief plus knowledge
of something, and the word you were trying to define is back inside its own definition.
A circle. Does a check get out of it? It gets the word out: a test that ran and found the
mark isn’t defined in terms of knowing. Whether the test was any good is still a real
question, and it’s the question the rest of this section puts a price on. So I’d say the
circle moves. It doesn’t vanish. It moves somewhere you can look at it, which is the


                                           167
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


most I’d claim.

8.3 The shape, said once
So here’s what I mean by entitlement, and it has three parts, and I’ll try to earn each.

A run is entitled to a claim when three things are present. First, an object, carried in the
state: a grouping, a relation between groups, a counter, a package of constraints. That’s
a thing you could print. A belief doesn’t count. Second, a checked relation between
that object and the claim: a test that was actually run, with its result on hand. “A test
exists” doesn’t count. Third, an event on the record that says this object was put there
and paid for, so that anyone auditing the run can point back at the moment the claim
was marked.

Said as a definition, so the rest of the section has something to point at:


Definition 8.1 (Entitlement). A run is entitled to a claim when three things are on hand:
an object carried in the run’s states; a checked relation between that object and the claim,
meaning a test that was run and whose result is on the record; and a paid event, a move
of the run at which the object was put in place and which the price list charged at least
one. In a certification system (Definition 3.1) a move that takes the reading from no to
yes is a paid move, because the toll charges it; whether the object went in at that move
is a separate question. This is the book’s word.


Keep the second and third parts separate. A note saying “coin under cup one, checked”
can be written without anyone lifting a cup. That gives an object, but no checked
relation. Now actually lift the cup, find the coin and write the result. Suppose this is a
free move: the note is on the sheet, the check really happened, but the NO box stays
NO and the tally line stays blank. This time the object and the checked relation are
both there. What is missing is the paid event. The run isn’t entitled in this definition’s
sense; that doesn’t make the result of the check false.

The reverse distinction matters too. A move from NO to YES earns a mark on the
tally line, but the bare toll says nothing about what that move looked at. Payment
alone supplies neither a check nor its correctness. The later machine will bind those
acts together in its step rule. The five parts of a certification system do not do that by
themselves.

And here’s the part to hold on to. Nothing in the five parts makes a later move read the
reading. The step function is handed the state and a move name, and it’s allowed to
ignore the YES box completely; plenty of systems will. So when I say a run is entitled, I
mean what someone auditing the run may conclude from the reading and the receipt.
The system doesn’t have to enforce it, and unless somebody builds it to, it won’t.

This is a good place to line up the three things the word established has had to mean so
far, because they blur easily, and a blur here would make the book look like it proves

                                            168
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


more than it does. The yardstick is the opening chapter’s four conditions for a check
being about this very claim: the same property, the same thing, the same edition, and
an honest check.

After the column of questions, the first column is Section 3’s bare toll: a paid crossing,
and nothing says a check happened at all (Section 9 has a remark saying exactly
that). The second is this section’s entitlement. The third is the small machine of
Part IV, whose step won’t let a commit through without a passing check of the same
property, on the same thing, at the same edition, for every program from a clean start
(Theorem 16.8, and Theorem 16.9 for a run that ends certified), whose checker comes
with a proof that it says what it means (Lemma 16.1, Theorem 16.11), and whose
certified runs from a clean start cost at least three (Observation 16.16). Even there two
things are missing, and the first is in the table, where you’ll see it. The step doesn’t
police whether a check could have failed: a property every value has is a perfectly
legal check, sound and useless. And in all three columns the status belongs to whoever
reads the record. The machine doesn’t know anything. What its flag means is assigned
from outside, by whoever says what each property means.

Why does the honest check carry so much? The philosopher Linda Zagzebski, who
works on knowledge and the virtues of a careful mind, argued in 1994 that any ac-
count of knowledge whose justification leaves even a small gap between having good
reasons and being right lets a Gettier case through: take a case where bad luck makes
the reasons point the wrong way, then add a stroke of good luck that makes the belief
true anyway. The first three conditions plus an honest check close that gap by con-
struction, and only one half of honesty is needed for it, the half that says no when the
property is false. Saying yes whenever it’s true is extra. A check that can be wrong, a
test suite that sometimes passes broken code, puts you straight back in her gap, and
then the record certifies something smaller and still true: this procedure said yes.

                                           169
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


And who certifies that the check is honest? Not the record. Honesty is a fact about
what the check does on every input, and the opening chapter already said a finished
state can’t hold that kind of fact. It has to be carried by a proof about the checker, done
once, outside every run, and nothing on the record pays for it. So an established claim
is two things stuck together: a run property the record carries and a program property
a proof carries, and the proof is entitlement for the auditor. The machine gets none
from it. Section 16 shows where that chain of reasons stops on a real machine.

The engineering version of this was already built, in 1996 and 1997. The computer
scientist George Necula, then at Carnegie Mellon, called it proof-carrying code: when
you ship a program to a host that doesn’t trust you, you ship a proof with it that the
program obeys the host’s safety rules, and the host checks the proof that arrived before
running anything. Not your reputation. Not “a proof exists somewhere.” The one
in the box. A quarter century earlier Stephen Cook’s certificates had the same bones,
from Section 3: a claim comes with a witness that’s cheap to check, and the checker
checks that witness. And the Scottish philosopher David Hume, in 1748, arguing
about miracles in his Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, laid out the thing the
receipt replaces. He weighed testimony against evidence, and wrote that “a wise man,
therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.” The way I read him, the whole of
his argument is a method for how much to trust a witness when you have no receipt.
The move in this book is to stop weighing. A claim on the record is either backed by
its object and its paid event, or it’s testimony from outside, and a run that leans on
testimony hasn’t earned it itself. It can inherit it, but only as far as the copy it leans on
is genuine, which is Section 7’s problem of a record shown from outside.

Robert Brandom, a philosopher at the University of Pittsburgh, built a whole account
of language on two words this book leans on, commitment and entitlement, and his
Making It Explicit (1994) is where I’d send anyone who suspects I invented the pair.
In his picture, as I read it and as his reviewers describe it, people talking keep score
on each other: what each speaker is committed to, what they’ve put themselves on
the hook for, and what each is entitled to, what they’re licensed to claim. You can be
committed without being entitled (a reckless assertion), many claims count as entitled
by default until someone challenges them, and entitlement can be borrowed: I can
claim a thing on your say-so and defer to you when I’m challenged. Lay mine beside
his and the differences are the content. His score is kept by the other people in the
room; here it’s a reading in the state. His entitlement often comes by default; here it’s
an event that has to happen and is charged. And his deferral is my testimony, which
I’ve just let back in on a leash: borrowed entitlement is only as good as the copy is
genuine. The leash has an older formal cousin, the jurisdiction rule of Burrows, Abadi
and Needham’s logic of authentication (Section 7), where you take a statement on
an authority’s word only if you already believe the authority has jurisdiction over
it. It came first, presented in 1989 and printed in 1990, years ahead of Brandom’s
book of 1994, and its words are believes and jurisdiction where his are commitment and



                                            170
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


entitlement.

There’s a whole field that would want a word here too, the logic of belief revision,
which asks how a reasonable mind should change what it believes when something
new comes in. Its nearest neighbours are worth naming, and I couldn’t keep them
apart until I put them back on the table with the cups. Your friend believes the coin is
under cup one. They can learn something that doesn’t clash with that, say cup two is
empty, and just add it. They can lift cup one, find nothing, and have to change their
mind about a table nobody touched. Or you can tell them you moved the coin. The
last two felt alike to me at first. They aren’t. In one the friend was wrong. In the other
the friend was right, and then the table changed.

Krister Segerberg, a Swedish logician at Uppsala, built a logic of irrevocable revision
in 1998: accepting something so that it can’t be given up. That’s the firmness question
taken to its end. Isaac Levi, a philosopher at Columbia who spent a career on how
beliefs get fixed and unfixed, split adding a belief into a deliberate kind and a routine
kind (I cite his 1991 book; the split goes back to his 1980 one). Deliberate is reasoning
your way there. Routine is where you take on whatever a procedure you committed
to in advance hands you, the way you’d accept a reading off a thermometer you’ve
already decided to trust, or what’s under a cup when you lift it. What I think the split
rests on is when the trust goes in: once, before the data comes. A passing CHECK is
routine in exactly that sense, with a checker proved honest once, outside every run.

Neil Tennant, a logician at Ohio State, and Gösta Grahne, a computer scientist at
Helsinki, I first filed as two separate complaints. They’re one move made from op-
posite sides. The target is the best-known impossibility in that field, the Swedish
philosopher Peter Gärdenfors’s 1986 theorem that a natural rule for conditionals, the
one his paper calls the Ramsey test, can’t live with rational revision. Tennant argued
in 2008 that it goes through only by treating some additions as revisions: the friend
who learned cup two was empty gets counted as having changed their mind. Grahne,
working on updates and counterfactuals, argued in 1998 that Gärdenfors’s theorem
bites only revising, so the friend whose coin was moved is out of its reach. Side by
side, they squeeze the theorem from both ends into one case: being wrong about a
table nobody touched.

The line this book leans on hardest is between two kinds of change. Revising is
changing what you believe about a world that stayed put. Updating is changing it
because the world moved. Two computer scientists, Hirofumi Katsuno and Alberto
Mendelzon, drew that line for knowledge bases in a 1991 paper on the difference
between updating a knowledge base and revising it; database researchers had been
working on updates with incomplete information since the mid-1980s, Arthur Keller
and Marianne Winslett among them. Grahne’s result stands on it. And look at what
the friend sees: an empty cup one is the same empty cup whether they misremembered
or you moved the coin. The evidence alone can’t tell revising from updating; that’s


                                           171
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


a fibre. What tells them apart is a count of how often the cups were touched. The
machine in Part IV keeps that count as an edition number for each thing, and its
version rule treats every write as an update: a write moves the edition number, so
every fact about the old edition stops counting for the new one.

And Alexandru Baltag, Bryan Renne and Sonja Smets, three logicians at Amsterdam,
gave a logic in 2014 that keeps apart three things Gettier’s cases blur: justified belief,
explicit knowledge and conclusive evidence. The friend who watched has justified
belief; the friend who lifted the cup has conclusive evidence. Explicit knowledge I
read as knowing with the justification written out beside it, the way the record keeps
its check, and I’m less sure of that one. Put them together and they say something
exact about this book’s record. A record that’s never wrong and never corrected would
be a dogmatist’s dream if its sentences were about the present. They aren’t. Each says
a property held of a thing at one edition, and that sentence stays true after the edition
number moves on. The record can be infallible and never corrected only because its
sentences are edition-stamped. Strip the stamps, and the first write would turn it into
a liar that can’t take anything back.

Push on that and it gives twice. The record is Segerberg’s irrevocable acceptance every
time, with no revising in it. If a check was dishonest, the only fix that fits a record like
this is a second record on top saying “withdrawn,” the way a revocation list works,
so the infallibility leans on the checker, proved once, outside. And the record is never
wrong partly because it only talks about past editions. Whoever reads it wants now,
and getting from “held at that edition” to “holds now” crosses every update since.
The record doesn’t make that step for you.

And the logicians the opening chapter named in passing, the ones who taught the
logic of knowing to count. Here they are properly, and this time I want to see what
each price rests on. Ho Ngoc Duc, in 1997, gave the logic of knowing an operator
for “true after some train of thought”: an agent doesn’t know every consequence of
what it knows now. It can come to know any of them by taking steps of reasoning.
Steps. I took that at first for the thing I was after, until I saw which way it points.
His operator points forward, at what the agent could come to know. A record points
back, at what was checked. One arrow, read from opposite ends. And Sergei Artemov
and Roman Kuznets, in 2014, turned logical omniscience into a question of cost: a
logic escapes it when every valid claim that something is known comes with a proof
whose size is bounded by a polynomial in the size of the claim. The usual modal
logics of knowledge can’t pass that test unless NP equals coNP, which most people
would bet against, and justification logic passes it for knowledge stated together with
its justification, because the size of the justification pays for the search. That last
clause took me a few reads. What I think it means is Cook’s certificate from the proof-
carrying-code paragraph above: put the justification inside the claim, and the hard
part, finding it, was paid before the claim was written. Their price rests on an open
bet, and it’s a price on looking. A price, of a sort. Steps and a price are both there,


                                            172
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


then, in their own form. What I still don’t find in them is the one I care about: a single
act that closes a question for good and is charged as that act. Their steps are steps of
reasoning, and their price is on finding a proof. Neither is on settling. I couldn’t get
past the journal’s paywall to Artemov and Kuznets’s paper, so my account of it comes
from how other people describe it.

Push on mine the same way and it gives. A check is one of Duc’s trains of thought,
so my act is the last step of his train, where the walking stops. What I’ve added is a
direction and a charge on stopping. And the charge rests on a choice. I put it inside
the step, and nothing forced me to.

Three things entitlement is not. It isn’t permission: an access control system says who
may write to what, and that’s granted from outside and says nothing about truth;
a process with permission to write the note still has no entitlement. It isn’t “true,
therefore usable”: that’s the cups. And it isn’t “sound by luck”: a shortcut that gives
the right answer because the inputs happened to cooperate is the stopped clock. The
count below has one condition aimed at it, and I’ll tell you what the condition says
and how much it actually catches.

8.4 What narrowing costs: count the rivals
Now the number, because a book about a bill has to say how much. Here’s the idea in
a form you can do with three playing cards. Shuffle cards marked 1, 2, 3 face down.
Sort them using only questions of the form “is this one bigger than that one?”, and
count the questions. There are six orders the cards could be in. Each question has two
answers, so after one question you’ve split the six into at most two piles, after two
questions at most four, and you need to get down to one. Four is less than six, so two
questions can’t always do it, and three can, and you can draw the tree of questions
on paper and see it: six leaves, three deep. The number of questions you need is at
least the base-two logarithm of the number of possibilities you started with, rounded
up: that’s log2 of 6, which is a bit under 3, rounded to 3. Donald Knuth, a computer
scientist at Stanford, gives this, in the volume on sorting of his The Art of Computer
Programming, as the lower bound for all comparison sorting, and the shape of the
argument is just: a tree f questions deep has at most 2 f leaves, so it can’t tell apart
more than 2 f cases.

And then the obvious next question: is the floor always the price? Try five cards.
There are 120 orders, log2 of 120 is a bit under 7, so you need at least seven questions,
and seven is enough, though not by the obvious method. Finding the way is a good
evening with a deck of cards (Knuth has it, under the name merge insertion, from the
mathematicians Lester Ford and Selmer Johnson in 1959). Now twelve cards. They
can be in 479,001,600 orders, log2 of that is about 28.8, so the count says at least 29.
Ford and Johnson’s method takes 30, and in 1965 Mark Wells, a mathematician at
Los Alamos who built a programming language for exactly this kind of combinatorial
search, showed by a computer search that nothing does better: twelve cards need 30.


                                           173
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


The floor was 29. The price is 30. So the count is a floor and only a floor; it never
promises the floor can be reached, and the bound later in this section has to be read
exactly the same way.

Ralph Hartley, an electronics researcher at the lab that became Bell Labs, writing in the
Bell System Technical Journal in 1928, before Shannon, measured information exactly
this way: the logarithm of the number of possibilities, no probabilities, just a count.
That’s the measure here, and I’ll say plainly it’s Hartley’s. Shannon’s would need a
distribution over the list, and there isn’t one. There’s just the list’s length.

Here’s the same count with something you can hold. Put three coins under three cups.
Each coin is heads or tails, so there are eight possible rows under the cups. Someone
hands you two answers: heads under the first cup, tails under the second. Lift the
first cup and compare. A matching answer leaves four possible rows. Lift the second
and compare. A match leaves two. The last coin can still be either way. The list really
shrank: eight, four, two. Nothing in that count needed a claim about which way the
last coin faces.

This is a parlour game, and an old one. In A Christmas Carol, in 1843, Scrooge’s nephew
Fred plays a game called Yes and No at his Christmas party: he thinks of something,
and everybody else asks questions he may only answer yes or no. He’s thinking of
an animal, a disagreeable, savage one that growls and grunts and lives in London,
and the answer is Uncle Scrooge. Most people know the game as twenty questions,
and twenty is a good number for it: a balanced question splits the remaining field in
half, and twenty such questions can guarantee identification among 220 = 1,048,576
possibilities. A lucky answer to “is it this one?” can finish immediately; the count
is about handling every possible answer. Push on that, though. The halving only
happens because Fred answers truthfully about what’s actually in his head. Lie once
and the count still shrinks; it shrinks around the wrong animal. That’s the cups again:
the four and the two are real because you lifted the cup and compared. Being told
what was under it wouldn’t have made them real.

Now put it on a run. Say a run comes with a list of states that are “still on the table,”
the candidates, and a shorter list, with some ruled out. Call the first the prior and
the second the posterior, and I want you to hear those as a list you could print. They
aren’t “the space of possible worlds.” Picture the ruling-out as observations, each
observation that ruled something out being one branch point in a tree like the card
tree. And here’s the claim: if that tree is no deeper than the number of paid steps the
run took, and the tree has enough leaves to cover the narrowing in a way I’ll spell out
in a moment, then the counter rose by at least log2 of the prior’s length, rounded up,
minus log2 of the posterior’s length, rounded up. At least as many marks as index bits
the list lost, where the index bits of a list are the yes/no questions it takes to point at
one entry of it, the card count again. That’s the bound.

“Paid step” needs its own sentence. It means a step the price list charges at least one for.


                                            174
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


In a certification system the toll guarantees that every crossing of the reading is one; a
price list is free to put a floor under more steps than that (a look, a send, a check), and
the count takes every paid step there is. The tree is a bare shape, branches and leaves
with nothing written on them, and “no deeper than the number of paid steps” is a
count along the run that happened. It isn’t a walk down the tree. A paid step doesn’t
have to have asked any question at all.

Notice, too, what the bound does and doesn’t say about the run. It takes the two lists,
the tree and the covering as given. It doesn’t say the run produced the posterior from
the prior; nothing in it reads the lists off the run. What it says is that, given lists, a tree
and a covering that someone supplies, the paid steps of the run cover the rounded
drop in list length. That’s Section 5’s warning come due: watching can narrow for free,
so the payment can’t be dug out of the narrowing. It goes in as a premise, the tree’s
depth against the paid steps, and I’ll keep calling it one. At the end of the section the
run makes the posterior itself, from a prior and the tests it passed (Theorem 8.4), and
then the premise is a share each test keeps.

8.5 What “narrower” buys: a stronger test
Before the count, one link that’s pure logic, and Plato’s third account is the whole
of it. Take a list of candidates and an observation, a function that says what each
candidate looks like from outside. The list’s membership test accepts an observation
when some candidate on the list shows it. Shrink the list, and the test can only get
pickier: anything the short list’s test accepts, the long list’s accepts too. The word for
that, and it runs backward from English, is stronger: the stronger test is the one that
lets fewer things through.

Pickier, though, isn’t the same as strictly pickier, and the cards show the gap. Take
all six orders as the prior, and as the posterior the three where card 1 sits left of card
2: 1-2-3, 1-3-2 and 3-1-2. First observation: “is 1 left of 2?” Every survivor says yes,
and the removed 2-1-3 says no, so the prior’s test accepts yes and no, the posterior’s
only yes. Strictly stronger. Second observation, same two lists: “is the first card a
3?” Now 3-1-2 says yes and the other two survivors say no, and among the removed
orders 3-2-1 says yes and 2-1-3 says no. Both tests accept yes and no. Same strength,
even though three orders are gone. What made the difference is a removed candidate
whose observation no survivor shares. That’s Plato’s mark, the thing that sets this case
apart from everything it could be confused with, turned into a function. Narrow the
list and keep one distinguishing removed candidate, and the test is strictly stronger;
narrow it without one, and the test may not have moved at all.

8.6 The count, exactly
Here are the words and the count, for any system with Section 6’s counter. A list is
a finite list of candidates, repeats allowed, and |Ω| is the length of the list Ω, repeats
counted. ⌈log2 x ⌉ is the base-two logarithm of x rounded up: the smallest k ∈ N with
2k ≥ x. At x = 0 it is 0, the convention for empty lists set in Section 5. And a −̇ b is


                                             175
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


subtraction on whole numbers that stops at zero, so 3 −̇ 5 = 0.


Definition 8.2 (Decision tree). A decision tree is a leaf, or a branch with two subtrees.
Its depth is 0 for a leaf and one more than the deeper subtree for a branch; its leaf count
L( T ) is 1 for a leaf and the sum of the two counts for a branch. Nothing is written on
a tree: no question, no answer, no candidate.


Lemma 8.1 (A tree is no wider than two to its depth). For every decision tree T, L( T ) ≤
2depth(T ) , and so ⌈log2 L( T )⌉ ≤ depth( T ).

Proof. Induction on the tree. A leaf has one leaf and depth 0, and 1 ≤ 20 . A branch
with subtrees of depths d1 , d2 has at most 2d1 + 2d2 ≤ 2 · 2max(d1 ,d2 ) leaves, which is 2 to
its own depth. The second half: L( T ) ≤ 2depth(T ) means depth( T ) is one of the k with
2k ≥ L( T ), and the rounded-up logarithm is the smallest of them.

The definition and the lemma are stated over the tree type alone, a leaf or a branch,
with nothing about any machine in them.


Theorem 8.2 (Paid narrowing, counted). Take a system with a counter µ and a price list
c that obey conservation (Theorem 6.1): each step raises µ by exactly its charge. Let Ω and
Ω′ be lists with |Ω′ | > 0, let T be a decision tree with |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ | (the tree covers the
narrowing), and let t be a run from s ending at s′ in which at least depth( T ) steps are charged
at least one each. Then

                          ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ µ(s′ ) − µ(s).

Proof. The rounded-up logarithm respects order, so the covering gives ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ ≤
⌈log2 ( L( T ) · |Ω′ |)⌉. It is also subadditive on products of positive numbers, ⌈log2 ab⌉ ≤
⌈log2 a⌉ + ⌈log2 b⌉, because 2⌈log2 a⌉ · 2⌈log2 b⌉ ≥ ab. So

                  ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ ⌈log2 L( T )⌉ ≤ depth( T ),

the last step by Lemma 8.1. By hypothesis at least depth( T ) steps of the run were
charged at least one, and no step is charged less than zero, so the sum of the charges
is at least depth( T ). By conservation that sum is µ(s′ ) − µ(s).

For any system with a counter that obeys conservation, put the two arguments to-
gether. The tree bound applies to the sum of the charges of a run, without needing
|Ω′ | > 0; conservation identifies that sum with the counter’s rise. A system satisfying
both gets the theorem. The bill form is also part of Theorem 8.3 below. The tree half
is the lemma above; the rest is arithmetic on the two lengths, the leaf count and the
counter. Notice what’s missing from the hypotheses: anything tying the lists to the
run. That’s the shape of the bound.


                                               176
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Three honest small prints, all of them visible in the statement. Both logarithms round
up separately, and the subtraction stops at zero, so when the prior and the posterior
round up to the same number of index bits (four candidates narrowed to three, say)
the bound says nothing. The lists are plain lists, repeats allowed, so “index bits” is
a difference of rounded list lengths with repeats counted; a list can get shorter by
dropping a duplicate without losing a single candidate, and “a candidate was ruled
out” and “the list got shorter” are two different claims. And the difference isn’t the
number of questions anyone asked.

The covering condition, |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |, is the nearest thing the count has to an anti-
stopped-clock clause, and I have to be exact about how near. Picture each survivor
standing for a little crowd of the prior’s candidates, itself included, a crowd no bigger
than the tree has leaves. Then the condition says every candidate in the prior fits in
some survivor’s crowd. That limits how much can be deleted per leaf you paid for. It
doesn’t say why anything was deleted. So the condition rules out deleting too much
for the tree you’ve paid for. It doesn’t rule out deleting for no reason. A run can satisfy
every hypothesis of the count and have ruled nothing out on purpose; the count prices
the size of the drop. It says nothing about the honesty of it. And the covering can’t
just be dropped. On the small machine one yes-or-no question with a big constant in
it narrows 2n candidates to one, n index bits, for a ledger of three, so for any n ≥ 4 the
bound is false without it (Section 16.17).

Here’s a side trip worth taking, because it looks like it breaks the count and doesn’t.
Two information theorists, Rudolf Ahlswede and Gunter Dueck (1989), noticed that
asking “is it this one?” is a different job from asking “which one is it?” If each receiver
only wants to know whether the message is theirs, a noisy channel used n times
can serve a number of receivers that grows like two raised to two to the nC, with
C the channel’s capacity, where naming the message only gets you two to the nC.
That’s identification, and on its face it says checking can be exponentially cheaper than
naming. But their tests are allowed to say yes wrongly once in a while. Make the yes
sound, a test that never says yes to the wrong message, which is the only kind of check
this book lets raise a record, and the double exponential collapses. The argument is
two lines of pigeonhole. I argue it here, and nothing checks it. Each receiver’s test, to
be any use, says yes on some output its own message can produce, and soundness
means no other message can produce that output; so those outputs are all different,
one per receiver, and there can’t be more receivers than outputs, |Y |n for an output
alphabet Y. Single exponential, the same order as naming. So for a check that never
lies, the card count is the right scale after all, and the cheap trick needs a check that
can be fooled.

8.7 What you’ve got
A paid flag is not a true claim; Section 7 left it at “a paid flag is a paid flag,” and
Section 9 will say it flatly. What a paid flag with an object and a checked relation
behind it gives you is entitlement: anyone auditing the run may treat the claim as

                                            177
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


established, and can point at the event where that became legitimate. (Nothing in the
five parts makes the system itself read the flag; I said that above and I’m saying it
again because it’s the sentence most likely to get lost.) Entitlement costs at least the
index bits of narrowing it commits to, given lists, a tree and a covering somebody
supplies, and given a run that paid for the tree’s depth. The cups say why entitlement
and truth are different. Plato says what the checked relation has to do: distinguish.
Necula says how to build it. Hartley says what to count.

Put the three pieces on one hypothesis list (narrow the list with a test that separates,
find the paid event, count the bill against a tree the run paid for) and you get a
single statement, structural entitlement, once over any certification system and once,
under the longer name structural entitlement represented, for every Thiele-complete
machine, the small machine included (Section 16.17). The first one reads as follows.


Theorem 8.3 (Structural entitlement, over any certification system). Take a certification
system (Definition 3.1), a state s that reads no, and a run t from s that ends in a state that
reads yes. Take a type of candidates, a type of observations with an exact equality test, an
observation obs of each candidate, and a decoder d that turns a run into an observation (what
its record shows). Take lists Ω and Ω′ of candidates and a decision tree T such that: (H1) Ω′
strictly narrows Ω: every member of Ω′ is in Ω, and some member of Ω isn’t in Ω′ ; (H2) some
dropped candidate w, in Ω and not in Ω′ , shows an observation different from every survivor’s;
(H3) the decoded run d(t) is shown by some survivor; (H4) |Ω′ | > 0 and |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |;
(H5) at least depth( T ) steps of the run are charged at least one each. Then (1) the membership
test of Ω′ is strictly stronger than the membership test of Ω; (2) some step of the run took the
reading from no to yes, and that step was charged at least one; and (3) the sum of the charges
of the run’s steps is at least ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉.

Proof. (1) is the cards’ argument: the dropped w shows something no survivor shows,
so the posterior test says no where the prior test says yes, and every survivor was in
the prior, so nothing the posterior accepts is refused by the prior. (2) The run starts
at no and ends at yes, so at some step the reading goes from no to yes, and the toll
charges that step at least one. (3) is the proof of Theorem 8.2 with the sum of the
charges in place of the counter’s rise: the covering and Lemma 8.1 bound the index
bits by depth( T ), and the sum of the charges is at least the number of steps charged at
least one. On a system that obeys conservation the sum of the charges is the counter’s
rise.

Theorem 8.2 is the same count with the counter’s rise, so for a system that obeys
conservation it’s the special case. Three things in the hypotheses feed nothing, and
I’m naming them here so you don’t have to find them: (H3) isn’t used by any of the
three conclusions; from (H1) only the inclusion is used, and the gap goes unused; and
in (H2) the words “not in Ω′ ” go unused, since a candidate whose observation differs
from every survivor’s can’t be a survivor itself. And (H4)’s |Ω′ | > 0 is used in that


                                              178
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


proof but can be dropped too: the covering forces it once the prior has a member.

A statement like that is true by packaging: it takes the hypotheses in and hands the
conclusions back, and the right word for it is a checklist. A checklist for leaning on a
claim. It discovers nothing about leaning. The version in which the run itself does the
narrowing, Theorem 8.4, comes at the end of this section.

And a checklist isn’t nothing. On 30 October 1935, at Wright Field, northeast of
Dayton, Ohio, the Army was evaluating Boeing’s new four-engine bomber, the Model
299. Shortly after take-off it plunged back onto the field and caught fire; that’s how
the wire report of that day has it, and the later histories add that it pitched up and
stalled first, which is what elevators locked in a raised position would do. Two men
died of their injuries, the Army’s pilot, Major Ployer Hill, and Boeing’s chief test pilot,
Leslie Tower. The airplane was fine. The crew had left the gust locks on, a locking
mechanism worked from inside the cockpit that holds the control surfaces still while
the plane sits on the ground. There’s a famous line that a newspaper called it too much
airplane for one man to fly. I couldn’t find that line in any paper from 1935; the earliest
place I could find it is a New Yorker article from December 2007 by Atul Gawande,
a surgeon who writes about how people get complicated work right, and he names
no newspaper, so take it as a lead. What I can find is what came after. The answer
was a card: a list of things to check, in order, every time, and the crews of the airplane
worked through written checklists for each phase of flight. The most careful history
of it I found is by Walter Boyne, a retired Air Force colonel and a former director of
the National Air and Space Museum. By his account it wasn’t the first written routine
for a pilot; those go back before the First World War. And it’s this crash, he says, that
made the checklist the way a crew flew. The airplane went on to be the B-17. Nothing
on that card was a discovery. Every item on it was something the pilots already knew.
What the card did was make sure none of it got left out when it mattered. That’s what
putting entitlement’s hypotheses on one list does: it finds nothing new about leaning
on a claim, and it makes the hypotheses impossible to drop quietly.

8.8 When the run does the narrowing
Theorem 8.3 takes the lists in. Here is the version where the run makes the posterior,
and the count stops being an item on the list and becomes a consequence. It needs
one thing a bare certification system doesn’t have: which steps are tests, and what
each asks. So a reading names them. For each instruction it gives either nothing or
a yes-or-no question about the state the run is in when it gets there, and a test step
passes when its question says yes there. The candidates are states the run could have
started from. A passed test is asked of a candidate by running the same moves from
the candidate up to that step and asking the same question there. The posterior is the
candidates that pass every test the run passed, asked that way, in the order the run
asked them.




                                           179
The Thiele Machine                                                                       Devon Thiele


Theorem 8.4 (Structural entitlement, with the narrowing made by the run). Take a
certification system and a reading that names its test steps, every test step charged at least
one. Take a state s that reads no, a run t from s that ends in a state that reads yes, and a list
Ω of candidate starts that contains s. Let Ω′ be the posterior t makes from Ω, and let bi and
ai be the numbers of candidates standing just before and just after the ith test t passed. Then
(1) Ω′ sits inside Ω and contains s; (2) every candidate of Ω that isn’t in Ω′ fails, asked that
way, a test t passed; (3) |Ω| · ∏i ai = |Ω′ | · ∏i bi ; (4) if every test t passed keeps at least a 2−k
share of the candidates standing before it, bi ≤ 2k ai , then ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ is at most
k times the number of tests t passed, that number is at most the number of steps charged at
least one, and the index bits are at most k times the sum of the charges; and (5) some step of t
took the reading from no to yes and was charged at least one.

Proof. (1) The run passes its own tests from s, and a candidate is kept only if it passes
them all. (2) A candidate dropped failed one of them. (3) Each test turns a standing
list of bi into one of ai , and the products telescope. (4) Each test keeps at least bi /2k ,
so |Ω| ≤ 2kn |Ω′ | with n the number of tests passed, and the rounded logarithms
follow as in Theorem 8.2. Each test passed is a test step, charged at least one. (5) is
Theorem 8.3(2).

Part (3) is the exact count: take base-two logarithms and log2 |Ω| − log2 |Ω′ | is the
sum, over the tests the run passed, of log2 (bi /ai ), the bits each one took. Part (2)
answers the complaint I made about the covering, that it doesn’t say why anything
was deleted: here everything deleted was deleted by a test the run passed and paid
for. Two premises stay, the prior list and the share. The share is needed. On the small
machine one CHECK of “A ≥ 15,” asked of sixteen candidates, keeps one, a 2−4 share,
