and narrows by 4 index bits on a run of 3 record moves (Proposition 16.46); with k = 1
part (4) would say 4 ≤ 3. The same statement on every Thiele-complete machine,
where the tests are the CHECK moves and the bill is the ledger, is Theorem 16.45.

8.9 A grouping, checked and committed
Part I ended on buckets, and Part II dropped them on purpose: the toll prices any yes-
or-no reading. This is where the word in this section’s title gets attached to a partition
in a theorem. Take a pile, a finite list of items, and a grouping, a bucket label for each
item. Its partition is “same label,” and the classes of that relation are a partition in the
sense of Definition 2.1. The data is a key for each item, drawn from any type you like (a
grouping’s own labels can serve as a key), and a grouping is sound for a key when any
two items it puts in one bucket have the same key. The grouping says “these belong
together,” and the key says whether they do. One grouping refines another when every
bucket of the first sits inside a bucket of the second.

Put two red buttons and two blue buttons on the table, numbered 1 through 4, with 1
and 2 red. Let the key be colour. Circles round {1, 2} and {3, 4} give a sound grouping:
every pair inside a circle has the same colour. Split the red circle into two singletons


                                                 180
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


and it stays sound; splitting cannot introduce a mismatched pair. Join 1 and 3 instead
and it fails. Changing the circles’ names from A and B to North and South changes
none of these checks. That is why the reading below uses the partition, not the spelling
of its labels.

For the operational rule, put a tick beside a grouping only after comparing the colours
within each circle. Copy that ticked grouping onto a separate commitment card, then
place the card in a record envelope; charge one tally for each of those three acts.
Change a button’s colour between the check and the copy, and the old tick must no
longer authorize the copy. The machine’s SET rule below does that by clearing the
current table and channel. A record already kept remains about the old colours, which
it keeps with the grouping.

The bucket machine holds a key, a table of checked groupings, a channel, a record, a trap
latch and a ledger. SET replaces the key for nothing and throws away the table and the
channel, which were checked against the old key. CHECK g costs one and passes when
g is sound for the current key, and, when it passes, writes g in the table. COMMIT
g costs one and passes when the table holds a grouping with the same partition as
g, and puts g in the channel. CERTIFY costs one and passes when the channel holds
a grouping; if the record is still down it then keeps that grouping with the current
key, the key a grouping with its partition was checked against, and a record already
kept is left as it is. A CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY that fails traps, and a trapped
machine only pays. The reading for a grouping g is: the record holds a grouping with
g’s partition. That’s the reading “this grouping has been checked and committed.”


Theorem 8.5 (A committed grouping entitles exactly its refinements). (1) The classes of
“same label” under any grouping form a partition. (2) Two groupings with the same partition
 of the pile have the same reading at every state of the bucket machine. (3) For groupings g and
 h of the pile, soundness of g for a key gives soundness of h for that key, for every key, exactly
 when h refines g. (4) On every run from a clean state (table and channel empty, record down,
 trap down), if the reading for g is up, the record holds a grouping and a key for which g is
 sound, and so is every grouping that refines g; and for every grouping h that doesn’t refine g
 there is a key for which g is sound and h isn’t. (5) The bucket machine pays the toll, and a run
 from a clean state that ends with the record up has raised the ledger by at least three.

Proof. (1) “Same label” is an equivalence relation, so Theorem 2.1 applies. (2) The read-
ing asks only for a grouping with the same partition, and having the same partition is
symmetric and transitive. (3) If h refines g, two items h puts together g puts together,
and soundness of g gives them the same key. Conversely, take g itself as the key: g
is sound for it, so h is, and that says h refines g. (4) Along any run, every grouping
in the table is sound for the current key, the one in the channel is too, since it has the
partition of one in the table, and the one the record keeps is sound for the key kept
with it; SET empties the table and the channel when the key changes. Then (3), and


                                               181
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


its converse with g as the key. (5) Only CERTIFY raises the record, and it costs one.
A raised record needs a passing CERTIFY, which needs a grouping in the channel,
which needs a passing COMMIT, which needs a grouping in the table, which needs a
passing CHECK.

So “structural” has a theorem under it. The reading sees a grouping only through its
partition, which is item (2). Soundness of the recorded grouping guarantees soundness
of every refinement, uniformly over all keys. A grouping that is not a refinement may
still be sound for a particular key; the guarantee does not extend to every key. If all four
buttons have the same colour, every grouping is sound. The theorem identifies what
follows from the first grouping’s soundness alone. It’s the three parts of entitlement
from the start of this section in their smallest case: the object is the grouping, the
checked relation is soundness for the key, and the paid event is the CERTIFY, on top of
a CHECK and a COMMIT at one mark each. What it doesn’t do is make a later move
read the record. Like everything in this section, it says what someone auditing the run
may conclude.

Before the machine of Part IV, I owe you the word the toll is named after, the “insight”
in “No Free Insight” (Section 5), because I’ve been using it as if it meant one thing.

9 What insight is
I named the rule in this book “No Free Insight,” and the name ran ahead of any careful
account of what insight is. The book has been narrowing it ever since: not learning
(Section 5), not looking, not copying. It’s time to say what’s left, and to say it in a way
that someone who studies actual insight, in actual heads, wouldn’t laugh at. So who
are those people, and what did they find? Here’s what I ran into, pushed on as I go.
Where a story reached me secondhand, I treat it as a lead to check.

9.1 Sultan and the sticks
In 1913 the psychologist Wolfgang Köhler went to Tenerife to run a research station
with a colony of chimpanzees, and the First World War then kept him there until 1920,
five years longer than planned, with the chimpanzees to watch. The famous one is
Sultan. Food is outside the cage, out of reach; two sticks are inside, each too short, but
one fits into the end of the other. Sultan tries each stick, fails, sulks, plays with the
sticks, and then, by Köhler’s account, at a moment you can see, joins them and reaches
the food. Köhler’s words were Einsicht and einsichtig, which came into English as
“insight,” and the whole school of psychology he belonged to, the Gestalt school, said
that’s what thinking is: a restructuring, the moment two sticks stop being two sticks
and become one tool. Stacking up tries until one works was, for them, something else.
Karl Duncker gave the human version, in German in 1935 and in English in 1945, five
years after he died at thirty-seven; he’d spent his last years working with Köhler at
Swarthmore. You can set it up yourself: a candle, a box of tacks, matches, and the task
of fixing the candle to the wall. Almost nobody sees that the box is a shelf, until they


                                            182
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


do. And then he found that if you hand people the box empty, with the tacks poured
out beside it, they solve it far more readily. Same objects. What changed was which
relation among them was on the table.

I like both of these for the same reason: the insight didn’t add an object. Sultan had
both sticks the whole time. The box was there the whole time. What arrived was a
relation, which is to say a piece of structure in Section 2’s sense, and the arrival was
sudden. Hold that, because the thing the toll prices also arrives in one step, and at its
best it’s also a relation.

9.2 It isn’t a feeling
But here’s the finding I’d hand anyone who thinks insight is a feeling, and it comes
from someone who measured it. In the 1980s the psychologist Janet Metcalfe asked
people to solve problems while rating, every fifteen seconds, how “warm” they felt,
how close to the answer. On ordinary problems, algebra for instance, the warmth
climbs steadily and peaks at the answer, which is what you’d expect. On insight
problems, riddles of the candle-box kind, the warmth stays flat, flat, flat, and then the
answer arrives, and if anything the people who felt warmest beforehand were more
likely to be wrong. She put that last finding in the title of a 1986 paper: premonitions
of insight predict impending error. The feeling of being close is not a gauge of being
close. Try it yourself: write a number from one to seven every fifteen seconds while
doing a long sum, then while doing a riddle, and compare the curves.

And the most famous insight story there is fits Metcalfe uncomfortably well.
Archimedes, a mathematician who died in 212 BC, asked by Hiero, the king of Syra-
cuse, whether a goldsmith had cheated him on a crown, gets into a bath, sees the
water rise, and runs home naked shouting “eureka,” I’ve found it. That comes from
Vitruvius, a Roman writer on architecture, writing about two centuries later. Is it
true? Galileo Galilei, then a young Italian mathematician, at twenty-two, in 1586,
took it as known that Archimedes caught the goldsmith. What he didn’t buy was the
method. Water spilling over the side, as Vitruvius tells it, was to him “a crude thing,
far from scientific precision,” and he guessed some writer had set down a rumour. So
he wrote a little tract, La Bilancetta, proposing a balance weighed in air and in water
instead, which he thought was probably what Archimedes actually did, since it rests
on Archimedes’s own results. Whether there was ever a bath, or a shout, nobody can
check now. What survives is a story two centuries late, wrapped around a real man
and probably a real problem. Notice what the legend kept: the bath, the shout, the run-
ning home naked. The feeling. What it left shaky is the part that would count as the
check, the test that could have caught the goldsmith. The bit everybody remembers is
the bit that tells you least.

So any account of insight that keys on the sensation, the “aha,” is keyed to something
that the data says is unreliable. Whatever insight is, it isn’t the feeling of having it.
That’s a relief, because a system of states and moves doesn’t have feelings, and a word


                                          183
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


that only meant a feeling would be cheating if I hung it on one. The version this book
can price has to be keyed to an event, and the question is which.

9.3 What happens when a computation learns
Here’s the split, and I’ll say what the toll does with each part, and then I’ll say who
decided the split. Keep Section 3’s sheet of paper in front of you: the NO box, the YES
box, the tally line, and the three moves STAY, WORK and VOUCH.

The first thing: raw observation. Something comes in and gets written down. A counter
ticks. Nothing is claimed about what it means, nothing is marked as resting on it,
and the reading doesn’t move because of it. Later moves can read what it wrote,
but that reading is a move of its own. This is the demon’s pad in Section 5, and it’s
what the statistician Dennis Lindley measured in 1956 as the information provided
by an experiment, the words of his title, and defined as the expected drop in your
uncertainty: a real quantity, and a quantity about what was seen. It can be free. The
toll says nothing at all about a move that doesn’t cross from NO to YES, so a price
list may charge it zero: on the paper, STAY and WORK cost nothing, and Section 5’s
watcher narrowed a whole row of candidates without paying a mark. “Can be” is
the honest word. A price list is allowed to charge for looking anyway, and whether
looking costs anything in the physical world is a different question that this sheet of
paper doesn’t touch.

Lindley’s measure has a back story, and it runs through Bletchley Park. I. J. Good,
who was Alan Turing’s main statistical assistant at Bletchley Park in 1941, wrote in
1979 that Turing had worked out the expected weight of evidence an experiment
would give, to judge one of the codebreaking procedures before running it, and so
partly anticipated Lindley by about fifteen years, in work that stayed secret. Turing
measured evidence in bans, logarithms to base ten, with a tenth of one called a deciban,
and the name came from the town of Banbury, where tens of thousands of the sheets
used in that procedure were printed. It’s the same base-ten unit other people call the
hartley, after the Hartley from the last section. And Good adds that Turing didn’t
know the logarithm he was using had already appeared in 1878, in a paper by Charles
Sanders Peirce, the same Peirce from the opening chapter, who’d called it the weight
of evidence. Peirce is as far back as Good takes it. What it changes: nothing in the
argument, but it shows how well trodden this first kind of thing is. For a century and
a half careful people have measured what an observation tells you, and every one of
those measures is about what was seen. That’s the side of the line the toll leaves alone.

The second thing: certified insight. Some move turns the reading from NO to YES.
Here is where the toll lives. In any system with the five parts that obeys the toll, that
move costs at least one mark, and every run that starts at NO and ends at YES pays at
least one somewhere along the way, which is Section 3’s universal floor. What’s being
charged for, at its best, is exactly the Gestalt thing: a relation, committed to. One tool,
claimed, out of two sticks. “At its best,” because Section 3 was careful about what YES


                                           184
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


means: the flag is up, and nothing more. A crossing that writes down which relation
it’s committing to carries Sultan’s tool with it. A bare crossing, VOUCH on the paper,
commits to no relation at all, and it pays exactly the same.

The third thing isn’t a kind of event. It’s an observation about the price: it’s flat,
whatever is certified. Say the YES state also shows something striking, a deep relation,
a result nobody could have guessed, Sultan’s two sticks become one tool. The toll
charges the crossing at least one. It doesn’t charge the striking crossing more, because
the floor’s proof never looks at anything but the reading before and after. On the
paper: VOUCH from NO makes one mark whether you were thinking of Duncker’s
box or of lunch. Meaning is not cost. The depth of what’s certified adds meaning. It
doesn’t add a mark.

The candle box has a footnote that says the same thing from the other side. In 1962
the psychologist Sam Glucksberg ran Duncker’s problem with money on it: some
people were told they could win five or twenty dollars depending on how fast they
solved it. With the tacks in the box, the people chasing the money did worse than
the people who weren’t. With the box empty the problem was easier for everybody,
and the accounts I’ve read don’t agree on what the money did there, so I’ll leave that
half alone. Paying more didn’t buy the insight, and on the hard version it got in the
way. That’s a fact about heads. It says nothing about records, and I won’t push it
further than that. But it’s a nice mirror for the paper. On the paper a deeper crossing
isn’t charged more, and in Glucksberg’s room a bigger prize didn’t bring the crossing
sooner. In neither place does the price measure the depth.

Here they are, exactly, for any certification system (Definition 3.1). Runs are written
as lists, the way Section 3’s proof wrote them: [ ] is the empty run, and i :: t is the run
that starts with move i and carries on with the run t.


Definition 9.1 (Certified insight event, raw observation). In a certification system, a
step from state s by move i is a certified insight event when it turns the reading on:
cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes. A move i is raw observation when no step by it,
from any state, is a certified insight event.


Remark 9.1 (What the toll prices, and what it doesn’t). Read off Definition 3.1 and
Observation 3.1, and checked on the board as a certification system. (1) The toll puts
no bound on the cost of a raw-observation move; on Section 3’s board STAY and
WORK are raw observation and cost 0. (2) Every certified insight event is charged at
least 1, by the toll, and every run from a state reading no to one reading yes has total
cost at least 1, by the universal floor. (3) The price is flat: the floor’s proof uses nothing
about the end state but its reading, so that proof establishes the same lower bound 1
whatever else the end state shows. A stronger lower bound can follow from additional
hypotheses, but those hypotheses must do additional work; it does not follow from



                                             185
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


the toll alone. A system that wants to charge more for a deeper certification has to
write that into its price list, move by move; the toll doesn’t do it for anyone.


So the account comes down to two facts and a warning. Looking can be free. Turning
the reading on can’t. The toll alone does not charge more for a remarkable claim;
another pricing rule or an additional requirement could.

Who decided the split? Not the costs alone. The toll prices exactly one thing, the
crossing. A price list is free to put a floor under more moves than that (a look, a send,
a check) and free to leave other moves at zero, so the sorting into raw observation and
certified insight is by whether the reading moves, and that sorting is this book’s. The
part that’s forced is the floor under the crossing, and Section 4 is the argument for it;
anything a price list charges beyond that is a choice, and any concrete machine owes
you its whole table so you can see which choices it made.

9.4 Test, then commit, and nothing forces the second to follow the first
The philosopher Karl Popper said a theory earns its standing by being exposed: you
make a conjecture, you try to kill it, and what survives a real attempt counts for
something, where “real” means the test could have failed. His word for that earned
credit is corroboration. I’ve leaned on that idea through this whole book, and here’s
where a certification system has a version of it, and here’s where the version is weaker
than Popper and I have to say so.

Add a fourth move to the paper: CHECK. It looks at something (a sum, a coin under a
cup, a formula against a row of values), and it can come out pass or fail, and it doesn’t
move the box. Charge it whatever you like; charging it on the attempt, pass or fail,
fits Popper, because what made his test count was that it was really run and could
have failed. That’s the test. It’s raw observation in the sense above, because it never
turns the reading on. VOUCH is the commit. So the honest protocol is two moves:
test, then commit, and the costs are separate, one for the checking work and one for
the crossing.

But nothing in the five parts makes the second move wait for the first. The step is
handed the current state and a move name; the toll looks only at whether the reading
crossed. Play VOUCH from NO with no CHECK anywhere before it, and you land in
YES and make one mark, the same box and the same mark as the player who checked
first. The two tally lines differ by exactly what the CHECK was charged, and if you
charged it nothing they don’t differ at all. The mark for the crossing is the same mark
either way. The receipt says a commitment was paid for. It does not say it was earned.
Popper’s corroboration needs the test; the toll doesn’t.

You can build a system that makes the commit wait. Let CHECK leave a mark in the
state when it passes, and write the step so VOUCH only crosses when that mark is
there. That’s a design, written into the step function, and it’s a perfectly good one.


                                          186
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Nothing in the five parts or the toll asks for it. That’s a real gap between the word
and the bare system, and the only honest thing is to leave it visible: the toll prices the
commit, and whether the commit was preceded by a test is a fact about the run, or
about a design somebody chose. The five parts don’t guarantee it.


Remark 9.2 (Nothing makes the crossing wait). Read off Definition 3.1. The toll
constrains cost(i ) for moves that cross, and nothing else; the step function is any
function of the current state and the move. So a certification system may have a move
that crosses from a state no check has touched, and the toll still holds. On Section 3’s
board extended with CHECK, the run [VOUCH] from NO crosses with one mark, and
[CHECK, VOUCH] crosses with one mark for the crossing plus whatever CHECK was
charged, one mark in all if CHECK is priced at zero. Making a crossing depend on an
earlier check is a condition on the step function, which a particular system can impose
and the definition does not.


9.5 What the word means
Insight, in the sense this book prices, is a relation committed to, in a move that flips
a reading from off to on, and that move costs at least one mark, in any system with
the toll, for any relation, whatever its depth. (And one edge from the paper: a bare
crossing that commits to nothing pays the same mark, so “a relation committed to”
is what the crossing is at its best. The toll doesn’t guarantee it.) Three boundaries,
each from a different place. From Metcalfe: it isn’t a feeling, and a system’s version
has to be an event. From the proof: the price is flat; a shallow commit and a deep
one both cost at least one, and cost is not depth. A system can pay heavily to check a
trivial claim, and Duncker’s box, a real insight, is still one small commit. And from
the two-move protocol: a paid flag proves nothing on its own. Price and correctness
are separate books.

Which leaves a suspicion I’d have in your place. Everything so far has been one
reading on one sheet of paper, with a rule I chose and a count I bolted on. Is the shape
of that record something I picked, or is it what any base-driven record has to look
like, on any machine at all? That’s the next section: take any machine that steps, bolt
a record onto it, and see what shape it’s forced into. How a concrete machine hangs
actual claims on its parts, a checked property of one counter at one edition, and where
those sit in the state, comes in Part IV.

10 Records over any base: the latch
For the whole book so far I’ve been building up a thing with a flag and a counter,
and a fair reader is entitled to suspect that the whole apparatus is special pleading for
one machine, the one I keep promising to build. So here’s the section that answers
the suspicion with no particular machine in it at all, and sees what’s left. Take any
machine that steps deterministically: a Turing machine, a register machine (a few


                                           187
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


numbered boxes that each hold a whole number, and a program that adds, subtracts
and jumps), a lambda calculus (Alonzo Church’s way of computing by nothing but
plugging expressions into expressions; Section 13 builds one), anything. Call it the
base. Now bolt a record onto it, under rules I’ll state, and ask: what can the record be?

The answer is one shape, and I’ll show you the shape first because it’s a thing you can
build from a cup and a die.

10.1 A cup and a die
Put a cup upside down on the table. The rule: the first time a coin lands in front of
it, turn it right side up. There is no rule for turning it back over. Now roll a die, and
put a coin down on every six. Roll twenty times. If a six appears, the cup turns over
on the first one and stays turned over. Write down which roll did it. That number is
where the record happened, and the cup afterward is the record. If no six appears, the
cup stays down; a reachable event need not occur on every trial.

For the deterministic base in the theorem, write the rolls down first and replay them.
The base state is the fixed list and a finger pointing to its next entry; a step moves
the finger one place, regardless of the cup. The event asks whether that entry is six.
Nothing about the cup changes which entry comes next.

That’s a latch. Electrical engineers have had the circuit since 1918, when two British
physicists teaching engineering in London, William Eccles, a radio pioneer, and Frank
Jordan, applied for a patent on a two-valve arrangement that holds whichever state
you last put it in; it became the flip-flop, and the registers and caches in the device
you’re reading this on descend from it. Cut its reset wire and what’s left has one input,
“set,” and the rule new state = old state or set: once set, it stays set. The cup is that circuit:
a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off.

(Eccles and Jordan didn’t call it a flip-flop. Their 1919 paper calls it a trigger relay.
Where the newer, sillier name came from I can’t source, so I’ll leave it at that.)

Is a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off only a picture, or did anybody ever build one on
purpose? Somebody did, and for a reason that’s very close to this book’s. In the mid-
1950s Wen Tsing Chow, an engineer at the Arma division of the American Bosch Arma
Corporation in Garden City, New York, was asked by the United States Air Force,
in the accounts of his career I could find, for a more flexible and secure way to hold
the fixed numbers, the targeting constants, inside the guidance computer of the Atlas
missile. What he and his Arma colleague William Henrich patented (filed in 1957,
granted in 1962, under the plain title “Storage matrix”) was a grid with a connection
at every crossing, where you set the numbers by taking out the connections you didn’t
want, physically or by burning them out with too much current. The word burn is
right there in the patent, and people still say they burn a chip. The descendants are
called programmable read-only memories, PROMs, and a fuse blown in one stays
blown: there’s no current you can send to grow it back. A whole memory built out of


                                               188
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


cups with no reset wire, because somebody wanted numbers nobody could quietly
change later. Does that prove anything here? No. The theorem below doesn’t care
what a cup is made of. But it’s good to know the shape wasn’t invented for a sheet of
paper. Somebody needed it, for stakes a good deal higher than a die.

Now the claim, stated loosely and then exactly: every base-driven record, over any base,
is a cup with no reset wire, turned by some event the base passes through.

10.2 What “base-driven” has to mean
Here’s where the content is, and I’ll give you the five rules, because the theorem is
only as strong as they are.

A machine extends a base when there’s a map from the bigger machine’s states down
to the base’s, and that map starts in the base’s start states, reaches every one of them,
moves in step with the base (one step up top is one step down below, through the
map), and agrees about halting. The bigger machine may carry as much hidden state
as it likes beyond the base. That’s the “any base” part: the base doesn’t get to see the
extension, and the extension doesn’t get to change what the base does.

The extension carries a record, a yes/no reading, and a ledger, a counter. It’s a base-driven
record when five things hold. One: the record’s next value depends only on the base’s
current state and the record’s current value. (I’ll call this driven by the computation. It
says the record answers to what the machine is doing. A clock on the wall or someone’s
hand doesn’t get a say.) Two: the ledger never goes down (Section 6). Three: the step
that turns the record on costs at least one; that’s the toll (Section 3). Four: once on,
the record stays on; that’s permanence (Section 4). Distributed-systems people have
a name for a predicate like that. The computer scientists K. Mani Chandy and Leslie
Lamport, in their 1985 paper on taking a consistent snapshot of a distributed system,
called a property stable when once it holds it holds forever after, and stable properties
are the ones a snapshot can be trusted to detect. Five: some run from a start state
actually reaches a step that turns the record on; otherwise the record is decoration.

Here are the words exactly. On/off is true/false, ∨ is “or” (on when either side is on),
and nextk is k steps.


Definition 10.1 (Base, record-carrying machine, cover). A base B is a set of states with
a step function nextB , a set of starting states, and a halting predicate. A record-carrying
machine M is a set of states with a step function next M , a set of starting states, a record
rec from states to Booleans, a ledger µ from states to whole numbers, and a halting
predicate. The cost of a step is cost(m) = µ(next M (m)) −̇ µ(m). A cover of B by M is a
map π from states of M to states of B that sends starting states to starting states, has
every starting state of B as the image of some starting state of M, commutes with the
steps, π (next M (m)) = nextB (π (m)), and agrees about halting: m halts exactly when
π (m) does.


                                            189
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Definition 10.2 (Base-driven record, latch). M with cover π is a base-driven record over
B when (R1, driven by the computation) there is one function f such that, for every
state m, rec(next M (m)) = f (π (m), rec(m)); for every state m, (R2, ledger) µ(m) ≤
µ(next M (m)); (R3, toll) if rec(m) is off and rec(next M (m)) is on, then cost(m) ≥ 1; (R4,
permanence) if rec(m) is on, so is rec(next M (m)); and (R5, a reachable write) some
starting state m0 and some k have rec(nextkM (m0 )) off and rec(nextkM+1 (m0 )) on. An
event is a function h from base states to Booleans, and its latch is the step (b, r ) 7→
(nextB (b), r ∨ h(b)). M factors as the latch of h when, for every state m (reachable or
not),

        (π (next M (m)), rec(next M (m))) = (nextB (π (m)), rec(m) ∨ h(π (m))).


Now the theorem. Under those rules, the base state and the record move exactly as a
latch: the record switches on at the first base state where some event holds, and never
off, and the event is read off the extension’s own rule by asking it what it does when
the record is off (stated exactly below). That’s a statement about what the base and
the record do together. The hidden state the extension carries can’t push the record
anywhere (R1) doesn’t allow, since the record’s next value is a function of the base
state and the record’s own value. The theorem doesn’t say the whole extension is a
bare latch machine, and it doesn’t make hidden state show up anywhere in particular:
an extension can carry a field that touches neither the record nor the ledger. And the
event is pinned down only on base states that some state with the record off covers;
on a base state with no such state above it, f (b, off) is whatever (R1)’s function says,
and nothing in a run ever consults it.

I promised the content was in the definition, and here’s what that means: the proof is
a short case split on whether the record is already on, and it uses only two of the five
rules, “driven by the computation” and “permanent.” The ledger, the toll, and the
reachable-write clauses play no part in it. A latch is what you get from “answers only
to the base” plus “never comes back down,” full stop. The other three rules matter
for the converse: for any base and any event the base can reach, the latch of that event,
priced at one unit per write, is a base-driven record. Put the two together and you’ve
got: base-driven records are exactly latches. One shape, no others, over any base.


Observation 10.1 (The record is a latch). Let B be any base, π a cover of B by M, and
suppose M’s record is driven by the computation (R1), through a function f , and permanent
(R4). Then M factors as the latch of the event h(b) = f (b, off). In particular every base-driven
record factors that way; (R2), (R3) and (R5) are not hypotheses.

Proof. The base half of the equation is the cover’s step clause. For the record, split on
rec(m). If it is on, permanence (R4) makes the next value on, and on ∨ h(π (m)) is on.
If it is off, (R1) makes the next value f (π (m), off) = h(π (m)) = off ∨ h(π (m)). Only
(R1), (R4) and the cover are used; (R2), (R3) and (R5) are discarded.


                                              190
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


The latch’s nearest neighbours are in verification, and they’re old. The computer sci-
entists Martín Abadi and Leslie Lamport, then at Digital’s research lab in Palo Alto,
added history variables to specifications in 1991: extra state that records what has hap-
pened and never steers the system, used to prove that one specification implements
another. A history variable that only ever turns on is the cup. Temporal logic has the
same record as an operator. In the past-time temporal logic that Orna Lichtenstein,
Amir Pnueli and Lenore Zuck set out in 1985, “once h” holds now exactly when h has
held at some point so far, and a runtime monitor keeps it in one bit with the update
r ′ = r ∨ h. Klaus Havelund and Grigore Roşu, two computer scientists working on
runtime verification, synthesized monitors of exactly that kind for safety properties
written in that logic in 2002. That update is the latch of Definition 10.2, word for word.
What the observation adds is the other direction: a record driven by the computation
that never comes down can’t be anything else.

One thing about that proof deserves a second look, because it cuts both ways. It never
asks what the base is. The cover decides that: whatever the map sends down is base,
and the record’s rule is allowed to read all of it; whatever stays up top is extension,
and (R1) keeps the record’s rule from reading it. Draw the line low, so the base is only
the computation’s own working state, and (R1) is a real demand. Draw it high, put
every table and every refusal bit into the base, and (R1) is easy to meet, and the latch
shape comes out exactly the same. So the theorem holds wherever you draw the line,
and that’s exactly why it can’t tell you where a record’s meaning lives. The meaning
lives in what the event h reads, and that’s in the base by construction. The cover makes
the projected base step independent of which extension state lies above it. The record,
ledger and hidden fields may still affect other extension fields; the theorem does not
make the entire extension inert. On the small machine, the checks that give the flag its
meaning sit in the base chosen for this cover. So when the machine in Part IV arrives,
ask it first which parts it puts above the line.


Theorem 10.2 (Every reachable latch is a base-driven record). Let B be any base and
h any event. Let Latchh have states (b, r, x ), starting states (b, off, 0) with b starting in B,
step (b, r, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b), x + δ) with δ = 1 when r is off and h(b) is on and
δ = 0 otherwise, record r, ledger x, halting as b halts, and cover (b, r, x ) 7→ b. Suppose some
starting b0 and some k bring Latchh from (b0 , off, 0), in k steps, to a state whose record is still
off and whose base state satisfies h. Then Latchh is a base-driven record over B.

Proof. (R1) holds with f (b, r ) = r ∨ h(b). (R2): each step adds 0 or 1. (R3): a step that
turns the record on has r off and h(b) on, so it adds 1. (R4): on ∨ h(b) is on. (R5) is
the supposition. The supposition asks for the first time h holds on some run; any run
from a start that reaches an h-state has such a first time.

A reversible base needs one more thing to carry a record, and the next theorem says
exactly what. If the base never merges two states, keep every earlier record value in a


                                               191
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


growing history beside the latch, and the whole step merges nothing either; but on a
finite state space a permanent record can’t be written by a step that merges nothing
at all. A step that merges nothing is called injective: no two states go to the same next
state. And r :: H is the history H with r put on the front, as in Section 9.


Theorem 10.3 (Records on reversible machines). (1) Let B be a base whose step is injective.
The machine with states (b, r, H, x ), step (b, r, H, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b), r :: H, x + δ)
(δ as in Theorem 10.2), starting states with r off, H empty and x = 0, has an injective step,
and under the supposition of Theorem 10.2 it is a base-driven record over B. (2) On a finite
state space, a single injective step with a permanent reading never turns that reading from off
to on.

Proof. (1) Equal images have equal base parts, so equal base states by injectivity; equal
histories r :: H, so equal records and histories; and equal ledgers once the equal δ is
subtracted. That it is base-driven is the proof of Theorem 10.2 with the history carried
along. (2) is Theorem 4.1 of Section 4 with a single move.

So a base that never merges can still carry a record, if it’s allowed to grow a history
that never ends. A machine with finitely many states can’t carry one without merging:
on a finite machine an instruction that first raises a permanent reading must merge
some possible states. The entering state need not belong to the colliding pair; Section 4
prices the instruction under merge pricing.

Process-calculus people ran into the same thing from the other side. Vincent Danos
and Jean Krivine, two theoretical computer scientists in Paris, wanted to pin down
what a transaction is. They took in 2005 a reversible version of CCS, Robin Milner’s
calculus of processes that talk to each other, where every step can be rolled back, and
modelled a transaction as a process that wanders freely through everything that can
be undone until it performs an action declared irreversible, which is the commit. The
way I read it, they start from steps that all come undone and ask what has to be added
before anything sticks, and the theorem above starts from a record and asks what
the step under it must be. In their calculus, as in the theorem, a permanent effect
needs a step with no way back, and the calculus has to say which steps those are. The
word I tripped on was declared. Theirs are labelled. Mine, I thought, are picked out
by counting, since on a finite machine the first write merges whatever anyone calls it.
Push on that and it gives. I choose the event h, and on a base that grows its history
forever the write merges nothing (Theorem 10.3), so there my permanence is declared
too.

There’s an arrow of time in that theorem, and I should say where it came from, because
I put it there by hand. Every starting state has the record off. That’s the only reason a
raised record means the event happened: it was down at the start, and only h lifts it.
Turn the cup up before the first roll and it tells you nothing about the die. So the clean



                                              192
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


start is an assumed ready state, a past hypothesis in miniature. The past hypothesis
is the physicists’ name for an assumed low-entropy beginning of the universe, which
several of the accounts below lean records on. Whether every trusted record leans on
it is their argument, and I’m not settling it. Nothing in this book derives one; every
theorem here about records assumes its small version and starts from there.

When I went looking for who else had found the arrow hiding in the start, I got five
papers that read like five unrelated answers. They lined up once I asked each one the
same thing: what does the cup being down at the start rest on? There are two places
to put it. You can put it at the beginning, as a fact about how things started. Or you
can put it in the structure of what causes what. David Wolpert, then a physicist at Los
Alamos and the same Wolpert as the free-lunch theorem, sorted memory systems in
1992, and one of his kinds works only because it begins in a prepared state set up by
a process that runs one way, which is how it leans on the second law. That’s the cup
put down by somebody before the game, at the first place. Wolpert and Jens Kipper,
a philosopher at Rochester, put in 2024 that sorting on a formal footing, and they say
plainly that they have no formal proof this kind can only remember the past. I trust
them more for that sentence. What I think they’re saying is that a prepared start buys
you a memory, and getting its direction too takes something they can’t yet prove.

Aram Ebtekar, an independent researcher in Vancouver, and Marcus Hutter, who
works on the theory of general artificial intelligence at Google DeepMind and the
Australian National University, built in 2024 a reversible toy world, imposed a past
hypothesis on it, coarse-grained it, and got records of the past and none of the future.
As I read their route, the clean start doesn’t go straight to the records. It goes through
a causal structure first, and the arrows come out of that. Thomas Blanchard, a philoso-
pher of science at Cologne, got in 2024 the same lopsidedness of knowledge out of
the causal Markov condition, a condition on causal structure. So Blanchard starts at
the second place, which is the middle of Ebtekar and Hutter’s road. That took me a
while to see, because one is a toy world and the other is philosophy of causation. They
go from the start to causes to records; he goes from causes to records. The fit is my
reading, and it’s mine to defend. And Carlo Rovelli, two years before his paper on the
cost of choosing from the opening chapter, studied traces in “Memory and entropy”
(2022) and concluded that a memory turns low entropy into available information.
He’s at the first place, and he says what the beginning gets spent on. Read against the
latch, that’s the blank the record uses up: the flag can say yes once because it started
at no.

So does the latch explain why records point backwards? No. I’ll say that plainly, so
it doesn’t look like it does. The step runs forwards and the runs start clean, and a
theorem built on those two can only hand the arrow back. Push further and it gives in
a second place. The history that grows forever looked like a way around the clean start.
It starts empty, so it leans on the same blank. Under a step that forgets nothing, on a
finite set, no permanent record can ever be written, past or future, which is Zermelo


                                           193
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


again. On the map the book sits at the first place, with Wolpert and Rovelli, and it sits
there by assumption. Ebtekar and Hutter at least imposed their start on a world with
its own dynamics and watched what came out. I wrote mine into the definition.

Constructor theory, which Section 4 brings in as a neighbour of the chairs, has a paper
on time (Deutsch and Marletto, 2025) saying that laws stated as which transformations
a device can and can’t bring about can’t mention time at all, so duration has to come
from relations between physical systems, clocks, that have their own dynamics. What
I think they’re saying is that whenever you want a duration you point at a second
system and count what it did. That’s the position this book is in by construction. The
step count is the only time in it, and it comes from the machine’s own steps. The next
subsection has a record turned at the fifth tick of a hidden clock, and (R1) throws it out,
which read beside them is a rule about which system may be the clock: the one being
recorded. Push on it, though. Their laws have no step in them, and the paper’s work
is getting duration and dynamics out of clocks and timers. I put a step, nextB , into
the definition of a base. So I’m in their position only at the far end of their argument,
where a clock already exists. The base is my clock, and I assumed it.

Physicists have built this latch on paper too, in quantum mechanics, and it behaves
the way the last theorem says. The question that sorted them for me is where the
cup puts what it forgets, since a closed quantum system with separate energy levels
comes back (Bocchieri and Loinger, Section 4) and the theorem left only two ways out:
a history that never ends, or a merge. Klaus Hepp, a mathematical physicist at ETH
Zurich, wanted a measuring device inside quantum mechanics itself, and studied in
1972 a particle that flips spins in a long chain as it passes, now called the Coleman-
Hepp model (I know Hepp’s paper only from accounts of it), and John Bell (1975)
took it apart: the record is exactly definite only for an infinitely long chain, which is
the reversible escape above, a history that never ends, in quantum clothes. Jonathan
Halliwell, a theoretical physicist at Imperial College London, used in 1999 a two-state
detector that flips once when a particle crosses a point and is kept from flipping back
by a large environment, which is a latch with the environment holding the history. His
abstract calls it effectively irreversible, and I like that he puts the word effectively right
there where you can see it. And Murray Gell-Mann, the physicist who named the
quark, and James Hartle, of the University of California at Santa Barbara, gave in 1995
the property a name inside their framework of decoherent histories: the permanence
of the past, past alternatives that stay settled as the story is extended into the future.
They name (R4) for whole histories and leave the cup to others. So Hepp’s chain, as
Bell read it, is exact and infinite, and Halliwell’s detector is finite and only effectively
permanent. Mine is finite, exact and permanent at once, and it gets there by letting the
first write merge. Push on that and it gives: I never say where the merged state goes.
Hepp’s chain had to be infinite. Halliwell had to put his in an environment. Mine just
goes, and the toll writes a unit in a counter. That’s fine in a model of computation, and
it’s exactly where this stops being physics.

The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


10.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the clock
A theorem with two hypotheses should have two counterexamples, one for each
hypothesis dropped, and it does, and they’re the two ways a record goes wrong in the
world.

Drop permanence. Take a base that just counts, and a record that flips at every step:
on, off, on, off. It’s driven by the computation; it’s not permanent; and it’s not a latch
of any event. This is a toggle, a piece of working state. A record you can revoke is
working state wearing a record’s clothes, and if a revocation has to stick, that’s a second
latch (“revoked”), which is how certificate revocation lists actually work: you add
an entry; you never delete the certificate. Alin Tomescu, a computer scientist then at
MIT, and his coauthors (2019) built append-only authenticated sets and dictionaries
for transparency logs, and revocation fits that shape exactly: a revocation goes in once
and stays. The pair lemma (stated below) covers two latches that can each read the
other; do it with two cups where the second only turns over on an even roll if the first
is already up, and you’ll see the second can never turn before the first.

Dialogue theorists built a version of that two-latch rule for arguments. Give each
speaker a row of cups, one for every claim they’ve made. Everybody I read in this
field is answering two questions about those cups: whose hand turns them, and can
they come back down. C. L. Hamblin, an Australian philosopher and logician who
also came up with reverse Polish notation for early computers, wrote Fallacies (1970),
and it has a chapter on formal dialectic where each speaker has a commitment store,
a list of what they’re on the hook for, and the rules of the dialogue update it. The
speaker doesn’t. I know that chapter from other people’s accounts of it. That’s an
answer to the first question, and it’s (R1) for arguments: the cup answers to what
happened in the dialogue, and the speaker’s hand is kept off it. Henry Prakken, who
works on AI and law at Utrecht, built in 2005 dialogue games for argumentation on
stores like that and made commitments sticky: a claim can be retracted only when
it has been challenged, and claims and backtracking carry a price. He also floats a
convention that once a player has retracted a proposition, that player can’t take it on
again, which is a revocation that stays revoked, the way an entry on a revocation list
does. That’s an answer to the second question, and it took me a second pass to see
that it’s two answers. A cup can come down, and coming down costs. And once it has,
the taking-back is itself a cup that stays up. Erik Krabbe, an argumentation theorist at
Groningen, names in 2001 the awkward part of that: retraction is frowned on, and yet
resolving a dispute takes somebody retracting a doubt or a point of view, so the rules
have to say when taking a commitment back is allowed. As I read him, he’s standing
between the two ends of the second question. A store that never gives can’t settle a
dispute. A store that gives freely isn’t a store. The part of all that I’d keep is Hamblin’s,
that the store belongs to the rules. It doesn’t belong to the speaker. Take the pen away
from the program. And this book answers Krabbe with a price: a take-back is a second
cup, “revoked,” and turning it costs at least one like any other write, so a retraction is


                                            195
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


allowed, permanent and paid for. That’s Prakken’s convention with the toll attached.
Where mine gives is his first condition. He lets a claim come down only when it’s been
challenged, and nothing in my latch asks why the second cup turned. The pair lemma
lets the second cup’s event read the base and the first cup, and nothing in it requires a
challenge to be there.

The same field has a notion that looks a lot like earning. In the abstract argumentation
of Phan Minh Dung, a computer scientist at the Asian Institute of Technology in
Bangkok (1995), arguments attack one another, and the grounded semantics starts from
the arguments nobody attacks and keeps adding the ones they defend. Look at how
it’s built: things go in and never come out, which is a row of cups turned one at a
time. Pietro Baroni and Massimiliano Giacomin, at Brescia, introduced in 2007, and
Martin Caminada, then at Aberdeen, revisited in 2014, strong admissibility: a set is
strongly admissible when every argument in it is defended by others in the set that
don’t lean back on it, so the support bottoms out. That’s the argumentation form of
an earned claim. Above the bottom, nothing in it is in by default, which puts it at the
far end from Burge’s default on the testimony map in Section 7. Caminada argues it
plays a vital part in the dialogue games that decide grounded acceptance. I’ve read
Caminada’s paper; Dung’s and Baroni and Giacomin’s I know through what later
papers say about them. Notice the bottom, though. An argument nobody attacks
gets in on a check that can’t fail, and this book says a check that can’t fail establishes
nothing. Now turn that on my own cups, because it lands. My first write needs only
that h holds, and what h reads sits in the base, where the latch theorem doesn’t look. I
charge a unit for it. A unit is a price. It isn’t a check. So my earned records bottom out
the way Dung’s do, in something let in without an argument, and the one difference
is that mine pays to get in. Whether a machine’s earned record certifies exactly the
strongly admissible sets is the kind of statement I’d have to prove before I said it, and
I haven’t.

A record that’s allowed to change its mind isn’t lawless, though. It’s somebody else’s
subject. Count how many times the cup may be turned. Once, from down to up, is the
latch. More than once and you’re somewhere else, and the people who went there sort
it two ways: by how many turns are allowed, and by how long the game runs. The
philosopher Hilary Putnam, then at MIT, and E. Mark Gold, a computer scientist at
a research lab in Santa Monica, in back-to-back papers in 1965, looked at questions a
machine answers by guessing and revising, where the answer is whatever the guesses
finally settle on. Putnam’s paper says outright that you’re never sure you have the
correct answer. That stopped me the first time. What kind of answer can’t you ever
be sure you have? The way I came to read it: the cup’s position at any moment is the
current guess, the answer is where it ends up, and nobody watching can tell when
it’s done moving. Yuri Ershov, a logician in Novosibirsk, sorted those in 1968 by how
many revisions they’re allowed (that’s how his hierarchy is described; I haven’t read
his paper). Allow one, from no to yes, and you get exactly the sets a program can list.



                                           196
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


That level I did check, in a modern account of the hierarchy by Rod Downey, Carl
Jockusch, Timothy McNicholl and Paul Schupp, four computability theorists, and it’s
a short exercise once you see it. That’s what a permanent record raised by a search
catches. Allow two, three, and so on, and every extra change buys new sets: the rungs
of the ladder are all different. A record that can come back down lives on that ladder.
Now put Putnam’s worry on my cup, because it lands. On the bottom rung a yes is
final the moment it appears, and a no never is. Down means not yet. A single cup of
mine can certify that something happened and can never certify that it didn’t; a final
no would take a second cup, turned by finding a reason, and that’s the pair of latches
again. That’s what the bottom rung costs, and I’d rather name it. This book stays on
the bottom rung. I’m pointing at the ladder. I’m not climbing it.

The ladder doesn’t stop at finite time, and the people who followed it past infinity
have names for the two kinds of record I just described. A definition that only ever
adds, stage after stage, and keeps everything it has at each limit, is an inductive def-
inition (the long treatment is a 1974 chapter by Wayne Richter and Peter Aczel, two
recursion theorists). That’s the latch run through the infinite, a cup that goes up at
some stage and is still up at every stage after. Let it take things back, and keep what
stays put from some stage on, and you have what John Burgess, a philosopher and
logician at Princeton, called in 1986 quasi-inductive definitions, which he met in the
revision theories of truth that grew up beside the logician Saul Kripke’s 1975 theory
of truth, which builds up the true sentences in stages. Burgess’s paper measures how
complicated the truths of those theories get. I’ve read its abstract. The place where
he names them I haven’t. What took me a few reads is that Burgess’s rule at a limit
is Putnam and Gold’s rule, keep whatever the guesses settled on, applied at every
limit stage along the way. That’s my reading of how the two fit. If it’s right, the split
between a cup that only goes up and a cup that settles is the same split at finite time
and past it. A permanent record is the first kind. A toggle that’s allowed to settle is
the second. Joel Hamkins and Andy Lewis, two set theorists, let a Turing machine
keep running through the ordinals in 2000. At a limit a cell keeps its value if it settled,
and reads 1 if it kept flipping back and forth forever, and the trick they use again and
again is the toggle: flash a flag on and off every time a guess changes, and at the limit
the flag is on exactly when the guess changed infinitely often. A flag that can come
back down is how that machine learns what no finite run could tell it. A permanent
one can’t do that trick, because at a limit a cell that only ever goes up just stays up. So
past infinity the toggle is the clever one. A latch tells you a thing happened at least
once. Their flashing flag tells you it happened infinitely often. I threw the toggle out a
few paragraphs back anyway, and I’d do it again, because before the limit its reading
can’t be relied on, and nobody using a machine of mine gets to wait for a limit. One
finite-time fact belongs beside it, so nobody concludes too much from permanence.
Hao Wang, a logician then at Oxford, described in 1957 a machine whose only write is
to mark a square and which can never erase one, and it computes everything a Turing
machine does. Permanence of a machine’s own memory costs it no computing power.


                                           197
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


What the book prices is a permanent reading raised by a step that has to work whether
or not the reading is already up, which is a different thing. So the cost I named a
paragraph ago is a cost in what a reading can claim. Computing power doesn’t pay it.

Drop “driven by the computation.” Take a base that counts, and a record that switches
on at the fifth tick of a hidden clock, whatever the base is doing. It’s permanent. The
computation doesn’t drive it. This is a timestamp. A timestamp is not evidence. It
says when. It doesn’t say what happened, and a record switched by an outside party or
a clock records that party or that clock and leaves the computation out. Try it with
the recorded die list. Keep a second tally hidden beside it, and turn the cup when
that tally reads five before a move; then advance both the tally and the finger on the
list. Run two trials from the same list entry with the cup down, but start the hidden
tally at five in one trial and zero in the other. The next cup values disagree although
everything the base shows agrees. That is the failure of being driven by the base. If
the tally always starts synchronized with the list position, the position can predict the
cup; the distinction matters below.

The examples establish exactly the facts I named for each: the toggle is driven, isn’t
permanent and isn’t a latch; the clock is permanent and isn’t driven. That each also
keeps the other rules (the ledger is the step count, the first switch-on costs one, a run
reaches it) is true by inspection.

Permanent but undriven is a clock, driven but impermanent is a toggle, and a record
is the thing that’s both. Undriven, for the clock, means that along the runs that
actually happen the base state doesn’t fix when the record turns; Lemma 10.7 below
says why that’s the condition, and what (R1) as written adds to it. That’s the whole
discrimination, and I think it’s the most useful single sentence in this book for looking
at systems other than the one I build, which is why it’s here.

The pair lemma and the two counterexamples, exactly. The base for both counterex-
amples is the counter: states are whole numbers, the step adds one, every state is a
starting state, and nothing halts. Two more bits of shorthand: ¬r is r flipped, and a
statement in square brackets, like [k = 5], reads on when it’s true and off when it isn’t.


Lemma 10.4 (Two records are two latches). Let c1 , c2 be two records on M, with cover
π onto a base B, such that: there is one function F with (c1 (next M (m)), c2 (next M (m))) =
F (π (m), c1 (m), c2 (m)); the ledger never goes down; a step that turns either record on costs
at least one; and each record is permanent. Then there are h1 , h2 with c1 (next M (m)) =
c1 (m) ∨ h1 (π (m), c2 (m)) and c2 (next M (m)) = c2 (m) ∨ h2 (π (m), c1 (m)) for every m.

Proof. Take h1 (b, r2 ) to be the first part of F (b, off, r2 ) and h2 (b, r1 ) the second part of
F (b, r1 , off), then split on each record as in Observation 10.1.


Lemma 10.5 (The toggle). Let the toggle have states (n, r ), step (n, r ) 7→ (n + 1, ¬r ),


                                               198
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


every state starting, record r, ledger n, cover (n, r ) 7→ n onto the counter. It is driven by the
computation, with f (b, r ) = ¬r; it is not permanent; and it factors as the latch of no event.

Proof. At (0, on) the next record is off, which breaks permanence; and any latch gives
on ∨ h(0) = on there.


Lemma 10.6 (The clock). Let the clock have states (b, k, r ), step (b, k, r ) 7→ (b + 1, k +
1, r ∨ [k = 5]), every state starting, record r, ledger b, cover (b, k, r ) 7→ b onto the counter. It
is permanent and not driven by the computation.

Proof. Permanence: on ∨ x is on. Not driven: the states (0, 5, off) and (0, 0, off) have
the same base state and the same record, and their next records are on and off, so no f
of the base state and the record can give both.

“Driven” is a condition on every state. The clock makes every state a starting state,
so the two states the proof compares are both ones a run can begin at, even though a
clock started at (0, 0, off) would never reach (0, 5, off).

That last sentence does more work than it looks, so here it is as a lemma. Start the
same clock in sync, at (b, b, off) only. On every state its runs reach, the hidden count
equals the base, and the clock is exactly the latch of [b = 5]. (R1) still rejects it, because
(R1) asks about every state, and (0, 5, off) is a state, though no run from a synchronised
start reaches it. So (R1) as written separates the clock from a latch partly by how the
cover is drawn and through states nobody visits. The separation I mean is the one
on reachable states: the clock with every state a start fails (R1) even when only states
some run reaches are counted, since two starting states sit over the same base state
with the same record and disagree about the next one. And the latch theorem holds in
that reachable form too.


Lemma 10.7 (The clock, on the states runs reach). Say M’s record is driven on reachable
states when (R1) holds for every state reached from a starting state in some number of steps.
(1) If M’s record is driven on reachable states and permanent, then on every reachable state M
steps as the latch of some event. (2) The clock of Lemma 10.6 isn’t driven on reachable states.
(3) The clock started in sync, with starting states (b, b, off) and the same step, record, ledger
and cover, is permanent, isn’t driven by the computation, is driven on reachable states, and on
every reachable state steps as the latch of [b = 5].

Proof. (1) is the proof of Observation 10.1, run on reachable states only. (2) The
states (0, 5, off) and (0, 0, off) are starting states, reached in no steps, and the proof of
Lemma 10.6 applies to them. (3) From (b, b, off) every step adds one to both counts,
so a reachable state has k = b and its next record is r ∨ [b = 5]. Over every state, (R1)
fails at the same pair as in Lemma 10.6.



                                                199
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


So “permanent but undriven is a clock” is a sentence about the clock with every state a
start, over the cover that hides its count, and it holds there in the strong form: undriven
on the very states its runs pass through. A clock started in step with its base is a latch
on the runs it has, and (R1) throws it out only because (R1) also looks at states those
runs never reach.

10.4 Is there only one such machine? No. One structure, two free choices.
Here’s a sentence I have to take apart: “there’s only one way to carry a record.” Three
different things get squeezed into that breath.

First claim: given the toll and a fixed price list, is there one way to keep the books,
starting at zero and adding each move’s price? Yes, on every state reachable from the
start; that’s Section 6’s initiality, and it assumes the price list.

Second claim: is every base-driven record over a base the same machine, charges and all?
No, and the counterexample is embarrassing in its simplicity. Take any base-driven
record and add one more coin to the bill on every step, whatever the step is. Now walk
the five rules. The record still answers only to the base and its own value (R1); the bill
never touches it. The ledger still never goes down (R2); it climbs faster, if anything.
The step that turns the record on still costs at least one (R3), because the toll is a floor
and a surcharge only raises the price. Once on, the record stays on (R4), and the same
run still reaches the write (R5). So the billed machine is base-driven, and it isn’t the
machine you started with: wherever the original sat still for free, the billed one pays a
coin a tick for sitting still. Do it with the cup and the die. Charge a coin for every roll,
six or not. The cup turns over on the same roll as before. You’ve changed the bill and
nothing about the record. A machine that charges for CPU time is base-driven and
isn’t the one that doesn’t.

But the billed machine isn’t a different structure. It’s the same record, steps and halting
with a different price list. So the claim worth keeping is sameness up to the price
schedule: compare two machines by their record, their halting and their steps, through
their maps down to the base, and don’t compare charges. Fix which event the record
is, and the bill stops mattering; a flat surcharge, or any surcharge that depends on the
current state, sits on the same structure. That’s the first free choice. The walk above
is the whole argument, and it works over an arbitrary base, with any surcharge that
depends on the current state: the billed machine is base-driven, has the same latch
event, steps along with the original on record, halting and base, and pays each step’s
cost plus the surcharge.

And then the second free choice, and this one still surprises me. Which event is the
record? Nothing in the five rules picks it. The converse above already says so, if you
read it twice: for any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one
unit per write, is a base-driven record. Do it with the die. One cup turns over on the
first six. Another turns over on the first one. Both are cups with no reset wire; both
are base-driven. Roll a one first, and until a six turns up the two cups disagree about

                                            200
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


whether anything has been recorded. So which permanent reading counts as the record is
a second thing nobody forces on you. The price list is one free choice. The event is the
other. That second choice is the question Section 15 is about: what, if anything, makes
certification the event worth recording. “The ledger passed one” is an event only if
the chosen base includes enough information to decide it. An extension-only ledger
is hidden from a base event, just as the hidden clock was. The free choice is among
functions of the chosen base.


Corollary 10.8 (The event is a free choice). Let B be any base and h1 , h2 two events, each
meeting the supposition of Theorem 10.2. Then Latchh1 and Latchh2 are both base-driven
records over B. If some base state b has h1 (b) on and h2 (b) off, then one step from (b, off, 0)
leaves the first record on and the second off.

Proof. That both are base-driven is Theorem 10.2 applied twice. The step is the latch’s
own rule: off ∨ h1 (b) is on and off ∨ h2 (b) is off.

Now let the cup wobble. Say whatever turns it over sometimes does and sometimes
doesn’t, with odds you could write on a card. Does fixing the price list fix the odds?
No, and the counterexample is two cups with the same price tag and differently
loaded coins. Here’s the setup, said carefully. Let a record be a single bit that moves at
random: from each value, a list of weighted next values, every weight positive, never
empty, never leaving on once on, and with the write from off to on charged at least
one. Call such a record a permanent probabilistic record. Call two such records the same
schedule when the same moves are possible and every move is charged the same, and
the same in probability when the weighted lists are equal.


Theorem 10.9 (The schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities). (1) There are two permanent
probabilistic records with the same schedule that are not the same in probability. (2) There is a
permanent probabilistic record that no deterministic latch on its current value describes.

Proof. (1) From off, one record moves to off or on with weights 1 and 1, the other with
weights 1 and 2; from on, both stay on with weight 1; both charge 1 for the write. Same
possible moves, same charges, different weights. (2) The first record moves from off
both to off and to on, while a latch r ∨ h(r ) gives one value.

These are finite-weight models on one bit with no base underneath; they say nothing
about any particular machine.

Third claim: is there one state space, up to renaming, that every base-driven record-
carrier has to have? I don’t claim it. Nothing needs it.




                                              201
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


10.5 Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about
The theorem is stated for any base, and this section instantiates it on three models of
computation that other people built: a small Turing machine (any program); a register
machine of the kind the computer scientists Stephen Cook (of the certificates) and
Robert Reckhow described in 1973, with unit-cost indirect addressing (any program);
and a lambda calculus (call-by-value, meaning an argument is worked out before it’s
plugged in, and made deterministic by letting a term with no step left to take step to
itself). On each, the latch form holds, by the one generic theorem applied to that base
(the bases are defined below). So a register machine with a base-driven record is a
register machine plus a cup. So is a lambda calculus. (There’s one more instance, the
machine I build later, where a particular flag is shown to be a base-driven record and
the same theorem makes it a latch, in Section 16.)

Here are the three bases explicitly. A base needs a state, a next-state function, a set of
starting states and a halting predicate; the latch theorem asks for nothing else about
its instruction vocabulary.


Definition 10.3 (Three concrete bases). The tape base has a finite Boolean list t, a head
index h, a program counter q and a natural-number cost field. Reading beyond the list
returns false. Writing at h extends the list with false cells if needed, then changes that
cell. Moving right increments h and extends the list through the new head position.
Moving left decrements a positive h; at h = 0, it prepends a false cell and keeps the
head at zero. A fixed finite program contains these instructions:

Instruction                                   Next state
Write a bit                                   Perform the write and advance q by one.
Move left or right                            Perform the move and advance q by one.
Branch to j                                   Set q := j if the current cell is true; otherwise
                                              advance q by one.
Halt                                          Leave the entire state unchanged.
ClaimTapeIsZero with a label ℓ                Advance q by one and do nothing else.



An out-of-range program fetch is Halt. Every state is allowed as a starting state,
and halting means the fetched instruction is Halt. The cost field is preserved by
every instruction in this base. In particular, its ClaimTapeIsZero instruction neither
erases the tape nor charges the cost field; neither the name nor the label supplies any
semantics.

The random-access base has a register function X : N → N and a program counter q.
For a fixed finite program its instructions are:

Instruction                                   Next state
Constant (i, c)                               Set X (i ) := c.


                                           202
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele



Instruction                                    Next state
Add (i, j, k )                                 Set X (i ) := X ( j) + X (k ).
Subtract (i, j, k)                             Set X (i ) := max(0, X ( j) − X (k)).
Indirect load (i, j)                           Set X (i ) := X ( X ( j)).
Indirect store (i, j)                          Set X ( X (i )) := X ( j).
Positive branch ( j, a)                        Set q := a if X ( j) > 0; otherwise advance q
                                               by one.
Jump to a                                      Set q := a.
Halt                                           Leave the entire state unchanged.



Each register-writing instruction advances q by one; its operands are evaluated in the
old state, and all other registers are preserved. A fetch outside the program also leaves
the state unchanged. Starting states have q = 0 and arbitrary register contents. A
state is halted when it fetches Halt or is outside the program. Unit cost here counts
instructions. It has nothing to do with the certification ledger.

For the indirect instructions, draw boxes 1, 2 and 3 and put 2, 7 and 0 in them. Indirect
load (3, 1) first reads the 2 in box 1, uses it as an address, and copies box 2’s 7 into box
3. Now put 9 in box 3 and execute indirect store (1, 3): the 2 in box 1 tells it where to
put the 9, so box 2 changes and box 1 stays 2. An address is being read from a box; it
is not necessarily the box’s own number.

The lambda base uses the terms and weak call-by-value rule defined in Definition 13.3.
To compute its next state, first try to reduce the function part of an application. If that
part cannot step and is an abstraction, either substitute an argument that is already
an abstraction or take a step in the argument. If neither applies, the term cannot
step. Variables and abstractions cannot step by themselves, and there is no reduction
under an abstraction. The base leaves a term unchanged when it cannot step and calls
precisely those terms halted. Every term is allowed as a starting state, including open
terms.


These definitions make the three examples bases in the sense of Definition 10.1. Apply-
ing the latch theorem to them does not assert universality, an execution-time bound,
or a simulation between the three bases.

There’s also a relation defined between bases, weak base equivalence: two bases are
equivalent when some correspondence covers their start states both ways, related
states agree on an observation and on halting, and one step on one side is matched by
some number of steps, possibly zero, on the other. That “some number of steps” is the
stuttering idea Leslie Lamport (the same Lamport as Section 6’s message counters) put
forward in 1983: a fine-grained machine and a coarse one shouldn’t count as different
because one takes three ticks to do what the other does in one. The relation carries no
cost; a machine that multiplies huge numbers in one step and a Turing machine differ


                                            203
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


in price. The relation never looks at price, so on what it does look at they can match.
It’s proved to be an equivalence relation, and the latch form is preserved across it.

Draw a coarse machine 0 → 1, with 1 halted, and a finer one a → b → c, with c halted.
Let a and b both show 0 and c show 1; halted states stay where they are. Relate 0 to
both a and b, and 1 to c. The fine move a → b changes nothing visible, so the coarse
machine matches it by taking no step. Its move b → c matches 0 → 1. Starting from a,
the coarse move is matched by two fine steps. This is what “possibly zero” allows; the
relation is about matching observations and halting, not matching the number of ticks
or their bill.

There is a limit to that statement. The “preserved across it” proof throws away its
equivalence hypothesis; the latch holds on every base regardless, so the preservation
is true for a boring reason. And nowhere in this book are two of the bases actually
related by this relation. The relation is defined, it’s an equivalence, and it is not used
to connect the Turing machine to the register machine to the lambda calculus, or any
of them to the machine in Part IV. It would be easy to read that list as if it did. What’s
proved is that each base, separately, carries a latch. That’s the honest sentence.


Definition 10.4 (Weak base equivalence). Bases B1 and B2 , with observations o1 and
o2 into one common set, are weakly equivalent when some relation R relates every
starting state of each to some starting state of the other, and any related x, y have
o1 ( x ) = o2 (y), the same halting, some n ≥ 0 with R(nextB1 ( x ), nextnB2 (y)), and some
n ≥ 0 with R(nextnB1 ( x ), nextB2 (y)).


Theorem 10.10 (Outside bases, and the relation). (1) Weak base equivalence is reflexive,
symmetric and transitive. (2) If two bases are weakly equivalent, Observation 10.1 holds over
one exactly when it holds over the other. (3) Observation 10.1 holds over each of the three bases
in Definition 10.3, for every fixed program where the base has one.

Proof. (1) Reflexive with equality as R and one step against one. Symmetric by revers-
ing R. Transitive by composing the two relations; a step on the first base is matched by
n steps on the second, and those n steps by some number on the third, by induction
on n. (2) and (3) apply Observation 10.1 directly. In (2) the equivalence hypothesis is
discarded.

10.6 Records with more than two values
A cup has two positions. Some records have more: a counter of how many checks
passed, a level that only rises. The same reasoning goes through one threshold at a
time. For each value a, “the record has reached a” is a yes/no reading, and each of
those readings is a latch. What doesn’t go through is squeezing the whole record into
one cup. “Rises” needs one word: the values come with an order ≤, “is at or below,”



                                              204
