substrate can represent and that’s correct on every program. That breaks the generic
proof at a named step, and I’ve named the steps.

Two: for the nat family, produce a d that correctly decides the predicate of the substrate
built from d.

Three: for L, produce a closed term that decides some extensional property holding of
one closed term and failing of another. That breaks Rice’s theorem for L, whose proof
rests on the reduction rules.

An outside decider alone doesn’t count against any of the three; the pencil argument
on Nd is why.

13.6 What this does to the book
It does two things. It keeps me honest: nothing in what follows claims that a system
with a record can check its own shortcuts on autopilot, because that’s a wall, the same
wall, and I showed you the bricks. And it tells you what a record can do, which
is the thing Part III has been about since the counter: it can carry a shortcut with
its receipt, so that the question “was this earned” is answered by an event you can


                                              229
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


point at. No decider has to exist for that, which is lucky, because on a system with a
recursion theorem no inside one can. The diagonal says such a system can’t automate
the judgement from inside, for any behavioural property with a yes and a no. The
latch says you can record the commitment. Those are different jobs, and a record does
the second.

The diagonal has a famous cousin that seems like it ought to bite a record too, so let me
walk right up to it. Gödel’s second theorem says a consistent system strong enough
for arithmetic can’t prove its own consistency, and Martin Löb, a logician answering
another logician’s question, sharpened that in 1955: if such a system proves “if this is
provable, it’s true,” it already proves the thing itself. So can a record vouch for itself,
and does Löb stop it? My first guess was that Löb stops it, since a record looked like
a system talking about itself. Here’s where I landed instead, and mostly it’s a relief.
Hold two things side by side: “there’s a receipt for this somewhere,” and the receipt in
your hand. Löb’s theorem is about provability, the bare claim that some proof exists, the
receipt somewhere. A record of the kind this book keeps is a different animal: an event,
a check of some claim that passed, a commitment to it, and a certificate, at a definite
step of the run. The receipt in your hand. It doesn’t say which claim or which step,
as the two runs in Section 16.18 show; it says the event happened. Sergei Artemov,
the logician from the opening chapter, drew exactly that line in 2001, between implicit
provability (“there is a proof”) and explicit evidence (“this is a proof”). As I read him,
for explicit evidence the reflection step “if this is a proof of F, then F” is harmless,
while for the bare “there is a proof” it’s what Gödel and Löb forbid. Why, in my
words: a receipt in your hand you can look at, and a receipt somewhere you take on
the system’s own word. A record sits on the explicit side.

Push on that and it gives, because a receipt is only as good as whoever wrote it. Its
trust rests on the checker meaning what it says, and that gets settled once, from outside
the machine. That’s where I chose to stop this machine’s chain of reasons. Gödel’s
second theorem does not forbid a machine from checking a proof about a checker. It
limits a sufficiently strong, effectively axiomatized theory’s ability to prove its own
consistency, if the theory is consistent. Eliezer Yudkowsky and Marcello Herreshoff’s
2013 draft on agents that trust their own rewrites describes a related problem, the
Löbian obstacle: how an agent can justify trust in a successor’s proofs. The relation is
worth examining, but it does not prove that my design is forced. So I didn’t get rid of
the receipt somewhere. I moved it out of the machine and handed it to whoever reads
the record.

One more thing follows from the same picture, by a short argument. Can a record
rest on itself, the way the sentence “this sentence is certified” would like to? Not if
it’s earned and permanent. The check that a certificate stands on happened while
the record was still down, because the record goes up only after that check passes,
and once up it never comes back down. So no claim whose truth needs the record
already up can be the claim a certificate stands on. Saul Kripke’s 1975 theory of truth


                                           230
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


calls a sentence like that, one that only ever leans on itself, ungrounded, and earned
records are grounded in his sense: every one bottoms out in a check that didn’t lean
on it. Caspar Oesterheld’s 2019 work on programs that cooperate by simulating each
other needed a grounding step of the same kind to stop an infinite regress. There is no
separate formal derivation of this argument; the claim is exactly what this paragraph
says.

One last distinction, because the two are easy to conflate and conflating them is the
easiest way to misread this book. There’s a second wall, nothing to do with the diagonal.
It’s Section 7’s kind of wall, a window with a colliding pair in it. Two states that differ
in their certification reading can look identical through a window that doesn’t show
that reading, the stamp inside the closed drawer and the drawer opened and shut,
and then no function of the window recovers the reading (Theorem 7.1: a decoder
has to give one answer on everything the window lumps together). That’s missing
information. Nothing about it is undecidable; it holds for finite things with nothing
to compute; and it sits beside Rice. None of Rice is underneath it. The property the
diagonal uses (any behavioural property of programs with a yes and a no) is a different
kind of thing from the reading the window hides, and nothing here says the two are
the same. Two walls, two axes. The diagonal is about what no inside procedure can
decide. The window is about what no outside observer can see. I’ll need both, and I’ll
try not to call one by the other’s name again. The machine I build later has a colliding
pair of exactly that kind (Theorem 16.14).

14 Five small models
A toll, a counter, two kinds of wall and a latch, and every one of them shown on paper,
on cups and cards and dice I made up. I’ve been building a toy and claiming it’s
the smallest version of something people actually do. Time to go and look at what
people actually do. I picked five systems that keep records other people rely on, with
real money or real security behind them, and asked each the pricing question from
the paper models: is there a price on the moment the record is written? Not on the work
around it. On the write. I’ll tell you the answer first, because it’s a single sentence
and it surprised me: of the five specifications, read through the transcriptions I made
of them, only one takes a fee at the moment of the write, and that one has a leak at
exactly the place Section 6 said a counter leaks, where it goes down.

“Price” needs one meaning for all five, or the answer is whatever I want it to be, so
here it is, and every system below gets classified by it. A specification prices an event
when it attaches one of three costs to it. A fee: something taken at the event itself,
whatever happens afterward. A bond: value put at risk by the event and lost only if
some later event happens, a contradiction, say. A budget: a finite allowance the event
draws down, so that only so many such events can ever happen. A wall isn’t a price
under this definition. Nobody pays a hash; reversing one is just infeasible. Neither is
work a protocol needs and never charges for. The table at the end of the section has


                                           231
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


a column for each of the three kinds, and what it shows is a finding about the five,
because the definition came first.

Three things are easy to blur in a section like this, so I’ll name them now and keep
them apart all the way through. There’s the real specification: the document real money
and real security run on. There’s my transcription: one mechanism copied out of that
document into a mathematical model, small enough to examine. And for some of the
five there’s a wrapper: a tiny abstract model that takes one premise as given and says
what follows from it. A claim proved at one level isn’t a claim at the level above it.
Near the end I’ll walk one system, gas, through all three, so you can see exactly where
each claim stops.

What I built for each is a fragment: a small mathematical model of the one mechanism
I’m asking about, transcribed from the system’s own specification where there was
one, and nothing more. Not the system. I’ll say for each one what the fragment is and
what it isn’t, because “Ethereum has been formalised” is the kind of sentence that gets
a book thrown across a room, and rightly.

14.1 Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back
Ethereum and chains like it decide which blocks are final by having validators, people
who’ve locked up money (their stake), vote on checkpoints: blocks picked out at
regular numbered rounds called epochs. A vote isn’t for one checkpoint. It’s a link from
a checkpoint the validator already trusts, the source, to a later one, the target, and
every chain starts from one first block, its genesis, which counts as trusted from the
start. In the design Vitalik Buterin and Virgil Griffith published in 2017, called Casper,
a checkpoint is justified when validators holding two thirds of the stake vote a link to
it from a justified source, and finalized when it is justified and a two-thirds link runs
from it to its direct child. The record is “this checkpoint is final.”

What’s priced? Two rules: don’t vote for two different targets in the same epoch, and
don’t cast a vote whose span, source to target, surrounds the span of another of your
votes. Break either and your deposit can be destroyed, which is called slashing. The
theorem they prove, called accountable safety, says that if two conflicting checkpoints
are ever both finalized, at least a third of the stake broke a rule and can be slashed.
So the price is on reversal, on making the record contradict itself. The write itself,
finalizing, takes no fee: honest validators finalize all day and nobody loses anything.
In the terms from the start of the section, Casper’s price is a bond. The deposit stands
behind every vote, the finalizing votes included, and it’s taken only if the record is
later made to contradict itself.

Do it with three validators of equal stake. Draw genesis at epoch 0, two competing
children at epoch 1, and one child of each at epoch 2. Let A and B vote both links on
the left branch, from genesis to its first child and from that child to the next. Let B
and C do the same on the right. Each link has two of the three votes. Both epoch-1
blocks are justified and have the required link to their child, so both finalize. B voted

                                           232
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


for different targets at the same epoch. B is the third that gets slashed; A and C are
clean. That’s what a fork costs and who pays, and Theorem 14.2 below has exactly
this instance, so the theorem’s premise isn’t vacuous: forks of that kind can be built,
and the theorem fires on them.

The fragment: a reconstruction of the published casper-proofs argument from Runtime
Verification and the University of Texas at Austin, based on Yoichi Hirai’s proof, with
validator sets and quorum intersection as a premise. A quorum is a set of validators
big enough to act, here two thirds of the stake, and quorum intersection is the arithmetic
of the three-validator example: two thirds plus two thirds is four thirds, so any two
quorums share at least a third. The fragment takes the overlap as given. It doesn’t do
that arithmetic. No deposits, no rewards, no fork choice (the rule for picking a branch
to build on), no connection to anything else in this book. A finalization fork implies
that a set of validators the size of that overlap, at least a third of the stake, is slashed.
And a one-validator chain finalizes and nobody’s slashed, which is the “write is free”
sentence in a degenerate setting, and only there.

Here’s the fragment, small enough to read in one sitting. Every name below is from
the transcription.


Definition 14.1 (Casper setting and votes). A setting has a type of validators, a type
of block hashes with a parent relation and a genesis hash, and two classes of validator
sets, the “two-thirds” sets Q1 and the “one-third” sets Q2 . It carries two premises:
quorum intersection, for any two sets in Q1 some set in Q2 lies inside both; and at most
one parent per hash. A state says, for each validator, target hash h, target epoch t and
source epoch u, whether that validator voted the link (h, t, u). A link from p at epoch
u to h at epoch t is justified by q when q ∈ Q1 , every member of q voted (h, t, u), h is
the (t − u)-th descendant of p, and t > u. Genesis is justified at epoch 0, and a block
reached from a justified block by a justified link landing at epoch t is justified at t.
Block h is finalized at epoch v with child c when c is a child of h, h is justified at v, and
the link from h at v to c at v + 1 is justified. A finalization fork is two finalized blocks
h1 ̸= h2 , neither an ancestor of the other. A validator is slashed when it voted two
different targets with the same target epoch (a double vote), or voted links (h1 , t1 , u1 )
and (h2 , t2 , u2 ) with t1 > t2 and u2 > u1 (a surround vote). The state is quorum-slashed
when some set in Q2 consists of slashed validators.


Theorem 14.1 (Accountable safety). In every setting (so under quorum intersection and at
most one parent), every state with a finalization fork is quorum-slashed.

Proof. Let the fork be h1 finalized at v1 and h2 at v2 . If v1 = v2 , the two links into
epoch v1 + 1 are each voted by a set in Q1 ; quorum intersection gives a set in Q2 that
voted both; their targets differ, since equal children would give h1 and h2 the same
child and so, by at most one parent, h1 = h2 . That set double-voted. If v1 ̸= v2 , say


                                            233
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


v1 < v2 , walk down the chain of justified links that justifies h2 . Every block on that
chain is an ancestor of h2 , so none descends from h1 . Some link in the chain starts at
or below v1 and lands above v1 . If it lands at v1 + 1, it and the finalization link of h1
have distinct targets at that epoch, and the intersection set double-voted. If it starts at
v1 , its source is a justified block at v1 other than h1 , and the links that justified those
two blocks give a double vote the same way. Otherwise it starts below v1 and lands
above v1 + 1, so it surrounds the finalization link of h1 , and the intersection set made
a surround vote.

The model takes quorum intersection and the accountable-safety setting as premises.
Its guarantees are conditional on those premises.


Theorem 14.2 (The premise can hold, and the write is free). (1) In the three-validator
setting where each validator has stake 1, Q1 is the sets of stake at least two thirds and Q2 the
sets of at least one third, the state where A and B vote one branch and B and C the other has
a finalization fork; B is slashed, A and C are not, and { B} is in Q2 . (2) In the one-validator
chain setting, one vote finalizes genesis and no validator is slashed.

Proof. Both are computations on fixed finite data. In (1) B voted two different targets at
epoch 1, which is the double vote; A’s and C’s votes are one link at epoch 1 from source
0 and one at epoch 2 from source 1, which neither double-vote nor surround.

One thing that means for the record itself: finality is revocable at a price, the price is
named, and a final block can hold a false statement.

And the obvious next question: is the 2017 design what Ethereum actually runs? Partly,
and the paper’s own title is the clue. It’s called Casper the Friendly Finality Gadget, and
its first sentence says it’s a finality system that overlays a chain still choosing its blocks
by proof of work. A gadget, bolted on top. In 2020 a larger group, Buterin among
them, wrote up Gasper, which joins Casper’s finality to a fork-choice rule called LMD
GHOST, and on 15 September 2022, in the switch people called the Merge, Ethereum
stopped choosing blocks by proof of work at all and went over to proof of stake. So
the checkpoints and the two slashing rules above are one part of a system that holds
real money today, and the transcription is of that part’s safety proof as the 2017 design
states it. Everything between the two, the fork choice and the rest of the running
protocol, is the gap between my transcription and the running system, which I walk
through near the end of this section with a photocopied recipe and a kitchen. Does
any of that move the price? No. Finalizing is still free for an honest validator. What
costs is contradicting yourself.

14.2 Gas: the one that charges a fee at the write
Every operation on Ethereum costs gas, paid in ether by whoever sent the transaction.
The yellow paper, Ethereum’s formal specification, gives the reason in one line: every


                                              234
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


computation is fee-bearing so the network can’t be abused and halting questions are
sidestepped. The record I care about is a nonzero slot in the shared storage, which
every full node in the world (every computer keeping its own complete copy of the
chain) has to keep until it’s cleared. Clearing a slot is allowed, and the refund rules
below exist to reward it.

And here it is: writing a fresh storage slot from zero to nonzero costs twenty thousand
gas, by the table in the paper’s appendix, plus twenty-one hundred for touching a cold
slot, one the transaction hasn’t touched yet (after the first touch it’s warm). As I read it,
the point is to discourage storage growth, since storage grows every node’s database.
That’s a fee on the write, at the moment of the write, and it’s the only fee in the five.
Gas has a budget too, in the sense from the start of the section: every block has a gas
limit, and the gas its transactions use can’t exceed it, so only so many writes fit in a
block.

Where does a number like twenty-one hundred come from? Somebody picked it,
so the obvious next question is who, and why, and the answer has a date on it. In
September 2016, just as Ethereum’s developers were gathering in Shanghai for Dev-
con 2, their developer conference (the third one, since they started counting at zero),
attackers started filling blocks with an operation that was cheap in gas and expensive
in fact: it sent every node off to read data from its disk, and nodes fell behind the chain.
The first repair, a fork that October called Tangerine Whistle, raised the prices of the
operations the attack had leaned on. The cold-slot charge came later, in a proposal by
Vitalik Buterin and Martin Swende called EIP-2929, switched on in the Berlin upgrade
of April 2021, and the motivation it gives is still those 2016 attacks. So twenty-one hun-
dred isn’t a law of nature or a measurement of anything deep. It’s a scar: a price set
after somebody found the place where the old price was wrong. That doesn’t change
the argument; the write is still priced at the moment of the write. It does change how
I read the rest of that table: some of its numbers, at least, are somebody’s answer to
“what did this cost last time,” which is a record of a different kind.

Now the leak, and it’s Section 6’s leak. Set a slot and then clear it in the same transaction
and you get a refund. Count it through: first write twenty-two thousand one hundred;
clearing it costs a hundred and credits a refund of nineteen thousand nine hundred;
net, twenty-three hundred. The other half is this: leave it set and you pay at least
twenty thousand. The write is priced. The revoked write nearly isn’t. But I have to
add what the fragment leaves out, because twenty-three hundred on its own misleads:
the realized refund is capped at one fifth of the gas the whole transaction used (that’s
the 2021 change from Section 6, the one that ended the refund-hoarding token’s ad-
vantage). So a real set-then-clear pays a lot more than twenty-three hundred. How
much more? The cap is a fifth of everything the transaction used, and that includes
the twenty-one thousand every transaction pays just for existing. Take a transaction
that does nothing but set and clear the slot: it uses 43,200 gas, so the cap is 8,640, so
it pays 34,560, which is 13,560 on top of the base. (Look at the slot alone and forget


                                            235
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


the base, which the rule doesn’t do, and you’d get 17,760.) Either way it’s far above
twenty-three hundred. The counter-level net is twenty-three hundred. The bill is not.

Here’s the arithmetic the way the specification has it, so you can redo it with a pencil.


Definition 14.2 (One slot in one transaction). A slot run records the slot’s value at
the start of the transaction (original), its current value, whether it has been touched
(warm), the gas charged so far, and the refund counter. A store of a new value charges
2100 if the slot is cold, plus 20000 if the slot still holds its original value, the new value
differs, and the original is 0 (2900 if the original is nonzero), and otherwise 100. If
the value is unchanged, the refund does not change. Otherwise add together these
applicable adjustments: add 4800 when the original and current values are nonzero
and the new value is zero; subtract 4800 when the original is nonzero and the current
value is zero; and, when the new value restores the original, add 19900 if that original
is zero, or 2800 if it is nonzero. Store the new current value, mark the slot warm, and
keep the original value unchanged. The run starts fresh: original and current 0, cold,
gas and refund 0. The net charge is gas minus refund.


Theorem 14.3 (Pricing the persistent write and the revoked one). (1) For every list of
stores from a fresh slot, if the slot ends nonzero then the net charge is at least 20000. (2) Storing
1 then 0 leaves the slot at 0 with net charge 2300; storing 1 alone has net charge 22100.

Proof. (1) By induction on the list, with the invariant: while the original value is 0,
the net charge is at least 0 when the current value is 0 and at least 20000 when it is
not. For the fresh original value 0, the four cases are short. Zero to zero adds 100
to net; zero to nonzero adds 20000; nonzero to nonzero adds 100; and nonzero to
zero adds 100 − 19900 = −19800. The last case starts with net at least 20000 and
therefore ends at least 200, still nonnegative. A cold access adds another 2100 in any
case. These updates preserve the invariant, and a fresh slot satisfies it. (2) Direct
computation: 2100 + 20000 = 22100 for the first store, 100 for the second, refund
19900, and 22200 − 19900 = 2300.

The arithmetic follows the execution specification’s storage instruction and gas table.
The end-of-transaction refund cap of one fifth is not in the fragment.

The fragment: one slot, one transaction, the gas and refund arithmetic transcribed
from the Ethereum execution specification at a named commit. No stack, no call
context, no other slots, and no refund cap.

Then the wrapper, which is a different kind of object, and the walk near the end is
about exactly that difference. It’s a gas schedule in the abstract: any states, any steps, a
cost per step, a yes/no commitment flag, and a charge predicate saying which steps
get billed. It formalises no EVM (the Ethereum virtual machine) at all. It is Section 7’s
result with the whole-run ceiling, the one that pins the amount as well as which steps

                                                236
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


pay, under a new name. Its two halves are worth reading separately. Leave one
committing step unbilled, and a one-step run commits for nothing, so the floor fails
outright; one missed commit is enough. Bill one step that doesn’t commit, and the
schedule charges more than the number of commits on that one-step run, so the ceiling
fails. And the class isn’t empty: in any system, the bill that charges one exactly on a
step that raises the flag and nothing on any other meets both halves (Section 7’s step
price).

And the wrapper itself, which is the cleanest thing in this section and has the least
Ethereum in it.


Definition 14.3 (A gas schedule). A gas schedule has states, instructions, a step, a cost
c(s, i ) ∈ N that may depend on the state, a Boolean commitment flag on states, and
a Boolean charge predicate χ(s, i ), with two premises: a charged step costs at least 1,
and an uncharged step costs 0. A step commits when it takes the flag from false to true.
For a run t from s, let c(t) be its total cost and n(t) its number of committing steps.
The schedule has the floor when c(t) ≥ n(t) for every run, and no overcharge when
c(t) ≤ n(t) for every run. It has unit pricing when c(s, i ) = 1 if χ(s, i ) and 0 otherwise.


Theorem 14.4 (Gas schedule exactness). For every gas schedule: it has the floor and no
overcharge if and only if χ(s, i ) holds exactly when the step from s by i commits, and it has
unit pricing. Moreover, (1) if some committing step from an uncommitted state is uncharged,
that one-step run costs 0 and the schedule fails the floor; (2) if some charged step does not
commit, the schedule overcharges.

Proof. The equivalence is Section 7’s characterization with the whole-run ceiling, un-
der another name. From right to left, each step’s cost is 1 on a committing step and 0
otherwise, so a run’s cost counts its commitments. From left to right, apply the floor
and no overcharge to one-step runs: a committing step must cost at least 1, so it is
charged; a charged step costs at least 1 and may not exceed its commitment count, so
it commits and costs exactly 1. Parts (1) and (2) are those one-step runs read the other
way.

Gas prices storage growth and computation. It says nothing about whether what’s
stored is true.

14.3 Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past
A trusted platform module, the small chip on most laptop motherboards, keeps a
handful of registers that can only be extended: the new value is a hash of the old value
together with a digest (a short hash) of whatever software just loaded. You can’t set
them; you can only fold more in. A quote is the chip signing those register values
together with a number the asker chose, a nonce, so the asker knows the quote is fresh.



                                             237
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Intel’s SGX does the equivalent for an enclave, a walled-off region a program runs in.
The record is the extended register.

What’s priced? On the registers, nothing in the specification: no fee, no bond, no
budget. Reversal isn’t expensive. It’s infeasible: you’d have to invert a hash or steal a
key. That’s the difference between a price and a wall, and it’s easy to blur, which is
why the definition at the start of the section leaves walls out. What stands behind a
cost can come in three currencies. It can be economic, a fee or a deposit the protocol
takes (Casper and gas are here). It can be cryptographic, a reversal made infeasible
by a hardness assumption, which makes it a wall with no exact price on it (attestation
and transparency are here). Or it can be physical, energy spent or hardware worn,
which none of these five specifications charges as a fee or a bond; the nearest thing is
the chip’s write budget, below. And the record’s permanence is only as long as the
register lives: a platform’s registers are cleared when it resets, so the permanence is
per boot.

Why the registers, then, when something that lasts would make a better record? Be-
cause the quote is what a remote asker reads, and the registers are what it signs. The
same chip has longer-lived records, and they’re closer to the cup than anything else
in this section. Version 2.0 of its specification has storage slots of a kind it calls a bit
field, changed only by a command that ORs new bits into the old value: a bit can be
set and never cleared, which is r ∨ h from Section 10, on a laptop motherboard. It
has counters that can only be incremented, and a counter’s first increment starts it at
the largest value any counter on that chip has ever held, so deleting one and making
a new one can’t wind it back. And those slots are rationed. Bryan Parno and his
coauthors, building a system called Memoir in 2011, noted that the specification of the
day only required a counter to be able to tick once every five seconds, and that the
chip’s storage was expected to survive about a hundred thousand writes in its whole
life, so writing once a second would wear it out in under twenty-eight hours. Memoir
writes to it twice per boot. Permanent, finite and rationed: the permanent record has a
budget, in exactly the sense from the start of the section, and it sits on these slots and
counters; the registers the quote signs have none. It’s the budget of Theorem 10.11’s
chain of k-bit words, which can only climb k times. Phones and small controllers go
one floor further down, to fuses like the PROMs in Section 10: a version number kept
as a row of fuses, one more blown at each security update, and boot code that refuses
anything older. An industry guide on it, Rob Smart’s 2021 explainer for PSA Certified,
a security certification scheme for chips and devices, tells designers to make sure there
are enough fuse bits to last the number of updates expected over the device’s lifetime,
which is part (5) of that same theorem, written as a design rule.

What all of this is for is rollback. Memoir’s example is a password checker restored
to an old saved state to undo a user’s password change, and in 2017 a system called
ROTE did the same job for Intel’s enclaves by having several machines vouch for each
other’s counters, with the stated result that the only way left to break it is to reset


                                            238
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


every one of them to its start. In 2016 Raoul Strackx and Frank Piessens’s Ariadne
got the cost of that job down to flipping a single bit of non-volatile memory per state
update, which they call the theoretical lower limit. Notice who the attacker is in every
one of these: whoever gets to put an old state back. A bad program doesn’t come into
it. A record kept by the step can’t see that attacker, which is why every guarantee in
Part IV about a record’s earned history is stated from a clean start, and a restored start
is outside all of them. The per-step toll still holds after a restore. It just can’t tell you
what happened before it.

Replicated services put the same kind of record somewhere else: inside each replica,
where a replica that’s been taken over still can’t make it say two different things.
Byung-Gon Chun and coauthors’ attested append-only memory (A2M, 2007) is a log
a replica can only add to; Dave Levin and coauthors’ TrInc (2009) shrinks that to
a trusted counter; MinBFT (Giuliana Veronese and coauthors, 2013) uses a trusted
counter to reach agreement with 2 f + 1 replicas when f of them can lie, where the
usual count is 3 f + 1; and Damysus (Jérémie Decouchant, David Kozhaya, Vincent
Rahli and Jiangshan Yu, 2022) has a small trusted service, the Checker, that keeps a
monotonic counter of where the protocol is. Allen Clement, Flavio Junqueira, Aniket
Kate and Rodrigo Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs, what such a record buys,
and as I read their result it’s a good warning for this book. On its own, stopping a
replica from saying two different things doesn’t lower the 3 f + 1 bound in an asyn-
chronous network at all. Add signatures that a third party can check, and it turns
any protocol that survives crashes into one that survives liars, with no extra replicas.
The way I read it, a record helps the others only as far as they can check what it says,
which is Section 7’s point from the other side.

There’s a fourth currency under those three, and it’s the one every permanent record
pays in. It’s the logical kind: Section 4’s room of chairs applies to any of these records.
On a finite state space, a step that switches a record on somewhere, and never switches
it off anywhere, forgets something. Forgetting alone doesn’t single out a record write:
any step that overwrites a field able to hold two values forgets something too. What
singles it out is where the forgetting lands. Take the states the record already reads
yes on, together with the one the step switches on. The step sends every one of them
to a yes state, and it can’t keep them apart, so what it destroys is a distinction on the
record’s own yes side: two states it already vouched for, or the state it just raised and
one that was up already. Any overwrite merges states somewhere; a permanent write
is forced to merge them on that side. That needs no premise about money, keys or
heat. The economic, cryptographic and physical payments each need a premise of
their own about their kind (a fee rule, a hardness assumption, Landauer’s principle),
and they hold exactly where that premise holds.


Theorem 14.5 (A permanent write forgets on its own yes side). For any states S, in-
structions I, step and Boolean reading: suppose a duplicate-free list names every state, the


                                            239
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


instruction i never turns the reading from on to off, and i turns it on at some state s. Then the
step by i is not injective. More: the step by i sends every state that reads on, and s, to a state
that reads on, and it is not injective even on those states.


The proof is Theorem 4.1 with permanence required only of the one instruction i. For
the second half: if the step were one-to-one on the states that read on together with s,
it would map the states that read on onto themselves, and then s would land where
some state that reads on already lands.

What the quote can do is say what was measured. It can’t say the measured code is
correct, and it can’t say anything about runtime state that was never folded in. A
correctly measured buggy program attests beautifully. The fragment proves that exact
limit: one register, a hash about which nothing is assumed, a quote as a pair, and no
function of the quote decides a runtime flag the quote ignores, which is Section 7’s
cube again. And a companion shows that a sign-and-verify interface alone gives no
authenticity (a scheme where verify always says yes passes the interface), so a crypto-
graphic premise has to be added; the fragment doesn’t model signatures, formats, or
a freshness check (the nonce is just a field the verifier fixes).

The same limit, turned outward, is the honest edge of the opening chapter’s four
conditions. Every one of them is about a thing the machine holds: same property,
same thing, same edition, honest check. For a claim about the world (the oven is hot,
the parcel arrived) there’s no edition the machine controls. Whatever reads the world
is a window onto it, and “nothing changed between the check and the commit” stops
being something a step can enforce and becomes a premise about the sensor. So a
record can establish claims about the machine’s own state, and claims about the world
only through named premises about whatever measured them. A correctly recorded
sensor reading certifies the sensor.


Definition 14.4 (Platform and quote). Fix any functions H : N × N → N (the extend
hash) and δ : N → N (the digest); nothing is assumed about either. A platform is a
measurement log (a list of numbers) and a Boolean runtime flag. Its register is the log
folded from 0 by H. The quote with nonce n is the pair (δ(register), n).


Theorem 14.6 (The quote cannot attest unmeasured state). For every nonce n there is no
function D from quotes to Booleans with D (quoten ( P)) = flag( P) for every platform P.

Proof. Take two platforms with the empty log, one flagged true and one false. Their
quotes are equal, since the quote never reads the flag, so D would have to return both
values on one input.

Any yes-or-no claim about δ(register) can be read off the quote. But a scheme whose
verification always says yes satisfies the sign-and-verify interface while accepting a


                                               240
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


signature no key produced.

14.4 Certificate transparency: visible, unpriced
The certificates that make your browser show a padlock are issued by hundreds of
authorities, and a bad or compromised one can issue a certificate for a domain it
shouldn’t. Certificate Transparency makes authorities submit every certificate to pub-
lic append-only logs built as Merkle trees, so that anyone can check that a certificate
was logged and that the log never rewrote its past. It was specified in RFC 6962 in
2013 and revised as RFC 9162 in 2021. I went looking for which one the running
logs follow, and it’s still 6962: Mozilla’s reference for web developers says browser
implementations are based on 6962, and as late as November 2025 Chrome’s team was
only proposing to drop its rule that every certificate carry a timestamp from at least
one 6962 log. The fragment I transcribe is 9162’s. A Merkle tree is Section 3’s hash
chain folded into a tree: hash each certificate (those are the leaves), hash the leaf hashes
in pairs, hash those in pairs, and so on up to one root hash. To prove one leaf is in, the
log hands you only the few hashes sitting beside the climb from that leaf to the root,
the path, and you redo the climb yourself. A second check, consistency, shows that a
bigger tree is a smaller one with leaves added on the end and nothing rewritten. The
record is a leaf in the tree.

The data structure has a history of its own in security. The computer scientists Scott
Crosby and Dan Wallach, at Rice University, built tamper-evident logs on the same
kind of tree in 2009, with a proof that an entry is in the log and a proof that a later
version of the log extends an earlier one, each a logarithmic number of hashes; a logger
that rewrites its past gets caught by the second.

Priced? Nothing. The RFC says it in its first section: logs let interested parties detect
misissuance afterward. They don’t prevent it. And a log that shows different views to
different people (a split view) can defeat the auditing, so logs are still trusted parties.
What it buys is visibility.

Which raises the obvious question: if nothing’s priced, why does any authority bother
logging? Nothing in the RFC makes it. The answer is a browser. Chrome’s team set
the rule, enforced from Chrome 68 in July 2018, that every certificate issued after 30
April 2018 had to meet its transparency policy, and a publicly trusted certificate that
doesn’t is simply not trusted by Chrome: the visitor gets a full-page warning in front
of the site. So there is a price after all. It isn’t anywhere in the specification. It lives
in one vendor’s browser, and it’s the price of being shown to that browser’s users at
all. Is that the bottom? Not quite, because it means the strongest lever on this record
is a policy one company can change, which is a fact about who holds the stamp. The
tree has nothing to do with it. That policy changes nothing in the table at the end of
this section, which asks what each specification prices. But it’s worth keeping two
sentences apart: “the specification prices nothing” and “nothing is priced.”

Do the inclusion proof by hand. Lay out seven cards d0 through d6 . Join neighbours

                                            241
The Thiele Machine                                                                      Devon Thiele


with paper brackets: a = ν(d0 , d1 ), b = ν(d2 , d3 ) and c = ν(d4 , d5 ). The last card stands
alone. Next join a to b, giving L = ν( a, b), and c to d6 , giving R = ν(c, d6 ). The root is
ν( L, R). Here ν means “put these two expressions, in this order, inside one labelled
bracket.” Equal symbolic hashes must have exactly the same bracket structure.

To check d3 , keep only that card and the three siblings d2 , a, R. Combine d2 on its left
to recover b, then a on the left to recover L, then R on the right to recover the root.
You never needed to open the cards inside a or R. That is the inclusion path. These
are symbolic hashes, so this trial checks the tree’s assembly; real short hashes need a
separate cryptographic argument. There are no signatures, gossip between auditors
or misbehaving logs in this fragment.


Definition 14.5 (Inclusion check, RFC 9162 section 2.1.3.2). Given a leaf index m, a tree
size N, a leaf hash, a root hash and a path, the check rejects unless m < N. Otherwise
start counters f = m, s = N − 1 and an accumulated hash r equal to the leaf hash. For
each path element p, reject if s = 0. If f is odd or f = s, replace r by ν( p, r ); in this
branch, while f is positive and even, halve both counters with rounding down. In the
other branch replace r by ν(r, p). After either branch halve both counters once more.
At the end accept exactly when s = 0 and r is the claimed root. A symbolic hash makes
a leaf hash ℓ( x ) and a node hash ν( a, b) distinct constructors: two hashes are equal
only when their entire constructions agree.

The consistency check used here takes old and new sizes M, N, roots u, v and a path,
and rejects unless 0 < M < N. If M is a power of two, prepend u to the path. Reject
an empty resulting path; otherwise its first element seeds two accumulated hashes
rold , rnew . Start f = M − 1, s = N − 1, and halve both while f is odd. Process each
remaining path element p: reject if s = 0; when f is odd or f = s, put p on the left
of both accumulated hashes and halve both counters while f is positive and even;
otherwise leave rold alone and put p on the right of rnew . After either branch halve
both counters once. Accept exactly when s = 0, rold = u and rnew = v. All halvings
round down.


Theorem 14.7 (The RFC’s own examples pass). With the symbolic hash, in the RFC’s
seven-leaf tree with leaves d0 , . . . , d6 (writing dk also for its leaf hash ℓ(dk )), the inclusion
check accepts leaf 3 with path [d2 , ν(d0 , d1 ), ν(ν(d4 , d5 ), d6 )], and likewise leaves 0, 4 and 6
with their paths; the consistency check from size 4 to size 7 accepts. For every input with
m = N, the inclusion check rejects.

Proof. Use the brackets a, b, c, L, R built above. For leaf 3, the counters start at (3, 6):
put d2 on the left, leaving (1, 3); put a on the left, leaving (0, 1); put R on the right,
leaving (0, 0) and root ν( L, R). Leaf 0 has path [d1 , b, R] and three right combinations.
Leaf 4 has path [d5 , d6 , L]: right, right, left. Leaf 6 has path [c, L]: left, then left; its
first branch shifts (6, 6) to (3, 3) before the ordinary halving, which accounts for the


                                                 242
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


unpaired last leaf. Each reconstructs the same root. For consistency from 4 to 7, the
old root is L and the supplied path is [ R]. Prepending L seeds both hashes with L;
shifting the initial (3, 6) gives (0, 1), so the sole remaining element leaves the old root
alone and makes the new root ν( L, R), with final counters (0, 0). The boundary case
m = N fails the first test m < N.

The append-only history is list append: appending keeps every old entry.

14.5 Proof-carrying code: no price, no permanence
Necula’s idea from Section 8: ship untrusted code with a proof that it obeys the host’s
policy; the host computes what would need to be true and checks the proof with a
small checker. The record is the checked proof, and it’s held only for the moment of
loading. Priced? No. Checking is cheap by design, which is the whole point, and
the producer paid to build the proof off the host. Permanent? No; nothing’s written.
The fragment is a three-instruction memory-bounds language with the policy “every
address is below the limit”: the checker accepts exactly when the condition holds, and
a certificate implies the condition. One example is checked on top of that: a program
that reads address two under a limit of two is rejected. Not the paper’s real case study,
and no bridge to anything else in this book. And its limit: a program that writes
garbage to address zero passes if zero is below the limit. The proof is of the stated
policy and nothing else.

And what was the paper’s real case study, the one my fragment isn’t? Network packet
filters: the little programs an operating system runs on incoming network traffic to
decide which program gets to see which packet. They run inside the kernel, the most
trusted part of the system, and they have to be fast, so they’re exactly the code you’d
most like to take from a stranger and least like to trust. In the 1996 paper that first
set out the idea, Necula and Peter Lee wrote several filters by hand in the assembly
language of a DEC Alpha, shipped each with its proof, and reported a one-time cost
of 1 to 3 milliseconds to check the proof, after which the filter ran with no checks at
all. That’s “checking is cheap by design” with a number on it. It changes nothing
about my fragment, which still isn’t that case study, and it doesn’t add a price: the
milliseconds are the checker’s work, and nothing is being written down for them to
be a toll on.


Definition 14.6 (The bounds fragment). Instructions are READ a, WRITE a v, and
HALT. For a memory limit L, the policy allows READ a and WRITE a v when a < L,
and always allows HALT. The verification condition of a program is that the policy
allows every instruction in it. A certificate is a list of per-instruction policy facts, one
for each instruction in order. The checker tests the policy on each instruction and
returns the conjunction.


Theorem 14.8 (The checker is the verification condition). For every limit L and program


                                            243
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


P: the checker accepts P exactly when the verification condition holds; any certificate for P
gives the verification condition; and with L = 2 the checker rejects READ 2 followed by HALT.

Proof. The first two are induction on the program and on the certificate, one instruction
at a time. The third is a computation: 2 < 2 fails.

14.6 One example, three levels
Before I lay all five side by side, let me walk one of them up and down the three levels
from the start of the section, because every claim in here lives at exactly one level and
it’s easy to let a claim slide up a floor without noticing. Gas, since it’s the one place all
three line up. Think of a restaurant’s real recipe, my photocopy of one page of it, and
a cookbook chapter on what any recipe has to contain. I can check my photocopy line
by line. That tells you nothing about what the kitchen cooks tonight.

The real specification. Ethereum’s execution specification says, in a document that
runs real money, what a storage write costs, what clearing it refunds, and how the
refund is capped at the end of the transaction. None of what I checked is at this
level. What the network actually charges is whatever the clients people run actually
compute, and the evidence for that is the clients and the chain. This book has none of
it.

The transcription. I copied one mechanism out of that document, one slot in one
transaction, gas and refund arithmetic only, at a named commit (Definition 14.2, Theo-
rem 14.3). What the result tells you: if the storage rule is what I copied, then leaving
a fresh slot set costs at least twenty thousand, and set-then-clear nets twenty-three
hundred at the counter. What it can’t tell you: anything about the refund cap (not
copied, which is why the bill came out so different from the counter earlier), the stack,
calls, other slots, or whether any client implements the rule as written. The boundary
of the claim is the edge of the copy.

The wrapper. The gas schedule of Definition 14.3 isn’t Ethereum. It’s any system
with steps, a cost per step and a yes/no commitment flag, plus one thing stipulated:
a charge predicate, with the premise that a charged step costs at least one and an
uncharged one costs nothing. That premise is the whole of what the wrapper adds,
and it’s added by hand; no specification supplies it. Given it, the theorem says the bill
is exact, never letting a commit go free and never billing a non-commit, exactly when
the charge predicate is the commit predicate at unit price. What that tells you is what
exact pricing would have to look like, in any system. It doesn’t say Ethereum meets
it, and Ethereum doesn’t: real gas bills computation that commits nothing, which the
transcription shows in numbers. So the wrapper prices a definition, the transcription
prices a copied rule, and neither prices the chain.

The other four sit on the same three levels, and only one more wrapper is spelled
out in this section. Casper’s transcription is the accountable-safety proof above; its


                                            244
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


wrapper is a small gadget with the stake at risk handed in. A finalize step that risks
nothing turns the record on for free, which breaks Section 3’s toll, and one that risks
at least one unit has a floor. It records exposure to loss (no collateral is destroyed in it),
has no Casper checkpoints in it at all, and is priced by stipulation, the same way the
gas wrapper is. Attestation, transparency and proof-carrying code have transcriptions
that prove what their verifiers do and no price theorem, because their specifications
carry no price. Their wrappers, which I don’t spell out here, are Section 7’s verifier
argument told in each system’s vocabulary, with a colliding pair behind each one, and
that argument is all they carry here.

How to knock down the four claims with the most weight on them, since the book’s
rule is that every claim gets a way to break it. For the gas transcription: a list of stores
from a fresh slot that ends nonzero with net charge under twenty thousand. For the
gas wrapper: a schedule that never lets a commit go free and never bills a non-commit,
whose charge predicate still differs from the commit predicate at some step. For the
finality gadget: a finalizing trace from unfinalized to finalized whose charged stake is
zero while the gadget claims a floor. For the attestation fragment: a verifier reading
only the quote’s fields that decides a runtime flag the quote ignores.

a bond behind the write and takes it on reversal (slashing). Gas takes a fee at the
write (and refunds the revocation, capped), and rations writes with a gas limit per
block. Attestation prices nothing on the registers the quote signs, and puts a budget
on its longer-lived slots and counters. Transparency prices nothing. Attestation and
transparency make reversal infeasible or visible. Proof-carrying code prices nothing
and keeps nothing.

Each row proves what its own transcription says. Reading a row as a claim about a
