So the thing my toy charges for, the moment the record is written, is charged a fee
in one of the five specifications I read, and in that one the designers had to patch the
place where the charge could be clawed back. I find that neither a vindication nor a
refutation. It’s a fact about what people built, and what they built was mostly walls
(hash chains, signatures) and penalties for contradiction. Tolls on commitment were
rare. Whether a toll on commitment is a better design than a wall is not something I
can prove, and I won’t pretend the five say so. What I read in them, and it’s a reading
of five fragments I chose, is that each has a condition treated as a record, though
the conditions differ in durability, and that the price axis is mostly empty. With one
definition of price fixed before the survey, that last part is a count: of fifteen cells in the
table, four are filled (one fee, one bond, two budgets), and only gas takes a payment
at the moment of the write.

That leaves the question Section 10 raised and Section 15 has to face. Five systems,
five different events chosen as “the record”: finalized, committed, attested, logged,
checked. Is there anything that picks out one event as the one worth recording, or is it
a free choice every time? I have a guess. It’s a thesis, and I’ll show you how to kill it.

15 The pointer thesis
The structural results leave a choice open. A base-driven permanent record is a latch
on an event, and the event is free to choose (Section 10, the two cups on one die). Five
real systems each picked a different one (Section 14). For the worked case in this book
I picked certification. This chapter asks whether that choice has a reason beyond the
construction: is there something about how people and machines rely on records that
selects this event?

I have a thesis, in the sense the Church-Turing thesis is one (Section 2): a claim tying
defined notions to the world. Its fate matters to that choice of event. The latch, the
windows and the counting arguments use their stated premises whichever event a


                                             246
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


system records. Here is the claim, where I got it, what can be checked, and how to kill
it.

15.1 The claim
Of all the events a machine could put on its meter, the ones its price list charges for
and its counter adds up, certification is the one whose records get copied and relied on
by parties who didn’t produce them: checked, stored, and acted on across independent
places that share no other state. Copying alone can’t be the test. A replicated system
copies everything it holds to every node, the gas used in a block header as faithfully as
the word final, so rival events get copied too. Nobody who didn’t produce them acts
on them. If that’s true, the choice of certification stops being free. It’s the one event
the world around the machine keeps redundant copies of and leans on, and that’s a
reason to price it and leave the others unpriced. So the thesis has two halves, and the
ways to kill it at the end aim at both: certification is that event, and where a deployed
discipline puts a price on writing a record, the record it prices is one that’s copied and
relied on in that sense.

There’s a second handle on the same question, and it comes from Section 4. The
permanent-certificate theorem never uses the word certification for anything special:
given Section 4’s rule that forgetting is charged, it prices any yes-or-no reading that,
once on, stays on, on a machine with finite memory. So it points at a narrower candi-
date: the events to price are the ones that write a record no later step can take back.
Certification is one of them. As an exact answer that candidate is false, because a
merging step can also revoke (Section 4’s three cards). Whether the records that are
copied and relied on are the permanent ones, and whether being copied and relied on
picks out anything the merge criterion doesn’t, is what the two handles have to settle
between them.

Two holes in that, which I can see from here, so you don’t have to find them for me.
The first is a missing premise. Even if the world copies certification records more than
any other kind, “copied” doesn’t give you “priced” on its own. Something has to
connect them, and the best candidate I have is a premise about incentives: a record
that many independent parties copy and lean on is exactly the record worth forging,
so it’s the one where a price buys the most protection. That’s a reasonable premise. It’s
also a premise. The thesis’s second half states the connection as a claim to be tested;
it doesn’t explain it, and nothing in this book supplies the explanation. The second
hole is a circle. If “certification” just means “the record other people rely on,” then
of course it’s the one that gets relied on and copied, and the claim says nothing. So
the event has to be picked out without mentioning reliance: here it’s a reading going
up for good right after a check of the same claim passed, which you can find in a run
without asking who reads it. Whether the world copies that event more than its rivals
is then a real question, and it could come out no.

That’s the whole thesis. Now the rest of what a thesis owes you.


                                           247
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


15.2 Where the shape comes from, and how much of it survived
The shape is from physics, and I want to tell you where exactly, because I borrowed a
word and I didn’t get to keep the whole thing.

Quantum mechanics has a famous problem: a system can be in a blend of states,
and when you measure it you find one definite state, and nobody agrees on what
“measuring” did. In 1981 Wojciech Zurek asked a sharper question: of all the ways a
measuring device could end up, why does it end up recording one particular kind of
quantity (the position of a pointer on a dial, say)? Why never some blend? His answer,
developed over twenty years and summarised in a 2009 paper called “Quantum
Darwinism,” is that the environment decides. The air, the light, the table, everything the
device touches, is constantly interacting with it, and only certain states of the device
survive that interaction; those are the pointer states. And more: the environment selects
them, and then it copies them. The light bouncing off a dial carries the dial’s reading
to every corner of the room, redundantly, so that a thousand observers can each read
a different scrap of the environment and all agree on where the pointer is, without
touching the dial. Objectivity, on this view, is redundancy: a property is objective
when many independent fragments of the world each carry it.

Zurek isn’t the only one behind it. Fernando Brandão, Marco Piani and Paweł
Horodecki (2015) published a proof that, as I read it, makes something like it generic:
under any quantum dynamics at all, observers who learn about a system only through
its environment get at most classical information, about one and the same measure-
ment of the system. That’s their theorem behind the word “objective,” and it’s a
statement about separate fragments, which is exactly the part I didn’t keep. Xiao-
Liang Qi and Daniel Ranard (2021), as I read their paper, sharpened it into a statement
about every possible evolution of system and environment: everywhere in the environ-
ment outside a region of fixed size, whatever an observer can learn about the system
is classical, read off one fixed measurement. A statement about every evolution and
every input is the quantum cousin of what the definitions below ask of an observer,
that it record the event in every state, including ones that never happen to turn up.

That’s the shape I borrowed. Certification is to a machine’s ecosystem (the machine
plus everything around it that reads, stores and relies on its records) what the pointer
reading is to the room: the thing that gets copied everywhere. It’s a good shape and I
think it’s the right intuition. Here’s what survived into the definitions below, and I’m
going to be exact because the word “redundant” is doing less than it does for Zurek.

Zurek’s redundancy is graded (each fragment carries almost all the information, with
some small loss) and it requires the fragments to be disjoint: different observers reading
different parts of the environment. The definition below is the zero-loss case with no
disjointness at all. An ecosystem is a state type, some number of observers, and one
bit per observer; an observer records an event when its bit is true exactly when the
event holds; an event proliferates when every observer records it. Nothing in that says


                                           248
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


two observers draw on separate parts of the state. They could all be reading the same
bit. The definition permits it. So I kept the word and dropped the independence
that makes Zurek’s version mean “objective.” That’s a gap between the thesis’s prose
and that first formal object, and the prose is where the thesis lives. The definitions
under the thesis below close part of the gap: they define independent carriers, and the
definition turns out to force something (Theorem 15.1).

The independence I dropped is exactly what the thesis’s closest published neighbour
keeps. Jess Riedel, Zurek and Michael Zwolak (2016) took histories of a closed quan-
tum system, the story a whole sequence of events tells, and asked which of them the
world keeps records of in many separate pieces of the environment. As I read their
paper, redundant records in separate pieces make a history consistent, so ordinary
yes-or-no reasoning about it works, and they pick out a small set of histories from
the huge number that are merely consistent: in their words, an objective past. That’s
“what proliferates is what counts” in quantum form, with the disjointness in it, and it
came before this book. Halliwell, in a second 1999 paper, “Somewhere in the universe,”
had already carried, as I understand him, the link between records and consistent
histories from pure starting states to mixed ones, where the records still exist but are
necessarily imperfect.

There’s a deeper mismatch in the borrowing, and it runs against the book, so it goes
here. In Zurek’s picture the whole thing, system and device and environment together,
evolves by quantum mechanics’ rule for closed systems, and that rule never sends
two states to one; every step can be run backwards. So, seen from the whole, the
environment’s copying is just that, copying: the dial’s reading gets written onto fresh
light, nothing anywhere is forgotten, and it’s Door one of Section 4 with the rest of
the universe as the endless strip. That’s the operation this book says is free, Bennett
writing on a blank page. The forgetting shows up only when you look at the dial alone
and ignore what the light carried off. Then a blend of pointer readings decays into a
plain either-or, and two different blends can decay into the same either-or: two states,
one result, a merge in the coarse picture. So the opening chapter’s “every settling
forgets” fits the dial’s own view. From the whole it fails, and the thing the thesis leans
on, copying, is the free half of the story. What that does to the thesis: if there’s a price,
it isn’t on the copying. It’s on whatever makes the copy final from the dial’s side, and
the claim above, as written, points at the copy.

A published no-go cuts closer still. Philippe Allard Guérin, Veronika Baumann, Flavio
Del Santo and Časlav Brukner (2021) gave an argument that, under assumptions that
look natural in quantum mechanics, an observer’s own perceptions of her outcome
at two different times can’t share one reality: no joint chance for the two, depending
linearly on the starting state, reproduces what unitary quantum theory predicts for
each. A record that persists, for the one holding it, is exactly what gets into trouble once
the whole is treated as one-to-one. It isn’t a theorem about my machine, which isn’t
quantum. It’s still the strongest published reason I know to hold the word “permanent”


                                            249
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


loosely when a physicist is in the room.

Which leaves the question to ask of any borrowed shape: has anybody checked the
original? For a long time quantum Darwinism was a theory without a lab. Then, in
2018 and 2019, three groups working separately, in Italy, China and Germany, went
looking for its fingerprint, as Philip Ball’s 2019 report in Quanta Magazine tells it. The
German one, at Ulm, with Zurek among the authors, watched the spin of a single
defect inside a diamond and the carbon atoms around it, and saw the redundancy
the theory predicts: the defect’s state turned up copied in its surroundings, and it
didn’t take much of the surroundings before more of them told you nothing new. The
other two did it with photons. Is that the bottom? Not by a long way, and the people
involved said so. Zurek himself pointed out that the photon experiments make their
copies artificially and that the diamond’s environment is small, and others noted that
all three are schematic versions of a real environment and don’t rule out rival accounts.
So the shape I borrowed has passed some first tests in a lab, at the scale of a handful
of atoms or photons, with the caveats written on it. None of that touches the thesis
here, which is about machines and never rested on quantum physics. It changes the
picture: what I borrowed is a lead somebody is checking. It isn’t settled, and I don’t
get to lean on it as if it were.

15.3 What’s proved
Definitions, two toys, a theorem about independence, a survey, and two refutations of
things that would have been stronger.

The definitions above, plus “unique pointer among rivals”: the event proliferates and
none of a listed set of rival events does. Uniqueness is relative to the list, necessarily,
since any event that holds on exactly the same states as a proliferating event prolif-
erates whenever it does: the same fact under another name, so someone has to say
which names count as rivals. And the first criterion, as a schema: for every ecosystem
in some class, its metered event is the unique pointer among its rivals. The class and
the rivals are inputs. Nothing about them is proved. A second set of definitions, after
this one, tightens “proliferates” to “copied and relied on” and drops the rival list.

Here’s the formal object, small enough to hold in one hand.


Definition 15.1 (Ecosystem, records, proliferates, pointer). An ecosystem is a type of
states, a number N of observers, and for each observer i a Boolean fragment Fi on
states. Observer i records an event E (a property of states) when, for every state s, E(s)
holds exactly when Fi (s) is true. E proliferates when every observer i < N records it. E
is the unique pointer among a list of rival events when E proliferates and no rival in the
list does. Given a class C of ecosystems, and for each member a designated metered
event and a list of rivals, the pointer criterion holds for C when every member’s metered
event is the unique pointer among its rivals.



                                           250
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Nothing in the definition makes two fragments read different parts of the state, and
“metered” is only a label: the definition has no metering in it.

One bit per observer can’t even state the objection a replicated system raises. Every
full node of a blockchain holds the whole shared state, so every fact about it, “gas
used is at least one” as much as “final,” sits on every node. The tightened definitions
give each observer whatever it holds, an action it takes on what it holds, and a flag for
whether it produced the record.


Definition 15.2 (Copied and relied on, independent carriers, the pointer). An ecosys-
tem with reliance is a type of states, a number N of observers, and for each observer i a
view Vi (a function from states to some type of things an observer can hold), an action
ai (a Boolean function of the view) and a producer flag. Fix a set R of reachable states.
An event E is copied on R when for each i < N some Boolean function d of the view
has E(s) exactly when d(Vi (s)) is true, for every s in R. Observer i relies on E when
ai (Vi (s)) true gives E(s) for every s in R, and ai (Vi (s)) is true for some s in R. E is
relied on by parties who didn’t produce it when some observer i < N is not a producer
and every such observer relies on E; it is copied and relied on when it is both. E is the
pointer on R when it is copied and relied on, and every event that is copied and relied
on holds at every state of R where E holds. An event a step rule could meter is one
decided by a Boolean function of the state, so a price list can charge exactly the steps
that turn it on. The carriers are independent under a family of relations Pi (states that
agree on observer i’s own part of the world) when each view gives equal values on
states related by its Pi , and for any two observers i ̸= j below N and any states s, t
there is a state u with Pi (u, s) and Pj (u, t): the two parts can be set separately.


Two pointers on the same R agree on every state of R, so the pointer is unique with
no list of rivals. And the definition of independence has a consequence I didn’t put in
on purpose.

Put one yes/no card in front of each of two readers. If the cards can be set separately,
all four arrangements are allowed: no/no, no/yes, yes/no and yes/yes. Ask each
reader to recover one shared event using only their own card. Suppose that event is
false at no/no and true at yes/yes. At no/yes, the first reader sees exactly what they
saw in the false case, while the second sees exactly what they saw in the true case.
Their answers conflict. That mixed arrangement is what the independence condition
supplies in the proof.

Now impose a copying procedure that only leaves no/no or yes/yes. On those reach-
able arrangements each reader can report the shared bit correctly. Separate cards are
possible carriers; correlated reachable contents make them copies. The theorem con-
cerns exact recovery on all arrangements, including the mixed ones that this copying
procedure never leaves behind.



                                           251
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


Theorem 15.1 (Independent copies on every state: the event is equivalent at any two
states). In any ecosystem with reliance whose carriers are independent and which has at least
two observers, an event copied on the set of all states holds at one state exactly when it holds at
any other, so it holds at every state or at none.

Proof. Let observers 0 and 1 decide the event by d0 and d1 . Given states s and t, take
u with observer 0’s part from s and observer 1’s from t. Then the event at s is d0 of
observer 0’s view, which is the same at u, so it equals the event at u; and the event at u
equals the event at t the same way through observer 1.

So separate parts of the world can each carry an exact copy of a real record only on
the states the world actually reaches, where the copying made them agree, and that’s
why the definition asks for copies on a set R of reachable states. Zurek’s copies are the
same: the light carries the dial’s reading because the dial put it there.


Theorem 15.2 (A replicated header: copying doesn’t separate, reliance does). Let the
states be a block header (a finalized bit, a gas-used count) and three nodes’ copies of it, with R
the states where every copy equals the header; node i’s view is its own copy, its part of the world
is that copy, node 0 is the producer, and every node acts exactly when its copy says finalized.
Then the carriers are independent; “finalized” and “gas used is at least one” are both copied
on R; “finalized” is the pointer on R; and “gas used is at least one” is not relied on by parties
who didn’t produce it.

Proof. Independence: to give node i the copy from s and node j the copy from t,
overwrite node j’s copy in s. On R every copy is the header, so each node reads either
fact off its copy. Node 1 acts only where its copy, and so the header, says finalized,
and acts at the finalized header with no gas used; that state shows gas used fails node
1’s reliance. Any event relied on by node 1 holds wherever node 1 acts, which on R is
wherever the header is finalized, so “finalized” is the strongest.

It’s a sanity check with maps I wrote, and it shows only that the tightened definition
can tell the two apart where plain copying can’t.


Thesis 15.3 (The pointer thesis). Let C be the class of ecosystems with reliance that faithfully
model deployed record-keeping disciplines, each with its reachable states, its observers reading
independent carriers in the sense of Definition 15.2, its certification event, and the records
its discipline prices. Then for every member of C: (1) the certification event is the pointer on
the reachable states, so it is copied and relied on by parties who didn’t produce it, and every
event copied and relied on in that sense, every event a step rule could meter among them, holds
wherever certification does; and (2) every record the discipline prices is copied and relied on by
parties who didn’t produce it.




                                               252
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


The thesis leans on two notions with no precise mathematical definition: what it is to
“faithfully model” a system, and which systems count as “deployed.” Those two tie
the definitions to the world, the way “computable in the plain-English sense” does
in the Church-Turing thesis, and no definition can do that job, so the claim is a thesis.
The other two terms it needs, independent carriers and the events a step rule could
meter, are defined in Definition 15.2. The schema takes the class, the reachable states,
the certification event and the priced records as inputs; it proves nothing about which
real systems satisfy them.

A toy: three observers on a replicated ledger, where certification proliferates and
“work done” doesn’t. It’s an illustration, and that’s all it is. It isn’t evidence.


Theorem 15.4 (The toy). Let the toy have states (a certified bit, a work count), three observers,
and every fragment equal to the certified bit. Then “certified” is the unique pointer among the
one rival “work at least 1”.

Proof. Every fragment is the certified bit, so every observer records “certified” by
definition. For the rival, take the state with the bit false and work 1: the event holds
and observer 0’s fragment is false, so observer 0 does not record it.

A survey of twelve events, one theorem: for each of the five systems in Section 14,
the designated event (finalized, committed, attested, logged, checked) proliferates
in the observer map I wrote for that system, and a rival (proposer work, a scratch
counter, measurement noise, submission latency, prover steps) doesn’t. The five to-
gether are one statement, an instance of the schema above. Plus a symmetric message-
authentication code, which does not proliferate, and a digital signature, which does.
Twelve rows. The five maps all use the same construction: a state has a designated
Boolean event and a separate nonnegative rival count, three observers each return
the event bit, and the rival asks whether its count is at least one. The bit and count
can vary independently. The signature map likewise gives all three observers the
authentic-signature bit. In the MAC map, observers 0 and 1 receive the authentic-tag
bit and observer 2 always returns false. These maps, not a protocol running on a
network, are the entire tests here. And a thirteenth that I think is the most important
one: swap which bit every observer copies, and the criterion picks the other event. The
criterion selects whatever the observer map copies. The map is where the argument
lives, and I wrote the maps. So the five “confirmations” are five instances of one
construction with the fields renamed. I’m saying that twice on purpose, so it can’t slip
past once.


Theorem 15.5 (The survey, and the swap). (1) In each of the five observer models (proof-
of-stake, gas, attestation, transparency, proof-carrying), the designated event proliferates and
the designated rival does not; in the symmetric-MAC model the authentic-tag event does not
proliferate; in the signature model the authentic-signature event does. (2) Let the states be


                                              253
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


 pairs of bits (first, second), with three observers whose fragments all equal the second bit. Then
“second is true” is the unique pointer among the one rival “first is true”.

Proof. Each confirmation holds by definition: each observer’s fragment is true exactly
when the event holds. Each refutation exhibits one state where the event holds and
some observer’s bit is down. In (2) that state is (true, false).

Two stronger claims, both refuted, and I’d ask you not to merge them because they
fail for different reasons.

The first stronger claim: every forgery-resistant commitment proliferates. If that were true,
certification would be the pointer because it’s the commitment. It’s refuted in three
observer models (deniable authentication, where only the designated verifier’s bit
tracks the event; a symmetric MAC, where the key holders share a secret and nobody
else can check; an object capability, an unforgeable token that grants access to whoever
holds it) and confirmed in two (a public log; a digital signature). Build the first with
three observers: give one a copy of the event’s bit and the other two a constant false.
The one records it; it doesn’t proliferate. The proved half is the map computation.
Whether my maps are fair to the real designs is argued in prose, and you should argue
back.


Theorem 15.6 (One blind observer is enough). (1) In any ecosystem, if some observer
i < N has Fi (s0 ) false at a state s0 where E holds, then E does not proliferate. (2) Let the
deniable model have states (authentic, verifier-accepts), three observers, observer 0’s fragment
the authentic bit and observers 1 and 2 constantly false. Then observer 0 records “authentic”,
and “authentic” does not proliferate. The symmetric-MAC and object-capability models also
fail to proliferate their events; the public-log and signature models proliferate theirs.

Proof. (1) Recording would require E(s0 ) ⇐⇒ Fi (s0 ), and the left side is true while
the right is false. (2) Observer 0’s fragment is true exactly when the event holds. Apply
(1) with observer 1 and the state (true, true). The other two refutations apply (1) to a
blind observer of their own model (the object-capability map gives the token holder
the bit and the other two constant false; the public-log map gives all three the logged
bit), and the two confirmations hold by definition.

The theorem is about the observer maps. That a third party in deniable authentication
really cannot be convinced is the modelling claim, and the model has no transcript,
key or verifier in it to check that against.

The second stronger claim: agreement plus accuracy plus locality imply permanence. That
is, if all observers agree, each sees the event exactly, and each updates by the same
local rule with no coordinator, then the recorded event can’t be undone. Refuted by
the smallest thing imaginable: one bit, two observers who both see it, and the rule
“flip.” All three conditions hold and true becomes false in one step. Do it on paper;

                                                254
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


it takes a minute and it’s humbling. What does give permanence is durability, “an
observer’s true view stays true,” added as a premise, and then it follows in a few lines.
So durability is the premise doing the work, and durability is Section 4’s permanence
wearing a different coat. Agreement doesn’t buy it. Do the paper version again with
one change, the rule “stay true once true” in place of “flip,” and the bit can’t fall,
because the rule won’t let it. The observers agreeing has nothing to do with it. (The
machine I build later has a reading that’s durable in exactly this sense: its flag never
comes down, by its step rule (Theorem 16.5).) None of this rules out a narrower
theorem with real assumptions about the network, the adversary or durability; it rules
out these two strong forms.


Definition 15.3 (Observation game). A game has states, a number N of observers, a
Boolean event e, a Boolean view Vi for each observer, and a step map. For i, j < N it
has consensus when Vi = Vj on every state; authenticity when Vi (s) = e(s) for every
state and every i < N; coordinator-free update when one function ℓ on Booleans has
Vi (step(s)) = ℓ(Vi (s)) for every state and every i < N; durable views when Vi (s) true
gives Vi (step(s)) true for every i < N; and a permanent event when e(s) true gives
e(step(s)) true.


Theorem 15.7 (What buys permanence). (1) It is false that every game with N > 0,
consensus, authenticity and coordinator-free update has a permanent event. (2) Every game
with N > 0, authenticity and durable views has a permanent event.

Proof. (1) The toggle game: states are Booleans, two observers, event and both views
the identity, step “flip”. Consensus and authenticity hold trivially, the local rule is
“flip”, and the state true steps to false. (2) If e(s) is true, observer 0’s view is true by
authenticity, stays true by durability, and authenticity turns it back into e(step(s)).

15.4 What isn’t proved, and must stay that way on the page
That certification in deployed systems is singled out by being copied and relied on across
independent carriers. The criterion defines independence; it has no precise definition of
“deployed” or “faithfully model,” and no cost law connecting being copied and relied
on to price. Every correspondence between a mathematical observer map and a real
system is a sentence I wrote. The thesis is a thesis, and anyone who says the formal
object proves it is reading more than is there.

15.5 How to kill it
Three ways, in the order I’d try them.

One: find a deployed discipline that puts a price on writing a record that parties who
didn’t produce it don’t copy and rely on. A real system with a toll on something
nobody else leans on. That breaks the second half, “the priced record is the copied
and relied-on one.”


                                            255
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Two: find a rival event, one certification doesn’t imply, that is copied and relied on
as well as certification in a real ecosystem. Then certification isn’t the pointer and
the first half’s “the one” is wrong. Or do it in a model: show that something like a
multiplication count, or the number of times a Turing machine’s head turns around,
is copied and relied on by the same standard, so the criterion picks out more than one
event and decides nothing.

Three: formalise an ecosystem honestly, with independence as Definition 15.2 defines
it, where certification fails the test. The symmetric-MAC row is already most of the
way there for a different claim; push it.

The theorems above have already refuted two stronger forms of its own claim, which
I take as a sign the method works and as a warning about the main claim.

15.6 The end of the logic
That’s Part III, and the end of the logic that started in Part II. Here’s what it earned. A
toll on raising a flag is forced by three premises (Section 4). Learning isn’t forced to
cost. Committing is (Section 5). The counter is arithmetic once the schedule is fixed
(Section 6). A window with a colliding pair in it can’t price the flag exactly (Section 7).
Entitlement is an object, a check, and a paid event, and, given lists, a tree and a
covering that someone supplies, and a run that paid for the tree’s depth, it costs at
least the index bits it commits to (Section 8). Insight is a committed relation (Section 9).
A feeling doesn’t qualify. Over any base a record that is driven by the computation
and never comes down is a latch, with two free choices, the price list and the event
(Section 10). With more than two places, a record that is driven by the computation
and climbs a partial order is a row of cups, each one a latch; the toll over the whole
row charges at least one on any step that turns up some cup, and a straight strip of
n + 1 stages needs exactly n cups that only turn up (Section 11). When the machine has
finitely many states, its record only grows, and the ordinary machine forgets nothing,
the toll prices crushing two states of one fibre, and a window can price exactly by
seeing the cups move (Section 12). No inside procedure whose flip a substrate can
represent decides a shortcut property, given a recursion theorem, which the nat family
has by construction. L is handled on its own terms rather than as a substrate, and on
L the same diagonal is proved again from a recursion theorem it has by proof. What
a record can do is carry the commitment (Section 13). Of five specifications, read
through my transcriptions, one charges a fee at the write (Section 14). For the choice
of event, the pointer thesis proposes certification and lists how that proposal could
fail (Section 15).

One accounting question remains: do the structural requirements select the toll alone?
A short list of requirements leaving only one price would settle that choice. The
requirements I tried do not do it, and the no is small enough to check on three states.
Call them blank, once and twice, with once and twice reading yes. The flip takes blank
to once and leaves the other two where they are. The smooth takes both once and


                                            256
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


twice to twice and leaves blank alone. The smooth forgets something, so the price
on merging from Section 4 charges it a mark. (The flip forgets too, blank and once
both land on once, so the price on merging charges it as well, as the list requires.) It
raises nothing, so the toll leaves it free. Now try requirements that name no reading:
no charge on a move that changes nothing, none on a move that forgets nothing, the
same bill when you rename the states, a total that adds up along a run, a bill that looks
only at the step, and one mark on the flip from blank. The toll, read as the bill that
charges the flip from blank and nothing else, meets every one of them on this machine.
So does the price on merging. They disagree on the smooth, so that list doesn’t pick
between them. What picks the toll is a requirement that names the record: over any
run the total is never more than the number of times the reading went up. With the
floor, that leaves exactly one bill, one mark per raise and nothing else (Section 7), and
it rules the price on merging out, because the smooth costs that price a mark and raises
nothing. The only renaming of the three states that respects the moves is the identity,
so the renaming requirement asks nothing there. So the uniqueness is real and it’s
small. It holds once you’ve said which reading you’re charging for, and which reading
deserves the charge is the pointer thesis, which is still a thesis.

The uniqueness theorems that do exist are about pricing information loss, and they’re
worth a look because they say what kind of bill the price on merging is. John Baez,
Tobias Fritz and Tom Leinster (2011), mathematicians who work in category theory,
the mathematics Lawvere’s diagonal theorem came from, asked what a measure of
information loss has to look like. As I read their paper, they proved that, for maps that
preserve a probability measure, Shannon entropy is up to a constant factor the only
measure of information loss that is functorial, convex-linear and continuous. János
Aczél and Bruno Forte, mathematicians at the University of Waterloo who worked on
functional equations, and C. T. Ng, who had taken his doctorate there under Aczél
in 1971, asked in a paper of 1974 which entropies deserve to be called natural, and
proved, by their account, that the entropies with a short list of natural properties are
exactly the linear combinations of Shannon’s and Hartley’s, where Hartley’s is the log
of the count, so even for merges the choice between the average and the worst case is a
real choice. Both price merges. Neither prices raises, so neither picks out the toll, and
that’s the three-state example in a bigger room. On the other side of the fence, Luciano
Pomatto, Philipp Strack and Omer Tamuz (2023), economists at Caltech and Yale who
asked what learning something should cost, proved, by their account, a uniqueness
result for what it costs to acquire information, with constant marginal costs. That’s a
price on producing a signal, a different bill from the free learning of Section 5.

What none of that is: a machine. Every theorem so far quantifies over “any states,
any steps,” or is about a small copy of somebody else’s system, or points forward at
a thing I keep promising. That’s the abstract part of the book, and it’s done. From
the next page on I stop saying “any machine” and build one, mine: the least I can
make that still shows the whole model, with every part named and every price written



                                          257
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


down, so that everything above finally has something to bump into, and then one
fixed program, run on a host with more counters, that runs every machine of the
model whose workings a program can compute. If a statement up there doesn’t mean
what I think it means, that’s where it’ll show. Part IV is the thing. I want to see if it
holds weight.



Part IV

The machine
16 The smallest honest machine
Parts I to III never built anything. They said “any states, any steps,” and whenever a
picture was needed, a board or some chairs or a cup stood in. Now I have to build a
machine, and the first worry I have about that is a slightly embarrassing one. I built a
big one first, the one from the origin story, with dozens of instructions, some picked
for reasons and some picked because I had to pick something, and theorems held of it.
What does that show? That the model works, or that I’m good at stacking instructions
until the proofs go through? A big machine is a wonderful place to hide a mistake. It’s
a garage so full of stuff that you could lose a car in it.

So the machine in this book is a small one. I want the state and every way of changing
it where you can inspect them. Six instruction kinds let us follow how a check stays
tied to an object, how a change makes it stale, and how the next move uses that relation.
Each kind takes operands, a counter or a property or a line to jump to, so there are
unboundedly many instructions. This is one construction of the model; the theorems
will say which facts depend on these particular choices. Smallest, in this chapter’s
title, is my account of building it. No comparison class, measure of size or proof of
minimality stands behind the word.

16.1 What the model actually asks for
Here’s what Parts II and III say the model adds to a machine. A record: a flag that
reads no or yes, “certified” or not. A toll: the step that raises the flag costs something
(Section 3). A ledger: the running total of those costs, a whole number that only climbs
(Section 6). And Section 10 proved the thing this whole chapter stands on: over any
base at all, a base-driven record is a latch, a bit that switches on at an event the base
decides and never switches off (Observation 10.1). The record watches the base. It
doesn’t compute anything the base couldn’t compute without it.

Push on that for a second, because it cuts the job in half. If the record adds no comput-
ing power, then all the computing power comes from the base, and the question “how
small can the machine be” splits into two questions that don’t touch each other. For


                                           258
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


the base: what’s the smallest thing that can compute everything there is to compute?
For the record: what’s the smallest set of pieces that makes the flag mean something?

One honest asterisk on “don’t touch,” because the machine below makes it matter.
What’s blind is the flag and the ledger: the base never reads either of them. But
the pieces that make the flag mean something (a table of checked facts, a slot for a
commitment, a trap that stops a refused run) have to sit where the step can read them,
which is in the base, and they do steer the run: a failed check stops a program dead.
The latch theorem holds wherever you draw the line between base and record, which
is exactly why it can’t tell you where the meaning lives. On this machine the meaning
lives on the base side of the line, in the bookkeeping, and the flag on top reports it.

The record question, the second of those two, is the one Part III left to the machine,
on purpose. Section 9 said that testing a claim and committing to it are two different
acts, and that nothing in the five parts of the model makes the second wait for the first.
Read Section 3’s definition again with that in mind: a machine where you pay one
unit and raise the flag over nothing in particular obeys every rule in it. That machine
is honest about the price and silent about what was bought. A receipt for nothing. The
toll alone can’t fix that, because the toll is a rule about cost, and “was this earned” is a
question about order: did a check happen, of this claim, before the commitment, with
nothing changing underneath in between?

This machine is my attempt to make the order part of the machine, in the smallest
place I could find to do it. I’ll show you the pieces, then the proofs, then the places it
falls short, which there are, and which I’d rather you hear from me.

16.2 Where the counters come from
The base first, and the base isn’t mine. It’s Marvin Minsky’s. In a 1961 paper in
the Annals of Mathematics, and then in his 1967 book Computation: Finite and Infinite
Machines, Minsky studied a machine so bare it’s almost a joke. Picture a few bins of
pebbles and a numbered list of instructions. There are only two kinds of instruction:
put a pebble in bin c and go to the next line; or, if bin c has a pebble, take one out
and jump to line j, and if it’s empty, just go to the next line. That’s it. No memory, no
tape, no arithmetic beyond plus one and minus one. When the line you’re on has no
instruction, the machine stops.

What Minsky proved, by hand, is that two bins are enough to compute anything a
Turing machine can compute, as long as you’re willing to pack the input in a strange
way. The trick is to keep many numbers inside one number, as the powers of different
primes (2x 3y 5z holds three numbers in one), and to do arithmetic on the exponents by
multiplying and dividing with the second bin as scratch space. That representation can
turn a modest input into an enormous pile, handled one pebble at a time. It is a way
to establish universality: the two bins can express every Turing computation under
the encoding. Here they give me a base whose ordinary moves are easy to inspect.
The structural results each say which properties of a base they need; Section 17 carries

                                            259
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


the earned layer to other bases under explicit interface conditions.

Who cares? Minsky did, because the question then was where the edge of computation
sits and how little machinery reaches it. You should, because it means the base of this
chapter’s machine hides nothing: if it can compute everything with plus one, minus
one and a jump, then nothing about the record can be smuggling computing power
in through some instruction I made fancy. For this construction I use the two-counter
result of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors. The halting reduction is their work;
the step-for-step connection to this machine is the part I have to establish.

And the pebbles aren’t only my picture. They were somebody’s actual machine, the
same year. In one issue of the Canadian Mathematical Bulletin, September 1961, Z. A.
Melzak, a mathematician at the University of British Columbia, described a computer
made of distinguishable holes and an unlimited supply of pebbles, with one three-
place operation, and a few pages later Joachim Lambek, a mathematician at McGill
University, trimmed it to two moves: put a pebble in hole X; take one out of hole X if
there’s one to take. He called it an infinite abacus, and early on he writes “Our method
is probably not new,” which is a hard sentence to beat. He also tells anybody who
distrusts infinity not to worry about all those holes, since any one computation only
ever uses finitely many of them. Is that two inventions or one? Lambek says his was
a modification of Melzak’s, so call it one and a half, with Minsky’s as a separate find
the same year. And then Lambek went somewhere you wouldn’t guess: in 1986, with
Philip Scott, a logician who had come to McGill to work with him and later taught at
the University of Ottawa, he wrote a book whose first part, as the publisher describes
it, shows that typed lambda calculi and a certain kind of category are essentially the
same thing. Pebbles to category theory in one career, twenty-five years end to end.
Does any of it change the argument? No. The machine uses Minsky’s version and
Minsky’s name. But a bare machine that several people reach for in the same year
looks like a shape that was sitting there. It doesn’t look much like anybody’s invention.

The title of Minsky’s 1961 paper is the clue I can’t leave alone. It’s about “Post’s
problem of tag.” Who’s Post, and what’s tag? Emil Post was a logician, a fresh PhD
from Columbia, who in 1921, on a fellowship at Princeton, was playing with about the
simplest rewriting game there is. Take a word of 0s and 1s. Look at its first letter, chop
the first three letters off the front, and stick something on the end: 00 if the letter you
looked at was 0, 1101 if it was 1. Repeat, and stop when fewer than three letters are
left. Try it at the table. Start from 1000: you get 01101, then 0100, then 000, then
00, and it stops. Start from 100: you get 1101, 11101, 011101, 10100, 001101, and
then 10100 again, and it goes round forever. Post wanted a rule that tells you, for
every starting word, which of those happens. He worked at it for months and later
called it hopeless, and as far as I can tell it still is: a hundred years on, nobody knows
whether that one little game, with that one rule, can be decided. Stephen Wolfram,
the physicist who built Mathematica, wrote a 2021 article on it that tells the Princeton
story, and it’s where I’d start. In his 1961 paper Minsky proved by hand that tag games


                                           260
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


in general can compute anything, which is why Post’s name is on it. It didn’t settle
Post’s own game. And the chase goes one step further. In 2008 Liesbeth De Mol, a
historian and philosopher of computing who wrote her doctoral work on tag systems,
turned the famous 3n + 1 problem (halve an even number, triple an odd one and add
one, and ask whether you always get down to 1) into a small tag game of the same
kind. So is Post’s game secretly as hard as everything, or just stubborn? I can’t tell
you, and as far as the published work goes, nobody can yet.

None of that changes the machine below. It changes the picture. The two-counter
machine came out of a hunt for the smallest thing that can’t be predicted, and the
smallest things are exactly where the open questions are still sitting.

One word clash, before it bites. Minsky’s machine is usually called a counter machine,
and its bins are counters. Section 6 also had a counter: the ledger µ, the number that
only climbs. Same word, two completely different things, and I’d love to say I set that
up on purpose. In this chapter, counter means one of Minsky’s two bins, called A and
B, and the climbing total is always the ledger µ.

16.3 The machine
Here’s the whole state. I’ll say each piece in words first.

   • Two counters, A and B. Each holds a whole number, with no upper limit.
   • A version for each counter, also a whole number with no limit. It starts at 0 and
     goes up by one every time its counter is written. Think of it as the counter’s
     edition number: a new value is a new edition.
   • A line number, which instruction comes next, counting from 1 (more on that
     choice just below).
   • A fact table: a list of facts. A fact is three things stuck together: a property, a
     counter, and a version. “A is even, as of edition 3” is a fact. The table has room
     for sixteen. Why sixteen? It’s a pick, with no derivation behind it, and what the
     pick costs is in the subsection near the end of this chapter on what the machine
     doesn’t do.
   • A channel: either empty, or holding one fact. This is where a commitment sits.
   • A trap: one bit, down at the start. When it goes up, the machine has refused
     something, and it stays up.

Counting lines from 1 looks like the least interesting choice in the chapter, and it’s one
of the oldest arguments in programming, with a famous referee. Edsger Dijkstra was
a Dutch computer scientist, one of the generation that founded the field, and for over
forty years he mailed numbered notes to a few dozen colleagues. In 1982 he wrote
one of them, EWD 831, titled “Why numbering should start at zero.” His case goes
through ranges first. Of the four ways to write “2 up to 12” with less-than signs, he


                                           261
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


picks the one that takes the bottom in and leaves the top out, 2 ≤ i < 13: two ranges
that meet end to end then share one number written once, and the length is just the
top minus the bottom. Start a sequence of N things at zero and it’s 0 ≤ i < N, and
each thing’s number is how many things came before it. He reports that programmers
on the language Mesa, which allowed all four conventions, found the other three a
steady source of clumsiness and mistakes, and he points out that FORTRAN starts
at one. Does that settle it? It settles which convention is tidier, by an argument you
can check. It doesn’t settle which convention somebody else’s work used, and that’s
the trap: the two-counter machine used by Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors
numbers its lines from 1, and so does this machine, because matching it line for line
is worth more here than tidiness. Is zero the right place to start counting? Dijkstra’s
title says it is, and I can’t tell you more than that. What his note carries is an argument
about which way makes fewer mistakes. That part you can check for yourself, and it’s
the more useful thing to have.

Everything in that list is the core, the part the base moves. Outside the core sit the two
pieces from the model: the ledger µ and the flag. The machine never reads either of
them to decide what to do next. I’m not asking you to take that on trust. It’s how the
step is written, and it shows up as a theorem below.

The properties a fact can name come from a tiny fixed language with three words: is
zero; is even; and is at least n, for any whole number n you like. Each one comes in two
forms. There’s the checker, a little program that computes yes or no: compare with
0, look at the last bit, compare with n. And there’s the meaning, the plain arithmetic
statement the checker is supposed to be checking: the number is 0; the number is two
times something; n is less than or equal to the number. Why both? Because a checker
is code, and code can be wrong in ways that look right, and “the checker says yes” is
only worth anything once somebody has proved it says yes exactly when the meaning
is true. That proof is one line per property, and it’s the first block below.

Why can a machine check a claim at all? Because a claim with a precise meaning is
something you evaluate: plug in the values and turn the crank. George Boole worked
out in 1847 that you can do arithmetic on claims this way, treating “and” like multipli-
cation and “or” like a kind of addition. Why multiplication? Try it at the table. Write
1 for true and 0 for false, and multiply: one times one is one, and anything times zero
is zero. That’s “and” to the letter. Then the stranger thing Boole noticed. Say “x and x”
and you’ve said nothing new; it’s just x. In numbers that’s x × x = x, and he made it
a law of his system, and it’s a law ordinary numbers mostly break. Which numbers
equal their own square? Two times two is four, no. A half times a half is a quarter,
no. Zero, yes. One, yes. That’s the whole list. So when Boole wrote his bigger book
in 1854, The Laws of Thought, he asked you to imagine an algebra whose letters take
the values 0 and 1 and nothing else. Every checker on this machine answers in that
algebra.



                                           262
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


And the 1847 book has a backstory worth a detour, which I found in the Stanford
Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s entry on Boole. Boole was largely self-taught and spent
about fifteen years as a schoolmaster, and what pulled him back to logic, early in 1847,
was a loud public quarrel between Augustus De Morgan and the Scottish philosopher
Sir William Hamilton over who had first thought of a small technical idea in the old
logic of syllogisms. Two well-known men fighting over credit, and a schoolmaster
watching from the side picks up the subject and writes the little book this paragraph is
about. Few people remember what the quarrel was over. Every checker in this chapter
runs on what the bystander wrote.

Then push on it, because Boole’s “or” isn’t quite the one a checker uses. His plus only
made sense for things that can’t both hold at once, so “x or y” with both of them true
had no meaning in his system. William Stanley Jevons, an English economist who
also worked on logic, read “or” as “either or both,” which gives “x or x is x,” the same
trick as before. He wrote to Boole in 1863 saying plus ought to work that way, and in
1864 he put it in a book called Pure Logic. Boole wouldn’t have it, since it broke the
tie to ordinary algebra his whole system stood on. The “or” in every programming
language I know is the inclusive one Jevons argued for. Does that change anything
about the checker? No; the crank turns the same way. It changes the picture: the “or”
a checker uses is the one the man who invented the algebra turned down.

Hanging a checked claim on a point in a computation is an old move too. Tony Hoare,
in 1969, built a whole way of reasoning about programs out of it: attach a claim to
a point in a program (“whenever execution reaches here, this is true”), and reason
forward from claim to claim. Robert Floyd had done it two years earlier on flowcharts.
Their claims were checked on paper by the person writing the proof. This machine’s
version is a property of one counter at one edition, checked by a step while it runs.

And is two years earlier the bottom? Not even close, and the next step down is a paper
this book already leaned on. In June 1949, at a Cambridge conference held for the
new EDSAC computer, Alan Turing gave a talk three pages long, “Checking a large
routine,” the same note the counter chapter used for stopping (Section 6). Stopping
was the second half of it. The first half is this move, twenty years before Hoare: the
programmer should make “definite assertions which can be checked individually,”
and the correctness of the whole should follow from them. His example program
computes a factorial using nothing but addition, and his picture for why you’d bother
is one you can do on the back of an envelope. Add up a long column of four-digit
numbers and hand someone only the total, and they have to redo the whole sum at
one sitting, because the carries tie every column to the one before it. Hand them the
total of each column as well, and the job falls apart into small checks they can do one
at a time. That’s a claim hung on a point in the middle of the work, so the person
checking never has to hold all of it at once. The paper got its due mostly later: in
1984 two computer scientists, F. L. Morris of Syracuse University and C. B. Jones of
Manchester University, who had worked on it together at Oxford, republished it, with


                                          263
The Thiele Machine                                                       Devon Thiele


its misprints corrected, as an early program proof by Alan Turing. Theirs is the text
I read, and the column of numbers is Turing’s own example in it. Does any of that
change the machine? No. It changes the date on the idea, and it tells you something I
like: the first person to ask how you’d check a program put the claims in the middle
of it. He didn’t save them for the end.

Now the six instruction kinds.

Instruction            What it does, when the trap is           Cost

The first three are Minsky’s machine, plus a HALT so a program can say it’s done.
The last three are the record’s. Read them as a chain: you can only certify with a
commitment in the channel, you can only commit to a fact in the table, and the only
way into the table is a check that passed. Three links, and each one costs.

One of what? One unit of µ, the same unit as Section 3’s toll. Why one? Why would
ten be worse? Because one is the smallest positive whole number, which is honestly
the whole defence, and Section 4 is the section where I tried to do better than that
for the flag. The finite whole-machine argument doesn’t apply here: these counters
are unbounded and some base moves merge for free. The record-layer argument
in Theorem 4.15 does give the toll if record-layer merges are priced. Choosing that
premise and choosing a unit for each of these three acts remain choices of the model.

                                             264
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


The whole numbers have a history of their own. In 1888 the German mathematician
Richard Dedekind published a little book whose title asks what numbers are and
what they’re for, and in 1889 the Italian mathematician Giuseppe Peano published
a booklet, written in Latin, that set out the axioms for the whole numbers in the
form people still teach: there’s a first number, and every number has a next one, and
a few rules about how “next” behaves. I had the two of them down as working
independently. I went looking, and the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on Dedekind
says Peano acknowledged Dedekind’s priority, which is why the axioms often go by
both names. (Peano’s booklet is also where the sign ∈ that you met in Section 2 comes
from: he wrote it as a Greek epsilon, for the Latin est, “is.”) Start from zero and take
“the next one” three times, and you have three. Once the prices are whole numbers,
one is the smallest positive price. Choosing whole-number prices, and choosing that
unit for CHECK, are still choices of this model.

The zeros matter just as much: computing is free on this ledger. Plus one, minus one
and jumping around cost nothing at all. Only the three acts that make a claim cost,
and each of them costs whether it passes or traps. Failing is not a discount.

The version rule. Here’s why versions exist, with numbers. Start with A = 4, version
0. CHECK is even A passes, and the table gets the fact (even, A, 0). Now INC A: A
becomes 5, and its version becomes 1. Now COMMIT is even A. The machine looks
for (even, A, 1), the claim about the current edition. The table only has (even, A, 0).
No match. Trap. The old fact is still sitting in the table, still true about edition 0, and
completely useless for committing to anything about edition 1. A fact is about one
edition of one counter, and an edition never comes back, because versions only go
up and never wrap. That’s the whole trick against stale evidence: you can’t check a
number, change it, and then commit to the check.

That’s the opening chapter’s time-of-check-to-time-of-use bug, the file checked and
then swapped, and the database answer to it is Kung and Robinson’s: at commit time,
check that nothing you read was written in the meantime, and back out if something
was. The version rule is that check, done by the step, on one counter. It also shows
where the guarantee ends. It works because one step does every write and every
write bumps a version. A second writer that changed a counter without bumping its
version, a second processor or a device writing memory on its own, would walk right
around it, and none of the theorems below are about a machine with one of those.

Processor designers put a cousin of this check in silicon. Jensen, Hagensen and
Broughton, at Lawrence Livermore in 1987, described a pair of instructions now called
load-linked and store-conditional: the load reads a word and the processor starts
watching it, and the store goes through only if nothing has written that word since;
otherwise it fails and the program tries again. It’s tempting to say CHECK is the load
and COMMIT is the conditional store, and it’s wrong in two places. COMMIT doesn’t
write the counter it checked, and the thing doing the watching, the fact, sits in a table


                                           265
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


the step keeps. No single processor holds it. The hardware version does cover the
second writer, because the watching happens on the memory everyone shares, which
is exactly the case the version rule leaves out.

The real kinship is older, and it’s somewhere else. Picture the table and the counters
shared by many processors, with CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY each done as one
indivisible step. Maurice Herlihy (1991), a computer scientist who has spent his career
on how many processors can share memory safely, ranked shared objects by how
many processors each one can bring to agree on a single value with nobody ever
waiting on anybody. Test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and reports what
was there, brings exactly two. A sticky bit, the idea of Serge Plotkin (1989), a Stanford
computer scientist working on distributed algorithms, is a cell the first writer jams for
good, with the first writer’s value, and everyone after can read it; it brings any number.
I guessed that the shared object would sit at the top with the sticky bit, because a write
that kills every fact about a counter, together with a commitment other processors
can see, looks like a way to build one. Ranking the object takes its operations, what
each one returns, which steps are indivisible, how it starts and which processes run
it, and then a proof that every processor decides, they all decide the same value, the
value is one somebody proposed, and nobody waits. Here it is, with every instruction
one indivisible step and the whole state readable, and the object is at the top. The
reason is the order of the fact table. Each processor CHECKs a property that holds of
a counter at zero, Zero to propose 0 and Even to propose 1, then reads the table and
decides the bit of its oldest fact. The table only gains entries at the front, and a CHECK
that finds it full trips the trap, after which nothing moves, so the first CHECK of the
run fixes the oldest fact for good. Every processor that decides decides that bit, the bit
is somebody’s proposal, and each one decides after two of its own steps whatever the
others do. The version rule and the commitment play no part. The trap alone doesn’t
do it: it records that something trapped, and it doesn’t hand everyone the first writer’s
value.

Now take the version rule away, let failures change nothing, keep only the properties
“at least n” so that a checked property only ever turns true, drop the decrement, and
make the fact table, the commitments and the flag sets and latches that only grow. I
guessed that then the object drops to the bottom rung, the level of plain memory, which
is the shared-memory face of what the database researchers Joseph Hellerstein and
Peter Alvaro (2020), at Berkeley and Santa Cruz, call CALM, where monotone means
nobody has to coordinate. That’s proved too, by Herlihy’s own kind of argument. Let
the updates return nothing and let the whole state be readable. If at every state, of
any two updates, one leaves the state alone, or the two commute, or one overwrites
the other, then no protocol brings two processors to agreement with nobody waiting.
The monotone object has that property, with registers beside it, because an instruction
that would succeed still succeeds after anything else has run. The toll changes neither
result. Neither idea is mine: the top is Plotkin’s and the bottom is the monotone fact



                                           266
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


that field already knows.

Process-calculus people have a statement of the same split. Johannes Åman Pohjola
and Joachim Parrow, computer scientists at Uppsala University (Parrow is one of
the inventors of the pi-calculus, a mathematical model of processes that talk over
channels), in 2016 proved that no model whose parallel composition is monotonic,
where a neighbouring process can never stop a step, has a consensus process. One of
their examples of a model that does is test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and
reports what was there. Test-and-set isn’t a sticky bit: in Herlihy’s ranking it brings
two processors to agree, and a sticky bit brings any number.

Their setting is small enough to check here whole. A model is any set of processes
with a step relation and a way to compose two processes that doesn’t care about order
or grouping. Composition is monotonic when whatever a process can reach alone,
it can still reach with anything set beside it. A consensus process is one where any
number of copies, run together, can end up agreeing on either of two outcomes, and
once a run has one outcome it can never show the other. Their theorem goes through
in a few lines: run half the copies to one outcome and the other half to the other, and
if neither half can block the other, the two outcomes meet on the same state. Then
the machine goes into it. A process is a shared machine state with a crowd of threads,
each proposing a bit, and composing two processes pools their threads on one state.
One thread proposing each bit is a consensus process in exactly their sense, for the
outcomes “some thread decided 0” and “some thread decided 1”, so by their theorem
that composition isn’t monotonic. The small machine sits on their non-monotonic
side. What puts it there in the run is the order of the fact table, the same as above; a
store that refuses a stale commit for good, as the version rule does, refuses in the same
spirit. The shared-memory version of their split is the pair of results above: the small
machine’s object reaches agreement for any number of processors, and the monotone
variant reaches it for none.

Security people know the pattern by a third name. A check that blesses a value, and
a write that takes the blessing away, is close kin to dynamic taint tracking, where a
label rides along with the data and a sanitizing step changes it; the labels go back
to the computer-security researcher Dorothy Denning’s 1976 lattice model of how
information is allowed to flow. How much a monitor like that has to remember is a
studied question too: Chamseddine Talhi, Nadia Tawbi and Mourad Debbabi (2008),
three security researchers at universities in Quebec, worked out which rules a monitor
can still enforce when its memory is bounded. The version rule is one small, specific
member of that family, done by the step.

Notice what isn’t a write. DEC on a counter that’s already 0 doesn’t change the counter,
so it doesn’t change the version. It’s a test that happens to move the line number.

The fact table. Facts go in and never come out. Nothing erases them and nothing
overwrites them. When the table is full, a seventeenth CHECK traps. It doesn’t push


                                           267
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


an old fact out to make room. That’s a choice with a bill attached, and I’ll put the bill
in the section on what this machine doesn’t do.

Traps. Any failure puts the trap up and changes nothing else in the core; the ledger
still takes the instruction’s cost. Once it’s up, every instruction leaves the core alone.
A stored program stops at a trap. But I also prove things about any list of instructions,
programs or otherwise, because an adversary doesn’t have to run my programs; they
can feed the machine whatever they want. For those lists, an instruction after a trap is
still charged its cost, and still changes nothing.

Now the exact version.


Definition 16.1 (Properties, checker, meaning). A property is one of: Zero, Even, or
Ge(n) for a whole number n. The checker eval( p, v) computes yes or no: v = 0 by equal-
ity, evenness by the parity function, n ≤ v by comparison. The meaning holds( p, v) is
the arithmetic statement: v = 0; there is an m with v = 2m; n ≤ v.


Lemma 16.1 (The checker says what it means). For every property p and every whole
number v, eval( p, v) = yes if and only if holds( p, v).

Proof. Split on the three properties. Equality with zero returns yes exactly at zero;
comparison with n returns yes exactly when n ≤ v. For evenness, the parity checker
returns yes at 0, no at 1, and the same answer at v + 2 as at v. Induction in steps
of two gives yes exactly at 0, 2, 4, . . ., the numbers 2m. Those are precisely the three
meanings.


Definition 16.2 (Core, state, claim, start). A core k holds two counters A, B and their
versions (whole numbers), a line number, a fact table (a list of facts, a fact being a
triple of a property, a counter and a version), a channel (empty or one fact), and a
trap bit. Write val(k, c) and ver(k, c) for counter c’s value and version. A state s is a
core, written core(s), with a ledger µ(s) and a flag cert(s). The claim p of c in k is the
fact ( p, c, ver(k, c)). The table’s room is 16. The start start( a, b) has counters a and b,
versions 0, line 1, an empty table, an empty channel, the trap down, µ = 0 and the flag
down. A state is clean when its table and channel are empty and its flag is down.


Definition 16.3 (Instructions, costs, the step). The instructions are INC c, DEC c j,
HALT, CHECK p c, COMMIT p c and CERTIFY, with effects on a core with the trap
down as in the table above. Passing any check, commitment or certification requires
the trap to be down. With that condition, CHECK passes when eval( p, val(k, c)) = yes
and the table holds fewer than 16 facts, COMMIT passes when the claim p of c is in
the table, and CERTIFY passes when the channel holds a fact; a failing one sets the
trap and changes nothing else. On a core with the trap up, every instruction changes
nothing. Costs: CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY cost 1, the rest 0. One step on a state


                                            268
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


is
                                                                                     
      exec(s, i ) = cexec(core(s), i ), µ(s) + cost(i ), cert(s) ∨ fires(core(s), i ) ,

where cexec is the core’s step and fires(k, i ) is yes exactly when i is CERTIFY and
passes at k. For any list t of instructions (a trace), run(t, s) applies them in order and
cost(t) adds their costs. A program is a list of instructions numbered from 1; a program
run fetches the instruction at the line number and executes it, and stops when the trap
is up, the line holds HALT, or the line holds nothing.


Read the step line slowly, because the rest of the chapter leans on its shape. The core
moves by its own rule and nothing else. The ledger adds the cost. The flag becomes
“it was up, or this is a CERTIFY that passed.” The core’s move doesn’t mention µ or
the flag anywhere. The base is blind to the record by construction.

A worked run, the shortest one there is. The program: CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is
zero A; CERTIFY. Start at start(0, b), for any b. Line 1: A is 0, the checker says yes, the
table is empty so there’s room, and the fact (zero, A, 0) goes in. µ = 1. Line 2: the claim
about A’s current edition is (zero, A, 0), and it’s right there. Into the channel. µ = 2.
Line 3: the channel holds a fact, the flag goes up. µ = 3. Line 4 has no instruction, so
the program stops. Three paid acts, in order, a flag that’s up, and a channel that names
the last earned commitment, which here is (zero, A, 0).

Now start the same program at start(5, b). Line 1: A is 5, the checker says no, the trap
goes up, µ = 1, and the program stops right there. The flag is down, and you can run
it as long as you like: it stays down. That second run is the point of the first. The same
three instructions certify from some starts and refuse from others, because the check
could have failed, and from most starts it does. A check like that has a no pile, which
is the only kind the opening chapter counts as establishing anything.

Could I have picked an even dumber claim? Sure, and the machine would have let me.
CHECK at least 0 A passes on every number there is, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY
on it raises the flag for 3 from every start (stop the presses: a number is at least zero).
The step doesn’t police that. It checks order, aboutness and that the checker tells the
truth; whether the question was worth asking isn’t something it looks at. A check that
can’t fail establishes nothing, and this machine will charge you three and raise the flag
for it anyway. Spotting that is the reader’s job, with the property in hand, and it’s on
the list at the end of the chapter.

Others walked into the same line from communication. Three theoretical computer
scientists, Oded Goldreich, Brendan Juba and Madhu Sudan (2012), built a theory of
communication with a partner you may not understand, in which getting a message
across counts only as a way to reach a goal, and the central notion is sensing: being
able to tell, from what you see, whether you’re making progress. The sensing they



                                            269
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


ask for is safe: when there’s no progress it says so, and so it never reports a success
that didn’t happen. Their main result, as I read it, is that safe sensing, with a partner
who could help if you spoke its language, is enough for one strategy that reaches the
goal with every such partner. A check that can fail and never lies, standing in front of
a verdict you can’t take back. That’s their theorem, in their setting, and it’s the same
shape.

16.4 It computes everything two counters can
First the base, because if the base can’t compute, nothing else here matters.


Definition 16.4 (Two-counter program, compile, window). A two-counter program M
is a list of instructions, each either MINC c or MDEC c j. A configuration is a triple
(line, a, b). One step of M: if the line holds no instruction, M has stopped; MINC adds
one to c and goes to the next line; MDEC subtracts one from c and goes to line j if c is
above 0, and goes to the next line if c is 0. mrun(n, M, x ) is n steps from x, staying put
once stopped. The compile of M replaces each MINC c by INC c and each MDEC c j by
DEC c j. The window of a core k is the triple (line number, val(k, A), val(k, B)).


Theorem 16.2 (Step for step). For every two-counter program M and every core k with the
trap down: M has stopped at window(k ) if and only if the program compile( M ) has halted
at k; and if M steps from window(k ) to y, then one program step of compile( M ) from k
lands on a core with window y and the trap still down. So for every n, n program steps of
compile( M ) from k land on a core whose window is mrun(n, M, window(k )), with the trap
down.

Proof. Look up the instruction at the line. If there is none, both sides stop. If it’s
MINC c, the compiled INC c adds one to c and goes to the next line, which is exactly
the window’s move (the version also moves, but the window doesn’t show versions).
If it’s MDEC c j, split on whether c is 0, and both sides do the same thing in each
case. Neither instruction can trap. The run statement is induction on n, one step at a
time.


Theorem 16.3 (Halting matches). For every two-counter program M and whole numbers a,
b: M stops after some number of steps from (1, a, b) if and only if the program compile( M)
halts after some number of program steps from start( a, b).

Proof. The start has window (1, a, b) and its trap is down. Apply Theorem 16.2 after
any number n of steps: the two configurations still have the same window, the trap is
still down, and one is stopped exactly when the other is halted. The same n witnesses
termination in either direction.

Now the part that isn’t mine. Two-counter universality is Minsky’s, and the construc-



                                           270
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


tions of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and their coauthors connect it to several other
models. The counter convention matters: DEC at zero goes on to the next instruction;
otherwise it takes one off and jumps. Appendix F builds the route from a tape to
counters, packs finitely many counters into two, and gives the halting diagonal. The
remaining step here is to match that two-counter machine to this machine’s INC/DEC
fragment, instruction for instruction.

Be precise about the reduction used below. A procedure deciding this halting question
would give a program listing the single-tape Turing machines that do not halt. Such
a listing cannot exist: halting runs can already be listed, and running the two listings
in parallel would decide halting. The undecidability statement below records that
reduction, so its meaning is in the connection between the two problems.


Theorem 16.4 (Halting is undecidable for this machine). The two-counter machine with
the instruction convention just stated agrees with the INC/DEC fragment: its step, its stop,
and its termination match those of the compiled program, so its halting problem at ( P, a, b)
has a positive answer if and only if the compiled program halts from start( a, b). Consequently,
the question “does program P halt from start( a, b)?” is undecidable in the following reduction
sense: a decider for it would make the complement of single-tape binary Turing machine halting
enumerable.
