Proof. The agreement is a case split on the counter-machine instruction at the cur-
rent line, and then induction along the run, ending in Theorem 16.3. Composing
a proposed decider for the compiled program with the compile map would decide
two-counter halting. The tape-to-counter reduction in Appendix F would then decide
single-tape binary halting and hence enumerate its complement, as claimed.

What that buys, and what it doesn’t. It buys: the base of this machine is a universal
machine in Minsky’s sense, and no algorithm can predict in general what it’ll do.
What it doesn’t buy is a fast machine, or one where your input arrives conveniently.
The counters start holding a and b, given directly; there’s no encoding layer in this
construction. Minsky’s prime-power packing is how you’d get from “any Turing
machine” to “two counters,” and I use that prior construction as it stands.

Is “given directly” just a convenience, or does it bite? It bites, and somebody found
exactly where. In 1972 Rich Schroeppel, then at the MIT AI Lab, wrote a ten-page
memo titled “A Two Counter Machine Cannot Calculate 2 N .” He spells out the con-
vention first: a counter machine computing a function starts with n in one counter and
zero in the others. Then he gives a proof that a two-counter machine started that way
can’t compute 2n . The same chain of stages that proves the theorem about multiplying
near the end of the chapter (Theorem 16.60) rules 2n out too, though I state only the
multiplying form: along an arithmetic progression of inputs the outputs grow by a
fixed amount, and powers of two don’t. So the packing Minsky needs is precisely the



                                              271
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


thing two plain counters can’t do for themselves. Hand the small machine its inputs
straight and there are functions of them it can’t compute; hand it the inputs already
packed and it computes anything a Turing machine can. That’s no contradiction with
the undecidability above, which ranges over every program and every starting pair,
packed ones included. The base hides nothing. It just needs its input pre-chewed, and
the chewing is somebody else’s.

16.5 It’s a certification system, and the flag is a latch
Now the record. Three facts first, all of them read straight off the step line.


Theorem 16.5 (Ledger, toll, permanence). For every state s and instruction i,
µ(exec(s, i )) = µ(s) + cost(i ), and for every trace t, µ(run(t, s)) = µ(s) + cost(t). If
cert(s) is down and cert(exec(s, i )) is up, then i is CERTIFY, it passes at core(s), and
cost(i ) ≥ 1. If cert(s) is up, so is cert(exec(s, i )).

Proof. Read the ledger component of Definition 16.3: it adds exactly cost(i ). Repeated
substitution along a trace gives the sum of its costs, or, equivalently, induction on the
length of the trace does. The flag’s new value is its old value or fires(core(s), i ). A
false-to-true change therefore requires that event, whose definition requires a passing
CERTIFY. CERTIFY costs 1. An already true flag stays true under the same disjunction.



That third clause in the middle is Section 3’s toll, for this machine. Which means this
machine is one of the things Section 3 was about, and Section 3’s theorem applies to it
without my lifting a finger.


Theorem 16.6 (An instance of the certification system). The states, the instructions, the
step exec, the cost and the flag, with the toll of Theorem 16.5, form a certification system
(Definition 3.1). So the universal floor (Observation 3.1) holds here: if cert(s0 ) is down and
cert(run(t, s0 )) is up, then cost(t) ≥ 1.

Proof. Take the state and instruction sets of Definitions 16.2 and 16.3, their step and
cost, and the flag as the reading. These provide the five components of Definition 3.1.
Theorem 16.5 supplies its one required rule. Applying Observation 3.1 gives the
claimed bound.

Then Section 10. Section 10 said: take any base, and any record that answers only
to the base and never comes back down, and the record is a latch. This machine has
a base: a program together with a core, stepping by the program step. And it has a
record, the flag, with the ledger riding along. So the question is whether it’s a base-
driven extension in Section 10’s five-rule sense (Definition 10.2), and if it is, Section 10
does the rest.



                                             272
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Theorem 16.7 (The flag is a latch of the base). Let the base have states (program, core),
stepping by the program step, starting at start( a, b)’s core for any a, b, and halting when the
program has halted. Map each (program, state) to (program, core). Then the machine, run
as a closed machine on (program, state), is a base-driven record over that base, and so its flag
factors as the latch (Observation 10.1) of the event “the next instruction is a CERTIFY that
passes.”

Proof. The rules of Definition 10.2 one at a time. Driven by the computation: the next
flag is the old flag or “the next instruction is a passing CERTIFY,” which is a function
of the base state and the old flag (that’s the step line). Ledger: µ only adds. Toll:
Theorem 16.5. Permanence: Theorem 16.5. A reachable write: the three-line program
of the worked run raises the flag from a start. Section 10’s theorem then gives the
factorization.

So far, nothing new. The toll, the floor and the latch are things Parts II and III already
promised about any machine of this kind. The next subsection is the part neither of
them could give.

16.6 Commitments are earned
Here’s the shape before the words. Pick any run from a clean start, any list of instruc-
tions at all, chosen by somebody who’d love to cheat. Look at the moment a COMMIT
would pass. Then, somewhere earlier in that run, there’s a CHECK of exactly the
same claim that passed and paid, at the same edition of the counter, and between
that CHECK and now, nothing touched the counter. Not “probably.” Not “on the
programs I wrote.” On every list of instructions anybody can write.

To say “nothing touched it” exactly, one word.


Definition 16.5 (Untouched). A list of instructions mid, run from a state s, leaves
counter c untouched when, for every way of splitting mid as t1 , then i, then t2 , executing
i at the core reached by running t1 from s leaves both ver(·, c) and val(·, c) as they
were.


Theorem 16.8 (A commitment was checked first). Let s0 be clean and pre any trace after
which COMMIT p c would pass. Then pre splits as pre1 , then CHECK p c, then mid, where:
the CHECK passes at the core reached by pre1 ; CHECK p c and COMMIT p c each cost at
least 1; c’s version after pre1 equals its version after pre; and mid, run from just after the
CHECK, leaves c untouched.

Proof. COMMIT passes, so the claim ( p, c, ver(c)) for the current version is in the table.
By the no-forging invariant (Theorem 16.12 below), that fact was written by a passing
CHECK p c at some point pre1 , with the version c had then; since it’s the current
version too, the two versions are equal. Versions never go down, and any instruction


                                              273
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


that changes a counter’s value also raises its version, so an instruction in mid that
touched c would have left c’s version higher at the end than at the CHECK. It isn’t. So
nothing in mid touched c.


Theorem 16.9 (A raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified). Let s0 be
clean and t any trace with cert(run(t, s0 )) up. Then for some p and c, t is

            pre1 , CHECK p c, mid1 , COMMIT p c, mid2 , CERTIFY, post,

where the CHECK passes at its state, the COMMIT passes at its state, the CERTIFY passes
at its state, c has the same version at the CHECK as at the COMMIT, and mid1 leaves c
untouched. And when the CERTIFY runs, the channel holds exactly the claim that COMMIT
made: the fact (p, c, c’s version at the CHECK). CERTIFY takes no operand; this is what ties
it to the claim.

Proof. The flag starts down, so some first instruction raised it, and by Theorem 16.5
it’s a passing CERTIFY. A CERTIFY passes only with a fact in the channel, the channel
starts empty, and only a passing COMMIT puts a fact there, so some earlier COMMIT
p c passed. Take the last one before the CERTIFY: the fact in the channel is the one it
wrote. Theorem 16.8 at that COMMIT gives the CHECK, the equal version, and the
untouched stretch, and the equal version makes the committed fact (p, c, c’s version
at the CHECK).

And the failure side, so you can see the refusals are clean, with nothing left half-done:


Theorem 16.10 (Unearned steps trap and change no claim). If COMMIT p c would not
pass at a core k, executing it puts the trap up and leaves the channel and the table as they were.
If CERTIFY would not pass at a state s, executing it puts the trap up and leaves the flag as it
was.

Proof. If the trap is already up, the core is unchanged and its trap remains up. Oth-
erwise, the failed COMMIT takes the failure branch of the instruction table: set the
trap, leave every other core field alone. A failed CERTIFY takes the same branch, and
its fires value is false. The flag update is then its old value or false, which leaves it
unchanged. The instruction’s charge still applies to the ledger.

If that rings a bell, it should. It’s Milner’s move from the opening chapter: in LCF
a theorem is a value that only the rules of the logic can build, so nobody can just
print one (Milner and two colleagues on his Edinburgh project, Michael Gordon and
Christopher Wadsworth, wrote the system up in 1979, and Gordon, who went on to
build the HOL prover at Cambridge, told its history in 2000). Here the thing nobody
can print is one bit, and what guards it is one step rule. Milner’s guard was a type
checker. Same architecture, much lower down.


                                               274
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


A provenance theorem is also an itemised receipt, and the itemised receipt has a
history that’s exactly this gap. James Ritty ran a saloon in Dayton, Ohio, and believed
some of his staff were pocketing money. On a steamboat trip to Europe in 1878 he
watched a mechanism that counted the turns of the ship’s propeller, and wondered
whether something like it could count the money instead. In 1879 he and his brother
John patented a “Cash Register and Indicator,” and they sold a version under the
wonderful name Ritty’s Incorruptible Cashier. The first model was this book’s counter
(Section 6) with brass on it: press a key, the amount goes onto a dial showing the day’s
running total. No drawer, no paper. At closing time you hold the dial up against the
cash. And that’s all a total can do. It tells you that the money is short. It can’t tell
you which sale went missing or who rang it up. The paper came later. The patents
passed to other owners, first a Cincinnati salesman named Jacob Eckert, and in 1884
to John H. Patterson, who renamed the business the National Cash Register Company,
and the story told about that company is that it added a paper roll: one copy kept
for the shop’s own books, one handed to the customer. That last part I only have
from histories of the company and of the machine, so hold it the way you’d hold
any company’s story about itself. The order is right either way: first a total that can
tell you something’s wrong, then a list that tells you where. The ledger µ is the dial.
Theorem 16.9 is the list: which CHECK, of which claim, about which edition, before
which COMMIT. The theorem supplies that list about the run. The machine doesn’t
keep it as data anyone can read back from the end state, and nothing in the theorem
gives a procedure for rebuilding it from there. A fact in the table holds a property, a
counter and a version number. That’s neither the counter’s value back then nor a log
of what happened in between.

Read Theorem 16.9 once more for what it doesn’t say. Between the CHECK and the
COMMIT, the counter is untouched. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, it isn’t
promised anything. You can check A is even, commit to it, add one to A, and then
certify. The flag goes up, and what it stands on is a commitment about the edition that
was current when you committed. The certificate is historical: it says “this was checked
and committed about this edition,” and it says nothing about whether that’s still true.
I think that’s the right meaning for a certificate (a birth certificate doesn’t expire when
the baby grows), but it’s a meaning, and you should know which one you’re getting.
So a certificate doesn’t say the claim holds at the CERTIFY, and it doesn’t say the
claim holds at the end of the run. A CERTIFY that rechecked the version would give
a different guarantee. That’s a possible extension, and the historical theorem doesn’t
need it.

16.7 What a passing check means
Provenance says a CHECK happened. It doesn’t yet say the CHECK was right, and
that’s a separate question with a separate proof. A machine could have a perfectly
ordered chain of check, commit, certify, all standing on a checker that says yes to
everything. So: what does a fact in the table actually tell you about the counter?


                                           275
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


Theorem 16.11 (Checker soundness). Let s0 be clean and t any trace, and let k be the core
of run(t, s0 ). For every fact ( p, c, v) in k’s table with v = ver(k, c), the property holds of the
counter’s current value: holds( p, val(k, c)). In particular, if COMMIT p c would pass at k,
then holds( p, val(k, c)).

Proof. Carry one sentence through every instruction: every fact in the table has a
version no higher than its counter’s, and if its version equals its counter’s, its property
holds of its counter’s value. A clean start has an empty table, so the sentence holds
there. A passing CHECK adds a fact at the current version, and the checker said yes, so
by Lemma 16.1 the property holds. A write raises one counter’s version, so every old
fact about that counter falls strictly behind and the second half no longer applies to it.
Nothing else changes a value or a version. The sentence holds after every instruction,
so it holds at the end. The part about COMMIT is the case where the claim is in the
table at the current version.

So, on a run from a clean start, a live fact means exactly this: one of three arithmetic
properties holds of one counter’s current value. Not “the program is correct.” Not
“the number is interesting.” The property, of the value, now. That’s all “checked”
means on this machine, and it’s enough to be true. Three events stay separate here.
The property holding of the value is one. A CHECK passing is another: a CHECK of a
property that holds still doesn’t pass when the table is full or the trap is already up. A
certification is a third, and it needs a COMMIT and a CERTIFY after the CHECK. So a
CHECK that didn’t pass says nothing about whether its property is false.

So who checked the checker? Nothing on the record did. From a clean start, the record
carries the run’s half of the story: a CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same claim about
the same edition, then a CERTIFY. The other half, that the checker says yes exactly
when the property holds, isn’t in any run. It’s Lemma 16.1, a proof about the little
program the step calls, priced by nothing on the ledger. So a claim established here
stands on two legs: a fact about this run, carried by the record, and a fact about the
checker, carried by a proof that whoever reads the record has to accept. That’s the
Münchhausen trilemma from the opening chapter taking its third horn on purpose:
the chain of reasons stops at a proof, named and on the page, where you can decide
whether you’d have stopped there too. And the entitlement it gives is the reader’s.
The machine doesn’t know anything. It keeps the order.

The question in that paragraph is older than any checker, and its most famous wording
isn’t about what you’d guess. “Who will guard the guardians?” gets quoted about
governments and police and, lately, proof assistants. Where’s it from? Plato’s Republic
has the worry, sort of: in Book III (at 403e), Glaucon, Plato’s older brother and one of
the people Socrates is talking with, says it would be absurd for a guardian to need a
guardian, which is close in words and opposite in mood, a man calling the question
silly. The Latin, quis custodiet ipsos custodes, is from the Roman satirist Juvenal’s sixth
satire, and it’s a joke about a husband. His friends tell him to bolt his wife in and set

                                                276
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


guards on her; the line asks who’ll watch the guards, since she’ll start with them. And
it gets better. In 1899 an Oxford undergraduate, E. O. Winstedt, found extra lines of
that satire in a medieval manuscript in the Bodleian Library, lines the other copies
lack, partly overlapping the familiar ones, and the famous question sits in that tangle.
Scholars have argued ever since about whether those lines are Juvenal’s at all. So the
most quoted sentence about trusting the checker comes with a doubtful source of its
own. Does that change anything here? No. The answer used here is simple: you never
get rid of the last guard, you make the last guard small enough to watch yourself.
Lemma 16.1 is one line per property. Euclid had the instinct: five postulates you can
hold in your head, and everything else meant to follow from them.

That split, a fixed checker proved sound from outside and a process that only gets to
act when the checker says yes, has a name in the writing on self-improving programs.
The AI researcher Jürgen Schmidhuber, at the IDSIA lab in Lugano, described a Gödel
machine (2003) that rewrites its own code only after its built-in proof searcher has
proved the rewrite useful, and Benja Fallenstein and Nate Soares (2015), researchers
at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, survey agents that reason
about their successors through formal proofs a fixed checker accepts. Same architec-
ture, aimed at a different question: they want to know when a machine may trust a
smarter version of itself, and this machine only wants to know whether a flag was
earned. Keeping the checker’s proof outside the machine is my design choice. The
nearest theorem, in Section 13, is narrower: no procedure the substrate can represent
decides, for every program, a property that depends only on behaviour and holds of
one program and fails of another. It doesn’t say a machine can’t check a proof about a
checker, or verify a restricted part of itself.

Soundness rules out a lying checker. It doesn’t rule out a pointless question: at least 0
has a perfectly sound checker and an empty no pile, as the worked run showed.

Program checking has a theory of its own, and its founding paper asks for a checker
that could have said no. The computer scientists Manuel Blum and Sampath Kannan
(1989; journal version 1995) defined a checker for a computational problem: given a
program and an input, it may run the program as it likes, and it must say “correct”
with high probability when the program is right everywhere and “buggy” with high
probability when its answer on that input is wrong. A checker that always says
“correct” isn’t one. Here the checker is fixed, deterministic and proved sound once,
and the part of their demand that survives is the fourth clause of Thiele-complete
(Definition 16.7 below): some claim whose check can fail.

16.8 Nothing gets forged
The proof of Theorem 16.8 leaned on an invariant I promised to show you. Here it
is. The fear it answers: could some clever sequence of instructions get a fact into the
table without a CHECK writing it? A DEC with a funny jump target, a COMMIT after
a trap, something I didn’t think of? The answer is checked one instruction at a time,


                                          277
The Thiele Machine                                                                      Devon Thiele


which is the only way I trust myself to answer it.


Definition 16.6 (Earned fact; no forgery). After a trace t from s0 , a fact f = ( p, c, v) is
earned when t is pre, then CHECK p c, then mid, where the CHECK passes at the core
reached by pre, f is exactly the claim p of c at that core, and, if f is live at the end (v
equals c’s version after t), mid leaves c untouched. The trace has no forgery when every
fact in the table after it is earned.


Theorem 16.12 (No forging). For every core k, instruction i and fact f in the table after
executing i at k: either f was already in k’s table, or i is CHECK of f ’s property and counter,
it passes at k, and f is the claim it writes. Consequently, if a trace has no forgery, so does that
trace followed by any one instruction; and from every clean start, every trace has no forgery.

Proof. The first part is a case for each of the six instruction kinds: only a passing
CHECK adds anything, and it adds exactly its claim. For the second, a new fact is
earned by the CHECK that just wrote it; an old fact stays earned, and if it’s still live
after the new instruction, its counter’s version didn’t move, so the new instruction
didn’t touch the counter and the untouched stretch grows by one. A clean start has an
empty table, which has no forgery, and the step carries it along any trace.

The closest earlier result is in capability hardware, and it’s much bigger. The computer
scientists Jack Dennis and Earl Van Horn, at MIT, introduced capabilities in 1966: tokens
a process has to hold to touch an object, which it can pass on and can’t forge. CHERI,
a capability extension of real instruction sets built at the University of Cambridge
and SRI International, rests on that idea, and in 2020 Kyndylan Nienhuis and twelve
coauthors proved, for the whole CHERI-MIPS instruction set, that arbitrary code
given some capabilities can’t increase them as it runs (up to any change of protection
domain). That’s nothing gets forged across a full instruction set. Theorem 16.12 is the
same shape, one instruction at a time, for six instruction kinds and a table of checked
facts.

16.9 A full table traps
Sixteen facts of room, and no eviction. Two halves to prove: nothing ever leaves, and
nothing ever overflows.


Theorem 16.13 (Bounded table, no eviction). Every instruction keeps every fact already
in the table. If the table holds 16 or more facts, CHECK p c puts the trap up and leaves the
table as it was. If the table holds at most 16 facts, it still holds at most 16 after any instruction.

Proof. With a raised trap no instruction changes the table. With the trap down, only
CHECK can change it, and a successful CHECK adds one fact without removing an
entry. Success requires a previous length strictly below 16, so the new length is at



                                                 278
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


most 16. At length 16 or greater that branch is unavailable: CHECK raises the trap
and preserves the table. Every other instruction preserves it as well.

Why trap? Why not make room? Because “making room” means deciding which
fact dies, and a fact that can die is a fact whose absence you have to explain later. A
table that only grows keeps the checked facts available to read back, and the prove-
nance proofs above lean on exactly that. The bill for it is real, though, and it’s in the
subsection near the end of this chapter on what the machine doesn’t do.

16.10 The window can’t see the record
Section 7 was about windows: a view of a state that shows some of it, and the theorem
that a window which shows the same before-and-after pair for a raise and a non-
raise cannot price both exactly (Observation 7.2). Here’s the smallest pair I could
build where the window is Minsky’s view of the machine (line number and the two
counters) and the record is everything else.

Run two traces from start(0, 0). The earned run is CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is zero
A; CERTIFY. The idle run is DEC A 0, three times. In the idle run, A is 0 every time,
so each DEC just goes to the next line and writes nothing. Both runs end on line 4,
with A = 0 and B = 0, both versions 0. Through the window, identical. One of them
has paid 3, holds a fact, could commit again, and has its flag up. The other has paid
nothing, holds nothing, can’t commit, and its flag is down. Two photographs, same
picture, different people.


Theorem 16.14 (Same window, different record). The earned run and the idle run from
start(0, 0) end at cores with the same window and the same versions of A and B, and with
different ledgers, different flags, different tables, and different answers to “would COMMIT is
zero A pass.”

Proof. In the earned run, CHECK adds (Zero, A, 0), COMMIT puts that fact in the
channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. The ledger is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. No counter is
written. In the idle run each DEC sees zero, so it advances the line without writing a
counter or raising a version. Its three costs are zero and it adds no fact or commitment.
Thus both final windows are (4, 0, 0) with versions (0, 0). The earned table contains the
current zero claim and the idle table is empty, giving the stated difference in whether
another COMMIT would pass, as well as in the ledger and flag.


Theorem 16.15 (No window oracle). There is no function g from windows to whole num-
bers with g(window) = µ at the end of every trace from start(0, 0). Likewise there is no
function from windows to yes or no that gives the flag at the end of every such trace, and none
that gives whether COMMIT is zero A would pass.

Proof. Such a g would have to give both 3 and 0 on the one window the two runs of


                                             279
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


Theorem 16.14 share. The same for the flag and the commit right.

This is Section 7’s shape, made of pebbles: the record lives off the window. Anybody
who only watches the counters and the line number, which is everything Minsky’s
machine is, can’t tell you what was paid, what was committed, or whether the flag is
up. Not because they looked carelessly. Because it isn’t there to see.

Two things the same in everything you look at and still two things: philosophy has
an old fight about exactly that, and it’s worth a detour, because it tells you which
side of the fight these theorems stand on. Leibniz said that for real things it can’t
happen. There are no two individuals indiscernible from each other, he wrote in 1716
to Samuel Clarke, the English philosopher and theologian who was taking Newton’s
side against him in an exchange of letters, and he told a story to go with it. A clever
gentleman of his acquaintance, talking with him in front of the Electress Sophia of
Hanover, Leibniz’s friend and patron, in the garden at Herrenhausen she had helped
lay out, thought he could find two leaves perfectly alike. She dared him to. He “ran
all over the Garden a long time” looking, and it was “to no purpose.” You can run his
search tonight with a handful of anything, leaves or coins or grains of rice: look hard
enough and every pair differs somewhere. Then in 1952 Max Black, a Russian-born
philosopher teaching at Cornell, pushed back with a universe you can’t build at the
table. Nothing in it but two iron spheres, the same size, the same colour, the same
everything, some distance apart. Name a difference between them. There isn’t one,
and there are still two of them. People have argued about Black’s spheres ever since,
and I’m not going to settle it.

Here’s why I don’t have to. Leibniz’s claim is about every property a thing has. The
theorems above are about three: the line and the two counters. The two runs aren’t
indiscernible in his sense at all: one has a fact in its table and its flag up, and the other
doesn’t. They’re indiscernible to a window, which is a much cheaper thing, and it’s
the thing that matters for a machine, because an observer of a machine only ever gets
a window. Leibniz’s gentleman would always find his difference if he could look at
everything. It doesn’t help him if all he’s allowed to look at is three things about each
leaf.

There’s a horse in this, too, if you squint. In Germany in the early 1900s a mathematics
teacher named Wilhelm von Osten showed off a horse called Clever Hans, who an-
swered arithmetic questions by tapping a hoof, and got them right, in front of crowds.
Same answers out as a horse that could count: that’s the idle run’s matching win-
dow. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst stopped looking at the answers and started
changing the conditions, and published what he found in 1907. Put blinders on Hans,
or have him asked by someone who didn’t know the answer, and the arithmetic fell
apart. Hans was reading the questioner: tiny, unintended movements of the head and
body as the hoof reached the right number. That’s the probe. Pfungst didn’t argue
with the answers. He asked a question the answers couldn’t fake, one that needed


                                            280
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


the real thing to be there, the way a COMMIT needs a checked fact to be in the table:
run COMMIT is zero A after each of the two runs, and one passes and the other traps
(Theorem 16.14). And the part of the story I like best: nobody was lying. Von Osten
was never persuaded by Pfungst and kept showing his horse. A matching window
doesn’t need a cheat behind it, which is why you want a probe. An accusation is the
wrong tool for it.

16.11 The exact price is three
Section 3 said a raised flag costs at least one. On this machine that’s true and too
modest. A raised flag needs a CERTIFY, a CERTIFY needs a COMMIT, a COMMIT
needs a CHECK, and each of those is its own instruction costing one. So at least three.
One of what: three units of µ, one per paid act, each one the “one” I picked back in
the table. And three is the number of links in the chain. It isn’t a guess that happens
to hold.


Observation 16.16 (The minimum price of a certificate). If s0 is clean and
cert(run(t, s0 )) is up, then cost(t) ≥ 3 and µ(run(t, s0 )) ≥ µ(s0 ) + 3. For programs:
if the flag is up after n program steps from start( a, b), then µ ≥ 3 there.

Proof. Theorem 16.9 finds a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three different
places in t, each costing 1, and every other instruction costs at least 0. The ledger
statement is Theorem 16.5. A program run is the run of the instructions it actually
executes, so the program form follows.

The three is three independent units, one for each part of a clean start. A flag that is
down buys the first: a run that raises it costs at least one. An empty channel buys the
second: with the flag down and the channel empty, a run that raises the flag costs at
least two. An empty table buys the third, and that is the theorem above. Leave out
any one part and its floor fails, and a cheaper certificate is there: with the flag already
up it costs 0, with a commitment already in the channel 1, and with a live fact already
in the table 2. The exact condition is this: every run from a state that ends with the flag
up costs at least three exactly when the flag is down and one of two things holds: the
trap is up, or the channel is empty and every fact in the table is about an older version
of its counter. And three is paid exactly from every clean start whose trap is down.


Theorem 16.17 (Three is tight). For all whole numbers a and b, run the program CHECK
is zero A; COMMIT is zero A; CERTIFY for 4 program steps from start( a, b). If a = 0, it
ends with the flag up and µ = 3 exactly. If a ̸= 0, it ends with the flag down and the trap up,
and for every n, n program steps from start( a, b) leave the flag down.

Proof. If a = 0, the checker for Zero says yes at 0, so the first instruction adds
(Zero, A, 0) to the empty table and charges 1. No counter changes, so the second
instruction finds that same fact, puts it in the channel and charges 1. The third finds

                                             281
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


the channel occupied, raises the flag and charges 1. The line is now 4, beyond the
three-instruction program, and the fourth program step adds no charge. The final
ledger is exactly 3. If a ̸= 0, the checker says no, so the first instruction sets the trap
and leaves the flag down. A program run takes no step once the trap is up, so every
later program step leaves the state, flag included, exactly where it is.

The version whose check can’t fail, CHECK at least 0 A; COMMIT at least 0 A; CERTIFY,
certifies from every start for exactly 3. So the floor of three is reachable from every
loaded start, and that’s the machine declining to police trivial checks. On that program
the check distinguishes no inputs.

That’s the worked run from the start of the chapter, now as a theorem. The floor is 3,
and a run whose check could have failed pays exactly 3, so 3 is the price. The bound
has no slack in it.

Don’t mistake that 3 for a measure of how hard a claim is to certify. It’s the same 3
for every claim, easy or hard, because only the three acts that make a claim are priced
and the counters work out whatever the check needs for free. A cost of certifying that
grows with the claim would have to price the checking itself, and that’s a different
question with its own literature. Four theoretical computer scientists, Guy Blanc,
Caleb Koch, Jane Lange and Li-Yang Tan (2022), studied one version of it under the
name the query complexity of certification: how many questions an algorithm has to
ask a black-box function to hand back a small certificate for its answer. Their count
moves with the function. Mine doesn’t move at all.

And that’s every piece of the model, standing on six instruction kinds: a base that
computes everything two counters can, a ledger that’s exact, a toll the universal floor
applies to, a flag that’s a latch of the base, a window that can’t see the record, and,
from a clean start, a commitment that can’t happen unless a check of the same claim,
on the same edition, came first and was right.

16.12 What it takes to be Thiele-complete
The front matter promised a definition of Thiele-complete with teeth, so here it is. First,
why it needs teeth. The easy definition goes: a Thiele machine is Thiele-complete when
its base can compute anything a Turing machine can (under Minsky’s 2n encoding,
done outside the machine). It looks fine, and it’s nearly empty. Take Minsky’s two-
counter machine, charge one mark for every move, and pick any yes-or-no question
about its configuration as the record. Every move costs one, so every move that raises
the record costs one, so it obeys the toll. That’s a Thiele machine with a universal base:
a clock bolted to a computer. A machine whose record never goes up passes too, since
a toll on a raise that never happens is never broken. Neither one earns anything, and
a name both of them get for free isn’t saying much.

So the definition below asks for what the small machine actually does, written so that
any machine at all can be held up against it. You name a language of claims first, then

                                           282
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


hand over a reading of the machine in that language, a list of things, and then the
reading has to pass four clauses.


Definition 16.7 (Thiele-complete). A machine has states, moves, a step, a cost for each
move and a yes/no reading of each state, the record. A claim language for it is fixed first:
a type of claims with an exact equality test; a meaning for each claim, a statement about
a state; for each claim, a relation “the thing this claim is about is unchanged” between
two states; and a proof that a meaning that holds keeps holding while the thing it’s
about is unchanged. An interface over that language hands over the rest: a universal
base, meaning a two-counter configuration shown by each state (its window), a class of
live states, a move for each two-counter instruction, and a loaded state for each start
(1, a, b); a checker that says yes or no to a claim at a state, with a proof that a yes means
the claim’s meaning, as the language gives it, holds of that state; a set of clean states; a
ledger, a whole number for each state; and a kind for each move: a base move, CHECK
of a claim, COMMIT of a claim, or CERTIFY. The machine is Thiele-complete over the
language when some interface over it meets four clauses, and Thiele-complete when
some interface, with claims, meanings and “unchanged” of its own, meets them. (a)
Universal base. Each two-counter instruction’s move is a base move; from every live
state it acts on the window exactly as the instruction acts on a configuration, and the
state stays live; each loaded state shows (1, a, b), is live and is clean; no base move
changes the record; and a record that’s up stays up under every move. (b) Earned
record. Clean states have the record down. Every run from a clean state that ends
with the record up contains a CHECK of some claim c that passes, then a COMMIT
of c with the thing c is about unchanged at every state in between, then a CERTIFY,
with the record down just before that CERTIFY and up just after it. A passing check
means its claim’s meaning holds of the state it checked, and a meaning that holds
keeps holding while the thing it’s about is unchanged. (c) Exact toll. Base moves cost
0, each CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY costs exactly 1, and each move adds its cost
to the ledger. (d) Non-vacuity. Some claim c has a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY
such that those three moves alone, from a loaded state, raise the record exactly when
c’s meaning holds there; and c holds at some loaded state and fails at another. A Thiele
machine whose base is universal, with no more asked, is weakly Thiele-complete.


An interface over a language becomes an interface of the plain kind by taking the
language’s claims, meanings and “unchanged” as its own, and the four clauses are
asked of that.

Why the language comes first. If the interface could name the meanings, it could take
“the checker says yes” as the meaning of every claim, and checker soundness would
hold for nothing. In the language-first form the meanings are written down before any
checker is handed over, so “a checker proved to mean what it says” has the content it
has on the small machine: what the claim says is the language’s, and the proof is that
a yes from the checker makes it true. The plain form stays because the theorems that

                                            283
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


follow hold for any interface at all, so they hold over every language too.

Read the four clauses as four plain sentences. (a) It computes anything a Turing ma-
chine can, under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine, and the computing
can’t reach the record: the base moves are the two-counter machine, they leave the
record exactly where it was, and a record that goes up stays up. (b) From a clean start,
the record goes up only on top of the small machine’s chain: a check that passed, a
commitment to the same claim with nothing changed underneath, then a certificate.
(c) Computing is free and each of the three acts costs one, so the ledger counts the acts.
The steps in between go free. (d) Somewhere there’s a claim whose check could have
said no. A machine whose every claim is “at least 0” doesn’t qualify, and neither does
one with nothing to certify.

And look where the checker’s honesty sits. In (b), “a passing check means its claim
holds” is a condition on the interface, proved once, outside every run, exactly where it
sat for the small machine (Lemma 16.1), and over a claim language it’s proved against
meanings the interface didn’t write. The definition doesn’t ask the machine to vouch
for its own checker. The nearest reasons not to ask are Gödel’s second theorem, about
a system proving its own consistency, and the diagonal of Section 13, about deciding
a property of every program. Neither forbids a machine checking a proof about a
checker, so keeping that proof outside is a choice. Nor does it ask the checker to be
something a machine could run. Clause (b) wants a yes or no for every claim at every
state, sound for the claim’s meaning, and nothing in it says that answer has to be
computable. Every instance in this book has a checker that’s an actual program, so
anything those machines certify could be listed by a program that runs them. For
example, take a function that answers whether an arbitrary program runs forever. It
need not be computable. Hand the definition a checker like that and it’s still met,
and the machine certifies claims no program could ever confirm. Nothing in this
book builds one. So “a Thiele-complete machine certifies exactly the claims a program
could list” is true only with “and its checker is computable” added, and the definition
doesn’t require that.

The same scope goes on the front matter’s “it isn’t more computing power.” The
record (the flag and the ledger) is never read by the step that computes the next core,
so erasing it changes no run, and it makes nothing faster. The checker is part of the
machine under the record. With an oracle checker that machine decides what the
oracle decides, since whether a CHECK traps is there for anyone to see; with a checker
that’s a program, it does what programs do. And a checker that’s a program still
makes CHECK a test at unit cost.


Theorem 16.18 (CHECK is a unit-cost test). From any start ( a, b), the single move CHECK
Ge(m) A costs 1, and the trap latch is down after it exactly when a ≥ m.

Proof. At a start the latch is down and the table is empty, so the check passes exactly


                                           284
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


when eval(Ge(m), a) says yes, that is when m ≤ a; a failing check sets the latch. The
price table charges a CHECK 1.

The two counters alone look at A only through the zero test of DEC, and from a =
m − 1 and a = m that test can’t come out differently in fewer than m steps, so they need
about m steps for what CHECK does in one. Theorem 16.50 gives the precise lower
bound and the matching ladder. So the record makes nothing faster, and CHECK, a
primitive test, can.

One word needs pinning before the theorems, using the three names set at the front
of the book. In clause (c), the exact toll is instruction-exact pricing: each of the three
acts, CHECK and COMMIT included, costs exactly one, so the ledger counts the acts
that make a claim. Back in Section 6, one result is about rise-only pricing in its tightest
bill, the exact schedule: one mark on the step that raises the flag and nothing on any
other step. Measured against the flag alone, the small machine isn’t rise-only, since
CHECK and COMMIT raise no flag and cost one each; measured the way (c) asks,
it is instruction-exact. Neither is wrong. They answer different questions: does the
ledger count the acts, or does it charge the flag and only the flag? Simulation-exact
accounting, the third name, comes up with the universal program U below.


Theorem 16.19 (What every Thiele-complete machine has). Let a machine be Thiele-
complete through an interface. (1) It obeys the toll and has a universal base, so it’s weakly
Thiele-complete; its base runs every two-counter program step for step from every live state,
and halting from a loaded state matches halting from the configuration it shows. (2) Along
any run, the ledger rises by exactly the number of CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY moves
in it. (3) A run from a clean state that ends with the record up contains at least three of those
moves and raises the ledger by at least 3. (4) Some CHECK fails at some loaded state, on a
claim that is false there, and some run from some loaded state raises the record. (5) On a run
from a clean state, the move that raises the record is a CERTIFY. (6) Every move costs 0 or 1,
and some move costs 0.

Proof. (1) A raise of the record isn’t made by a base move, by (a), so it’s a record move,
which costs one by (c). Running a program on the base is induction on its steps, each
matched by (a). (2) is (c), added up along the run. (3) Clause (b) finds a CHECK, a
COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three different places, and (2) counts them. (4) is (d): the
three moves certify exactly where the claim holds, the claim fails at some loaded state,
and the check can’t pass there because (b) says a passing check means the claim holds;
at the loaded state where it holds, the three moves raise the record. (5) Clause (b) puts
the record down right before a CERTIFY and up right after it, and the record never
comes down, so that CERTIFY is the first and only move where it rises. (6) Every
move is a base move or a record move, and (a) supplies base moves.


Theorem 16.20 (The language first, and what a certificate then means). (1) A machine


                                              285
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


that is Thiele-complete over some claim language is Thiele-complete, so every part of Theo-
rem 16.19 holds of it. (2) If a machine is Thiele-complete through an interface whose claims
have an exact equality test, it is Thiele-complete over the language made of that interface’s
claims, meanings and “unchanged,” with clause (b)’s proof that a meaning keeps holding as
the language’s own. (3) If a machine is Thiele-complete over a claim language L, some interface
over L meets the four clauses and has this property: every run from one of its clean states that
ends with the record up contains a CHECK of a claim c of L that passed, then a COMMIT of
c, and L’s meaning of c holds at the state the CHECK saw and at the state the COMMIT saw.

Proof. (1) Take the plain interface the language-first one becomes. (2) The checker’s
soundness and the keeping proof are the ones clause (b) already supplies. (3) Clause
(b) gives the chain; the checker’s soundness proof against L gives c’s meaning at the
state checked; L’s keeping proof carries it, through states where the thing c is about is
unchanged, to the state committed.

Part (2) says where the strength of the language-first form lives: in the naming. Any
reading can be turned into a language, so “Thiele-complete over some language” asks
no more than Thiele-complete does. “Thiele-complete over L,” for an L written down
without looking at the checker, says that what the machine certifies is what L says.
Every instance below is stated that way.

Each item in the proof names the clause it comes from, and that’s all the definition
gives. A Thiele-complete machine needn’t have a fact table, a CHECK that traps
when it fails, a COMMIT that looks anything up, or claims about counters. The
definition asks for an earned chain on the runs that raise the record and leaves the rest
to the machine. So the small machine’s table provenance, its trap, and its channel are
facts about that machine, and they don’t carry over to every machine that meets the
definition. Through a plain interface its claims can be any labels the interface names;
over a claim language they are the language’s. Either way its checker can be an oracle,
as the paragraph above says.

The second half of (6), that some move costs 0, is the one that kills the clock.


Observation 16.21 (A clock is a Thiele machine and isn’t Thiele-complete). Take the
two-counter machine, let every move cost 1, and take as the record any yes/no question about
its configuration whatsoever; or take a flag that switches on, and stays on, the first time any
chosen test of the configuration says yes. Either way the machine obeys the toll and has a
universal base, so it’s weakly Thiele-complete, and it is not Thiele-complete. More generally,
no machine whose every move costs at least 1 is Thiele-complete.

Proof. Every move costs one, so any raise costs at least one: the toll holds for any
record. The machine’s own moves are the two-counter instructions, which gives the




                                              286
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


universal base. But a Thiele-complete machine has a free move, by Theorem 16.19(6),
and this one has none.

That’s short, and it’s short because clause (c) does exactly the job it was written for:
it says computing is free, and a clock charges for computing. The other clauses earn
their keep too, and that’s worth checking, because a definition with a clause nothing
needs is a definition hiding something.


Theorem 16.22 (Each clause does work). (1) Take a free two-counter base with a ledger
beside it, and one extra move TICK that costs 1 and raises a flag. It obeys the toll, and read
with TICK as CERTIFY it meets the universal base clause and the exact toll clause; it is not
Thiele-complete, and more generally no machine with a move that raises the record from every
state is. (2) Take a free two-counter base and a record that never rises. It obeys the toll and
meets clauses (a), (b) and (c); it is not Thiele-complete, and more generally no machine whose
record never rises is.

Proof. (1) From a clean state, TICK alone raises the record. Clause (b) would need a
CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY inside that one-move run, and one move can’t
be three. (2) Clause (d) needs a run from some loaded state that raises the record, and
none does.

The paid latch is the receipt for nothing from the opening chapter, wearing a universal
base: honest about the price, silent about what was bought. The definition throws it
out.

The silent machine meets three clauses and fails only (d). The paid latch fails (d) as
well as (b), so it doesn’t show (b) doing work alone, and nothing above says whether
a clock meets (a), (b) and (d). So here’s the sharper check, the usual evidence that a
definition isn’t written around one machine: for each clause, a machine that meets the
other three and fails it.


Theorem 16.23 (The four clauses are independent). For each clause of Definition 16.7
there is a machine with an interface that meets the other three clauses and fails that one. Each
of the four machines obeys the toll and has a universal base, so it’s weakly Thiele-complete, and
none of them is Thiele-complete through any interface at all. (a) fails for this chapter’s machine
with one more move, DROP, free and read as a base move, which lowers the flag and trips the
trap latch. (b) fails for this chapter’s machine with one more move, FREE, costing one and read
as a CERTIFY, which raises the flag on any state whose trap is down, with no commitment
behind it. (c) fails for this chapter’s machine with every move costing one. (d) fails for the
silent machine of Theorem 16.22(2).

Proof. (a) Nothing moves a trapped state’s flag, so a run that uses DROP ends with
the flag down. A run from a clean state that ends with the flag up never used DROP;


                                               287
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


it’s a run of this chapter’s machine, and Theorem 16.9 gives its chain. DROP is free
and read as a base move, so (c) holds, and (d) holds as it does for the plain machine.
A state with the flag up has it down after DROP. That breaks the permanence in (a),
and permanence is about the machine alone, so no interface meets (a). (b) FREE never
lowers the flag, costs one and is read as a record move, so (a), (c) and (d) hold as before.
From a clean start FREE alone raises the flag, and a run of one move has no room for
a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY. Through any interface: (d) gives a loaded state
from which the record rises, so its trap is down; (a) makes that state clean, so its record
is down by (b); and FREE alone raises it, which (b) forbids. (c) Clauses (a), (b) and (d)
never mention a price, and they hold as for the plain machine. Base moves cost one,
so (c) fails, and every Thiele-complete machine has a free move (Theorem 16.19(6)).
(d) is Theorem 16.22(2).

Three of the four are this chapter’s machine with one thing changed, and in each case
the one clause it fails is the only thing keeping it out. Clause (c) also fixes something
it has no business fixing: the size of a mark. Double every price on the small machine
and it leaves the class, because its CHECK now costs two and (c) asks for one. A
definition that a change of currency breaks would be a strange one, so here is (c) with
the unit left open.


Theorem 16.24 (Any unit). Call a machine Thiele-complete at unit c, for a whole number
c ≥ 1, when some interface meets clauses (a), (b) and (d) and this form of (c): base moves cost
0, each CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY costs exactly c, and each move adds its cost to the
ledger. (1) At unit 1 that is Thiele-complete. (2) Multiply every price of a Thiele-complete
machine by c ≥ 1 and the machine is Thiele-complete at unit c; divide every price of a machine
Thiele-complete at unit c by c and the machine, with the same states, moves, step and record,
is Thiele-complete. (3) At every unit some move costs 0, so the clock of Observation 16.21,
with any reading or any latch as its record, is Thiele-complete at no unit, and neither is any
machine whose every move costs at least 1. (4) At unit c, a run from a clean state that ends
with the record up contains at least three of the three acts and raises the ledger by at least 3c;
the claim it stands on held when it was checked and still held when it was committed; and the
move that raises the record is a CERTIFY. (5) The small machine with every price doubled is
Thiele-complete at unit 2 and isn’t Thiele-complete.

Proof. (1) 1 · r = r. (2) Clauses (a), (b) and (d) never mention a price, and the two
machines have the same runs. The ledger is multiplied or divided along with the
prices, and (ℓ + c r )/c = ℓ/c + r exactly, so the divided ledger still adds each divided
price. (3) The move compiled from INC A is a base move, so it costs 0. (4) Clause
(b) finds the three acts in the run as before, and each costs c. The other two parts
are the unit-1 results on the divided machine, which runs exactly as this one does.
(5) is (2) with c = 2, and the doubled machine has a CHECK that costs 2, which no
Thiele-complete machine has (Theorem 16.19(6)).



                                               288
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


So the class doesn’t care what a mark is worth. It cares that computing is free and that
the three acts cost the same. The clock fails at every unit for the reason it failed at one:
it charges for computing. I keep unit 1 in the definition because the small machine is
built that way and every count in this chapter is in its marks.

Now the other direction. A definition nobody meets is as useless as one everybody
meets.


Theorem 16.25 (The small machine, the generic one and the sorted one are Thiele–
complete). (1) This chapter’s machine is Thiele-complete, read with INC and DEC as base
moves, CHECK p c and COMMIT p c as record moves on the claim “p holds of c,” CERTIFY
as CERTIFY, the window as (line, A, B), “unchanged” as “same value and same version
of c,” clean states as clean starts and the ledger as µ. (2) So is the same machine over any
property language with an exact equality test and a checker proved to mean what it says, as
long as some property is true of one number and false of another. (3) In particular the ma-
chine whose property is “this counter, read as a list, is sorted” is Thiele-complete. (4) Every
Thiele-complete machine is a certification system (Definition 3.1) and obeys the universal floor;
for this chapter’s machine, that system agrees step for step and cost for cost with the one of
Theorem 16.6, and for the generic machine with the generic machine’s own. (5) Each of the
three is Thiele-complete over its own claim language, fixed before the checker. For this chapter’s
machine the language’s claims are pairs of a property and a counter, equal when both parts
are, the meaning of “p holds of c” is the meaning holds of Definition 16.1 applied to c’s value,
written without the checker, and “unchanged” is “same value and same version of c.” For the
generic machine the language is built from the properties, their equality test and what they
mean, and the checker isn’t part of it; the sorted machine is that case.

Proof. (1) Clause (a) is Theorem 16.2 together with the step line: INC and DEC never
touch the flag, and the flag never comes down. Clause (b) is Theorem 16.9 with
checker soundness (Lemma 16.1), and a meaning about c keeps holding while c’s
value doesn’t move. Clause (c) is the price table. Clause (d) is Theorem 16.17 with
the claim “A is zero,” which holds at (0, b) and fails at (5, b). (2) and (3) are the same
argument with the property language left open, and the sorted claim holds of the list
numbered 18, which is [1, 2], and fails of 20, which is [2, 1]. (4) is (1) of Theorem 16.19
and Section 3’s floor. (5) The interface over the language is the one of (1), (2) and
(3) with the meanings handed over by the language, and the checker’s soundness is
Lemma 16.1 and its generic form.

Section 17 carries the same fixed-language form to other bases. The claims keep their
stated meanings; the new interfaces supply the checkers.

And here’s the thing every machine that meets the definition can’t help doing. It’s
Section 7’s shape again, only this time it isn’t about one machine. It’s about all of them.




                                               289
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Observation 16.26 (Every Thiele-complete machine hides its record and its ledger
from its window). Let a machine be Thiele-complete through an interface, and let its window
be the two-counter configuration its universal base shows. (1) For every state s there’s a loaded
state and one free base move from it that lands on a state with s’s window, with the record
down and the ledger unchanged. (2) There’s a loaded state and two runs from it that end with
the same window, one with the record up and one with it down; and likewise two runs from
one loaded state that end with the same window and ledgers at least 3 apart. (3) So no function
of the window gives the record at the end of every run from every loaded state, and no function
of the window gives the ledger. (4) The same holds of the certification system built from the
machine.

Proof. Theorem 16.19(4) gives a loaded state and a run from it that raises the record,
and (3) says that run paid at least 3. Say it ends with window (line ℓ, x, y). Two-counter
instructions can steer any configuration to any other: empty A, fill it to x + 1, empty
B, fill it to y, then one DEC of A that jumps to line ℓ. Those are base moves, so from
the same loaded state they reach the same window, cost nothing, and leave the record
down, by (a) and (c). That’s two runs, one window, two records and two ledgers,
which is (2). A function of the window would have to give both answers on that one
window, which is (3). For (1), load ( x + 1, y) and take just the last DEC. (4) is (3) read
through the certification system, whose runs are the machine’s.

The observer in that theorem sees one thing, the final window. An observer who
sees the window before and after each step, or the whole trace of windows, or who
is also handed the program and the start, is a different observer, and the collision
says nothing about them; given the program and the start, the run is fixed and so is
its record. The theorem’s two runs also start from the same loaded state, so they’re
reachable witnesses, which is stronger than two arbitrary states that happen to look
alike. And “no function of the window gives the record” is all it says. It doesn’t say
the window tells you nothing about it.

Notice how little that took, and say it out loud so nobody mistakes it for more. It’s the
fibre fact from Section 7 plus one observation: a universal base can print any window
for free. Which is the point. The window here is everything a Turing machine would
call the machine, the line and the counters. On a Thiele-complete machine, that’s
never enough to tell you what was established or what it cost, and it can’t be, because
computing is free and can’t touch the record. A richer window, one that shows the
flag, is a different window, and nothing above says it fails.

16.13 One machine that runs them all
The small machine raises its flag only by checking, committing and certifying, and it
pays for that. The next question is whether one machine can stand in for all of them,
the way Turing’s universal machine stands in for every Turing machine. Here’s what
I mean by that. A universal Thiele machine is one fixed machine running one fixed


                                              290
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


program that runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with the guest’s record
kept and the guest’s toll collected by the host’s own steps. No program running on
the host has to keep a convention for it.

And I want it the hard way. The easy way is to give the host a move that means “take
one step of the guest,” and then “it runs any guest” is true because I wrote it that way.
There’s a host like that two subsections on, after the two programs, and it’s useful
as a picture. It isn’t Turing’s kind of universal. Turing’s universal machine has no
instruction for “do what the machine on the tape would do.” It has the same kind of
instructions every other Turing machine has, and one fixed table, and the table does
the reading and the deciding and the carrying out. That’s the bar here: one fixed
program, written in the small machine’s own six kinds of instruction, with no step of
the guest built into anything.

Turing’s own explanation is worth having in your head, because the program below
copies its shape. In the 1936 paper the universal machine’s tape starts with the machine
to imitate, written out as a string of letters, its standard description, and after it the
imitated machine’s complete configurations, one after another: where its head is, what
state it’s in, what’s on its tape. To take one step, the universal machine finds the last
configuration, looks through the description line by line, comparing, until it finds the
line for that state and that symbol, and then writes out the next configuration the way
that line says. Then it goes back and does it again. It leaves marks on squares so it
doesn’t lose its place. Every bit of that is ordinary instructions on an ordinary tape,
and nothing in its table knows any particular machine.

Turing’s universal program came first on paper, and one that people actually came
to use arrived through the side door. John McCarthy, who had started the artificial
intelligence project at MIT with Minsky, was writing up his new language Lisp around
1960 and wanted to show it was neater than Turing machines, so he wrote a universal
function for it, eval, the language describing how to evaluate itself, and argued it
was shorter and easier to follow than a universal Turing machine. In his own history
of Lisp, that was for the paper, a thing to read; the notation for writing programs
as data was made up for the paper with no thought of using it in practice. Then
Steve Russell (S. R. Russell in McCarthy’s account), a programmer on that MIT project,
noticed that eval could serve as an interpreter and coded it by hand, and there was a
running language with an interpreter that nobody had planned. McCarthy adds that
the surprise froze some decisions he’d made “rather lightheartedly” for the paper. So
the trick has a habit: written to be read, it ends up being run. The program below goes
the other way round, on purpose. It’s written to run, and the proofs check that what
runs is what the page says.

The host. The program runs on a machine with the small machine’s instructions
and the small machine’s prices: INC, DEC, HALT for free, and CHECK, COMMIT,
CERTIFY for one each, with the same table of sixteen facts, the same channel, trap,


                                           291
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


ledger and flag. One change: it has a counter for every whole number, each with its
own version, where the small machine had two. No new kind of instruction, no new
price. Take away the table, the channel and the flag and what’s left is old: a machine
with as many registers as it needs, adding one, taking one away and jumping on zero,
is the unlimited register machine of John Shepherdson and H. E. Sturgis, two logicians
who proved in 1963 that such machines compute every partial recursive function.


Definition 16.8 (The host machine). The host machine is the machine of Definition 16.3
with one change: it has a counter, with its version, for every whole number r (a
register), and INC r, DEC r j, CHECK p r and COMMIT p r name one register each. Its
property language has one property, Slot. Write ⟨m, n⟩ for the number (2n + 1) · 2m ;
every positive number is ⟨m, n⟩ for exactly one pair, and 0 is no pair. Number the
small machine’s properties Zero 7→ 0, Even 7→ 1, Ge(n) 7→ n + 2. The checker of Slot
says yes at a value x exactly when x = ⟨m, v⟩ and the small machine’s checker says
yes to the property numbered m at v; its meaning is the same with holds in place of
the checker.


There’s one place the guest’s machine shows up in the host. The host’s single property
knows how to read the small machine’s three-word property language: “this number
is the pair (property, value) and the property holds of the value.” It doesn’t know
the small machine’s step. That’s the counter version of Turing’s universal machine
knowing the alphabet its guests write in.

Two facts that force the design. Why more counters? Because of two facts, and the
program looks the way it does because of them.

The first is about reading. On this machine a program that wants a counter’s value
in its own control flow has to take pebbles out (DEC) and put them back (INC), and
every INC, and every DEC on a counter above 0, is a write, so the counter’s version
goes up. A fact is about one version, so a read done that way kills every live fact about
the counter. Not every look is a write: CHECK reads a value without writing it, a
DEC on 0 changes no version, and a fresh CHECK after such a read can make a new
live fact. But the guest’s counters are exactly the ones the host has to read by taking
pebbles out, again and again, to decide which way a DEC jumps and to work out a
property’s answer, and each of those reads kills whatever fact was kept there. So the
host can’t keep the guest’s facts on its copies of the guest’s counters.

The second says that even if reading were free, a fixed program couldn’t keep them by
sending each guest property to one of a fixed, finite list of host properties and checking
it on the same register the guest’s fact is about. That’s all the theorem below rules out,
and it’s the pigeonhole.


Theorem 16.27 (No host fact on an exact copy of the guest’s counter). Take any host


                                           292
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


property language with an exact equality test and any checker, a finite list Q of host properties,
and any translation of the small machine’s properties into members of Q whose host check
passes whenever the guest’s check passes on the same number. Then there are n ̸= m, with
Ge(n) and Ge(m) translated to the same host property, such that the guest program CHECK
Ge(n) A; COMMIT Ge(m) A traps within two steps from every start, while on every host
state with the trap down and room in its table, and some register holding a number at least n,
the translated CHECK and COMMIT on that register both pass and put the committed claim
in the channel.

Proof. A fixed program mentions finitely many properties, so Q is finite, and the
translation sends the infinitely many Ge(0), Ge(1), . . . into it: two of them land on
the same member. The guest’s COMMIT asks for Ge(m), and its table can only hold
Ge(n), so it traps (or its CHECK already trapped). The host sees one property twice:
its CHECK passes, since the guest’s would, and its COMMIT finds exactly what that
CHECK wrote.

So the host keeps the guest’s facts somewhere else: in slots, extra registers used for
nothing but holding facts, one per checked fact, each holding the pair (property num-
ber, value) that the guest checked. The pigeonhole doesn’t bite a slot, because the
property lives in the slot’s number. The instruction doesn’t have to carry it: CHECK
Slot on a slot asks about whatever pair is sitting there, and there are infinitely many
pairs. A slot is written only when the program is moving a fact into it. And when
the guest writes the counter a fact was about, the program gives every slot about that
counter a nudge, one INC and one DEC, which leaves the number alone and pushes
the version up, so the host’s facts go stale at exactly the moment the guest’s do.

Do one slot by hand. The property “even” has number 1. Checking it on value 4 puts
⟨1, 4⟩ = (2 · 4 + 1)21 = 18 in a separate slot. To read that pair, divide 18 by two until
the remainder is odd: one division gives 9, so the property number is 1; subtract one
from 9 and halve to recover value 4. The host checks that property of that value. A
second card, the mirror, says 2: the property number plus one. COMMIT can read this
second card while leaving the checked slot untouched.

When the guest changes the counter that fact concerned, nudge the slot 18 → 19 → 18
and set the mirror to zero. Its number came back, but its version rose twice, so the
old host fact is no longer current. A restored number does not restore an old check.
The mirror tells the search not to use that slot’s old fact; the version rule enforces the
refusal even if it tries.

The program. Here’s U the way Turing would describe it, one register at a time and
then one job at a time. Registers 0 and 1 hold the guest’s A and B. Register 2 holds
the guest’s whole program as one number: each instruction gets a number (an opcode
paired with its operands, INC as 0, DEC as 1, HALT as 2, CHECK as 3, COMMIT as 4,
CERTIFY as 5), and the list of them is packed with ⟨·, ·⟩, the empty list as 0. Register 3


                                               293
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


is the guest’s line. Registers 4 to 13 are scratch. Registers 14 and 15 count how many
CHECKs on A and on B have passed. Registers 16 to 47 are mirrors, sixteen for each
guest counter, and registers 48 to 79 are the slots, sixteen for each guest counter. The
guest’s table holds sixteen facts in total, across both counters, and all sixteen can be
about one counter, so the host gives each counter room for all of them. That’s a host
reservation, and the guest’s own capacity stays sixteen in all. Register 80 is a dead end
that’s never written.

Each guest step goes like this. At line 1 the program copies the program number and
the guest’s line into scratch, putting the originals back as it goes, because copying
a counter on this machine means emptying it into two others and refilling it. If the
guest’s line is 0, or past the end of the program, it stops. Otherwise it peels instructions
off the front of the copy, one per line, until it holds the one at the guest’s line, and
splits that into opcode and operands. Then a chain of DECs on the opcode sends it to
one of six handlers.

   • INC c: INC the guest’s counter c, nudge every slot about c and zero its mirrors,
     add one to the guest’s line, back to line 1.
   • DEC c j: DEC the guest’s counter c. If it was 0, add one to the guest’s line. If it
     wasn’t, nudge every slot about c, zero its mirrors, and set the guest’s line to j.
     Back to line 1.
   • HALT: stop.
   • CHECK p c: let k be the count of passed CHECKs on c. If k is below 16, build
     ⟨number of p, value of c⟩ in slot k of c, run CHECK Slot on that slot, set its mirror
     to the number of p plus one, add one to the count and to the guest’s line, and go
     back to line 1. If k is 16, run CHECK Slot on the dead end, which holds 0, which
     is no pair, so it traps, just as the guest’s seventeenth CHECK does.
   • COMMIT p c: look through the sixteen mirrors of c for one equal to the number
     of p plus one. At the first match, run COMMIT Slot on that slot. With no match,
     run COMMIT Slot on the dead end, which traps.
   • CERTIFY: run CERTIFY, add one to the guest’s line, back to line 1.

Why the mirrors? COMMIT has to find the slot holding the claim, and it can’t read
the slot to find out, because reading would make the fact stale. So beside every slot
sits a mirror the program is allowed to read: the property’s number plus one while
the slot’s fact is live, 0 once the guest has written the counter. If a guest CHECK fails
its property, the host’s CHECK on the slot fails too, since the slot holds exactly the
pair the guest checked. If the guest table is full across both counters, the host’s own
sixteen-entry table is full as well, even when this counter’s slot count is below sixteen;
its CHECK then traps for lack of room. Both kinds of refusal are preserved.

Count what costs anything. Fetching, unpacking, copying, nudging, branching: all


                                            294
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


INC and DEC, all free, the way computing is free on the small machine. The only paid
instructions are the CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY sites, and each guest CHECK,
COMMIT or CERTIFY makes the program run exactly one of them. So the host’s
ledger lands on the guest’s, mark for mark. And when the guest’s flag goes up, the
host’s goes up by the host’s own CERTIFY, standing on the host’s own COMMIT and
CHECK on a slot. It isn’t copying a bit. It runs the same chain on its own registers.


Definition 16.9 (The program U, and loading a guest). U is the fixed list of 3728 host
instructions specified by the block expansions in Appendix G, starting at line 1 and
mentioning registers 0 to 80; exactly 69 of them cost anything. For a guest program P
and a start ( x, y), the loaded host hload( P, x, y) has register 0 at x, register 1 at y, register
2 at the number of P, register 3 at 1 and every other register at 0, every version 0, line
1, an empty table and channel, the trap down, ledger 0 and flag down. Write grun(m)
for m program steps of P from start( x, y), and hrun(n) for n program steps of U from
hload( P, x, y).


Theorem 16.28 (U keeps pace with its guest). For every guest program P, start ( x, y) and
number of guest steps m, there’s a number of host steps n such that one of two things holds.
Either the host is back at line 1 with m ≤ n and related to the guest: registers 0 and 1 hold
the guest’s A and B, register 3 holds the guest’s line, the guest’s trap is down, the two ledgers
are equal, the two flags are equal, and the host’s table and channel hold, fact for fact, slot facts
matching the guest’s facts and channel. Or both have stopped, with the same counters, the
same trap, the same ledger, the same flag, and matching tables and channels. And from any
related pair where the guest hasn’t stopped, one guest step is matched by at least one host step
that lands related again, or with both stopped.

Proof. The one-step part is a case for each thing the guest can do at its line: stop;
INC; DEC, taken or not; CHECK, passing, failing, or with a full table; COMMIT,
found or not; CERTIFY, passing or not. The block invariants and the case analysis
in Appendix G show where each matching stretch lands. The relation carries the
bookkeeping that makes the next case go through: each count register equals the
number of slots in use for its counter, each slot in use holds (property number, checked
value), a slot’s fact is current exactly when the matching guest fact is, a live slot’s mirror
is the property’s number plus one and a stale one’s is 0, and unused slots, unused
mirrors and the dead end are 0. A freshly loaded host is related to the guest’s start.
The run statement is induction on m.


Theorem 16.29 (Halting and answers match). For every P, x and y, the guest’s run of
P from start( x, y) halts if and only if U’s run from hload( P, x, y) halts. And whenever the
guest has halted at step m and U at step n, the host’s registers 0 and 1 hold the guest’s A and
B, and the two traps, the two ledgers and the two flags are equal.



                                                295
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Proof. Theorem 16.28: a halted guest is matched by a stopped host, and a host that has
stopped can’t be back at line 1 with the guest still running, because line 1 isn’t a stop.
A halted machine stays halted, so the two halting points carry the same values.


Theorem 16.30 (The host’s flag is the guest’s, and its ledger is exact). (1) The guest’s
flag is up at some step of its run if and only if the host’s flag is up at some step of
U’s run. (2) For every m there’s an n at which the two are related, with m ≤ n, or
both stopped, with µ(hrun(n)) = µ(grun(m)). And for every n there’s an m with
µ(grun(m)) ≤ µ(hrun(n)) ≤ µ(grun(m + 1)): in between matching points, the host’s
ledger never gets ahead of the guest’s next step.

Proof. (1) Flags are equal at matching points and never come down. (2) Ledgers are
equal at matching points; inside the stretch of U that runs one guest instruction, at
most the one paid site of that instruction runs, so the host’s ledger sits between the
guest’s before and after it.

That’s a third sense of “exact,” and it’s the plainest of the three: two ledgers, one
number.


Theorem 16.31 (The host earns its own flag). If the host’s flag is up after n steps of U from
hload( P, x, y), then the instructions U executed contain, in order, a passing CHECK Slot on
a slot, then a passing COMMIT Slot on the same slot, with the slot untouched and its version
unchanged in between, then a passing CERTIFY; the slot held ⟨number of p, v⟩ at the CHECK,
with holds( p, v). And the guest’s own run from start( x, y) contains a passing CHECK p c,
then, with c untouched and its version unchanged, a passing COMMIT p c, then a passing
CERTIFY, with c holding v at its CHECK.

Proof. By Theorem 16.30 the guest’s flag rises too; find the guest step where it rises, a
passing CERTIFY, and the related host point just before it. The guest’s channel there
names a fact, and the relation says the host’s channel names the matching slot fact. The
host’s own flag rises at its own first passing CERTIFY, and nothing paid runs between
the related point and that CERTIFY, so the host’s channel hasn’t moved: it names that
