slot fact. The host machine’s version of Theorem 16.9 gives the host’s CHECK and
COMMIT on that slot. The record kept with the slot says what pair it held and when,
and the checker’s meaning gives holds( p, v). The same theorem on the guest’s run,
up to the step where its flag rose, gives the guest’s chain on the same p and c, and the
record says c held v at its CHECK.


Theorem 16.32 (The host is Thiele-complete, and U’s halting is undecidable). (1) The
host machine, with Slot as its property and one move per instruction, is Thiele-complete (Defi-
nition 16.7), and Thiele-complete over its own claim language, whose claims are “Slot holds
of register r,” whose meanings are written without the host’s checker, and whose “unchanged”


                                             296
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


is “same value and same version of register r”; and U’s run from hload( P, x, y) is a run of it.
(2) Read as a certification system it obeys the universal floor; a run of U that raises the host’s
flag costs at least 3 there. The system built from its Thiele-completeness agrees with it step for
step and cost for cost, so the same run costs at least 3 on that one too, and the universal floor of
1 holds there directly. (3) U halts from hload( P, x, y) exactly when P halts from start( x, y),
so the question “does U halt from this loaded host?” is undecidable in the reduction sense of
Theorem 16.4.

Proof. (1) The base is registers 0 and 1, run by INC and DEC; the claims are “Slot
holds of register r”; the rest is the host machine’s own versions of the small machine’s
theorems, and for non-vacuity, register 0 loaded with 1, which is ⟨0, 0⟩, the pair of
Zero and 0, against register 0 loaded with 0, which is no pair. Over the claim language
the interface is the same one, with the meanings handed over by the language. (2)
is Theorem 16.25(4) and Theorem 16.31. (3) is Theorem 16.29, and the loading map
reduces the small machine’s halting question, undecidable by Theorem 16.4, to this
one.

Put it together, plainly. One fixed program, 3728 instructions of the small machine’s six
kinds, with no guest step built into anything, runs every program of the small machine
from every clean start start( x, y). It halts exactly when its guest halts, with the guest’s
answer in its first two registers. Its flag goes up at some step of its run exactly when
the guest’s goes up at some step of the guest’s run, by its own check, its own commit
and its own certificate. Its ledger is the guest’s, mark for mark, wherever the two line
up. And the machine it runs on is Thiele-complete. Since the small machine runs every
two-counter program, U runs every computation, under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done
outside the machine. That’s the universal Thiele machine of this book, for the small
machine’s programs; the next subsection carries it to every computably presented
Thiele machine.

The fine print, before you take that anywhere. The guests start clean, from start( x, y);
the whole-run theorems are about loaded hosts, and only the one-step theorem is about
any related pair. The host’s property reads the small machine’s three-word language,
so a guest with a different property language needs a different host property; the
host of the next subsection has one, a single property that reads a universal claim
language. Sixteen slots per counter is the guest’s whole table size, reserved for each
counter in case every fact is about that one. This interpreter unpacks the program
number from the front for every guest step, and copies a number one pebble at a time.
That determines the running time measured in Section 19; the simulation result above
compares the states and ledgers at matching points.

Enforcement in the step is the reference monitor’s move from the opening chapter,
Anderson’s 1972 move: one mechanism everything has to pass through. What’s put
together here is a priced, earned record under that move, carried to every guest by
one fixed program. The move itself is Anderson’s. Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett and

                                                297
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


Fred Schneider (2006) worked out, in their model, which policies mechanisms like
that can enforce at all, and their paper is where I’d go to see why enforcing a property
of every run escapes the Rice-style walls that deciding one runs into.

Why make such a fuss about proofs that walk every case? Because the first universal
machine had bugs. It’s the machine in Turing’s 1936 paper, and nobody gets to call
Turing careless. In 1947 Emil Post, in an appendix to a paper on a problem of Thue,
pointed out that the construction leaned on a convention it hadn’t earned, and he
patched a small defect in how the universal machine writes out each complete con-
figuration. Around the same time Donald Davies, who joined the National Physical
Laboratory in 1947, where Turing was designing a computer, worked through the
universal machine’s tables and found more mistakes, much to Turing’s annoyance, as
the accounts of Davies’s life have it. (It’s the same Davies who later named the packet
in packet switching.) His corrections were finally printed in a collection edited by Jack
Copeland, a philosopher and historian of computing who runs an archive of Turing’s
papers, The Essential Turing, in 2004. They may be some of the first bugs ever written,
in a program for a computer that didn’t exist yet. That’s a lovely claim and a hard one
to check, so take it as a lead. I can’t give it to you as a fact. What it changes here: a
universal machine is exactly the kind of construction where a careful person leaves a
hole, U has 3728 lines for a hole to hide in, and each case of its simulation argument
has to hold. The definitions are on the page so you can examine what those cases
establish.

16.14 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided,
      priced in whole units, carried as a latch
U runs the small machine’s programs, and through them every computation, under
Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine. But a Thiele machine from some-
where else has its own states, its own moves, its own prices and its own reading, and
running it through the two-counter encoding keeps its computation and nothing else.
So the question Turing’s machine raises for this book is the bigger one. Take any Thiele
machine whose workings can be computed. Is there one fixed program that runs every
such machine as a guest, keeping its halting, raising its own flag exactly when the
guest’s reading would rise, on an earned chain of its own, and keeping a ledger equal
to the guest’s own prices, with the host’s flat ones nowhere in it? There is, within
limits I’ll list, and here it is.

First the class, said plainly. A computably presented Thiele machine is a certification
system in Section 3’s sense (states, moves, a step, a price for each move, a yes/no
reading) together with a driver that picks the next move from the current state or says
stop, and a way of writing states and moves as whole numbers. “Computably” means
four little programs, written in the plainest language of computable functions there
is, the one built from zero, plus one, picking an argument, composing, recursion and
search: one computes the driver, one the step, one the price, and one the reading, and
the reading’s program answers yes or no on every state there is. Run from a start s0 ,

                                          298
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


the driver’s moves give one run. Its ledger after n moves is the sum of their prices, and
its latch after n moves says whether the reading has been yes at any state so far.

The host gets one thing the small machine doesn’t have: a paid move that certifies
nothing. On the small machine every charge comes from a CHECK, a COMMIT or
a CERTIFY, and those can bill seven: one passing CHECK and six COMMITs of the
same claim cost seven and raise no flag. But every passing CHECK takes one of the
table’s sixteen entries for good, every COMMIT rewrites the channel, and a failing
CHECK traps. So the host machine gets a seventh instruction kind, PAY: it costs one,
goes to the next line, and changes nothing else; it never raises the flag, takes no table
entry and leaves the channel alone. That’s why the compiler uses it.

How far the small machine gets without it is proved, and the count is short. Take
a run that never traps and ends with the flag down. No CERTIFY ran in it, since a
passing one raises the flag and a failing one traps. Every CHECK in it passed, since
a failing one traps, and each passing CHECK filled one of the table’s sixteen entries,
so there were at most sixteen. Every COMMIT in it committed a claim the table holds,
and the table holds at most sixteen, so at most sixteen COMMITs can be of claims the
run hadn’t committed before. That’s 32, and the only way past it is a COMMIT of a
claim already committed earlier in the run. A claim names its counter’s version, and
the version changes at every write, so a repeat needs its counter left alone since the
earlier COMMIT. A guest whose every move writes its counters can’t do that, so it
runs out of ways to pay after 32. A simulated program that runs longer than that has
to bill somewhere, and PAY is where. Whether some other host without PAY could do
the same job is a question I haven’t settled, and I don’t claim it.

The definition of Thiele-complete sorts every paid move into CHECK, COMMIT or
CERTIFY, so PAY has to be filed under one of them, and it’s filed as a CHECK of the
empty claim, a claim that never holds. That’s a filing for the interface. It isn’t what
PAY does on the machine: a CHECK that fails on this machine traps, and PAY goes on
to the next line. With PAY filed that way the host stays Thiele-complete, and Thiele-
complete over its own claim language, in which the empty claim means nothing, and
its floor of three for a flag raised from a clean start still holds with PAY present.

The program is U with one more handler: a seventh branch on the guest’s opcode,
for PAY, that runs the host’s own PAY once. Call it UP ; it’s 3735 instructions, with
70 paid sites, the 69 of U plus the PAY. The guest it runs is a program of the small
machine with PAY added, and that guest is where the presented machine goes. Its
four programs are compiled into two counters, by the packing Minsky used, using the
translations of Appendix F from computable functions to counter programs; the guest
keeps the presented machine’s state coded in its counter B, takes one of its moves by
running the compiled step, pays the move’s price in PAYs, and, when the compiled
reading says yes, checks, commits and certifies. The host’s one property is fixed too: a
claim is either one of the small machine’s three words about a number, or “run reading


                                          299
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


program r on the coded state v,” and the host’s checker evaluates that with one fixed
routine for every presented machine there is. So nothing in UP knows any particular
presented machine. The machine arrives as data, the way Turing’s guests arrived on
the tape.

A fixed checker that runs whatever program it’s handed and always answers needs
saying how, so here is the routine. A claim of the second kind carries a number r. The
checker decodes r as a counter-machine routine: its instructions, where they sit, which
register holds the answer, which register holds the fuel, and how many registers to
load. If r doesn’t decode to a routine, the answer is no. Otherwise the checker loads
the routine’s registers from v, reads a fuel number f out of v too (the fuel register’s
entry in v’s prime factorisation), runs the routine for at most f steps, and says yes
exactly when by then the routine has left its code with 1 in its answer register. Every
input gets an answer within f steps, so the checker is total, and what it means is that
bounded run: yes if and only if the routine halts within the fuel the value carries,
with answer 1. That’s how it stays clear of the diagonal. A total evaluator E that
agreed with every total yes-or-no program on that program’s code alone would let
g(n) = ¬ E(n, n) contradict itself at its own code. This checker never evaluates a
program on its code alone: the fuel comes with the claim’s value. The guest compiled
from M runs M’s reading routine itself and puts at least the step count it took into the
fuel register, and at such a value the checker says yes if and only if the reading says
yes.

For the fuel rule, take a routine containing just one instruction: increment an answer
register initially holding 0, then leave its one-line code. Give it fuel 0 and the check
says no: it has not completed. Give it fuel 1 and the check says yes: it has left the
code with answer 1. The first no did not mean the routine would never answer yes. It
meant “not within this allowance.” You can run that distinction with a pebble and a
single instruction card. The general checker does the same job for an arbitrary finite
list and an allowance supplied with it.


Theorem 16.33 (One host runs every computably presented Thiele machine). Let M be
a computably presented Thiele machine, so that a driver picks its next move (one run per start),
a program decides its reading on every state, and its prices are whole numbers; and let s0 be
a start state. Load UP with the guest compiled from M’s presentation and s0 coded in. What
the host carries of M’s reading is its latch. Then: (1) UP halts exactly when M’s run stops.
(2) For every n such that M hasn’t stopped before move n, there’s a host time t at which the
host’s register for the guest’s counter B decodes to M’s state after n moves, the host’s ledger is
M’s ledger after n moves plus a surcharge, and the host’s flag is M’s latch after n moves; and
if M stops at n, such a t has UP halted as well. (3) The host’s flag is up at some time exactly
when M’s reading is yes at some state of its run. (4) If the host’s flag is up at time t, the host’s
own instructions up to t contain a passing CHECK on a slot, then a passing COMMIT on the
same slot with the slot untouched in between, then a passing CERTIFY; and the slot held the


                                                300
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


claim “reading program r says yes of v” for M’s own reading program r, that claim holds, and
v decodes to a state of M’s run where the reading is yes.

Proof. Two layers, each proved on its own. The bottom layer is the compiler: for every
presented machine, its guest program’s run passes through points that code M’s states
in order, with the guest’s ledger equal to M’s ledger plus the surcharge and the guest’s
flag equal to M’s latch, and the guest’s own flag stands on an earned chain whose
claim is M’s reading program applied to the coded state where the reading first said
yes. The top layer is UP , proved the way U was in the previous theorems, with the PAY
case added: it keeps pace with any guest of this kind, halting and flag matched, ledger
equal at matching points, and its flag earned on a slot. Compose the two. The earned
part takes one more step: the host’s chain gives a guest CHECK that passed, and a
guest run that ends with its flag up has exactly one passing CHECK, the compiler’s
CHECK of the reading on counter B. So the guest CHECK the host’s chain points to is
that one, and its claim is M’s reading at the first state where it said yes.

Two things the theorem doesn’t say. First, the host’s flag is M’s latch. If M’s reading
says yes at some state and no at a later one, the host’s flag stays up, so it says the
reading was yes somewhere in the run, and it doesn’t say the reading is yes now.
Second, what the host re-establishes is the reading: the claim it checked is “M’s reading
program says yes of this coded state,” and that’s all. A bare certification system needn’t
tie its reading to anything true about sorting, proofs or the world outside. If M’s
reading is meant to say a list is sorted, that it does is a separate correctness theorem
about the reading, and the host doesn’t supply it. The two universal programs also
keep their own guests: U runs the small machine’s programs over its three words
about numbers, and UP runs computably presented machines over the universal
claim language.

Now the surcharge, because that’s where the ledger stops being exact, and it can’t be
helped. The host raises its flag the only way the host machine allows, by a CHECK, a
COMMIT and a CERTIFY, and those cost three. If M’s first move that turns its reading
to yes costs at least three, the host pays the difference in PAYs and nothing more is
owed. If it costs less, the host pays three there anyway, which is the larger of three
and the move’s price. The surcharge starts at that move: while M’s latch is down it’s
zero, so a run that never certifies is matched exactly. Whether anything could do better
depends on what M paid before. When M’s whole ledger at the raise is below three,
no program on the host machine can match it, since a raised host flag costs three from
a clean start. When M paid more than that earlier, nothing here says this compiler’s
surcharge is the least possible: part (1) of the theorem below bounds this compiler,
and part (3) is the only lower bound proved.

Keep two tally lines for a guest whose first three moves each cost one and whose
reading first says yes after the third. The guest’s totals are 1, 2, 3. This compiler pays
one PAY on each of the first two moves, then its three-act chain: the host totals are

                                            301
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


1, 2, 5. The excess is two, added once. If the third move instead costs four, the host
runs the chain and one PAY there; both totals then read 6. These are counts of charged
instructions, not counts of all the work needed to decode the guest.


Theorem 16.34 (Exact, within two, and no better). Let M, s0 and the loaded host be as in
Theorem 16.33, and let M’s reading be no at s0 . (1) For every n before M stops there’s a host
time at which the host’s ledger lies between M’s ledger after n moves and that plus two, with
the state decoded and the flag matched as before. (2) If moreover every move that first turns
M’s reading to yes costs at least three, the surcharge is zero and the host’s ledger equals M’s
exactly at those times. (3) If M’s latch is up after n moves while its ledger is below three, then
no run of the host machine from a clean start, under any program at all, ends with its flag
equal to that latch and its ledger raised by exactly M’s ledger.

Proof. (1) and (2): the guest pays M’s prices in PAYs, a unit at a time, except at the
move where M’s reading first says yes. There it has to run its CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY, three units, and it makes up the rest of the move’s price in PAYs, so it pays
the larger of the price c and three. The price is at least one, because the move raised a
reading (the toll), so the excess is at most two, and none when c ≥ 3. (3): a raised flag
on the host machine costs at least three from a clean start, whatever the program, and
M’s ledger is less.

Part (3) is an observation in the sense of Section 3: it reads off Observation 16.16. If the
reading is already yes at the start, the host has to raise its flag at once, and that costs
three on top of a ledger of nothing.

And one machine carried all the way, by proof, so the class isn’t empty. Its states are
whole numbers, its one move adds one and costs three, its driver always picks that
move, and its reading is “at least three.” The driver returns the fixed move; the step
adds one; the price returns three; and the reading compares the state with three. The
counter constructions in Appendix F implement all four. Loaded into UP from 0, the
host never halts, its flag goes up, at the host time matching move n its ledger is exactly
3n and its flag is up exactly when n ≥ 3, and the raised flag stands on a host chain
whose slot claims the machine’s own reading of a state at least three. That’s proved.
Nothing executes UP on that guest.

Now the limits, each of which is in the statement, said plainly.

   • Readings that are decided. The reading’s program has to answer yes or no on
     every state. A reading a program could only confirm, waiting forever on the no
     cases, isn’t covered, and neither is a reading no program computes at all.
   • One run per start. The driver picks the move, so the guest is deterministic.
     A machine whose next move is somebody’s free choice gets in only with that
     choice written into its driver.


                                               302
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


   • The record is the latch. The host’s flag is up once M’s reading has been yes at
     any state of the run, which is exactly the latch of Section 10. A reading that goes
     yes and then back to no is carried as “it was yes once.”
   • The ledger is exact up to the surcharge. When the reading starts at no, at most
     two, and zero when the first raising move costs three or more; when it starts at
     yes, three. And no program on this host, run from a clean start, can do better
     when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three.
   • Prices in whole units, paid one at a time. A move that costs a million is a million
     PAYs. The compiler also uses Minsky’s packing. These choices determine the
     time needed to realize the guest’s charge on this host.
   • Proved; never run. The demonstration machine’s numbers come from theorems.
     Nobody has run UP on it. An executable version of the full construction has not
     been produced, and its compiled programs are impractically large. Section 19
     says what was run.

16.15 A simpler host, with the guest step built in
There’s a much simpler host than U, and I keep it in the book because it’s easy to read
and it shows the copy rule in one line. Its universality is by construction: it has a
move that runs one guest step by calling the small machine’s own step. So it isn’t the
universal Thiele machine of this book. U is. Read it as a picture of what U does the
long way, and as a host that starts from any guest state at all, clean or not.

It carries a guest inside its own state: the guest’s program as data, the guest’s counters,
its table, its ledger, its flag. The host has one extra move, run one guest step. In that
one move it looks at the guest’s flag, takes the step, looks again, and if the flag went
from down to up, the host’s own copy of that flag goes up in the same move, and the
host pays for it.


Definition 16.10 (The host). A guest is a program P of this chapter’s machine to-
gether with a state g of it (Definition 16.3). A host state h has six parts: its own
core core(h), its ledger µ(h), its own flag own(h), the guest program P(h) held as
a list of instructions, the guest state g(h), and the mirror m(h), a yes/no copy of
the guest’s flag. The host has two kinds of move. OWN i runs the instruction i
on the host’s own core, costs what this chapter’s machine charges for i, and raises
own exactly when that machine’s flag would rise. GSTEP b costs b. If the host’s
core is trapped it does nothing else. Otherwise it moves the host to its next line
and, if the guest’s next instruction costs at most b, runs that instruction on g(h);
in the same move the mirror becomes m(h) ∨ (¬cert( g(h)) ∧ cert( g′ )), where g′ is
the new guest state. The host’s reading is own(h) ∨ m(h). Its stored program is
U0 = [GSTEP 1; OWN (INC A); OWN (DEC A 1)]: one guest step, then two moves
that bring the host back to its first line.



                                           303
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Every instruction of the small machine costs at most one, so GSTEP 1 runs every
guest instruction there is. Why charge the budget b? Why not the cost of whatever
instruction got fetched? Because charging the budget keeps the price a function of the
move alone, which is what the certification system of Part II asks for: you read the
price of a host move off the move, the way you read the small machine’s prices off
its table, without peeking inside the guest. The bill for that is easy to see. A host that
steps a free guest instruction, an INC say, still pays one for the move.

So the host’s ledger is closer to a clock than to a receipt for its guests: one unit per
guest step, whatever the step was. It never falls behind the guest’s own bill (part (3)
of Theorem 16.37 below), and it matches that bill only when every guest step happens
to cost one. Could a cleverer host have simulation-exact accounting, a ledger equal
to its guest’s? This one fixed-price move cannot: GSTEP 1 is the same move whether
the guest’s next instruction is a free INC or a paid CHECK, so its one price cannot
match both. That does not rule out other primitive-step designs with different moves
or state-dependent prices. U achieves the match using ordinary instructions: it pays
only on the record moves it runs itself, so its ledger equals its guest’s (Theorem 16.30).

And one thing about the definition before the theorems, so you know which of them
carry weight. GSTEP runs the guest’s instruction by calling the small machine’s own
step on the guest’s state: the guest’s step is a primitive of the host. So “the host runs
any guest” (Theorem 16.35) is true by construction. The host was built to do exactly
that, and the proof is mostly unfolding. The theorems with something in them come
after it. From a loaded host, or any state where the two agree, the mirror always equals
the guest’s flag (Observation 16.36). Nothing raises the mirror unless the guest itself
passes a CERTIFY inside a guest step the host paid for (Theorem 16.38). No OWN
move, in any host program at all, touches the guest’s state or the mirror (the second
sentence of that same theorem), and no host move of either kind rewrites the guest’s
program. And the mirror is tied to the guest’s earned chain: after any host run from a
loaded host, if the mirror is up, the guest’s own run from its start contains a passing
CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same claim, then a CERTIFY. So this host runs any
guest by construction and keeps the guest’s record by theorem, as a copy of the guest’s
flag. The mirroring program U0 does not earn the host’s own flag; a different program
could do so with the host’s OWN CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY. U does both the
long way: it runs the guest with its own instructions, and it earns its own flag.


Theorem 16.35 (The host runs any guest). (1) If the host’s core is not trapped, then after
n moves GSTEP 1 the guest state is the guest program’s own run of n steps from g(h), the
guest program is unchanged, and the host is still not trapped. (2) If the host’s core is at line
1 and not trapped, then 3n steps of the program U0 leave the guest exactly where n steps of
its own program put it. (3) For every two-counter program M and inputs a, b: M halts from
(1, a, b) exactly when the host program made of OWN moves of the compiled M halts, from a
host whose core starts at ( a, b), whatever guest that host carries.


                                              304
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Proof. (1) Induction on n: a host that isn’t trapped stays untrapped through a guest
step, and with budget 1 the guest step is the guest’s own step. (2) One pass of U0
is a guest step, then INC A and DEC A back to line 1, so it is (1) once per pass. (3)
A host program made only of OWN moves is the small machine, core for core, and
Theorem 16.3 does the rest.


Observation 16.36 (The copy is the record). Say a host state h agrees when m(h) =
cert( g(h)). Every host move takes an agreeing state to an agreeing state, so every host trace
and every stored host program does too, and a freshly loaded host agrees. In particular, if h
agrees and is not trapped, the mirror after n moves GSTEP 1 is the guest’s flag after n steps of
its own program.

Proof. One move at a time. An OWN move touches neither the mirror nor the guest. A
trapped GSTEP touches neither. An untrapped one sets the mirror to the old mirror or
the crossing, and the guest’s flag is a latch (Theorem 16.5), so if the old mirror equalled
the old flag, the new mirror equals the new flag. The last sentence is this together with
Theorem 16.35.


Theorem 16.37 (The host’s step collects the guest’s toll). (1) If h agrees, is not trapped,
and the guest step that budget b allows takes the guest’s flag from down to up, then the mirror
is down before GSTEP b and up after it, the host’s ledger rose by exactly b, and b ≥ 1. (2) In
the run of (1) of Theorem 16.35, from a host that agrees, if the guest’s flag goes up between its
steps n and n + 1, the mirror goes up between the host’s moves n and n + 1, and that move
costs 1. (3) For every host trace t, µ( g(run(t, h))) + µ(h) ≤ µ(run(t, h)) + µ( g(h)): the
host’s ledger grows at least as fast as the guest’s.

Proof. (1) The guest’s flag rises only on a passing CERTIFY (Theorem 16.5), which costs
1, and the budget let it run, so b ≥ 1; the mirror was the guest’s flag, so it was down,
and the move sets it to the crossing. (2) is (1) at the matching move. (3) Induction on
t: a guest step that runs costs the guest at most the budget the host paid, and every
other move leaves the guest’s ledger alone.


Theorem 16.38 (No free host certification). If the mirror is down at h and up after a host
move i, then i is GSTEP b with b ≥ 1, the host was not trapped, the guest’s next instruction
was CERTIFY, and the guest’s flag went from down to up in that move. A trace made only
of OWN moves leaves the mirror and the guest state exactly where they were. And the host’s
own flag rises only by an OWN CERTIFY that passes on the host’s core.

Proof. An OWN move copies the mirror unchanged, and a trapped GSTEP does too,
so the rise is an untrapped GSTEP b whose guest step crossed; a crossing is a passing
CERTIFY, which costs 1 and needed the budget. The own flag moves by this chapter’s
step line.


                                              305
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Theorem 16.39 (The host is a Thiele machine). For every host state and move, if the host’s
reading goes from no to yes, the move costs at least 1; the same holds for the mirror alone and
for the own flag alone. So the host read through own ∨ m, the host read through m alone, and
the guest class are certification systems (Definition 3.1), and any host trace that raises the
host’s reading costs at least 1.

Proof. The mirror’s half is Theorem 16.38; the own flag’s half is the small machine’s
toll on the host’s core. The trace form is Section 3’s universal floor.


Remark 16.1 (Two guests, run). Load the guest CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is zero
A; CERTIFY; HALT with both counters at 0. After two moves GSTEP 1 the mirror is
down; after three it is up, the guest’s flag is up, the host’s own flag is still down, and
the host has paid 3. Under the program U0 the mirror is down at host step 6 and up
at step 7, with 3 paid. The guest CERTIFY; CERTIFY traps on its first step: after five
moves GSTEP 1 the mirror is down, the guest is trapped, and the host has paid 5 for
nothing.


That copy can’t be faked. The proof walks every host move there is, and the copy only
rises in a guest step where the guest itself ran CERTIFY and passed. A host program
that never touches the guest leaves the copy exactly where it was. From a loaded host
the copy always equals the guest’s flag, and the host’s ledger always grows at least
as fast as the guest’s, and a three-instruction loop runs any small-machine program
one guest step per pass. Here the mirror, the crossing test and the charge sit in the
host’s step rule, so Theorems 16.37 and 16.38 hold for every sequence of host moves,
including ones that never run a guest. That’s the simple version. Everything it gets
from its built-in move, U gets from ordinary instructions, plus an exact ledger and a
flag of its own.

16.16 The machine versus the program it runs
All three hosts in this chapter come down to one distinction, and it’s worth saying on
its own, because the two halves are easy to run together: the machine doing the stepping
(what the machine is) and the program it runs (what runs on it). The toll of Section 3 is
a property of the machine doing the stepping. A rule a program keeps holds as long
as the program keeps it.

Here’s the picture I keep for it. Play Monopoly on the counter of a real bank. The
game has a bank of its own, with its own rules, and one of them is printed in the
rules sheet: the Bank never goes broke, and if it runs out of money the Banker may
issue more by writing on any ordinary paper. Inside the game that’s fine; the players
agreed to it. The real bank’s teller, standing right there, has no opinion about any of it.
Push a thousand in Monopoly money across her counter and her ledger doesn’t move,
because her rules are about her own money. The game’s money is nothing to them.
The real bank is the machine doing the stepping. The game is a program it happens to


                                             306
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


be hosting. A rule that lives in the game holds as long as the players keep to it. A rule
that lives in the bank holds whatever the players do.

(And since the game is on the table: its box told an origin story for decades, that
an out-of-work salesman named Charles Darrow invented it during the Depression.
The board is older. Elizabeth Magie, an American writer and game designer with
an economic argument about land to make, patented The Landlord’s Game in 1904,
with a square track, railroads and a square that sends you to jail, and in 1902, in The
Single Tax Review, described it as “a practical demonstration of the present system
of land-grabbing with all its usual outcomes and consequences.” Darrow sold his
version to Parker Brothers in 1935, and the company bought Magie’s patent for a few
hundred dollars, five hundred by the accounts I found. A story told by the company
selling the product is a lead to check, every time. It changes nothing about banks. It’s
a good reminder of who writes the story on the box.)

A fixed machine can enforce an invariant in its own transition table, and that includes
a Turing machine. Give its tape a ledger track and a certification cell, and write a
table that never sets the cell without bumping the ledger: that machine obeys the
toll in its step relation. It’s an instance of the abstract certification system, so it can’t
be a counterexample to it. What it doesn’t do, built the ordinary way, is enforce
the toll on the programs it runs. A universal machine whose table was written only
to interpret carries the simulated certification bit as plain data on its tape. If the
host is programmable, so that other code shares that tape with the guest, any of that
code can flip the bit without paying, because the host’s step has no opinion about
it. So an ordinary programmable computer, as built, doesn’t enforce the toll for its
programs. That’s how it’s built. It could. The simpler host above enforces it by having
its own step mirror the guest’s bit and charge for its crossing (Observation 16.36 and
Theorem 16.38), and the universal programs U and UP are fixed tables that go one
better: they earn their own flag, by their own check, commit and certificate, exactly
when the guest’s would rise, and pay on their own ledger what the guest pays, U
exactly and UP to within a surcharge of at most two when the guest’s reading starts at
no (Theorems 16.31, 16.30, 16.33 and 16.34). That’s a statement about which reading a
step rule prices. It isn’t a claim that Turing machines can’t price one.

Computing ran into this exact gap in hardware, and how it got out is worth the detour.
In 1974 two computer scientists, Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg, asked when
a machine can run guests, a whole operating system inside another, efficiently and
safely. Their answer is one sentence you could check against any instruction set. Call
an instruction sensitive if it reads or changes the machine’s own settings, the things
the host has to keep for itself, and privileged if running it outside the host’s own mode
makes the machine stop and hand control to the host, which is called a trap. For the
kind of machine they modelled: if every sensitive instruction is privileged, a host can
be built. The guest runs at full speed, and whenever it touches something that matters,
the machine itself stops it and lets the host decide. That’s a host whose step has an


                                            307
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


opinion.

Then the obvious next question: did the machines people actually bought pass the
test? The most common one didn’t. In 2000 John Scott Robin, an Air Force officer, and
Cynthia Irvine, a computer-security researcher at the Naval Postgraduate School, went
through every instruction of Intel’s Pentium and found seventeen that are sensitive
and not privileged; POPF, which loads the processor’s flags, is the one usually pointed
at. A guest could run them and the host would never hear about it. The fixes came
two ways: VMware rewrote the guest’s code on the fly so the troublesome instructions
never ran as written, and in the middle of the 2000s Intel and AMD added hardware
support so they’d trap. Does that change anything here? Not the theorems. Popek and
Goldberg were after speed and isolation. A record and a price weren’t their question,
so their result isn’t mine and mine isn’t theirs. It changes the picture, though. The
universal programs sit where they’d want a host to sit: the host’s own steps collect
each guest’s toll and earn each guest’s record again. And an industry learned the same
lesson the expensive way: a rule binds the guest only if it lives in the step underneath.

The smallest version of “a ledger beside an ordinary machine” is a Turing machine
configuration with a counter next to it, where each step adds one, plus one more if it
writes a nonblank symbol. The counter doesn’t disturb the machine.


Theorem 16.40 (A counter beside a Turing machine changes nothing). Let a Turing
machine with transition table δ step a configuration c to tmn (δ, c) after at most n steps
(stopping when δ has no entry). Pair each configuration with a counter, and step the pair by
stepping the configuration and adding the step’s charge. Then for every n, δ and pair (c, m),
the configuration part after at most n steps of the pair is tmn (δ, c). In particular this holds
from (c, 0).

Proof. By induction on n. For n = 0 both sides are c. For n + 1, if δ has no entry at
c, both runs stop and both sides are c. Otherwise the pair steps to (c′ , m′ ) where c′ is
exactly the Turing machine’s next configuration, whatever m′ is, and the induction
hypothesis at (c′ , m′ ) finishes it.

The construction here is a Turing configuration paired with a number. It isn’t a Thiele
machine in this book’s sense, so it does not establish a Thiele simulation of Turing
machines. A counter beside a machine is the scorekeeper’s tally from Section 3: honest
about the machine, and kept by whoever holds the pencil.

One limit on all of this, so it isn’t read as more. Certification is one event. Other kinds
of observable a machine might carry would each need their own event, their own
evidence and their own cost law, and nothing here supplies those.




                                              308
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


16.17 Parts II and III, run on this machine
Parts II and III proved their counts and their collisions for any system with the named
pieces, and they left a promise: that the machine of this part would be put through
them. Here it is. The eight-state machine of Section 4 gets run by the small machine,
price for price. Structural entitlement, the count of what narrowing a list of rivals costs,
is proved for every Thiele-complete machine, with the small machine as a worked
member, a larger search on the host that has a counter for every number, and a run
that shows the count’s one awkward hypothesis, the covering, can’t be dropped. And
the time a check saves gets an exact exchange rate, for the part of the machine that
has no record. (The no-bare-verifier result is in Section 7, next to the collision it comes
from.)

The eight-state machine, run by the small machine. Look at the small machine
through a window that shows two things: its line number read modulo four, which
I’ll call its slot (the eight-state machine’s word from Section 4, unrelated to U’s slot
registers), and its flag. Call a state live when its trap latch is down, the fact “A ≥ 0”
about A’s current version is in its table, and its channel holds a commitment, which is
what CERTIFY needs in order to run.


Definition 16.11 (The eight-state machine, compiled). Stamp is the single instruction
CERTIFY. Next-slot is the single instruction INC B. Jump to slot a, for a one of 0, 1, 2, 3,
is the four instructions COMMIT (A ≥ 0) A; COMMIT (A ≥ 0) A; INC B; DEC B a.
The setup is the two instructions CHECK (A ≥ 0) A; COMMIT (A ≥ 0) A.


The two COMMITs in a jump change nothing but the line and the channel, and each
costs one, which is where the jump’s price of two comes from. The INC makes B
positive, so the DEC takes one off and jumps to line a for nothing, and B is back where
it was.


Theorem 16.41 (The small machine runs the eight-state machine). (1) For every live
state s and every move m of the eight-state machine, running m’s instructions from s ends in
a live state whose window is the eight-state machine’s step of s’s window by m, and the ledger
has risen by exactly m’s charge: one for stamp, two for jump, zero for next-slot. (2) The same
holds for any list of moves: the window after the compiled list is the eight-state machine’s run
of the list, the state is live, and the ledger has risen by the sum of the charges. (3) So a run of
compiled moves from a live state that takes the flag from down to up has raised the ledger by
at least one. (4) From any start ( a, b), the setup ends in a live state with window (slot 3, flag
down) and the ledger at 2; after it, any compiled list runs as on the eight-state machine from
(slot 3, flag down), with the ledger at 2 plus the sum of the charges; and if the flag is up at the
end, the whole run, setup included, contains the earned chain of Theorem 16.9.

Proof. (1) By cases on the move. On a live state CERTIFY runs, because a committed


                                               309
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


claim is on the channel; it raises the flag, moves the line on by one and charges one.
INC B moves the line on by one and charges nothing, and it touches only B and B’s
version, so the fact about A and the commitment stand and the state stays live. In a
jump, each COMMIT finds its fact in the table and succeeds, charging one, and the
INC and the DEC are free and end at line a, whose slot is a; the flag isn’t touched.
(2) is (1) over the list, by induction. (3) The eight-state machine’s own toll (Section 4)
says a run of its moves that takes the flag from down to up is charged at least one,
and (2) carries that charge across. (4) CHECK (A ≥ 0) passes at every value of A and
the COMMIT after it passes, which takes line 1 to line 3, slot 3, with two marks paid;
then (2) applies. A raised flag was raised by a CERTIFY, and Theorem 16.9 gives the
chain.

Three reservations, said now. The setup’s claim is true of every value, so its CHECK
can’t fail; it’s there because the small machine won’t CERTIFY without a checked,
committed claim. It isn’t there as a test. And the jump’s price of two is two paid
COMMITs, a choice a program makes that the machine allows and doesn’t force. The
window is a projection, too: the small machine’s full state keeps far more than eight
states’ worth.

And the whole small machine isn’t the eight-state piece it runs. It merges some states
for free.


Theorem 16.42 (The small machine’s merges). (1) A move of the small machine that takes
the flag from down to up is CERTIFY; CERTIFY merges two different full states into one (a
state with the flag down and the same state with the flag up land on the same state), and it
costs at least one. (2) DEC A 2 also merges two different full states, and it costs nothing. So it
is false of the small machine that every move that merges is priced.

Proof. (1) Only CERTIFY changes the flag, and it costs one. The two states with the
flag down and up, and a committed claim, are the same state after CERTIFY. (2) Take a
core at line 1 with A at 1 at version 0, and the same core with A at 0 at version 1. DEC
A 2 takes the first to A = 0 at version 1, line 2, a write; it takes the second to line 2
with A still 0 at version 1, because DEC on zero is no write. Same state, price zero.

It’s the same fact as the last item of the list of what this machine doesn’t do, which
comes near the end of this chapter, now with names: the chairs argument needs a
price on every merge, this machine’s schedule puts the floor on the flag only, and
that’s why the eight-state piece is a piece. The record layer closes the rest: asked
only of merges between states with the same line and counters, the merge premise
holds for this machine’s own prices and forces the toll on it with no finiteness premise
(Theorem 4.15).

Structural entitlement, for every Thiele-complete machine. Theorem 8.3 was about



                                               310
The Thiele Machine                                                                      Devon Thiele


any certification system and handed the run’s payments in as a bill. For a Thiele-
complete machine (Definition 16.7) the bill is known. Call the CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY moves of a run its record moves; each costs exactly one, so the ledger rises by
the number of record moves, and clause (b) says what a raised record must contain.


Theorem 16.43 (Structural entitlement represented). Let a machine be Thiele-complete
through an interface. Take a clean start s0 and a run t from it; a type of rivals and a type of
observations with an exact equality test; an observation obs and a representative observation
r of each rival; a decoder d from runs to observations; lists Ω, Ω′ of rivals and a decision tree
T. Suppose (M1) Ω′ strictly narrows Ω, as in Theorem 8.3, and (M2) some dropped rival
shows an observation different from every survivor’s; (M3) the run ends with the record up
and the decoded run d(t) is shown by some survivor; (M4) depth( T ) is at most the number
of record moves in t; (M5) |Ω′ | > 0; and (M6) the covering is by fibres: there is a map F
from rivals to lists of rivals such that every rival x of Ω lies in F (u) for some survivor u with
r ( x ) = r (u), the lengths of the lists F (u) over the survivors add up to at least |Ω|, and no
F (u) is longer than L( T ). Then (1) the membership test of Ω′ is strictly stronger than that
of Ω; (2) t contains the earned chain of clause (b), with the meaning of the claim true at the
CHECK and at the COMMIT; (3) ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ is at most the number of record
moves of t; (4) the number of record moves of t is exactly the ledger’s rise; and (5) the ledger
rose by at least 3.

Proof. (1) is Theorem 8.3(1). (2) Clause (b) applied to a run from a clean state that ends
with the record up gives the chain, and a passing check means the claim’s meaning
holds, which keeps holding while the thing it’s about is unchanged. (3) The fibres
cover: summing their lengths gives |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |, and Theorem 8.3’s count finishes
it, with the record moves, which are the paid steps, in place of the charged steps. (4) is
clause (c) added up. (5) is Theorem 16.19(3).

It’s a checklist, as I said in Section 8, and the small print is the same kind. (M3)’s
second half feeds no conclusion: only the record’s being up is used. (M1) is used only
for the inclusion. Its gap feeds nothing. And the first clause of (M6), the representative
observation, isn’t used by the count either. What the machine adds to Theorem 8.3
is conclusions (2), (4) and (5): the payment is the machine’s own three acts, each at
exactly one, and a raised record carries the earned chain.

Two further statements, about the run’s own questions and about the record clause.


Theorem 16.44 (A floor with no supplied tree). Take a machine and an interface that
meets the exact-toll clause (c) of Definition 16.7, so each record act costs exactly one. Call the
questions of a run the claims of its CHECK moves, and say two rival states answer alike
when every one of those claims gets the same verdict at both (each verdict taken at the rival
itself, as it starts; the states the run passed through don’t enter). If, for a list Ω of rival states
and a number m > 0, the rivals of Ω that answer alike with any one rival, itself included, are


                                                 311
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


never more than m, then ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 m⌉ is at most the number of CHECK moves of
the run, which is at most its number of record moves, which is the ledger’s rise.

Proof. A run’s questions give each rival an answer list, and answer lists are lists of
Booleans of length equal to the number of CHECK moves, so there are at most 2c
answer classes among the rivals, c the number of CHECK moves. The classes have at
most m members each, so |Ω| ≤ 2c · m, and the rounded logarithms follow. The rest is
clause (c).

The tree has gone: it is the run’s own questions. There are limits, and they’re the ones
in the statement. The verdicts are taken at the rivals as they start. The states the run
had reached when it asked don’t come into it, and a free branch, DEC on zero, can still
narrow a list for nothing. So this prices a narrowing that the paid checks explain, and
no more.

The next statement takes the verdicts where the run took them. A rival is a state the
run could have started from; a CHECK the run passed is asked of a rival by running
the moves before it from the rival and checking the same claim at the state that reaches.
Nothing is supplied but the prior.


Theorem 16.45 (Structural entitlement, with the narrowing made by the run). Let a
machine be Thiele-complete through an interface. Take a clean start s0 , a run t from it that
ends with the record up, and a list Ω of rival starts that contains s0 . Let the posterior Ω′ be the
rivals that pass every CHECK t passed, each asked as above, in the order t made them, and let
bi and ai be the numbers of rivals standing just before and just after the ith. Then (1) Ω′ sits
inside Ω and contains s0 ; (2) every rival of Ω that isn’t in Ω′ fails, asked that way, a CHECK
that t made and passed; (3) |Ω| · ∏i ai = |Ω′ | · ∏i bi ; (4) if every CHECK t passed keeps at
least a 2−k share of the rivals standing before it, bi ≤ 2k ai , then ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ is
at most k times the number of CHECKs t passed, that number is at most the record moves of t,
the record moves are the ledger’s rise, and so the index bits are at most k times the ledger’s rise;
(5) t contains the earned chain and the ledger rose by at least 3; and (6) with no share assumed,
the index bits are at most the sum over the CHECKs t passed of ⌈log2 ⌈bi /ai ⌉⌉.

Proof. (1) The run passes its own checks from s0 , and a rival is kept only if it passes
them all. (2) A rival dropped failed one of the tests, and each test is a CHECK of t at
the prefix where it passed. (3) Each test turns a standing list of bi into one of ai , and
the products telescope. (4) Each test keeps at least bi /2k , so |Ω| ≤ 2kn |Ω′ | with n the
number of tests, and the rounded logarithms follow. The tests are among the run’s
CHECK moves, which are record moves, and clause (c) makes the record moves the
ledger’s rise. (5) is clause (b) and Theorem 16.19(3). (6) is (4) with 2k replaced at the
ith test by the smallest power of two at least ⌈bi /ai ⌉; every ai is positive because s0 is
never dropped.



                                                312
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Part (3) is the exact form of “index bits are the sum of what each test took”: take
base-two logarithms and log2 |Ω| − log2 |Ω′ | is the sum of log2 (bi /ai ). Parts (4) and
(6) are what survives rounding to whole bits. Here the run does the narrowing, every
candidate dropped was dropped by a check the run paid for, and what stays a premise
is the prior and the share. The share can’t go.


Proposition 16.46 (One CHECK can take four bits). Take the sixteen starts ( a, 0) with
a = 0, . . . , 15, and the run CHECK (A ≥ 15) A; COMMIT (A ≥ 15) A; CERTIFY from
(15, 0). It raises the record. Its one passing CHECK keeps one rival of sixteen, so the posterior
is (15, 0) alone and the index bits are 4, while the run has 3 record moves. So index bits at
most the record moves, the bound of Theorem 16.45(4) read with k = 1, fails here.


The share here is 2−4 , and with k = 4 part (4) reads 4 ≤ 4. It’s the example of Section 8
that showed the covering can’t be dropped, seen from the run’s side: one test can take
many bits, and the bill covers the bits per test times the tests.


Theorem 16.47 (What the record adds). Let a machine be Thiele-complete through an
interface. (1) From a clean start, the record is up at the end of a run exactly when the run
contains the earned chain, and a run with the record up raised the ledger by at least 3. (2)
Conclusions (1), (3) and (4) of Theorem 16.43 hold without a clean start and without the record
being up, for a machine that only meets the exact-toll clause (c): the hypotheses (M1), (M2),
(M4), (M5) and (M6), and the decoded run being shown by some survivor, are all it needs.


So the record doesn’t make narrowing cost more. It adds the earned chain and a floor
of 3, and that’s all it adds: a run meeting the same counting and payment hypotheses
is still bound by that index-bit floor even if it never raises the record, and the floor of
3 no longer applies to it.

Weights, and the partition form. Two more pieces of the same count. First, suppose the
rivals aren’t equally many: give each a whole-number weight, a multiplicity, and call
the sum of the weights of a list its mass. The count survives with masses in place of
lengths. If the prior’s mass is at most L( T ) times the posterior’s, the rounded index
bits of the two masses differ by at most depth( T ); so for any certification system a
run that paid at least that many charged steps has a bill at least the drop, and for a
Thiele-complete machine the representation theorem goes through with masses and
the same five conclusions. On such a machine the ledger rises by the same number
from every start, the number of record moves, so the weighted sum of ledger rises
is the prior’s mass times the record moves, and the drop in rounded bits times that
mass is at most the weighted sum. Dividing by a positive total mass would give an
expected rise; the statement here leaves the weights unnormalized. The weights are
whole numbers, cross-multiplied, and no probability enters. Second, the covering by
fibres has a plainer form that doesn’t need the clause that the fibres add up to the prior.


                                              313
The Thiele Machine                                                                      Devon Thiele


Say the rivals are partitioned by the representative observation when every rival looks
like some survivor under it and no observation class, counted inside the prior, has
more than L( T ) members. The fibre lengths then add up to at least the prior, because
every rival is in the class of some survivor, so a partition gives the covering, and the
count holds under it. The converse is false: there are coverings that aren’t partitions.

A worked member on the small machine. Eight rivals: the starts ( a, b) with a ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}
and b ∈ {0, 1}, counter A at a and counter B at b. The run is CHECK (Even) A; CHECK
(A ≥ 2) A; COMMIT (A ≥ 2) A; CERTIFY, from (2, 0). The program raises the flag
from a rival exactly when a is even and at least 2, so exactly from (2, 0) and (2, 1),
and the posterior is those two. The decoder reads one “passed” for each CHECK in
the run’s receipts; the representative observation is “B is 0,” which isn’t constant; the
fibres are the four rivals that share B; the tree is the complete tree of depth 2.


Proposition 16.48 (The eight-start member). For every a and b, the run raises the flag
from ( a, b) exactly when a is even and at least 2. All hypotheses of Theorem 16.43 hold, with
eight rivals narrowed to two: the test of the posterior is strictly stronger; the index bits are
3 − 1 = 2; the run has 4 record moves and the ledger rises by exactly 4; and the earned chain
is in the run. The run’s own questions (Theorem 16.44) are its 2 CHECKs, so the floor is met
with equality. With the two CHECKs alone, the record stays down, the ledger rises by 2, and
the bound 2 ≤ 2 still holds.


It’s a real narrowing. The cups of Section 8 aren’t sitting under it in a costume, and
the posterior is exactly the set of rivals the run certifies, so here a proof ties the lists
to the run. Nobody supplies them. Read with Theorem 16.45, the run’s two passing
CHECKs, replayed from the eight rivals, leave four and then two, the same two, so
the posterior is the one the run makes; each keeps half, so k = 1, and the index bits, 2,
are at most 1 · 2 and at most the ledger’s rise of 4.

A search through n bits. The same shape at a size you can’t enumerate, on the machine
of Definition 16.8, the one with a counter for every number, with the small machine’s
property language of Zero, Even and At-least-n, read at registers, in place of Slot. That
machine is Thiele-complete too. Hide n = k + m bits, one in each of registers 0 to n − 1.
The program asks k questions, one per bit of the first k: CHECK “at least 1” of register
i for a 1, CHECK “is 0” for a 0. Then it COMMITs the first claim and CERTIFYs. The
prior is every n-bit value; the posterior is the 2m values that begin with the answers;
the tree is the complete tree of depth k.


Theorem 16.49 (A search through n bits). For 1 ≤ k ≤ 16 and any m: from a world
holding a value v of at least k bits, the program certifies exactly when v begins with its answers,
so the posterior is exactly the set of rivals it certifies from; the test of the posterior is strictly
stronger than the prior’s; the earned chain is in the run; the prior has 2k+m members and the
posterior 2m , so the index bits are exactly k; the run has exactly k + 2 record moves and the


                                                 314
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


ledger rises by exactly k + 2; and the run’s own questions are k CHECKs, so Theorem 16.44 is
met with equality. With the COMMIT and the CERTIFY left off, the questions alone narrow
2k+m values to 2m , the record stays down, and the ledger rises by exactly k. And no run from a
clean start that raises the record contains more than 16 CHECKs before its CERTIFY, so with
17 questions no start certifies.

Proof. Each question is a CHECK of whether one register holds a given bit, which
passes exactly when it does; a failing CHECK traps. So the program certifies exactly
when every answer is right, which is when v begins with the answers. The counting is
the count of bit strings, and the representation theorem applies with every hypothesis
a theorem. The cap is the fact table: it holds sixteen facts, never evicts, and a CHECK
on a full table traps (Theorem 16.13), so a seventeenth CHECK before the CERTIFY
ends the run in a trap.

The sixteen belongs to the machine. The program has no say in it: it’s the same ceiling
as the item “Sixteen checks per run, ever” in the list of what the machine doesn’t do,
near the end of this chapter, and it’s why this search has k ≤ 16 however many bits are
hidden. Unasked bits can be any number. The lists, the tree and the fibres are supplied
here, as in the representation theorem, and tied to the run only for this member. The
covering still prices only the size of the drop. Its reason goes unpriced.

The covering can’t be dropped. It’s a hypothesis, and one might hope it’s a nuisance one
could remove. It isn’t, and the small machine shows it. Fix n ≥ 4, take the 2n starts
with A below 2n as the rivals, and run the three-move chain on the claim “A ≥ 2n − 1”:
CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY. It certifies exactly from A = 2n − 1, so the posterior
is one start, n index bits are gone, and the ledger rose by 3. So for n ≥ 4 the claim
“the index-bit drop is at most the ledger’s rise” is false for this run, and no tree of
depth at most 3 covers the narrowing, whatever the representative observation. One
property with a big constant in it carries n bits in a single yes-or-no question; what the
bound prices is a narrowing whose classes are balanced, a tree with enough leaves. A
narrowing of any other shape is outside it.

The time a check saves. The question is whether counter A is at least m. There are
two ways to find out. The free way uses base moves only, INC and DEC, which cost
nothing. But a base move reads A one unit at a time: a DEC takes a unit off A or finds
it empty. After n moves, a run that started with A at least n has never seen A empty,
so it can’t have behaved differently for different such A except by a constant shift in
A itself. The paid way is one CHECK (A ≥ m): one move, a ledger of one, and the
line it ends on says which way it went. Certifying the answer takes the whole chain,
CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY.


Theorem 16.50 (The time tax). (1) No program of two-counter instructions that runs fewer
than m moves has its final line number and its final B determine whether A ≥ m at every



                                             315
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


start; in particular none tells A = m − 1 from A = m. (2) A program of m DEC/INC pairs
(a ladder: DEC A and on success go on to the next pair, otherwise INC B) decides it in exactly
m moves, from the line number and B, and costs 0. (3) Executed as a three-move trace from
start( a, b), the paid chain raises the flag exactly when a ≥ m and has a ledger of exactly 3,
whatever m is. As a stored program it pays 3 on success and stops after its first failed CHECK
with a ledger of 1. (4) A single CHECK (A ≥ m) decides it in one move from the line number,
with a ledger of exactly 1, whatever m is. (5) So if a ledger unit is worth λ moves, the paid
route to deciding costs 1 + λ and the free route costs at least m, and the paid route is cheaper
exactly when 1 + λ < m; the paid route to certifying costs 3 + 3λ.

Proof. (1) Take the starts (m − 1, b) and (m, b). When n < m both have A ≥ n, so in
the first n moves no DEC finds A empty in either run, and the two runs differ only by
the shift of one unit in A. They end at the same line with the same B, though A ≥ m
holds of one and not the other. (2) Run the ladder: each pair either takes a unit off A
and moves on, or finds A empty and falls through to the INC. The line after m moves
is 2m + 1 exactly when all m units were there. It’s all DEC and INC, so it costs 0. (3) is
the price table: CHECK (A ≥ m) passes exactly when A ≥ m, a failing CHECK traps
and the flag stays down, and the three moves cost three. (4) is the same price table
with one instruction: a passing CHECK goes on to the next line and a failing one traps.
(5) is arithmetic on (1) to (4).

The certifying comparison is 3 + 3λ < m; the deciding comparison 1 + λ < m is
arithmetic on the free lower bound and the one-move decider. The exchange is sharper
than a comparison of two particular programs: the free side is a lower bound over
every program of INC and DEC, so no choice of program is involved, and the paid
side is constant. The limits: the bound is for programs that make no record move, INC
and DEC with falling off the end as stopping. It doesn’t cover every Thiele-complete
machine, because the definition doesn’t forbid a base move that changes a counter by
more than one unit, and such a machine is a different machine, one the bound doesn’t
speak for. And the two routes put their answers in different places, the free one in
the line number and the paid one in the flag; this compares two ways to answer one
question. It doesn’t compare two certifications.

16.18 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs
Section 13 left the diagonal standing on any substrate and on a little family built to fit
it, reproved it on L, handled on its own terms rather than as a substrate, and said what
a machine has to supply to fill in the same shape, two things: programs that can be
handed to programs as numbers, and a recursion theorem for the transformations it
can carry out. This machine’s universal program reads a whole guest program out of
one register, with a numbering of programs that goes there and back (Definition 16.9),
and halting is undecidable here in the reduction sense of Theorem 16.4. What’s left are
the two classical results that turn a universal machine into a place where the diagonal
bites: Rice’s theorem and Kleene’s recursion theorem. They come with a wrinkle I


                                              316
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


should put first, because it decides which machine they’re about.

The wrinkle is the one from earlier in this chapter, at the end of the subsection on what
two counters compute. The small machine takes its inputs straight into two counters,
and Schroeppel’s memo gives a proof that two plain counters can’t even compute 2n
from n. Rice’s reduction has to keep a program’s input safe while a copy of a halting
instance runs. Kleene’s construction has to run an evaluator while keeping its input.
Two counters have nowhere to keep it. So the two theorems land where they’re true
and where I could prove them. The host machine of Definition 16.8, the one with a
counter for every number that U runs on, is a fine programming system: its programs
are numbers, an input sits in register 1, and there’s room to spare. On it both theorems
hold in full. On the two-counter machine itself the story splits, and I’ll tell it at the
end of the subsection: Rice’s theorem holds on every input, by a trick for keeping the
input that I’ll show you; Kleene’s holds when inputs are written as powers of two, the
way Minsky packed them; and on plain inputs Kleene’s is false, and that’s a theorem
too.

The host machine’s programs are numbered the way U numbers a guest’s. Write
⟨m, n⟩ for (2n + 1) · 2m . INC r is ⟨0, r ⟩, DEC r j is ⟨1, ⟨r, j⟩⟩, HALT is ⟨2, 0⟩, CHECK r is
⟨3, r ⟩, COMMIT r is ⟨4, r ⟩, CERTIFY is ⟨5, 0⟩, and a program is the list code: the empty
program is 0, and an instruction x followed by a program t is ⟨ x, code(t)⟩. Every
number decodes to some program, and decoding a program’s code gives the program
back. Say a host program outputs y on input x when, started with x in register 1 and
every other register 0, with a clean table, it halts with y in register 0.

Rice first, because it’s the shorter road. Henry Rice, whom you met in Section 7,
proved in his 1951 doctoral thesis, and published in 1953, that no program decides any
property of what programs do unless every program has it or none does. Properties
of how a program is written aren’t covered. The road from halting is a single detour.
Take a property of what programs do, a program y that has it, and a program n that
doesn’t. Given an instance of two-counter halting, a Minsky program H with starting
counters a and b, build a host program that first loads a and b into two fresh registers,
then runs a copy of H moved onto those registers, then empties both, then runs y. If H
halts on ( a, b) the built program behaves like y and has the property. If H runs forever
the built program never stops on any input, and it behaves like the program that loops,
which lacks the property (if the looping program has it instead, swap the roles of y and
n). Everything the built program does before y is INC and DEC, which pay nothing
and touch no fact, channel, trap latch or flag. So a decider for the property would be
a decider for halting, with the consequence stated in Theorem 16.4: the complement
of single-tape Turing-machine halting would become something a program could list,
the same reduction sense of “undecidable” as Theorem 16.4. Two words carry the
weight, and they’re the ones to check in the statement: what “behaves the same” sees,
and where the program starts.



                                             317
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


Definition 16.12 (Behaving the same, on the host). A host program ends in a state
when it halts there, from the start with x in register 1 and the rest clean; a trap counts
as stopping. Two host programs behave the same when for every input x, any state one
ends in has a state the other ends in that agrees with it on every register’s value, the
fact table, the channel, the trap latch, the ledger and the flag, and the same the other
way round. The line number and the versions aren’t compared. A property of host
programs is extensional when behaving the same carries it from one program to the
other.


Theorem 16.51 (Rice’s theorem on the host machine). Let Π be an extensional property
of host programs that some program has and some program lacks. Then Π is undecidable in
the reduction sense of Theorem 16.4.

Proof. The reduction above. The prefix before y leaves every register but the two fresh
ones as it found them, and empties those, so when H halts the built program ends in
whatever state y ends in from the same input, with the same ledger, table, channel, trap
and flag. When H doesn’t halt, the built program stops on no input. The reduction is
from the complement of halting, so no excluded middle is needed; the proof splits on
the decider’s own answer for the looping program.

A property that depends only on the partial function a program computes, whether
it stops and what it leaves in register 0, is extensional, so it is covered. That case also
follows from the recursion theorem below.

On the small machine itself the same road works from the clean start, and only from
there. Say two two-counter programs behave the same from the clean start when, what-
ever state one halts in from counters (0, 0), the other halts in a state with the same
counters, trap latch, ledger and flag, and the same the other way round. The fact table
isn’t compared, because the prefix moves the versions of A and B by fixed amounts
and the facts carry versions. There is no input to keep, since the program starts at
(0, 0), and H’s instance is loaded straight into A and B.


Theorem 16.52 (Rice’s theorem for the small machine, from the clean start). Let Π be a
property of two-counter programs that’s carried from a program to any program that behaves
the same from the clean start, held by some program and lacked by some other. Then Π is
undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 16.4. In particular “halts from the clean start”
is undecidable.


That’s the clean start only. Every input is harder, because the standard reduction has
to keep the input safe while the halting instance runs, and two counters have nowhere
obvious to keep it. The way through is at the end of the subsection.

Kleene’s recursion theorem is the deeper one, and it’s a construction, which is Sec-


                                             318
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


tion 13’s point about Kleene’s little gem (Moschovakis’s phrase): the content is the
building, and the contradiction in Section 13 was just the last line. It says: for every
transformation F of programs that some program can carry out on numbers, there’s a
program p that computes the same thing as F ( p). The shape of the building is the old
one. From the program that carries out F, build an evaluator that reads a number, treats
it as a program’s code, specialises that program to its own code, runs F’s program
on the result, and runs whatever program comes back. The specialising step is what
logicians call s-m-n: fix one input of a program and get a new program that needs one
input fewer. Then the witness is the evaluator specialised to its own code. Run on any
input, it builds its own code, hands it to F’s program, gets the code of F ( p), and runs
that.

Here’s each piece on the host machine, with its exact premise.


Theorem 16.53 (s-m-n, and a universal program for host programs). (1) For a number c
and a host program V, let spec(c, V ) be c copies of INC 2 followed by V with its jumps moved
to follow them. Then for all x, y, spec(c, V ) outputs y on input x if and only if V, started with
x in register 1 and c in register 2, halts with y in register 0. (2) There is a host program W
made only of INC, DEC and HALT such that, for all c, x, y, W started with x in register 1 and
c in register 2 halts with y in register 0 exactly when the host program numbered c outputs y
on input x.

Proof. (1) The prefix writes register 2 c times and nothing else, so it moves that reg-
ister’s version from 0 to c. A fact records a version, so after the prefix every later
version of register 2, and the version in every fact the run records about register 2,
is c more than in a clean run. A CHECK or a COMMIT reads versions only to ask
whether two versions of the same register are equal, and adding c to both keeps the
answer, so the two runs take the same steps. The run is V’s run from the stated start,
moved down by c lines. (2) is the evaluator. A finite algorithm decodes a number into
a program, runs it step by step on given registers, and, searching over the number of
steps, returns the output of the first halting run. Appendix F implements this search
with a finite counter program. The host runs those INC and DEC instructions on the
required registers, with HALT marking the returned output. This supplies W.

Be exact about one thing: U is not that universal program. U runs two-counter guests,
and a two-counter guest given its input plainly can’t run the evaluator. With inputs
written as powers of two one can, as Theorem 16.59 near the end of this subsection
shows. W runs host programs, and it can, because it’s a host program on a machine
with registers.


Theorem 16.54 (Kleene’s recursion theorem on the host machine). (1) For every host
program T there is a host program e such that for all x, y: e outputs y on input x if and only if,
for some d, T outputs d on the number of e, and the program numbered d outputs y on x. (2)


                                               319
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


So for every transformation F of host programs that some host program carries out on numbers
(on the number of p it outputs the number of F ( p), for every p), there is a host program e such
that for all x, y, e outputs y on x if and only if F (e) does. (3) The same on numbers: for every
function f on numbers that some host program computes, some number e has the program
numbered e and the program numbered f (e) output the same on every input.

Proof. (1) Let E be the following program of INC and DEC, built the same way as W
from one finite evaluator, with T’s number t written in. On inputs x and c it computes
the number of spec(c, Pc ), where Pc is the program numbered c, runs T on that number
to get d, and then runs the program numbered d on x. Let c0 be the number of E, and
let e = spec(c0 , E). By (1) of Theorem 16.53, e on input x does what E does on x and
c0 . And E on c0 builds the number of spec(c0 , Pc0 ), which is the number of e, since Pc0
is E. So e hands its own number to T, gets d, and runs d on x. (2) and (3) are (1) with T
carrying out F or f .

That fixed point is of the function: e and F (e) stop on the same inputs and leave the
same number in register 0. Their ledgers, flags and fact tables can differ, because the
marks e pays are the evaluator’s. I’d like a fixed point that agrees on the record too,
and the next two theorems say how much of that can be had. The ledger and the flag
can be had. Every register can’t.


Theorem 16.55 (The recursion theorem, up to the record). Let F be a transformation of
host programs that some host program T carries out on numbers. Then there is a host program
e such that, for every input x, any state e ends in has a state F (e) ends in that agrees with it on
register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of facts in the table, and whether the
channel is empty, and the same the other way round. So e stops on x exactly when F (e) does,
and the ledgers are equal exactly, with no surcharge. T may itself check, commit and certify.

Proof. The construction is Theorem 16.54’s, with a different evaluator. The first step
is to see that a record is small. From a clean start, a host program that stops has a
record I can read off five numbers, in this order: what it left in register 0; how many
facts the table holds; what is left of the ledger once the facts, the trap and the flag
are paid for, which I’ll call the replay allowance; 1 if the flag is up and 0 if not; and
1 if the trap latch is up and 0 if not. The record obeys a short rulebook. The table
holds at most sixteen facts. The latch is a single bit. A commit needs a fact behind it, a
certify needs a commit, and the channel is empty exactly when the replay allowance
is zero. The ledger is the facts, plus that allowance, plus the flag, plus the trap. The
allowance includes repeated CERTIFYs as well as COMMITs; it counts marks the
replay can spend on commitments, not the original commitment events. Those are the
only properties of a record the replay will use, and I proved them by following the
plain machine alongside the real one, one step at a time.

The second step is five blocks, one for each number. Each block reads the code of T,


                                                320
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


runs T on the number of the specialised program, runs the program that comes out on
x, and returns its number. All of that happens on plain data: the blocks are programs
of INC and DEC, built the way W was, from an evaluator expressed as a term of L and
translated to Minsky programs. So if T has marks of its own, they are simulated and
never paid.

The third step is the payment. The evaluator puts 1 in a fresh register, which satisfies
the host’s one property, and CHECKs it once for every fact. It COMMITs to that claim
