19.1 Taking the coat off
The first executable is generated from the formal definitions. The second is written
separately from the same specification. Both implement the small machine, the host
with a register for every whole number, the host with PAY, the universal programs
and the loaders. The compiler below has an executable runner too.

Whole numbers matter here. Machine words in one build are 63 bits wide, while the
guest codes U reads go up near 2100 , so ordinary fixed-width arithmetic would wrap
around. The mathematical machine has no such overflow. Its executable therefore
uses unbounded integers, with arithmetic chosen to match the definitions: subtrac-
tion stops at zero and division by zero returns zero. The mappings, compilers and
input/output routines remain implementation dependencies; testing them does not
change the mathematical definitions.

19.2 A second machine, written by hand, to check the first
A run shows what a build did on those inputs. Comparing two implementations step
by step can expose a disagreement with the specification; agreement on tested runs
leaves other runs open.

They’re compared on the whole state after every step: the program line, every counter
and register and its version, the fact table in order, the channel, the trap latch, the


                                         342
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


ledger and the flag. The comparison covers exhaustive sets of short programs, random
programs, both hosts and the small guests listed below. They agree on every tested
step. I also broke the machine on purpose, giving it a fact table one too small, a
free CHECK, a commitment that ignores versions, and a write that doesn’t bump the
version, and each break gets caught. A second set pins the boundaries this book draws
in words, and those runs come out as the words say: two runs that end in the same
state with different first certifications, a check that can’t fail certifying from every start,
six commitments billing seven without a flag, a write after the commitment and a flag
over a claim that’s now false, sixteen copies of one CHECK filling the table, a CERTIFY
costing one at a ledger already at two, and a merge between two yes-states that leaves
the entering state alone.

A shared mistake can survive both implementations. The comparison doesn’t test
whether the definitions say the right thing, since both implementations follow them.
That’s what having the definitions and arguments on the page is for.

19.3 U on a real guest
Now the universal program, which is where I expected trouble. The guest I wanted
to run first was the obvious one, a guest that goes the whole way: CHECK, COMMIT,
CERTIFY, flag up, run inside U on the built machine. Here’s why that’s not what ran.
U keeps the whole guest program as one number, a number that grows like two raised
to the sum of the codes for the guest’s instructions (for a guest of one instruction it’s
exactly a power of two), and it reads that number the only way a counter can, one unit
at a time. So its speed depends on the code, and the code grows fast: a guest with one
CHECK in it has code 224 , and a guest with the whole chain has a code near 2100 .

So I came down to what could finish. Here’s what ran, on the executable host, com-
pared against a separate guest implementation at the end: the host stopped exactly
when the guest did, and showed the guest’s counters, latch, ledger and flag.

                     guest                    host     host steps    time
                     count A down from 2      U        25,953,317
                     one passing CHECK        U       402,654,059    618 s
                     one failing CHECK        U       201,327,155    305 s
                     one passing CHECK        UP      402,654,059    617 s
                     one failing CHECK        UP      201,327,155    313 s

The first row’s count is pinned exactly: if the build changed so that it moved by one
step, the comparison would fail. The times are from one ordinary computer and are
only there to give you the scale. That’s about twelve host steps for every unit of the
guest’s code, for every guest step, which is exponential in the size of the guest. A guest
with one CERTIFY in it would have code 232 , about fifty billion host steps, and at the
measured rate of about 650,000 steps a second it would take something like twenty-
two hours, nearly a day. The guest I wanted, with the whole chain, has a code near
2100 , which at the same twelve steps a unit is more than 1031 host steps a guest step;


                                             343
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


at the measured rate, with this encoding on that computer, that’s around 1018 years.
So U on a guest that certifies is covered by the mathematical simulation argument,
but this execution has not been performed. Runs this long only fit in memory at all
because the host’s register store can be squeezed during the run without changing any
state, which is a theorem too.

The large counts come from this encoding and the unit operations used to read it. They
measure the work done by this interpreter. The structural comparison asks whether
the related states preserve the guest’s computation, record and ledger; the execution
tests check that comparison on the cases in the table. Whether another interpreter or
another base realizes the same relations efficiently needs a separate construction and
a running-time analysis. Nothing in these measurements gives a lower bound for all
such realizations.

19.4 From source programs to the host
Running guests one CHECK at a time doesn’t tell you whether the built machine
can do anything you’d recognise as a program. You’d want to hand it gcd, or a sort,
written the way people write them, and get the answer out, and writing gcd by hand
in INC and DEC is no way to find out. So the last piece in the drawings is a compiler.
The source is a small language you could write by hand: whole-number variables,
addition, subtraction that stops at zero, comparisons, if, while, and procedures that
return several results, with the rule that a procedure can only call ones defined before
it, so there’s no recursion. Each translation stage has a proof that it preserves the
program’s result: the procedures are inlined, the result is flattened to assignments and
jumps, that is compiled to Minsky’s counter machine through the counter-machine
compiler, that to a program for the host machine, that to a two-counter guest, and the
guest to a run of UP .


Theorem 19.1 (The compiler is correct). For every source program with no recursion, and
every input: the program computes y exactly when the runner (the bounded evaluator of the
compiled host program) halts with y for some amount of fuel; exactly when the compiled host
program halts with y; exactly when the two-counter guest halts with y; and exactly when UP
running that guest halts with y, with its first counter at 0, its ledger at 0 and its flag down. So
a terminating compiled program delivers its answer and certifies nothing. To certify a claim
about that answer, a target program must add a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY; this
compiler does not insert that chain. The runner also takes exactly as many steps as the host
program does, with the rest of its fuel left over, and a run that doesn’t halt has used all its fuel.


The statement says nothing about how many steps the compiled program takes. It’s
about answers.

The runner and the compiler are implemented, and the build has been run on a set
of programs I picked to be annoying: gcd, factorial, a primality program written


                                                344
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


with procedures, an Ackermann tower, a sorting network on a list packed into one
number, and a tiny interpreter for another machine written in the source language.
Then 220 random programs that halt, 160 random programs with loops that might not,
programs that never halt run for a fixed budget, and programs mutated on purpose to
make sure the comparison notices. Answers are compared with direct arithmetic and
separate interpreters of the source and compiled programs. Ackermann’s function at
(3, 5) is 253; the source program takes 64,768 operations to get there, and the compiled
host program takes about 119 million steps. The executable runner does a few million
host steps a second, so that’s about a minute.

That’s about 1,800 host steps per source operation for Ackermann, and up to about
a hundred thousand for multiplication by repeated addition, because every addition
copies a running total one unit at a time. This implementation’s unit operations make
the work grow with the values being handled. I haven’t measured how it grows with
program size. The last two stages, the two-counter guest and UP running it, are proved
but have not been run. An executable version of those stages has not been produced,
and UP on a compiled guest would be slow for the same reason U on a certifying guest
is. Still, I like that 253. It came out of nothing but INC and DEC, and a proof that they
mean what the source meant.

19.5 What wasn’t built
No chip. The drawings were never cut into metal. Earlier work on this project went
into hardware, a chip design for a much bigger machine, and none of it was carried
over: there’s no circuit for the small machine, no simulation of one at the level of
gates, and no board ever ran any of this. The small machine exists as mathematical
definitions and executable implementations that agree on every tested step. That’s the
whole of what “it runs” means in this book.

I’d love to see it in metal some day. But builds that can be held against each other on
every step are worth a lot to me. A board with nothing to hold it up against isn’t, and
that’s the trade I made.

20 The CHSH check
The small machine checks whether a number is zero, even, or at least something.
That’s a fine way to show the chain, and a dull thing to certify. Here’s a check worth
earning, built from zero, and then the one thing the small machine’s host does with it,
which is smaller and more exact than “it checks for quantum behaviour,” a sentence
that’s tempting and wrong. The short version, so you know where this is going: the
check never computes the famous number and never writes down the famous bound.
It tests seven facts about integers in eight counts. If they pass, a certain five-by-five
table has a property called positive semidefinite, and that property forces the famous
number under the famous bound. The wall is a consequence of the check. It never
goes into it. Everything else is explaining those sentences.


                                          345
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


What does this example contribute to the structural question? It separates the counts,
the relation they satisfy, the act of checking that relation and the record kept of the
act. A tally is written down for nothing on this machine. Its checker uses integer
arithmetic to decide a precise matrix condition. The step then ties the passing check
to this edition of the tally, and the earned chain costs three marks, just as it does for a
simpler claim. The mathematical depth of the condition and the price of those three
acts are different quantities. That makes this a useful case to hold against the small
examples.

The tally alone supplies no history of how it was obtained. A made-up tally can pass
the same arithmetic test as a played one. The claims here concern its numbers and the
machine’s treatment of them; the guarantee paragraph below says exactly how.

20.1 The game
Two players, Alice and Bob, in separate rooms. A referee flips two independent fair
coins, independent also of the players’ plan, and hands Alice a question x, zero or one,
and Bob a question y, zero or one. Alice answers a, zero or one; Bob answers b. No
talking during the game. They may agree on a plan beforehand, as detailed as they
like. They win a round when their answers differ exactly when both questions were one.
In words: if either question is zero, match; if both are one, differ.

Try to win every time. A plan is a list: what Alice says to x equals zero, what she says
to x equals one, and the same two for Bob. Four bits. Now write the four requirements
the rounds impose: a0 equals b0 (both asked zero); a0 equals b1; a1 equals b0; a1
differs from b1. Chain the first three: a0 equals b0 equals a1, and a0 equals b1, so
b0 equals b1. But the fourth says a1 differs from b1, and a1 equals b0 equals b1.
Contradiction. One of the four must break. So any plan loses at least one of the four
question pairs, and if the referee asks all four equally often, the best a plan can do is
three out of four. Seventy-five percent. Do it the long way too: there are sixteen plans
(four bits), and if you write them all out and count wins you’ll find eight win three
rounds and eight win one, and none wins four (the broken requirements always come
in odd numbers, which you can see by adding up the four equations and keeping
only whether the totals come out even or odd, with “equal” as 0 and “differ” as 1:
each of the four answers appears twice on the left, so the left sides add to an even
number, and the right sides add to one). Sharing a coin before the game to pick a
plan at random doesn’t help; a mixture of numbers no larger than three-quarters is no
larger than three-quarters. Arthur Fine, a philosopher of physics at the University of
Washington, much of whose work is on the physicist Albert Einstein and the quantum
theory, proved in 1982 that the whole “pre-agreed answers, no influence between
rooms” story is exactly the mixtures of those sixteen lists, one scoreboard for all four
questions at once; the sixteen are the whole classical story. That one I don’t have to
take on his word: the form of his theorem that speaks of the four averages is checked
in this book, and the end of this section says how.



                                           346
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


The number. Recode answers zero and one as plus one and minus one. For each
question pair, let E be the average, over many rounds, of Alice’s answer times Bob’s.
The CHSH quantity is S equals E00 plus E01 plus E10 minus E11. For one fixed plan
each win adds one to S and each loss subtracts one, so S is wins minus losses: a three-
win plan has S equal to two, a one-win plan has minus two. With equal question
frequencies, the win rate is one half plus S over eight. So “seventy-five percent” and
“S at most two” are the same fact, and the second is the one that got the name.

The ceiling is easy to reach and costs nothing to write down. Tally one round per
question pair with both players answering zero every time: after the recoding every
answer is plus one, so all four correlators are one. That’s the plan that answers zero
to everything, which matches on every pair and so wins the three pairs that ask for
a match, S = 1 + 1 + 1 − 1 = 2. On the small machine’s host a tally like that is a
few INCs on counters, and INC is free. Nothing in it says the rounds were played;
anybody can tally anything for nothing. The other side, that no finite mixture of plans
beats two, is Theorem D.2 in Appendix D, one direction of Fine’s result. The full
equivalence, in the form that speaks of the four averages, appears in the last part of
this section.

20.2 Where it came from, and why anyone cared
So who started this, and why would anybody care whether two rooms can win a coin
game? The names come in a line, and the line didn’t mean much to me until I saw
that each of them moved the same thing a notch: from an argument about what’s real,
which you can only agree with or not, toward a pile of counts a referee can judge. Each
one rests on a different piece of the game above.

The trail starts in 1935, with Einstein, by then at the Institute for Advanced Study
in Princeton, and two younger colleagues there, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen,
asking whether quantum mechanics describes everything that’s real about a pair of
particles. Their argument: if measuring one particle lets you predict the other’s result
with certainty, the result must already have been fixed, and the theory leaves that out.
What they rest on is the plan in each player’s pocket, a pre-agreed list of answers,
the plan above. And the first thing worth checking is whether the paper even says
what Einstein meant. By his own account, not quite. Podolsky did the writing, and
that June Einstein wrote to Erwin Schrödinger, the Austrian physicist whose 1926
wave equation is at the heart of quantum mechanics, that the essential thing had been
“smothered by formalism.” The person who lays that letter out is Arthur Fine, the
same Fine whose theorem closed the sixteen plans above, in his encyclopedia entry on
the argument. So Fine stands at both ends of the line: he checked the founding paper
against what its author meant, and he proved exactly what the plans can do. Even the
founding paper is a lead to check. It isn’t a verdict.

For thirty years that was philosophy. In 1964 John Bell turned it into arithmetic: if each
particle carries pre-agreed answers and nothing travels between the rooms, certain


                                           347
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


averages can’t exceed a fixed number, and quantum theory predicts they do. What
that rests on took me a few reads. His inequality rules out the pair of assumptions
together, called local realism (answers exist before you ask, and no influence across the
gap). Either one alone survives it. And where does a paper like that get published? In
a brand-new journal called Physics Physique Fizika, which charged authors no page fees
and in fact paid them by the word, ten cents a word, and which folded in 1968 after
four volumes, or three. I went looking for that count, and the sources don’t agree on it:
four is the number the American Physical Society’s archive of the journal gives, and
Iulia Georgescu, writing about the journal in Physics World in 2026, says three. She’s
also where the ten cents comes from. As Andrew Whitaker tells it in his biography of
Bell, the journal gave out no free copies, so Bell spent his payment buying copies of his
own paper to mail to other physicists. A result nobody else holds a copy of hasn’t left
the room yet, and Bell paid to send his across. In 1969 four physicists, John Clauser,
then a graduate student at Columbia, Michael Horne and Abner Shimony at Boston
University, and Richard Holt at Harvard, rewrote it as the four-average form above,
S at most two, which could be tried in a lab with imperfect equipment. It’s called the
CHSH inequality, after their initials. That notch rests on what a real lab can deliver.
Shimony was in philosophy and in physics at Boston University both, which is the
whole line in one man.

Then the obvious next question: did anybody actually try it? Stuart Freedman, a grad-
uate student at Berkeley, and Clauser, by then a postdoc there too, tried it in 1972. The
physicist Alain Aspect’s group at the Institut d’Optique in Orsay, with two colleagues
there, Jean Dalibard and Gérard Roger, did it in 1982 with the measurement settings
switched while the photons were in flight, which in the game’s terms, as I read it, is the
referee handing out the questions too late for any note about them to cross between
the rooms. Before that, in 1975, Aspect went to see Bell at CERN to tell him what he
planned, and by Aspect’s own account Bell heard him out in silence and then asked,
first thing, whether he had a permanent position. Aspect did. Bell’s reason, as Aspect
tells it, was that most physicists would take the experiment for a waste of time, or take
him for a crackpot. I read that as the toll in its oldest form: a check that could have
come out the other way costs somebody something to run, and Bell wanted to know
who’d pay. And in 2015 three groups of experimental physicists (Bas Hensen’s in Delft,
with electrons 1.3 kilometres apart; Marissa Giustina’s in Vienna; Lynden Shalm’s at
NIST, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, in Boulder) closed the two
main escape routes at once. In 2022 Clauser, Aspect and the Austrian physicist Anton
Zeilinger shared the Nobel Prize “for experiments with entangled photons, establish-
ing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science.”
The 2015 tests came out of that line of work, and Zeilinger was one of the authors of
the Vienna one. So in under fifty years the subject went from a question you needed a
permanent job to risk to a Nobel. The lab number sits above two. A remaining escape,
that the referee’s coins were secretly correlated with the particles, is a philosophical
one and I’m not going to pretend it’s closed.


                                           348
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


Now put this book’s check on the same line, because that’s where my position gives.
It sits past the far end, at the counts. Those fifty years went into making the counts
worth judging, rooms really apart, questions really late, escape routes really shut, and
my check starts after all of it. It’s handed eight counts and can’t tell a lab’s tally from
one somebody wrote down for free. So the check is a referee of counts, and everything
that made these counts worth refereeing happened upstream of it.

What quantum play does: if the players share an entangled pair and choose what to
measure from their question, the best they can do is S equals two times the square
root of two, about 2.83, a win rate of about eighty-five percent. Boris Tsirelson, a
Soviet mathematician who later taught at Tel Aviv University, in a 1980 paper called
“Quantum generalizations of Bell’s inequality,” proved that that’s a ceiling: quantum
correlations violate Bell, but only up to there. That ceiling, and the state that reaches it,
are checked for strategies in finite dimension, with real amplitudes and with complex
ones; and the ceiling holds in any dimension at all, infinitely many levels included
(the next part says how). What’s proved below, besides, is the algebra.

And the wall above that, which is the one I find most instructive. In 1994 the physicists
Sandu Popescu and Daniel Rohrlich asked: what if you only demand that nothing can
be signalled, that Alice’s answers on their own have the same odds whatever Bob is
asked, and the other way round? Then you can write down a “box” (the PR box, after
their initials) that wins every round (its answers differ exactly when both questions
are one, by fiat, each answer alone a fair coin), S equals four, and nothing about it
lets either room send a message. So the no-signalling condition alone doesn’t explain
the quantum ceiling; the PR box meets that condition and beats 2.83. That does not
supply a physical theory satisfying every requirement of relativity. The order is: two
for plans, 2.83 for quantum, four for no-signalling.

And the box has the same kind of history as everything else in this book: somebody
got there first. Popescu and Rohrlich’s initials stuck, but the big review of the field by
Nicolas Brunner and four coauthors credits boxes like it to Peter Rastall, whose 1985
paper on locality and Bell’s theorem appeared in Foundations of Physics, and, separately,
to Leonid Khalfin, a physicist at the Steklov Institute’s Leningrad branch, and Tsirelson
himself, both in 1985, nine years before. Then the question that really matters: if
relativity isn’t what stops things at 2.83, what is? People have tried candidates. In
2005 the computer scientist Wim van Dam, who works on the theory of quantum
computing, argued, in a paper on the implausible consequences of such boxes, that
with enough PR boxes, Bob could work out any yes-or-no function of both their inputs
after Alice sends him a single bit, which would make the whole question of how much
two parties need to talk collapse, and that’s a strong hint the boxes are too good to
be real. In 2009 Marcin Pawłowski, a physicist at the University of Gdańsk, and five
coauthors proposed a principle they called information causality: Bob can’t get more
information about Alice’s data than the bits she actually sends him. They argue that
ordinary and quantum physics both obey it, and that any theory that beats 2.83 breaks


                                            349
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


it. How much of the rest of the quantum boundary it reaches is something I haven’t
checked. Which principle fixes the whole quantum boundary, if any one does, this
book won’t answer. The check below is a fence at the middle step.

20.3 Five sentences that are easy to say by accident
Here they are, each with what I can stand behind beside it.

“Faster than light.” Nothing travels. Each room alone sees fair coins; the correlation
shows up only when you lay the two columns side by side afterward. “Quantum
means random.” The average S is fixed by the state; what’s random is each single
answer; the plans are the less random side. “A Bell violation proves nonlocality.” It
rules out local realism, both assumptions together, and every real test has loopholes
with names. “A tally above two proves nonlocality.” No: S is a population average,
and one finite tally can land above two by luck. Four rounds, one per question pair,
with coin-flip answers, reach S equals four one time in sixteen. That gap between
a population bound and a finite sample is the problem Yanbao Zhang, Scott Glancy
and Emanuel Knill, at NIST in Boulder, work through for real Bell tests (Physical
Review A, 2011 and 2013), and the book doesn’t solve it. The way they solve it is
worth knowing, because it has the shape of this book’s record. Turn each round into
a small bet that no local plan can expect to win, even a plan that remembers every
earlier round, multiply the bets as the rounds come in, and the French mathematician
Jean Ville’s inequality, from his 1939 thesis, one of the works that started the theory of
martingales, says the chance the product ever climbs past one over δ is at most δ. So a
flag can go up for good the moment the product crosses, with its error stated up front.
It needs one thing the small machine doesn’t have: settings drawn underneath the
program, where the program can’t choose them. And how much can one round tell
you? Wim van Dam, Richard Gill, a mathematical statistician who later held the chair
in that subject at Leiden, and Peter Grünwald (2005) measured exactly that, in bits
of evidence against every local plan. Of the two-party proofs they compare, CHSH
comes out the strongest, “much stronger” than the others in their words, at about
0.046 of a bit per round, a few hundredths, so a convincing record takes hundreds of
rounds. Four won’t do. This book proves only the narrow thing, that a tally above two
is not explained by one fixed plan replayed every round, and that narrow thing is what
the sentence has to stay. And “the PSD test proves the data is quantum.” (PSD is short
for positive semidefinite, the property of the five-by-five table from the short version;
the next part builds both.) It doesn’t, and the direction matters. Passing implies the
five-by-five table, pinned in a way the next part explains, is PSD, and that implies S
squared is at most eight; both are proved. The correlators of a PSD table like that are
the correlators of some quantum strategy. That’s Tsirelson’s representation theorem,
and it’s proved here: the strategy is built on two systems of eight levels each. The exact
edge of the quantum set for this game was found by Lawrence Landau, whose 1969
Berkeley thesis was on the quantum theory of local observables, and Lluís Masanes,
then at the University of Barcelona (next part), and that’s proved here too. Failing says


                                           350
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


nothing about whether the play was quantum: the check is complete for the pinned
matrix, the quantum set is wider than that, and quantum behaviour can fail it. Every
one of the sixteen plans fails it, and I’ll show you why. What it guarantees is in one
paragraph, once the check is on the host machine.

20.4 The five-by-five, and what positive semidefinite means
Here’s the mathematics the check rests on, and it’s one idea: a table of numbers could be
a table of dot products. Take a two-by-two symmetric table with a and c on the diagonal
and b off it. It’s positive semidefinite (PSD) when a and c are at least zero and a times
c minus b squared is at least zero. Check two by hand: ones on the diagonal and one
half off, the determinant is three quarters, passes; ones on the diagonal and 1.2 off,
the determinant is negative, fails. The reading: PSD means the table could be the dot
products of some arrows, and 1.2 is too big a dot product for two arrows of length one.
That’s the whole idea, generalised to bigger tables.

Now the table. Rows and columns labelled I, A0, A1, B0, B1 (the identity, Alice’s
two questions, Bob’s two). Diagonal all ones. The I row and column zero off the
diagonal (that’s “zero marginals”: the table takes each answer alone to average to zero,
a fair coin; the counts record no marginals and the check doesn’t test this). A0 with
A1 zero, B0 with B1 zero (no round asks Alice both questions, so no tally holds that
average, and the table sets it to zero). Those zeros are choices. They pin the table to
one slice, and I’ll come back to what they cost. And the four Alice-Bob cells hold the
four correlators E. That’s a five-by-five with four free numbers in it. It splits into the
one in the corner and a four-by-four block made of an identity and the two-by-two
grid E of correlators, and PSD of that block is the same as saying E shrinks every vector
(E is a contraction), which is three inequalities: one minus E00 squared minus E10
squared at least zero; one minus E01 squared minus E11 squared at least zero; and
their product at least the square of (E00 E01 plus E10 E11).

Run it. All four correlators 0.6 except E11 at minus 0.6, S equals 2.4: the two diagonal
terms are 0.28 and 0.28, the cross term zero, passes; above two, below 2.83. All four
at one over root two (E11 negative): diagonals zero, cross term zero, passes with no
slack, S equals two root two exactly, the 2.83; nudge any entry’s size up and a diagonal
goes negative. The all-ones plan (one, one, one, one): first diagonal is one minus one
minus one, negative, fails, though S equals two and it’s a perfectly legal classical play.
The PR box (one, one, one, minus one): fails the same way. A fence at the middle step,
and a fence that keeps out every one of the sixteen plans: each has all four correlators
at plus or minus one, so the first diagonal is always one minus one minus one. Of the
classical plays, only diluted mixtures of plans get through.

That point, one over root two in size in every entry, is four real numbers, and no tally
of rounds ever lands on it. A tally’s correlators are ratios of whole numbers, and
the point needs each of them to be one over root two, which would make root two a
fraction, and you killed that fraction with a pencil in Part I. That point and its mirror


                                           351
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


image, every sign flipped, are the only places the bound is reached (Remark D.2 in the
appendix). So a passing tally always has S squared strictly below eight. It can get as
close as you like: the (17, 3) tally in the five examples below has S squared equal to
7.84, and tallies of the same shape with a fraction nearer one over root two get nearer
still. Two root two is the least bound the check can promise, and no tally the check
accepts ever reaches it. Hold on to that corner; it comes back.

Picture what quantum play can reach as a field, and every test as a fence. In 2007
Miguel Navascués, Stefano Pironio and Antonio Acín, in a paper called “Bounding
the Set of Quantum Correlations” (NPA, after their initials), came at the edge from
outside, resting on necessary conditions. In their terms a table like this one is the
first rung of a ladder: bigger tables of expected products, each PSD, each a necessary
condition for quantum behaviour when its entries are left free, each rung tighter, and
(their 2008 paper) converging to the quantum set (strictly, the set from commuting
operators, which can differ from the tensor-product set in general scenarios). Each
rung is a fence with the whole field inside it. The check’s table is the first rung with
the marginals and the two within-party entries pinned to zero. Pinning is a stronger
demand than the rung makes, so passing puts you inside the first rung, and a quantum
point can still fail. My fence cuts across the field. Lawrence Landau in 1988 and Lluís
Masanes in 2003 came at the edge itself, for this two-questions-each case only. I’d
have drawn a flat wall at 2.83. The exact boundary they found is a curved surface
(the arc-sine form) touching 2.83 at one point. It’s checked here: a table has a PSD
completion exactly when its entries lie between minus one and one and their arcsines
pass four inequalities, so those are exactly the quantum tables.

So the obvious next question: if every rung is tighter than the last, does some rung
finally land exactly on the quantum set and stop? My first guess was yes, at least
here. A 2026 paper by Anubhav Chaturvedi, a quantum-information theorist at the
University of Gdańsk, says no: no finite rung of the ladder captures the whole quantum
set even in this simplest case. And for the four correlators alone, a 2008 paper by the
same Navascués, Pironio and Acín works out that the first rung already lands on
Landau and Masanes’s curved edge. That looked like a contradiction until I saw what
each one fences. Landau and Masanes draw the edge for the four correlators alone.
Chaturvedi’s is the full behaviours, each room’s own odds included. So there’s the
corner again from the other side: tallies never reach it, and, if his proof holds, rungs
never close on the field. I wanted that to be one fact. It’s two. Mine is root two again,
about which points a count can hit. His is about the fences. His result backs, from
outside, the caution this book keeps about the ladder, that no finite rung may close
on the whole quantum set. It says nothing about my own check, though. My check’s
caution, that a quantum point can fail it, comes from the pinning, and his paper never
pins anything.




                                          352
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


20.5 The check, in integers
Eight counts: for each of the four question pairs, one counting rounds where the
answers matched and one where they differed. A round is one bump to one count;
nothing about the round is tested, and no marginals are recorded. Then the check
reads the eight and tests seven integer facts. For each pair, let N be same plus different
and D be same minus different (so E is D over N). The seven: the four N are strictly
positive (every pair was sampled; a pair with no rounds is rejected outright, and never
read as a correlator of zero); A, which is N00 squared N10 squared minus D00 squared
N10 squared minus D10 squared N00 squared, is at least zero; B, the same with the
other column, is at least zero; and with C equal to D00 D01 N10 N11 plus D10 D11 N00
N01, C squared is at most A times B. Those are the three contraction inequalities with
the denominators cleared. No division, no reals, no square root, no S. Try it: counts
(same, different) of (4, 1), (4, 1), (4, 1), (1, 4) give E of 0.6, 0.6, 0.6, minus 0.6; N is five
and D is three (minus three for the last); A is 175, B is 175, C is zero; passes. That’s the
first example above, the S equals 2.4 one, in integers.

The theorem chain, in words: a passed check gives PSD of the five-by-five built from
the counts; contraction and PSD are equivalent, both directions; and PSD forces S
squared at most eight. The names are in the statements below. The underlying algebra
is one identity: four times the sum of the four correlators squared, minus S squared,
is a sum of six squares, so if the row sums of squares are at most one, S squared is
at most eight, and the point one over root two reaches it. That’s Tsirelson’s bound as
algebra, with no Hilbert space (the mathematical home of quantum states) in it.

Here is the chain as three statements. The derivations are in Appendix D; this is what
they prove.


Definition 20.1 (Correlators from the counts; the pinned matrix). For eight counts
and a question pair xy, let Exy = (samexy − diffxy )/(samexy + diffxy ), read as 0 when
both are 0. For reals Exy , M ( E) is the symmetric five-by-five matrix on I, A0 , A1 , B0 , B1
with ones on the diagonal, Exy in the cells ( A x , By ) and ( By , A x ), and zero everywhere
else (Definition D.5). M is PSD when vT Mv ≥ 0 for every real vector v, and S( E) =
E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 .


Theorem 20.1 (The integer check implies the pinned matrix is PSD). If eight counts pass
the seven integer facts, then M ( E) for their correlators is symmetric and PSD.

Proof. The four positivity facts make every denominator positive, so each Exy is
Dxy /Nxy , and dividing the other three facts by positive squares turns them into the
three contraction inequalities (Lemma D.15). Contraction is equivalent to PSD of M( E)
by a Schur complement on the four-by-four block (Corollary D.13).

Theorem D.16 and Corollary D.13 in the appendix give the two directions.

The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


Theorem 20.2 (PSD forces the Tsirelson bound). For all real E00 , E01 , E10 , E11 : if M( E) is
symmetric and PSD, then S( E)2 ≤ 8.

Proof. A PSD matrix with unit diagonal has every three-by-three principal minor at
                                                    2 − E2 , and on rows A , B , B it is
least zero. On rows A0 , B0 , B1 that minor is 1 − E00   01                1  0   1

Corollary 20.3 (A passed check means the bound). If eight counts pass the seven integer
facts, their correlators satisfy S2 ≤ 8. In fact S2 < 8, and passing tallies come as close to 8 as
you like.

Proof. Theorem 20.1 supplies positive semidefiniteness of the pinned moment matrix
for these four correlators. Theorem D.14 in the derivation appendix applies to every
such matrix and gives S2 ≤ 8. Its quadratic form calculation is printed there. The
score is a ratio of whole numbers, and no such ratio squares to 8, so the bound is strict.
The tallies whose four correlators are n/q, n/q, n/q, −n/q with 2n2 ≤ q2 pass, and

their scores 4n/q come as near 2 2 as you like.


Remark 20.1 (Sound, and incomplete). The pinned matrix is stricter than the quantum
question it is usually read against. PSD of M ( E) gives the correlators a PSD completion,
since the zeros are one choice of the two free entries. The converse fails. The all-ones
plan has a PSD completion, and every deterministic plan is a quantum strategy; yet
its minor on rows A0 , B0 , B1 is 1 − 1 − 1 = −1, so M( E) is not PSD there, and a tally
of one matching round per pair gives A = 1 − 1 − 1 = −1 in the integer check, so
the check fails. The second failure is a named theorem on the machine: the tally of
one matching round per pair is refused forever (Proposition 20.6). Every deterministic
plan fails the same way. The tally of one round per pair fails the check for each of the
sixteen plans, so does a plan replayed over any number of rounds once pairs 00 and
10 have been sampled, and no deterministic plan’s pinned matrix is PSD. So a pass
proves the bound, and a failure proves only that the tally’s pinned matrix isn’t PSD
or a pair went unsampled; it says nothing about whether the play was classical or
quantum. The free tally from the start of this section is exactly such a tally: it reaches
S = 2 and the check throws it out.


None of that algebra is new, and I don’t want it to read as if it were. Tsirelson’s bound
has been formalised before, in Isabelle/HOL by Mnacho Echenim and Mehdi Mhalla,
computer scientists at Grenoble (2023), and in Lean’s mathlib, and Navascués, Pironio
and Acín already analyse this very matrix by Schur complement and discuss the level




                                               354
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


above it. What I think is mine here is smaller: an integer decision procedure on the
counts, and a checked link from “the check passed” to PSD to the bound.

The picture under the check is older still. Tsirelson showed, in a longer paper of 1987
after his 1980 note, that the correlations two separated quantum parties can reach are
exactly the tables of inner products of unit vectors, one vector for each question on
each side. With the marginals pinned to zero the pinned matrix is that picture, and
by its Schur complement it is PSD exactly when the two-by-two table of correlators,
read as a matrix, has operator norm at most one. The physicists Reinhard Werner and
Michael Wolf’s survey of Bell inequalities (2001) sets out that correlation-matrix view
for two-party inequalities in general.

20.6 The check, earned on the host machine
Now put it on the machine. A check on the small machine is a property: a checker,
which is a little program that says yes or no, a meaning, which is a statement, and a
proof that the two agree. The version of the small machine with its property language
left open (Section 16, Theorem 16.25) takes any property language with an exact
equality test whose properties come with those three things, and for every one of
them a flag raised from a clean start stands on a passing CHECK of one claim, a
later COMMIT of the same claim with its counter untouched in between, and a later
CERTIFY, the three acts costing one each. So here’s the plan for the game. Pack the
eight counts into one counter, as a list, the way the sorted-list machine packs a list
into one number (Section 16). Let the checker be the seven integer facts read off the
unpacked counts. And let the meaning be what the facts are for: every pair was
sampled, and the pinned five-by-five is positive semidefinite. Then the proof the
generic machine asks for, that the checker says yes exactly when the meaning holds,
is the chain above with the denominators cleared in both directions, and a flag raised
on that machine from a clean start means: these counts, at this edition of their counter,
passed the check, somebody committed to that with nothing changed underneath, and
the correlators they give satisfy S2 ≤ 8. Here is that, stated exactly, and it’s stronger
than the chain above in one way I want to say once and plainly. The earlier theorems
said that a passed check makes the pinned matrix PSD. The check is also complete
for it: it passes if and only if every pair was sampled and the pinned matrix is PSD,
because clearing the denominators works in both directions. The statement is over the
machine of Definition 16.8, the small machine with a counter for every number, with
PCHSH in place of its one property, Slot. A CHECK reads one counter, which is why
the eight counts have to travel in one.


Definition 20.2 (The packed tally, and the property PCHSH). Read a whole
number as a list in the list code (0 is the empty list, and 2x (2y + 1) is x fol-
lowed by the list y), and take as its tally the first eight entries, in the order
same00 , diff00 , same01 , diff01 , same10 , diff10 , same11 , diff11 , a missing entry reading 0.
Every number is some tally. The property PCHSH has the checker “the tally passes


                                              355
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


the seven integer facts” and the meaning “every question pair was sampled, and the
pinned matrix M ( E) of the tally’s correlators is symmetric and PSD.”


Theorem 20.4 (The check is exact). (1) The seven integer facts hold of a tally if and only
if every pair was sampled and M( E) is symmetric and PSD. (2) For every whole number v,
the checker of PCHSH says yes at v if and only if the meaning holds of v’s tally. (3) Reading
the number that packs a tally gives that tally back. (4) If the facts hold, the score of the tally
                            √                                  √
satisfies S2 ≤ 8 and |S| ≤ 2 2; in fact S2 < 8 and |S| < 2 2, and passing tallies come as
close to 8 as you like.

Proof. (1) The forward half is Theorem 20.1. For the backward half, PSD gives the
three contraction inequalities (Corollary D.13); with every N positive, multiplying
them through by the squares of the denominators gives A ≥ 0, B ≥ 0 and C2 ≤ AB,
which is Lemma D.15 read the other way. (2) is (1) with the packing, since every
number is a tally. (3) is the code and its decoder being inverse. (4) is (1) forward, then
Theorem 20.2; the strict form and the closeness are Corollary 20.3.

    τ = pre · CHECK PCHSH c · mid1 · COMMIT PCHSH c · mid2 · CERTIFY · post,

Proof. A raised flag from a clean start has the earned chain (Theorem 16.9, which
holds for this machine as for the small one): a passing CHECK, then a COMMIT of
