CHECK of PCHSH at c means the checker says yes at c’s value, which is the meaning
by Theorem 20.4(2), and the bound is (4) of the same theorem. An unchanged edition
means an unchanged value. For the converse, the CHECK passes exactly when the
tally passes; if it does, COMMIT and CERTIFY find their facts and the three acts cost
three; if it fails, the trap latch goes up, and a run takes no step once the trap is up (as
in Theorem 16.17), so the flag never rises.


                                                356
The Thiele Machine                                                                      Devon Thiele


That’s the one thing the machine does with the check, as the section’s opening said:
a raised flag can stand on it. Five tallies, each a theorem with its counts written out,
show the check isn’t vacuous and where its edges are.


Proposition 20.6 (Five tallies). Counts are given as (same, diff) for the pairs 00, 01, 10, 11.
(4,1), (4,1), (4,1), (1,4) has S = 12/5: the check passes, the flag rises, the ledger reads 3. (17,3),
                                                              √
(17,3), (17,3), (3,17) has S = 14/5 = 2.8, just under 2 2, with S2 = 7.84: it passes, the
ledger reads 3. (9,1), (9,1), (9,1), (1,9) has S = 16/5 with S2 > 8: refused forever, whatever
follows. (1,0), (1,0), (1,0), (0,1), the PR box, has S = 4: refused forever. (1,0), (1,0), (1,0),
(1,0), the all-ones classical plan, has S = 2: refused forever.


The last one is the check being stricter than the bound, as a named theorem: a perfectly
legal classical play with S = 2 is turned away.

What the theorem doesn’t say stays what it was. The tally is placed. Nobody plays it on
the machine: the theorem starts from a counter that already holds the packing, and no
instruction plays a round, so a program can put any code in a counter for free. There
are no marginals. The pinned matrix is stricter than the quantum set, so failing says
nothing about whether the play was quantum, and there is no margin for sampling
noise at Tsirelson’s point.

A tally stays free. Each count is a counter, a round is an INC on one of them, and
INC costs nothing, so a pile of trials costs nothing to write down; the packing into
one counter is a program’s business, and in the theorem the packed counter is simply
there at the start. What costs is the claim about the pile. Statistics are free; the claim
about them is what costs.

So here, in one paragraph, is what the check guarantees. If it passes, then every ques-
tion pair was sampled, the four empirical ratios satisfy three polynomial inequalities,
hence the fixed five-by-five is PSD, hence S squared is at most eight. It does not guar-
antee that the tally came from honest play (a program can INC whatever counts it
likes for nothing, including four rounds that put S at four). It does not guarantee any
marginal is zero (no marginals are recorded and none are tested). It does not put the
players’ state behind the counts. What it does give is a quantum strategy with the
same correlators: a passing tally’s correlators have a PSD completion, and every point
with one is the correlator table of a strategy on two eight-level systems. And it fails the
tally of every single plan, honest classical play included. It has no margin for sampling
noise either. Honest play at Tsirelson’s point aims at correlators of plus or minus one
over root two, and there every pair of squared correlators the check adds up comes
to exactly one, the edge of what it accepts. So an honest tally aimed at that point sits
right on the line, and ordinary luck over a finite number of rounds pushes it over most
of the time. I simulated it, drawing each round’s answers at Tsirelson’s correlators: the
check fails 92 percent of the time at 10 rounds per question pair, 87 percent at 100, and



                                                 357
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


about 85.5 percent from 1,000 to 100,000. In those simulated trials, fair coins passed
every time from 100 rounds per pair on, and failed about 2.5 percent of the time at 10.
That is an observed frequency, not a guarantee for every possible tally. The limit has a
closed form. To first order the largest singular value of the noisy correlator matrix is
one plus the larger eigenvalue of a random symmetric two-by-two with independent
Gaussian entries, and the check passes only when that eigenvalue is at most zero,
                                        √
which happens with probability (2 − 2)/4. So honest play at Tsirelson’s point fails
                       √
with probability (2 + 2)/4 ≈ 0.854 in the long run. That’s simulation and arithmetic;
no proof of that limit is given here.

The check can also allow a tolerance. For ε = p/q it tests the same seven facts in
integers with the 1 in the contraction inequalities replaced by (1 + ε)2 . At ε = 0 it is
the check above. A pass means the two-by-two correlator matrix has operator norm
at most 1 + ε, and S2 ≤ 8(1 + ε)2 . A tally of 100 rounds per pair with correlators
0.72, 0.70, 0.72, −0.72 fails the exact check and passes at ε = 1/10. In the same simu-
                      √
lation, with ε = 3/ n for n rounds per pair, honest Tsirelson play fails it about five
                                                                              √
times in a hundred thousand. The price is in the bound: a pass caps S at 2 2 (1 + ε),
a little outside Tsirelson’s number. The exact check remains the default. With p and
q fixed for a machine instance, the tolerance check also runs as CHECK on the same
versioned registers: its CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY chain certifies exactly when the
integer tolerance test passes, pays three marks on success, and traps permanently on
failure. From a clean start, every raised flag has that earned chain behind it, with
the same register value at CHECK and COMMIT, and establishes the relaxed bound
above. The check certifies a shape of the tally. What the shape means is a question for
whoever supplied the rounds.

And notice which way the fence faces. The most practical use anyone has found
for a Bell test, certified randomness, needs the opposite bound. Stefano Pironio and
colleagues (2010) argued, and backed with an experiment, that a Bell violation, with
settings the devices can’t choose, certifies that the outputs are random, and a group
of quantum cryptographers, Rotem Arnon-Friedman, Frédéric Dupuis, Omar Fawzi,
Renato Renner and Thomas Vidick (2018), made the accounting tight with what they
call entropy accumulation. A string printed in advance passes no such test, so it’s the
cleanest case I know, outside this book, of a check that can fail, separating output that
was established from output that was printed. That needs S bounded from below, with
an error probability. This check bounds S from above and fails every single plan, so it’s
a fence that keeps out the super-quantum and the fixed plan. As a nonlocality test it’s
no use. The deployed version exists, too: Gautam Kavuri and colleagues, physicists at
NIST and the University of Colorado (2025), run a public randomness beacon whose
outputs each trace back through a Bell test to a public record, the nearest working
system I know to a certified claim written down for good. And records cut both
ways there. Jonathan Barrett, Roger Colbeck and Adrian Kent, working on quantum
cryptography (2013), pointed out that a device which keeps its own memory of earlier



                                          358
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


rounds can leak it through outputs it makes public later, so reusing a device can undo
a guarantee the user thought was settled. A permanent record in the wrong box is an
attack.

20.7 A rational stand-in for an irrational number
One useful rational bound: 5657 over 2000, which is 2.8285, and two root two is
2.82842... It’s the four-decimal round-up, chosen so that rational arithmetic can test
“above the Tsirelson bound” without square roots, and it’s safe because 5657 squared
is 32,001,649 and eight times 2000 squared is 32,000,000, so the fraction sits above root
eight by about seven hundred-thousandths. It’s used in a few rational theorems. It is
not used in the integer check, and the real-number theorems use root eight.

20.8 Two more tests, as mathematics
The second rung: a nine-by-nine table on I, the four questions, and the four Alice-Bob
products, with the correlators and five extra free numbers for three- and four-body
entries. Its two four-body entries are tied, one the negative of the other. That tie is a
constraint, ⟨{ A0 , A1 } ⊗ { B0 , B1 }⟩ = 0: the zero entries of the first rung don’t imply it,
and a classical strategy breaks it. So the second rung is level 1+AB on that slice, and
that’s what I mean by level 1+AB everywhere in this book. Its PSD is again equivalent
to a contraction-like condition. The check for it proves something stronger, that the
matrix is positive definite, by a cascade of two Schur steps down to a four-by-four
that Sylvester’s criterion closes. Sylvester’s name on a test about matrices fits in a
way I enjoy, because the word matrix is his. In 1850, in the Philosophical Magazine, the
English mathematician James Joseph Sylvester used it for an “oblong arrangement of
terms” out of which you cut square blocks and take their determinants, and matrix
was already an old word for the place something grows from. That’s exactly what
the test does: it cuts the top-left square blocks out of the big grid, one row deep, two,
three, four (the leading minors), and asks each one’s determinant to be positive. Was
he the first to state the test? The name doesn’t settle that; names stick to people for all
kinds of reasons, and I’d treat this one as a lead. And a fact that’s easy to list without
noticing what it means: with all five extra numbers at zero, the condition certifies a
strict subset of the classical set (the ball where the four correlators’ squares sum to at
most one), forcing S at most two; it can’t certify anything above the classical line. To
get a point above two you have to supply the extras (S equals 2.4 with one extra at
minus one half). Appendix D has the algebra.

The two sizes are one test. A single positive-semidefinite predicate takes the size as a
parameter, and the five-by-five and the nine-by-nine are it at two sizes.


Definition 20.3 (The size-generic PSD test). A claim is a top index n and a ma-
trix M indexed by naturals. It is realizable when Mij = M ji for all i, j ≤ n and
∑i≤n ∑ j≤n vi Mij v j ≥ 0 for every real vector v. The CHSH claim of E is top index
4 with the matrix M( E) of Definition 20.1; the level-1+AB claim uses top index 8 and


                                             359
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


the nine-by-nine matrix.


Corollary 20.7 (The level-1 test is the size-five case). For all real E00 , E01 , E10 , E11 : the
three contraction inequalities hold if and only if the CHSH claim of E is realizable. The same
holds at size nine for the level-1+AB contraction condition and its claim.

Proof. Realizability at top index 4 unfolds to symmetry and PSD of the five-by-five, by
computing the finite sums, and that is equivalent to contraction by Corollary D.13. At
size nine the same unfolding meets Theorem D.19. Nothing new is proved about the
matrices; the point is that one predicate covers both.

The third thing: the elliptope, the set of correlators for which some choice of the two
missing entries (A0 with A1, B0 with B1) makes the five-by-five PSD. Every one of
the sixteen plans is inside it, mixtures stay inside, every point inside obeys S2 ≤ 8,
Tsirelson’s point is inside and reaches it, the PR box is out, and it’s strictly bigger
than the classical set. There’s a certificate checker for it with a soundness proof, in
two branches: a strict Sylvester check with the completion supplied, and a rational
factorisation certificate of the completed matrix, checked in integers. What’s proved is
that a pass puts the correlators inside the set and that no choice of inputs gets the PR
box through, and, by computation, that some named points pass, the all-ones plan and
a point that the arc-sine boundary puts exactly on the quantum edge among them. The
further claim that every point with a rational PSD completion has such a certificate is
not proved here. The certificate checker is sound, as mathematics; none of the small
machine’s properties is the elliptope check.

20.9 The quantum set
Three descriptions of the same set have been running through this part: the tables
some quantum strategy can produce, the tables whose five-by-five matrix has a PSD
completion, and the tables inside Landau and Masanes’s curved edge. They are the
same set, for strategies on finitely many levels. Here’s how each piece goes, because
the constructions are the part worth seeing.

Quantum tables are inside the completion set. A strategy’s correlator is the inner
product of two unit vectors: Alice’s observable applied to the shared state, and Bob’s
applied to it. Four unit vectors always have a PSD table of inner products, so every
quantum table has a completion, and Tsirelson’s bound follows from that: S2 ≤ 8 for
every strategy, and its level-one moment matrix passes the PSD test with the marginals
in. Quantum mechanics uses complex amplitudes, and the complex case goes through
by a plain trick: a complex vector of length n is a real vector of length 2n, its real
parts followed by its imaginary parts, and the real part of a complex inner product
is the ordinary inner product of those longer real vectors. So the real argument runs
                                                                           √
unchanged. The two-qubit strategy from the start of this part reaches 2 2 in both
readings.


                                              360
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


The completion set is inside the quantum tables. This is Tsirelson’s representation,
and the construction is his. Take a table with a PSD completion. A PSD matrix is a
table of inner products of vectors, always: peel off one row at a time, and a zero on
the diagonal forces its whole row to zero. So the completion hands over four unit
vectors in four dimensions, a0 , a1 for Alice and b0 , b1 for Bob, with a x · by equal to the
table’s entries. Appendix D, Section D.8, gives the factorization and the measurements
explicitly. Now the trick. There are four real eight-by-eight matrices, built from the
two-by-two ones that swap two entries or flip the sign of one, that each square to the
identity and anticommute in pairs: multiply any two of them in either order and the
answers differ only in sign. Use a vector’s four components to mix those four matrices,
and you get an observable that squares to the identity, a legitimate measurement. Give
Alice and Bob a maximally entangled pair of eight-level systems, and the correlator
of two such observables comes out as exactly the inner product of their vectors. So
the strategy built from the four vectors produces the table, for both real and complex
amplitudes. Eight levels on each side is always enough.

The curved edge is the same set again. Each correlator is the cosine of an angle, the
angle between one of Alice’s vectors and one of Bob’s. Walk the loop a0 , b0 , a1 , b1
and back to a0 : the angle across any one leg can’t exceed the sum of the other three,
because angles on a sphere obey the triangle inequality. Flip one vector to its opposite
and you get the other four inequalities, with 2π in them. Written in arcsines, those
eight inequalities are Landau and Masanes’s four. Going the other way, any four
angles that pass them can be met by actual vectors: choose an angle between Bob’s
two that meets both pairs of constraints, build each of Alice’s from the two angles
it has to make with them, and check that the determinant that says such a triangle
exists comes out nonnegative. So a table has a PSD completion exactly when its
arcsines pass the four inequalities, and those are exactly the quantum tables. The
point (3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5) sits on the edge, because arcsin 53 + arcsin 45 = π2 by the
3-4-5 triangle, and so does Tsirelson’s point. The interval construction, including both
endpoint cases, is in Section D.9.

20.10 What isn’t proved
One step on paper, and then nothing about dimension. Quantum mechanics also
allows systems with infinitely many levels, and the checks don’t need finitely many.
Whatever the dimension, a shared state v gives an expectation on the operators the
players measure with: x 7→ Re ⟨v, x v⟩. That one line is the step on paper. The proofs
use only what that expectation always has: you can add, multiply, scale and take
adjoints, the product spreads over sums, and the expectation of x ∗ x is never negative.
Each measurement is its own adjoint with the expectation of its square at most one,
which covers unsharp measurements too, and Alice’s commute with Bob’s. That last
demand is weaker than putting them on two separate systems, so the result covers
the wider, commuting model as well. On that footing Tsirelson’s sum of squares goes
                                          √
through, and the CHSH value is at most 2 2. The same nonnegative form, with each


                                            361
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


diagonal entry raised to one, completes the correlator table to a PSD matrix, so the four
arcsine inequalities hold, and with a unit the full first-level moment matrix, marginals
and all, is PSD. The other direction needs no help from infinity: every point inside the
arcsine edge is reached on two eight-level systems.

Also: the finite-mixture theorem proves only one direction, that a finite local model
satisfies the bound, and its converse as stated is false: a table with S = 0 that no
local model produces. Fine’s own theorem, in the form that speaks of correlations, is
proved separately as an equivalence: a table of four correlators comes from a local
model exactly when each is between −1 and 1 and all eight CHSH inequalities hold.
Section D.10 constructs the finite distribution. And one more thing about tallies, which
the guarantee paragraph above already used: a free tally is not thereby classical (the
four rounds with S equal to four). The correlators (one, one, one, minus one) are the
PR box, which no classical play produces; the classical vertex this section used, which
fails the check like every plan, is (one, one, one, one).

That’s the game, the number, the two walls, and the check. Last of the machine
sections: what all this costs against physics.

21 The counter against physics
Section 4 did the physics argument once: on a finite machine a permanent flag merges
states, Landauer’s principle (a named premise) prices merges, and the toll follows.
I’m not going to do it again. This section is about what a machine’s counter, the small
machine’s µ included, has to do with any of that, and the answer is: less than naming
Landauer might suggest, and I want you to hear the exact amount from me.

21.1 The calibration is a unit conversion
Multiply the counter by a chosen energy per mark, and a theorem that a state with
one mark, at the scale kT ln 2 per mark, carries kT ln 2 of energy for every k and T.
Read that for exactly what it is: a unit conversion, true by definition, with the scale
as a free input. Nothing in it picks the scale. The theorem would be just as true with
the scale set to a dollar a mark. What would connect marks to joules is the premise
in Section 4, Landauer’s principle, which is a physical premise. And even as a scale,
k B T ln 2 a mark is the floor for one particular squeeze, a halving. Corollary 4.9’s floor
for a flip that brings k states into a room already holding m, starting from the even
spread on those m + k states, is k B T ln mm+k , and for one newcomer into a big room
that’s far below a halving, roughly k B T/m. Price every mark at k B T ln 2 and you can
overstate the floor of a single narrow flip by a factor that grows with m.

Remember the constant from Boltzmann’s grave in Part II, the exchange rate between
a count and heat? It has a newer chapter, and it makes the point sharper than I can.
The k B in k B T ln 2 turns a temperature into an energy, and for most of its history it was
a measured number, with error bars, pinned down by careful experiments. Since 20
May 2019 it isn’t. That day the international system of units was redefined so that


                                            362
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Boltzmann’s constant is exactly 1.380649 × 10−23 joules per kelvin, by definition, and
the kelvin is whatever makes that true. So the conversion from temperature to energy
has been a convention since then, in the strictest sense: its numerical value in those
units is fixed. Realising the kelvin in a laboratory still requires measurements, with
uncertainty. What’s still physics is everything around it, whether wiping a bit at a
temperature really sheds that much heat, which is what the Lyon bead was measuring.
The calibration theorem is the same kind of move as that redefinition. It fixes a
conversion, and the physics, if there is any, is somewhere else.


Definition 21.1 (Energy at a scale). For a real number c (joules per mark) and a state s,
the energy of s at scale c is µ(s) · c. The Landauer calibration at k B and T is the statement
that every state with µ(s) = 1 has energy k B T ln 2 at scale k B T ln 2.


Theorem 21.1 (The calibration is a unit conversion). (1) For all real k B and T, the
Landauer calibration at k B and T holds. (2) For any counter, there are two real-valued func-
tions of the state that give 1 and 2 on every state with one mark, so the counter alone fixes no
energy value.

Proof. (1) Substitute µ(s) = 1: 1 · k B T ln 2 = k B T ln 2, by ring arithmetic, for any k B
and T, positive or not. (2) Take the two functions to be the energy at scales 1 and 2. At
µ(s) = 1 they give 1 and 2.

The physics is the premise of Section 4, restated here once in the form the next theorems
test. In words first: a dissipation hands each instruction a whole number of heat units,
each unit worth kT ln 2. The floor premise says an instruction that takes at least one
state where some yes-or-no property is false to a state where it’s true, never sends a
true one back to false, and sends two different states to one, dissipates at least one unit.
That’s a different statement from Landauer’s principle as Premise 4.5 has it. That one
depends on the spread over states, Q ≥ k B T ln 2 · ∆H, and gives nothing for a known
state. This one gives every such instruction a floor of one whole unit, whatever the
spread. To get the second from the first you’d need more, at the least a spread with a
full bit of uncertainty removed at every such step, and the known-state theorem and
the narrow squeeze of Section 4 show that isn’t automatic. So I give it its own name,
structural dissipation pricing. The calibration says no instruction dissipates more units
than the counter charges it. One word about that word: “dissipation” here means heat
handed to the surroundings, in the sense Section 4 took from Sagawa: a bill for where
the forgotten bit goes. It has nothing to do with waste, or with doing the job badly.
Two premises, nothing proved about either, and the only question is whether they can
sit in the same room:


Premise 21.2 (Structural dissipation pricing). A dissipation is a function δ from instruc-
tions to naturals, counted in units of k B T ln 2. The floor, a hypothesis separate from


                                              363
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Premise 4.5 of Section 4: every instruction that collapses a yes-or-no property has
δ(i ) ≥ 1, where i collapses P when some state with P false is sent to a state with P true,
every state with P true is sent to one with P true, and some two different states are
sent to the same state. The calibration: δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ) for every instruction. Neither is
proved anywhere; the theorems below ask whether they can hold together.


The last clause of the floor is there because the first two don’t make a step forget
anything on a machine with infinitely many states. INC A sends a state with A = 0
to one with A = 1 and keeps every positive A positive, so it raises “A ≥ 1” one way,
and it is one-to-one. Any one-to-one map that misses some state does the same to the
property “is in my image”. Its input can be recovered from its output, and its entropy
loss is zero. The adopted Landauer premise therefore supplies no positive heat floor;
this does not promise that an implementation gives off no heat. A floor read without
the last clause would charge a whole unit. On a finite machine the clause comes for
free. A step that sends one false state into the true ones and keeps every true state true
puts one more state into the true set than the set holds, so two of them land on the
same state.

21.2 The premises have to be able to hold together
Here’s the one piece of this section that I think is good physics discipline, and it’s a
consistency test. Suppose you want to claim the counter tracks dissipation. You need
two premises: that every step you’ve chosen to count dissipates at least one unit, and
an upper calibration that bounds dissipation by the charge. Can those two hold at
once? There’s a theorem saying exactly when: a model satisfying both exists precisely
when every operation you’ve chosen to count (the statement below calls those eligible)
costs at least one. I should say how cheap that is. The model the proof builds takes
the dissipation to be the cost itself, so the theorem shows the two premises don’t
contradict each other. It doesn’t show that the counter tracks any dissipation. Still, it
does bite on a schedule: if you count a zero-cost step, no such model can exist. One
example where the premises hold is a one-bit reset, where resetting costs one and
idling costs nothing; the small machine’s flag-raising steps, below, are another.

Now point the test at the small machine of Section 16, counting every step that col-
lapses some yes-or-no property, and it fails. Read without the last clause of the floor, it
would fail at a step that forgets nothing: INC A raises “A ≥ 1” one way, is one-to-one,
and costs zero. With the clause in place the failure sits at a merge. Its free instructions
merge states (the last item of the list at the end of that chapter has the pair: two cores
that one DEC sends to the same core, for nothing), so DEC A 2, which collapses the
property “A is zero or the line number is 2” by sending a state where it’s false and
a state where it’s true to the same state, costs zero there, and (1) below says no dis-
sipation can charge it one and stay under its cost. The machine prices the certifying
chain and leaves its other merges free, so the premise pair holds for the steps the toll
is about and fails for the whole instruction set. That’s the honest shape.


                                           364
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


Theorem 21.2 (When the premises can hold together). (1) For any set of operations, any
predicate “eligible” on them, and any cost, a dissipation with δ(i ) ≥ 1 on every eligible i and
δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ) on every i exists if and only if every eligible operation costs at least one. (2) On
a one-bit machine with a reset of cost 1 and an idle of cost 0, taking “eligible” to mean “sends
two different states to one”, such a dissipation exists.

Proof. (1) If such a δ exists, 1 ≤ δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ). Conversely, take δ = cost. (2) The reset
is the only operation that sends two states to one, and it costs 1; apply (1).

Three statements are in play, and each points its own way. Energy at a scale, µ · c,
is a conversion and points nowhere. The calibration, δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ), puts the charge
above the dissipation: an upper bound. Landauer’s principle puts the heat above
an entropy loss: a lower bound. The theorem above says the assumptions can hold
together. That’s compatibility, and it isn’t evidence. It doesn’t make the ledger the
least energy anything needs, and it doesn’t make it the heat anything gives off.

But now the history escape from Section 4, pointed at a machine. Keep the previous
state in a history list (push it onto the front each step; below, s :: h is the list h with
s put on the front) and every fixed-instruction step becomes injective, while the step
you can see stays the same; the line number can collapse to one place while the bigger
state keeps its past. The free merge, lifted to a machine with history, isn’t a merge. So
“this step merged, therefore it dissipated” can’t be said of the visible step alone. It’s a
sentence about the whole state including whatever history is retained, and a physical
model has to say what’s retained. The permanent-certificate theorem in Section 4
supplies that for the certifying step on finite memory. For the rest of a machine’s steps
it’s unsaid.


Theorem 21.3 (Keeping history makes every step injective). Let the history step send a
pair (s, h), a state and a list of past states, to (apply(s, i ), s :: h). For any step function, the
history step with a fixed instruction is injective, and its first component is the original step.

Proof. Undoing the history step, by popping the list, returns the old pair, so two pairs
with the same image are equal.

21.3 The calorimeter protocol, as a specification
Here is how one would measure this, and it’s here because it makes the boundary exact.
Take a two-state register with energies zero and a gap, a population p in the excited
state, and the simplest possible rate equation for how p changes in one time step (a
rate for climbing into the excited state, a rate for falling out of it, and the length of the
step). For the canonical reset (population one half to zero, with the rates chosen so the
equation closes), the heat delivered to the bath is exactly half the gap. Choose the gap
to be twice kT ln 2 and that heat is exactly kT ln 2.



                                                365
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Read that twice, because the temptation is to read it as a derivation of Landauer’s
number and it’s the opposite. The gap was chosen to make the heat come out as
Landauer’s number. The same populations and rates with half that gap give half
the Landauer value, and there’s a theorem exhibiting identical population dynamics
with different heat. The rate equation fixes the shape; the energy scale is a selected
Hamiltonian (the physicist’s name for the rule that says what energy each state has),
and selecting it is not deriving it.

The canonical reset is a bookkeeping toy, and its rates show it. A register that trades
heat with a bath at temperature T has rates in detailed balance: the rate up over the
rate down is e−∆/k B T , which at the gap 2k B T ln 2 is 1/4. The canonical rates are 0 and
1, and the factor e−∆/k B T is never 0, so no gap and no temperature put them in that
ratio. With rates that are in it, a relaxation at a fixed gap moves toward the equilibrium
population 1/(1 + e∆/k B T ) and, with steps short enough not to overshoot, never goes
below it. At the gap 2k B T ln 2 that population is 1/5. The toy has no work term either;
nothing in it pays for the squeeze. Part (4) of the theorem below says what that costs:
at the gap k B T ln 2 the toy books less heat than Landauer’s bound asks for the same
squeeze from one half to zero, so the toy has no second law.


Definition 21.3 (The two-state protocol). For a gap ∆, the register’s mean energy at
excited population p is ∆ · p. One step of the rate equation is

                              p′ = p + δt k01 (1 − p) − k10 p ,
                                                             


and the heat to the bath over a step from p to p′ is defined as ∆p − ∆p′ . The canonical
reset takes p = 21 , δt = 1, k01 = 0, k10 = 1, ending at p′ = 0, and counts one logical
event.


Theorem 21.4 (The heat is fixed by the chosen gap). (1) The canonical numbers satisfy
the rate equation. (2) For every ∆, the canonical reset’s heat is ∆/2. (3) For all k B , T, the
gap ∆ = 2k B T ln 2 gives heat k B T ln 2. (4) If k B > 0 and T > 0, the gap k B T ln 2 gives
heat strictly below k B T ln 2. (5) There are two different gaps for which the same canonical
populations satisfy the rate equation and the heats differ.

Proof. All five are field arithmetic on the definitions: 12 + 1 · (0 − 12 ) = 0; ∆ · 12 − ∆ · 0 =
∆/2; and ln 2 > 0 for (4). For (5) take gaps 1 and 2.

A reset that pays its way is driven. Raise the gap a little, let the register settle with rates
in detailed balance, raise it again, and so on, starting from a gap of zero, where the two
states are alike and the population is one half. Raising the gap while the population
holds is work done on the register; settling at the new gap is heat to the bath. That’s
the textbook way to wipe a bit slowly, and here it’s checked.




                                              366
The Thiele Machine                                                                       Devon Thiele


Definition 21.4 (The driven reset). Write kT for k B T. At gap ∆ the equilibrium ex-
cited population is π (∆) = 1/(1 + e∆/kT ) and the register’s free energy is F (∆) =
−kT ln(1 + e−∆/kT ). Rates satisfy detailed balance at gap ∆ when k01 = k10 e−∆/kT . A
driven reset along a schedule of gaps g0 , g1 , . . . , gn takes, at step m, the gap from gm to
gm+1 with the population held at π ( gm ), which is work π ( gm )( gm+1 − gm ), and then
                                                                                   
lets the register settle to π ( gm+1 ), which is heat gm+1 π ( gm ) − π ( gm+1 ) to the bath.
The reset’s work and heat are the sums over its steps. The uniform schedule from 0 to
D in N steps has gm = Dm/N.


Theorem 21.5 (A driven reset pays kT ln 2 in work). (1) With rates in detailed balance
at gap ∆, one step of the rate equation takes p to π (∆) + 1 − δt (k01 + k10 ) p − π (∆) ;
                                                                                                    

when δt (k01 + k10 ) = 1 it lands on π (∆) from any p. (2) For any schedule, work minus
heat is gn π ( gn ) − g0 π ( g0 ), the change in the register’s mean energy. (3) If kT > 0 and the
schedule never falls, the work is at least F ( gn ) − F ( g0 ); if also every step raises the gap by at
                                                                         
most h, the work is at most F ( gn ) − F ( g0 ) + h π ( g0 ) − π ( gn ) . (4) If kT > 0, D ≥ 0 and
N ≥ 1, the uniform reset from 0 to D in N steps does work between kT ln 2 − kTe− D/kT and
kT ln 2 + D/(2N ), and leaves an excited population of at most e− D/kT .

Proof. (1) Under detailed balance k01 = (k01 + k10 ) π (∆), so the step is linear in p −
π (∆) with that factor. (2) The terms telescope. (3) The slope of F is π, which falls as the
gap rises, so the mean value theorem gives π (b)(b − a) ≤ F (b) − F ( a) ≤ π ( a)(b − a)
for a ≤ b; add over the steps. (4) F (0) = −kT ln 2, π (0) = 12 , ln(1 + x ) ≤ x for x ≥ 0,
and π ( D ) ≤ e− D/kT ; put these into (3) with h = D/N.

Try one finite step in units where kT = 1: start with gap zero and half the registers
excited, then raise the gap to ln 2. The work is 12 ln 2. After settling, the excited share
is 1/3, so the bath receives ( 12 − 31 ) ln 2 = 16 ln 2 and the registers retain 13 ln 2 more
energy. Work equals those two amounts added together. A third are still excited: one
such step has not wiped the bit.

Here nobody picked the gap to make the number come out. Take D large and N much
larger than D: the work closes in on kT ln 2 from both sides, and the population left in
the excited state goes to zero. The bit is wiped, and Landauer’s number is the work it
took. The temperature gets in through detailed balance, which is the thermal premise
the toy didn’t have. It’s still a model. The settling step is the one part (1) describes,
and the work and heat are the standard bookkeeping for a slowly driven two-state
system.

What ties it to a machine: the protocol counts one logical event, by definition, and one
is what the small machine’s CERTIFY charges, the last of the three paid acts behind
a raised flag (Section 16). That’s a match of two numbers, both one by choice, and
nothing more. There is no theorem mapping the protocol’s two register states to any
machine state. Here “heat to the bath” is the register’s mean energy before minus



                                                 367
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


after, so it assumes the bath receives what the register loses. That physical relation is
not established here. So a device test would have to measure the gap, the populations,
the rates, and the bath heat independently; separately establish that the device’s rates
are in detailed balance (that the up and down rates stand in the ratio the temperature
dictates), which the driven reset assumes and the canonical one breaks; and separately
establish that the device’s physical reset is the machine’s certify event. The driven
reset is an executable experimental specification. The canonical reset is a bookkeeping
toy. Neither is a measured device, and neither is an unconditional conversion of marks
to joules, and anyone who tells you otherwise has skipped the conditions.

21.4 What permanence adds to Landauer: nothing new, said plainly
Here’s a fair question: is there a prediction the permanent-certificate theorems make
that Landauer’s principle alone doesn’t? No, and the reason is short. The smallest case,
one certified state and one flipping in, is “set a bit to one whatever it held,” which is the
reset Landauer described and Bérut measured; Landauer’s own name for it is “restore
to one,” and Section 3 put it beside the toll at the start. The general bound, kT ln((m
plus k) over m) for squeezing m plus k equally likely states into m, is what Landauer’s
principle gives for that squeeze, at kT ln 2 for each bit removed. What the permanence
theorems add is a structural derivation: finiteness and a permanent reading force
any flag-raising instruction to merge some full states. They do not identify the newly
certified state as part of that collision, or supply the input distribution and physical
conditions for a heat bound. With those supplied, Landauer’s premise applies to
the uncertainty actually removed. The machine result and the physical premise do
different jobs.

21.5 What this section is
A calibration that’s a unit conversion; a pair of premises, consistent on the steps the
toll is about and inconsistent on the whole instruction set; a history that makes any
step injective; and a measurement protocol that’s a specification with a selected scale.
The physics in this book is in Section 4, as a named premise with its critics named.
Here there’s accounting, and I’ve tried to call every line by its right name. That’s the
end of the machine. What’s left is what it took to check any of this, and where the
checking stops.

Part V

Checking it, and its edge

22 How to break this
Every main claim in this book comes with the exact shape of the thing that would kill
it. I went to the trouble on purpose. A claim you can’t break is a claim that wasn’t
saying anything. So I’m handing you a loaded gun pointed at my own work, with
every sentence sharp enough to aim at. These are written as instructions: here is the
trace to find, the object to build, the theorem to exhibit. Build one and the proof tree
falls, and I mean that as an invitation.

The invitation is an old one, and people have put prices on it. Donald Knuth gives the
first person to find each error in his books one hexadecimal dollar, 0x$1.00, which is
$2.56, deposited these days at the Bank of San Serriffe, a bank that doesn’t exist, since
real checks turned out to be an open door for fraud. Why pay strangers to find your
mistakes? His own page says it plainly enough: a careful reader makes the book better
for everyone who reads it next. This chapter doesn’t come with a bank, real or made
up. What it comes with is, for every claim, a description of the exact object that would
make it fall, so you know before you start what counts as winning.

Before the list, three places to aim at me. A sentence of mine that says more than the
mathematical statement and argument it refers to. A definition that doesn’t capture
the English word it’s named for: on the small machine, “is at least 0” is a check that
can’t fail, and the step certifies it anyway, so “certified” there doesn’t mean “found
something out” (Section 16 says so, and that’s the kind of gap to hunt). And a list of
premises that only its own example satisfies.

22.1 The abstract claims (Parts II and III)
The universal floor (Section 3). Build a certification system that satisfies the one-step toll
and give a run from uncertified to certified with total cost zero. The universal floor
falls. If you instead drop the toll, you’ve built a free-certification system. That’s a
different system, and it counts for nothing against the theorem.

The toll from premises (Section 4). Exhibit a finite, duplicate-free list of every state, a
certificate no step revokes, and an injective step that switches it on. The permanent-flip
theorem falls, and the derivation of the toll with it. An infinite state space, a revocable
certificate, or an unpriced merge is not a counterexample; the chapter already builds
one of each. For the squeeze bound, a finite permanent machine with a cost meeting
the halving premise where one step switches k states on beside m certified ones and
two to the cost times m is less than m plus k; the squeeze bound falls. For merge-or-
revoke, a finite machine and an injective instruction that switches a reading on without
switching it off anywhere; the merge-or-revoke claim falls. A move that merges and

                                             369
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


also revokes counts against nothing. It’s the three cards. For the eight-state machine,
a move of it that merges two states and costs nothing; merge pricing on that machine
falls.

The bill in bits (Section 4). Exhibit a finite machine with a permanent certificate, a
move that switches k states on beside m certified ones (k at least one), and a spread
of probability over those m plus k states whose image under the move has entropy
above log base two of m. The entropy ceiling falls. For the general form, a step and a
spread on a finite list of every state under which two different states, each with some
probability, land on the same state while the entropy doesn’t drop; the strict entropy-
drop claim falls. A heat measurement on a real device below what the bound asks
doesn’t touch either theorem. It refutes Landauer’s premise for that device, and that’s
a fight with physics. The counting stays where it was. And a certifying step from a
state already known that gives off no heat isn’t a counterexample: the known-state
argument says the premise sets no positive floor there.

Learning is free (Section 5). Show that the four-state demon’s measure step merges two
states, or that its observer’s candidate list doesn’t shrink. The free-learning example
falls. A different price schedule that charges the measure step is allowed and isn’t a
counterexample. The claim is “not forced.” It never says “always free.”

The counter (Section 6; on the small machine, Section 16). Find a state of the small machine
and an instruction such that the ledger after is anything other than the ledger before
plus that instruction’s cost; the loud version is a ledger that goes down. Conservation
falls. The uniqueness half, that only one bookkeeping starts at zero and follows the
schedule, holds over any counter machine (Section 6); a reachable state where two
such bookkeepings disagree makes it fall.

Windows (Section 7). Exhibit a window and a price computed from the observed
before and after that meets the floor and never overcharges, on a machine where
two steps share their before and after pictures and only one certifies. The window-
pricing obstruction falls. A window that shows certification is not a counterexample;
the theorem says exactly that such a window prices exactly. For the three escapes, a
verifier of one of the three kinds that’s wrong about the pair, under its own relation;
the argument after Definition 7.1 falls.

Entitlement (Section 8). Produce a strict narrowing of a candidate list, with a distin-
guishing observation, that does not yield a strictly stronger membership test; the card
argument falls. Or exhibit a run with a tree no deeper than its paid steps, covering
the narrowing, whose counter rose by less than the index bits lost; Theorem 8.2 falls.
On every Thiele-complete machine: a run from a clean start that ends with the record
up, meets the hypotheses of Theorem 16.43, and has fewer record moves than the
index bits it narrowed, or has no earned chain in it; the entitlement bound falls, and
the weighted form falls the same way. A narrowing with a big drop and a small bill
is not a counterexample unless a tree no deeper than the record moves covers it: the


                                            370
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


covering is a hypothesis, and the uncovered-narrowing counterexample says why it
has to stay one. On the host machine, a run from a clean start that raises the record
only after more than sixteen CHECKs; the sixteen-check ceiling falls. On the small
machine, a program of INC and DEC that runs fewer than m moves and whose final
line number and B determine whether A ≥ m at every start; the free-step lower bound
falls.

The latch (Section 10). Exhibit an extension of a base whose record is driven by the
computation and never switches off, and which is not a latch on any event. The latch
theorem falls. A record that switches off, or one driven by a hidden clock, is the two
counterexamples already given.

The diagonal (Section 13). Two routes. A decider for some substrate with a shortcut
predicate whose flip the substrate can represent and which answers correctly on every
program; the generic proof fails at a named step. For the nat family, a d that correctly
decides the predicate of the substrate built from d. L has its recursion theorem by
proof, so it gets a target of its own: a map on L’s terms, computable by an L term,
with no term that behaves like its own image; L’s recursion theorem falls. On the host
machine: a host program that decides an extensional property of host programs that
some program has and some lacks, or a map of host programs that a host program
carries out, with no host program that computes the same function as its image; Rice’s
theorem for the host or its recursion theorem falls. On the small machine: a decider for
a property of what two-counter programs do from the clean start that some program
has and some lacks; the fixed-input Rice theorem falls. A decider for such a property
over every input of two-counter programs; the all-input Rice theorem falls. A two-
counter program that multiplies every plain input by the number of Theorem 16.60;
the multiplication obstruction falls. A map of host programs that a host program
carries out, with no host program that stops when its image stops and agrees with
it on register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of facts and whether
the channel is empty, is a counterexample to the fixed-point theorem for the record.
A map whose fixed point disagrees with its image on some other register is not one:
some computable map has no fixed point that agrees with its image on every register.

The pointer thesis (Section 15). It’s a thesis, so the three routes are its own: a deployed
discipline pricing a record that parties who didn’t produce it don’t copy and rely on;
a rival event copied and relied on that fails at a reachable state where certification
holds in a real ecosystem; an honest formalisation, with independence as defined
there, where certification fails the test.

One concession goes with it, and I make it in full. The window results, the separation
of the two runs, and the counter’s uniqueness don’t single out certification. Their
proofs use only that the step carries something the classical picture doesn’t determine,
so the same shape of result holds for any such field. Nothing in Parts II to IV proves
that certification is the one event a model is forced to price; Section 4 forces a price on


                                           371
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


every merge, certifying or not. That’s the thesis, and Section 15 is the case I make for
it.

The five models (Section 14). Each fragment has a theorem with a named falsifier: a
finality fork with nobody slashable; a gas schedule meeting floor and no-overcharge
whose charging predicate differs from the commit predicate on some step; a nonce n
and a function from quotes to Booleans that returns flag( P) on quoten ( P) for every
platform P; one of the RFC’s own example proofs that the transcribed inclusion check
rejects, or an input with leaf index equal to tree size that it accepts; a program the
bounds checker accepts whose verification condition fails. Each kills one fragment.
None of them, and I want this clear, says anything about the real system beyond the
fragment.

22.2 The machine claims (Part IV)
The small machine (Section 16). Four targets. From a clean start, a run that raises the flag
without an earlier passing CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY of the same claim, with
the counter’s version unchanged between the CHECK and the COMMIT; certification
provenance falls, and commitment provenance for a COMMIT alone. From a clean
start, a trace that leaves a fact in the table nobody checked; the no-forging claim
falls. From a clean start, a run that ends certified for a total charge under three; the
minimum-price theorem falls, and a run at exactly three is not a counterexample:
CHECK “A is 0”, COMMIT, CERTIFY from a start where A is 0 is one, and the same
program from any other start is refused forever. A check that can’t fail certifying for
three isn’t a counterexample either; the step doesn’t police trivial checks, and the book
says so. A two-counter machine and a program whose run on the small machine
disagrees with it step for step, or halts when it doesn’t; the step correspondence or the
halting correspondence falls.

Thiele-complete (Section 16). A machine that charges at least one for every move and
still meets the four clauses; the free-move requirement falls, and with it the exclu-
sion of clocks, whose proof uses it. A Thiele-complete machine and a function of its
window that gives its record at the end of every run from every loaded state; the
window obstruction falls. For clause independence, take one of the four witnesses in
Theorem 16.23 and show that it also fails one of the three clauses it is said to meet, or
that it meets the clause it is said to fail. That would break the claimed independence
witness.

The universal program (Section 16.13). A program of the small machine and a start on
which U halts and the guest doesn’t, or the other way round; the halting equivalence
falls. One on which the flags disagree, or the ledgers differ at a matching point; the flag
equivalence or the ledger equality falls. A run of U whose raised flag doesn’t stand
on a passing CHECK, then COMMIT, of one slot, then CERTIFY; the earned-chain
guarantee falls.

Every computably presented machine (Section 16.14). A computably presented Thiele

machine and a start on which UP ’s flag goes up while the machine’s reading never says
yes, or the other way round; the reading equivalence falls. With the reading starting

a ledger more than two above the machine’s; the surcharge bound falls. A program

The classical CHSH bound (Section 20). Exhibit four fixed bits and a tally consistent with

The integer check (Section 20). The game check has two walls, and here’s how to knock

The nine-by-nine (Section 20). A point and five extra numbers where the contraction-like

22.3 What’s mine and what isn’t
This is not a claim to have been first. Appendix C does the sorting item by item, with

Interpretation, which is mine and not proved. That structure is what a computation

I’ve given, and the proposals are where I’d aim first if I were you.

23 The claim ledger
Here’s everything this book claims, one line each: what kind of claim it is, and where it
lives. “Proved” means proved under the premises printed in that section, and nothing
more. If a line here ever says more than its section does, the section is right and the
line is wrong. “By unfolding” after it means the proof does little more than read the
answer off the definitions, a case split whose every branch is a line: true, checked, and
carrying almost nothing the definitions didn’t already say. If you’re counting results,
count those differently. I mark them so they don’t pad the list, and where they’re
stated in the book they carry the label observation.

Ledger is a good word for it, and it’s older than bookkeeping. Around 1400 a ledger
was a book that lay permanently in one place, a big church breviary, say, from the old
verb leggen, to lay; the account-book sense turns up in the 1500s. A book that stays
put. That’s the job here too. The home sections are long and they wander, and this is
the one place where every claim lies still, so you can come back and find it where you
left it.

The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


23.1 Claims about the model
First the model. Every line in this table is about any system that has the pieces the
line names: a state and a step, plus whatever the result asks for, a reading and the toll,
a counter and a price list, a window, programs. None of them is about my machine,
except the lines that run these results on it, which say so and point to Section 16.17.
The table runs over several pages, in reading order.

Here’s one way to use it, and it takes five minutes. Pick the sentence in this book you
trust least. Find its line. Read the Kind column before anything else. Then go to the
home section and check that the line says no more than the section does. If it says
more, you’ve found my mistake, and the end of this section says what I’d like done
about it.

23.2 Claims about the machine
Part IV built one small machine and the hosts that run it, and the ledger keeps them
apart from the model. The machine is the small one of Section 16, two counters and
six instruction kinds, where commitments are earned and universality is proved, with
the definition of Thiele-complete that every machine can be held against, the universal
program U on a host made of the same instruction kinds, and the priced program UP
that runs every computably presented Thiele machine. Every line in the next tables is
about those machines, or about every machine meeting that definition, or about the
game check and the physics section that close Part IV, and nothing else, under the
premises printed in its section.
