23.3 What I propose
The proposal joining these results is to make structural relations and their accounting
part of the state and the step. The items below spell out that proposal and a narrower
choice within it, the pointer thesis about certification. They reach further than the
theorems; none puts an unavoidable physical price on every observable change.

   • That the axis belongs in the step (Section 24, Section 25).
   • That the usual account of a computation is a shadow of the step (Section 25).
   • Within the record construction, that certification is the event selected by the
     reliance criterion of the pointer thesis (Section 15).
   • That this is a structural account of computation, with a cost model as one part of
     it (Section 24).
   • That the toll is the right thing to price. The alternatives are a wall or a penalty
     for contradiction (Section 14, Section 25).

And three things this book doesn’t settle, with what would settle each. Whether
Landauer’s critics are right, which would leave every theorem standing and one
premise unowned by the world: that takes measurements of real devices (Section 4).
Whether certification really is the pointer event: that takes a way to tie the definitions

                                                399
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


to the systems the thesis is about, and Section 15 gives three ways to kill it. And
whether there’s a smaller start than a partition: that takes a ruler someone can state
and a smaller structure measured by it (Section 2).

That’s the whole ledger. If you find a claim in this book that isn’t on it, or a line that
says more than its home does, that’s my mistake, and I’d want to hear about it.

24 Scope
This is the line around what I’ve proved. Inside it: an accounting law for one event,
a derivation of that law from premises each with its own counterexample, a set of
windows that provably lose it, a record axis that’s a latch over any base, a diagonal
that holds by proof on L, a machine of six instruction kinds on which commitments
are earned and which computes what two counters can, one fixed program in its
instruction kinds, run on a host with more counters and one paid move, that runs
every computably presented Thiele machine, and an integer check that implies a
bound by algebra. Outside it: everything that follows. This is the fence. I built it
myself, so lean on it before you trust it.

G. K. Chesterton, the English writer who has been called the prince of paradox, has a
famous fence, in a 1929 book called The Thing. A reformer finds a fence across a road,
can’t see what it’s for, and wants it cleared away; the wiser one tells him to go off and
find out why it was put there, and only then come back and argue for tearing it down.
This section runs the other way round. Every post below comes labelled with what
it’s there for, the overclaim it stops, so you don’t have to go off and find out first. Pull
up any post you like. Just look at what walks through the gap when you do.

Physical interpretation of the counter. The ledger is unique once the start and schedule
are chosen. That doesn’t make it entropy, and it doesn’t make it energy. A physical
bridge needs a model of which states carry information, premises that can all hold
at once, and a real argument tying the formal charge to dissipation. The permanent-
certificate theorems supply the first for an abstract finite machine with a permanent
reading. The two premises are shown able to hold together whenever every counted
step costs at least one, and for a one-bit reset. The small machine’s free steps merge
states and are charged nothing, which breaks the bridge for its whole instruction set
(Section 21), and the calorimeter protocol shows that population dynamics don’t fix
the energy scale. No joule value attaches to one mark without thermal and device
premises (Section 4, Section 21). Once you pick the start and the price list, the number
is forced by arithmetic, and it isn’t energy. What I’d need before it could be is the list
at the top of this paragraph.

Class separation. The witnesses show specific windows losing specific fields. They
don’t stop a conventional simulator from keeping those fields in its encoding. No
separation of standard complexity classes follows from the collisions (Section 7, Sec-
tion 16). I’ll be blunt about why I’m careful here. Whether P equals NP is one of the


                                            400
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


seven problems the Clay Mathematics Institute put a million dollars on, at a meeting
in Paris in May 2000. One of the seven has been solved since, the Poincaré conjecture,
by the mathematician Grigori Perelman, who posted the proof as preprints in 2002
and 2003. P versus NP hasn’t. If a two-state collision on my machine settled it, I’d
be owed a million dollars. Nobody owes me anything. A window that loses a field
is a fact about that window. A complexity class is a fact about what every possible
program can do within a budget, and nothing in these collisions reaches that far.

Trace initiality, and what it doesn’t settle. The universal property of the trace fold is
about evaluating lists of instructions: pick where a target starts, and there’s exactly
one way to fold a list into it (Section 6). The counter’s uniqueness assumes a schedule.
Rise-only pricing assumes an event, and a reference count that says what charging too
much means (Section 7). Those results make the construction precise. None of them
shows that the schedule I chose, or the event I chose, is physically necessary.

Other observables. Certification is one worked example. A family of other observations
might turn up other structural laws, but each would need its own events, its own
evidence, and its own cost rules, justified on their own terms. The window and oracle
results are about what specific maps keep, and nothing more.

Program predicates versus state observations. The state-level collision (Section 7’s wall)
and the program-level diagonal (Section 13’s wall) live in different domains. Linking
them would take a theorem of its own. The nat family and L (Section 13) keep their
explicit quantifiers and representability premises.

Entitlement bounds. The count is handed its tree and its covering, along with the
payment condition. It doesn’t dig the tree out of an arbitrary run, and it isn’t a
Shannon bound on every trace (Section 8). On every Thiele-complete machine the
payment is the record moves, each exactly one mark, and a floor that takes no tree
exists when the questions are the run’s own CHECKs; but its answers are taken at the
rivals as they start, a free branch can still narrow for nothing, the lists, tree and fibres
are supplied except in the worked members, and the covering can’t be dropped. The
search through n bits is capped at 16 questions by the machine’s fact table, and the
time tax is a lower bound for programs of INC and DEC only. Nothing here extends it
to every Thiele-complete machine (Section 16.17).

Quantum behaviour. The fixed-matrix equivalence is about one completion with zero
marginals and zero within-party moments. The elliptope lets the within-party mo-
ments move, at the level of correlators. That correlator completion has an opera-
tor realisation by the construction in Appendix D. Full behaviours with prescribed
marginals ask for more: the correlator construction does not establish those extra prob-
abilities. A sound check isn’t complete for those bigger sets, and the elliptope decider
is mathematics. None of the small machine’s properties is it (Section 20).

The record axis. The proved structural result is: a permanent record driven by a base


                                            401
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


computation is a latch on an event; on a finite machine its write merges states; and the
named windows don’t recover it. Certification is one instance. No theorem selects it as
the unique event every system must record (Section 10, Section 15). A finite monotone
multi-valued record decomposes into threshold latches. One Boolean latch can’t hold
it. Revocation, including revocation priced from the other side as in Casper, lies
outside the permanent-record axis; a price on revocation doesn’t transfer to a price on
the write (Section 14). Probabilistic records don’t inherit the uniqueness result either.
Two honest random records can have the same branches and the same charges and
still give those branches different weights, one choosing evenly and one two to one, so
the schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities. And no single deterministic latch explains a
record that can branch both ways from the same observation. Weak base equivalence
is defined and is an equivalence; no two of the three bases of Definition 10.3, and
none of them and the small machine, are related by it in this book, and the latch form
holds on each separately, so it doesn’t tell them apart (Section 10). A record driven
by the computation that stays up is a latch, and on a finite machine its write merges
states; which event deserves the latch isn’t proved; records that can come back down
lie outside all of this (they’re limit computability’s, and Section 10 points at Ershov’s
ladder), and random ones lose the uniqueness.

Who it’s safe against. Every guarantee about the record is about programs: any list of
instructions, run from a clean start on a step that does what its definition says, one
writer stepping at a time. That covers the buggy program and the hostile one. It
doesn’t cover whoever sets the start (a snapshot put back, a table loaded with facts
nobody checked), a reset or a power cycle, whoever picks the program, the wire that
carries the report, someone who flips the flag with a probe, the tools that built the step,
or a second writer that changes a counter without bumping its edition. Those are the
operator, the device and the tool chain, and they’re outside this fence. A record read
by someone who didn’t watch it being made is only as good as their reason to believe
the box that shows it. The ways across that I know of, a quote over measured state and
a proof that travels on its own, are in Section 7 and Section 14, and this book builds
neither. What the guarantee gives inside the fence is safety: no program forges the
chain. Availability is a different promise, and it isn’t given. A hostile program can put
the trap up or fill the table, and after that nothing useful gets done. The mathematical
machine uses whole numbers, which never overflow, so versions and the ledger grow
without bound. A build with fixed-width counters, versions or ledger has to stop
before any of them wraps, failing safe with the trap up, because a wrapped version
could make an old fact look live again and a wrapped ledger would fall. Starting,
restoring, resetting and that overflow stop belong to the implementation, and none of
them is proved here.

The diagonal on the machine. What’s proved for the small machine’s programs is that
halting is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 16.4, for them and for the
universal program (Section 16). L has its recursion theorem, Rice and halting by proof



                                           402
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


(Section 13). On the host machine, the one with a counter for every number, Rice’s
theorem holds for properties that depend on everything a program ends with (every
register, the table, the channel, the trap, the ledger and the flag; the line number and
the versions are left out), for programs run on an input in register 1; s-m-n holds with
no premise on register 2; and Kleene’s recursion theorem holds for the transformations
a host program carries out on numbers, with a fixed point that agrees with its image
on stopping, register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of facts and
whether the channel is empty; for some of these transformations no fixed point agrees
on every register. On the two-counter machine itself Rice’s theorem is proved on
every input, with facts compared by what they’re about, their versions left out of the
comparison; Kleene’s is proved with inputs written as powers of two and refuted with
plain inputs (Section 16.18).

The five models. Each is a fragment transcribed from a specification, with a named
theorem and a named limit: the Casper transcription has no deposits or fork choice;
the gas fragment omits the refund cap; the attestation fragment has no signatures;
the transparency verifier covers control flow and leaves collision resistance out; the
proof-carrying checker is a three-instruction memory-bounds language. None is a
claim about the real system beyond its fragment (Section 14).

The machine. Part IV has one small machine, with the hosts that run it, and here’s its
fence. The small machine of Section 16 (two counters, six instruction kinds) is where
commitments are earned: from a clean start, a raised flag went through a passing
check, a commitment and a certification of the same claim, nothing is forged, and the
cheapest such run adds exactly three to the ledger, a price reached by a check that could
have failed (the step doesn’t police trivial checks: a check that can’t fail certifies for
three too). It’s also where universality is proved, by matching Minsky’s two-counter
machines step for step and using the halting reduction of Forster, Larchey-Wendling
and coauthors. It’s Thiele-complete under a definition every clock-style machine fails,
and every machine meeting that definition hides its record and ledger from its own
window. The universal Thiele machine is one fixed program, U, on a host with the
small machine’s instruction kinds and more counters, with no guest step built in: it
runs every program of the small machine from every clean start start( x, y), halts when
the guest halts, raises its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate if and
only if the guest’s flag rises somewhere in the guest’s run, and keeps a ledger equal to
the guest’s at every matching point. With one paid move added, one fixed program,
UP , runs every computably presented Thiele machine: its step, prices and reading
computed by programs, the reading decided on every state, the run fixed by a driver.
The host halts when the guest stops, its flag is the latch of the guest’s reading, raised
on its own earned chain whose claim is that reading, and its ledger is the guest’s plus a
surcharge of at most two when the reading starts at no, a surcharge no program on that
host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest certifies with its whole ledger
below three. A machine whose reading no program decides is outside. A simpler host



                                           403
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


with a guest step built in runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror of the guest’s
flag; its ledger only covers the guest’s. The small machine’s check price is flat, its fact
table holds sixteen, and its certificate is historical (Section 16 lists the rest).

The comparison machines. The bases I put the latch on are fragments too. The register
machine of Section 10 is the one with indirect addressing in Definition 10.3, and that
theorem is about it. The reversible result (Theorem 10.3) covers any base whose step is
injective, and on a finite state space says only that no injective step raises a permanent
reading. None is a theorem about real memories or full reversible languages. The cost-
semantics results are local correspondences, short of full cost-framework embeddings:
the trace’s cost is a writer cost and a grade, and the toll is the potential method with
one potential (Section 6). Nobody’s whole type system gets embedded either.

Outward consequences. I looked for results about real systems that would need the
record axis. What’s proved are the five fragments of Section 14, each a transcription
with its own named limit, and none is a theorem about the deployed system. Stronger
candidates would need protocol or hardware semantics I haven’t formalised, and I’ve
proved nothing about them. So none of this yields a new outside result that both
needs the record axis and is ready to use.

Where each result lives. Every system that follows the toll, whatever its states: the floor,
at most as many certifications as cost, and the potential-method reading. Every finite
machine whose price covers merges: the toll for permanent records, and, when its
move names can be decided equal or different, which instructions every such price
must charge. Every finite machine paying per halving: the machine’s own narrowing
bound. Every machine extending a base with a driven, permanent record: the latch.
Every window through which a certifying and a non-certifying step look alike: no
exact price from the window. Every machine meeting the definition of Thiele-complete:
a free move, at least three marks on any run from a clean state that ends certified, and
a final window that doesn’t determine the record or the ledger. Any eight counts:
the integer check and its PSD bridge, which are mathematics. This machine only: its
six instruction kinds and their prices, its sixteen slots, its own colliding pair, and the
encodings its universal programs use.

What I’m proposing beyond that. A structural account of computation: the relations it
carries belong in the state, their treatment belongs in the step, and a cost model is
one part of that account. The permanent record supplies a case we can take apart.
The pointer thesis asks whether certification deserves that record in the systems it
describes. It can fail without changing the latch or window arguments, which use no
such selection criterion.

The larger proposal is about which distinctions an account of computation ought to
preserve. The constructions show particular ways to preserve them and what follows
under the stated premises. Their worth depends on the questions we need the account
to answer. If a program’s log and a proof about that program recover every distinction


                                            404
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


we need, that weakens the case for requiring the account in the step. If a deployed
system has good reasons for a wall or a penalty rather than a toll, that weighs against
the proposed pricing there. Those are ways to examine the proposal, alongside the
counterexamples that test individual theorems.

25 Conclusion
Put the triangle, the cups and the two computers back on the table. Turning the
triangle preserves relations you can check with your fingers. Turning a cup records an
act; a row of cups can distinguish stages that one cup cannot. The two computers can
leave the same answer while differing in what they did to reach it. In each case we had
to say what the things were, which moves were allowed, which relations survived,
and what our way of looking could tell apart.

Part I gave that question its vocabulary: structure as relations among things, kept
under chosen changes, carried by whatever stuff, relative to a frame. A partition
supplied the smallest sorting by the ruler I chose. Making a grouping, keeping it,
checking it and standing behind it separated into different acts. That gave me a case
in which to ask how an account of computation could carry the difference and price a
change.

The record case got an exact form in Part II: five parts, one rule, one theorem you
proved at the table. Then the rule stopped being only my preference. With finitely
many yes-states and a flag that stays up, every move that raises it merges states, and
under the merge-pricing rule the toll follows. The collision is a property of the instruc-
tion on its allowed states; it need not involve the state that just entered. A heat bound
additionally needs the input distribution and a physical model. That’s a derivation
under three premises you can refuse one at a time, each with its counterexample built.
It isn’t a proof that every computation has to adopt the rule; and the charge on forget-
ting is a named premise with its critics named. Learning can be free; committing to a
record that stays put can’t be, on those premises. That’s as far as physics goes in this
book, and I’ve tried to keep it exactly that far.

Part III was the logic, and here’s what it earned, in the order it was earned. The counter
is arithmetic once the schedule is chosen. A window in which a raising step and a
quiet one look the same can’t price the raise exactly, by a fact about functions far older
than the machine. Entitlement is defined as an object, a checked relation, and a paid
event; given lists, a tree and a covering somebody supplies, a run that paid a charged
step for every level of the tree has paid for the index bits it commits to (no run is shown
to have to pay them, the run doesn’t recover the tree, the lists count repeats, and the
index bits aren’t the questions anybody asked); on every Thiele-complete machine the
same count, for a run from a clean start, is a theorem about its record moves, with the
earned chain inside the run, and the count can’t do without the covering; and it is a
license to lean on a claim. It doesn’t prove the claim true. Insight, in the sense the toll
prices, is a committed relation. A feeling doesn’t count. Its floor is flat: at least one,

                                           405
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


however deep. The claim behind the flag is something a check could have refused,
and in the bare model nothing makes the commit wait for the check. Over any base, a
base-driven record is a latch, with two free choices, the event and the price list; “only
one substrate” is false and “one structure, many price lists” is true once the event is
fixed. No procedure the substrate itself can represent decides the shortcut predicate,
given a recursion theorem, by the same diagonal that broke Frege’s floor, and the
machine’s answer is to record the commitment. It leaves the judgement unautomated.
Of five record disciplines I modelled in fragments, one charges a fee at the write. And
which event to record is a thesis, with its refutations listed.

Part IV made the relations operational. The small machine’s state ties a checked claim
to an edition of a counter. Its step uses that tie: change the counter and the old check
no longer authorizes a commitment. From a clean start, a raised flag therefore requires
a passing check, a commitment about the same edition and a certificate, in order.
Three marks suffice and no such run pays less. These are facts about the construction,
including the case of a check that cannot fail. Its two-counter base supplies universality
under the stated encoding.

The universal programs ask whether those relations survive another machine doing
the work. On the host with more counters, U runs the small machine’s programs from
clean starts, matches halting and answers, earns its own flag exactly when the guest
raises one, and matches the ledger at corresponding points. With PAY added, UP runs
every computably presented Thiele machine, latches the guest’s reading through its
own earned chain, and carries the guest’s ledger with the stated surcharge: at most
two at the raise when the reading starts at no. The simulation arguments describe
which states correspond; the execution chapter measures the time this particular rep-
resentation takes.

Changing the base and joining machines ask the structural question more widely. The
lift works under its interface conditions, with counterexamples where those conditions
fail (Section 17). Side-by-side machines need both records; a single total can lose which
side acted. Sequential hand-offs and nested runs each need their own conditions
(Section 18). These constructions make us say which relation is carried through a
change and which is lost. The six instruction kinds are one place to inspect that work.

Then a check worth earning, the two-player game with an integer test whose pass
forces Tsirelson’s bound for the tally it’s handed. And what the counter has to do with
physics, which is less than the name Landauer might suggest. The places where the
machine came up short of the idea stayed on the page: its free steps merge states, so
the chairs don’t force the toll on it, and only the merge premise asked of the record
layer does; and a check that can’t fail certifies for three like any other. Part V was
where to challenge it and what would break it. Every result carries the shape of
the thing that would kill it, gathered in one place (Section 22): a state of the small
machine and an instruction after which the ledger goes down; a contractive correlator


                                           406
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


whose pinned matrix isn’t positive semidefinite; a certification system that follows
the toll and certifies at total cost zero; a function on numbers that correctly decides
the shortcut predicate of the substrate built from it. Any one of them brings down
the theorem it matches. I hunted. I came up empty. That leaves the arguments here
for you to examine. Even where a theorem holds, my sentence can say more than it
establishes, or a definition can fail to catch the word it’s named for. Section 22 starts
with those.

If you asked what’s new here, I wouldn’t give you one thing, because there isn’t one.
There are four, and each comes with its fence and its neighbours. First, the toll isn’t
only my preference: on a finite machine a reading nothing turns off can only be turned
on by a step that merges states, so if merges are priced, raising it costs (Theorem 4.1,
Observation 4.2). The counting under it is the finite cousin of the recurrence argument
Zermelo threw at Boltzmann in 1896, and the abstract merge price is motivated by
Landauer’s reset example. Identifying that price with heat needs the further premises
stated in Part II. Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) had already put a physical price on
that merge for finite automata, so what’s here is the toll as a rule on a ledger. Second,
a window that shows a raising step and a quiet one the same can’t price the raise
exactly (Observation 7.2); that a price computed from what a window shows can’t
tell apart two steps the window shows the same is elementary, and what’s here is the
pricing form. Third, a record driven by the computation that never switches off is a
latch on one event, over any base (Observation 10.1); latches and history variables
are old, and the theorem covers only records that never come down. Fourth, a record
that’s priced, and on the small machine earned (Theorem 16.9), under the move of
guaranteeing something about every program. That move isn’t mine at all. It’s the
reference monitor’s (Anderson, 1972), made precise for monitors that watch a run
(Schneider, 2000), and proved for monitors checked at every instruction (Azevedo de
Amorim and coauthors, 2015). What’s put together under it here is built and checked,
and its idea isn’t new: the check bound to the edition it looked at, the toll paid on
top, and universal programs that carry both to every program of the small machine
and to every computably presented Thiele machine, earning their own flag as they go.
Appendix C sorts all four with sources.

And two things I’d point at if you asked how far the checking reaches. Neither is a
fifth new thing.

In the game: an integer check on eight counts forces a five-by-five matrix to be positive
semidefinite, and from there the Tsirelson bound follows, and the chain never once
reaches for physics. No Hilbert space, no operators, no observables. The route through
the matrix is the first rung of a ladder Navascués, Pironio and Acín built in 2007. None
of that route is mine, and the semidefinite road to Tsirelson’s bound is older than that.
What’s here is the check that runs in whole numbers, and the checked link from “the
check passed” to the bound. It’s algebra you can follow line by line. The reason this
is an algebraic claim is in its definitions and the argument: no premise identifies the


                                          407
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


counts or matrices with a physical device. And on the small machine’s host a raised
flag can stand on that check: from a clean start a raised flag contains a passing CHECK
of the packed counts, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY, and the check passes exactly when
every pair was sampled and the five-by-five is positive semidefinite (Section 20).

In the model: the diagonal rules out a correct decider whenever its flip can be ex-
pressed inside the substrate and the substrate supplies the fixed point; in L the fixed
point is proved from the reduction rules and the diagonal is Rice’s theorem. On the
small machine’s host, Kleene’s recursion theorem and Rice’s theorem are proved for
its own programs, so the wall stands there by proof, with its premise a theorem: no
host program decides a property of what a program computes that some program has
and some lacks; such a property is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 16.4
(Section 16.18).

What this book doesn’t settle, by my count. Whether the toll is the right thing to
price. The five real systems mostly built a wall or a penalty for contradiction. Whether
certification is the pointer event. Whether Landauer’s critics are right, which would
leave every theorem standing and one premise unowned by the world. And the
question I’d most like someone to take from me: is there a smaller start than a partition,
by a ruler they can state? I said in Section 2 it would change this book. It would.

And the two computers from the first pages, the sorter and the copier, holding the
same list. Walk the warehouse again. The list is in order on both. On the machine
with the earned layer, a different part of the state tells you whether a check and a
matching commitment occurred. Its rules maintain the relation to the edition that was
checked. Cover that part of the machine and the distinction disappears from your
view. Change the counter and you can watch the old check become stale. Those are
different operations, with different consequences, and you can follow each one.

A report carried out of the warehouse raises another question: what connects that
report to the machine? The flag alone supplies no answer. A window, a copying
operation, a second machine and a reader each introduce relations of their own. The
book’s constructions ask explicitly which of them hold. That is how the example
reaches beyond the lamp: through what survives a change of view, a change of state,
or a change of machine.

So that’s the Thiele Machine: structure held as state, acted on by a step, with an
account of the changes and a view that may keep or lose their distinctions. The record
and its toll give that proposal a worked mathematical core. The small machine and its
interpreters give us particular constructions to take apart. The argument is for treating
those relations as part of computation itself. Each theorem answers a stated question
under stated premises; the choice of which questions an account ought to preserve
remains there for you to challenge.

The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele



A Things I had to learn first
I came in with none of the formal fields this work turned out to need. By the time the
argument had taken shape I’d needed enough of half a dozen of them that I had to put
down somewhere what those fields had words for. This appendix is that place. None
of it is the argument. It’s what I needed to be able to make it. Everything below is
what I understood after I went and read about it; I’m not claiming to teach you these
subjects, and if you already know a part, skip it.

A.1 Bits, bytes, and what a CPU sees
A bit is one digit that’s either zero or one, the smallest fact a machine can hold. Every-
thing else is bits stacked up. Eight of them make a byte, which lands you any number
from 0 to 255, and the first thing that genuinely surprised me is that the same byte is
also a letter: a convention called ASCII simply agrees to call 65 the letter A, 48 the digit
0, 32 a space. Nothing in the byte knows which it is. The meaning is a convention laid
on top.

You can see the convention’s seams with a pencil. Write 65 in binary: 1000001. Knock
off the first two digits and what’s left, 00001, is 1, and A is the first letter. B is 66, which
ends in 00010, two. Now lower case: a is 97, which is 1100001, the same pattern with
one more bit switched on, the one worth 32. Every capital and its small letter differ in
exactly that bit. That’s on purpose. The first version of the code, in 1963, had no lower
case at all; when lower case arrived, in the 1967 revision, it was placed so the two cases
differ by one bit, which made matching them, and building keyboards and printers,
simpler. Nothing in the byte knows it’s a letter, but somebody made the letters easy
for a circuit to tell apart.

Everything in this subsection is about real CPUs. None of it belongs to the abstract
model, which has a kind of state and a step rule and nothing about widths or slots,
and the small machine of Part IV needs very little of it: its two counters have no width
at all, and hold any whole number.

A word is a chunk of bits the CPU treats as one unit, in 2026 usually 64 bits (0 to
about 18 quintillion) on a desktop or server and 32 (0 to about 4 billion) on many small
devices. The abstract model doesn’t care which width.

A register is a named storage slot inside the CPU that holds one word, the fastest
place to read or write. Memory is a longer list of word-sized slots accessed by index,
the address. The program counter is one specific register that tracks where in the
program the machine is; after every instruction it moves on to the next instruction
unless the instruction says jump. On the small machine it’s called the line number. A
stack pointer is a register pointing at the top of a region used for nested calls. A port
is a named channel for talking to the outside world.

Modular arithmetic means counting wraps around: counting modulo 16, the numbers
run 0 to 15, and 17 wraps to 1. Bitwise operations work on the bits of a value one

                                              409
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


position at a time: AND is 1 only when both bits are, OR when either is, XOR (exclusive
or) exactly when they differ. A logical shift moves bits left or right: for unsigned values
it multiplies or divides by a power of two, discarding overflow on a fixed-width left
shift and rounding down on a right shift. Popcount is the count of one-bits in a value.
Hexadecimal is base 16, digits 0 to 9 then A to F, written with a 0x prefix: 0xFF is 255.

A trap, on a CPU, transfers control to a handler; the interrupted program may later
resume. It can report an error or request a service. On the small machine a trap is
one bit that goes up when an instruction refuses, and then the core stops moving. An
ISA, instruction set architecture, is the list of every instruction a CPU recognises, each
identified by an opcode, a numeric tag the CPU decodes. The small machine’s has six.
The abstract model has none; it has a step rule.

A.2 The notation the formal parts use
I don’t think in these symbols, and I had to learn to read them. The natural numbers
are 0, 1, 2, and so on, written with a double-struck N; the integers add the negatives;
the reals are the whole number line. A function from a set A to a set B is written
with an arrow. For a finite set, vertical bars around it mean its size; for a number, its
absolute value. A big sigma is a sum over every member of a set. A delta before a
quantity means the change in it. An upside-down A means “for every”; a backwards
E means “there exists.” A double arrow is implication; a double-headed one is “if
and only if.” A small circle between two functions is composition, apply the right one
first. Angle brackets mean one of three things, and the sentence around them says
which: a pair of numbers packed into one, ⟨m, n⟩ (Section 16.13); a dot product of
two vectors; or, around a random quantity, its long-run average, which I picked up
from the Bell-test papers. The circled times ⊗ in the quantum derivation combines
two systems: A ⊗ B acts as A on the first and B on the second; the appendix gives
its entries. The integer check itself uses neither operation nor quantum systems. A
superscript T on a matrix is its transpose, rows and columns swapped, and I with a
subscript n is the identity matrix.

A.3 Category theory beyond Part I
Section 2 sketches objects, arrows, composition, identities, associativity, and the iden-
tity laws. Beyond that: a functor is a structure-preserving map from one category to
another, sending objects to objects and arrows to arrows while respecting composition
and identities; think of it as a translation rule between two worlds of structure. An
embedding is a functor that throws nothing away, and faithful is the precise version
for arrows: two distinct arrows never land on one. Conservative is the version for
inverses: if the image of an arrow has an inverse, the arrow already had one, so the
functor can’t manufacture an isomorphism (an arrow with an inverse) that wasn’t
there. The two properties are different, and neither gives the other. Read the natural
numbers under addition as a category with one object and an arrow for each number,
and the same for the integers. The inclusion of the first into the second is faithful, since



                                            410
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


distinct naturals stay distinct integers. It isn’t conservative: 1 has no inverse among
the naturals, and its image has one, minus 1. The other way round, the functor from
the integers onto the trivial one-arrow group is conservative, since every arrow of the
integers already has an inverse. It isn’t faithful: it sends every integer to the same
arrow. An embedding needs faithfulness specifically. A monoidal product combines
two objects or two arrows into one, with a unit and laws that make the combining
behave. An initial object has exactly one arrow into every object; the counter’s unique-
ness in this book is a uniqueness-on-reachable-states fact, and no category-theoretic
initial object is involved. Yoneda’s lemma is where the categorical engine first clicked
for me, the night I quit borrowing other people’s runtimes (Section 1), and nothing in
the formal development uses it.

A.4 Bell-test vocabulary
A correlation between two outcomes is the average of their product; with outcomes
plus or minus one it lies between minus one and one, plus one meaning always match,
minus one always differ. A correlator is one such average in a labelled setting, E00 for
Alice’s setting 0 and Bob’s 0. The marginal of a joint distribution is the distribution of
one side alone with the other averaged out; zero-marginal means each side’s outcome
is plus or minus one equally often on average. A local hidden-variable model is one
where both outcomes are fixed by a shared random variable agreed before the game
plus each side’s own setting; Bell’s theorem says no such model produces certain
correlations quantum mechanics does. No-signalling means neither side’s marginal
depends on the other’s setting. Quantum-realisable means compatible with some
quantum state and measurements; the NPA hierarchy gives a ladder of necessary tests,
each a positive-semidefiniteness condition on a moment matrix, and no single rung is
known to be sufficient in general (Chaturvedi’s 2026 preprint argues none is, even for
this game). The PR box is the no-signalling correlation that wins the game every time,
stronger than quantum mechanics allows. Cauchy-Schwarz is the inequality that a
dot product is bounded by the product of the lengths. The Tsirelson bound is two root
two, the largest game score quantum mechanics allows; the classical bound is two and
the PR bound is four. (If you go looking for Boris Tsirelson’s 1980 paper, look under
Cirel’son, the spelling the journal printed, or you may not find it.) The elliptope is the
set of correlators that can be filled out into a positive-semidefinite matrix.

A.5 Other terms I use without rebuilding
Provenance is the recorded chain of where an object came from; on the small machine,
a commitment’s provenance is the passing check that came before it (Section 16). Simu-
lation, in computer science, is one system imitating another’s input-output behaviour;
a Turing machine can simulate a system with effective finite encodings of its states
and moves and a computable step on those encodings, my small machine included, by
representing its state on tape, and the difference this book is about is what a window
on that tape shows. That’s real, and it raises a fair question: if a tape can stand in for
the state, what was the difference? The tape carries a picture of the state, the way a


                                           411
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


photograph carries a fire, and a photograph of a fire keeps you exactly as warm as any
other photograph. The counter and the toll live in the step rule. An encoding copies
the bytes, and the step rule isn’t in them. A Turing machine built with the toll in its
own transition table is a different case: it directly satisfies the model’s rule. Whether
it also simulates another machine is a separate question. What no machine can do is
make a simulated rule binding just by writing it down on tape.

Projection is a function that drops information on purpose. The window on the small
machine keeps three things, the line number and the two counters, which are what
Minsky’s machine already has, and that’s why projecting lands you back in ordinary
computation. It drops everything else, including the parts doing the new work: the
versions, the table of checked facts, the channel, the ledger and the flag. Nothing is
wrong with it. It’s a perfectly good function. It just costs you what made the state more
than a pair of counters. A quotient is the operation of declaring two things the same
when they agree on what you chose to look at and working with the classes instead.
A projection does exactly that. Dropping fields one at a time also glues together states
that the dropped fields kept apart. The fibre of a function over a value is everything
the function sends to that value. An injection sends no two inputs to the same output;
a surjection covers every output. Decidable means an algorithm always halts with a
yes-or-no answer; keep the claim and the algorithm apart, since the algorithm decides
the claim only once there’s a proof that its answer matches. Polynomial time means
running time bounded by a power of the input size; P is the problems solvable that
way, NP the problems where a candidate solution can be checked that way, and whether
the two are the same is open.

“Kernel” has two uses here. In mathematics, the kernel of a map is what it sends to the
identity; for a projection the useful version is the relation “these two states project to
the same thing.” An operating-system kernel is the core of an operating system, as in
the packet-filter example in Section 14.

A.6 Matrices
A matrix is positive semidefinite (PSD) when vT Mv ≥ 0 for every vector v; the game
check is all about one matrix being PSD. The determinant of a square matrix is a single
number that is zero exactly when the matrix squashes some direction flat. For a two-
by-two matrix with rows ( a, b) and (c, d) it’s ad − bc. For a bigger one, expand along
a row: for each entry, delete its row and column, take the determinant of what’s left,
multiply by the entry, alternate the signs, and add up; the recursion bottoms out at
two by two. A principal submatrix is what you get by choosing some of the indices
and keeping only those rows and the same columns; its determinant is a principal
minor. A symmetric matrix is PSD exactly when every principal minor is at least zero,
every one of them, and the game check uses the three-by-three ones (Appendix D.4).
The Schur complement turns a question about a block matrix into a question about
a smaller one. For a symmetric block matrix with corner block P, off-diagonal block
Q and other corner R, it’s R − QT P−1 Q, and when P is positive definite the whole

                                           412
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


matrix is PSD exactly when that complement is (Lemma D.8). Positive definite matters;
invertible isn’t enough. Take P = −1 and every other entry zero: the complement is
zero, which is PSD, and the whole matrix isn’t.

A.7 Borrowed ideas the book pushes on
These get their full story in the chapter that uses them; here’s the one-line version for
when you’ve forgotten which one Landauer was.

The pigeonhole principle: put more pigeons than holes and some hole holds two. Sec-
tion 4’s room with too few chairs is that, and so is the proof that a permanent flag can
only be raised by a step that forgets something. Landauer’s principle (Rolf Landauer,
1961): a step that wipes information, lowering the entropy of what a machine holds
by some number of bits, gives off mean heat at least Boltzmann’s constant times the
temperature times the natural log of two per bit, under a physical model relating that
logical entropy to the memory’s thermodynamic entropy. In this book it’s always a
premise with its name on it. Nothing here derives it (Section 4, Section 21). Entropy,
in Claude Shannon’s sense: for a spread of chances over states, roughly the average
number of yes-or-no questions you’d need to pin the state down, so an even spread
over n states has log2 n bits. A spread, in this book, is just a list of chances that add up
to one. Maxwell’s demon (Section 5): a little creature that watches molecules and sorts
fast from slow, seemingly for free; Charles Bennett’s answer was that the measuring
can be free and the wiping of the demon’s notes is what costs. The potential method
(Robert Tarjan, 1985): pay for a run with a quantity stored in the state, so a step’s bill
plus the change in the stored quantity is what you count; Section 6 reads the toll as
that method with one particular potential.

The halting problem (Alan Turing, 1936, who essentially proved it without stating it
in this form; Stephen Kleene stated it in 1952, and Martin Davis seems to have been
the first to name it, in 1958, Section 13): no program decides, for every program and
input, whether it stops. Kleene’s recursion theorem (Stephen Kleene, 1938): for any
transformation of programs that can itself be computed, some program computes the
same partial function as its own transform. Its timing, storage and records need not
agree. Rice’s theorem (Henry Rice, 1953): any property that depends only on what a
program does, and isn’t true of all programs or of none, can’t be decided by a program.
The diagonal is the move under all three: build the thing that does the opposite of
what the table says about it (Section 13). L is a small lambda calculus, a language
made of nothing but functions applied to functions, which Yannick Forster and Gert
Smolka presented and which Section 13 uses as a tool. A cryptographic hash is a
short fingerprint of a longer piece of data, made so that finding two inputs with the
same fingerprint is supposed to be hard; a hash chain folds each new record into the
fingerprint of the last, and a Merkle tree folds them pairwise into one root (Section 3,
Section 14).




                                            413
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


A.8 Words this book builds
These are mine, or mine in the sense that I pinned them down for this book. Each is
built properly in the chapter named; this is only a reminder.

A few words first, because everything else hangs off them and each has exactly one
meaning. The model (or the abstract model) is a kind of state and a rule for stepping,
plus exactly the extra pieces a given theorem asks for: a certification reading and the
toll, or a counter and a price list, or a window, or programs written as states and a
recursion theorem. The name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. Parts I to III
develop those general arguments, alongside particular examples and applications to
the later machine. A substrate is the model’s shape with whatever extension a theorem
names, and nothing else; the word never means my machine, and never the side
of a simulation that does the stepping (Let me be straight with you). My machine
(also the machine I build, the build, the small machine, the smallest honest machine,
Section 16) is the concrete machine of Part IV that fills in those pieces at once: two
counters with their versions, a table of checked facts, a channel, a trap, a ledger and a
flag, six instruction kinds and their prices, with its hosts and universal programs. The
scaffolding is that machine and everything built on it, and Part IV lives there. A Thiele
machine, lower case, is any system proved to be an instance of the certification system
(Definition 3.1), five parts and the toll; the paper toys are, and so is the small machine.
Weakly Thiele-complete means a Thiele machine whose base is Turing-universal; that
bar is nearly empty, since a clock that charges one for every move pays the toll for any
record. Thiele-complete means more (Definition 16.7): a universal base whose moves
are free and can’t touch the record, a record that stays up once it’s up and is raised
from a clean state only after a passing check, a commitment to the same claim and a
certificate, one mark for each of those three acts, and a claim whose check, commit and
certificate raise the record on some loaded starts and leave it down on others. Every
clock-style machine fails it; the small machine meets it; and every machine that meets
it hides its record and ledger from its own window. A universal Thiele machine is
one fixed program that runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with the guest’s
record earned again and its toll paid by the host’s own steps. The ones in this book are
U (Section 16.13), a fixed program in the small machine’s instruction kinds, with no
guest step built in, that runs every small-machine program with halting and flag exact
and its ledger equal to the guest’s at every matching point, and UP (Section 16.14),
the same program with one paid move added, that runs every computably presented
Thiele machine, one whose driver, step, prices and reading are computed by programs
with the reading decided on every state, keeping its reading as a latch and, when the
reading starts at no, its prices to within two, a surcharge no program on that host, run
from a clean start, can avoid when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three.
The simpler host with a built-in guest step runs guests by construction and keeps
a mirror of the guest’s flag. A computer running the small machine isn’t a Thiele
machine; it implements one, inside bounds, the way a laptop implements a Turing
machine. When a word below belongs to only one of the two layers, the entry says


                                           414
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


which.

A partition is a sorting of a pile into groups, nothing in two groups and nothing left
over (Section 2). A certification system is a state type, moves, a step, a cost per move,
and a yes-or-no reading, plus one rule, the toll: a move that turns the reading from
no to yes costs at least one (Section 3). The rule is called A2 in the conditions table
(Appendix B). A move merges when two different starting states land on the same end;
one that never does is injective, it forgets nothing. A reading is permanent when no
move turns it from yes back to no (Section 4).

The counter, which I also call the ledger: in the model, a number carried in the state
that starts at zero and that every step raises by exactly that step’s charge (Section 6).
My machine has exactly one, the ledger µ (Section 16). Two other things get called
counters, and each chapter says which: Minsky’s two bins on the small machine, and
the eight counts that tally the game’s rounds (Section 20). Neither is the ledger. A price
list says what each move costs; the model takes it as given, and my machine’s table of
what each instruction costs is in Section 16. A receipt is a total that lives in the state,
only climbs, equals the sum of the charges on every path including the failures, and is
the only such total for its price list (Section 6 proves it for any system with a counter
and a price list; on my machine the sum is a theorem too, Section 16). In the model
there is just a certification reading, yes or no (Section 3); on the small machine it’s the
flag, set by a CERTIFY that passes and never cleared.

These belong to the small machine only (Section 16). A two-counter machine is Minsky’s:
two counters holding whole numbers with no upper limit, and two instructions: add
one, and subtract one and jump if the counter is above zero, or else go on to the next
line; already enough that nobody can decide in general whether one halts. The small
machine is a two-counter machine plus HALT and three instructions for the record,
six in all: INC, DEC, HALT, CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY. A counter’s version is its
edition number: it starts at 0 and goes up by one every time the counter is written, so
an edition never comes back. A fact is a property, a counter and a version together, such
as “A is even, as of edition 3”; the properties come from a fixed language with three
forms, is zero, is even and is at least n. The same theorems also hold for any property
language with an exact equality test whose checker is proved to mean what it says,
and one such language reads a counter as a list and asks whether it’s sorted. The fact
table holds up to sixteen facts, and the only way in is a CHECK that passed; nothing
ever leaves it. The small machine’s channel holds one committed fact or nothing, and
COMMIT puts a fact there only if the table has it about the counter’s current edition.
With the flag up from a clean start it names a commitment earned that way, and a later
COMMIT replaces it, as a two-commit run shows. The trap is a bit that goes up when
an instruction refuses, and then nothing in the core moves again. A commitment is
earned when a passing check put its fact in the table first, about the same edition, with
no write to that counter in between; on the small machine every flag raised from a
clean start is earned, and that’s a theorem. CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY cost one


                                           415
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


each and everything else costs nothing, so from a clean start a run ending with the
flag up adds at least three to the ledger, and a run whose check could have failed adds
exactly three: CHECK is zero on A, COMMIT, CERTIFY, from a start where A is 0. The
step doesn’t police trivial checks; is at least 0 passes every value and certifies for three
too. The host machine is the small machine with a counter, called a register, for every
whole number, and one property, Slot, true of a number that packs a property of the
small machine together with a value it holds of. A slot is a register of the host used
for nothing but holding one checked fact about the guest, and its mirror is a register
beside it, safe to read, that says which claim the slot holds while its fact is live. U is the
fixed program of host instructions that runs every small-machine program; it reads
guest instructions out of one register, keeps the guest’s counters in two others, and
puts every checked fact in a slot, because on this machine reading a counter writes it.
The universal program’s guest is a program of the small machine, held as one number
in a register of the host and run one instruction at a time by U’s fetch and decode. UP
is U with one more handler, for PAY, an instruction that costs one and does nothing
else; its guests are programs compiled from computably presented Thiele machines
(Section 16.14).

A window is any function that shows you part of a state (Section 7); a shadow, said
loosely, is what a window leaves you with. A collision is two steps that look the same
through a window, before and after, where one raises the flag and the other doesn’t
(Section 7). Entitlement is what a run has when it carries an object, a checked relation
between that object and a claim, and a paid event that put the object in place: a license
to lean on the claim. It doesn’t prove the claim true (Section 8). A latch is a record
that switches on the first time some event holds and never switches off (Section 10).
The diagonal’s substrate (Section 13) is the model’s shape extended with programs, a
run that may give nothing back, a counter that never falls, a way to write programs
as states, the transformations the substrate counts as its own, and its own recursion
theorem for those; the proof of the diagonal uses neither the counter nor the toll.

B Every assumption in one place
This book uses systems defined by stated conditions, and theorems with stated
premises. I’ve named each condition where it’s used. Here they are side by side,
because a reader who wants to break this book should be able to see every place
where it says “suppose,” in one list, with what each “suppose” buys.

The labels A2 to A6 in this appendix are shorthand for the conditions listed below.
They are not additional claims: each label names the rule written beside it.

B.1 Systems and their conditions
Definition B.1 (Certification system). A certification system consists of a set of states
S, a set of moves I, a step function step : S × I → S, a cost cost : I → N, and a reading
cert : S → {no, yes}, satisfying the toll: every move that turns the reading from no to


                                             416
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


yes costs at least one. This is the condition of Section 3, called A2 in the table below.
Every result stated “for any certification system” assumes it.


Definition B.2 (Quantitative certification system). A quantitative certification system
is a certification system with a witness, a function W from states to N, and a threshold
N ∈ N, satisfying: (A3) W (s) + cost(i ) ≥ W (step(s, i )), the witness grows by at most
what the move cost; and (A5) a state that reads yes has W (s) ≥ N. An optional
additional condition is (A4) W (s) ≤ W (step(s, i )).


Theorem B.1 (The floor raised to a threshold). In a quantitative certification system, every
run from a state with witness 0 (this starting condition is called A6) to a state that reads yes
has total cost at least N.

Proof. Adding A3 along the run telescopes: the witness at the end is at most the
witness at the start plus the total cost, so at most the total cost. A5 says the end witness
is at least N. Neither A4 nor the toll is used.

A3 and A4 bound opposite directions, and neither implies the other: witness 1, cost 0,
witness 0 satisfies A3 and breaks A4, and witness 0, cost 0, witness 1 does the reverse.
These conditions describe a general setting. The small machine’s own floor of three is
proved directly (Observation 16.16) and never goes through it.

Here are the labels side by side, so none of them is left without a meaning.

 Label                 Condition
 A2                    the toll
 A3                    the witness grows by at most the cost
 A4                    the witness never drops
 A5                    yes needs a witness at the threshold
 A6                    the run starts with witness zero
