Three remarks on the table. First, the recursion premise holds by construction for the

                                             418
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


nat family and by proof for L (Section 13) and for the programs of the small machine’s
host (Section 16.18). Second, the substrate used for the diagonal also carries a different
rule from the toll: the counter never goes down on a step. Neither implies the other,
and the diagonal uses neither. Third, merge pricing is an abstract lower bound on
every merging instruction. It is the pairwise restriction of worst-case entropy pricing,
which is equivalent to the halving price. Landauer’s premise instead bounds heat from
the uncertainty actually removed under its thermal conditions. A known starting state
supplies no positive floor from that premise (Theorem 4.13). Riechers, Boyd, Wimsatt
and Crutchfield (2020) derive additional work bounds under time-symmetric control
of metastable memories. Their low-error bound depends on the initial distribution
and the memory’s time-reversal behaviour; it is not a universal heat charge on each
logical move.

C What’s mine, and what isn’t
Every chapter of this book leans on somebody, and I’ve named them where I lean.
This appendix does a different job, and it’s the one where I’d most like to be caught
out, and caught out early. For each thing the book could be accused of claiming as its
own, it says what was already known, what this work actually defines, builds, proves,
or connects, and what kind of contribution that is. Six kinds, and they aren’t the
same claim: a new result (a statement nobody had); a new proof of something known; a
mechanization (a known result checked by a machine); an implementation (something
built that runs); a synthesis (known pieces put together under one question); and a
conjecture or thesis (a claim stated and not proved; a thesis ties defined notions to the
world, so no proof can settle it). Every kind can be worth doing. None of them is the
others. And if you read down the list and notice that “new result” hardly shows up,
good. You’re reading it right.

Two warnings about my own evidence before the list. First, “I didn’t find it” is a fact
about my searches. The literature is bigger than my searches. I searched with every
tool I had, and some tools will cheerfully invent a citation if you let them, so where it
matters I say where I looked, and you should assume it may well be sitting in a paper
I’d need a few more lifetimes of homework to read. Second, nothing below is inferred
from how many theorems there are, from a proof assistant’s clean bill, or from a good
story about who came before. Those tell you the work was checked. They don’t tell
you it’s new. Thousands of checked theorems could, in principle, be thousands of
careful ways of agreeing with Tarjan.

C.1 The universal floor and the potential method
Known: the potential method of amortized analysis, a function on states whose drop
bounds the cost of a run, is Tarjan’s (1985), and it has been mechanized more than
once (Nipkow in Isabelle/HOL, 2015 and 2019; Charguéraud and Pottier’s time credits,
2019), built into type systems for automatic resource analysis (from Hofmann and Jost,
2003, and Hoffmann and coauthors, 2011, onward), and recast in cost-aware type


                                           419
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


theories (Niu, Sterling, Grodin and Harper, 2022). Mine: choosing the potential that is
one when a designated reading says no and zero when it says yes, so that “the crossing
costs” (the toll) and “every run that crosses paid” (the floor) are the potential method’s
two halves (Section 6). Kind: a mechanization of a known technique with a particular
choice of potential. The choice is the point: it makes “was certified” something the
account must carry. The theorem is not new mathematics. If it looks clever, that’s
Tarjan’s cleverness; my part was picking which number to plug in.

Go back to Tarjan’s paper and there’s a sentence that sits right on the line this book
draws. He opens with the dictionary (to amortize is to put money aside at intervals,
as in a sinking fund) and then gives two views of the method. In the banker’s view
the computer is coin-operated, and each operation is handed credits to spend or save;
in the physicist’s view, which he credits to Daniel Sleator, every state has a potential
and you count its changes. Then he stops to say that the credits are only an accounting
device: the programs that actually run contain no mention of credits or debits. That’s
exactly right for what he wanted, a bound proved about a program from outside. It’s
also exactly the gap. In his method the coins live in the proof. The one move I chose
was to put them in the step, where no program takes a step without it being counted.
Same arithmetic, different place.

C.2 The toll from finiteness, permanence, and a price on merges
Known: that steps which merge states (no single-valued inverse) are what Landauer’s
principle charges for is Landauer’s (1961), sharpened by Bennett (1973, 1982, 2003; the
words “the erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths” are from the 2003
abstract); generalizations and the dependence on the input distribution are Maroney’s
(2009), Sagawa’s (2014), Wolpert’s; the critique is Earman and Norton’s and Norton’s.
Write-once memory is an old topic in coding theory (Rivest and Shamir, 1982), where
the question is reuse and price never comes up, and Chris Heegard (1985) worked
out the capacity of permanent memory with noise, again a question of how much fits.
What it costs doesn’t come into it. Statisticians priced permanence on finite memory
in their own currency: in Hellman and Cover’s analysis of hypothesis testing with
finite memory (1970), a machine that settles its answer by falling into states it never
leaves does worse than one that doesn’t, so a decision held for good costs memory
states. Heat never enters their analysis. And the counting under the theorem is older
than any of that, twice over. Theorem 4.1 is the finite, discrete cousin of the recurrence
argument Zermelo, using Poincaré’s theorem of 1890, turned on Boltzmann in 1896,
here aimed at a reading. Zermelo aimed it at entropy, and Bocchieri and Loinger gave
the quantum recurrence in 1957. In automata form it is classical: a finite machine
whose moves are all one-to-one reshuffles recognises only group languages, and the
inputs that raise a permanent reading form a language that is never one of those
unless it is empty (Pin’s 1992 paper on reversible automata is the reference I’d check;
automata theorists treat the step as folklore), and going quantum doesn’t change it
(Brodsky and Pippenger, 2002: quantum finite automata that measure once, at the


                                           420
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


end, accept with bounded error exactly the group languages). The closest of all is
recent. Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) give a proof that if the smallest automaton
for a language has a step that merges states, every automaton for it does, and argue
that recognising it on a device that repeats one local step produces entropy, while a
language whose smallest automaton only reshuffles can be recognised for free; one of
their worked examples is the strings with no b, the complement of the latch’s language.
That’s the core with a physical price already on it. And the logarithm in the heat
floor matches the absolute-irreversibility bound of Murashita, Funo and Ueda (2014),
which Manzano, Kardeş, Roldán and Wolpert (2024) carried over to computation. The
logarithms coincide for the stated counts. This does not supply a physical reverse
process: absolute irreversibility needs forward and reverse path probabilities that the
logical map alone does not specify. Constructor theory states a cousin of the same core
for devices that run in a cycle: Marletto, Vedral and coauthors (2022) and Violaris and
Marletto (2022) built an irreversible task out of the quantum homogeniser and argued
that erasure may cost more than Landauer’s bound. Section 4 tells all of it. Mine: the
price as a named rule on a ledger, a premise that merges cost at least a mark, which
turns “the flip merges” into “the flip costs” on any machine whether or not anybody’s
physics is right, and the toll derived from it (Observation 4.2); what comes with that
form, namely the characterisation of the moves every merge-pricing schedule must
charge, when move names can be decided equal or different (the merging moves, so
the core again in pricing words), the merge-or-revoke dichotomy for a single move,
the squeeze and entropy forms for a permanent flip, and a built counterexample for
each premise (Section 4). Kind: the core is classical, and somebody else’s: Zermelo’s
in physics, folklore in automata theory, with Pin’s paper as the place to check it. The
pricing form isn’t wholly mine either: priced in entropy, for automata, it’s Ouldridge
and Wolpert’s. They derive the price from the physics. I assume mine. What’s mine
is the price as a named rule on a ledger, the toll derived from it, its single-move and
counted forms, and the counterexamples. The physics is a named premise and is
Landauer’s. Searches: the core turned up in the places just named, and its physical
price in Ouldridge and Wolpert; I didn’t find the ledger form or the derived toll stated
anywhere I looked, and nobody’s search covers a whole field, mine least of all.

C.3 Learning free, committing priced
Known: that measurement can be done at no fundamental cost and the cost sits
in erasing the record is Bennett’s resolution of Maxwell’s demon (1982), with the
quantitative trade-off by Sagawa and Ueda (2009). The closest physics I found to the
line between learning and committing is Ouldridge and ten Wolde’s fundamental
costs of persistent copies (2017; with Govern, 2017), copies that stay correlated with
their originals after the two come apart; theirs is heat for a correlation in chemistry,
and Section 5 says how it differs. The sharp chemical form, that a persistent copy
grown at equilibrium carries no information about its template, is Poulton, ten Wolde
and Ouldridge’s (2019), and that the bill can be split between measuring and erasing
in more than one way is Fahn’s (1996). Mine: the four-state demon, the three-state ring


                                          421
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


and the two-state impossibility (Section 5). Kind: finite models illustrating a known
physical point inside my ledger. Not a new physical claim. Bennett did the hard part
in 1982; my four-dot example puts the difference between learning and committing
where you can work through it yourself.

C.4 Windows that can’t price what they hide
Known: a function of an observation is constant on the observation’s fibres; that’s ele-
mentary, and the systems version of it is Moore’s distinguishing experiments (1956),
Kalman’s observability (1960), and the completeness question of abstract interpreta-
tion (Cousot and Cousot, 1977; Giacobazzi, Ranzato and Scozzari, 2000); in control
theory it is diagnosability and opacity of discrete-event systems (Sampath and coau-
thors, 1995; Saboori and Hadjicostis, 2007), where a collision is a hidden event no
observer can diagnose without delay; in economics it is the hard-evidence view of
mechanism design (Green and Laffont, 1986; Bull and Watson, 2007), where what a
mechanism can tell apart is limited by the evidence on offer; and its sharp form for
fingerprints is Naor and Rothblum’s lower bound for checking a stored file (2005); in
distributed systems it is Haeberlen and Kuznetsov’s (2009), that only omission and
commission faults can be detected from outside, and in philosophy it is Easwaran’s
transferability (2009). Mine: stating the pricing version (no window price is exact
across a collision), exhibiting a colliding pair for the small machine’s window, and the
theorem that every Thiele-complete machine has two runs from one clean start that
end looking the same through the window its base shows, one certified and one not
(Section 7, Section 16). Kind: an elementary observation about what a window hides,
plus specific facts about the machine and the definition.

C.5 Structural entitlement and its bound
Known: decision-tree counting bounds (a tree that tells N cases apart has depth at
least log2 N); certifying algorithms that hand over checkable certificates (McConnell,
Mehlhorn, Näher and Schweitzer, 2011); proof-carrying code (Necula, 1997); the gap
between justified true belief and knowledge (Gettier, 1963). Mine: the definition of
entitlement as an object, a checked relation, and a paid event on the record, and the
count that, given lists, a tree and a covering, a run that paid for the tree’s depth
pays at least the index bits it commits to (Section 8). Kind: synthesis; the counting
idea is standard, the assembly and its vocabulary are this work’s, the pricing policy
is assumed (nothing derives it), and the count is proved in its bill form over any
certification system, and for the record moves of every Thiele-complete machine on a
run from a clean start, with the earned chain in the run, a floor that takes the run’s own
checks in place of a tree, and a counterexample showing the covering can’t be dropped
(Section 16.17); and in a form where the run makes the posterior from a prior, every
drop is made by a check the run passed, and the index bits are at most k times the bill
when each passing check keeps a 2−k share, a hypothesis the same counterexample
shows is needed (Theorems 8.4 and 16.45).



                                           422
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


C.6 The record axis is a latch
Known: monotone, write-once state is old: the latch (Eccles and Jordan, patent filed
1918, paper 1919), sticky bits (Plotkin, 1989), grow-only state in replicated data types
(Shapiro and coauthors), history variables and stuttering in refinement (Abadi and
Lamport, 1991), append-only authenticated sets for transparency logs, which fit re-
vocation as a once-only event (Tomescu and coauthors, 2019), and, in program logic,
monotonic state, where a property witnessed once on state that only moves forward
can be recalled at any later point, with a soundness proof and a working home in
F⋆ (Ahman, Fournet, Hriţcu, Maillard, Rastogi and Swamy, 2018): the type-theory
name for a record that stays up. Past the finite case, inductive and quasi-inductive
definitions (Richter and Aczel, 1974; Burgess, 1986) and the flag trick of infinite time
Turing machines (Hamkins and Lewis, 2000) are the transfinite versions of a record
that only grows and a toggle, and Danos and Krivine’s (2005) reversible calculus needs
an action declared irreversible in order to commit. Mine: the exact statement that a
record driven by the computation that never switches off is, over any base, a latch
on one event, with its converse and a counterexample for each of the two conditions,
and the argument that base-driven records agree up to the price list while the stronger
uniqueness fails (Section 10). Kind: a small structural lemma, I think not stated before
in this form (I found no prior statement in the searches I ran), built from old notions.
The proofs show why the record must latch and why its price list remains a separate
choice.

C.7 The diagonal and L
Known: Kleene’s recursion theorem and Rice’s theorem; Lawvere’s fixed-point form
(1969) and Yanofsky’s retelling (2003); mechanized recursion theorems and Rice (Nor-
rish in HOL4, 2011; Carneiro in Lean; Forster, Kunze, Smolka and coauthors, including
L itself, 2017, and their library of undecidability results). Mine: the diagonal stated
once over any substrate that supplies a recursion theorem; and Rice and halting proved
again for L from its reduction rules (Section 13); and the same two theorems built for
the small machine’s host, with Rice’s on every input of the two-counter machine and
Kleene’s with inputs written as powers of two, and Kleene’s refuted for plain inputs
(Section 16.18). Kind: checked instances of known theorems of computability. They
hold for any model with universality and s-m-n, and the work is in building those for
this machine.

C.8 The game check
Known: that positive semidefiniteness of a correlation matrix gives the Tsirelson
bound is Tsirelson’s (1980) and Stephanie Wehner’s semidefinite proof (2006), from
a paper on Tsirelson bounds for generalized CHSH inequalities; the moment-matrix
hierarchy, the Schur-complement analysis of this very level-one matrix and the level
1 + AB are Navascués, Pironio and Acín’s (2007, 2008), with both four-body cells free
where my matrix ties them; that every point with a PSD completion is the correlator
table of a quantum strategy, built from anticommuting observables in a maximally


                                          423
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


entangled state, is Tsirelson’s too (1980); the arcsine characterization is Landau’s (1988)
and Masanes’s (2003); and Tsirelson’s bound has already been checked by machine,
in Isabelle/HOL (Echenim and Mhalla, 2023) and in Lean’s mathlib. Rational sum-
of-squares certificates are Helfried Peyrl and Pablo A. Parrilo’s (2008), from a paper
on computing sum-of-squares decompositions with rational coefficients. Mine: a
decision procedure in integer arithmetic on outcome counts; a checked chain from
“the counts pass” to “the pinned level-one matrix is positive semidefinite” to “S2 ≤ 8”;
explicit constructions of the representation in finite dimension, real or complex, on
two eight-level systems, and a proof of the arcsine characterization; proofs of the
contraction equivalence by explicit test vectors; and the level-1 + AB cascade (on
the slice ⟨{ A0 , A1 } ⊗ { B0 , B1 }⟩ = 0) and an elliptope gate in whole numbers, with a
soundness proof (Section 20 and its derivation appendix). Kind: an integer procedure
connecting counts to these known bounds, with a new proof of a known equivalence
in one slice. I found no prior formalization taking counts as input, and that’s a report
on where I looked, and the literature is bigger than where I looked. The same check
earned on the small machine’s host, a raised flag standing on it, is built and checked;
the idea isn’t new (Section 20).

C.9 Five record disciplines, one question
Known: each system and its guarantee belongs to its designers: Casper (Buterin and
Griffith, 2017), Ethereum’s storage gas and refunds (EIP-2200, EIP-3529), extend-only
TPM registers, Certificate Transparency (RFC 9162), proof-carrying code. Mine: asking
all five whether the write is priced, with a small checked fragment of each (Section 14).
Kind: synthesis and an organizing reading; the fragments are not verifications of those
systems.

C.10 The pointer thesis
Known: Zurek’s quantum Darwinism (2009), with Ollivier, Poulin and Zurek (2004)
and Blume-Kohout and Zurek (2006): preferred states are the ones whose records
proliferate redundantly in the environment. Mine: borrowing that shape for the
question of which event deserves a record, with definitions (copied and relied on by
parties who didn’t produce it, independent carriers), two toys, and refutations of two
stronger forms (Section 15). Kind: thesis. No claim about quantum physics.

C.11 The counter as a receipt
Known: one-way counters that give order and termination are old: Turing’s 1949 note
on checking a large routine, Floyd’s ranking functions (1967), Lamport’s clocks (1978).
Carrying a run’s cost beside its result is the writer cost of Danner, Licata and Ramyaa
(2015) and of Danner and Licata (2022), and the graded effect semantics of Katsumata
(2014), with a working-language version in Orchard, Liepelt and Eades (2019). The
receipt side of time credits is Mével, Jourdan and Pottier’s (2019): in their extension of
the Iris logic every step uses up a credit and produces a receipt, receipts prove lower
bounds, and enough of them prove that a counter can’t overflow in any feasible time,


                                           424
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


which is the closest published neighbour of a total that only climbs. Mine: putting
three properties side by side (the total only climbs, it equals the sum of the charges
on every path including the failures, and it is the only such total for a given price list),
the argument for any system with a counter and a price list, and the checked sum on
the small machine (Section 6, Section 16). Kind: synthesis; the abstract statements are
checked over any counter machine, and on the small machine the sum is too. Against
the graded frameworks the answer is split: the counter is their writer exactly, and
their type systems, bounding relations and before-the-run checking of grades are not
embedded, because the grade here is written by the step during the run (Section 6).
For the well-graded, loop-free programs defined in Section 6, on runs that do not trap,
the counter’s rise equals the fixed grade. The loop built there costs its input value, so
no fixed whole number is its exact grade on every input; an input-dependent grade is
exact. The arguments and their formal counterparts are given there. Cost-aware type
theories such as calf allow grades that depend on the inputs.

C.12 The small machine
Known: two-counter machines and the undecidability of their halting are Minsky’s
(1961, 1967), mechanized by Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors (2019, 2020).
The guarantee about every program is older than any of this, and it isn’t mine either.
It’s the reference monitor (Anderson, 1972): a check that sits in the path of every op-
eration, so no program gets around it. Schneider (2000) worked out what a monitor
that watches a run can enforce: only safety properties, the kind a bad run breaks at
some finite moment, and “no CERTIFY without an earlier earned COMMIT” is one
of those. Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors (2015) verified monitors that check tags
at every instruction. The shape of “earned,” a certificate nothing can make except
through the rules, is Milner’s LCF, where a theorem is a value only the logic’s rules
can build (Gordon, Milner and Wadsworth, 1979; Gordon, 2000); the small machine
is that architecture at the level of single instructions. “No certify without an earlier
commit” is also a correspondence assertion in the sense of Woo and Lam (1993), which
Gordon and Jeffrey (2003) check with a type system, and a store of commitments that
the rules of a dialogue keep, each speaker’s updated by the rules as the moves are
made, is Hamblin’s (1970, chapter 8, on formal dialectic); the difference from all three
is again that here the step enforces it. A check that blesses a value and a write that
takes the blessing away is close kin to dynamic taint tracking, whose labels go back to
Denning’s lattice model of information flow (1976), with the blessing itself, controlled
endorsement, given a type system and a security theorem by Cecchetti, Myers and
Arden (2017), and what a monitor can enforce with bounded memory is Talhi, Tawbi
and Debbabi’s question (2008). A small monotone record inside each replica of a repli-
cated service is A2M (Chun and coauthors, 2007), TrInc (Levin and coauthors, 2009),
MinBFT (Veronese and coauthors, 2013) and Damysus (Decouchant and coauthors,
2022), and Clement, Junqueira, Kate and Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs,
what such a record buys and what it doesn’t. The signature route to the same goal,
which needs no trusted step, is IA-CCF (Shamis and coauthors, 2021): replicas sign


                                            425
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


and log their protocol messages in the ledger, so blame lands on individual members
however many of them misbehave. And “check once, issue a capability the system
trusts, rely on it later” is built and deployed in Garg and Pfenning’s proof-carrying file
system (2010), whose logic lets a policy’s consequences change with time and state,
and in Sirer and coauthors’ logical attestation for the Nexus operating system (2011),
unforgeable statements about programs used as credentials; those are the closest sys-
tems I’ve found to check, commit, certify. Mine: a machine of six instruction kinds on
two counters, with a version for each counter, a bounded fact table and a channel; its
theorems that, from a clean start, a committed fact was checked first about the same
edition, that nothing is forged, that nothing is evicted, that with the flag up from a
clean start the channel names a fact an earlier passing COMMIT committed, and a
later commit can replace it, as a two-commit run shows, and that a run from a clean
start to a raised flag adds at least three to the ledger, with three reached by a run whose
check could have failed (the step doesn’t police trivial checks, so one that can’t fail
costs three too); the same theorems for any property language with an exact equality
test whose checker is proved to mean what it says, a sorted list read out of a counter
included; and the step-for-step match with the two-counter machine, so halting is
undecidable for it (Section 16). Kind: an instance of monitor enforcement with two
things on top that I didn’t find put together where I looked: the check is bound to
the edition of the thing it checked, and a toll is paid for the commitment. The first of
those alone is old: checking at commit time that nothing you read has changed since is
optimistic concurrency control (Kung and Robinson, 1981), and each counter’s version
is its version number. What I didn’t find is that check put together with a toll. The
universality and the undecidability are borrowed, and the other properties are short
consequences of the step rule. Whether the design is new I can’t say, and I make no
claim beyond the proofs.

C.13 The universal host
Known: Turing’s universal machine (1936), which runs any machine given as data,
and the universal register machines that run two-counter programs. Keeping a guest
and the code running beside it out of each other’s state is what a virtual machine
monitor promises (Popek and Goldberg, 1974). Compiling computable functions into
counter machines is established by Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors. Mine:
one fixed program, U, written in the small machine’s own six kinds of instruction on
a host with a register for every whole number, with no guest step built in, that runs
every program of the small machine from every clean start start( x, y), halts exactly
when its guest does, raises its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate if and
only if the guest’s rises somewhere in its run, and keeps a ledger equal to the guest’s
at every matching point; its host machine is Thiele-complete, and whether U halts
on a loaded guest is undecidable (Section 16.13). Two small facts force its shape, and
they’re stated there: reading a counter on this machine writes it, and a finite program
can’t keep the guest’s facts on a copy of the guest’s counter, by the pigeonhole. Beside
it, a simpler host with a built-in guest step runs guests by construction and keeps a


                                           426
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


mirror of the guest’s flag, with the mirror, isolation and earned-chain theorems. Code
that shares unprotected memory with a record can overwrite it. Ordinary computers
can also isolate memory and enforce rules through monitors. The claim here is the
specific simulation and record guarantee proved for the fixed interpreter U. Kind:
implementation and mechanization of a design whose shape is Turing’s universal
machine, with the record and the toll carried through. The universality is borrowed
from the small machine and from Minsky. And the same program with one paid move
added, UP , runs every computably presented Thiele machine, with its halting matched,
its reading carried as a latch on the host’s own earned flag whose claim is that reading,
and its prices to within a surcharge of at most two when the reading starts at no, which
no program on the host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest certifies with
its whole ledger below three (Section 16.14); the counter-compilation construction is
given in Appendix F. Kind for that part: implementation and mechanization again.
That a universal machine runs any computable machine is Turing’s; what’s carried
through here is the record, earned again, and the prices, exact up to the surcharge, and
I didn’t find that put together where I looked.

C.14 Thiele-complete, defined so a clock fails
Known: Turing completeness, and the observation every theorist makes in four sec-
onds, that a toll alone is cheap: a machine that charges for every step pays any toll.
Enforcement mechanisms have been compared and sorted before, and they aren’t
one notion seen several ways: James Morris (1973) separated access limitation from
authentication in programming languages, and Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett and
Fred Schneider (2006) classified which policies execution monitors, program rewriters
and static analysis can each enforce, and they differ; Wai Wong (1995), on a neighbour-
ing track, recorded and checked HOL proofs so a theorem could carry its derivation.
Mine: a definition of Thiele-complete with four clauses (a free universal base that can’t
touch the record and a record that stays up once it’s up, an earned record, an exact
toll on the three record acts, and some claim whose check can fail), the proofs that
every clock-style machine and a paid latch and a silent machine fail it while the small
machine, the same machine over any property language with an exact equality test, a
proved checker and a property that holds of one number and fails of another, and the
universal program’s host meet it, and the theorem that every machine meeting it hides
its record and ledger from its own window (Section 16). Kind: a definition with short
consequences. The window theorem is the fibre fact of item 4 plus one observation,
that a universal base prints any window for free. I’m not claiming the definition is
the only reasonable one, or that LCF kernels, reference monitors and proof-carrying
code are all Thiele-complete machines in disguise; Hamlen, Morrisett and Schneider’s
sorting says such mechanisms genuinely differ, and the book doesn’t have a theorem
showing the definition holds up across such differences.




                                          427
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


C.15 What that adds up to
Read straight down the list. The mathematics underneath this book is mostly known,
and some of it is very old. The question organizing this book is what structural
relations an account of computation should carry in its state and step, with certifica-
tion and its price as the worked case, and the answer isn’t one result. It’s four, and
I name them the same way wherever they come up. The toll derived from finite-
ness, permanence and a price on merges (item 2; the counting is classical, the finite
cousin of Zermelo’s recurrence objection and folklore about permutation automata,
and Ouldridge and Wolpert already priced it in entropy for automata, so what’s mine
is the price as a rule on a ledger and the toll it gives, and the price is an abstract premise
motivated by Landauer’s reset). The pricing form of the window fact (item 4; the fact
itself is elementary). The latch form of a record that never comes down (item 6; latches
and history variables are old). And a record that’s priced, and on the small machine
earned, under the reference monitor’s every-program move (items 12, 13 and 14; the
move is Anderson’s, Schneider’s and the micro-policy authors’, and what’s added is
the check bound to its edition, the toll on top, a definition of Thiele-complete that a
clock fails, and universal programs that carry both to every small-machine program
and to every computably presented Thiele machine, earning their own flag). The first
is a ledger form of a core that’s classical and already priced in physics; the second
and third are small exact statements I didn’t find stated where I looked; the fourth is
built and checked, and its idea isn’t new. The proofs connect those statements to one
small machine and the programs that run on it. Around it is my best attempt at saying
which is which, which you should check as hard as anything else in here. Item 2’s
core, the finite cousin of Zermelo’s recurrence objection, was folklore among automata
theorists, with Pin’s paper as the place to check it, long before I found it, and its price
in physics was Ouldridge and Wolpert’s. If someone shows me its ledger form, the
pricing form in item 4, or item 6 stated earlier, I’ll move it up the list and be glad to,
and a little embarrassed, in that order.

D The CHSH derivation, in full
This appendix supports Section 20. That section tells the story; this one does the
algebra. Each item gives the statement with its hypotheses and the steps needed to
check it. Nothing here identifies an arbitrary matrix with a physical state. Where
quantum strategies enter, their relationship to the matrices is stated explicitly.

D.1 Setting and notation
Definition D.1 (Settings, outcomes, correlators). Alice receives a setting x ∈ {0, 1}
and Bob a setting y ∈ {0, 1}. Each answers a bit, recoded as an outcome a, b ∈
{+1, −1} (bit 0 becomes +1, bit 1 becomes −1). The correlator Exy is the average of
the product ab over the rounds with settings ( x, y). The CHSH quantity is

                                S = E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 .

The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele

whose rows are indexed by Alice’s setting and whose columns by Bob’s. The rows of
E are ( E00 , E01 ) and ( E10 , E11 ); the columns are ( E00 , E10 ) and ( E01 , E11 ).


Definition D.2 (Counters). There are eight counts: for each setting pair, samexy counts
rounds whose two answer bits matched and diffxy counts rounds whose bits differed.
A round adds one to exactly one of the eight. Write

                                                                                 Dxy
          Nxy = samexy + diffxy ,        Dxy = samexy − diffxy ,         Exy =       .
                                                                                 Nxy


A matched round contributes ab = +1 and a differing round ab = −1, so Dxy is the
sum of the products and Dxy /Nxy is their average. Since | Dxy | ≤ Nxy , every correlator
from counters lies in [−1, 1]. When a bucket is empty, its correlator is defined as 0. The
score is E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 .

D.2 The classical bound
Lemma D.1 (Deterministic strategies). Let a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ∈ {+1, −1}. Then −2 ≤ a0 b0 +
a0 b1 + a1 b0 − a1 b1 ≤ 2.

Proof. Factor: a0 b0 + a0 b1 + a1 b0 − a1 b1 = a0 (b0 + b1 ) + a1 (b0 − b1 ). If b0 = b1 then
b0 + b1 = ±2 and b0 − b1 = 0; if b0 ̸= b1 the other way round. In both cases exactly
one of the two brackets is ±2 and the other is 0, so the expression is ±2 times a sign,
which is +2 or −2. There are sixteen sign choices, and every one of them gives exactly
±2. None gives 0 or ±4.

The same bound follows by checking the sixteen sign cases. For rational-valued
functions f A , f B : N → Q whose values are ±1, the absolute value of f A (0) f B (0) +
f A (0) f B (1) + f A (1) f B (0) − f A (1) f B (1) is at most 2. The real-valued version has the
same bound.


Definition D.3 (Finite factorizable model). A real-valued correlation function
E( a, b, x, y) is factorizable when there exist response functions A( x, λ), B(y, λ),
weights p(λ) and a natural number λmax such that: 0 ≤ p(λ) ≤ 1 for λ ≤ λmax ;
∑λmax

   =0 p ( λ ) = 1; every A ( x, λ ) and every B ( y, λ ) is −1 or +1; and for all a, b, x, y,
E( a, b, x, y) = ∑λλmax
                     =0 p ( λ ) A ( x, λ ) B ( y, λ ). The outcome arguments a, b are dummies;
only correlations are modelled.


Theorem D.2 (The classical bound for a finite local model). If E is factorizable, then


                                              429
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


−2 ≤ E(0, 0, 0, 0) + E(0, 0, 0, 1) + E(0, 0, 1, 0) − E(0, 0, 1, 1) ≤ 2.

Proof. Substitute the factorization: S = ∑λ p(λ)Sλ , where Sλ is the deterministic
expression of Lemma D.1 at the signs A(·, λ), B(·, λ). Each Sλ ∈ [−2, 2], the weights
are nonnegative and sum to 1, so −2 = ∑λ p(λ)(−2) ≤ S ≤ ∑λ p(λ) · 2 = 2.


Remark D.1 (Scope of the classical bound). Fine’s 1982 theorem is an equivalence
between several descriptions of local models and the Bell inequalities. The preceding
theorem proves one direction: a finite factorizable model obeys the bound. The con-
verse of this single inequality is false. The correlation-form equivalence requires each
correlator to lie between −1 and 1 and all eight inequalities. The preceding theorem
covers finitely many hidden states (λ ≤ λmax ), not an arbitrary probability space. It
applies to rational boxes as well: if their correlations form a factorizable model, their
rational score has absolute value at most 2.


The finite-tally statement concerns one fixed strategy replayed on every recorded
round.


Definition D.4 (A tally consistent with one local plan). For bits a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ∈ {0, 1}
and a counter record w, w is locally consistent with ( a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ) when, for each
setting pair ( x, y): if a x = by then diffxy = 0, otherwise samexy = 0; and every bucket
is sampled, N00 , N01 , N10 , N11 > 0.


Theorem D.3 (A tally above 2 is not one replayed strategy). Let w be a counter record
whose rational score S(w) is greater than 2. Then for all bits a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 , w is not locally
consistent with ( a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ). A stronger statement is that a locally consistent record has
score of absolute value at most 2; read through its contrapositive, it gives the first statement.

Proof. Under local consistency each sampled bucket is pure: if a x = by every round
in the bucket matched, so Exy = Nxy /Nxy = +1; otherwise every round differed and
Exy = −1. In signs, Exy = α x β y with α x = (−1) ax and β y = (−1)by . The score is then
the deterministic expression of Lemma D.1, which is at most 2 in absolute value. A
score above 2 contradicts this.

The theorem rules out one explanation, a single four-bit plan used on every round. It
says nothing about a local model that redraws its hidden state every round; Section 20
gives a four-round coin-flip tally with score 4.

D.3 Tsirelson’s bound from algebra
Lemma D.4 (The six-square identity). For all real a, b, c, d,

          4( a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ) − ( a + b + c − d )2
             = ( a − b )2 + ( a − c )2 + ( a + d )2 + ( b − c )2 + ( b + d )2 + ( c + d )2 .

Proof. Expand the square on the left: ( a + b + c − d)2 = a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 + 2ab + 2ac −
2ad + 2bc − 2bd − 2cd. So the left side is

               3( a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ) − 2ab − 2ac + 2ad − 2bc + 2bd + 2cd.

On the right, each variable appears in exactly three of the six brackets (a in a − b, a − c,
a + d; b in a − b, b − c, b + d; c in a − c, b − c, c + d; d in a + d, b + d, c + d), so the
squared terms add to 3( a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ). The cross terms are −2ab from ( a − b)2 ,
−2ac from ( a − c)2 , +2ad from ( a + d)2 , −2bc from (b − c)2 , +2bd from (b + d)2 and
+2cd from (c + d)2 . Both sides agree term by term.

Lemma D.9 (The 2 × 2 test). If α ≥ 0, δ ≥ 0 and αδ − β2 ≥ 0, then αu2 + 2βuw + δw2 ≥

Remark D.3 (What PSD of the pinned matrix means). M ( E) is the level-1 moment
matrix with the two within-party entries ⟨ A0 A1 ⟩ and ⟨ B0 B1 ⟩ pinned to zero. Its PSD is
sufficient for the correlators to admit some PSD completion (Section D.7), and it is not
necessary: the all-ones plan has a completion but fails here. So a check built on M( E)
is sound for the completion set and not complete for it, and it rejects some honest
classical tallies. That correlators with a PSD completion are exactly those reachable
by quantum measurements is Tsirelson’s theorem, and both halves are proved here
in finite dimension. For real and for complex amplitudes, a strategy’s correlators are
inner products of unit vectors (with complex amplitudes, use real vectors of twice the
length) and its level-1 moment matrix is PSD, so they have a PSD completion. The
other half, that every PSD completion comes from a quantum strategy, comes from this
construction: the strategy is built on two eight-level systems from the completion’s
Gram vectors (Section D.8).


D.5 The integer check
Definition D.7 (The seven-integer check). From the counters of Definition D.2, with
all arithmetic in Z, let

                                      2   2     2   2     2   2
                                 A = N00 N10 − D00 N10 − D10 N00 ,
                                      2   2     2   2     2   2
                                 B = N01 N11 − D01 N11 − D11 N01 ,
                                 C = D00 D01 N10 N11 + D10 D11 N00 N01 .

The check is the conjunction of seven facts, in this order: 0 < N00 , 0 < N01 , 0 < N10 ,
0 < N11 , 0 ≤ A, 0 ≤ B, and C · C ≤ A · B.


There is no division, no real number, no square root and no S in it.

Theorem D.16 (Soundness of the integer check). If a tally w passes the seven-integer

pinned matrix is positive semidefinite.

D.6 Level 1+AB
The five additional parameters name the moments γ1 = ⟨ A0 A1 B0 ⟩, γ2 = ⟨ A0 A1 B1 ⟩,
γ3 = ⟨ A0 B0 B1 ⟩, γ4 = ⟨ A1 B0 B1 ⟩ and γ5 = ⟨ A0 A1 B0 B1 ⟩. These are labels for the entries;
the definition below does not construct operators.


Definition D.8 (The level-1+AB matrix). The 9 × 9 real matrix on rows and columns
I, A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 , A0 B0 , A0 B1 , A1 B0 , A1 B1 , with the following entries:



                              I   A0 A1 B0          B1 A0 B0 A0 B1 A1 B0 A1 B1
                      I    1 0 0 0 0                      E00     E01     E10      E11
                     A0    0 1 0 E00 E01                   0       0       γ1      γ2
                     A1    0 0 1 E10 E11                  γ1       γ2      0        0
                     B0    0 E00 E10 1 0                   0       γ3      0       γ4
                     B1    0 E01 E11 0 1                  γ3       0      γ4        0
                    A0 B0 E00 0 γ1 0 γ3                    1       0       0       γ5
                    A0 B1 E01 0 γ2 γ3 0                    0       1      −γ5       0
                    A1 B0 E10 γ1 0 0 γ4                    0      −γ5      1        0
                    A1 B1 E11 γ2 0 γ4 0                   γ5       0       0        1

Two constraints are fixed by this layout. First, the four-body cells carry opposite signs:
+γ5 at ( A0 B0 , A1 B1 ) and −γ5 at ( A0 B1 , A1 B0 ). In a real moment matrix those two cells
are ⟨ A0 A1 B0 B1 ⟩ and ⟨ A0 A1 B1 B0 ⟩, so the tie says ⟨ A0 A1 ( B0 B1 + B1 B0 )⟩ = 0, which for
a real matrix is ⟨{ A0 , A1 } ⊗ { B0 , B1 }⟩ = 0. The level-1 pinnings don’t imply it. Take
a classical strategy: Alice’s two answers a0 , a1 are independent fair signs, and Bob
copies them, b0 = a0 and b1 = a1 . Every pinned cell of its moment matrix is 0 and both
four-body cells are 1, so no choice of the nine numbers gives its matrix. The matrix
here is therefore level 1+AB on the slice ⟨{ A0 , A1 } ⊗ { B0 , B1 }⟩ = 0, and that is what
“level 1+AB” names in this book. The slice holds whenever A0 and A1 anticommute.
The soundness theorems below are about this matrix, so they stand as stated. Second,
the matrix keeps the level-1 pinning: every cell whose label reduces to a marginal or
to ⟨ A0 A1 ⟩ or ⟨ B0 B1 ⟩ is zero, for instance ( A0 , A0 B0 ), ( A0 B0 , A0 B1 ) and ( A0 B0 , A1 B0 ).
The displayed matrix is symmetric.

Write a vector as (v I , v A0 , v A1 , v B0 , v B1 , v00 , v01 , v10 , v11 ), where v xy is the coordinate of
A x By . Put

The condition called column contractivity at level 1+AB is R ≥ 0 for all six real inputs.


Lemma D.18 (Three squares plus the residual). For every vector,

                  vT M9 v = (v I + L1 )2 + (v A0 + L2 )2 + (v A1 + L3 )2 + R.

Proof. The coordinates v I , v A0 , v A1 appear in the form only through their diagonal
squares and the cross terms 2v I L1 , 2v A0 L2 , 2v A1 L3 , read off rows I, A0 , A1 of the matrix.
Completing each square adds L21 + L22 + L23 , which the residual subtracts. What is left
in R is the diagonal of the remaining six coordinates and the cross terms among them,
read off the lower right 6 × 6 block.


Theorem D.19 (PSD at level 1+AB). For all real Exy and γ1 , . . . , γ5 , the matrix of Defini-
tion D.8 is positive semidefinite if and only if the residual R is nonnegative for every choice of
its six real inputs.

Proof. If R ≥ 0 everywhere, Lemma D.18 writes the form as three squares plus R.
Conversely, given the six residual inputs, choose v I = − L1 , v A0 = − L2 , v A1 = − L3 ; the
three squares vanish and PSD gives R ≥ 0. This is the level-1 argument of Section D.4
one size up.

Definition D.10 (What the integer check computes). The supplied moments arrive

Each cleared integer, read as a real, equals the corresponding real quantity times the
stated positive power of K. A k × k leading minor of a matrix scaled by c > 0 scales
by ck . So every integer positivity holds exactly when the real one does.

Proof. The bucket conjuncts make every denominator positive, the bridges carry the
six integer positivities to the real cascade, and Lemma D.20 twice plus Lemma D.21
give R ≥ 0, hence positive semidefiniteness by Theorem D.19.

of M( E) implies membership.


Theorem D.24 (Deterministic plans are inside). If a20 = a21 = b02 = b12 = 1, then
( a0 b0 , a0 b1 , a1 b0 , a1 b1 ) is elliptope realizable, with x = a0 a1 and y = b0 b1 .

Proof. With these entries the form equals v20 + ( a0 v1 + a1 v2 + b0 v3 + b1 v4 )2 . Expanding
the second square gives a20 v21 + · · · on the diagonal, which is v21 + · · · by the unit
squares, and the cross terms 2a0 a1 v1 v2 = 2xv1 v2 , 2a0 b0 v1 v3 = 2E00 v1 v3 , and so on for
all six pairs. A sum of two squares is never negative.

The all-ones plan is one instance. The classical mixture (1, 0, 1, 0) has a completion at
x = 1, y = 0, with form v20 + (v1 + v2 + v3 )2 + v24 .


Theorem D.25 (Convexity and finite mixtures). For 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1, if E and F are elliptope
realizable, so is λE + (1 − λ) F. For finitely many members with nonnegative weights sum-


                                               442
The Thiele Machine                                                                        Devon Thiele


ming to at most 1, the weighted sum is realizable. Every finite mixture of deterministic plans
is realizable.

Proof. The form is affine in ( E, x, y) for each fixed v. Take the completion (λx1 + (1 −
λ) x2 , λy1 + (1 − λ)y2 ); the form at the mixture is the same mixture of two nonneg-
ative forms. The finite version is induction on the number of members, with the
shortfall in weight absorbed by the zero point. The last statement combines this with
Theorem D.24.


Theorem D.26 (Tsirelson’s bound holds on the completion set). If E is elliptope realizable
then S2 ≤ 8.

Proof. For a symmetric PSD matrix the bilinear form obeys Cauchy-Schwarz,
B(u, w)2 ≤ Q(u) Q(w), because Q(u + tw) = Q(u) + 2t B(u, w) + t2 Q(w) ≥ 0 for
all t and Lemma D.11 applies. Take u1 = e A0 and w+ = e B0 + e B1 : B(u1 , w+ ) =
E00 + E01 , Q(u1 ) = 1, Q(w+ ) = 2 + 2y. Take u2 = e A1 and w− = e B0 − e B1 :
B(u2 , w− ) = E10 − E11 , Q(w− ) = 2 − 2y. So c21 ≤ 2 + 2y and c22 ≤ 2 − 2y
with c1 = E00 + E01 , c2 = E10 − E11 , and both budgets are nonnegative. Then
c21 c22 ≤ (2 + 2y)(2 − 2y) = 4 − 4y2 ≤ 4, so c1 c2 ≤ 2, and S2 = (c1 + c2 )2 =
c21 + 2c1 c2 + c22 ≤ (2 + 2y) + 4 + (2 − 2y) = 8.

The completion can make a row of E longer than 1 (the all-ones plan has rows of
squared length 2), which is why this proof does not use the row bounds of Section D.4.


Corollary D.27 (The PR box is outside). (1, 1, 1, −1) is not elliptope realizable, since its
S2 = 16 > 8.


Theorem D.28 (Strictly beyond the classical bound). (3/5, 3/5, 3/5, −3/5) is elliptope
realizable and has S = 12/5 > 2.

                                           25 and cancel; the cross terms are 2 · 5 v1 v3 , 2 · 5 v1 v4 ,

By Theorem D.2 no finite factorizable model has S > 2, so this point is not a finite
mixture of plans, while Theorem D.25 puts every such mixture inside. The completion

The gate is an integer decider with a soundness proof. Its completion entries arrive
as bucket pairs, and an empty bucket is read as 0/1, so unlike Section D.5 it does not
require every pair to be sampled.

The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Definition D.12 (The two branches). The positive-minor branch: with the completion
supplied as buckets and all entries scaled to integers by a positive common factor
K, the four leading minors of the 4 × 4 block on A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 are strictly positive.
The factorization branch: with the completion and a rational certificate supplied (six
subdiagonal entries over a common positive denominator, four pivots dk ≥ 0 over
another), the ten entry equations of M = LDLT hold in cross-multiplied integer
arithmetic. The full gate is their disjunction.


Theorem D.29 (Soundness of the gate). If the full gate returns yes on a counter record,
any completion buckets and any certificate, then the four correlators of the record are elliptope
realizable. On the PR box tally the gate returns no for every choice of the remaining arguments.

Proof. The first branch reduces to Lemma D.21 through the same fraction-free identity.
The second is a weighted sum of squares: given the ten equations, the form is ∑k dk Pk2
with dk ≥ 0. The PR statement is soundness followed by Corollary D.27.

Examples by direct computation: the all-ones plan passes through the factorization
branch at x = y = 1; the classical mixture (1, 0, 1, 0) passes; the 12/5 point passes
through the positive-minor branch at x = y = 0; and (3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5) passes
through the factorization branch with pivots (1, 1, 0, 0).

The gate is a decider with a soundness proof, and that’s all it is: no property of the
small machine is built from it.

D.8 The four-vector construction
Put two equal-length pencils down with their ends together, and draw a line along
one of them. Keep that pencil still and turn the other. Use the square corner of a sheet
of paper to bring the moving pencil’s tip straight across to the line, and mark where
it lands. The mark moves from a full pencil-length forward, through the joined ends
when the pencils make a square corner, to a full pencil-length backward. Call those
readings 1, 0 and −1. That is the signed shadow we want. Between those positions
the reading is the cosine of the angle. A dot product of unit vectors measures that
shadow.

Now ask for four directions, two labelled Alice and two Bob, with a prescribed shadow
for each Alice–Bob pair. Try this request: Alice’s first points exactly along both of Bob’s;
Alice’s second points along Bob’s first and exactly against his second. Each request
alone is easy. Put them together and your hands cannot do it: Bob’s pencils would
have to point both the same way and opposite ways. Four numbers in range need not
describe four directions that can coexist.

Write those four readings as x = E00 , y = E01 , z = E10 and w = E11 . We have not
specified the shadow between Alice’s own two directions, or between Bob’s own two.
Those are the two blanks, t and u, in the following table. Can we fill them so that the


                                              444
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


whole table comes from directions? The pencils let us ask it in a plane; the construction
will allow four coordinates. A completion is a positive-semidefinite matrix
                                                      
                                      1 t          x y
                                                      
                                    t 1           z w
                                  G=
                                    x z
                                                       .
                                                  1 u
                                      y w          u 1

The extra row and column labelled I in Section D.7 have diagonal 1 and all other
entries zero, so they do not change this condition.

Why positivity? Lay arrows end to end, allowing a backward arrow when its weight is
negative. Square the length from the start to the finish. Expanding that square adds up
the arrows’ pairwise shadows, with their weights. It cannot be negative. A proposed
shadow table that gives a negative answer for some choice of weights cannot come
from arrows. That is the PSD test. A Gram matrix is simply the table of all those
pairwise dot products.

The converse has to build the arrows. Pick the first direction as a baseline. Give
every other arrow the component along it that its shadow demands, then build the
remaining components perpendicular to it. What remains to be fitted is a smaller
shadow table. Here is that construction, including its boundary. If its first diagonal
entry is zero, positivity of h11 a2 + 2h1j ab + h jj b2 for every a, b forces h1j = 0: with
b = 1, a nonzero h1j would let the linear term go negative without bound. Delete that
zero row and column, construct vectors for the smaller matrix, and put back the zero
vector. If h11 > 0, set
                                           h1i h1j
                              Kij = hij −            (i, j > 1).
                                            h11
In the quadratic form of h, take the first coordinate to be − ∑ j>1 h1j v j /h11 . The remain-
ing form is vT Kv, so K is PSD. Induction supplies vectors ri with ri · r j = Kij . Then
       √                       √
u1 = ( h11 , 0) and ui = (h1i / h11 , ri ) have Gram matrix h. The dimension is at most

the required cross inner products.

The next question is harder: how do directions become a prescription for a quantum
measurement? Start with two signed cards in a row. One move swaps them; another
changes the sign of the card in the right-hand place. Start at (+, +). Swap then change
the right sign: (+, −). Start again, change the right sign then swap: (−, +). Every
sign is reversed. Try unequal numbers on the cards: the two orders still give negatives
of each other. “Anticommute” means exactly that relation between the two moves. Do
either move twice and everything is back.




                                             445
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


Write the swap as X, the sign change as Z, and doing nothing as I:
                             !                        !                   !
                         0 1                     1 0                  1 0
                 X=            ,       Z=               ,       I=          .
                         1 0                     0 −1                 0 1

For the larger construction, label eight places by the three-bit words 000 through 111
and put a signed number at each. An X in one bit-position swaps each pair of places
differing at that bit; a Z reverses the signs at places whose bit there is 1. The three
positions give us the following four moves, written as real 8 × 8 matrices:

       Γ1 = X ⊗ I ⊗ I,    Γ2 = Z ⊗ X ⊗ I,         Γ3 = Z ⊗ Z ⊗ X,      Γ4 = Z ⊗ Z ⊗ Z.

The tensor product has entries ( A ⊗ B)(i,k),( j,l ) = Aij Bkl . Each Γi is symmetric and
squares to the identity. For i < j, the first position where the two products differ has X
against Z, and XZ = − ZX; all other positions commute. Thus Γi Γ j = −Γ j Γi . For a unit
vector a, the symmetric matrix A( a) = ∑i ai Γi therefore satisfies A( a)2 = ∑i a2i I = I.
Its two-outcome measurement has projectors ( I + A( a))/2 and ( I − A( a))/2: they are
symmetric, square to themselves, are orthogonal, and sum to the identity.

Take |Φ8 ⟩ = 8−1/2 ∑8k=1 |k ⟩ ⊗ |k ⟩. Expanding this sum gives

                                               1              1
                                               8∑
                       ⟨ Φ8 | A ⊗ B | Φ8 ⟩ =         Aij Bij = tr( AT B).
                                                 i,j
                                                              8

For i ̸= j, cyclicity of the trace and anticommutation give tr(Γi Γ j ) = − tr(Γi Γ j ) = 0;
for i = j the trace is 8. Consequently the correlator of A( a) and A(b) is a · b. Give Alice
A( a0 ), A( a1 ) and Bob A(b0 ), A(b1 ). Their strategy realizes x, y, z, w. All four Γi have
trace zero, so the one-party expectations vanish too. The same real matrices and state
are also a complex strategy.

What would that mean at a bench? Prepare the stated shared state, choose one of the
two specified measurements on each side, and write down the two signs returned. For
each pair of settings, count agreements as +1 and disagreements as −1. Their average
is the correlator. The model predicts the four averages x, y, z, w; a finite tally fluctuates
around its expectation. The signed-card moves let us check the measurement algebra
by hand. Realizing that state and those measurements in a device, and comparing its
tallies with the predictions, is the physical experiment.

Conversely, in a normalized quantum state ψ with self-adjoint measurements A2x =
By2 = I on separate systems, put a x = ( A x ⊗ I )ψ and by = ( I ⊗ By )ψ. They are unit vec-
tors and Re⟨ a x , by ⟩ = Exy . Replace each complex coordinate by its real and imaginary
parts. This preserves those real inner products, and their Gram matrix is a completion.
A mixed state gives the same construction by taking the direct sum of the vectors of
its pure components, weighted by the square roots of their probabilities. Thus the
completion condition and finite-dimensional quantum realizability are equivalent.



                                                446
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


The necessary direction does not require finite-dimensional vectors. If a positive
normalized expectation ω on an algebra has self-adjoint A x , By , with ω ( A2x ), ω ( By2 ) ≤
1, then the real symmetric matrix with entries Re ω ( Xi X j ) is PSD: its quadratic form is
ω (C ∗ C ) ≥ 0 for the real linear combination C of the four observables. Increasing each
diagonal entry to 1 preserves PSD. When Alice’s observables commute with Bob’s, its
cross entries are precisely the real correlators. This supplies the same G. Including the
unit as a fifth observable also gives the level-1 moment matrix with its marginals. The
sufficient direction already used only two eight-level systems.

D.9 The arcsine boundary, in both directions
Keep Bob’s two directions hinged at one end. Alice’s first direction has to make a
specified angle with each. How far can Bob’s hinge open while that is possible? Hold
Alice’s direction upright and sweep each of Bob’s around it at its required angle. Point
them towards the same side to close the hinge as far as it will go; point them towards
opposite sides to open it as far as it will go. There is a whole interval of openings
between those limits. Alice’s second direction asks for another interval.

Draw both intervals on one strip marked from 0 to 180 degrees. If they miss, no
hinge setting satisfies both. If they overlap, choose an opening in the overlap and
construct each Alice direction at that opening. The algebra below permits each its
own perpendicular component in four dimensions. The pencils show why the shared
opening is the question; they need not fit the entire construction on a tabletop. In the
impossible request above, one interval is just 0 degrees and the other just 180. There
is nowhere to put the hinge.

Assume x, y, z, w ∈ [−1, 1], and put s x = arcsin x, with analogous notation for the
other three entries. A unit vector making angles α, β ∈ [0, π ] with two unit vectors can
exist at an angle δ between those two exactly when

                          |α − β| ≤ δ ≤ min(α + β, 2π − α − β).

To see this, decompose the two vectors along and perpendicular to the first. Their inner
product ranges from cos α cos β − sin α sin β to cos α cos β + sin α sin β, by Cauchy–
Schwarz; every value in that interval is attained by choosing the angle between their
perpendicular components. Taking arccosines gives the displayed interval, including
zero perpendicular components.

Apply this to Alice’s first vector and Bob’s two. Since α = π/2 − s x and β = π/2 − sy ,
Bob’s angle must lie in
                              I0 = [ |s x − sy |, π − |s x + sy | ].

Alice’s second vector gives I1 = [ |sz − sw |, π − |sz + sw | ]. Each interval is nonempty
because | a − b| + | a + b| = 2 max(| a|, |b|) ≤ π for a, b ∈ [−π/2, π/2]. They intersect




                                             447
The Thiele Machine                                                                       Devon Thiele


exactly when

                 |s x − sy | + |sz + sw | ≤ π,           |sz − sw | + |s x + sy | ≤ π.

Using | a| + |b| = max(| a + b|, | a − b|), these are the four inequalities

                     |s x + sy + sz − sw | ≤ π,          |s x + sy − sz + sw | ≤ π,
                     |s x − sy + sz + sw | ≤ π, | − s x + sy + sz + sw | ≤ π.

So a completion implies all four.

For the converse, choose any δ ∈ I0 ∩ I1 and set b0 = e1 , b1 = cos δ e1 + sin δ e2 . If
0 < δ < π, put

                            y − x cos δ                                  w − z cos δ
                     c0 =               ,                         c1 =               ,
                               sin δ      q                                 sin δ
                  a0 = xe1 + c0 e2 +          1 − x2 − c20 e3 ,
                                        q
                  a1 = ze1 + c1 e2 +        1 − z2 − c21 e4 .

The interval conditions say exactly that the two radicands are nonnegative: after mul-
tiplication by sin2 δ, the first is 1 + 2xy cos δ − x2 − y2 − cos2 δ ≥ 0, and likewise for
z, w. These four vectors have unit length and the prescribed cross inner products. If
                                                                                √
δ = 0, the intervals force x = y and z = w; take b0 = b1 = e1 , a0 = xe1 + 1 − x2 e3 ,
            √
a1 = ze1 + 1 − z2 e4 . If δ = π, they force y = − x and w = −z; use the same Alice vec-
tors and b1 = −b0 . Their Gram matrix supplies the completion in every case. Together
with the preceding construction, this proves the stated quantum characterization.

D.10 The finite local model, in both directions
Make sixteen cards, each with four boxes labelled A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 , and put every possible
arrangement of plus and minus signs on them, one arrangement per card. Draw a
card before choosing which setting to ask each player about. Alice reads her chosen
box; Bob reads his. Neither needs the other’s setting. How often each card is drawn is
the only choice left in this model.

Try to get perfect agreement for the first three pairs and perfect disagreement for the
fourth. Any card that ever gets drawn would need A0 = B0 , A0 = B1 and A1 = B0 ,
which makes A1 = B1 too. Changing how often you draw the cards cannot fix it. For
less extreme requests the question is quantitative: can we assign nonnegative weights
to the cards, adding to one, that give all four requested averages? The following
construction supplies those weights exactly when all eight CHSH inequalities hold
and the correlators are in [−1, 1].

There is a useful way to assemble the deck. First allow only Bob’s first question and
make a distribution of the three answers A0 , A1 , B0 . Then do the same for his second
question. Both smaller decks must draw Alice’s answer pairs in the same proportions.


                                                   448
The Thiele Machine                                                                              Devon Thiele


The adjustable number t is Alice’s agreement-minus-disagreement average across her
two boxes. Choose it in both intervals

        J0 = [ −1 + | x + z|, 1 − | x − z| ],                   J1 = [ −1 + |y + w|, 1 − |y − w| ].

Each interval is nonempty. They overlap exactly when | x + z| + |y − w| ≤ 2 and
|y + w| + | x − z| ≤ 2, which expand to the eight CHSH inequalities. For a0 , a1 , b ∈
{−1, 1} set
                                            1 + ta0 a1 + xa0 b + za1 b
                        P0 ( a0 , a1 , b) =                            ,
                                                        8
                                            1 + ta0 a1 + ya0 b + wa1 b
                        P1 ( a0 , a1 , b) =                              .
                                                        8
When a0 = a1 , nonnegativity of P0 is 1 + t ≥ | x + z|; when a0 = − a1 , it is 1 − t ≥ | x − z|.
These are precisely t ∈ J0 . The same check for P1 uses J1 . Summing signs shows that
both distributions have mass 1 and the desired pair correlators. Their common Alice
marginal is PA ( a0 , a1 ) = (1 + ta0 a1 )/4.

To join the two smaller decks, first draw Alice’s pair with its common probability.
Among the first deck’s cards bearing that pair, draw Bob’s first answer; among the
second deck’s cards bearing the same pair, draw his second. Those conditional draws
give a four-answer card. A pair that never occurs needs no card. Written as probabili-
ties, this procedure is
                                  
