If PA = 0, nonnegativity forces both corresponding triple distributions to be zero.
Otherwise summing over either Bob answer cancels the denominator. Thus P has
the two triple distributions as marginals and total mass 1. Sample one of its sixteen
answer quadruples and let each party answer with its assigned sign. This is a finite
mixture of deterministic local plans with exactly the four required correlators.

D.11 Scope of the constructions
The constructions above establish the correlation characterizations. The following
paragraphs distinguish their scope from the completeness of a particular integer test,
from full behaviours with marginals, and from claims about experimental data.

The arcsine boundary. For two settings and two outcomes per side, Tsirelson, Landau
(1988) and Masanes (2003) give theorems characterizing the correlators reachable by
quantum measurements: | arcsin E00 + arcsin E01 + arcsin E10 − arcsin E11 | ≤ π and
its sign variants. The characterization holds as an if and only if with the comple-
tion set and, through Tsirelson’s representation, with the quantum set. The point
(3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5) is on the boundary: arcsin 35 + arcsin 54 = π2 by the 3-4-5 triangle,
so the sum is π; Tsirelson’s point is on it too. The necessary direction holds in any
dimension, for any expectation on an algebra of observables in which Alice’s commute


                                                          449
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


with Bob’s.

Equality with the quantum set. That the completion set of Section D.7 is exactly the
set of quantum correlators is Tsirelson’s representation theorem, and it is proved in
finite dimension: for both real and complex amplitudes, with two eight-level systems
enough for every point. That PSD of the level-1 moment matrix is necessary for
quantum behaviour is proved for strategies in finite dimension, with real amplitudes
and with complex ones, and in any dimension, marginals included, for any expectation
on an algebra of observables.

Achievability. Theorem D.6 is a point of R4 . A state and measurements that reach it are
                                            √                                        √
explicit: the two-qubit state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/ 2 with A0 = Z, A1 = X, B0 = ( Z + X )/ 2
                     √                      √     √      √       √             √
and B1 = ( Z − X )/ 2 has correlators 1/ 2, 1/ 2, 1/ 2, −1/ 2 and S = 2 2, and
every strategy in finite dimension has S2 ≤ 8, with real amplitudes and with complex
ones. No experiment stands behind either.

Completeness of the checks. The 1+AB cascade and the elliptope gate are proved
sound, and neither has a proved converse. The level-1 integer check is the exception:
on the small machine the same seven integer facts hold exactly when every pair was
sampled and the pinned matrix is positive semidefinite (Theorem 20.4), so that check is
complete for what it tests. The 1+AB cascade is strict and misses boundary points. The
assertion that the factorization branch accepts every rational PSD completion needs a
completeness argument for its rational certificates; no such argument is supplied here.
Nor is it shown that the 1+AB checks accept nested sets.

Finite levels. For full behaviours, marginals included, the NPA levels are relaxations.
Chaturvedi (arXiv 2607.14569, 2026) argues, in a preprint, that no finite NPA level
characterizes the complete quantum set even in this simplest Bell scenario. Nothing
in this book checks that proof.

Statistics and physics. Nothing here says how many rounds make a tally informative,
and nothing says the counters came from honest play; a program can INC whatever
counts it likes.

D.12 Prior work
                                         √
Tsirelson’s 1980 paper gives the bound 2 2 for quantum correlations, and his theorem
says that quantum two-outcome correlators are inner products of real unit vectors.
Landau (1988) and Masanes (2003, arXiv quant-ph/0309137) each give a condition
that, by their proofs, characterizes the quantum correlators exactly for two settings
and two outcomes. Wehner (2006, arXiv quant-ph/0510076) gets Tsirelson bounds,
CHSH among them, from a semidefinite program on the 4 × 4 Gram matrix of those
vectors. Navascués, Pironio and Acín (2007, arXiv quant-ph/0607119; 2008, arXiv
0803.4290) built the hierarchy of moment-matrix tests; their 2008 paper applies a Schur
complement to the level-1 matrix of this scenario, recovers the arcsine condition, and
discusses the 1+AB level. I went back to each of those papers for these points, and that


                                          450
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


is what I found in them. The results are theirs. Two of them are proved again here, in
finite dimension: Tsirelson’s representation and the arcsine characterization; the rest
of their proofs are not redone. Formal proofs of Tsirelson’s bound already exist, by
Echenim and Mhalla in Isabelle/HOL (arXiv 2306.12535) and in Lean’s mathlib, and
exact rational sum-of-squares certificates go back at least to Peyrl and Parrilo (2008).
                                   √
So the moment-matrix route to 2 2 is standard. What is specific here is narrower:
an integer certificate computed from outcome counts, and the argument from “the
counts pass” to PSD of the pinned matrix and on to S2 ≤ 8. I did not find that chain
elsewhere, and I make no claim beyond it. On the host machine, the same chain is
earned: a raised flag from a clean start stands on a passing check of the packed counts,
and the check passes exactly when the pinned matrix is positive semidefinite and
every pair was sampled (Section 20, Theorems 20.4 and 20.5). The converse direction
of the integer check, integers from PSD, is checked there too, and there too I make no
claim beyond the chain.

E Constructing the quoting operation
The proof in Section 13 uses a program that takes the code of a term and returns the
code of that code. Here is its construction.

Draw the instruction “add one” on a card. Now make a second card describing the
first card’s marks, rather than carrying out the addition. The count has not risen:
you have described an instruction. Describe the second card in turn and you have
a description of a description. Quoting does that second job mechanically. In the
language below, take the variable of index 0. Its code is a tree with three lambda
nodes, then an application of variable 2 to the numeral for 0. Quoting that code builds
a description of those three lambdas and that application; it does not look up variable
0 or execute the term it describes.

Nothing in the operation lets a program inspect itself by magic: its input is an ordinary
tree encoded as a closed lambda term.

The construction follows Forster and Smolka (2017), whose construction for L has
the same three syntax builders on Scott-encoded children, an auxiliary procedure for
numerals, and a quote procedure Q with the same specification, defined by the same
recursion on codes; the self-application that uses Q in Section 13 is their fixed-point
lemma, after Barendregt’s (1984) proof for the full lambda calculus. What follows is
my rebuilding of it, with the reductions written out.

E.1 Numerals and syntax as data
For readability, the formulas below give names to bound variables. Renaming a
bound variable changes nothing; the underlying syntax uses the de Bruijn indices
of Definition 13.3. Applications associate to the left. Write X ⇓ Y here for a finite
sequence of the weak call-by-value steps ending in the value Y.



                                          451
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Scott numerals are the following closed values:

                           0 = λz.λs.z,      n + 1 = λz.λs.s n.

Thus a numeral selects either the supplied zero case or the supplied successor case,
passing its predecessor to the latter. The cases below are values, so choosing one does
not prematurely run the other.

The three syntax constructors, operating on already encoded children, are

                             mkvar = λn.λv.λa.λl.v n,
                             mkapp = λp.λq.λv.λa.λl.a p q,
                             mklam = λp.λv.λa.λl.l p.

Each builder is a term of the language L of Definition 13.3. For a variable of index
n, an application and an abstraction, respectively, define their codes by the following
resulting values:
                             ⌜#n⌝ = λv.λa.λl.v n,
                               ⌜ p q⌝ = λv.λa.λl.a ⌜ p⌝ ⌜q⌝,
                               ⌜λp⌝ = λv.λa.λl.l ⌜ p⌝.
In particular, mkvar n, mkapp ⌜ p⌝ ⌜q⌝ and mklam ⌜ p⌝ reduce to these three codes. A
code is closed even when the term it describes has a free variable: the index of that
variable is stored as a numeral. It is data inside the code, and the code itself has no
free variable.

E.2 Recursion without running under a lambda
The usual self-application trick has to delay its recursive call in a call-by-value lan-
guage. Use

               W = λx.λ f .λv. f (λa.x x f a) v,     rec( F ) = λv.W W F v.

When F and u are closed values, beta reduction gives

             rec( F ) u −→ W W F u −→∗ F (λa.W W F a) u = F (rec( F )) u.

The recursive argument is a lambda, hence already a value. It starts work only when
F applies it to an argument. That is the whole reason this construction survives the
call-by-value rule.

E.3 Quoting numerals
Let Ej = ⌜#j⌝ for j = 0, 1, 2, and let Z = ⌜0⌝, obtained directly from the finite syntax
of 0 = λλ.1. Write mklamk ( X ) for k nested applications of the syntax builder mklam
to X; it is an abbreviation for constructing k lambda nodes, and the language gains no
new operation from it.


                                            452
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Define

          FN = λr.λn. n Z (λk.mklam2 (mkapp E0 (r k))),              Q N = rec( FN ).

Then Q N n ⇓ ⌜n⌝, by induction on n. At zero the Scott numeral selects Z. At a
successor it passes n to the second case; the induction hypothesis supplies the code of
n, and the builders produce the code of λλ.(#0 n), which is exactly the syntax of n + 1.

E.4 Quoting terms
For a proposed recursive call r, define three handlers:

                      HV = λn.mklam3 (mkapp E2 ( Q N n)),
                H A (r ) = λp.λq.mklam3 (mkapp (mkapp E1 (r p)) (r q)),
                HL (r ) = λp.mklam3 (mkapp E0 (r p)).

Now set
                     FQ = λr.λt.t HV ( H A (r )) ( HL (r )),   Q = rec( FQ ).

The handlers are lambdas and so are values. The Scott code of the input chooses one
of them and hands it the encoded children. Induction on the represented term proves
Q ⌜t⌝ ⇓ ⌜⌜t⌝⌝:

   • For t = #n, the first handler constructs three lambda nodes over an application
     of variable 2 to the quoted numeral. That is the syntax of λλλ.(#2 n), the code of
     #n.
   • For t = p q, the induction hypotheses quote both child codes. The second handler
     constructs three lambdas over variable 1 applied to those two codes. That is the
     syntax of the application code.
   • For t = λp, the last handler constructs three lambdas over variable 0 applied to
     the quoted child code. That is the syntax of the abstraction code.

Each recursive call works on a proper child of the finite input tree, or on a smaller nu-
meral. Each builder takes finitely many beta steps. The induction therefore establishes
termination as well as the value returned.

The mkapp used in Section 13 is this builder. With Q and that builder written out, its
self-referential term has every piece on the page.

F Computing with counters
Put a few beans in one cup and leave a second empty. Write a short list of orders: add
one, take one away if there is one, go to this line, stop. A finger on the page keeps
your place. Carry out the orders literally. The question in this appendix is how to give
the same job to another person with different equipment—a strip of paper, stacks of
cards, or a different set of cups—and get the same answer whenever the first person

                                                 453
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


stops.

Agree on how the input is laid out and how to read the output before either starts.
One person must not quietly solve the problem while preparing the other’s cups.
The reductions in this appendix concern functions on natural numbers. To compute a
relation R(⃗x, y) means to halt with output y exactly when R(⃗x, y) holds, and to produce
only numerical outputs on halting runs. The machines below are deterministic, so any
relation they compute is the graph of a partial function. A translation must preserve
both the output and whether the run terminates. Its input and output encodings are
part of the translation.

F.1 Finite programs made from two instructions
A counter holds a natural number. INC adds one and advances to the next line. DEC
subtracts one and jumps to its named line when the counter is positive; at zero, it
leaves the counter alone and advances. A finite program uses finitely many counters.
An unconditional jump to j is INC r followed by DEC r j: it restores r’s value and
always jumps. A zero test is DEC r to a positive branch that first restores r; its fall-
through is the zero branch. These operations preserve values, not versions. They are
used here for computation, where there are no live facts to preserve.

Try copying a cup with three beans. Put two empty cups beside it and keep a supply
of spare beans. Each time you remove a bean from the first cup, put one in each of
the other two. When the first is empty, move the third cup’s beans back into it. Now
the first and second each have three, and the third is empty. Try zero beans, then five.
At every pass one more of the original beans has been counted into both other cups;
that is why it works for any starting count, not just the three you tried. These are the
moves behind the copy C (r, s, t) below.

Emptying a counter is a DEC loop back to its own line. Moving a pile decrements its
source and increments its destination until the source is empty. Copying uses two such
destinations and then restores the source from one of them. Addition, multiplication
by a fixed natural number, and bounded loops are finite combinations of these moves.
Division by a fixed positive number b needs only b control states: decrement the input,
cycle through remainders 0, . . . , b − 1, and increment a quotient counter whenever the
cycle returns to zero. On exit the quotient is in that counter and the remainder is in
the control state.

F.2 A tape in finitely many counters
Cut a strip into numbered squares and put a finger on one square. Lift the squares
on its left into a stack, nearest on top, and do the same on its right. Moving your
finger one place right is now two acts: put the square you were reading on top of
the left stack, then take the top of the right stack as the new square. Write a new
mark before moving and the stack keeps the changed square. Move left and the two
stacks exchange jobs. You can walk the strip either way without losing its order. An


                                          454
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


exhausted stack supplies a fresh blank square.

Now replace each stack by a count. Use digit 1 for a blank and digit 2 for a mark, with
base 3. Push a mark onto an empty stack: its code is 2. Push a blank on top: its code
is 3 · 2 + 1 = 7. Count seven beans in groups of three. The one left over says “blank
on top”; the two groups say the remaining stack has code 2. Pop that and the marked
square comes back. Multiplication pushes and division pops.

In general, number a finite tape alphabet by 1, . . . , q, including its blank, and put
b = q + 1. Encode a finite stack whose top symbol is d and whose remaining stack
has code n by bn + d; the empty stack is 0. A push is multiplication by b followed
by d increments. A pop is division by b: the remainder is the top symbol and the
quotient is the remaining stack. The digits are nonzero, so no nonempty stack has
code 0. Popping an empty stack gives remainder 0, which is no digit; the control reads
it as the blank and leaves the stack empty.

A tape configuration is a control state, the scanned symbol, and two stacks: the sym-
bols to the left of the head, nearest first, and the symbols to its right, nearest first. The
control state and scanned symbol have finitely many possibilities, so they fit in the
program’s line number. To write d and move right, push d onto the left stack and
pop the right stack for the new scanned symbol. A left move does the reverse. The
arithmetic just described implements each transition in a finite terminating stretch of
counter instructions. Extra stored blanks do not change the represented tape. A finite
number of tapes uses two stacks per tape and finitely many scratch counters. Halt-
ing states translate to halting lines. Induction over tape steps proves the simulation;
termination of every arithmetic stretch proves its converse.

In the other direction a tape can hold the finitely many counter values as unary strings
separated by delimiters. INC appends a mark in the selected string; DEC erases one
when present and otherwise detects the empty string. The current instruction is finite
control. Each scan and rewrite terminates, so halting and the output are preserved.
Multiple tapes may be represented on one tape by a list of tracks with marked head
positions: a complete scan reads the marked symbols, a second scan writes their
changes and shifts their markers. Extend the represented interval by a blank cell when
needed. A fixed-length binary code for the finite alphabet implements each scan with
binary symbols and finitely many intermediate control states. Thus this argument also
applies to the single-tape binary halting question.

F.3 Packing finitely many counters into two
Try holding two counts in one pile of eighteen beans. Count how many times you
can halve eighteen exactly: once. Count how many times you can divide it exactly
by three: twice. Reassemble the eighteen beans after each reading. Those are the
two stored counts, 1 and 2. Double the pile to 36 and only the first stored count rises.
Divide 36 by three to get 12 and only the second falls. Divide by three again: four
beans, storing 2 and 0.

                                            455
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Try taking one more off that second count. Four beans do not divide evenly into
threes. The attempted division must restore the four and take the zero branch; keeping
only the quotient would corrupt the first count. This is why the procedure below
remembers the remainder. Two and three share no factor, so changing the number of
one kind of factor leaves the other alone. Assign another prime to each extra count.
An all-zero collection is represented by one bean: the empty product is 1.

Let p0 , . . . , pk−1 be distinct primes. At the boundary between simulated instructions,
keep
                                      k −1
                                 A = ∏ pri i ,     B = 0,
                                      i =0

where ri are the simulated counter values. The simulated line is finite control. The
representation is unique by prime factorization. There are enough primes for any
finite program: a prime divisor of 1 + ∏i pi is not among the primes already chosen,
so the list can always be extended.

To simulate INC on ri , empty A into B, adding pi to B per decrement, then move B
back to A. The result is pi Aold and B = 0. To simulate DEC, divide A by pi using
the finite remainder cycle described above. On exit A = 0, B = q and the control
holds d, where Aold = pi q + d and 0 ≤ d < pi . If d = 0, the original number was
divisible by pi , hence ri > 0. Move B to A and take the positive branch. Its exponent
of pi has decreased by one and every other exponent is unchanged. If d > 0, then
ri = 0. Restore A by moving B back with pi increments per unit, add d, and take the
zero branch. Both branches restore B = 0. All loops terminate because their source
counter decreases. Induction gives the represented run at every simulated instruction
boundary, and no simulated instruction can conceal an infinite internal run.

This is universality with an encoding. With input n in the first simulated counter and
the others zero, the packed input is 2n when p0 = 2. It is supplied to the two-counter
machine as its input; the construction does not claim that two counters starting at (n, 0)
can first manufacture 2n . That is precisely the distinction needed by the one-counter
and Schroeppel arguments in Section 16. For a tuple of inputs, supply its product
of prime powers. If a numerical output is needed in ordinary notation, the external
decoding reads the designated prime’s exponent. A host with finitely many additional
counters can perform this decoding itself by repeated fixed-prime division.

F.4 Why halting has no decider
Write two responses on a card: “If the predictor says STOP, keep going forever. If it
says KEEP GOING, stop.” Suppose somebody offers a predictor that always finishes
and always gets a program’s eventual behaviour right. Give it this very card, with
these instructions for using its answer. Work through both possible answers. STOP
makes the card keep going; KEEP GOING makes it stop. Waiting longer for the
predictor does not create a third correct answer: its promise was to finish with one of
the two.


                                             456
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


The card can be a program because each response is a finite instruction, and waiting
for and branching on the predictor’s answer are computable operations. Here is how
to include the input explicitly. Finite tape programs can be written as finite binary
words, and a program can interpret such a word by looking up the next transition and
maintaining the simulated tape. Invalid descriptions may be assigned one fixed halt-
ing program. Suppose a terminating algorithm H ( p, x ) decided whether the program
described by p halts on x. Build a program D which, on input p, computes H ( p, p),
loops forever if the answer is yes, and halts if it is no. Let d describe D. Either answer
to H (d, d) contradicts what D (d) does. Therefore no such deciding algorithm exists.

Translate a tape program and its input by the stack construction and then prime pack-
ing. Both translations are finite algorithms, and the translated two-counter run halts
exactly when the tape run halts. A decider for two-counter halting would therefore
give H. The same reduction, followed by Theorem 16.3, applies to the small machine.
Halting instances can be enumerated by simulating every description and input for
successively larger finite budgets. If the nonhalting instances could also be enumer-
ated, interleaving those two enumerations would decide each instance. This proves
the impossibility underlying the reduction formulation of Theorem 16.4.

F.5 Seven descriptions of the same computation
The equivalence in Theorem 17.4 can be obtained by the following translations. They
preserve the partial function, including divergence. The constructions are the familiar
ones behind the results of Minsky, Shepherdson and Sturgis, and Forster, Larchey-
Wendling and their coauthors; the encodings and the reason each translation works
are given here.

Binary stacks. A binary stack is a finite word with push and pop operations, with a
distinct empty case. Encode the empty word as 1 and pushing d ∈ {0, 1} as n 7→ 2n + d.
Division by two pops it, with 1 tested before division. Finite counters implement these
operations. Conversely two stacks hold a tape as above; encode every symbol of a
larger alphabet by a fixed-length binary block. A push or pop of that block takes a
fixed finite number of stack operations, and the control stores a partially read block. A
tape simulates counters, so the translations connect binary stack machines and counter
machines in both directions.

The two decrement conventions. Some counter machines jump on zero and fall through
after a positive decrement; the convention of this book does the reverse. To translate
a conditional decrement, send its two outcomes to separate short blocks that uncon-
ditionally jump to the intended destinations. An unconditional jump is the restoring
INC/DEC pair above. Thus either convention implements the other’s instruction,
with the same final counter values and one finite stretch per step. Relabel each target
to the beginning of its translated block. This proves the equivalence of the two Minsky
instruction conventions without identifying their individual steps.

FRACTRAN. A program is an ordered finite list of positive rational numbers. At a

                                           457
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


positive integer N, multiply by the first fraction whose product with N is an integer;
halt if none applies. Counter machines simulate this by fixed-denominator division,
multiplication and an ordered scan of the finite list. For the reverse translation, assign
distinct primes pr to counters and qi to control states. Represent a counter configura-
tion by qi ∏r prnr . Every translated instruction uses a fresh intermediate state prime,
so its state marker never cancels out of a fraction. For INC r going to j, use ti pr /qi ,
followed by the transfer q j /ti . Try it with a counter represented by factors of 2, a
starting line marked by 5, a destination marked by 7 and an intermediate marker 11.
Ten beans, 5 · 2, mean line 5 with counter value 1. The fraction 22/5 takes ten to 44;
7/11 takes 44 to 28. Divide the result by its line marker 7: four remains, two factors of
2. The line has changed and the counter has risen by one. The intermediate 11 keeps
the two parts of the instruction separate. For DEC r with positive target j and zero
target k, use, in this priority order,

                                       ti         ui
                                            ,        ,
                                      qi pr       qi

with transfers q j /ti and qk /ui . All state and intermediate primes are distinct from
the counter primes. Exactly one state marker is present. Fractions belonging to other
states cannot apply. At state i, the first decrement fraction applies exactly when nr > 0;
otherwise the second applies. The next fraction transfers the intermediate marker to
the destination marker. A halting state has no outgoing fraction. Each counter step
therefore takes two fraction steps, and the prime exponents preserve all counter values.
Read the output as the exponent of the output counter’s prime.

Partial recursive functions. Compare two orders. “Try the first ten tickets” gives you
a stopping point before you begin. “Try tickets in order until one passes” does not.
If each test finishes, the second order can still keep you working forever because
every ticket fails. If one test itself never finishes, you never reach the next ticket.
Those are the differences between a bounded loop and the search used here. Start
with zero, successor and projections; close under composition, primitive recursion
and minimization. In minimization, search 0, 1, 2, . . . for the first argument where the
tested function returns zero; every earlier test must terminate with a positive result. A
counter program implements the initial functions directly. Disjoint scratch counters
preserve arguments across composition. For primitive recursion it keeps the recursion
index and accumulated result, increments the index, and runs the step program until
it reaches the supplied bound. For minimization it runs the tests successively; an un-
defined test leaves the run there forever, as the definition requires. Induction on these
constructions supplies a finite counter program for every partial recursive function.

Conversely encode a counter configuration by nested pairs ⟨m, n⟩ = (2n + 1)2m , with
a separate finite code for the line. Addition, multiplication, powers, bounded division
and bounded search are primitive recursive: their loops have a supplied natural
bound and can be written as recursion on that bound. Pair decoding is bounded by



                                            458
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


the encoded positive number. The next configuration and the halt test are therefore
primitive recursive for any fixed finite program. The configuration after t steps is
primitive recursion on t, keeping halted configurations fixed. Minimize the total halt
test over t, then read the output counter. This is the program’s partial function, and it
is undefined exactly when the program never halts.

The language L. Fold two instruction cards shut. One says “put three beans in the
output cup and stop”; the other says “keep adding beans forever.” A zero input is
to choose the first card. If your rule makes you carry out both cards before choosing,
you never deliver the three beans. You have to keep the instructions folded until the
choice is made. An abstraction does that job in weak call-by-value: its body waits until
the abstraction is applied. The Scott numeral definitions and the delayed recursion
construction in Appendix E give zero, successor, predecessor, case distinction and
guarded recursion as terms. A case on a numeral n can be delayed explicitly as

                              n (λd.u) (λp.λd.v p) (λa.a) :

at zero it evaluates u, and at a successor it evaluates v on the predecessor. Both
branches are values until selected, so call-by-value does not evaluate the unused
branch. Composition is application; primitive recursion repeats a step on the pre-
decessor; minimization is a guarded search that evaluates each test before moving
to its successor. These term constructions implement the partial recursive functions
just described, by induction on their definitions. On numerical inputs a terminating
construction returns a Scott numeral, and an undefined computation has no resulting
value.

In the other direction, encode a finite term as a finite string or as the nested-pair code
of its syntax tree. Reading the outer constructor, finding a variable index, renaming
bound indices and substituting a finite term are terminating traversals of finite trees.
A tape algorithm performs them with an explicit stack of unvisited children. For
weak call-by-value evaluation it evaluates an application’s function and argument,
then substitutes the argument value in the abstraction’s body; it never reduces inside
an unapplied abstraction. Each operation is a finite tape computation. Induction
on a terminating evaluation gives a terminating tape run with its value; reading a
terminating run backwards gives the evaluation tree. Scott numerals are decoded by
counting successor constructors. Thus an L computation of a numerical relation is a
tape computation of it.

The tape and counter translations, the two counter conventions, binary stacks, FRAC-
TRAN, partial recursive functions and L now lie in one connected family of trans-
lations. Composing the translations preserves their input/output relation. None
preserves time, space, or a certification ledger merely because it preserves a partial
function; the record-preserving constructions in the main chapters establish those
additional properties.


                                           459
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


F.6 Searching for a finite computation
Give yourself one token and run one instruction of the program you want to test. If
it has not stopped, reset its starting arrangement, give yourself two tokens and try
again. Then three. A program that stops after seven instructions is found on the
seven-token attempt. Seeing six attempts fail says only that it has not stopped within
six instructions; it does not tell you it runs forever.

The evaluators used in Section 16.18 work by that search. A program and a natural
budget determine a finite simulation. Enumerate budgets 0, 1, 2, . . ., and stop at the
first one that exhibits a halting run, returning its output. If no such run exists, the
search continues forever. Encoding a finite program, decoding an instruction, and
performing one step use the finite operations above, so this search is itself a partial
recursive function and has a finite counter program. The host can execute that program
instruction for instruction, using as many registers as the construction requires. Its
computation uses only INC, DEC and HALT, hence costs zero and leaves the fact table,
channel and flag alone. This supplies the evaluators and program transformations
used in the host’s s-m-n and fixed-point arguments.

G The universal program in blocks
Put the guest’s instructions on one sheet and the host’s on another, with a finger
marking the current line on each. The guest takes one instruction. The host takes
as many of its smaller instructions as it needs, then returns to the head of its sheet.
Compare the two arrangements there: counts, live facts, commitment, flag and ledger.
The host is allowed to do more work between comparisons. It is not allowed to lose a
fact, revive a dead one, or charge another mark for its bookkeeping. The lists below
let you carry out that comparison instruction by instruction.

This gives the finite instruction list defining U. A block is a list, not an extra instruc-
tion: replace every block name by its list, place the lists consecutively, and resolve each
label to its instruction number. The first instruction is at address 1. Within a block, o is
its first address and o + k its offset k. Unless a branch says otherwise, execution con-
tinues into the next block. The only final instructions are INC, DEC, HALT, CHECK,
COMMIT and CERTIFY, with the meanings and prices of Definition 16.3 on the host’s
registers (Definition 16.8).

G.1 Arithmetic blocks
Write J ( a, p) for the two-instruction list INC a; DEC a p. It jumps to p and restores
the value of a. The following lists specify the other arithmetic blocks. Semicolons
concatenate lists; a named block in a list is placed at the next available address. A
target such as o + 3 refers to the enclosing block’s start, not the nested block’s start.

  Block               Expansion at address o
   Z(x)               DEC x o

The Thiele Machine                                                                                Devon Thiele

   J0 ( x, p)            DEC x (o + 3); J ( x, p); INC x
   M ( x, y)             J ( x, o + 3); INC y; DEC x (o + 2)
   M2 ( x, y, z)         J ( x, o + 4); INC y; INC z; DEC x (o + 2)
   C ( x, y, t)          Z (y); Z (t); M2 ( x, y, t); M (t, x )
   H ( a, x, p)          Z ( a); M( x, a); J ( a, o + 8); INC x; DEC a (o + 11); J ( a, p); DEC a

   N ( a, x, y)          J0 ( x, 0); Z (y); J ( a, o + 8); INC y; H ( a, x, o + 7)



Their lengths, in the order Z, J0 , M, M2 , C, H, P, N, are 1, 4, 4, 5, 11, 12, 23, 20. The source
and destination of a move are distinct; M2 may have equal destinations, as in P. In C
the three registers are distinct; in H, a ̸= x; in P and N, all three are distinct.

Each claim about these blocks follows from a decreasing counter. Z decrements to zero.
M adds the old source to the destination and empties the source; M2 does it to both
destinations. Consequently C leaves x unchanged, writes its old value to y, and leaves
t = 0. J0 tests zero without changing the value: a positive counter is decremented and
then restored, while zero takes the jump.

In H, first move the old x into a. Each complete pass removes two from a and adds
one to x. Thus it leaves a = 0 and x = ⌊ xold /2⌋; an even old value jumps to p, an
odd one falls through. In P, the first four blocks make x = 2xold + 1 and a = 0. Each
subsequent pass doubles x while decrementing y, so it ends at x = (2xold + 1)2yold ,
with a = y = 0. In N, zero jumps to address 0, which holds no instruction, so the run
stops. A positive number is repeatedly halved until odd, counting the even divisions
in y. Therefore N sends x = ⟨m, n⟩ to x = n, y = m, a = 0. These invariants prove
both the returned values and termination on the stated inputs.

G.2 Selection, comparison and fetching
The selector D ( x, t; p0 , . . . , pk−1 ) has length 3k. For i = 0, . . . , k − 1, place at offset 3i
the three instructions DEC x (o + 3i + 3); J (t, pi ). If the entering value is i < k, it takes
target pi with x = 0. If it is at least k, it falls through with x reduced by k. This follows
by counting the decrements before the first zero.

The equality block E( x, y; t1 , t2 , u; p) first makes copies C ( x, t1 , u) and C (y, t2 , u), occu-




                                                    461
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


pying offsets 0 to 21. Its remaining list is

                                      22 :    DEC t1 (o + 29),
                                      23 :    J0 (t2 , p),
                                      27 :    J (u, o + 32),
                                      29 :    DEC t2 (o + 22),
                                      30 :    J (u, o + 32),
                                      32 :    Z ( t1 ); Z ( t2 ).

The listed offsets count expanded instructions, so the block has length 34. The tempo-
rary registers are distinct from each other and from x, y. The two copies count down
together. If they reach zero together, the block jumps to p; if one reaches zero first,
it clears both and falls through. Thus it preserves x, y, leaves its temporary counters
zero at either exit, and branches exactly on equality.

For fetching, define F (q, l; w, k, h, a, t; p0 , pe ) by the list

                                        0:    C (q, w, t),
                                       11 :   C (l, k, t),
                                       22 :   J0 (k, p0 ),
                                       26 :   DEC k (o + 27),
                                       27 :   J0 (w, pe ),
                                       31 :   N ( a, w, h),
                                       51 :   J0 (k, o + 56),
                                       55 :   DEC k (o + 27).

Its length is 56. Register q holds a list encoded by 0 for empty and ⟨head, tail⟩ for a
nonempty list, and l is a line number. The scratch registers are distinct and separate
from q, l. A zero line takes p0 . Otherwise decrementing the line copy once makes
k = l − 1. Each pass removes the next list head into h and its tail into w. If k = 0,
that head is the selected instruction and the block exits; otherwise it decrements k and
repeats. An exhausted list takes pe . The original program and line values are restored
by the copies. Every call terminates: each complete pass decreases k, or exits.

G.3 Registers and instruction codes
Put Ti = i + 4 for 0 ≤ i < 10. For bank c ∈ {0, 1} and slot 0 ≤ k < 16, put

           Rc = c,     Qc = 14 + c,       Vc,k = 16 + 16c + k,       Sc,k = 48 + 16c + k.

Register 2 is the program, register 3 its line, and register 80 is the dead end. V are
the mirrors, S the slots, and Q the counts of successful checks in each bank. Property
codes are 0 for zero, 1 for even, and n + 2 for at least n. The code of an instruction is
the pair of its opcode and operand: INC has opcode 0 and operand c; DEC has opcode
1 and operand ⟨c, j⟩; HALT has opcode 2 and operand 0; CHECK has opcode 3 and
operand ⟨c, p⟩; COMMIT has opcode 4 and that same operand form; CERTIFY has


                                                  462
The Thiele Machine                                                                       Devon Thiele


opcode 5 and operand 0. A program is their list code. These rules specify the loaded
number in register 2.

A bump of slot S and mirror V is INC S; DEC S to the following instruction; Z (V ). It
has length 3. It leaves the slot’s value alone, increases its version by two, and empties
the mirror. Let Bc concatenate the sixteen bumps of bank c, in increasing slot order; its
length is 48.

The CHECK bank block at o is C ( Qc , T7 , T4 ), then a selector on T7 whose sixteen targets

the move into it installs exactly the pair of property code and guest value. The host’s
own table has capacity sixteen: if it is full, its CHECK traps even when this bank’s
count is below sixteen. Thus the capacity is shared between the banks, just as it is in
the guest. A count of sixteen in one bank already fills the table, so the dead-end check
and the full-table trap are the same case.

A COMMIT slot block is COMMIT Slot Sc,k ; Z ( T2 ); INC 3; J ( T4 , H ), of length 5. The

more than the property code. It then runs, for k = 0, . . . , 15, E(Vc,k , T2 ; T7 , T8 , T4 ; o +

the sixteen slot blocks. Its length is 1 + 16 · 34 + 1 + 2 + 16 · 5 = 628. The comparison
reads the mirror, leaving the slot untouched. Its first match commits that slot’s current
fact; absence of a match reaches the dead end and traps. The CERTIFY block is
CERTIFY; INC 3; J ( T4 , H ), of length 4.

These expansions determine every instruction and target. Adding the fifteen lengths
gives 3728. There are sixteen ordinary CHECK sites and one dead-end CHECK in each
bank, sixteen ordinary COMMIT sites and one dead-end COMMIT in each bank, and
one CERTIFY site: 2 · 17 + 2 · 17 + 1 = 69 paid sites. Every other instruction is free.

G.5 Why the blocks simulate a guest
Run a case that catches more than a wrong sum. Start the guest with four beans in
A and run CHECK Even A. Put its fact on a card saying “even, version 0.” The host
copies the value into an unused slot as the pair (Even, 4), whose code is (2 · 4 + 1)21 =
18, and checks that slot. Put one mark on each ledger.

Now let the guest add one bean and take it away. Its pile is four again, but its version
is 2. The old fact still says version 0. On the host, each of those guest writes bumps
the slot by one and back: 18 to 19 to 18. The slot’s value ends where it began, while its
version rises and its mirror is cleared. Try COMMIT Even A using the old check. Both
machines must refuse, even though four is even. Both pay one more mark for that
failed attempt. A translation that merely compares the piles at the end would miss the
failure this experiment is designed to catch.

Start again and leave out the two bean moves. CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY must
succeed on both sheets, raising both flags for exactly three marks. The longer list of


                                                     464
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


host instructions earns no extra marks for copying or looking up a line. These two
runs test the reason for keeping both values and versions. The argument for all runs
has to keep the following correspondence at every return to the head.

At the head, registers 0, 1 and 3 give the guest counters and line. Each successful guest
CHECK has one host slot fact holding its property and checked value. Its mirror is
the property code plus one while the guest fact is current, and zero after the guest
counter has been written. The matching host slot fact is current in exactly the first case.
Count registers say how many slots have been used in their bank; unused slots and
mirrors are zero. Tables have corresponding entries in the same order, and channels
name corresponding entries. The ledgers and flags agree. Loading a guest establishes
every part of this relation.

Fetching and dispatching terminate and preserve that relation’s stored values. For INC
or a positive DEC, the guest writes its counter; the selected bank’s bumps invalidate
exactly its former slot facts and clear their mirrors. A zero DEC writes nothing and
bumps nothing. These cases pay zero on both machines. For CHECK, a free slot
receives the exact pair tested by the guest. Both checkers answer the same, and the
tables have the same length. A passing check appends the corresponding fact and
updates its mirror and count. A false check or a full table traps both machines, after
the same single paid act. For COMMIT, a nonzero mirror matches exactly a current
guest fact with the requested property and counter. Its host slot has not been read or
changed, so the corresponding COMMIT succeeds. If none matches, both machines
trap. Again exactly one mark is paid. For CERTIFY, channels are either both empty or
both hold corresponding commitments, so the instruction either traps both or raises
both flags, for one mark.

All arithmetic between these paid acts terminates by the block invariants. A normal
case returns to the head; a halting or trapped case stops. No arithmetic block has a
paid instruction. This proves the one-step correspondence and bounds every inter-
mediate host ledger between the guest’s old and new ledgers. Induction proves the
run correspondence of Theorems 16.28 and 16.30. It also proves the reverse halting
implication: an infinite guest run entails infinitely many nonempty host stretches, and
a running guest instruction cannot produce a stopped host except in its own halting
or trapping case.

G.6 Adding PAY
For UP , use opcode 6 with operand 0 for PAY, append a PAY handler to the six handlers,
and append its block after CERTIFY. The block is PAY; INC 3; J ( T4 , H ), of length 4.
The head’s selector now has seven entries and is three instructions longer. Every
block after the head therefore starts three addresses later. Resolve targets to those
new addresses; the head itself remains at address 1. The new PAY block starts at 3732.
The total length is 3728 + 3 + 4 = 3735 and there are 69 + 1 = 70 paid sites. The
interpretation of Slot uses the priced host’s property language from Section 16.14; the


                                           465
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


arithmetic blocks and their invariant do not depend on the particular meaning of a
property code. A PAY guest step is one PAY host step surrounded by free arithmetic,
so the same ledger argument applies.

H Methodology note
I used a proof assistant to constrain formal derivations produced with language mod-
els and to catch errors. It checks derivations within its logic. It does not establish that
a definition captures the intended idea, that a model describes a physical device, or
that a result matters. Those questions belong to the argument.

I Sources
These works are cited for their results, history and intellectual context.

The universal programs and the compiler that puts every computably presented Thiele
machine on the universal host use effective computability and counter-machine sim-
ulation; their construction is given in Sections 16.13 and 16.14 and Appendices E–G.
The counter and lambda references credit the established constructions. The thermo-
dynamic references do not remove the explicit physical premise of the heat bound.
The environmental-record papers motivate Section 15; they do not prove this book’s
pointer thesis.
